# **The First Volume of All the Works**
# **of Angelo Poliziano**
(at least those known to exist), in which are contained:
Twelve books of Letters, with certain additions which are indicated in the following table.
Plato’s *Charmides*, translated into Latin <note>The original text says "donated with Latinity," a Renaissance idiom for translation</note> by Poliziano, an unfinished work. Page 96.
The First Century of the *Miscellanea* <note>A "century" refers to a collection of 100 philological essays or notes</note>. Page 98.
There has been added a most accurate translation by Giacomo Tufano of all the Greek passages found in the entire work.
Explanations of the Letters and the *Miscellanea*, with an index for them.
**His other works and**
minor treatises will be listed in the later Volume or part.

<meta>This page begins a formal dedicatory epistle by the renowned printer Jodocus Badius Ascensius. The tone is highly rhetorical and laudatory, typical of early 16th-century humanist prefaces.</meta>

# Jodocus Badius Ascensius to Master Louis Roux, a man of the highest integrity and by far the most prudent Civil Sub-prefect—holding, as is well known, the Royal seat for civil judgments in the illustrious tribunal of the Parisians: Greetings with all respect.

->**P**<-

I feel, most equitable of judges, that the cause of good literature is now finally being treated most excellently and fortunately, since they have you as a brave champion and a veritable Hercules <note>A common humanist metaphor for a powerful protector of the arts</note>, from whom all those harmed in their affairs both implore and obtain the aid of undefiled justice and a powerful arm. You, who for many years now have fulfilled the duties of Royal Majesty in civil judgments at Paris in every respect, have at last, with a wonderful sense of extra devotion, looked toward good literature. For its sake, you have raised a signal from the royal watchtower, to which countless men will flock in throngs to enlist—not slaves called to the cap of liberty <note>original: "ad pileum vocati" - a Roman ritual where slaves were freed</note>, nor the landless poor seeking a handout, but even the noble leaders of the first class, ready to serve at their own expense. For behold, like a fearless standard-bearer or a lead centurion <term>primipilaris: the highest-ranking centurion in a Roman legion</term>, the most learned and modest youth Jacques Tusan of Troyes <note>Jacques Tusan (Jacobus Tufanus) was a noted Greek scholar and student of Budé</note>, educated in your own home and having made wonderful progress in letters, steps forward.

<summary>A dedicatory letter from the printer Jodocus Badius Ascensius to the Parisian magistrate Louis Roux, praising Roux's patronage of the humanities and introducing the scholar Jacques Tusan.</summary>
<keywords>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, Louis Roux, Jacques Tusan, Paris tribunal, humanism, patronage, legal history</keywords>

*   but rather always praising the diligence of the man: Aldus Manutius the Roman <note>Aldus Manutius (c. 1449–1515) was a famous Venetian printer and inventor of Italic type</note>; nevertheless, we ourselves might desire Greek characters that are a bit more rounded and

<meta>This page begins a dedicatory epistle from the printer Jodocus Badius Ascensius to the jurist Nicolas Bérauld. It establishes a tone of scholarly respect and sets the stage for a work that bridges legal studies with humanist eloquence.</meta>

# Jodocus Badius Ascensius: To Nicolas Bérauld of Orléans: Lawyer: most learned: & most eloquent: sends greetings. <note>The Latin "S. D." stands for "Salutem Dicit," a standard formal greeting.</note>

**I** summon you, most learned Bérauld, and your persuasive eloquence to this register. Why do you tremble? Why do you prepare to flee? I am not calling you back to scholastic trifles: nor to poetic games: nor am I inviting you to a waste of good hours on dialectical riddles <note>The author is distinguishing this serious work from the overly complex or "frivolous" logic puzzles common in medieval university education.</note>. For I know how devoted you are to the profession and the public reading of the sacred laws. Nor is it hidden from me how much you have profited since you were first initiated into them. Nor does it escape me what great hope you have stirred up concerning yourself. Indeed, such is the dexterity of your intellect: such is your erudition in fine letters: such is your indefatigable alacrity in discussing and reviewing the opinions and secret meanings of the legal experts: that no one who knows you even by a "single fingernail" (as they say) <note>A classical idiom meaning to know someone intimately or by a small part of their work.</note> could doubt that very soon, with you as champion and leader, the sacred laws—having driven out all barbarism—will recover their ancient glory and standing. This is a conviction I have also formed most beautifully from your discourses and orations, which were gathered even without your knowledge; to me...

<summary>A formal dedication from the printer Jodocus Badius to the legal scholar Nicolas Bérauld, praising Bérauld's intellect and his efforts to restore classical elegance to the study of law.</summary>
<keywords>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, Nicolas Bérauld, legal humanism, Orléans, classical education, legal reform</keywords>

--- Page 6 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedicatory preface by the printer Josse Bade (Badius) to Louis de Berquin, likely following a discussion of the intellectual merits of the works being published.</meta>

The extraordinary deeds of the most excellent heroes, your ancestors and parents, will come to light. Then, by frequently reading those philosophical lectures and prefaces, with what great excitement will you be seized! You will surely recognize things similar to your own genius and your own discoveries. Then, while meditating upon the precepts of Epictetus <note>A Stoic philosopher whose works Berquin translated into French</note> and Athanasius <note>Saint Athanasius, a Church Father; Berquin was known for translating patristic texts to make them accessible</note>, with what a thorough searching of the mind will you be moved! "This is how I am accustomed to act," you will say to yourself, "this is how I speak, and this is how I worship the gods above."

Finally (not to delay you with many words), when wandering through those "forests" <note>original: "syluis"; likely referring to a collection of miscellaneous poems or "Silvae"</note>, when measuring out songs, and when unravelling epigrams—who will be able to restrain you as you leap for joy, Berquin? And will you still be angry with Badius <note>The printer, Josse Bade, referring to himself in the third person</note> because, shut out by unfair constraints of time and space, he has not yet sounded the "Beraldine" <note>A reference to the scholar Nicolas Bérault, a mutual friend of Berquin and Badius</note> trumpet-blast of your name? I hope you will return to his good graces even while you read these words.

"But," you will say, "I recognize nothing of yours here, Badius; everything was printed previously (I will not mention that they were printed better) and previously dedicated to others." But under your patronage, Louis, and by the skill of your name, all of France will enjoy these goods at a far lesser expense. Therefore, look upon this with favor, and protect the things dedicated to your name. Farewell. From our copper-plate printing office <note>original: "officina nostra chalcographa"</note>, on the day before... <note>The date is cut off in this transcription</note>

<summary>In this concluding portion of a preface, the printer Josse Bade (Badius) praises Louis de Berquin’s intellectual lineage and encourages him to accept this new, more affordable edition of philosophical and patristic works.</summary>
<keywords>Josse Bade, Louis de Berquin, Epictetus, Athanasius, printing history, humanism, patronage, book trade</keywords>

--- Page 7 ---
<meta>This is the dedicatory epistle for the works of Angelo Poliziano, printed by Aldus Manutius in Venice, 1498. It establishes the relationship between the printer and the Venetian scholar-patrician Marino Sanudo.</meta>

->Aldus Manutius the Roman to Marino Sanudo, son of Leonardo, a Venetian patrician. Greetings.<-

**I** often find myself marveling at this city of Venice, most excellent Marino Sanudo, for its nearly infinite wonders—so many that it seems to me more like another world than a mere city. I marvel especially at its supreme men, endowed with the highest intellects and the greatest skill, not only in administering the Republic and ruling peoples (in which they are so admirable that they must, without controversy, be placed above all governors of states, both present and past), but also in the faculty of oratory and in every kind of learning, the number of whom I could not easily say. Among these men, you, Marino, are deservedly numbered by virtue of your sharp intellect, singular learning, and greatest modesty. Though you are constantly devoted to public business, you never cease from writing and composing works most worthy of being read.

I saw, in days past, in your library—which is packed with books of every kind—the volumes you have written with such ingenuity and erudition concerning the Venetian magistrates and the lives of the Doges <note>original: "principum"</note> who have existed from the founding of the city to these present times. I also saw those books on the Gallic War <note>Sanudo's "La spedizione di Carlo VIII in Italia"</note> which you finished many months ago and are keeping suppressed in both Latin and the vernacular, so that they may be read by the learned and unlearned alike. And although you are most learned, you nevertheless always read something by both the ancients and the moderns, mindful of that saying of Pliny: *that there is no book so bad that it cannot be of use in some part.*

Therefore, since you learned that the "Lucubrations" <note>Literally "works composed by lamplight"; scholarly night-studies</note> of Angelo Poliziano, a man of supreme genius and singular learning, were being printed with type in our house, you have not ceased to urge me to hasten the edition, as you desire with your own excellent mind to read the labors of a supreme mind. You added, however, the Greek adage: *hasten slowly* <note>original: "σπεῦδε βραδέως" (speude bradeōs). This was Aldus's famous motto, often paired with the anchor and dolphin image.</note>. Wherefore, most sweet Marino, we send to you as a gift all the works of Poliziano we were able to obtain; you may see what they are in the index which is read immediately after this letter.

If anything should offend your learned ears as being insufficiently polished or refined, know that these were not published by the author himself, but by his friends—and especially by Alessandro Sarti of Bologna, a man dear to all the literate, who took care to have printed whatever works of his most dear friend he could find after a long and accurate search. Our Poliziano is therefore most worthy of pardon if any fault is detected in his writings, since he would have corrected them had he been permitted; indeed, had he lived out his years, he would have restored the laws from the Pandects <note>The Digest of Roman Law; Poliziano was a pioneer in legal philology</note> (which were formerly at Pisa) to their original reading, as he had begun to do. He would have completed his commentaries on them—as he used to declare—not in a "barbarous" <note>A reference to the "Dark Ages" or medieval legal Latin</note> style, but in the Roman manner and with the greatest learning. He had also begun, happily and with marvelous success, to rescue Philosophy herself from the "barbarians." He also promised that within ten years he would most brilliantly explain all the liberal arts both by living voice and in writing.

O premature and cruel death, which strikes most especially at the highest geniuses! O loss forever to be lamented, since that man would have left to posterity many things most worthy of being known, which perhaps will never be known. But would that we had also possessed the second century of the *Miscellanea*, and the *Epiphyllides*, and his ingenious and learned annotations on Suetonius <note>original: "Tranquillum"</note>, Terence, Statius, and Quintilian, and so many other things from which he could have made a hundred "centuries" <note>Poliziano's *Miscellanea* were organized into groups of 100 philological observations called "centuries."</note>. Those works would have come out into the public for the benefit of mankind, which (as I hear) certain people in Florence are hiding away so that they may publish them as their own. But they act foolishly indeed; for they will achieve only this: that if they ever find or publish anything worthy of being known, all the learned will contend that it belongs to Poliziano rather than to them—men who are not ashamed to try to fly with borrowed feathers while suppressing so many of Poliziano's works. Farewell.

<margin>Those things which are missing from Poliziano's lucubrations</margin>

<column-break/>

<summary>Aldus Manutius dedicates his edition of Angelo Poliziano's works to the Venetian scholar Marino Sanudo, praising Sanudo's own historical writings while lamenting Poliziano's early death and the potential loss of his unfinished scholarly projects.</summary>

### THE FIRST BOOK OF THE LETTERS OF ANGELO POLIZIANO. Letter I.
### Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to his friend Piero de' Medici. <note>Latin: S.D. stands for Salutem Dicit, a formal Roman greeting.</note>

**Y**OU HAVE OFTEN URGED ME, great-souled Piero de' Medici, to collect my letters and publish them gathered into a single volume. I have now collected them, lest I fail to obey you in all things—you, in whom all my hopes and resources are placed. Yet I have not collected every single one, for that would be a task more laborious than gathering the scattered leaves of the Sibyl. <note>A reference to the Cumaean Sibyl of Roman mythology, whose prophetic oracles, written on leaves, were easily scattered by the wind.</note> Clearly, I did not write them with the intention of them being brought together into one body, but only for the immediate occasion, based on topics that presented themselves rather than being sought out. Thus, I did not even keep copies for myself, except for a few—the less fortunate ones, I think—which have for a long time now been struggling against bookworms and moths. Nevertheless, to give the collection the appearance of a proper volume, I have also inserted several letters sent to me, though only those from learned men, which...

# Book of Letters. I. Folio II.

...which is the seasoning of both food and prayer, is modestly advanced in the letters of friends and denied to the author. *Inconsistent with himself:* what Horace <note>original: "Flaccus"</note> considers a vice in poetry, but in letters variety is becoming, since each one constitutes a new little work. *Stylus* is the instrument for writing on wax tablets, but it is used to represent the quality or genre of writing. *By which name:* an allusion to the names of debtors inscribed in account books; whence we often use "names" <note>Latin: *nomina*</note> to mean debts. Sometimes also for a "cause," as here. *Lest anywhere:* that is, in any letter. *Patronage:* defense. *In the epistolary style:* Cicero seems to him too grave and obscure in his letters. Or, *the shadow:* that is, a likeness of imitation, just as a shadow follows the body. *In prayers:* that is, in desires. *The Orator:* the nephew, whose letters are extant and truly charming. *The whole age of Pliny:* because the Latin language had already begun to degenerate through the affectation of new words. The letters of Symmachus also, and of Dio, Brutus, and Libanius are extant, very brief in the Laconian <note>Spartan/concise</note> manner but full of meaning. Such letters of Cicero to Atticus also exist. *He will claim:* that is, he will vindicate and defend from slander. *He fashions:* that is, he adorns; just as in a beautiful girl, the neglect of grooming adds to her grace. *By a little old woman:* that is, an Attic old woman. *Character:* that is, innate virtue and the quality of the latent mind. *In a circle:* so that it ends where it began. *It does not displease Aquila:* <margin>Aquila.</margin> the orator, whom Quintilian mentions quite often. He wants a speech to be entirely free-flowing; Quintilian, however, wants it to have "feet," but his own—that is, bound together in a way entirely different from poetry, so that he hates nothing worse than a closing phrase that sounds like the tail of a heroic verse, which is a dactyl ending with a spondee. *You might join poorly:* the feet of Aquila. For he is speaking of rhythms and oratorical feet. *He will not act:* that is, if there are letters in which there are no persons speaking to one another and doing a thing, not just narrating it. *He will respond:* it is not a dialogue and so it ought not to "act." *The things indeed etc.:* "ta" is the article, like the French "les"; "men" means "indeed"; "koina" means "common things," whence "epicene" means "sub-common"; "kaino" means "newly" or "in a new way"; "ta" is also the article; "e" means "or"; "kaina" means "new things"; "koino" means "commonly"; understand "you should say" or "they are to be said." *To shuffle:* to escape the things objected. *I will certainly satisfy:* a beautiful conclusion and almost circular, for it agrees with the beginning. Sylvius recently explained the rest, and perhaps he would have added these or similar things if he had been present, and perhaps would have recognized his own; so I will fulfill the role of the absent friend as best I can.

## Angelo Poliziano to his Peter de' Medici. II.

Since you have often heard from us that Florence—the city in which you deservedly hold the leading place, just as your ancestors did for a long time—had an entirely different origin than what is reported by the writers of our history, you most kindly requested (as is your custom) that I commit to writing whatever I had discovered on that matter. For you said it would be something the whole city would rightly owe me: that I had shown them their own origins, especially since they were such that, if they had to be chosen from any history at all, more excellent ones could not have been selected. Therefore, my Peter, both to do a favor for the city which has always treated me kindly and humanely, and to obey you in your honorable request (than which nothing more pleasing to me lives on earth), I shall briefly encompass in this letter what I have found in the monuments of literature concerning the founders of this city; then I shall add a few things about the name itself. Since it is well enough established that the people of Fiesole were also accepted into a part of the city—whence I believe Fiesole was also named—I shall explain. The Triumvirs Gaius Caesar (who was later Augustus), Mark Antony, and Marcus Lepidus (who was also the High Priest) led the colony to Florence. The colonists led there were Caesarian soldiers, to whom two hundred acres were assigned through the *cardines* and *decumani*. This I find in Julius Frontinus, a most celebrated writer who flourished in the age of Nerva, in his book on the measurements of fields—a very ancient book of which you, Peter de' Medici, have a copy at home. Thus, what happened to no other city: Florence arose from three commanders, one of whom was the greatest of all, and another also the High Priest. The first citizens of Florence were those men whose virtue no arms, no fortifications, and no strength could resist. Having explored the origin, let us also investigate the cause of the name. He reports that the city of Rome had a triple name: one is this common one we have said; the second was secret—whence the poet turned his "Amaryllis" (which properly signifies "love" <note>Greek: *Amor*</note>) into bucolic song; the third was owed to sacrifices, from which the name was given to the Floralia, which the learned man Philadelphus (from whom we received these things) interprets as *Anthusa* in Greek. This you may translate into Latin as "Flourishing," or perhaps more aptly "Flora" or "Flo—"

<column-break/>

F. S. He calls *cardines* <margin>Cardines.</margin> those boundaries of fields which run from south to north, and *decumani* those from east to west. Pliny is the authority in the thirty-third and thirty-fourth chapters of the eighteenth book. They are called *cardines* because they look toward the "hinges" <note>Latin: *cardines*</note> of the sky. It is called *cardo* as if it were "cor" <note>heart</note>, for "kardia" is called "heart" by the Greeks. <margin>Decumanus</margin> Poliziano thinks the *decumanus* boundary is so called in the eighty-sixth chapter of his *Miscellanea* because it is the longest. For it is very common for *decumanus* to be used for "the greatest," such as a "decuman egg" <note>the 10th egg, believed to be largest</note>, a "decuman wave," or the "Decuman Gate" in a camp, through which (according to Vegetius in the twenty-third chapter of the first book) delinquent soldiers are led out to punishment. Lucilius in his *Lapathus*, as found in Cicero's second book *On Ends*: "You never dined well in your life, since you consume everything on that shrimp and a sturgeon with a *decuman* [huge] one." Why *decumanus* signifies that which is greatest, many think the reason is this: because they assert the tenth wave becomes the largest, and the tenth egg born is the largest. Ovid in the first book of *Tristia*: "The wave that comes from here towers over all waves; it is after the ninth and before the eleventh." The same in the eleventh book of *Metamorphoses*: "So when the high waves beat the steep sides, the onset of the tenth wave, rising more vastly, rushes on." Whether that be true or not I shall not dispute; yet I could easily persuade myself of this reason: that in the number of simple units, the tenth is the greatest and highest. For according to Plutarch in the first book *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, both Greeks and barbarians count all things from one to ten; when they have reached that, they return to unity. This same opinion is in Aristotle's fifteenth section of *Problems*, except that he says the Thracians end their counting at four. <margin>Why the number proceeds only to ten.</margin> Aristotle writes this as one reason among many why the progress is made to ten and no further: because all men were created with ten fingers by natural law. Having obtained, as it were, the counting-tokens of their own number, they enumerate all other things by this same multitude. Concerning the significance of numbers by fingers, other than the common way, our Jodocus Clichtove writes much skillfully at the end of his book on the mystical significance of numbers. *Decumanus* is said as if it were *decimanus*, just as you can read *optumum*, *maximum*, and many others of this kind written with a "u" instead of an "i" in Plautus. ¶ *The second which was secret.* <margin>Tutelar gods.</margin> Macrobius reports in the third book of *Saturnalia* that all cities are under the protection of some god, and that it was a custom unknown to many Romans that when they besieged a city and trusted it could now be taken, they would "call out" <margin>The custom of calling out.</margin> the tutelary gods (commonly called patrons) with a certain song. Either because they despaired of the city being taken otherwise, or if it could be, they thought it a sin to hold gods captive. For on that account the Romans themselves [kept] both the god and...

...that the protection of the city of Rome might be secured: and the Latin name of the city itself was kept hidden, unknown even to the most learned. They wished it to remain secret, taking care lest they suffer the same "hostile evocation" <note>A ritual (evocatio) where an enemy commander invited the guardian deity of a city to leave and come to Rome</note> which they knew they had often performed against the cities of their enemies, should the name of their own protector be made public. Sempronius turns away from this opinion: he denies that Rome was named by Romulus, but rather believes that Romulus was named after Rome. Otherwise (he says), the name and origin of Rome would be common and manifest, whereas a most salutary religion ordained they be hidden; for if the origin of the name of Rome became clear, the god under whose protection Rome stood and from whom it derived its name would be exposed to the nations, and for that reason, others might call that god away. For this reason, Angerona, the goddess of silence, is worshipped before the doors on the festival days of Janus, so that no one may be permitted to bring into the open that which the ancients, with sealed mouths, wished to be contained within the secrets of the heart for the safety of the republic. Soranus was the first to pay the penalty for violating this religious law. Servius, commenting on that line of the first book of the *Aeneid*, "and he shall call the Romans by his own name," says: "He says 'the Romans,' not 'Rome.' For no one utters the true name of that city, even in sacred rites." Whence a Tribune of the Plebs, as Varro says, having dared to name it, was hoisted onto a cross. Not even Hyginus, speaking of the site of the city, expresses this. Fearing this "evocation" of the gods, the Tyrians used to cast chains upon their statues, as Plutarch is the author of in his *Roman Questions*. Crinitus, in the last chapter of his first book, records that the city of Rome was called *Indiges* <note>original: "indigetem"; a term for a local or patron deity</note> by Julius Frontinus. Anthusa, etc. This you have in Latin. *To anthos* <note>original: "το αφθοσ" (error for τὸ ἄνθος)</note> means "the flower." Ptolemy II was called Philadelphus. Flora was a noble courtesan who named the Roman people the heir to all she had amply accumulated through the courtesan's art, so that her birthday might be celebrated with the annual interest. But so that a certain dignity might be added to a shameful matter, they feigned that she was a goddess who presides over flowers, and that she must be appeased so that the crops, along with the trees or vines, might blossom well and prosperously. Following this color in the *Fasti*, Ovid told of a noble nymph called Chloris, who, having married Zephyrus, received this gift from her husband as a dowry: that she should have power over all flowers. These things are from the twentieth chapter of the first book of Lactantius's *Divine Institutes*. Regarding the city of Constantine, which is called Constantinople, Cassiodorus writes thus in the eighteenth chapter of his second book, which he calls the *Tripartite History*: "When all things were proceeding prosperously for Constantine," he says, "he wished to have a city; and coming to the plain before Ilium <note>Troy</note> near the Hellespont above the tomb of Ajax, where the Achaeans had their camp while fighting against Troy, he marked out the city and made the gates, which are seen to this day by sailors." As he was doing this at night, God appeared, warning him to seek another place; and moving him to Byzantium in Thrace, He ordered him to dwell there. Though it was originally called Byzantium, he enlarged it and surrounded it with a very great wall. Adorned with various structures, he established it as equal to Imperial Rome, and confirmed by law that, being named after Constantine, it should be called the Second Rome. These things are from Cassiodorus. Philostratus, in the fourth book of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, falsely claimed that the Trojans could not obtain their request from the hands of Achilles through sacrifices for Troy to be restored, because of their violated faith. In Pliny, etc. Pliny, in the fifth chapter of the third book, says: "The Fluentini are situated by the flowing Arno." Platina mentions Desiderius, King of the Lombards, in his book on the *Lives of the Popes*. Boccaccio, in the fourth book of the *Genealogy of the Gods*, mentions that Atlas of Italy (who is commonly said to be the most ancient) died at Fiesole (which Pliny names after the Fluentini). The same author, in his book on *Mountains*, says that Fiesole was a twin-peaked mountain above Flo-

[Main Text - Right Column]
-rence. We know, moreover, that the colonies of the Roman people were like small images and likenesses of it. It is also established that Florence was founded in the image of Rome: which (to pass over other things) even the name of the Capitol and of certain regions still testifies. Furthermore, both Philadelphus and the most learned Eustathius have recorded that the name *Anthusa* was given to the city of Constantine, which is called New Rome. From there, therefore, the name was drawn, from whence the city itself was drawn. For in Pliny, I would believe that either by a corrupted word "Fluentini" is read for "Florentini," or that the ancient peoples who inhabited the banks of the flowing Arno were once so called; who then, however, migrated into the "Florentines" once the city was founded and the colony led forth. Thus the edict of Desiderius, King of the Lombards, calling them "Fluentini," could easily be reduced to either cause. Ptolemy certainly (as certain ancient manuscripts admit) called it Florence. And Pliny says the same in the fourteenth book of his *Natural History*, although in the common manuscripts the passage is altogether full of errors. Paulinus, the disciple of Ambrose, also mentions Florence, and he offers a most rich testimony of holiness to our own Bishop Zenobius. Procopius also indicates how strong and powerful this city was even then, which, though often attempted by the Goths, could not be taken by storm. One most beautiful vestige of antiquity still exists in it: this temple of wonderful structure, formerly bearing the title of Mars, now of the Precursor <note>St. John the Baptist</note>. For the Romans worshipped Mars as the author of their race; the Caesarian soldiers, victors of the world, worshipped Mars above all; and Augustus, the principal founder of your city, worshipped Mars, as he also built a temple to him in the middle of the forum at Rome with the surname "the Avenger." Wherefore it is the less to be wondered at that the Florentine youth, although by ancestral custom they abstain from arms, still excel in playful contests even among the most practiced soldiers. For concerning you, Peter, I need say nothing in this place, you who have recently carried off so many palms as victor so many times in a few days; lest I should seem to anyone to have sought an opportunity for praising you by this letter of ours. Fiesole remains: which ancient fame reports was founded by that heaven-bearing Atlas, and Giovanni Boccaccio, a man most learned for those times, confirms it. Lest its authority waver any longer, I can cite Hesiod, the most ancient poet, who declares that Fiesula was one, and indeed the first, of the nymphs by whom the constellation of the Hyades (or in Latin, the *Suculae* <note>Little Pigs</note>) is represented; whose position the moon represents, which is still the emblem for the people of Fiesole—unless they rather carry the moon because it, the last of the wandering stars, especially presses upon the very summit of Atlas who supports the heavens. But hear now the verses of Hesiod, which the grave author Theon and that grammarian Tzetzes repeat in the commentaries of their letters from his book titled *Astraea*—a man of incomparable memory and almost infinite reading:

# **Book of Letters. I. Folio III.**

<column-break/>

->Nymphs, whom they call Hyades, a race of men.<-
<note>original: "Νύμφαι, ἃς Ὑάδας καλέουσι φυλὴν ἀνθρώπων." A quote from the Greek poet Hesiod.</note>

You see how Hesiod names Fiesole <note>original: "Fæsulam"</note> especially among the Hyades; you may find this also in the writings of Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar and archbishop</note>, although in those faulty manuscripts it is written as "Aesula." Furthermore, Ammonius the Grammarian mentions Fiesole as one of the nurses of Bacchus <note>The god of wine and ecstasy</note>. I believe no one with even a slight education is ignorant of the fact that the Hyades were the daughters of Atlas and the same who served as the nurses of Bacchus. 

Indeed, Silius <note>Silius Italicus, a Roman epic poet</note> teaches us that in that city there were famous interpreters of lightning according to the ancient Etruscan discipline <term>Etruscan discipline: the traditional religious and divinatory practices of the ancient inhabitants of Tuscany</term>. He writes: *Fiesole, the interpreter of the lightning's wings, was present at the sacred rites.* 

Because I have always, for some reason, favored this city more than others, I cannot remain silent on this point: the very safety of all Italy ought to be credited to the people of Fiesole. It was, of course, on their mountain ridge that Radagaisus—once the most savage King of the Goths—was divinely [defeated] with two hundred thousand men who were laying waste to the world...

<margin>Suffenus</margin>
Livy, chapter four of the fourteenth book. *Erasures* <note>original: "lituras"</note> from *smearing* <note>original: "linendo"</note>, that is, corrections. *Lest I be a Suffenus* is a proverb; that is, lest I flatter myself and foolishly admire my own work. For Suffenus was by far the most absurd poet: sharp-tongued regarding the faults of others, but blind to his own. Hence, those who are vainly pleased with themselves are called "Suffenuses." These things are from the proverbs of Erasmus.

<column-break/>

[I send this] first, intending to send others as well: if in this one instance I find you to be a friend and not a flatterer. For they come to you under this law: that they be chastised, that they be beaten, and that they pay the penalty for their errors by both the fingernail <note>The "fingernail" (unguis) refers to the Roman practice of testing the smoothness of a surface with a nail to find flaws.</note> and the obelisk <note>The "obelisk" (obeliscus) was a traditional mark used by editors to denote suspicious or spurious passages.</note>. **Book of Letters. Book I. Folio IV.**

Those whom we love, we are accustomed to praise and love even for their faults. From this comes that common proverb of Ausonius: *We love our own moles and scars.* <note>original: "Næuos nostros & cicatrices amamus." Ausonius was a 4th-century Roman poet.</note> Regarding this matter, we hope to say more in the second book. I am adding a Stoic companion—that is, the book of Epictetus, which I have translated from Greek into Latin; he was a philosopher from the Stoic sect. The Law of Retaliation <margin>Retaliation.</margin> <term>Talio: the principle of "an eye for an eye."</term> is the law which commands that a person be punished with the same kind of injury that he himself committed. In the writings of Aulus Gellius, in the first chapter of the final book, those words of the Twelve Tables <note>The earliest code of Roman law, c. 450 BCE.</note> are preserved for memory: *If he has broken my limb, unless there is an agreement, let there be retaliation.* Gellius says more regarding this law. Charondas of Thurii <note>A famous lawgiver of Sicily/Southern Italy.</note> enacted the same law, as is found in the "Reasonings" of Battista Egnazio. From this comes "to retaliate"—that is, to repay an injury received, or to punish by the law of retaliation. In the same place, Gellius says: *That which was done through imprudence ought to be retaliated through imprudence.* "Senecio" <margin>Senecio.</margin> <note>A plant name (Groundsel), but here discussed as a diminutive of "Senex" (old man).</note> is a diminutive from "old man." Afranius says: *It is enough if you look after this little old man.* The authority for this is Priscian in his third book. Supercilious...

The word "Urban" is derived from "City" <note>Latin: *urbs*</note>, referring to one who is courteous, pleasant, and refined; for such people are generally found in the city in contrast to those who live in the countryside, whom we therefore call "rustics"—that is, harsh, wild, and of unpolished manners—whom the common tongue calls "villains" <note>original: "villanos," referring to inhabitants of a villa or farm, which later took on a negative moral connotation</note>. It might perhaps seem that he was alluding to the names of those great men, Urban and Hilary <note>Hilary derives from the Latin *hilaris*, meaning cheerful</note>; even if he did not do so, I think it should nevertheless be noted that, whether by chance or—as I rather believe—by the deep providence of God, happy names have been bestowed upon excellent men. For example, look at those four leaders of Church doctrine: Jerome, Ambrose, Augustine, and Gregory. How auspicious and how fitting to their circumstances are the names imposed upon them! For "Jerome" signifies a "holy name" <note>derived from the Greek *Hieronymos*</note>, which is certainly most appropriate for a man so anxiously holy and so pure in both character and doctrine...

**Book of Letters. Book I. Folio VII.**

[Left Column]

concerning your brilliance: and finally concerning your studies: I might almost deliver a formal oration. My friend Lorenzo de' Medici is witness; so too is Pico della Mirandola here—two heroes, I believe, not merely men—whom I have as either the most attentive listeners to your praises, or as most devoted heralds of them. Already among the learned youth and our circle of friends, we have made such progress by speaking of you that you are regarded as the one man who is not only most learned, but also most refined and most wise. Furthermore, whether I bring up the letters or the speeches in which illustrious mention of you has always been made by us, or even these *Miscellanea* <note>Poliziano’s famous work of philological "Miscellanies"</note> of ours which will soon be published: since a certain "knot worthy of a deliverer had fallen," as Horace says <note>original: "dignus vindice nodus" - a reference to Horace's *Ars Poetica* regarding when a god should intervene in a plot</note>, they have named you, along with Lorenzo and Pico, as their judge against rude ignorance. Nor indeed have you been idle, or unprepared for opportunities to honor and extol me, perhaps even beyond what I can bear; so that you have most beautifully redeemed yourself from this silence of letters by your frequent conversations about me. Therefore, we do not nourish our friendship with those flatteries and unseemly, inept fawning—which are most suspected by all the best men, and are, I add, common. We are never lacking to one another in any place, study, or duty. Those showy and popular displays of goodwill, like so much rouge and trickery, I believe you do not desire, and I abominate. They say "there is no need for hanging ivy for wine that is sellable" <note>A proverb meaning good quality needs no advertisement; ivy was the sign of a tavern.</note>. And so let us, as becomes learned men, despise all outward show and noise, and let us "strip away the mask" (as the saying goes) of friendship. But to finally come to the point for which I had intended to write this letter: when Francesco Gaddi of Florence, who was acting as ambassador there a little while ago—a man most closely joined to both of us—happened, as it goes, to mention in a conversation with Lorenzo de' Medici that you desired a volume of Dioscorides <note>An ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> if we had a corrected one here, Lorenzo immediately—as he is a man most devoted to you—commanded me, according to his custom and authority, to take care of that matter as quickly and diligently as possible. Here then is the book for you, my dear Barbaro: sufficiently corrected, unless I am mistaken; certainly an ancient one. When you have used it, you will return it to me—not so much unharmed (such is your diligence), but rather noted by that most learned hand of yours, so that some value and authority may be added to the volume from you. Farewell.

and integrity: which are so manifest that they do not require foreign commendation. Plautus in *The Little Carthaginian* employs almost the same idea: "One must," he says, "bring a buyer to unsellable goods." Good merchandise easily finds a buyer. ¶ To "strip away the mask of friendship" is to show oneself as a true friend: and as if with a "windowed breast" (as they say), to show what you have inside. For there are very many men whose faces do not agree with their hearts. This kind of men Caecilius pursues in these verses noted by Aulus Gellius in chapter nine of book ten. For those are the worst enemies who have a cheerful face but a sad heart: whom you know neither how to grasp nor how to let go. "Mask" (*Persona*) is a covering for the face (commonly called a *larva*); it has its origin from "sounding through" (*personando*). For the voice is not wandering or diffused, but collected and forced, having only one exit, which makes the sounds clearer and more melodious, as the same Gellius says in chapter seven of the fifth book. To "tear the mask" is said by Pius in his commentaries on Plautus's *Amphitryon* to be a proverb; it signifies to affect someone with shameful disgrace. For when the mask was torn from unskilled actors, they were branded with such disgrace that they thought it shameful for themselves to return to the stage after this. *Istic*: that is, with you or where you are. *Ista manu*: that is, by your hand. For "that" (*istud*) most often refers to the second person.

**CASCEN.**
¶ "To give work" (*Operam dare*) is a common expression. That is, to expend labor and activity: it is distinguished by the context: hence "to give work" is not "to sacrifice," but "to give work to divine matters"; just as it is not "to procreate" or "to copulate," but "to give work to children or to wifely matters"; nor is it "to study," but "to give work to study" is to study with deliberate effort: and so with similar things. "Heroes, I believe": understand "as." For the order is: "Medici and Mirandola are witnesses: as I believe, two Heroes, not men." ¶ "You have redeemed yourself from silence": that is, you have released yourself from debt and made yourself free from the fault which you had contracted by the silence of letters: that is, by writing nothing. He says "sellable" (*vendibili*), not "for sale" (*venali*): and rightly so, as with the rest. For "for sale" is whatever is put up for sale; "sellable" is that which is easily sold because it is good. "That for the sake of which" (*Ut eo qua gratia*): For the sake of which. ¶ "For sellable wine, etc.": that is, a thing that is manifestly good does not need a herald.

[Right Column]

friendship. For some friends, living together, rejoice in one another and provoke each other with mutual gifts. Others, sleeping or separated by locations, do not indeed "act": but they are so disposed that they would act as friends. For locations do not absolutely dissolve friendship, but only the "operation" of it. Which, if it be long-lasting, seems to bring forgetfulness to friendship as well. Whence it is said: "Silence dissolves many friendships." A "silent person" is named from silence, one who is of rare speech. ¶ "Heroes, I believe, two, not men." Between the circle of the moon and the peaks of the clouds and winds, there are aerial souls which they call heroes, lares, or geniuses: which are seen by the mind, not the eyes. Marcus Varro thought this, as Saint Augustine records in chapter six of the seventh book of *The City of God*. Martianus Capella, however, in the second book of *The Marriage of Philology*, says: "From the middle of the air down to the borders of the mountains and the earth, Demigods and Heroes dwell." They are called Heroes from the fact that the ancients called the earth "Hera." Therefore, Heroes are intermediaries between gods and men, whose wives or daughters are called Heroines. ¶ "As Horace says, etc." Horace says in his *Poetics*: "Let no god intervene, unless a knot worthy of a deliverer has fallen." In a poem, the persona of some god is not introduced (as Acron says) unless a matter worthy of his intervention is expressed; otherwise, he is poorly placed. This happens especially when we sing of some matter which cannot be grasped by the mind. For what Virgil devises in the ninth book of the *Aeneid*—that Turnus, King of the Rutulians, entered the city of the Trojans alone and turned all the Trojans themselves to flight—would not seem believable unless he had added: "Juno supplies strength and courage." In the same author, in the second book, Aeneas would not have been believed to have escaped from Troy amid the flames, weapons, and enemies, except with a god leading him—namely, Venus. ¶ "Redeeming yourself from silence": that is, departing, you will have withdrawn or vindicated yourself. ¶ "Rouge" (*Fucum*): that is, an adulterated and external display. For a "rouged" thing—that is, colored—is one thing and seems to be another. ¶ "Trickeries" (*Præstigias*): that is, a display other than what the thing itself is. They want "trickeries" to be named from "binding" or "dazzling" (*perstringendo*). For to "dazzle," as Nonius Marcellus says, is to darken. Plautus in *The Braggart Warrior*: "Let him dazzle the sharp sight of the eyes in the battle line for the enemies." Thence they are called "prestigiators" (magicians) who so dazzle the sight of the eyes that things appear other than they are. Or because, by the authority of the same Marcellus, to "graze" is to touch. Whence "grazed olives" is a proverb concerning those men who, unless they are struck and punished, bring no usefulness. Moreover, when someone has "grazed" (struck) our nose, we seem to see certain aerial images, and things offer themselves to be seen by us other than they are. ¶ "For sellable wine, there is no need for hanging ivy." A proverb used here for this sentiment, which is known of itself: it does not need proof. It is likewise applied to excellent things.

To the Brutes, that is, the dull-witted and those devoid of reason. For "Brutus" means dull. For this reason, Junius, who concealed his wisdom, was surnamed Brutus <note>Lucius Junius Brutus, the founder of the Roman Republic, who famously faked idiocy to survive the tyranny of Tarquin the Proud</note>. Pacuvius also speaks of "brute fortune," whose verses Crinitus cites in the fifth chapter of his first book. Philosophers assert that Fortune is insane and brute, and that "Brute Fortune" is unable to distinguish between the worthy and the unworthy. Therefore, among brute living creatures, both friendships and enmities exist. For example, the crow is a friend to the fox; the heron to the crow; the fox to the serpent; and the turtledove to the blackbird. But others are divided by mutual hatred: the eagle and the dragon <note>often referring to a large serpent or python in classical texts</note>; the crow and the owl; the weasel and the crow; the kite and the raven; the eagle and the heron. The raven is also an adversary to the bull and the donkey. The wolf is an enemy to the donkey, the bull, and the fox. Aristotle records other enmities of this kind among living creatures more extensively in the first chapter of his book *On the Nature of Animals* <note>original: "de natura animalium"</note>. The Hedge-sparrows and the Linnets <note>original: "Aegithalli & Acanthylides"</note> have such well-attested enmities...

[Large woodcut initial Q depicting a scholar in a study] I recently received your letter: it was so pleasing to me, my dear Pomponius <note>Pomponio Leto (1428–1498), a famous Italian humanist</note>, that I feel as though I have been gifted with immortality by its words. Furthermore, the *Six-Month Calendar* was wonderfully welcome, as was the map you mention regarding the Marsic War <note>The Social War (91–87 BC) between Rome and its Italian allies</note>. However, if that map is the same one I happened to read in passing while in Rome, I fear it was not transcribed with enough accuracy. Indeed, the name was written as *Aimilius* on the stone, not *Aemilius*. I had also noted that same diphthong <note>The "ai" spelling instead of "ae"</note> upon the dome of the Pantheon itself. As for your consulting me (if the gods permit!) regarding obscure passages of the poets—you, who are the most learned man in all literature—I realize you grant me this out of love, whereas it is truly owed to you. I understand what I must pass on, how much you favor me, and what a burden of expectation I carry. Nevertheless, I shall say what I think; if I cannot prove the facts themselves to you, I will certainly prove my zeal and goodwill. The specific verses which you rightly consider corrupted are these:

*The native of eternal Jove’s rock; hence for you, Mars,*
*The green lakes are given behind the back; where with a lazy miter*
*The pregnant woman gathers; and she herself warms the man in the released birth.*

I believe, for my part, they should be read as follows:

*Thence the rock of Genetæan Jove; hence of the Tibareni*
*The green lakes are given behind the back; where with a lazy miter*
*The pregnant woman binds; and she herself warms the man in the released birth.*

So that the sense is: after the Chalybes <note>An ancient Iron Age people of Anatolia</note>, they leave the promontory of Genetæan Jove behind their backs; that is, they sail past it. Then come the "green lakes" of the Tibareni—green, of course, because they abound in livestock and therefore in pastures. It is the custom of these Tibareni that when their wives are in labor, or even just released from childbirth, the men are placed in bed wearing miters <note>A type of headband or cap</note>; they themselves are warmed and tended to in place of the women who have just given birth. This was translated with wonderful brevity from Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Rhodes, author of the Argonautica</note>, whose second book contains these verses:

*And after them, then the peak of Genetæan Jove* <note>original Greek: Τοὺς δὲ μετ' αὐτίν' ἔπειτα Γενηταίου Διὸς ἄκρην</note>
*Rounding it, they were driven past the Tibarenian land.* <note>original Greek: Γνάμψαντες, σώοντο παρὲξ Τιβαρηνίδα γαῖαν.</note>
*There, whenever wives have borne children to their husbands,* <note>original Greek: Ενθ' ἐπεὶ ἄρκε τέκωνται ὑπ' ἀνδράσι τέκνα γυναῖκες,</note>
*The men themselves groan, falling into the beds,* <note>original Greek: Αὐτοὶ μὲν στενάχουσιν ἐνὶ λεχέεσσι πεσόντες,</note>
*Their heads bound. But the women, in turn, sustain with food* <note>original Greek: Κράατα δησάμενοι, ταὶ δ' αὖ κομέουσιν ἐδωδῇ</note>
*The men: and laboriously provide the birthing-baths for them.* <note>original Greek: Ανέρας, ἠδὲ λοετρὰ λεχώϊα τοῖσι πένονθ.</note>

The commentators on Apollonius add: this was also written by Nymphodorus in the *Laws of the Barbarians*; he says the Genetæan promontory was named after the river Genetes, where there is a temple to "Jove the Hospitable," whom they call *Xenion*. Apollonius writes the same in that same book:

*And nearby dwell the Tibareni, rich in lambs,* <note>original Greek: Αγχι δὲ ναιετάουσι πολύρρλωνες Τιβαρηνοί</note>
*Under the Genetæan peak of Jove the Hospitable.* <note>original Greek: Ζηνὸς ἐνξείνοιο γενηταίω ὑπὸ' ἄκρηω,</note>

In this passage, they are called "rich in lambs" from their abundance of sheep, which is why Valerius <note>Valerius Flaccus, Roman poet</note> learnedly called them "green lakes," on account of the pastures, as I believe. Orpheus also writes of the Tibareni in the *Argonautica* after the Cha-

Dionysius, in his book *On the Situation of the World* <note>Dionysius Periegetes, a 2nd-century geographer</note>, mentions that the Tibareni are the most excellent of all shepherds. **Xenion**: that is, hospitable. Homer, in the sixth and ninth books of the *Odyssey*, declares that guests, the poor, and suppliants are under the protection of Jupiter. Virgil says in the first book of the *Aeneid*: "Jupiter, for they say thou givest laws to guests." For *xenios* <note>original Greek: ξενιοσ</note> is said for "hospitable," and *xeniou* <note>original Greek: ξενιου</note> for the "gift of hospitality." *Xenos* <note>original Greek: ξενοσ</note> means a foreign guest. *Xenikou* <note>original Greek: ξενικου</note> means a place of hospitality.
<margin>Xenodochium. Nosocomion.</margin> Note besides these that the Greeks use the term **Xenodochium** for what is commonly called a hospital. That which they call a "hospital of God" or an infirmary, the Greeks call a **Nosocomion**; for *nosos* <note>original Greek: νοσοσ</note> means disease, and *komion* <note>original Greek: κομιν</note> is said to be a village or ward. **Orphanotrophion**: where those bereft of parents are nourished. **Ptochotrophion**: a house erected for feeding beggars. **Gerontocomion**: where nourishment is supplied to the elderly whose strength is exhausted by old age.
**ASCENSIUS.** <note>The commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note> **Semestre**: now commonly called "six-month period"; it is more correctly formed from *semis* (half) and *mensis* (month). **Consultissimus**: that is, most skilled or most learned. Thus one says "learned in the law" (*iuris consultus*) and "consulted by the law" (*iure consultus*), between which there is this distinction: the *iure consultus* is he whom we consult regarding the law because we think him skilled; the *iuris consultus* is he who is well-versed in the counsels of the law and is thus an expert. **From the truth**: from the just, or from what is due. For "truth" is used everywhere by the learned to mean "justice." **Intetlego**: an ancient spelling where, in composition, the letters remained almost entirely intact.
**F.S.** **Appetit**: that is, it is near. **Let him hang entirely from your file**: that is, let him be shaped completely, and with superfluities removed, let his talent be polished. This is a metaphor drawn from blacksmiths, whose finished works hang in the workshop.
<margin>Like jackdaws. Starling.</margin> **Like jackdaws and like starlings**: that is, in a very great number. For jackdaws and starlings are accustomed to fly in flocks. The starling is (as Aristotle says in chapter 26 of his book *On the Nature of Animals*) black, distinguished by white spots, and the size of a blackbird. It is characteristic of the starling kind (says Pliny in chapter 24 of the tenth book) to fly in crowds and to be driven in a sort of ball-like circle, with all tending toward the center of the flock.
<margin>Jackdaw.</margin> The **Jackdaw** (as Marcus Varro writes in the first book *On the Latin Language*) is so named because it flies in flocks (*gregatim*). The interpreter of Homer, at the end of the seventeenth book of the *Iliad*, writing of the fight of the Trojans with the Greeks over the corpse of Patroclus, says: "Just as a multitude of starlings or jackdaws fills the air with cries when they see a hawk threatening destruction to smaller birds, so under Aeneas and Hector the Greek youths, with a great shout and forgetting the fight, retreated." **You seem to have recalled the ancients from the underworld**: that is, there is no other learning of the ancients than that which is yours.
<margin>Quirinus.</margin> **Quirinus**: that is, to me who am his Quirinus, meaning "master." For *Quirinus* is said to mean master, or because the Greeks call a master *koiranos* and *kyrios*. By this name Romulus was called because of his mastery of the city of Rome—unless we agree with Lactantius that he was called Quirinus after death so that men would not think he had been a mere man.
<margin>To be amazed.</margin> **To be amazed**: In those manuscripts which are thought to be corrected, they claim it is written with deliberate care as *obstypescere* rather than *obstupescere*. Thus Benedictus the Philologist, regarding Virgil in the first book of the *Aeneid*—"Sidonian Dido was amazed (*obstypuit*) at the first sight"—thinks one should read *obstypuit*, not *obstupuit*. For all the commentaries of Tiberius Donatus say that the ancient manuscripts have *obstypui* and *obstypescere*. For *y* and *u* have such an affinity between them that when you make Latin words from Greek, you sometimes keep the *y* unchanged and sometimes change it to *u*. In this latter case, we imitate the Aeolians, who, on the authority of Priscian in his first book, were accustomed to pronounce *y* with the sound of *u*, as in *dakryon* <note>original Greek: δακρυον</note> for *lachryma* (tear). Yet the ancients wrote *lachrymas* and *lachrymare*...

**Pomponius Laetus to Angelo Poliziano, greetings.**
**Letter XVII.**

It is now time, most learned and sincere of Italians, that you return the books of Lucretius, so that as an upright man you may fulfill your promise. You will give them to be carried to the City <note>Rome</note> by Petreius, a man of the highest faith, who, because of the fame of your name, loves, honors, and venerates you along with the rest of our order. For whoever has a good opinion of himself ought to congratulate our age greatly that it has such men as our ancestors would have considered to be in the highest glory. He is traveling to Florence with deliberate purpose to visit you more often, and so that he may emerge entirely from your "file" <note>i.e., your corrective polishing</note>; I wish that I could do the same. When I think of the height of your genius, I cannot help but wonder why our people do not fly to you "like jackdaws and starlings" (if I may speak so). I have read your work, in which you most clearly seem to have recalled the ancients from the underworld by a certain singular learning. But I shall be more sparing in your presence; you do not need my proclamation. For you are famous enough by your own labor. Truly, whenever there is an interpretation of something sublime, you, Poliziano, are the only one who comes to mind. I have explained what I feel about your most piercing genius in one letter, and a long one indeed—though what can be too long in such a matter? I believe you delayed returning the poems of Lucretius because of your occupation with various disciplines. I beseech and entreat you, see to it that they return to their "Quirinus" <note>their master/owner</note>. I have certain very ancient monuments which, when you see them, you will be amazed and wonder at; they were recently dug up, unearthed, and found, and they are reflected in those observations of yours. Regarding which, I perceive a certain divinity to be in you, so that truly your soul is a fire taken from heaven. May the gods keep you. Commend me to the Medici, the father and the children, patrons of letters. Then, impart my best greetings to Demetrius. Farewell. At Rome, the fifth day before the Kalends of June.

Battista Guarini sends greetings to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola.
Letter 19.

I do not yet concede that the lawsuit should be decided in your favor. For I can easily turn those clever arguments of yours back against you <note>original: "αντιστρεφειν" (antistrephein) - a Greek rhetorical term for turning an opponent's argument against them</note>. If I am your teacher, why do you not obey me? If I am not, why do you call me teacher? Nor do I refuse this title because I look down on you as a student—for I assert that you are *my* teacher—but because I both venerate and proclaim your learning. In that learning, I am conscious that you have advanced so far that I have not needed to mark your work with my fingernails <note>a metaphor for scratching out errors</note>, nor with the stroke of a pen, nor with red ink, nor finally with a critical mark <note>original: "obelisco" - a symbol used by ancient editors to mark doubtful passages</note> or an asterisk. But we have fallen, as I see it, into a new kind of legal dispute: while you strive to award me that possession <note>referring to the title of "Teacher"</note>, I am trying to surrender it. What rhetorician has ever had a plaintiff or a defendant in a case of this kind? My dear Pico, I will never "extend the blade of grass" to you in this fight <note>original: "herbam porrigam" - a Latin idiom meaning to admit defeat or surrender</note> unless we first settle on good terms, so that (since you will not yield otherwise) both of us...

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the letters of Angelo Poliziano, specifically focusing on classical idioms for victory, legal terms, and the beginning of Letter XX to Battista Guarino.</meta>

**Book of Letters. Book I. Folio XI.**

Neptune produced the horse, Minerva the olive. Minerva was declared the victor: whence it became the custom that when someone judges another to be their superior, they offer an olive branch. From this comes that proverb, *I give the grass* <note>original: "herbam do"</note>, that is, I yield the victory. Marcus Varro posits this, noting that in contests, someone gives grass in the manner of a palm branch to the one with whom he no longer attempts to contend, confessing him to be the better man. These things are from Servius. Pliny, in the fourth chapter of his twenty-second book, speaking of the "siege crown," says: This was given from green grass taken from the spot where someone had saved the besieged. For among the ancients, the highest sign of victory was for the vanquished to proffer grass: that is, to yield the very earth, their nurturer, and even the right of burial. The same author, in the fifth chapter of the eighth book, concerning the intelligence of elephants, says: Their shame is wondrous. When defeated, the elephant flees the voice of the victor and proffers earth and vervain. *To give the hands* <note>original: "dare manus"</note> is used by Cicero in *On Friendship* <note>Lælius de Amicitia</note> for the same meaning. At the end, he says, "let him give his hands," and allow himself to be conquered. <margin>To give the hands. To pass the torch.</margin> *To pass the torch* <note>original: "lampada tradere"</note> signifies the same. For in the Academy there is an altar of Prometheus, from which they run to the city with lit torches: if the first man's torch is extinguished, the victory passes to the second runner; if the second's, to the third; if none of them win, the victory goes to no one. See more in Battista Pio, chapter 114 of his *Annotations*; in Beroaldo’s *Annotations*; and in Hyginus. Appian writes in the second book of the *Civil Wars* that it was also a sign of surrender when they covered their heads with shields. <margin>To cover the head with a shield. Experience is the best teacher in writing.</margin> Experience is usually considered the best teacher in writing. Aulus Gellius, in the second chapter of the thirteenth book, writes about the utility that experience brings to writing. The poet Accius read his tragedy, titled *Atreus*, to Marcus Pacuvius at his request. Then they say Pacuvius said: that what he had written was indeed sonorous and grand, but it seemed to him a little too harsh and bitter. "It is as you say," said Accius, "and I am certainly not sorry for it. For I hope that what I write hereafter will be better. For they say it is the same with talents as it is with fruits: those which are born hard and bitter later become mellow and pleasant. But those which are produced immediately withered and soft, and are lively in the beginning, do not soon become ripe, but rotten." Therefore, it seemed necessary to leave something in talent for time and age to mellow. *By the pebble* <note>original: "calculo"</note>, that is, by judgment. For by throwing pebbles into an urn, they indicated a judicial sentence. In these, there was a triple mark: **θ** <note>Greek letter Theta, for 'thanatos' or death</note> was the mark of condemnation; **τ** <note>Greek letter Tau</note> for absolution; **A** for enlargement <note>ampliatio</note>, that is, whenever they indicated that the matter was not yet clear to them and the case ought to be argued anew. The authority for this is Asconius Pedianus. <margin>Marks of judgments. The die (chance).</margin> *Outside the die of learning*, that is, one whose learning is certain and solid. Pliny uses this proverb regarding Cicero. These are his words from the preface to his books of *Natural History*: "There is a certain public rejection even of the learned. Marcus Tullius also uses it, placed outside every die of talent." *The works of the Sibyl are required*, that is, they are full of errors and cannot be corrected by a man. *Not by a long recovery of rights* <note>original: "postliminio"</note> etc. *Postliminium* <margin>Postliminium (Recovery of rights).</margin> is when our things, having been taken from us or departing from us, are received back or return to us, which we possess again by the same right as before. I subscribe to the words of Pompeius: He is received by *postliminium*, he says, who had been captured outside the thresholds—that is, the boundaries of the province—and returns again to his own property. Gallus the Aedile, in the first book of *Significations Pertaining to Law*, says that one received by *postliminium* is he who, having departed as a free man from his own city to another, returns to that same city by the law established concerning recoveries. Likewise, a slave who passes from us into the power of the enemy and later returns to us is in the power of his former master by the right of *postliminium*. Horses, mules, and ships are received back by *postliminium* in the same way as slaves. Those kinds of things which return to us from the enemy return by *postliminium*; the same kinds can return from us to the enemy. Thus says Pompeius. We shall write later concerning the word *Postliminium* and its reasoning.

**ASCENSIUS.** *According to himself*: i.e., according to your matter or utility and convenience. *The mark of the nails*: which is impressed into poorly written wax. *Transverse pens*: by which things poorly written on paper are erased, like the deleting part of a stylus. *Vermilion*: made red by mixing in cinnabar. Cinnabar is a red earth with which sheep are usually marked. *With an obelisk*: i.e., a spit, with which bad verses are usually transfixed. *With an asterisk*: i.e., a little star with which things lacking light are usually marked. Sylvius explains all these fully; therefore I do not repeat them. But lest the novice reader stumble in the order or meaning: the order is: "In which learning: I am not conscious to myself," i.e., I do not acknowledge that you have promoted, i.e., profited and stretched toward further things, "so much," i.e., to such an extent or so greatly, "the mark of my nails; nor do I mark the same with the transverse [pen]" etc. *Into a new kind of claim*: i.e., a dispute over the possession of the name of "teacher." For those who litigate about possessing want to possess, but we flee from it. Regarding the *proffering of grass*, besides those which Sylvius learnedly collected, this seems to me the reason: that in a single combat of those fighting, he who succumbs and is knocked to the ground, since he has nothing else in the name of surrender, plucks grass from the turf upon which he fell and proffers it to the victor. This surrender is done both more quickly and more openly than with words, since the victor perhaps might not wish to hear one preparing to say many things, or indeed might not hear him; also the spectating people might more easily see the grass than hear words, and thus it inhibits further raging. The *Heptaplus* of Pico [della Mirandola] is usually placed first among his printed works. <margin>The pebble (Calculus).</margin> *Calculus* is a small stone, named from *calcando* [treading]; before the use of counters, they used to use them in making accounts: whence it is usually used for a computation. It was also cast into an urn by judges just as points were impressed into wax: and therefore both "pebble" and "point" are accepted for a "vote" <note>original: "suffragio"</note>, which word the common people use. *The works of the Sibyl are required*: i.e., they are so disturbed and inverted that they could be restored and properly replaced by no one except the authors themselves; just as the Sibylline verses written on palm leaves, if once disturbed by the wind, could be replaced by no one. And therefore, as it says in the *Aeneid*, book III: "They depart unadvised and hate the name of the Sibyl." It was likely, however, that they could have been restored by the Sibyl herself.

Pliny, in the eighth chapter of the thirty-third book, says: "The mention of gold and silver is accompanied by a stone (which they call a touchstone) formerly not accustomed to be found except in the river Tmolus, as Theophrastus is the authority, but now found everywhere..."

From every direction, letters come to us—or are written about us—by excellent men: letters full of zeal, full of praise. First, there are the two from you: how noble, good God, how simple, how generous! Finally, with what great and what kind of marks of affection are they distinguished! I pass over how elegant and learned they are. This is clearly the characteristic of that house of yours, in which the very cradle of the liberal arts is found. Therefore, what stings these great judgments or favors of yours ought to apply to me—or rather, what spurs for writing they ought to provide—if I easily despise (as I have indeed always despised) the follies of the malevolent and those trifles which I might truly call "abortive." <note>original: "abortiuas." The author suggests his critics' works are stillborn or fail to develop into anything meaningful.</note> (For they are almost dead before they are even published.) With your letters supporting me, which are more long-lived than even the Phoenix, I am now eager, aided by the shouts of the learned, and I hasten toward the finish line of this race. <note>original: "ad huius calcem curriculi." A classical metaphor for reaching the end of a task or life stage.</note> Indeed—

Pico della Mirandola, the pure flower of genius <note>original: "Picus Mirandula flos Illibatus Ingeniorum"</note>

# **Of Illustrious Men**

<column-break/>

François Dubois <note>original: "Franciscus Sylvius," a 16th-century French humanist</note> in his commentary on the second book of the Letters of Angelo Poliziano.

<margin>Pure <note>original: "Illibatus"</note></margin>
Pure: that is, inviolate, untouched, or whole.

<margin>Sacrificial cakes <note>original: "Liba"</note></margin>
Sacrificial cakes <note>original: "Liba"</note> (to seek the origin a little deeper) were so named according to Marcus Varro in the sixth book of *On the Latin Language*, because they are made for the sake of "libation" <note>original: "libandi," the act of pouring a ritual offering</note>. These cakes are pastries made of flour, honey, and oil, as Servius says regarding that passage in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 7: "They set out the feast, and place wheaten cakes <note>original: "adorea liba"</note> upon the grass beneath the food." Properly speaking, therefore, "to offer a libation" <note>original: "libare"</note> is to sacrifice with these cakes. These cakes were "wheaten" <note>original: "adorea"</note>, that is, made from grain. Furthermore, Fabius Pictor, in his book *On the Golden Age*, is the authority for the fact that grain and wine are offered first to Janus in every sacrifice, because he was the first to discover wine and grain. This is what I consider "to offer a libation" to properly mean. But because not much was consumed during that ritual offering, it happened that the word "to taste" or "to touch" <note>original: "libare"</note> came to mean to diminish something slightly. See Aulus Gellius, Chapter 3 of the first book.

# On the Nature and Effects of Ivy

The plant which the Greeks call *Kittos* <note>original: "κισσός"</note> and we call Ivy, possesses a dual nature that has long fascinated both physicians and poets. It is said to be dedicated to Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine and ecstasy</note>, not merely for its evergreen beauty, but because of its strange power over the effects of wine.

### The Testimony of the Ancients

As recorded by the ancient authorities:

*   **Socrates** spoke against the tragic poets, claiming they were intoxicated by the "ivy-juice" of their own verses.
*   **Pliny the Elder**, in his tenth book, chapter thirty-five, discusses the ivy at length, noting its ability to cling and climb.
*   **The Physicians** observe that ivy has a cooling property, yet its berries can provoke a heat in the blood.

<column-break/>

### The Varieties of the Plant

The ivy is divided by the learned into the male and the female varieties. It is noted that the flower of each is remarkably similar to the wild rose. Furthermore, in the twenty-fourth book of his natural history, Pliny describes how the plant:

1.  Creeps along the ground if denied a support.
2.  Strangles the very trees it seeks for protection.
3.  Produces a resin that is useful in certain medicinal plasters.

<margin>Ivy is harmful to stone walls and buildings.</margin>

It is a wonder of nature that a plant so associated with the revelry of Bacchus should also be used as a remedy for the heaviness of the head <note>a hangover</note> caused by that same god's gift. When the mind is dispersed by wine, the ivy-garland was thought to draw out the superfluous vapors.

<summary>This page explores the botanical characteristics and classical associations of ivy, citing Pliny the Elder and Socrates regarding its medicinal and symbolic relationship with Bacchus and wine.</summary>
<keywords>Ivy, Hedera, Bacchus, Pliny the Elder, Socrates, Botany, Ancient Medicine, Wine</keywords>

**Letter VIII.**

[Large decorative initial 'I'] In a certain letter of yours to our friend Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous philosopher and close friend of Poliziano</note>, while many things delighted me, I was further prompted to write to you by the judgment you assert regarding our *Rusticus* <note>Poliziano’s poem *Rusticus* (1483), a Latin work celebrating country life</note>. Would that it were as true as it is honorable! However, I interpret this not so much as a judgment of me, but rather as your zeal and kindness toward me. For I am not so unexamined by myself that I would decide to believe more about myself from you—a most dear friend and therefore a less impartial judge—than I believe about myself. Unless perhaps that "amiable insanity" of poets, as Horace calls it <note>original: *amabilis insania*; Horace, Odes 3.4.5</note>, so mocks me that I never "meet with myself," and never "bring the knapsack from my back to my chest" <note>A reference to Aesop’s fable where people see the faults of others in a bag hanging in front, but their own faults in a bag hanging behind</note>. But if that blind self-love called *philautia* <note>Greek: φιλαυτία; excessive self-love or conceit</note> follows poetry like a shadow follows a body—infatuating most men and raising a head empty of all but excessive vanity—I confess it already irks me to be considered a candidate for poetry at such an ungrateful turn, and for such a sad and regrettable reward. Otherwise, not even that famous Lycian <note>Glaucus, in Homer's Iliad</note>, more foolish than I, would have exchanged "gold for bronze" <note>Greek: χρύσεα χαλκείων; a proverbial bad trade</note>, "a hundred oxen's worth for nine." Furthermore, I owe you no less for what you feel about us, or for what you ask others to feel, than what my conscience refuses to acknowledge and my modesty refuses to bear. For whether you do this to deceive others—not even envying me your own ornaments, that is, the furniture of your own praises—or whether you yourself are deceived and even my faults delight you, both are signs of love, and certainly no common love. Indeed, Achilles also dressed his Patroclus in his own armor, and a mole even on a boy’s knuckle delighted the poet Alcaeus. Therefore, if you love me—which I know you do—you certainly cannot doubt that I love you in return. For they say that love is bought by nothing more than by itself. And yet, just as I love the one who loves me, I do not likewise praise the one who praises me. For in returning favors, that law of Hesiod must be observed: that you should return in the same measure, or even with a heap on top if you can. But when you, with the riches of speech you possess—when you, I say, a man of such genius and such learning—have heaped such great praises upon me, a single little man from the crowd, from your very "granary" (as they say), how can I, from the return of a stingy and uncultivated soil, measure back to you even half as much, let alone something more? Unless, like that Echo, I reflect and pour back your own voices to you. But I fear that if I unseal whatever you have given and send back your own praises which I hold only on loan, I shall stand naked myself and, like Aesop’s little crow when its borrowed feathers were taken away, I shall provoke laughter. And yet, you cannot even prosecute me as guilty of ingratitude, since this Pico—should I call him a man or a Phoenix?—voluntarily undertakes a substitute payment for me and relieves my role. You are always in his mouth, which is full of the Muses and the Graces. Inspired by him, we too are driven to extol you even beyond our strength, though still below our desire. For he alone is equal to carrying such a great burden. We, however, hang from him like the iron rings from Plato’s magnet <note>A reference to Plato's *Ion*, describing how poetic inspiration passes from the Muse through the poet to the listener like magnetic force through rings</note>. He himself rains down a certain secret virtue upon us, as if a divine inspiration <note>Greek: ἐνθουσια... (enthousiasmos); divine frenzy or inspiration</note>...

[Right Column]

<margin>On the *Rusticus*.</margin> Our *Rusticus*. That is, our forest/poem which is called *Our Rusticus*. So Terence says in the prologue to *The Eunuch*: "Which we are now about to perform, the *Eunuch* of Menander." Therefore, he does not deny that he transferred those characters into his *Eunuch*, that is, the comedy which is called *The Eunuch*. For often an adjective refers to the thing signified in place of the noun.
