# BOOK X. Of Illustrious Men

[margin: Various causes of love.]
...was delighted by that specific part. We were saying that even the vices of a beloved thing please us. Ovid says in the second book of his *Elegies*:
<note>original: "Non est certa meos quae forma invitet amores..." Ovid, Amores 2.4.9-14</note>
There is no fixed beauty that invites my loves:
There are a hundred reasons why I am always in love.
If there is one with modest eyes cast down before me:
I burn: and that bashfulness is a snare for me.
If there is one who is bold, I am captured because she is not rustic:
And she gives hope of being nimble on a soft bed.
If she seemed harsh, and rigid like the Sabine women:
I think she wants it, but is feigning from deep within.
If she is learned, she pleases me, endowed with rare arts.
If she is unrefined: she is pleasing in her own simplicity.
Plato, in the fifth book of the *Republic*, writes toward this same opinion. He says it does not befit a man who indulges greatly in love to be ignorant: that all those established in the flower of youth stir up and excite a lover of boys in some way, since they seem worthy of care and affection. Are you not affected thus toward beautiful youths? One, because he is snub-nosed <note>original: "simus"</note>, is judged gracious by you and is praised. Another, with a hooked nose, you call "royal." Another, because he is between these two, seems to you to be quite well-proportioned. The fair-skinned are "sons of the gods." But who called a youth "pale-ish" <note>original: "pallidulum"</note> except a lover himself, flattering in a certain way, and easily enduring the pallor in young men under the name of "semi-pale"? And to speak briefly: you seize whatever little excuses you can, so that you reject no youth at all of a flowering age. To these things, the same applies to you. What of those greedy for wine? Do you not see them similarly affected, seeking any wine whatsoever, seizing any occasion? Tibullus seems to have borrowed these things from Plato. His words are:
<note>original: "Ne fuge te tenerae puerorum credere turbae..." Tibullus 1.4.9-14</note>
Do not flee from trusting yourself to the tender crowd of boys:
For they always have a cause for a just love.
This one pleases because he restrains the horse with tight reins.
This one drives the calm water with a snowy breast.
This one, because a brave boldness is present, has captured me: but for that one
A virginal shame stands before his tender cheeks.

...[impulse]: which compels us even more than we are able of our own accord. He himself, like a choir-master <note>original: "pausarius"</note>, gives us the rhythms and incitements for praising you: for praising together with you Hermolaus Barbarus <note>A famous Venetian humanist (1454–1493)</note>: a man (as it seems to me at least) who is one of the remains of the Golden Age: than whom he himself is far more learned, and none are more holy than he. But having entered upon something concerning you, we often "imagine" <note>original: "φαντάσεσθαι" (phantasesthai)</note> so many things that the breeze lifts us into the sky, so that we sometimes dread an Icarian fall. You see now also that I, as if "possessed by nymphs" <note>original: "νυμφόληπτον" (nympholepton)</note>, exhibit in this letter something I know not what, rather "dithyrambic" <note>original: "διθυραμβικώτερον" (dithyrambikoteron) - meaning wild or passionate</note>. Why then do you knit your brow? Does it escape you that I must be indulged in this, whatever fury it is, either because I love all who are a little more refined, and am, as they say, a "white level" <note>original: "amussis alba" - a proverb for something easily influenced or without bias</note>; or because I seem to you also not to be abhorrent to the Muses: and likewise to Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> himself: and perhaps to Hermolaus: the "literary triumvirs," so to speak. If you approve of me even a little bit: I now show the middle finger not only to the common folk and the grammarians, but even to the philosophers themselves: not even excluding Plato, but the Florentine one <note>Likely referring to Marsilio Ficino</note>. Farewell.

[margin: Echo.]
That is the law of Hesiod. Cicero says in the first book of *On Duties*: No duty is more necessary than returning a favor. If Hesiod commands you to return those things which you received for use in greater measure (if only you can), what then ought we to do when provoked by a benefit? Hesiod, in the book titled *Works and Days*, writing to his brother Perses, says: Measure what is received, and return it with the same weight to your neighbor: so that he may help you again when you are in need. "Malignant" <note>original: "maligni"</note> means sterile, less fertile. Virgil in the second book of the *Georgics*: "First, difficult lands and malignant hills." Echo was a nymph living in the woods and mountains who, at the time when Juno wanted to catch Jupiter lying with the nymphs, would detain her with her speech until the nymphs had escaped. After Juno realized this, she said: "Small power of this tongue, by which I have been deluded, shall be given to you: and the shortest use of the voice." And she confirms the threats with the deed. Yet this nymph doubles the voices at the end of speaking, and reports back the words heard. The author is Ovid in the third book of the *Metamorphoses*. Aesop’s little crow. Horace in the epistle to Julius: "Lest perhaps, if the flock of birds should come one day to reclaim their feathers, the little crow, stripped of its stolen colors, should move people to laughter."

[margin: The fable of the little crow in Aesop.]
In the second book of Aesop which we have in Latin, it is called a jackdaw <note>original: "graculus"</note>, not a little crow. There the fable is written to roughly this effect: A jackdaw adorns himself with the feathers of a peacock which (as happens) had fallen: despising jackdaws, he desires to be associated with peacocks. The peacocks weary the unknown and impudent jackdaw, stripped of his snatched feathers, with bites and claws: and they leave him half-dead. Thus miserably tortured, he fears and blushes to return to his own kind (to whom he had been injurious). To whom one of the other jackdaws says: "If you had been content with the garments of nature, you would neither have been miserably punished by the peacocks, nor rejected by us." Plato in the *Ion*, concerning iron rings and the magnet hanging from them, writes toward roughly this opinion.

[margin: The power of the magnet.]
He says: "It is a divine power that moves you, just as in the stone which Euripides named the Magnet, and some call the Heraclean stone. This stone not only attracts iron rings, but even pours power into the rings themselves, by which they can do this same thing, and just like the stone, attract other rings. Whence a long concatenation of iron and rings often hangs from one another: and for all of these, the power is drawn from that stone." Thus he says. St. Augustine writes more diffusely in the fourth chapter of the twenty-first book of *The City of God*. He says: "We know the magnetic stone to be a wonderful snatcher of iron: which, when I first saw it, I greatly shuddered at. For I perceived an iron ring snatched and suspended by the stone. Then, as if it had given its own power to the iron it had snatched, and made it common, the same ring was moved toward another: and it suspended it: and just as that first one adhered to the stone, so the second ring adhered to the first ring. A third was added in the same way: and a fourth was added: and now a chain of rings hung, connected to each other by mutual circles, not intertwined from within, but adhering from without. Who would not be amazed at that power of the stone, which was not only in it, but also passed through so many suspended things, and bound them with invisible bonds?" But it is much more wonderful what I learned from my brother and fellow bishop Severus of Milevis concerning this stone. For he recounted that he himself had seen how Bathanus, formerly a Count of Africa, when the bishop was dining with him, brought out the same stone and held it under silver, and placed iron above the silver. Then, just as he moved his hand underneath, in which he held the stone, so the iron was moved from above, with the silver in the middle, and suffering nothing. With a very rapid running to and fro, the stone was snatched below by the man, and the iron above was snatched by the stone. Thus Augustine. Pliny understands this virtue of the magnet and the rings when, in the fourteenth chapter of the thirty-fourth book, he says: "We shall speak of the magnetic stone in its own place, and the concord which it has with iron. This material alone receives strength from that stone, and retains it for a long time: apprehending other iron so that a chain of rings is sometimes seen. Which the unskillful common people call 'living iron,' and wounds from such become more severe." The magnet (as Pliny says in the sixteenth chapter of the thirty-sixth book) was named after its discoverer, found in India. For they are found everywhere, as in Spain. He is said to have found it when the nails of his sandals and the tip of his staff stuck to it while he was pasturing his herds. **Book of Letters. Book II. Folio XVIII.**

They are more blue. Just as the magnet draws iron to itself, so the Theamedes stone found in Ethiopia drives away and rejects all iron. Pliny also writes in the Preface of his twentieth book: iron is drawn to itself by the magnet, and again driven away from itself by another <note>The Theamedes was believed to be a "negative" magnet</note>. St. Augustine says in the same place from which we were calling evidence: When a diamond is placed next to a Magnet, it does not seize the iron, and if it had already seized it, as the diamond approaches, it soon lets go. Pausanias is said to be the one who makes pauses among singers, <margin>Pausanias.</margin> who, if he pauses slowly, the song is slowed; when he hurries, one must hurry. For a pause is a rest or a delay. Lucilius: "When he gave these words, he made a pause in his mouth from speaking." Of the Golden Age: about which and others Hesiod writes much, learnedly and prudently enough, in the book called *Works and Days*. "Having entered," that is, beginning. "The Icarian [sea] at some time," etc., that is, let us fear lest we fall: as did Icarus the son of Daedalus, when he fell into the Icarian sea. We omit the fable as it is well enough known. "Next to," that is, similarly. <margin>Next to.</margin> Sallust in *Catiline*: "I value their life and death next to each other <note>original: "iuxta"</note>, since you are silent about both." "A white plumb-line," that is, a white line: about which we shall remember more hereafter. "To the Triumvirs": he alludes to the fact that Octavius Caesar, Mark Antony, and Marcus Lepidus, as triumvirs, ruled almost the whole world subject to Roman jurisdiction. Pomponius Laetus and L. Fenestella write amply about the triumvirate. "I show the middle finger," that is, not only do I not fear, but I even despise. Moreover, to show the middle finger is a proverbial sentiment for the contempt of those whom they point out. <margin>To show the middle finger.</margin> For the middle finger has I know not what infamy; as in Laertius, book six: When foreigners desired to see Demosthenes, the Cynic Diogenes, stretching out his middle finger, said, "This, for you, is the orator of the Athenians." For he wished to signify that he was hardly a man. The same Diogenes used to say that most people were insane, except for a finger <note>meaning they are only a finger's breadth away from madness</note>. If someone, therefore, should go along stretching out his middle finger, he will seem to be insane; but if the index finger, not so. Porphyrio, in the commentaries on the last satire of Horace’s second book of *Sermones*, calls the fingers by these names: thumb, index, famous <note>the middle finger</note>, medical <note>the ring finger</note>, and smallest. Persius in the second satire calls it the "infamous" finger: "And she purifies the forehead and damp lips with the infamous finger and purifying spit beforehand." Martial in book six: "He shows his finger, but the lewd one." Juvenal in the tenth satire: "He might bid a halter for him, and show the middle nail."
ASCENSIUS. <note>The commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note>

"From our *Rusticus*." Therefore, Rusticus had also sent out these letters before, or at least shared them with friends. *Philautia* <note>original: Φιλαυτι</note>, that is, self-love. For *philos* is dear and a friend; *autos* is self and one's own. "Gold for Bronze" <note>original: Χρυσέα Χαλκείωμ</note>, that is, golden things for bronze ones; "valued at a hundred oxen for nine oxen" <note>original: εκατομβοια εννεα βοιωμ</note>. Namely, the arms of Glaucus the Lycian [valued at 100] for the arms of Diomedes [valued at 9]. In another sense, as the Aldine edition has it. The Law of Hesiod: that we should imitate fertile fields, which return more than they received. "But nothing less," namely, because I might repent of my undertaking. "I shall have resigned," that is, I shall have returned with whole faith: for if someone received sealed things to be guarded as deposits, if he restored them with the same seal safe, he is said to "resign" <note>to unseal/return</note>. Or rather, with the seal broken so the depositor may see if all are safe; if he finds it so, and the depositary returns them sealed and closed again, he may be said to resign. "You will have gathered in the granary." In the Aldine impression it is written thus without the 'h' <note>original: "orreum" instead of "horreum"</note>: perhaps to distinguish it from "I shudder" <note>horreo</note>, or because he thinks it derived from "barley" <note>ordeo</note>. <margin>Granary.</margin> "From the midst," common. "He puts his own arms on Patroclus." So also Maro <note>Virgil</note>: "He puts his own arms on the youth." It seems to have more grace than if he said "he dressed Patroclus" in whatever way; but "on Patroclus" <margin>He puts on Patroclus.</margin> for his favor, ornament, or something of his kind. "Concerning the return" <note>original: "De reditu"</note>: in the Aldine it is written with a single 'd'; it is however from the verb *redo* <note>to give back</note>, for which *reddo* is more frequently written, not from *redeo* <note>to return/go back</note>. "Just like Echo," a beautiful allusion: especially since through it he signifies that he cannot report the whole, but only the ends. I might say "Picus" <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>, because he is so called by surname, or "Phoenix," because he is uniquely learned. "It rains down": what is commonly called "it flows in." *Enthousiasmon* <note>original: ευθουσιασμον</note>, that is, the inspiration of a divine power or divine substance: this is poetic madness. *Rhapsodein* <note>original: ραψωδειμ</note>, that is, to sing out as if through rhapsody. "A breeze lifts." So Horace concerning Pindar: "A great breeze lifts the Dircaean swan." *Nympholeptos* <note>original: νυμφυληπτομι</note>, that is, caught by nymphs, driven by madness. *Dithyrambikoteron* <note>original: Διουραμ βικωτερομ</note>, that is, more furious or more like a bacchante.

**Poliziano. Greetings.**
**Letter IX.**

**I** indeed, most learned Poliziano, feel that I have received the most grateful and pleasant fruits of your love toward me; nor do I expect more fertile or more honorable yields from elsewhere. For I see that you have responded in friendship "in the same measure and better" <note>original: αυτω μέτρω καὶ λώϊομ</note>; and I perceive that which I never doubted: that you are not only "Poliziano," but also "most political" <note>original: πολιτικώτατομ - a pun on his name and the Greek word for a statesman/civilized man</note>, having joined such rare and exact eloquence to almost infinite humanity and modesty. But if I examine the accounts of my business and report them in turn, I shall find that I have made no more excellent profit since that day on which I last wrote to Pico than this letter of yours: Good gods, how Attic <note>refined/pure</note>, how upright, how polished, how lovable it is! So much so that the highest love and the highest erudition seem to contend in it, nor can it easily be discerned which excels. It is very easy to guess the most evident causes of both things. For your erudition is the highest, coming entirely from yourself through divine genius and indefatigable study. Your benevolence, truly, cannot be anything but immense, with which you embraced me at the suggestion of Pico. I, however, had already begun to love you before; but that "meeting and conversation in the same place" <note>original: εις ταυτὸμ σύνοδός ἡ ὁμιλία</note> was lacking. Yet in the future, we shall not lack this through the benefit of letters. However, I suspect you remember—for it is nearly five years ago when you were staying with us—that you recited to Hermolao and to me (then wretched and in mourning clothes due to the death of my father and uncle) that golden poem concerning the sacrilegious and bloody murder of Giuliano. Since then, no mention of learned men has ever been made in my presence without you occurring to me first of all. Soon, in that most elegant *Rusticus* of yours, you were always held great by me; you were found even greater. Wherefore—

**F. S.** "If I examine the accounts of my business." He alludes to the custom of merchants, who, having examined the accounts of given and received, easily know what profit they have made. For they call "accounts" <margin>Accounts.</margin> what are commonly called "reckonings." Whence they wish the book in which they write accounts to be called an "Account-book" <note>original: Rationarium</note>. <margin>Account-book.</margin> "Attic," that is, wiped clean, polished, whole. We write about the Asiatic style of speaking in the *Griphus* of Ausonius. "The murder of Giuliano": <margin>The murder of Giuliano.</margin> Giuliano, the brother of Lorenzo de' Medici and uncle of this Pope Leo X (who was called Giovanni before his papacy), was slain on account of a certain faction in Florence in a sacred building, at the very time when the priest was showing the most holy body of the Lord to be adored by the people. Which deed, having been committed, it seems can be expiated by no victim, by no sacred rites.
ASCENSIUS.
"In the same [measure]," etc., that is, to the same measure and better or more abundantly. "Most political," that is, most civil and most "Politian-like." Moreover, he alludes to the name Poliziano: which I would prefer to derive in Latin from "polishing" <note>poliendo</note>. For his speech is most polished. "Which excels": it could also be said "excelleat." "Which," namely of the things mentioned before, love or erudition; since these are things of the soul, he referred it to neither <note>using the neuter gender</note> (just as I do now). "Into the same," etc., that is, conversation and social habit bringing people together.

# **On Illustrious Men**

I would wish you to be persuaded of this: that you have laid such foundations of love and duty with me that they can be ruined by no misfortune, nor torn asunder by any force. I await the most pure fruits of this bond—which are by far the most pleasing of all things to me—that is, your letters. And not only letters, but occasionally also those most delightful Muses; when they come to me, then I shall especially sing that sweetest song of Theocritus:

->May my whole house be filled with them; for neither sleep,<-

# Book of Letters. II. Folio XIX.

[Left Column]

I do not deny that laziness is the primary cause; it has always, I know not how, been my greatest delight. But nevertheless, certain small preoccupations—or rather, foolish trifles, exceedingly annoying—divide almost all my leisure among themselves, bit by bit <note>original: "scrupulatim," referring to small weights or stones</note>. For if anyone wants a brief motto to be engraved on a sword hilt or a ring's emblem; if someone wants a verse for a bed or a bedroom; if someone desires some insignia, I won't say for silver, but even for their common earthenware: immediately they run to Poliziano. You can see all the walls now smeared by me, as if by a snail, with various themes and titles. Look, one man demands witty Fescennine verses <note>ribald, improvised Roman wedding songs</note> for the Carnival; another asks for sacred discourses for assemblies; another for mournful dirges for the lute; another for licentious songs for a night-watch. That fool tells me of his own loves—to an even bigger fool. This one asks for a "symbol" <note>a private device or emblem</note> that should be clear only to his mistress, while others exercise their conjectures in vain. I pass over the untimely chattering of students, the trifles of versifiers, and those who, according to custom, admire themselves and their own works—all of which I endure daily with drooping ears. What shall I say of the common people, whether urban or rustic, who drag me by the nose through the whole city to their business like a buffalo? Therefore, while I dare to deny nothing to those who impudently insist, I am forced both to vex my other friends and (what is most annoying) to abuse the kindness of my dear Lorenzo de' Medici himself. Consequently, no room remains for me among these things for writing or composing, so that even the Priest's Office of the Hours <note>the daily required prayers</note> is cut into tiny pieces—which I believe is scarcely expiable. Finally, though I do nothing, I am never at leisure; indeed, while I am compelled to belong to everyone, I can neither be plainly my own man, nor anyone else's. Hence, if hereafter I delay or omit a response to you, know that I was immediately occupied, as is my custom, in doing trifles. Our Lorenzo de' Medici—either from your letters, which I always read to him for the sake of my honor, or from the testimony of this great Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>, who is accustomed to attribute much to you—now loves you so much that he almost competes with us. He truly rejoiced that Hermolaus himself would be an ambassador in Rome—that is, in a most visible place—even for the sake of studies. We await him so eagerly that we have almost consumed him entirely with hope. But if, once received on his journey, he hastens to depart from us, I say now, and I proclaim: woe to the man's toga, woe to his hems! <note>meaning they will grab his clothes to keep him from leaving</note>. As for the books of Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias</note> on the soul which you mention, we have none of them here at all; indeed, we suspect they do not even exist, which you will notice from the index itself that Seraticus sent to you. Rather, Pico and I ask that when you return to Venice (which they announce will be shortly), you grant Lorenzo de' Medici's librarian the opportunity to copy it. Indeed, I translated some very sharp questions on philosophy by this Alexander into Latin just last year. But Seraticus reports that you also are interpreting some works of the same writer. Then Grimani voluntarily promised that next summer he would send me another copy, which he had lent to you long ago; from which I conjecture that it might have happened by chance that we both translated the same book. If I am not reasoning falsely, I am already thinking of the sponge <note>i.e., erasing his own work in favor of the better one</note>, and I ask...

[Right Column]

"This gift of long-lived Anchises himself you shall have, a mixing bowl impressed with signs." "Impressed," he says, that is, having signs pressed into it, which is an emblem. From the Greek *emballesthai* <note>to throw in or insert</note>. I see the word was made because they are pleasant to the sight. Also, a work constructed from small tiles and elegantly variegated is called an "emblem" by the Greeks; such are many floors of houses, and likewise we have seen not a few sideboards and tables. Fescenium (as Servius says in his commentary on the seventh book of the Aeneid) is a town in Campania where wedding songs were invented. These people, however, derive their origin from the Athenians. Whence they are called Fescennine verses. <margin>Fescennine verses.</margin> Or according to Pompeius, because they think they ward off "fascinum" <note>evil spells or the evil eye</note>, they think the Fescennine song was made with itching and lascivious words. By "witticisms of the Fescennines," he therefore means lascivious songs. A "conciliabulum" is a place where a council is held, that is, as they commonly say, a congregation, a chapter, or a preaching; it is also used for the council itself. A "symbol," that is, an enigmatic motto, as we call the symbols of Pythagoras. "To her own." "Conjectures." "With drooping ears" <note>original: "dimissis curriculis," though the text likely means "demissis auriculis"</note>, that is, with the exercise of studies or the interpretation of readings set aside. For a "curriculum" is a place where one contends in a race; those things which properly belong to contests are attributed to literary matters. <margin>To lead a buffalo by the nose.</margin> "To lead a buffalo by the nose" is a proverb against those who are led wherever by another's will. For with a ring inserted in the top of the nostril, a buffalo—that is, a wild ox—is led around no differently than a horse with a bridle. Erasmus is the authority. "I am never at leisure." He alludes to the saying of Scipio, about which Cicero writes these words in the preface to the third book of *On Duties*: Cato (who was almost his contemporary) wrote that Publius Scipio, the son of Marcus, he who was first called Africanus, was accustomed to say <margin>The famous saying of Scipio.</margin> that he was never less at leisure than when at leisure, nor less alone than when he was alone. A magnificent voice indeed, worthy of a great and wise man, which declares that he thought about business even in leisure, and was accustomed to speak with himself in solitude, so that he never ceased and sometimes did not need the conversation of another. Poliziano, however, understands this sentiment thus: "Since I do nothing in serious studies, I am nevertheless never at leisure," for the common people hinder me. "Woe to the man's toga," etc., that is, I would much rather not have seen him. For the departure of friends is heavier than the longing for them. "Woe" is an imprecatory interjection. The "lacinia" is the extreme part of the toga. He mentions the toga and the hem so that he does not seem to call down a curse upon his friend. Poliziano translated the *Problems* of Alexander of Aphrodisias, that is, his questions, into Latin. "The sponge," that is, the deletion of those things which I have done. We write more concerning the sponge and its function in our commentaries on Ausonius's *Gryphon*. "Of the file," that is, of emendation.
ASCENSIUS <note>The printer/editor Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note>.
"Scripulatim" (I found it written thus, but I think it should be written "scrypulatim"; for 'y' and 'u' have much affinity). That is, minutely, as if by *scrypula* or *scrypuli* <note>scruples</note>, three of which make a drachma according to Priscian. Pliny uses this adverb in Book 22: "To collect and mix powers by scruples is not a work of human conjecture but of impudence." "Woe to the man's toga," because we shall hold him by it so that if he prefers to go, it will be utterly torn; and I understand the same regarding the hems. Nor do I think he would not want to have seen him. "I think of the sponge." Drawn, I believe, from the witty laugh of Augustus, who, when he had written a tragedy about Ajax and regretted it, being asked what Ajax was doing, replied that he had "fallen upon the sponge" <note>a pun on Ajax falling on his sword; the sponge erases the ink</note>. It is well known that painters and writers delete from tablets things that displease them with a sponge.

### Franciscus Sylvius on the Third Book of Letters of Angelo Poliziano.
[Decorative initial H] That Homeric Hero, etc. To Achilles, angry on account of the seizure of Briseis and refusing to fight with the Trojans, Agamemnon sends three heroes: Nestor, Ulysses, and Phoenix, the tutor of Achilles: so that they might reconcile Achilles to him by the offering of many gifts. When the envoys attempted this in vain, Achilles replied nearly to this effect: "What has been determined for me," he said, "can in no way be revoked. And lest anyone should perhaps think I speak otherwise than I feel: that race of men who have one thing shut in their breast and another ready on their tongue <margin>One thing in the breast, etc.</margin> is as hateful to me as the very gates of hell." In the fourteenth book of the *Odyssey* by the same author, Ulysses says: "I hate that man like the gates of hell who tells lies for the sake of poverty." **To push a stroke** <note>Latin: *palpum obtrudere*</note>, that is, to stroke or flatter. For a "palp" is an enticement. Persius in his fifth Satire: "Does that man have mastery of himself, whom white-robed ambition leads gaping with a stroke?" "Palpatio" is used for "palpo." Plautus in the *Menaechmi*: "Away with your strokings." "Palpo" and "palpor" (for both are used) mean to flatter and to ensnare with flatteries. Plautus in the *Poenulus*: "Flatter him, stroke him." Lucilius, as found in Marcellus: "When he sees me here, he fawns, he strokes, he scratches my head." Thence comes "palpator" (a flatterer). Plautus in the *Menaechmi*: "Pleasure-seekers and great drinkers, then swindlers and many flatterers dwell in this city." Erasmus <note>Desiderius Erasmus, the great humanist scholar</note> supposes the reasoning for this proverb, "to push a stroke" or "to strike with a stroke," was made by grooms who soothe horses with the clapping of the hand. Horace in the *Satires*: "Who, if you stroke him clumsily, kicks back, safe on all sides." **Naevian Hector.** Since no books of the poet Naevius have fallen into our hands, we still seek who it was that praised Hector. **Marketable rather than for sale.** <margin>Marketable and For Sale.</margin> They think "marketable" and "for sale" are distinguished thus: that "marketable" is that which easily attracts a buyer, even if the owner does not wish to sell. "For sale," however, is whatever is exposed in order to be sold. "Whatever praise you have added," that is, placed upon, "will accrue to you." He alludes to the lot of slaves. For slaves, whatever they acquire beyond their personal allowance, they acquire for their master. **I am in your debt.** <margin>I am in your debt.</margin> This is a proverbial sentiment, meaning: I am bound to you, I am in your service. For before the use of silver and gold, all money was bronze <note>Latin: *aes*, hence the phrase "in tuo aere"</note>; from which the treasury was called the *aerarium*. **Caskets** and by diminution **small cases** are minor boxes made of wood, ivory, or other things, in which coins are kept. <margin>Caskets.</margin> Whence many thought the word "wealthy" <note>Latin: *locuples*</note> was derived. <margin>Wealthy.</margin> However, Pompeius Festus supposes a wealthy man is one said to be rich in many places. Pliny explains the words of Pompeius; for he says in the third chapter of the eighteenth book: "They called those 'wealthy' who were full of places, that is, fields."
**ASCENSIUS.** "More friendly than truly." This manner of speaking has grown strong and was not avoided even by Valerius Maximus: by which, in order to join equal grades, he places a comparative between two preparatives, although the matter itself seems to require an absolute after the latter. For if we resolve "more friendly" by saying "in a more friendly way," we would not add "than more truly" but "than truly." Let those who dreamed of forming "friendlier" be gone. **Deceptions**, that is, as if by a binding and illusion or a catching of the senses. **With Naevian Hector**, who is frequently cited by Cicero, especially in his letters, and by Valla in the preface to the first book of *Elegancies*.

# BOOK THREE.
### Angelo Poliziano to his friend Callimachus, Greetings.
### Letter I.

[Decorative initial T] Although I see that what you feel and proclaim about me is much more friendly than it is true: both in what is felt and what is proclaimed: nevertheless I rejoice that those things are attributed to me by you which I myself do not recognize in me at all. For why should I not rejoice that I gain that feeling and proclamation of yours even by a certain deception of the senses? For it is not at all doubtful to me that you have persuaded yourself that what you write is even true; since you are not of that brand of men whom that Homeric Hero confirms he hates so greatly—having one thing ready on the tongue and another shut in the breast—nor is there any cause why Callimachus should seek to "push a stroke" upon Politian. Therefore you do not deceive me, but you are more deceived by yourself. And yet you are not deceived: you feel truly, you proclaim truly of me. Congratulate yourself, therefore, on your judgment of us, and hold fast to that opinion forever, provided you maintain your love and benevolence; indeed, praise me also as you have begun, so that I, that "praised man," may rejoice to be "praised by a praised man" along with Naevian Hector. Furthermore, with you as my praiser, I am marketable rather than for sale. For I am never going to change my master. Therefore, whatever you have added to me will accrue to you. For I am indeed in your debt; whence perhaps you sent those little cases from there all the way to me, and they are pleasing, namely because they are festive, because they are yours; but I do not give thanks: for you yourself received the benefit by giving it: not because you gave to one worthy, but because you gave to your own—indeed to yourself, for a friend is a second self—and for that reason you gave to one worthy, that is, to Callimachus himself. Farewell.

### FRANC. SYLVIVS.
**You will have intercepted.** That is, you will have taken away. **It is not enough to have seen, etc.** Virgil in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*: "Nor is it enough to have seen him once; it pleases them to delay long, and to keep pace, and to learn the causes of his coming." **Most unworthy of the title.** For a rustic speech is called uncultivated <margin>Rustic speech.</margin> and barbarian. Aulus Gellius in the sixth chapter of the thirteenth book: "When we now say someone speaks 'barbarously,' that vice of speech is not barbarian, but rustic; and those speaking with that vice, they used to say spoke 'rustically'."
**ASCENSIUS.** **You intercept from me.** That is, when I prepared to respond while reading the beginning, you, having been substituted, responded the same thing I wished, and you intercepted my faculty of responding. For when you said, "you are deceived by yourself," you would have wished to respond, "I am not deceived," but immediately you countered: "And yet you are not deceived," etc. **The useful with the sweet.** This refers to that Horatian line in the *Art of Poetry*: "He has won every vote who has mixed the useful with the sweet." **Your Rustic.** <margin>Your Rustic</margin> This refers to the appearance or a proper name, not to the type: just as Politian himself said "Our Rusticus" in the feminine gender, as the Comic poet called his play *The Eunuch*. Callimachus, however, follows that line of Juvenal: "Orestes, written even on the back and not yet finished," when he speaks of tragedy.

...than by whom you are cherished with greater either goodwill or respect. F.S. Lynceus. That is, most sharp in the foresight of the eyes. For Lynceus is named by Strabo as the son of Aphareus <note>The OCR "Sohno" is likely a corruption of "Aphareo"</note>; according to the same author, he excelled greatly in sight: whom Varro declares could see for thirty-five miles: and that he was accustomed, when leaving Carthage, to clearly note the Punic fleet and the number of ships from the watchtower of Lilybaeum. <margin>Lynceus.</margin> Cicero relates that the entire *Iliad* was written by him so finely on parchment that it could be enclosed in a walnut shell. Erasmus writes that Lynceus was so sharp-sighted that he even penetrated the earth itself with the sharpness of his eyes, and perceived what was happening among those in the underworld. It is commonly believed that Lynceus's vision was named after the Lynx beast (into which Ovid, in the fifth book of the *Metamorphoses*, feigns that Lyncus, the king of Scythia, was transformed). <margin>Lynx.</margin> Therefore, "a Lynceus" is said proverbially of one who is most keen-sighted: just as "Blind Tiresias" is one whose sight is quite dull. <margin>Tiresias.</margin> Concerning the position of the human heart, etc. We remembered that Momus is the god of fault-finding. Lucian (as found in Erasmus) relates in his book on heirs that Minerva, Neptune, and Vulcan contended among themselves for the leadership in craftsmanship; and so that each might produce a certain chief specimen of his art, Neptune fashioned a certain bull; Minerva devised a house; and Vulcan composed a man. <margin>Momus.</margin> Momus was chosen as the arbiter of the contest and the evaluator of the art. Having inspected the work of each, besides other things which he blamed in the works of the others, he noted this especially in the craftsmanship of the man: that the artisan had not added windows or little doors in the breast, so that it could be seen what lay hidden in the heart; which he had fashioned as a hollow place, winding with many recesses. Therefore, "He who [fears] the judgment of Momus," etc. That is, sincere love is so sharp-eyed that it easily discerns what is inside the heart, just as if the breast were windowed. He does not, therefore, wish for that judgment of Momus. "Each is a large enough theater for the other." That is, mutual friendship is easily enough observed and known. For *theatron* is the Greek word for a spectacle. "At hand." That is, in readiness. "Examination." That is, judgment. A "Love-charm" <margin>Love-charm.</margin> is a certain poison or medicine by which we compel others to love us, which is called a *philtron* by the Greeks. <margin>Philtron.</margin> I confess I have not read what the "Love-charms of Hecato" might be. "Against one's will." <note>original: "Ingratis"</note> That is, unwillingly. Plautus in the *Amphitryon*: "He roused them from the harbor at this time of night against their will." Moreover, *ingratis* is an adverb, meaning "unwillingly." <margin>Against one's will.</margin> *Didaktra* from the verb *didasko*, that is, "I teach": these are the rewards for teaching, which Politian writes at length are called "Minerval fees" in the twenty-first chapter of his *Miscellanea*. <margin>To return love for love.</margin> *Antipelargein* among the Greeks is to repay a mutual turn of duty: especially the nourishing and cherishing of those by whom you were once nourished or instructed. As if children should in turn feed and cherish parents weary with age; or if a disciple should in turn instruct a teacher. It is taken from the nature of the Stork, which in Greek is called *pelargos*. These things are from Erasmus. Moreover, Storks, as Pliny says in chapter 23 of the tenth book, in turn support the old age of their parents. Aristotle in chapter 13 of the [ninth] book... <margin>Stork.</margin>

# LXX. **Of Illustrious Men**

Angelo Poliziano <note>Poliziano (1454–1494) was a leading Italian humanist scholar and poet of the Renaissance.</note> sends greetings to his friend Lodovico Odasio.
Letter IV.

Your letter caught me in the middle of my literary work; therefore, having read it, I set it aside for a little while for the present, intending to examine it more diligently at my leisure and to respond to it, as was fitting, as soon as I was able. If this happens later than either you endure or I would have wished, it is nevertheless a mark of your kindness to take whatever we do in good part. For we do not require some small service from one another so much as we require the spirit itself; nor indeed is a man immediately lacking in love because he is lacking in formal duty. For which reason I do not even strongly approve of that point in your letter: that you excuse yourself so scrupulously for why you either wrote nothing to me before, or why you have only now finally written. For if we love one another from the soul (as we certainly do), whatever is convenient for one is surely convenient for both. Therefore, neither silence can dissolve nor can it weary our wills, which are bound together as if by a Herculean knot <note>original: "nodo Herculaneo"; a proverbial expression for an unbreakable bond.</note>; or rather...

Aeneid, Book I. *Ambrosial*: which refers to the hair that breathed a divine fragrance from the crown of the head. *Ambrosial* (says Servius <note>Maurus Servius Honoratus, a 4th-century grammarian famous for his commentary on Virgil</note>) means either divine, or anointed with ambrosia. *With the spices of the myrothecium*, that is, with the ointments which are preserved in a *myrothecium*. **Letters Book III. Folio XXIII.**

by the restored intimacy of such a charming youth: which I shall even envy for a little while, until I come into the embrace of you both. **F.S.** <note>Likely the commentator Franciscus Sylvius</note> *Sketched out.* That is, denoted with lines. The metaphor is drawn from painters, who first mark out their images with outlines. *I bore the latter and I shall bear the former.* They use this form of speech in the same way as "I sell or buy for more or less." *I bore the latter.* That is, I allowed myself <margin>I bore the latter, and I shall bear the former.</margin> to be the inferior. For you were the first. Terence in *The Brothers*: "I also demand to be loved and highly valued by my people; if that happens through giving and complying, I shall not bear the latter part." *I shall not bear the latter* (says Donatus <note>A famous 4th-century grammarian</note>)—understand "parts," or "I shall not make little of it." That is, I shall not be outdone by Mition. It is a metaphor from the parts of actors in a play. *I shall not bear the latter, therefore.* That is, I shall be first in giving and complying. This is from Donatus. However, I think nothing needs to be understood as missing, but rather I consider it spoken for the sake of the genitive case.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer and commentator</note> *In his own name:* by his own merit, for his own sake. *Not so much in his own.* Namely, in the name of letters. *I had heard a rumor.* That is, inwardly; that is, so that I might know it inwardly as if "under the skin," I had heard it. *Sketched out:* this is what they call "drawn forth." *Of the former*—understand "parts," as Donatus rightly says. Nor is the expression similar to "I sell or buy for more." For he does not mean to say "I bore," that is, "I valued as the latter" (meaning of less value), but "I bore," that is, "I acted or carried or took away the parts of the latter," that is, of him who acts later, etc. Or "the parts of the latter" in the same case.

->**Angelo Poliziano to Marcus Antonius Sabellicus. Hearty Greetings.**<-
->**Letter VIII.**<-

[Large decorative initial S] Atlas used to return in his own name formerly so welcome, that content with having received my friend, I desired no further service. But now, in the name of your letter which he faithfully delivered, he has returned so pleasant to me that I almost did not require his presence, and Atlas had something with him which was clearly more desired by me than Atlas himself. Now that same man returns to you with my letter, which I think will be pleasing to you, not so much in his own name as in the name of the carrier. I had indeed known before how much you excelled in genius and literature, and how much also in style and eloquence. Concerning your kindness, I had truly heard nothing as yet; but your letter has now *sketched it out* for me. Atlas, indeed, has expressed it with brush and colors. I was truly already lying in wait for some occasion of entering into your favor, when you, of course, anticipated me while I was doing this: not only more kind for this reason than the former, but also because the proposed reward was smaller. Therefore, I must take care that, just as in entering into friendship with you *I bore the latter part*, so in protecting and cherishing the same *I shall bear the former.* Farewell. The 6th day before the Calends of September <note>August 27th</note>, 1488.

**F.S.** *Of our poverty.* That is, of our infancy and lack of skill. He persists in the metaphor of borrowed property. *To that very man.* That is, to you. *He shall have begged.* That is, received in the manner of beggars. *Those things of yours.* For you will find that pronoun "istud" refers more often to the second person <note>the person being spoken to</note>.

**ASCENSIUS.** *What sort, finally.* Put "finally" first, and it will be a verse. *I may attempt.* Correct: for we attempt in vain.

->**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giovanni Lorenzo Venero. Greetings. Letter IX.**<-

[Large decorative initial N] Phaedrus is returning to you, a man most devoted to us both, to whom you gave a letter for me some months ago, full of love toward me, upright, elegant—the sort, in short, that could proceed from you alone. I shall respond to them as briefly as possible. You praise me, Giovanni, as if I were one of the number of the most learned men and those like yourself. You, I say, praise me—you who are by far the most learned of all whom I have seen or heard. I, therefore, although I am not ignorant of myself, nevertheless bear it most calmly, either that you yourself are deceived by too much love for us, or that you wish others likewise to be deceived. There is no reason, however, why I should attempt to return equal things. For since you have bestowed so much praise upon me—who scarcely follow a light shadow of your learning and kindness—as much as should rightly be owed to you, if I myself should attempt to return praises in turn, those very words which I had received from you as a loan would have to be restored and resigned by you: so that the clumsy ambition of our poverty might be rightly laughed at, showing off riches to that very person from whom, of course, it begged them. Your little books, and likewise those volumes which we have from that library, we shall send back as soon as our Florentine Ambassador has betaken himself there. We are waiting for Pausanias, however, when it shall be convenient for you. Farewell. At Fiesole, on the Ides of October <note>October 15th</note>, 1486.

**F.S.** *Of both of whom.* To read accurately, and to read with pleasure. I see an honest face. Smeared with the honeyed sweetness of Poliziano. *You interrupt.* That is, you hinder me and speak while I am talking so that I may not praise Poliziano, or Cortesi, or anyone else absent, as he addresses one present. *You make a noise against me.* That is, you make a noise with hands, feet, or voice against me while I am already praising Poliziano. *Away with you!* <margin>Away with you!</margin> That is, remove yourself. Plautus in *Amphitryon*: "Bah, away with you from here!" It is, moreover, a Greek word; others think it an adverb. <note>original: "απαγω"</note> *Apago* means I lead away, I drive off, I remove; it signifies when someone is led to death. *Let the shoemaker not go beyond his sandals.* <margin>Let the shoemaker not go beyond his sandal.</margin> It is a proverb signifying that judgment should not be passed on those things which are foreign to our art and profession. Pliny writes from where the reason for it originated. His words are from the tenth chapter of the thirty-fifth book, when he speaks of Apelles <note>The most famous painter of antiquity</note>. "The same man," he says, "used to display his finished works in a stall to those passing by; and hiding behind the painting itself, he would listen to the faults that were noted, preferring the common people as a more diligent judge than himself. And they say he was rebuked by a shoemaker because he had made one fewer loops on the inside of the sandals. When the same man the next day was haughtily quibbling about an emendation of the previous warning regarding the leg, the indignant artist looked out and denounced him, saying that the shoemaker should not judge above the sandal: which itself has come into a proverb." *Sandals* <margin>Sandals.</margin> are what are called *soleae* by the Latins. Aulus Gellius in chapter 20 of the thirteenth book says: "Almost all things of that kind by which only the heels of the soles are covered at the end, while the rest is nearly naked and joined by smooth straps, they called *soleae*; sometimes by the Greek word *crepidulae*." But I think the word *Gallic* <margin>Gallic shoes.</margin> is new, having begun to be used not long before the age of Marcus Cicero. Therefore, it was used by him in the second of the *Philippics*. "You ran," he says, "with Gallic shoes and a cloak." The same Gellius reports that Cicero was the only one among writers of at least serious authority to have used that word. Perhaps it is a Gallic word. For our people call them *gallociae* <note>clogs or galoshes</note> in our domestic tongue. The same author says that the makers of that footwear (which the Greeks call <note>original: "κρηπιδας"</note> *crepidas*) were called *crepidarii*. Sempronius Asellio in the 14th book of his *History* says: "He asked for a *crepidarian* knife from a *crepidarian* shoemaker." <margin>Crepidarius. What sort of shoemaker.</margin> By which you easily enough understand that he is called a shoemaker (*sutor*) who sews shoes; for he who sews clothes is called a tailor (*sartor*) by a more common word.

**Mystery.** <note>original: "Mysterium"</note> It is brought forth. As if speaking with me, that is, in secret. "In the ear" is more elegant than "to the ear." Mysteries, that is, secrets. For this is what secrets were called by the Greeks. From this, the discussion of divine matters is called "mysteries." For we write in our commentaries on the *Gryphus* of Ausonius <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius, a 4th-century Roman poet; the "Gryphus" is his poem on the number three</note> that divine matters ought to be kept secret. However, the origin of why they are called "mysteries" is a matter of doubt in Eusebius <note>Eusebius of Caesarea, a 4th-century Christian historian</note>, who suggests that mysteries were first named by idolaters. He writes to nearly this effect in chapter five of the second book of *The Preparation for the Gospel*: "Ceres," he says, "and the Good Goddess <note>original: "bona dea"</note> were a mystery; whose sorrows, abduction, and grief Eleusis teaches." Therefore, it seems to me, if one wishes to attend to the derivation of the words: from *orge* <note>original: "οργη"</note>, which in Latin is "anger," which Ceres felt against Jupiter, come the "orgies." But "mysteries" were named from *mythos* <note>original: "μυθος"</note>, which in Latin is "wickedness" <note>The author is likely confusing the Greek 'mythos' (story) with 'mysos' (pollution/crime)</note>, which happened to Dionysus. But if they also call them mysteries after that Attic man Myes, who perished while hunting, as Apollodorus wrote, then these mysteries certainly will not be something glorious, having been handed down as a kind of funeral honor. But perhaps mysteries—that is, *mytharia*—were named in Latin as if they were certain fables. Thus far Eusebius. For *mythos* is called a fable. "Four hundred years ago," etc. For nearly five hundred years, both the Latin and Greek languages lay almost dead; at which time lived Giovanni Boccaccio, a man of almost infinite reading, but who was more elegant in his mother tongue than in Latin. Encaustic ta—

<margin>Ink</margin>
**Encaustic Ink.** <note>original: "Atramentum Encaustum"</note> —bles they burned in, that is, they disgraced and contaminated those things which they wrote. For "encaustic" is that ink with which printers <note>original: "informatores"</note> stamp letters; it is so called because it is usually made from the smoke of pitch and other things burned together, as if made from combustion. The Greeks call it *enkaustikon* <note>original: "ευκαυσικον"</note>, meaning "burnt in." Likewise, "encaustic" is said to be painted by fire. For certain people used to paint and burn in the picture, which they called encaustic paintings. On this matter, see Pliny, book 35, chapter 11, and book 33, chapter 7. Domitius

**Defense of Calderini.** <note>Domizio Calderini was a 15th-century Italian humanist</note> Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a famous Renaissance scholar and rival to Calderini</note> pursues Calderini in the ninth and seventy-fifth chapters of his *Miscellanies* <note>original: "Miscellaneorum"</note> too much like a dog and with envy, in my own opinion. I confess, indeed, that Calderini erred in many things. But who can make a completely straight path in an impassable place? It is much easier to make a crooked path straight than to make a straight path where no path exists. Since, therefore, no path lay open to the Latin poets except for a very few, Domitius was the first to open it. "The others." These are the words of Crassus in the first book of Cicero's *On the Orator*. "The power of Antonius's genius," he says, "seems to be something incredible and almost singular and divine; even if it were stripped of this knowledge of the law, he could easily protect and defend himself with the other weapons of wisdom. Therefore, let him be excepted by us. But as for the others, I shall not hesitate first to condemn them for laziness in my judgment, and afterwards even for impudence." "For not everyone can be a Cato." Cicero in his book *On Old Age*: "Nor," he says, "can everyone be a Scipio or a Maximus, or a conqueror of cities, so as to remember pedestrian and naval battles, or wars waged and triumphs led by themselves." "Some," says Cicero in the first book of *On Duties*, "either by a certain good fortune, or by goodness of nature, or by the instruction of parents, have followed the right path of life." "From the city having been destroyed," etc. Dona—

**Book III of Letters. Folio XXIII.**

Lucius Phosphorus, Bishop of Segni, to Alessandro Cortesi. Greetings. **Letter X.**

[Large decorative initial P] I have read the letters of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Italian humanist and poet under the patronage of the Medici.</note>, Alessandro, most carefully and with the greatest pleasure. Both were nearly inevitable: because they were written to a very dear friend, and because they were written by a most learned man. I see an honest face—now you interrupt and make a noise. Away with you! Do you wish to know what I think? Watch what you are doing: am I able to judge? "Let the cobbler stick to his last," <note>original: *ne ultra crepidas sutor*</note> as the Greek proverb goes. Do you continue to press me? I shall answer, lest I seem proud. Remember, however, that I am speaking with an intimate friend, as if to myself. I know that judgments of this kind, even when correct, are an envious matter—let alone mine, such as they are. Receive this, therefore, into your ear like mysteries <note>original: *μυσήρια* (mysteria)</note>; take care not to announce them. I love our Poliziano exceedingly, my Alessandro, and I admire him, and I attribute all the highest qualities to him. And to speak freely what I feel: I do not think he is to be condemned any more than those are to be praised who, four hundred years ago, burned into papyrus and paper—as if stained with spots—ink-blotted tablets rather than illustrating them with any distinguished form or image. I except one or two: Lorenzo Valla <note>A famous humanist known for proving the "Donation of Constantine" was a forgery.</note>, when I was a boy, and recently Domizio Calderini. I consider it a crime and plainly impious not to praise and admire them. As for the rest, as either Antonius or Crassus says in Cicero, I shall not hesitate to condemn them for sluggishness and utter ignorance. Yet I hold them excused as well. For if the judge is fair, they provided what they were able to. For we cannot all be Catos, or Scipiones, or Laelii (as Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> says), although some (as he also says), whether by a certain happiness or by the goodness of nature, have followed the right path of life. I think it went excellently for those who attempted it in any way, even if they did not achieve it. Add to this that it is to be attributed not so much to themselves as to the times: the scarcity of good literature and teachers. For who is ignorant that ever since the city was destroyed and the empire lost—with Italy occupied by Barbarians—Roman eloquence, and indeed all literature and all arts, perished? So it pleased your Caesar <note>Likely a reference to the historical decline under the later Emperors.</note> that all these things went to ruin and were plainly lost. But at last some genius emerged, and like a fire revived from ashes and coals, it shone forth; from which these men have shone upon us like lights. Since this is so, sweetest Alessandro, let us congratulate our age; and all the more because now that pair has become an "uneven" group. I propose a riddle <note>original: *ἄἰνιγμα* (ainigma)</note> to you: I make those who were equal, unequal. Do you not understand? Why not consult Apollo? Why not the Cumaean Sibyl? Why not Ammon? Why not your Etruscans? Why not whatever soothsayers there are? But there is no need. Behold the riddle solved for you: to Lorenzo Valla and Domizio Calderini, I add Angelo Poliziano, and I create, as it were, a triumvirate. This is my opinion; this is my judgment; I whisper it into your ear. But I am free to cry it out; thus, I say, I deliver my sentence from the tribunal, and I proclaim it for all good and learned men, and indeed the whole world, to hear. "Thracians, Sarmatians, Getae, Britons, I can show you letters; come!" as the charming Poet says. You have my judgment of Poliziano, Alessandro. Nor would I wish anyone to think this is given to flattery; for I cannot win over the others, who are dead and deprived of their senses; the other <note>Poliziano</note> I do not yet know living, I confess. I vehemently desire it, and to lay such foundations of friendship that no injury of time can ever abolish them. That you may do this, our Alessandro, I ask you in a greater way, that by your introduction you make me master of my vow, and reconcile and plainly hand me over to the prince of letters. As for Poliziano himself: do you hear, most learned man (I am speaking with you), I would wish him to be asked that he does not despise what he receives from others as a favor when asked by me, so that he may respond in love and goodwill. At the same time, let him return me commended to the most famous man and leading citizen, Lorenzo de' Medici. For several years have passed since I have desired exceedingly to dedicate myself to such a great and powerful friend, and to hand myself over into his clientage and voluntary servitude. Farewell. March 13, 1485.

P.S. *Exceptam* for *scriptam*. For to "except" is to lift up a falling thing. Unless you write down the words of a speaker, they fall and perish. Socrates' *Busiris*. One should read Isocrates, not Socrates. Servius, in his interpretation of that poem of Virgil from the third book of the *Georgics*: <margin>Isocrates praised Busiris.</margin> "Or who knows not the altars of the unpraised Busiris?" Busiris (he says) was a king of Egypt who, when he sacrificed guests he had received, was killed by Hercules, when he had also wished to kill him. Isocrates wrote his praise. Thus far Servius. Libanius was a Greek rhetorician. We have mentioned Thersites elsewhere. Favorinus on the quartan fever. Aulus Gellius in chapter 12 of the seventeenth book is the authority that not only sophists, but also philosophers, undertook to write on infamous subjects—or if one prefers to say, "unexpected" subjects. <margin>Quartan fever praised by Favorinus.</margin> Favorinus spoke on those subjects quite willingly, thinking them suitable either for sharpening the intellect, or for exercising wit, or for mastering difficulties through use, just as when he sought the praises of Thersites, and when he praised the fever recurring every four days. He said many charming things, and not easy to come by, on both sides of the case, and left them written in books. But in the praises of the fever, he even produced Plato as a witness, who he says wrote: he who has recovered from a quartan fever and regained full strength will be more faithfully and constantly healthy. You may read other things there as well. Therefore, Favorinus the philosopher praised Thersites and the quartan fever. In Philostratus, book 4, a certain boastful youth says he wrote praises of gout, deafness, and blindness. Polycrates likewise praised Busiris, as Erasmus writes in the preface to the *Praise of Folly*; Glaucus praised injustice; Synesius, baldness; Lucian, the fly and the parasite. Stratocles, just as if he had received news of a victory in a well-managed affair, reported and persuaded that a public thanksgiving to the immortal gods be decreed. Not long after, a messenger arrived with certain news of a defeat; for which the people (as was right) bore Stratocles' deed with indignation. Stratocles asked them one by one whether he had caused any loss, since for three whole days they had been affected by joy and good opinion. Plutarch is the authority in his *Politics*. In the *Life of Demetrius*, he records almost the same sentiment: that the Athenians were defeated in a naval battle near Amorgos, yet those in the city lived for two days in pleasure. *Pendimus*, that is, we estimate. "No more than," etc. This is derived from Aulus Gellius. His words are from the sixteenth chapter of the thirteenth book: "Those who made Latin words," he says, "and those who used them properly, did not wish 'humanity' (*humanitas*) to be what the common people think, and what is called *philanthropia* by the Greeks—even if it signifies a certain benevolent dexterity..."

**Book of Letters. Book III. Folio XXVI.**

You said those letters were mine: so that you might examine them more easily. **The mask.** <note>Latin: *persona*</note> We spoke of the mask previously. Here, however, he alludes to the mimes: who performed with gestures on stage while wearing masks. **You will have fulfilled.** i.e., you will fulfill. **You play.** You mock. From which we get "mockery." <note>Latin: *ludibrium*</note> **Which you produce** etc. You who write in such a hurried tumult, yet so precisely: that one who had premeditated could scarcely write more exactly. **If you dwell with yourself.** <margin>Dwell with yourself</margin> i.e., if you know what is truly suitable for you: if you are not ignorant of your own nature: if you know yourself: if you descend into your own soul: if you have not sought yourself outside of yourself: or if you are adorned with letters just as you are. This is a Persian phrase from Satire IV: *Dwell with yourself so you may know how short your household furnishings are.* <note>A reference to Persius, Satire 4.52, meaning "know your own limitations."</note> Erasmus, however, turns this toward a different meaning. Let them live (he says) at your own home: so that you may understand how slender your fortune is. He thinks this is a metaphor taken from those who live in the households of princes: and as commonly happens, they swell up with the wealth of others as if it were their own: but if they had to live at home, they would scarcely have a salt-cellar to set on the table. **A great [theater] for you** etc. i.e., when you are alone, the Muses will be with you: in whatever crowd of people you may be, you will think of the Muses and literature: and thus you will consider yourself to be as if in solitude. **That having been interrupted.** i.e., though the frequent sending of letters be interrupted, our love shall not be diminished.

->**ASCENSIUS**<- <note>Referring to the commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius.</note>

**For [all things] are common** etc. <note>original Greek: *κοινα γαρ*</note> i.e., for the things of friends are common: "all things" is understood. **You will have fulfilled.** This seems to be placed in its own mood, for the order is: just as I shall have fulfilled (if I am able, it is understood) this triumvirate of friends: so you will have rightfully fulfilled (if you wish) that triumvirate of men of letters: instead of "of letters." But I suspect the printer, even Aldus, made an error. For if he had meant "of letters," he would also have said "of friendships."

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Lucio Phosphoro, Bishop of Segni, Greetings. Letter XIII.**

My friend Alexander did no wrong in sending me the letter that was owed to me. He would have sinned more—a crime expiable by no sacrificial victim—if he had begrudged me those praises of me. Although those are not my praises, but rather yours; and for that reason, they are also mine. **For the things of friends are common.** <note>original Greek: *κοινα γαρ τα τῶν φιλων*</note> But you, having borrowed a mask from us, have brought your own self onto the stage. For just as I gladly fulfill this triumvirate of friends, so you rightfully fulfill that triumvirate of men of letters. As for your complaint that those letters were written with too little care: either you are mocking me, or you are the most fortunate of all men, who can produce from the surface of your mind what hardly anyone else could produce from the depths of their heart. There is no reason for you to long for the city while in the country, or the country while in the city: if you dwell with yourself: if wherever you go, you follow yourself: you will find a great theater for yourself in any solitude, and you will create a great solitude in any theater. Furthermore, the duty of letters which you require, I promise on this condition: that you in turn promise that even if that duty is interrupted (when circumstances require it), no loss of love shall occur between us. For I am sometimes so distracted and busy that it is not permitted to write: sometimes so sad and weary that I have no desire to write. You, therefore (as the old saying goes), should know your friend's faults, not hate them. Farewell.

F.S. **They speak against.** i.e.

# 24. Of Illustrious Men

It was necessary to consider—though perhaps less aptly—whether anyone can be truly learned unless they are also eloquent. This point was not introduced without reason, for many claim learning for themselves without possessing eloquence; on the other hand, those who are truly eloquent without being learned are either few or non-existent. For eloquence is not acquired without great judgment, provided we distinguish the truly eloquent from the merely fluent <note>original: "facundis"</note> and the talkative. I said "few" because if eloquence could not be possessed without wisdom, Cicero would not have called it "dangerous" <note>A reference to Cicero's *De Inventione*, where he argues that eloquence without wisdom is a threat to the state.</note>. Nevertheless, although I might concede that it can be held without wisdom (which is a virtue), it certainly cannot be held without much learning. I would even say "not unless" <note>original: "pro nisi dicerē q̄ nō"</note> rather than "except." 

### Assertions regarding Aesop
Sylvius <note>Likely referring to the humanist scholar Aeneas Silvius Piccolomini, later Pope Pius II.</note> asserts many learned things concerning Aesop, but what is relevant to the matter is also a common story among the people. For when he was put up for sale with other slaves, and a buyer asked an elegant slave what he knew, he replied: "Everything that is fitting for a free man to know." Then, when he asked Aesop what *he* knew...

Locus Studendi <note>Latin: "A Place for Study"</note> [handwritten]

# Book of Letters. III. Folio XXVII.

and from these they melted down vessels. The author is Plutarch in his *Political Precepts*. The same author writes more copiously on this in the *Life of Demosthenes*. However, regarding that judgment of Demosthenes' speech "smelling of the lamp," he ascribes it to Pytheas, not Demadrus. Pytheas (he says) was accustomed to say that the speech of Demosthenes smelled of the lamp, being composed with exquisite and curious refinement, with long periods, exactly according to the rule and the plumb-line. The same author relates in what sense this was said, writing in the *Life of Demosthenes* to this effect: It was not easy (he says) to find anyone who had heard Demosthenes speaking off the cuff; it was well known that even when often called by name by the people while sitting in the assembly, he refused to stand up unless he had already meditated on the matter about which he was to speak. Certain other famous men of that time mocked this. And Pytheas once said that Demosthenes' <term>enthymemes</term> <note>rhetorical arguments based on a syllogism</note> smelled of the lamp. To him, Demosthenes replied with no small amount of bitter mockery: that his lamp and Pytheas's did not serve the same purpose. "To smell of the lamp" [Marginal note: To smell of the lamp.] is a proverb concerning a matter that has been meditated upon and worked out with much study. From this, it became a custom that those who studiously keep watch by the lamp are said to work elaborately if they wish to forge something more accurately. Erasmus relates that this was cast as a slur against Demosthenes: that he said everything at home having premeditated it. Concerning him, that famous eulogy was also celebrated: that he consumed more oil than wine. Demosthenes (as Plutarch says in the book *On the Education of Children*), when summoned by the people to give counsel, resisted. "For I am not prepared," he replied. Pericles likewise, often called by the people to speak, used to say he was unprepared. For the nighttime is much more fit [Marginal note: Studying at night.] and accommodating for the study of letters than the daytime. For as Saint Jerome writes in his letter to the brothers on the holiness of vigils: during the day, various necessities make a noise; occupations distract the mind; a double care disperses the senses. A quiet night, a secret night, offers itself opportunely for prayers; it is most fit for those keeping watch, while it presents the senses—freed and collected from fleshly occupations—to divine sight. Therefore, by keeping watch, all fear is excluded; confidence is born; the flesh is wasted away; vices wither; charity is strengthened; foolishness recedes; prudence approaches; the mind is sharpened; error is blunted; and the devil, the head of crimes, is wounded by the sword of the spirit. Saint Jerome prudently records many other things of this kind concerning the night vigil and nocturnal prayer. Philostratus writes in his third book that the nighttime is more accommodating for taking counsel. Likewise, with Aristotle as the author in the sixth chapter of the first book of *Economics*, rising before dawn is most beneficial for health, for the care of the household, and for the study of philosophy. From this, "to work by the lamp of Aristophanes and Cleanthes" became a common proverb when we say someone weighs every single thing with the greatest study and care. Also against Ctesiphon, etc. An accusation was driven against Ctesiphon; no public trial was more famous, both because of the excellence of the orators and because of the magnanimity of the judges, who in no way gratified the adversaries of Demosthenes (for Demosthenes was the patron of Ctesiphon), who were most powerful in the republic at that time. Instead, they acquitted him so remarkably that the accuser Aeschines did not even carry a fifth part of the votes. Aeschines, therefore, cast into exile, taught rhetoric around Rhodes and Ionia. These things are from Plutarch in the *Life of Demosthenes*. Then, with Valerius as the author in Book VIII under the title "On Pronunciation," Aeschines was asked by the Rhodians to recite first his own speech against Ctesiphon, and then that of Demosthenes for the same man. When he had done this with a very clear and sweet voice, while everyone was admiring the eloquence of both pillars of oratory, but somewhat more that of Demosthenes, he said: "What if you had heard the man himself?" So great an orator, and just now such a hostile adversary, so respected the force and fire of his enemy that he proclaimed himself an inadequate reader of the writings. Thus Aeschines praises Demosthenes. But Politian here adheres to the opinion of those who say Aeschines replied to the Rhodians: "What if you had heard the beast himself bellowing with his own voice?" To this, bloodless and worn out, etc. Marcus Tullius Cicero, when he had devoted himself entirely to the imitation of the Greeks, expressed the force of Demosthenes, the abundance of Plato, and the [Marginal note: Praise of Cicero.] pleasantness of Isocrates, as Quintilian writes in the tenth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*. Yet (as the same author records in the final book), men of his own times dared to attack him as being too tumid, and "Asian," and redundant, and excessive in his petitions, and sometimes cold in his wit, and broken in his composition, exultant, and almost (far be it!) softer than a man. But after he was consumed by the triumviral proscription, those who hated him, those who envied him, those who emulated him, and even flatterers of the present power everywhere invaded a man who would not answer back. Yet he, who is held by some to be meager and dry, could be criticized by his enemies for nothing other than excessive "flowers" and an affluence of genius. Both charges are false, but the latter is closer to a plausible lie. Especially, however, those who desired to be seen as imitators of the "Attic" style preferred him. This hand, as if initiated into certain sacred rites, pursued him as a foreigner, a superstitious man, and one bound by those laws. Whence even now they are dry, and juiceless, and bloodless. For these are the ones who hold out the name of "health" (which is the exact opposite) for their own weakness; because they cannot bear the brighter force of eloquence like the sun, they hide in the shadow of a great name. These are the words of Fabius <note>Quintilian</note>. Rufus (as Merula says) called Cicero overflowing and talkative, and called him an "Allobrogian"; Brutus called him spineless and soft; Calvus called him thin and bloodless. [Marginal note: Calvus Licinius.] Crinitus writes in his second book on the Latin Poets that Calvus Licinius had a dispute with Marcus Cicero concerning the leadership of eloquence. [Marginal note: L. Brutus.] Lucius Brutus was a Latin orator in whom Cicero records there was much gravity in the first book of *Offices*. "Titles," that is, praises or the numbers of praises. For on the statues of those whose statues they were, the titles of their virtue were written. "Until now," that is, to this day. "To be ascribed," that is, to be given. "Danger" <note>original: "periculum"</note>, that is, experience.

ASCENSIUS <note>The printer/editor Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note>

I have perceived all. In Virgil, one reads "I have anticipated" <note>original: "praecepi"</note>; and I think Angelo wrote it thus. "Wheaten bread" <note>original: "siligineus panis"</note> is made from the flower of wheat, though there are those who think winter wheat is inferior to common wheat. "I claim" <note>original: "vindico"</note>: so the ancients wrote; now one writes "vendico" for it, just as "penna" for "pinna." "These are of envy," etc., a whole verse. "Danger" <note>original: "periculum"</note>: a testament.

Angelo Politian to Lucio Phosphoro, Bishop of Segni, greetings. 15th.

[Large decorative P] You are angry at our detractors, most learned Phosphoro, because they say in my *Miscellanies* I speak "monsters of words," and while they admit I am a learned man (as you say), they deny I am eloquent. Then they also charge that I have heaped such great praises upon Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note> alone that I have left absolutely none for others. Truly, Phosphoro, these things do not move me; for no news of such talk reaches me, nor does it arise unexpectedly. I have perceived all, and I have already gone over it in my mind. Indeed, I would not even respond to them unless I felt you wished it so, to whom I can deny nothing. Therefore, as for the "monsters of words" which those men call out: I confess I am ignorant of them, unless they believe they are monsters because they themselves now for the first time either hear or understand words that are like owls <note>original: "notua," perhaps meaning rare or night-words</note>. For I have neither given birth to any words unheard by the ancient Cethegi, nor do I have any authors except the most accepted ones. Yet I am not of the number of those who allow the Latin language to cease for the most part, while each person shrinks from those things which have been generally unknown until now. Indeed, things have come to such a pass that we do not even speak safely in the language of the great authors, because it is less known to the common crowd. Therefore, we prefer to use barbarian words rather than Roman ones; and while there is wheaten bread at home, we eat begged-for bran instead. But as for their taking away my eloquence while granting me learning: I am not only not angry, but I even give thanks. Do not, I pray, indulge too much in your love for me, Phosphoro, nor...

D.iii.

**Of Illustrious Men**

You might think I am being praised if I were lauded after the example of Marcus Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar often called "the most learned of the Romans."</note>: whom the ancients themselves believed possessed much knowledge, but no eloquence. If, however, in these *Miscellanies*, I appear to someone to be even slightly knowledgeable—even without eloquence—it is well. I have won. For that was exactly what I was seeking. Of what use is eloquence to me in this work, which is prepared not for persuasion, but for teaching? 

Furthermore, regarding what you write about my style: I certainly think it is true that a work is not immediately worse because it varies, since eloquence itself does not have a single face or a single color. For this reason, no one has yet been considered eloquent by a unanimous vote; either because each person pleases himself above all others, or because different forms of speaking captivate different people more. Consider Demosthenes and Cicero. To some, the speech of the former was dry; to Demades it seemed to smell of the lamp <note>original: "lucernam olere" – a common idiom meaning a work was over-studied or labored over at night.</note>; to Aeschines (if the gods please!) it even seemed barbaric. Calvus called the latter [Cicero] bloodless and worn out; Brutus called him broken and weak; others called him meager and...
