# **Of Illustrious Men**

<note>The author is discussing the Greek statesman Alcibiades</note> He preferred to respond according to the occasion <note>original: "ex tempore"</note>. Furthermore, Theophrastus records on the same authority that Alcibiades, while speaking, was accustomed to seek out not only what he should say, but also in what style of speech and, finally, in what manner those things ought to be said by him. For this reason, he was frequently observed to hesitate over his subject matter and to stumble in the very course of his oration. On that account, Pericles—on whose lips we used to say Peitho <note>The Greek goddess of persuasion</note> sat—was accustomed to pray and make vows before his speech began, lest any word should come into his mind which might seem somewhat foreign to the matters at hand.

Wherefore the same Plutarch learnedly teaches in his book *On the Education of Children* that one must take care that boys do not speak extemporaneously. For that which is said or done without counsel and rashly cannot be beautiful. And as the proverb goes, "Honorable things are difficult." For there is no weight in extemporaneous oratory, and no end coheres with the beginning; wandering and straggling loquacity is never absent from it.

**"Do you, a maiden, dare to clash with men?"**
<note>original: "Audesq; viris concurrere virgo"</note>
This is a half-line of Virgil's from the first book of the *Aeneid*.

**Book of Letters. III. Folio XXIX.**

Those souls which have been released from the bonds of the body, and have fulfilled the duty of life—which is a general term applicable to all souls—are categorized as follows. From these spirits, the one who has obtained the care of his descendants and possesses the home with a peaceful and quiet divinity is called the **Household Lar** <note>The Lares were ancient Roman guardian deities of the home and fields</note>. However, he who, on account of the adversities of a life of vice, is received into no good dwellings, but is punished by wandering as if in a kind of exile, is a vain terror to the good and harmful to the wicked; most people call this one a **Larva** <note>A malevolent spirit or ghost in Roman mythology</note>. Since it is uncertain which lot has fallen to each—whether one is a *Lar* or a *Larva*—they are addressed by the name **Manes God** <note>The Manes were the collective spirits of the dead, often treated as divine</note>, and the title of "god" is added as a mark of honor. "Among the first," that is, from the foremost. "A man of the first rank," that is, a **Primipilus** <note>The highest-ranking centurion in a Roman legion</note> and a leader; this is a metaphor transferred from military matters to literary ones. Furthermore, the **Pilum** <margin>The Javelin</margin> <note>original: "Pilum"</note> is so named from "perishing" <note>Latin: *perimendo*</note>, as if it were "perillum" (as Varro prefers in the first book of *On the Latin Language*). The missiles used by the infantry army are called *pila*.

This was done at the villa of the Caesars situated on the Tiber River near the ninth milestone of the Flaminian Way, which for that reason is called "At the Hens" <note>Latin: *ad gallinas*. This refers to the Villa of Livia, where legend says an eagle dropped a white hen holding a laurel sprig into Livia's lap</note>; and the grove grew marvelously. From that grove, Caesar, when triumphing thereafter, held a laurel in his hand and wore a crown upon his head; and subsequently, all the Caesar emperors did the same. It became an established custom to plant the branches they had held. It is recorded that upon the death of each Caesar, the tree planted by him withered away; and in the final year of Nero, the entire grove, along with all the hens, perished. Suetonius records this in his *Life of the Emperor Galba*. Regarding his authority, etc.—that is, because his authority is so great among all people—even the things he said incorrectly are believed as if they were true.

"A snake lurks in the grass" <note>Latin: *Anguis in herba latet*</note> is a proverb applied to those things which appear beautiful, sweet, pleasant, and delightful on the outside, yet contain some harm within. Such is that line from Ovid: "Poisons lie hidden beneath the honey." <note>Latin: *Latent sub melle venena*</note> Virgil says in the *Bucolics*: "You who gather flowers and strawberries growing on the ground..."

**Book of Letters. III. Folio XXX.**

<meta>This page continues a discussion on literary criticism and the reputation of ancient authors, specifically focusing on the Greek tragedian Aeschylus before transitioning into a letter from Angelo Poliziano to Jacopo Antiquario.</meta>

Who indeed has ever moderated their criticism of Plato or Socrates? Take Aeschylus, the greatest of tragedy. Aeschylus (as Quintilian writes in the tenth book of his *Institutes of Oratory* <note>A foundational Roman textbook on rhetoric</note>) is sublime, grave, and grandiloquent, often even to a fault; but he is unrefined in many places and disorganized. Because of this, the Athenians permitted later poets to bring his corrected plays into competition. In this way, many were crowned with laurel. He was the first to bring tragedies into the light. According to Volaterranus <note>Raffaele Maffei, a contemporary humanist scholar</note>, it was his fate to die by a blow coming from above. Therefore, having left the walls of the city in Sicily where he was living, he sat down in a sunny spot. An eagle carrying a tortoise was deceived by the brightness of his head (for it was bald) and dropped it on him as if onto a stone, so that it might eat the meat of the broken tortoise. By that blow, the origin and beginning of the stronger tragedy was extinguished. The author of this story is Valerius <note>Valerius Maximus</note> in his ninth book, under the title "On Unusual Deaths." *Decuriatus*: that is, from a decuria <note>A division or group of ten</note>. *By no means negligently*: that is, not too negligently, but diligently. For "by no means" contains a sense of affirmation. *I have weighed*: I have examined. *With a critical scale*: that is, with a judicial examination. *It is not whole to us*: that is, it is not in our power.

<margin>Aeschylus.</margin>

*How much less I owe to myself*: I think it should be read as "I ought." *As it is agreed between me and you*, etc. The context of the words seems to require that it be struck out, or "it is agreed" should be read. *Cottidie* for *cotidie* <note>daily</note>: those who write it this way claim it is said as if for a "continuous and continued day."

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Jacopo Antiquario. Greetings. 19.**

Would that the praises you bestow upon me in your letter were as true as they are deep, proceeding no less from your judgment than from your kindness. You might then persuade me—just as I have always recognized the very weighty judgment of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," Poliziano's patron</note> regarding this letter of yours. For while that greatest of men in every walk of life defers most highly to you in his conversations, he also says he sees no one to whom you yield in letters, integrity, and prudence. I would indeed easily believe the things you write about me so heartily and, so to speak, with a "true face," and I would favor these praises as if they were entirely my own, were it not that, besides my own conscience, fame itself publicly cries out against your kindness. Therefore, I accept this entire eulogy not as something assigned to my merits, but to your character; feeling that I owe you all the more, the less I owed to myself. 

But as for what pertains to our *Miscellanea* <note>Poliziano's famous work of philological criticism</note>, either I am mistaken, or nothing in them is as fruitful as that liberty and simplicity—perhaps incautious, but nevertheless noble—which, if it proceeds less from prudence, certainly proceeds from a love of our common studies; a quality which is clearly most desired in the writers of this age. For as to why you did not wish me to "cross swords" with Domitio <note>Domizio Calderini, a rival scholar</note>, I understand indeed what you are looking at. Nor was I blind to something of that sort even then, when I took upon myself that most hateful role of the censor and affected a nearly wicked diligence, exposed to every boastful word and singsong chant. Neglecting cautions, I directed all my skill, to the best of my ability, toward repairing the losses of literature. I have always feared, however, into what part my plan might be snatched—I do not say by detractors—but how it would be received by the most prudent and cautious of men. 

And although it is altogether necessary that I agree with you—that is, with a man most friendly and learned—nevertheless, because some see things clearly in their own hearts, I shall say something to those points which you wisely and kindly object to in this part of your letter. You say one should not fight with the dead, as if with a ghost. To me, however, the opposite usually seems true; for what we pronounce against the dead is usually accepted as true, as it ought to be; whereas what is said against the living often suffers from the suspicion of hatred or envy. "But he helped the cause of literature," who would deny it? Is he not praised by me by that very name more than by anyone else, and indeed on the same page where he is also criticized? "But he would have corrected those things if he had lived longer." How should I know that? Is one always to hope for the best regarding the progress of talents? Were not his very last works his best? What if he were to become daily less at leisure due to the pursuit of honors, and more inflated by his own opinion? But suppose he would have corrected them. Shall Domitio alone, among all writers, be exempt from the censor's rod? Shall he alone be (if the gods permit) "the son of a white hen" <note>original: "Gallinae filius albae" - a Roman proverb for a lucky or privileged person</note>? Why should his name be hidden, in whose authority there is poison, lurking like a "snake in the grass" <note>original: "anguis in herba"</note> within his own commentaries? I show Domitio to students as if showing a pitfall to travelers. Nor do I seem to forget humanity; rather (as I now seem able not just to hope, but to judge with certainty), I shall deserve somewhat better of life through this censorship of mine than perhaps another does through indulgence. Add to this that it has been done by illustrious examples—unless the authority of Horace is light to anyone, who at once "cut the throats" of Ennius, Plautus, Lucilius, Dossennius, and that whole cohort of ancient poets, even while the people protested. What? Did not Aulus Gellius also run into Seneca with great freedom of words? Does not Quintilian mark the same man with a "black pebble" <note>original: "atro notat calculo" - a vote of condemnation</note>? Does not Marinus [criticize] Ptolemy—

#### Jacopo Antiquario to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. XX.

**I** wrote to you in the best faith: knowing it would be: that my letters would be received with an equal openness of mind: which deed I do not change: and I rejoice greatly that it happened just as I hoped. The excuse regarding Domitius is superfluous: against whom I think all (for so I might say) your invectives <note>original: "vehellas"</note> were undertaken by you for the public utility of students. Nor would I wish them to be pricked back by me even by the smallest word or marked with a contrary judgment. But I would have wished—which is no longer free to change once the work is published—that you had more frequently refrained from the person while you attacked the matter. However you have undertaken that study: in the manner of the best farmer: I do not doubt that you wished whatever thorns were occurring to be thoroughly rooted out from your furrows along with the roots. Nor was it necessary to apply an old example: where the present business does not lack praise. Indeed, I feel only this is lacking in your writings: that you did not live in the ancient age: with which you seem to have attained the memory of all centuries: by industry and the likeness of labor. Those who have not given this testimony were born of an unhappy and adulterous birth of the Muses. Do not, therefore, macerate us in expectation with the offspring of a long incubation: but having also accepted Pico as a sponsor for the security of your name: whose whole life is full of glories: by whom I seek with all prayers to be received into the flock of friends through you: whose footsteps I always adore: whatever is born at home from the cohort of fattened birds <note>A metaphor for Poliziano's polished literary works.</note> you should send out to be looked at, read, and learned: you who are about to hold all those in your strings: who are led by some image of virtues or harmony. Farewell. Chalcus sends you greetings: he is yours: and your Antiquarius is yours: each desires to be held as a finger of your right hand. Milan. The fifth day before the Ides of December [December 9], 1489.

<gloss>F.S. Greater than merits, that is, than I have deserved. More of a pledge etc., that is, you have praised me more and more abundantly than I can repay. Moreover, the metaphor is started from those who, contending about some matter, are accustomed to deposit pledges. Unwashed fingers. He alludes to that proverb, to touch with unwashed hands: or to enter with unwashed feet, which is to approach an excellent thing unpreparedly, unskillfully, or overconfidently.</gloss>

# **Book of Letters. III. Folio XXXII.**

->Jacopo Antiquari sends greetings to his friend Angelo Poliziano.<-

Every day, letters are brought to you in bundles from the entire assembly of the most learned men; these seem to contribute greatly to your renown. I do not know with what expression you receive them. I suspect, however, it is with a modest and familiar one. Indeed, what they write congratulates both the age and you. Meanwhile, the letter from Pomponio <note>Julius Pomponius Laetus, a prominent humanist and founder of the Roman Academy</note> delighted me exceedingly; our friend Bernardo recently handed it to me to read—a young man polished to a fine turn in your school. I desire, however, to know from you whether you claim anything for yourself from such a crowded chorus of praise from so many. For wise men—among whose opinion I judge you to be—believe that whatever good they perceive in themselves is not produced or prepared by their own labor, but is granted by the benefit of nature and of God. But truly, those who credit such things to themselves are, without a doubt, to be compared to a painted harlot <note>original: "lenæ purpurissatę"; referring to someone using artificial makeup to hide reality</note>, or to Poggio’s fable <note>A reference to Poggio Bracciolini’s "Facetiae," specifically the fable of the dung-beetle swimming with apples</note>: "We apples are swimming too." I believe that these thoughts often enter your mind—that as you hold the trail of some discovery...

[Handwritten note at top: To call to the baggage. <note>Latin: "Ad vasa conclamare." A military signal to pack up equipment.</note> afternoon]

**Of Illustrious Men**

Francis Sylvius on the fourth book of the Letters of Angelo Poliziano.

<margin>To call to the baggage.</margin> **T**he second watch of the night: that is, between the ninth hour and midnight. Regarding the division of the watches, we have written in our commentaries on the *Gryphus* of Ausonius. *As if calling to the baggage*: that is, signifying that all things must be abandoned in the highest state of desperation. *To call to the baggage* is a proverb: used when we say, in a state of extreme desperation, that everything must be carried away with us. For when a situation is brought into danger, the General orders the "shouting out": so that the soldiers themselves may gather all their vessels <note>Latin: "vasa," referring to kit, equipment, or baggage</note> and impediments, so that if they are perhaps forced to flee, they are more prepared for flight; or when the camp must be moved elsewhere. Julius Frontinus, in chapter eight of the first book of his *Stratagems*: Gaius Caesar, having learned through a certain captured water-carrier that Afranius and Petreius intended to move their camp by night, in order to hinder the enemy's plans without harassing his own men, immediately at the start of the night [ordered] the call to the baggage <margin>With the baggage collected.</margin>

The substance is found in the extreme parts of the bones, such as in the ears. Aristotle writes about the difference between cartilage <note>original: "Carthaginis," likely a printer's error for "Cartilaginis"</note> and bone in the eighth chapter of his book *On the Nature of Animals*. The term **Hypochondrium** is derived from *hypo* <note>Greek: ὑπὸ</note> meaning "under" and *chondros* <note>Greek: χόνδρος</note> meaning "cartilage"; it was also a name used by the Greeks for the internal part of the stomach. Melancholic sadness follows hypochondriac and flatulent <note>referring to "vapors" or gas in the digestive system</note> conditions, just as dementia follows an acute fever, as Galen says in the third book of *On the Affected Parts*. Although **Artery** <margin>Artery</margin> is almost always used in the feminine gender, Lucretius nevertheless used it in the neuter in his fourth book: *The cry, passing outward, makes the artery rougher.* <margin>Neuter gender</margin> Aulus Gellius, in the tenth chapter of his eighteenth book, places this difference between a **vein** and an **artery**: A **vein** (he says) is a receptacle for blood mixed and blended with natural spirit, in which there is more blood and less spirit. <margin>Vein</margin> An **artery** is a receptacle for natural spirit mixed and blended with blood, in which there is more spirit and less blood. <margin>Artery</margin> **Wasted away**—that is, consumed by wasting and thinness. Cornelius Celsus, in his third book, posits three types of **wasting**: <margin>Three types of wasting</margin> The first is what the Greeks call *atrophy*, in which the body is not nourished; since some parts are naturally always passing away and none are taking their place, extreme thinness arises, and unless it is treated, it kills. The second the Greeks call *cachexia*, where there is a bad habit of the body, and therefore all nourishment is corrupted. The third is by far the most dangerous, which the Greeks name *phthisis* <note>tuberculosis or consumption</note>. It generally begins in the head, then drips down to the lungs. Ulceration occurs here. From this, a slight fever arises, which, even when it has subsided, nevertheless returns. **He would satisfy nature**—that is, he would die. For we owe death to Nature in exchange for life. For, as Valerius says in his sixth book: *A law was declared by the nature of things for both receiving breath and returning it at the same moment of time; and just as no one is accustomed to die who has not lived, so no one can live who is not destined to die.* **First**—that is, better, and therefore to be carried out first. **Contracted harms**—that is, committed sins. For **Harm** <note>Latin: *noxa*</note> is the punishment, while **Guilt** <note>Latin: *noxia*</note> is the fault, as Cornelius Fronto says. <margin>Harm</margin>

**Book IV of the Letters. Page 34.**

He received [the last rites] with awe-inspiring majesty. Then, beginning to console his son Piero (for the others were absent), he urged him to bear the force of necessity with a steady mind. He reminded him that heavenly protection would not fail him, just as it had never failed himself amidst such great shifts of affairs and fortune, provided he cultivated virtue and a good mind; for well-considered plans would yield good results. After these words, he rested for a while in a contemplative state. Then, having dismissed the others, he called the same son back to him. He advised him on many things, commanded many things, and taught him many things which have not yet been made public. All of them, however (as we have heard), were full of both singular wisdom and holiness. One of these, which I was permitted to know, I shall record here. "The citizens," he said, "my dear Piero, will undoubtedly acknowledge you as my successor. Nor do I fear that you will lack the same authority in this republic that we ourselves have held to this day. But since every city is a body (as they say) of many heads, and one cannot cater to every individual, remember in such variety to always follow that counsel which you understand to be the most honorable; and have regard for the whole community rather than for the private interests of any individual." He also gave instructions concerning his funeral: namely, that following the example of his grandfather Cosimo <note>Cosimo de' Medici (1389–1464), the founder of the Medici political dynasty</note>, the rites should be performed for him within the modest limits that befit a private citizen. Then came Lazarus, your physician from Pavia <note>Lazzaro da Ticino, a famous doctor of the era</note>, a man of great experience (as it seemed). Having been called in late, however, and wishing to leave nothing untried, he attempted certain very costly medicines made by grinding up all kinds of gems and pearls. Lorenzo <note>Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent" (1449–1492)</note> then asked one of his servants (for some of us had been admitted) what that doctor was busy with or what he was preparing. When I replied to him that he was mixing a topical application <note>original: "epithema"</note> to warm the region of the heart, he immediately recognized my voice. Looking at me cheerfully, as was always his custom, he said, "Ho there, ho there, Angelo!" <note>The author is Angelo Poliziano, the famous humanist scholar and tutor to the Medici</note> At the same time, with his arms now exhausted of strength, he painfully raised them and grasped both my hands very tightly. When I was overcome by sobs and tears, which I tried to hide by turning my head away, he remained entirely unmoved and held onto my hands again and again. But when he perceived that I was still hindered by weeping from being able to attend to him, he gradually and as if not noticing let them go. I immediately threw myself into the inner chamber of the bedroom, weeping, and gave free rein (so to speak) to my grief and tears. Soon, however, I returned to the same spot, having dried my eyes as much as I could. When he saw me—and he saw me immediately—he called me to him again and asked very kindly what his friend Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the celebrated philosopher</note> was doing. I replied that he remained in the city, fearing that he might be a burden if he came. "But I," he said in turn, "if I did not fear that this journey would be burdensome to him, would desire to see and speak with him one last time before I depart from you entirely." "Do you wish for him to be summoned?" I asked. "I do indeed," he said, "as soon as possible." I did exactly that. He had already arrived and sat down; I also knelt beside them so that I might more easily hear my patron speaking, as his voice was now failing.

# Of Illustrious Men

<note>original: "Virozum Illuſtrium"</note>

He was inspired, a man born for all the highest things: and one who, though fortune stood still or resisted him so often, moderated himself with such alternating navigation that you would not know whether he appeared more steadfast in prosperity or more level-headed and temperate in adversity. Indeed, his genius was so great, so effortless, and so perceptive that in those individual qualities where others think it a great feat to excel, he stood out equally in all of them. For as for his integrity, justice, and faith: I believe no one is unaware that the heart and soul of **Lorenzo de' Medici** <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent" (1449–1492), the de facto ruler of the Florentine Republic and a massive patron of the Renaissance.</note> were chosen by these virtues as if for some most pleasing dwelling and temple. Furthermore, how great his courtesy, humanity, and approachability were is declared by a certain extraordinary goodwill toward him from the entire populace and clearly from all social ranks. But indeed, among all these things, his liberality and magnificence nevertheless shone forth, which had carried him forth to the very gods with a nearly immortal glory; while in the meantime, he pursued nothing merely for the sake of fame and reputation, but rather followed all things out of a love for virtue.

**Book IV of the Letters. Folio 35.**

While a preacher was delivering a sermon from the pulpit, a woman suddenly rose up from the midst of the dense crowd, terrified and dismayed. Running as if possessed <note>original: "lymphato cursu" - a frantic state attributed to water-nymphs</note> and letting out terrifying cries, she shouted, "Ho there! Citizens, do you not see this ferocious bull, who is casting down this vast temple to the ground with flaming horns?" Furthermore, during the first watch of the night, when the sky was suddenly fouled by clouds, the very peak of the great cathedral <note>The Duomo of Florence, Santa Maria del Fiore</note>—which, by a singular and marvelous work, towers over the whole world with its dome—was struck by lightning from heaven. Huge masses of stone were cast down, and enormous pieces of marble were hurled with a certain horrific force and momentum toward that specific area where the Medici palace is seen. In this event, a certain omen was not lacking: one of the gilded balls <note>The "palle" or balls were the heraldic symbol of the Medici family</note>—like the others seen on that same peak—was shaken off by the lightning bolt, so that the loss proper to that family might be foretold by their own emblem. But it is also memorable that as soon as the thunder ceased, serenity was immediately restored. Moreover, on the night that Lorenzo died, a star brighter and larger than usual was seen hanging over the villa <note>The Villa at Careggi</note> where he was spending his final moments; it appeared to fall and be extinguished at the very instant it was later discovered he had departed from life. Indeed, it is said that for three continuous nights, ghostly figures <note>original: "facies"</note> rushed down from the Fiesole mountains and were seen sparkling above the temple where the remains of the Medici clan are buried, soon after vanishing. What of the fact that a pair of the noblest lions, kept in the public cage, clashed so fiercely in combat that one was badly mauled and the other put to death? At Arezzo <margin>At Arezzo</margin> also, twin flames—like the "Castors" <note>St. Elmo's Fire, traditionally associated with the twins Castor and Pollux</note>—are said to have burned for a long time over the citadel in the plain. And a wolf repeatedly let out terrifying howls beneath the city walls. Some even interpret this as a marvel (as people’s minds are inclined to do): that the most excellent physician of this age (for so he was held), when his art and foresight had failed him, lost heart and threw himself into a well of his own accord, thus offering a sacrifice by his own death to the leader of the "Medic" <note>A pun on "Medici" (the family name) and "medicus" (physician)</note> family. But I see that, although I have kept silent about many great things lest I fall into the appearance of flattery, I have nonetheless been carried further than I had originally intended. I did so partly out of the very desire to comply with and obey you—a most excellent, learned, and prudent man, and a friend to me.

Forgive my many preoccupations, Caesar: and do not believe me to be either arrogant or neglectful of my duties because I have not replied to your letters until now. The better part of my day is worn away by various readings; the remaining effort is given to my friends. Night divides itself between rest and sleep, along with prayers, the <term>horarium</term> <note>A book of hours or a schedule for daily prayers</note>, and the pen. F.S. You write that Marianus etc. In the preface of the *Miscellanies*, Poliziano mentions him in these words: "Wherefore," he says, "your favorite seems the more admirable to me, this Marianus of Genazzano, second to none in theology, and of all those whom we have heard preaching in the <margin>Praise of Marianus of Genazzano.</margin> church, he is not only the most prudent but also the most eloquent. His eloquence is not viewed with suspicion by people striving toward good fruit <note>original: "bonam frugem," meaning spiritual improvement</note>, because it is commended by an incredible severity of life; nor, on the other hand, is his austerity gloomy or formidable, because he does not despise the charms of poetry and that beautiful variety, brilliance, and delight of literature." I recognize the **phrase** <note>original: "incisum"</note>, as the discourse is distinguished by phrases and members, just as by commas and other marks. A **phrase** (as Diomedes says in his second book) consists of single <margin>Phrase.</margin> words, as we have said: "we wished to give witnesses." "We said" is a phrase. A **member** <note>original: "membrum," a clause</note>, however, is a sense-unit, but broken off from the whole body <margin>Member.</margin> and accomplishing nothing by itself: as "O clever men" is complete in itself, but removed from the rest it has no force, just as by themselves a hand, foot, head, and other members of the body. **It would drag a tail** means it would be superfluous. **Of the churches** means of the Christian people. For *ekklesia* <note>original: "εκκλησία"</note> <margin>Church.</margin> is a gathering, a council, an assembly, a congregation. **He flees the light** means he flees eyes; that is, one who loves solitude and does not desire to be seen by others. **Conscience**, namely, a good one. For just as baseness demands darkness, so virtue demands the light; as Plutarch relates in his *Political Precepts*, when the house of Julius Drusus, a man of the people, stood exposed to view from many neighboring parts, a certain craftsman promised that for a cost of five talents he would turn it away and arrange it more privately. "I will give you ten," Julius said, "if you lay it all out so conspicuously that all the citizens, not just the neighbors, can see by what principle I live at home." Truly he was a modest and worthy man, nor perhaps did he need the transparency of such a house, since he daily gave the most learned proofs of outstanding virtue and examples of a noble life in public.

ASCENSIUS. **Behold for you then.** This "for you" is taken from the middle of common speech; it points to no specific person. For it does not point to Chalcus, who was far away. **What tail it would drag.** It is explained by Sylvius as meaning it would be superfluous, but he had put "empty" in its place. Therefore, advised by a reading of Horace, I would prefer to explain it as: nothing that would be ridiculous. For it is still the custom in Italy and in some parts of France for boys to hang a fox's tail on the backs of those they hold in derision. **Lorenzo de' Medici.** From this it is clear that the letters were not printed in the place or chronological order in which they were sent. For the second letter of this book describes his death. **Because a good conscience**: understand "is."

# Book IV of the Letters. Folio 37.

Our most diligent Pico <note>Likely referring to Gianfrancesco Pico della Mirandola, nephew of the famous philosopher</note> has delivered Lactantius to me: that is to say, he has given both to both of us. <meta>This page continues the astronomical and philological commentary on the celestial spheres, specifically focusing on the lunar orbit and the terminology of planetary motion.</meta>

# On Illustrious Men

The moon moves obliquely along the ecliptic line <note>The ecliptic is the apparent path of the sun across the sky; the moon's path crosses this at an angle.</note>. Therefore, the lunar circle intersects the solar circle. The **Ray**—that is, a stylus made of bronze or iron. In the "sign-bearer," which in Greek is called the *zodiac* <note>original: "ζωδιακος" (zodiakos)</note>. It carries the signs such as Aries, Taurus, and others of that kind, although there are other signs in the heavens. For Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author of an influential encyclopedia on the seven liberal arts.</note> says in his eighth book that the entire sky shines with thirty-five signs. Of the moon itself—namely, on its **edge** <margin>Edge</margin>—that is, on its extremity and surface. For an "edge" <note>original: "limbus"</note> is that which is sewn onto the outermost part of a garment for the sake of ornament. Virgil says in the first book of the *Aeneid*: "Wrapped in a Sidonian cloak with a decorated border." Nonius <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note> calls the "edge" a woman's garment that has purple at the bottom.

The center of the lunar **epicycle** <margin>Epicycle</margin> etc. What an "epicycle" (or as they commonly call it, an *epicyclus*) is seems to require a deeper explanation drawn from the commentaries of Pierre d'Ailly <note>original: "Petri Alliacensis"; a 14th-century French theologian and astronomer.</note> on the books *On the Sphere*. The altitude (which they call thickness) of the individual orbs in which the planets reside is divided into three orbs placed one on top of the other and touching; of these, the two outermost—the highest and the lowest—are not of equal thickness in their parts.

# Letters, Book IV, Folio XXXVIII

<note>The top of the page continues a technical commentary on the motions of the spheres.</note>

...likewise it moves around the poles of the equator: which by its own force carries all the lower orbs along with it: this is the diurnal <note>daily</note> motion: because it usually occurs in the space of a natural day, that is, twenty-four hours. The remaining lower orbs, however, move by their natural motion from the west through the south to the east around the poles of the zodiac. The widest orb, that is, the "prime mover" <term>Primum Mobile: the outermost moving sphere in geocentric astronomy</term>. Which all things, etc. This automaton was not much different from an artificial sphere. Something of such a kind was fabricated by Archimedes, etc. Lactantius, in chapter five of his second book, mentions this machine of Archimedes. "Doubtless," he says, "God the artisan of the universe so disposed those things, so engineered them: that they might run through the spaces of the heaven by an admirable logic, to produce the varieties of the seasons succeeding one another. If Archimedes the Sicilian could engineer a likeness and figure of the world in hollow brass, in which he placed the sun and moon so that they might produce unequal motions similar to the celestial movements for each individual day: and not only the setting and rising of the sun, or the waxings and wanings of the moon, but even the disparate courses of the stars, whether fixed or wandering <note>planets</note>, while that orb turns? Could God therefore not have engineered and produced those true things, which the skill of man was able to simulate by imitation?" Thus far Lactantius. Plutarch, in the *Life of Marcellus*, says that machines of this kind were composed by Archimedes. For when he writes various opinions concerning the death of Archimedes, he says: "A third rumor is tossed about concerning him. While he was carrying spheres, angles, and certain other mechanical instruments to Marcellus—by which he was accustomed to adapt the magnitude of the sun to the sight—soldiers encountered him: and thinking he was carrying gold, they killed him." Plutarch records many other things there about his ingenious industry; Pliny in chapter thirty-seven of the seventh book, Valerius in the eighth book under the title of study and industry, and Titus Livy in the fourth book of the third decade also hand down these memories. **Faith wavered.** That is, it could scarcely be believed. **All praise is inferior to the work.** That is, the work cannot be praised enough. **Unequal.** That is, inferior.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>The commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note> **Concerning which he treats.** That is, "of which": a not inelegant transposition. **The highest margin.** This margin is also defined. **Coitus.** The meeting of the sun and moon, as in the new moon. **Insinuates.** Commonly accepted for that which "indicates" and "makes certain": as if it "brings into the bosom" <note>Latin: *in sinum*</note>; for those things we have in our bosom are known and certain. Whence it is said: "This hope of mine is laid up in my bosom." **It happens.** That is, it frequently occurs. **Epicycles.** This is the nominative case.

<margin>Archimedes</margin>

->**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Francesco Casa, Greetings.**<-
->**Letter VIII.**<-

[A] I have received your letter, in which you signify to me that a report has been brought there concerning a small mechanical **Automaton**: which was recently constructed by a certain Lorenzo of Florence <note>Lorenzo della Volpaia</note>: in which the course of the stars is explained, congruent with the logic of the heavens. And you say that you desire—since the credibility of the rumor is being questioned—that I write to you about it, if I have any certain knowledge. I will comply with your wish: and although I have not seen that work for a long interval, living in the country: nevertheless, I shall briefly set forth what its form is, or its logic, or its use, as much as I can follow from memory. If this explanation seems a little obscure to you, you should attribute it not entirely to my speech, but to the subtlety and even the novelty of the matter itself. It is a square column: which, ending in a point in the manner of a pyramid, is topped at a height of nearly three cubits. Above it, as a capital, is a flat bronze disk, distinguished with gold and colors: and on one part of it, the entire course of the wandering stars <note>planets</note> is explained: its dimension is shorter than a cubit, and it is driven by small toothed wheels inside: with an immobile circle embracing the highest margin, marked by the spaces of twenty-four hours. Within it, on the highest rotating disk, the twelve signs <note>of the Zodiac</note> are discerned by their degrees. Inside are seen eight small disks of nearly equal size among themselves. Of these, two occupy the center point: one fixed upon the other, so that the lower, slightly larger one represents the Sun, and the upper one the Moon. From the Sun, a ray reaching to the circle indicates the hours on the circle itself, and on the zodiac it indicates the months, days, number of degrees, and the "mean motion" (as they say) of the sun. Likewise from the moon a stylus comes forth as an index of its hours, which are designated lower down on the rim of the larger disk: and passing through the center of the lunar **Epicycle** and touching the zodiac, it declares the mean motion of its star. Another likewise arising from the same place and cutting the center of the lunar body—that is, the edge of the Epicycle—manifests its true location. By which it happens that slowness and speed, and all motion and course, and likewise conjunctions and full moons are seen. Around these are six small disks, one of which—which they call the **Head and Tail of the Dragon** <note>the lunar nodes where eclipses occur</note>—insinuates the eclipses of both the Sun and the Moon. The rest are attributed to the planets, from each of which two points emerge as indices of motions, just as we showed in the moon. But these also move backward <note>retrograde</note>, which never happens in the moon, since its Epicycle carries it in the opposite direction. Thus the logic of conjunctions, retreats, and latitudes is manifest in each. There is besides another rim, like a zodiac, cutting those six small planetary disks from above, from which the degrees of the rising signs and the spaces of the days—that is, at what hour the sun rises—appear. From which the individual planets are carried by their disks, and in turn move toward the east by day, and toward the west by night. Conversely, the widest orb itself turns the planets toward the east by night and toward the west by day in the space of twenty-four hours. All of which, indeed, both logic proves and every most skillful person agrees, are congruent with the heaven itself. Nor is there any reason you should wonder that these things seem incredible to many. For (as it is said by a certain author): *Faith is usually slow to believe in great things.* We ourselves, I say, scarcely believe our eyes when we look upon these things daily. And so, when I was reading at one time that Archimedes of Syracuse had fabricated something of the kind, my faith wavered even in so great an author: which this man of ours has plainly fulfilled. And indeed, all praise is inferior to the work itself, nor can it be praised according to its dignity in any other way, except that we confess all praise to be unequal to it. It is certainly doubtful whether we should admire the craftsman himself more for his character and probity, his candor and sanctity, or for his genius: so that we might think him both sent down from heaven and to have learned the heavens in heaven itself. Farewell. Fiesole, August 8th, 1484.

# F.S. In the Capitoline courtyard, etc.
Pomponius Laetus writes in his book *On Roman Antiquities* that there was a temple of Hercules almost in the middle of the back of the Capitoline Hill. Pliny likewise mentions the Capitoline Hercules in the seventh chapter of his thirty-fourth book. Strabo also writes in his sixth book that after Tarentum was conquered by the valor of the Romans, a sublime bronze image of Hercules was carried away to Rome with other spoils and fixed upon the Capitol. This was offered as a gift by Fabius Maximus, who had captured the city. **Hardly so**—that is, not very much. **Palatine, etc.** The Philologist <note>Likely referring to a specific scholar or commentator known by this title in the Renaissance</note> frequently cites this manuscript from the Palatine library. **Anio**, genitive **Anienis**, just as **Nerio** becomes **Nerienis**, according to the authority of Gellius in the twenty-second chapter of his thirteenth book. However, Servius, in his commentaries on the seventh book of the *Aeneid*, records that Ennius said **Anionem**. The Anio is a river not far from the city of Rome, which took its name from Annius, a king of the Tuscans. For according to Plutarch in his *Parallels*, Annius had a daughter of extraordinary beauty named Salia, whom he kept under diligent guard as a maiden. A certain very noble youth named Cathetus saw the girl playing; he loved her, and urged by the force of love, he seized her and carried her off to Rome. The father pursued the abductor of the maiden, and when he despaired of the power to catch him, he threw himself into the river of the Parensii, bestowing his name upon the river along with his body. For they afterwards called it the **Annio**. Therefore, correct orthography requires "Annius" with two 'n's. From Cathetus and Salia were born Latinus and Salius, from whom the most noble families originated. **Narses** was at first a bookseller. When the Emperor Justinian had received him into his bedchamber and recognized the man's virtue, he admitted him into the order of the patriciate. He then sent him to Rome against the Goths; having also received auxiliary forces from Alboin, King of the Lombards, he attacked, slaughtered, and pursued the enemies. The author is Platina in his book *On the Lives of the Popes*. Regarding the life of Narses, Paul the Deacon writes more in the second book of *The Deeds of the Lombards* and the eighth book of *The Deeds of the Romans*; Procopius and Aretino also write much. It has the genitive **Narsis** and **Narsetis**, like **Chremis** and **Chremetis**, **Daris** and **Daretis**, **Lachis** and **Lachetis**. **To follow Quintilian.** These are the words of Quintilian from his first book: *That distinction was also preserved by many, so that "ad" when it was a preposition took the letter 'd', but when it was a conjunction <note>original: "at"</note> it took 't'. Likewise, "quum" if it signified time was written with a 'q', but if it signified a companion <note>original: "cum"</note> it was written with a 'c'. But if "quum" was written with a 'q', it would be followed by two 'u's.* Other things are even more trivial than these: such as writing "quicquid" with a 'c' in the fourth place so that we do not seem to be asking a question twice. And "quotidie," not "cotidie."

**Book IV of the Letters. Folio 39.**

Meanwhile, that oak had produced mistletoe, and men had noticed it. Therefore, all the wretched birds were suddenly caught there by the birdlime <note>A sticky substance used to trap birds</note>, and a late repentance came upon them in vain for having despised that wholesome counsel. But they say this is why now all birds, when they see an owl, flock to her as if to greet her, escorting her, following her, sitting around her, and flying about her. For, mindful of her counsel, they now admire her as wise; they throng in a dense crowd so that they might gain some wisdom from her. Thus far Poliziano, who attributes excessive wisdom to the owl.

**ASCENSIUS.** As to what you ask regarding the reasoning for this kind of orthography <note>spelling systems</note>, about which there is great controversy even among the primary grammarians: it seems to me that Angelo Poliziano, easily the most learned of men, brings forward a weak argument. For those who decorate coins or stones or temples with titles and other writings are generally unlearned, just like those who used to write books for hire. Wherefore, in many cases following common pronunciation, they distorted not a few things from true writing; among which they say *Vergilius* for *Virgilius*, for the common people say *verga* and *vergine* instead of *virga* [rod] and *virgine* [virgin]. Quintilian, however, seems to have contended that it is not a capital crime if someone confuses *cur* and *quur* [why], or *cum* and *quum* [when/with]. Nor am I unaware that the ancients wrote indeclinable parts whole in compounds; but because whatever is brought forth more sweetly or written more distinctly is pleasing so that speech may be held more lucid, the perception of Priscian, Diomedes, and similar men, or the custom of learned men—even recent ones—is not to be rejected. Therefore, although between *quod* and *quot*, *quam* and *quanquam*, *quae* and *que*, and similar things there is no legitimate distinction, I would nevertheless preserve the difference now known to almost everyone. Truly, I would not easily be induced to write *quod* for *quot* [how many], or *quodannis* for *quotannis* [yearly], since *quotus* is derived from *quot*, not *quodus* from *quod*. I will easily concede, however, that no conjunction should be written with a *d* at the end; therefore I would write *at*, *atque* [and], *sed* [but], and its daughters; and if anything by its own elements, rather *quot* than *quod*—except that *quod* has been assumed as a conjunction. But because *sed* seems composed of *se* and *et*, I shall write it entirely with a *t*. I mentioned the custom of the learned: by which, although *quin* is rightly written, I would nevertheless write *aliquoi* [to someone]; and *toties*, *quoties* [as often as] without the *n*, just like *septies*, *octies* [seven times, eight times]. Nor shall I follow the writing of the Greeks in purely Latin words, who, following common pronunciation, are not rarely deceived. But enough on these matters.

**Angelo Poliziano to Filippo Posco, Greetings.**
**Letter 60.**

[Large initial G] You have done a favor by sending the letter and the little verses. You ask what I think. I shall be brief. They are correct, festive, sharp, full of meaning and stings. I would call them consummate, were I not comparing them with antiquity rather than with this age. As to why you ask why I mark these particles *quod* [that/which] and *adque* [and] with the letter *d* rather than *t*, the answer is easy. And lest you think you are being led around or even deceived, I will cite a few witnesses, and those not foreign to you. There is in the Capitoline courtyard to the left, I believe, a certain marble of the bronze Hercules found not so long ago, inscribed with ancient and now almost obsolete verses, the beginning of which is: *Hercules Invictus*. In it, this is also read: *Administrandum quodannis* <margin>Yearly.</margin> [To be administered yearly]. That most ancient manuscript of Virgil also supports this spelling, which is kept there in the innermost Palatine library, written in capital characters. You may review a few things with me from the *Bucolics* and *Georgics* now, lest the whole volume must be unfolded for you: "Two bowls foaming with fresh milk *quodannis* [yearly]." And a little after: "As to Bacchus and Ceres, so to you the vows *quodannis*." And again: "Unless human force *quodannis*." Likewise: "For every *quodannis* the soil must be cut three and four times." But it also marks *adque* <margin>And.</margin> [and] by the same reasoning. Nor should it move you that you find it otherwise on that bridge of the Anio constructed by Narses: "And the interrupted journey is continued." Unless you think we must stand by that unlearned age. I would prefer to follow Quintilian, who in the first book of the *Oratorical Institution* mocks as a "chilling" practice that a distinction was preserved by many so that *ad* as a preposition took the letter *d*, while *at* as a conjunction took *t*. Therefore, you may find traces of the old spelling still in the same Virgil, such as: "And to inhabit humble cottages." "But he offers himself to me of his own accord." "And again to Troy." "And the altars, Menalcas." "And he raises tall alders from the soil." "And would that one of you." "And he detains the opposing enemies." And a thousand others, so that I may circumscribe myself with a smaller boundary than I promised. Furthermore, our friend Lollius asks of us why we preserve the same in the verb *adgredior* [I approach/attack]. And (unless I am mistaken) both the force of custom and the authority of Priscian lead him. But I appeal from this depraved custom to correct antiquity. Inspect (if there is leisure) his book. So, I think, you will find: "Approach, O great honors, the time will soon be here." And likewise: "They approached: for often the old man had mocked both with the hope of a song." Nor indeed does the authority of Priscian seem to me in this place to be anything but weak (if I may be pardoned for saying so) and wavering; since he even thinks it happened more by the error of writers than by reason that *adfatur*, *adludo*, *adrideo*, *adnitor*, *adfumo* retain the *d*. For who would think that even on coins consecrated to the Caesars themselves, this fault was admitted? In which, as other things are in the same manner, certainly *adlocutio* [allocution] is marked with the letter *d*, never *l*. But you, being too much men of wit and clearly facetious, are mocking me, since you have Pomponio at home: a man most consulted in all antiquity and indeed all literature. Therefore, I am the foolish one: "bringing an owl to Athens" <note>A Greek proverb meaning to do something superfluous, like "carrying coals to Newcastle."</note>. But now farewell; and excuse my preoccupations to Lollius, to whom I have given no letters by this particular carrier. Farewell.

F.S. "In trades" (as Plautus says) etc. Plautus in the Prologue of *Amphitryon*: "As you wish me to affect you with joyful profits in buying and selling your trades, and to help in all things." "From Illyria": that is, the Illyrian land, as from Arimathia. Moreover, Illyria is (as Appian writes in *Illyrica*) a region of the land of Greece measured above Macedonia and Thrace <margin>From Illyria.</margin>; they found it to be six thousand stadia long and one thousand two hundred wide. It was so called because Polyphemus had three sons by Galatea: Celtus, Gallus, and Illyrius, who, proceeding from Sicily, gave their names to the Celts, Gauls, and Illyrians whom they ruled. "From malice": that is, from Momus <note>The god of mockery and blame</note>, of whom we spoke before. "Destined to overcome the injury of time": that is, never to perish, nor to be involved with things handed over to oblivion.

I should certainly trust my own style. ->**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Andrea Magnanimo. Greetings. Letter XIII.**<-

[Large initial E] You write that my *Herodian* <note>Poliziano’s Latin translation of the Greek history by Herodian, covering the Roman Empire after Marcus Aurelius.</note> is being demanded there by those who print books with type. For I call it mine by right: as if I have gifted it with Latinity <note>original: "latinitate donauerim" — a common humanist phrase for translating a Greek work into elegant Latin.</note>. Then you ask that I eventually return your own manuscript to you, corrected by our own hand (which you say they desire). I am returning it: but, to tell the truth, corrected lightly rather than severely: so that you may find more of our errors in it than those of the bookseller. I should certainly trust my own style: that is, the style of the interpreter: that somewhat more indulgence is owed to it than to the author’s: since things usually respond somewhat better when you write where there is a free course, so to speak, than when you translate where nothing is permitted outside what is prescribed. Added to this is the fact that this task of interpreting was for me a work of lighter effort: seeing as I dictated it in a few short days while walking about. Therefore, I am so far from seeking praise for myself from it, that I think it would even be abundantly fine if I avoid serious blame. Wherefore, to my other friends, and especially to you, I do not only release the entire defense of this work, but I even strictly forbid it: I reserve you, untouched, for other things which will be published later. But although there are very many among you who favor me even more than is right: yet you are the one, Andrea Magnanimo—most worthy of that family name of yours <note>"Magnanimo" means "Great-souled" or "Magnanimous" in Latin/Italian.</note>—whom I indeed value most highly; since you are sprung from good stock, and flourish in wealth and honors, and most especially because you are of the most elegant wit, the sweetest character, and possessed of a singular grace in whatever you do or say—indeed, even if you do nothing and say nothing—and finally, by your very countenance, as they say, you conquer men. Therefore, I fear no one as long as you are devoted to me. For no one will ever think ill of Poliziano who understands that he also pleases Magnanimo. There is only one thing which I now strive for from you. Take care, with your usual diligence in our affairs, that the volumes which they will soon form [print] degenerate as little as possible from the original; and that not even those little annotations which I have written in the margins be omitted. Among those, indeed, I think you will find three or four places at most where I had to use an excuse for a corrupt Greek manuscript. To manage these things easily, you could have no one more suitable or more useful to you than Alessandro Sartio: your citizen, a man of letters, and a devotee of ours, which I consider the most important thing in this matter.

# Of Illustrious Men

## BOOK V.

-> **Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to Bartolomeo Scala. LETTER I.** <-

**[E]**ven you told me openly in recent days—and many have reported hearing it from you—that my style of writing does not please you. This is because I pursue words that are too adopted <note>original: "ascita," meaning foreign or far-fetched</note> and remote. You also claim that I am a certain (for so you are accustomed to say) *cementer* <note>original: "ferruminatorem," literally one who solders or glues things together</note>. For this word has long since begun to signify, in your usage, one who employs words that are somewhat less than common. Indeed, you are usually (as I hear) joking when you call Hermolao Barbaro <note>A famous Venetian scholar and diplomat</note> a *cementer*, perhaps because he had used that very word on several occasions.

But I, my dear Scala, just as I easily grant you that an infrequent word should not be adopted rashly, so on the other hand I would contend that it ought not to be held against anyone if they restore to use Latin words found in suitable authors, and strive to give novelty to the ancient, nor allow those words to lie entirely idle which, through the fault of the times, have fallen utterly into disuse. For if our speech were to receive only those words which are obvious to everyone, we would be using nothing better than the language of public notaries. 

As for your calling me back to Cicero—who is indeed the supreme author of the Latin language, yet not the only one—I ask what you would do with the others, whose testimonies have always held the weight of authority among the most learned? I ask likewise: what answer would you give to Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, a prolific Roman scholar</note> at least, who, while he yields the palm of oratory to Cicero, retains for himself the palm for speaking Latin? I ask also: would you reject as if they were barbarians Livy, Sallust, Quintilian, Seneca, and both Plinys, besides many others approved by the consensus of so many centuries? Especially since, in their great diversity, some have made the prize of victory doubtful—just as among the Greeks with Herodotus and Thucydides in history, so among us with Livy and Sallust. What of the fact that Cicero is most unlike Demosthenes? For nothing can be added to the one, nor taken from the other; clearly, that "juice" of oratory is almost lacking in one, while in the other it as if overflows. 

Furthermore, why is this very word *Ferrumino* <note>To solder or cement</note> <margin>On several occasions.</margin> uttered with such laughter? Since it is proper, simple, not ill-sounding, and not obsolete; a word from which neither Pliny himself (that lover of propriety) nor the legal experts abstain—who claim for themselves the force of vocabulary by a certain right above others. Is it therefore, because Hermolao used it once or twice, deservedly despised or mocked? You have written much, I believe, though you have not published so much that is commonly circulated. But you are certainly composing a history: a long and arduous work, I think. What example, then, do you set for yourself if we cannot safely use the words even of good authors? 

I confess, however, that regard must be had for the subject matter you write, the person to whom you write, or the time in which you write. <margin>Propriety must be observed.</margin> For the same style would not suit the *Speeches* of Cicero and the *Milesian Tales* of Apuleius. For there is, as it were, one language in which we play, and another in which we conduct serious matters. You would not speak to a boy in the same tone as to a learned man. Nor again should you write in the same way to friends as to strangers, nor the same to princes as to private citizens. Wherefore your Cicero—and perhaps mine too—is sometimes found so unlike himself that not everything he writes seems to belong to the same author. 

But we easily endure you as a censor, Scala, a man who has been engaged in letters for so many years not without glory. What we cannot endure are certain poorly-learned men who nevertheless demand that everything be measured against the "taste" of Cicero. For it often happens—and indeed sometimes to my great laughter or stomach-turning—that they especially rebuke those very things in our writings which are found in the good and corrected manuscripts of Cicero, while they themselves use utterly barbarian words as if they were Ciceronian—words which these German <note>original: "Teutones"</note> printers of new books have sometimes most perversely invented. 

Now, that precept of Caesar which is immediately thrown in our faces—that we should "shun an infrequent word as if it were a reef"—was perhaps more valid in that age when everyone still spoke Latin than in ours. For then, one who was not content with the vocabulary of his own age could rightly be argued against. But now, the Latin language is not known by the common people. It is no longer learned from nurses, but from teachers. Among them, surely no words ought to be considered more "usual" and "accepted" than those brought forth from those ancient treasuries of the great authors. 

I have written these things to you freely, my dear Scala, but also as a friend; not so much asserting myself against your laughter (by which I am certainly not offended) as lightly defending Hermolao Barbaro himself: the most learned man of our century, who deserved the best from literature and philosophy while he lived. May I be permitted by you (as I expect from your fairness in all things) to feel entirely differently in literature than you do, provided that no loss of love or mutual goodwill occurs between us on this account. Farewell. December 25, 1493.

**Letter II.**

[Large decorative initial E] ven if I do not doubt that you have felt great grief at the death of King Ferdinand <margin>Ferdinand</margin> <note>Ferdinand I of Naples, d. 1494</note>—because in him there was such authority and wisdom as we scarcely remember in any other king—nevertheless, when I consider within myself who succeeds that King as King, I think it almost a sin for either you, or anyone of those who favor your affairs (among whose number we also belong), to be engaged in any greater mourning or sadness. For since the heir to the kingdom (may it be happy and auspicious) has fallen to Alfonso, <margin>Alfonso</margin> <note>Alfonso II of Naples</note> the eldest son, whose excellent character, singular virtue, and incredible wisdom have shone in war and peace, we should certainly be ungrateful if we looked not at how much has been left to us, but only at how much has been taken away. Especially since the kingdom is supported by so many and such great aids. For Ferdinand the second, <note>Ferdinand II of Naples, known as Ferrandino</note> another son of Alfonso, has been substituted as Duke of the Calabrians; fame reports to us that he himself excels in all gifts of body and mind, so that he has already given a doubtless specimen of a certain royal nature in many magnificent things. Added to this is Federico, <margin>Federico</margin> <note>Later Frederick of Naples</note> a man of great prudence, great dexterity, and great experience in affairs, but of even greater benevolence, faith, and piety toward the King his brother. I pass over other connections, wealth, armies, leaders, allies, the zeal of the common people, protections, fortifications, and bulwarks, which seem able to be shaken by almost no human forces. Indeed, who, I ask, can more hope for or promise himself divine aid than he who, pursuing the impious Turks with sword and fire, expelled them not so much from the town of Otranto as (so it seems to me) from Rome itself—which they were seeking first—and even from those most holy altars? Wherefore, although a great loss has altogether been made by the death of Ferdinand, yet because he handed over his "watch" to his son, and left as King the one he most desired for himself, a man excelling in every kind of praise, you ought not by any means, my dear Pontano—you and whoever else are among the officers of the King—give yourselves over to sorrow. Rather, with a ready mind (which I indeed think you are doing), you should be at hand and devote all your diligence to relieving him (as much as can be done) of care, labor, and trouble. It is fitting for you also separately to give thanks to God the Greatest, because him whom you educated for this hope from a tender age, whom you adorned with disciplines, whom you instructed with precepts, you now see as King; and such a King, that he is held most worthy not only of that most beautiful and opulent kingdom of yours, but even of the empire of the world. A certain special love of mine toward you and your princes impelled me to write these things to you. But also this pupil of mine, and likewise my patron, the pillar of our republic, Piero de' Medici, <margin>Piero de' Medici</margin> <note>Piero "the Unfortunate," successor to Lorenzo the Magnificent</note> a youth of excellent mind and character, has greatly exhorted me. Nothing can be more loving of you than he is, my Pontano. For as to your King himself, to whom he has surrendered himself entirely and inwardly, there is no need to write, especially to you to whom all things are known. But nevertheless, he always speaks of him so honorably and lovingly that he leaves almost nothing for the rest. But enough of these things. As for the fact that in previous days you diligently excused your occupations because you had not responded to a certain letter of ours: you are a man too dutiful (as I see) and too refined. For although I would indeed hold your letters most welcome, nothing can delight me which is granted with any trouble to you. I only wish you would forgive this: that while I follow my zeal and love for you, I have not feared to interrupt your occupations once or twice. It is permitted to you by me (provided you do not cease to love me) not only not to respond to my letters, but not even to read them if it is so convenient. Farewell.

*Insimulans*: that is, accusing. Plautus in the *Amphitruo*: "Nor let him find me falsely accused <note>original: *insimulatam*</note> of shame." *Reus* <margin>Defendant</margin>: that is, one who is conscious of a matter or accused. Cicero in the second book *On the Orator* calls *reos* not only those who are charged, but all those about whose business a dispute is held. *Voti reus* <margin>Bound by a vow</margin> in Macrobius, in the third book of the *Saturnalia*, is he who has bound himself by some vow. *Voti damnatus* <margin>Condemned by a vow</margin> is he who has been released from a vow <note>meaning he must now pay it because his prayer was answered</note>. *Temporariam*: that is, brief, shifting, lasting for a short time. *Rarum*: that is, famous. For on the authority of Cicero, "All famous things are rare." *Consuetudinem*: that is, as they say, "conversation" or "social intercourse."

**ASCENSIUS.**
*But yourself.* Someone is said to "conquer himself" who, although he has conquered others in other matters, is so diligent or so excellent in any one thing that he surpasses himself—that is, his usual diligence and excellence; as Livy says in the first decade. *Voti reus* is properly he from whom a vow is demanded like a debt. But he is *voto damnatus* who has been "convicted" of being a debtor of a vow because the condition which he had accepted has come to pass. Whence that passage in Virgil's *Bucolics*: "You also shall condemn [them] to their vows," is usually explained as the exhibition of vows, by doing those things for which they made the vow. For if one placed in danger, disease, or other evil has made a vow to God if he escapes it: then if through divine help he escapes it, he is "condemned to his vow" by God, that is, he is bound to perform the vow. He is not, however, absolved, but—

...having attempted to betray our Spaniards, it had failed, and they were being plundered: not a few coins of ancient currency were discovered. One of these my student Guttanus—certainly no one to be ashamed of—showed to me. It was roughly the size of those they call "Capital" coins, and certainly of the same thickness, but of purer silver. On it, the figure of a head was formed; around it, in larger letters that were entirely intact, I read: **VIRGILIUS MARO**. From this fact, I gather by conjecture that Virgil was granted the resources to provide for himself and his own titles on money; just as Crinitus <note>Pietro Crinito (1475–1507), a Renaissance humanist.</note> records in the first book of his work *On Latin Poets* that the name of the poet Fabius Dorsennus was written on bronze coins. Likewise, Priscian <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note> writes in his fourth book that *Virgilius* is derived from *virgula* <note>a small rod or wand</note>, just as *Sylvius* comes from *sylva* <note>forest</note>. They were calling it into reproach and accusing it. Time and time again. I believe you are not unaware that our opinion on this matter is joined with that of Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, a leading scholar of the Italian Renaissance.</note>, as seen from the commentary on the previous letter and from our *Progymnasmata* <note>preliminary rhetorical exercises</note>.

<margin>Analogy.</margin> **Analogy** (as Aulus Gellius says in the twenty-fifth chapter of his second book) is the similar declension of similar things, which some call "proportion" in Latin; for example, *amo* <note>I love</note> and *laudo* <note>I praise</note> vary with almost the same endings.

<margin>Anomaly.</margin> **Anomaly** is an inequality of declensions following custom; for instance, *tempus* <note>time</note> and *locus* <note>place</note> do not have the same endings everywhere in all cases. This word Priscian, etc. The words of Priscian are from his second book. "In certain compounds," he says, "I find *r* is converted into *l*: as in *intelligo* <note>I understand</note> and *pellicio* <note>I entice</note>, instead of *interlego* and *perlicio*; *pellego* for *perlego* <note>to read through</note>, *pelluceo* for *perluceo* <note>to shine through</note>." Plautus in the *Asinaria*: "Come now, show that contract you wrote between me, my girlfriend, the madam, and the laws. Read it through [*pellege*], for you are truly a unique poet for that task." The same author in the same play: "You shine through [*pelluces*] as if you were a Carthaginian lantern." Thus far Priscian. The same author in book ten, when speaking of the perfect tense of verbs ending in *-go*, says: "*Perlego*, I have read through [*perlegi*]; *relego*, I have read again [*relegi*]." From this they except the compounds *negligo*, I have neglected [*neglexi*], and *intelligo*, I have understood [*intellexi*]; which the ancients used to say as *interlego*, *interlexi*. In the manuscripts of Plautus which Battista Pio <note>Giovanni Battista Pio (1460–1540), an Italian humanist editor.</note> saw through the press, I find it written almost always as *pellego* and *interlego*; as in the *Mercator*, *neglego*. "I now disregard [*neglego*] my mother's wrath," he says, emulating Cato.

<margin>Cato.</margin> **Cato** (as Cornelius Nepos records in his *Life*) was most fond of literature; therefore, although an elder, he took up the study and made such progress in it that it is not easy to find anything regarding either Greek or Italian affairs that was unknown to him. In Cicero's book *On Old Age*, these are the words of Cato: "What of the fact," he says, "that they even learn something new? As we saw Solon boasting in his verses, who says he becomes an old man learning something every day; as I have done, who learned Greek literature as an old man. Indeed, I seized upon it as greedily as if I were desiring to quench a long-lasting thirst, so that those very things which you now see me using as examples might be known to me. When I heard that Socrates had done this with the lyre <note>original: "fidibus"</note>, I would have wished for that as well (for the ancients used to call it 'playing the strings'), but in literature I certainly labored."

<margin>Papyrianus the grammarian.</margin> A joke lies hidden at the end, etc. In that part. And what he calls "the youth Papyrianus." **Papyrianus** was a grammarian whom Quintianus calls by name in the list of authors from whom he composed his epigraphs, and whom he cites not infrequently; Priscian cites him repeatedly. Perhaps Scala <note>Bartolomeo Scala (1430–1497), Florentine statesman and scholar.</note> seems to mention him here by name. But if it is a joke, as it certainly seems to be, he is calling Papyrianus a shameless sodomite. For Lucius Papyrius held the youth Publius in chains; because the boy refused to suffer debauchery, Papyrius afflicted him with insults and lashes. Concerning this, Livy says in the eighth book of his first decade: "In that year," he says, "a new beginning of liberty, as it were, was made for the Roman commons, because they ceased to be bound [for debt]. The law was changed on account of the lust and remarkable cruelty of a single moneylender. This was Lucius Papyrius, to whom Publius had given himself over as a bond-servant for his father's debt by a decree of the Senate; though the boy's age and beauty might have elicited mercy, they instead inflamed Papyrius's mind to lust and insult, and he believed the flower of the boy's age was an incidental profit of the loan, first attempting to entice him..."

# **On Illustrious Men**

I endure it: since a public scribe, accustomed to dictating letters, must especially approve of that style which shrinks less from common usage. Yet you are not to be blamed in this matter, since these letters are usually sent to the unlearned. We, on the other hand, who read through the writings of the ancients for the benefit of youth, have learned to exercise a choice of words and thoughts; nor have we ourselves willingly cut off the better part of eloquence just to serve the ears of the unlearned. Perhaps you think this is an affectation; however, it contains a certain majesty and sanctity of language. For this reason, even Sallust himself <note>Gaius Sallustius Crispus, a Roman historian known for his archaic and brevity-focused style.</note>—whom you rightly praised alongside me—was nevertheless attacked by certain people in a very well-known epigram as one who wrote with affectation. And now you so strongly disapprove of certain trifles, which pertain chiefly to orthography <note>The conventional spelling system of a language.</note>, that you almost stir up a tragedy. I ask you, my dear Scala <note>Likely Bartolomeo Scala, the Florentine chancellor and humanist.</note>, do not bring this ill-will upon me, nor let such disturbances be stirred up on that account.
