**Letters Book V. Folio XLV.**

Or *Carthaginiensis*: which I prefer to say, rather than the common *Carthaginensis*. What do you have to object to here, besides a long-standing error? First, that very Priscian <note>A famous 6th-century Latin grammarian.</note>, whom you call a noble grammarian, mandates by rule that one should say *Carthaginiensis*. After this, much is added to his authority by the verse of Ennius which Tully <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero.</note> cites: "He who strikes the enemy shall be to me a *Carthaginiensis*." For if it were read as *Carthaginensis*, the meter (as you see) would limp. Finally, I can produce many very ancient books whenever you wish. I can also cite an epigram carved in ancient marble that is still seen in Rome in the Transtiberine region <note>Trastevere.</note>, which supports our observation.

But I come now to the *Ferruminator* <note>Literally "one who solders" or "cements." Poliziano uses it as a metaphor for a restorer of texts.</note>: whom you avoid (to use the words of Flaccus <note>Horace.</note>) "worse than a dog or a snake." <margin>Carthaginian.</margin> If it must not be used because it has a doubled letter 'r', then by that example, my dear Scala, you will leave no iron (*ferrum*) to the soldier, nor his land (*terram*) to the farmer, nor even a hoe (*marram*). For all those words of yours (for so I like to joke)—that is, those which have a doubled 'r'—are no less in use than those you think are "soft." And if I must listen to you, my Scala, we shall all be forced to babble like children; and, what is laughable, flee to the "lambdacism" of Alcibiades <note>A speech impediment where 'l' is substituted for 'r'; Alcibiades was famous for this lisp.</note>. But if you use it properly, you say, perhaps you do not sin—but only if you use it metaphorically. As if this were truly repugnant to metaphor, or as if this word has not quite often, even among good authors, migrated from its own home into a foreign one. <margin>The Solderer.</margin>

As for your saying you do not know what is meant by the name *ferrumen* <note>Solder or cement.</note>: I certainly forgive you. For perhaps it was not permitted for one occupied with the Greeks to unroll our grammarians, by whom it is explained. Why you should take it for "bitumen," I do not see; however, I profess I will show what it means in Livy, provided you show the place where Livy uses it. Regarding Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, a contemporary scholar.</note>, you indeed act prudently in making excuses, fearing, I believe, ill-will. But return with me, I pray, into memory: how you both ardently accused him in previous days, and I constantly defended him. For you defamed this word *ferruminandi* for no other reason than that Hermolaus used it. For it is certainly not yet found in my writings.

There is also something else that I confess I greatly wonder at in your letter: for while you disparage this century in which we live and think it little learned if compared with the ancients, you nevertheless fight me using only the authorities of this same century. But you also judge those who publish their writings and allow them to be spread by printing presses to be arrogant and rash. As if those who write rightly do not, by that means, benefit even more people. Let those follow your advice who smear wretched papers only to bury them in perpetual darkness. I, truly, am not ashamed to amend in later writings if I have ever erred in earlier ones, so that, as someone said, "I may progress by writing, and write by progressing." For the glory of Hippocrates, or Augustine, or Cicero is not less on that account: that they condemned certain things long published by them in subsequent new editions. But I see I have gone on too long while responding to several "heads" of your letter. You will grant pardon (such is your kindness) not only to my talkativeness but also to my liberty. Your letter gave occasion for the one; your example invited me to the other. It seems, somehow, to befit friends—as in conversation, so also in letters—to have a certain "skirmishing" between them, which we hear those Socratic men, people of "wiped noses" <note>A Latin idiom for being sharp-witted or discerning.</note>, used most often, so that they might test their learning in speaking and their patience in listening. Farewell. Florence.

**F.S.** *Edentulum*: that is, old and without teeth. *Receptui canant signa*: I think the meaning of "to sound the retreat" is unknown to no man. It is a proverb whose reasoning is drawn from military affairs, in which trumpeters call soldiers to war and, conversely, sound the retreat. <margin>To sound the retreat.</margin> And when soldiers are to go out alone for some work, those same trumpeters sound. But the horn-blowers sound whenever the standards are to be moved or fixed. Whenever there is a fight, both the trumpeters and horn-blowers sound together. But the *classicum* <note>A trumpet signal.</note>—that is, what the buglers say through the horn—is usually sounded in the presence of the commander, or when a soldier is punished capitally. For the *classicum* is a mark of command. <margin>The *Classicum*.</margin> Vegetius is the authority in Book II, Chapter 21. The poets feign that Triton, Neptune's trumpeter, sounds the retreat for the rivers into the sea. After the retreat is sounded, no one is allowed to fight the enemy. Therefore, on the authority of Plutarch in the *Laconian Apophthegms*, a certain Spartan in the battle line, when he was about to thrust his sword into the enemy, did not thrust it once the signal for retreat was given. When asked by someone why he had not killed the enemy he had caught: "Because," he said, "it is better to obey the commander than to kill the enemy." *Nati* etc.: These are the words of Virgil from *Aeneid* Book VI, when he remembers those who are in the Elysian Fields: "Great-hearted heroes, born in better years." <note>Handwritten note: Note with flourish</note>

**ASCENSIUS.** "Did I not tell you" etc.: He responds in such a way that you may recognize the remains of a somewhat irritated stomach; you might not know whether he confesses himself defeated feignedly or truly—and perhaps rather feignedly, because he says at the end: "For there is something that could be said against it."

**Bartolomeo Scala to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. Letter VI.**

Did I not tell you that I am toothless? I protested before: that you would be dealing with an old man now worn out by age and exhausted in strength. I am truthful; I command that the signals sound the retreat. I would not commit myself, my Poliziano, to be shut up in that game of yours on these conditions. Shall I—an unarmed, unwarlike, cowardly, trembling soldier—descend into the dust and the field for an insipid and ridiculous skirmish? For having clashed with Hercules—whom so many and such great conquered monsters translated into heaven—I now give up the "herb" <note>A gesture of surrender.</note> and my hands, and I pray you save the conquered man. Do not be cruel; led among the captives on the day of triumph, I will be able to add to the pomp and the number. For certainly you can (so it seems to me now) lead a triumph not only over our letters, but over Letters themselves. Because you thought me so worthy as to respond so accurately...

**Of Illustrious Men**

If you have honored and exalted me in your writing, even beyond measure—and if that has always been your way—nevertheless, by this new kindness toward me now, I confess I owe you much. The elegance of your letter is truly admirable, your learning clearly fresh and incredible, and your refinement unusual and incomparable. There you have what I think of your writings; I have even confirmed it with my own signature, should any ill-willed person speak against it. I myself shall take delight in these more common letters, as I have done until now, content perhaps with this more obscure sort. Since you, being born (as they say) in better years, have occupied the more illustrious things, you certainly, my dear Poliziano, owe much to nature above all others. She gave you that genius of yours, by which you can do so many things, and a memory by which you can recall almost everything—to say nothing of the gifts of the body, which some think carry no small weight for happiness—and the advantages of fortune, which are certainly accustomed to aid natural virtue unless it abandons itself. He would be utterly blind who did not see these things. For the rest, I will end the letter, for I think it better done in person when the matter can be handled opportunely; we shall settle all the things about which you write (for there is indeed something that could be said to the contrary). Farewell. 1493. Florence.

P.S. As a bear is accustomed to do with a cub. A bear playing with a cub, which is more tender, lessens and tempers the fierceness of its teeth, as if it had no teeth. When, therefore, a bear—otherwise quite savage—plays with a cub, it seems to bite it; but it handles it so softly with its mouth that it appears toothless. This is what usually happens with dogs playing with us. *Light with a naked sword* etc. This is a Virgilian verse from the twelfth book of the *Aeneid*. Moreover, a *parma* is a short shield, as Nonius <margin>The Parma shield.</margin> Marcellus says: which was painted according to a man's virtue <note>i.e., his military merit or character</note>, as we have learned from Servius. Therefore, for recruits, or those who had not yet accumulated any military glory, the shield was white <note>blank</note>. We mention this in passing from chapter 17 of the second book of Vegetius on military matters. Lest soldiers wander away from their tent-mates in the confusion of battles, they painted different signs on the shields for different cohorts; indeed, the name of each individual soldier was written on the shield, and it was added from which cohort or century he came. *Tiger, leopard, lion* are names of beasts that are active and fierce. *For dogs* etc. Xenophon, in his book on hunting, instructs that the names of dogs <margin>To triumph over an enemy.</margin> ought to be short so they can be easily called. *To triumph over letters* etc. For we triumph over an enemy, that is, "on account of" an enemy, just as we say "to fight for life" <note>original: "de vita pugnare"</note>. For excellent writers rarely use the preposition *de* in place of *pro* <note>The commentator is discussing a grammatical nuance regarding the Latin preposition 'de'</note>.

ASCENSIUS <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the famous printer and commentator</note>. *If you are toothless* etc. Poliziano responds no less sharply and urbanely. For if Scala swears that he wrote everything from the heart, it is no less likely that Poliziano responded from the heart. But if he secretly boasts, or whispers into the ear of his admirers, that he has beautifully tricked Poliziano—who did not realize he was being mocked—Poliziano himself thought he was mocking the stupidity of a man who thought his bites were not felt. *Foolish I.* The word "O" is understood, which is not expressed lest he seem to be breaking out in anger. *This you did above,* he says. The noble author is Horace. *To triumph over letters,* that is, to hold a triumph over letters <margin>To triumph over.</margin> conquered by me as if over enemies. Whence I will not say "to triumph over an enemy" is the same as "to triumph for an enemy," but "over a conquered enemy," which he declares by adding: *For when were those my enemies?* as if to say: never. And yet we do not triumph except over a conquered enemy. *Even falsely.* Sharply said; because if he praised him falsely, it would be a great thing to have compelled such a man even to a simulated praise. *No delay* etc. In many places he alludes to Virgilian verses. For in the *Bucolics* he said: *In me there shall be no delay.* But he writes this freely lest he seem to have responded so blandly out of fear of a confrontation.

<margin>Letter VII.</margin> **Angelo Poliziano to his friend Bartolomeo Scala, Greetings.**

**S**ince you are toothless, my Scala, your letter was nevertheless "toothed" <note>meaning sharp or biting</note>. I certainly felt it. For it nearly broke me with its bite; yet it spared me somewhat, and played with me just as a bear sometimes does with a cub. Foolish was I, who did not immediately yield to a veteran so often crowned; being, as it were, still a raw recruit, *light with a naked sword, and inglorious with a white shield.* You, however, do this magnificently, as you do other things, you who do not even think me worthy of your anger. For as to why I am called "Hercules" by you: I do not take pride in it for that reason; for in that way (as the poet says) lazy dogs will have the names *Tiger, Leopard, Lion.* Moreover, I could no more conquer you than the ridiculous Pygmies in Philostratus could conquer Hercules; he snatched them all up and wrapped them in his lion skin. Furthermore, to "triumph over letters" is not my way; for when were they ever my enemies? That is the glory of Goths and Huns, not mine. But how, I ask, could I occupy the more excellent things? I was perhaps still wailing in my cradle while you were delivering orations. Finally, if I have shown you any honor, my Scala, I confess I did so because of your merit. If, in turn, I pricked you in jest: I now wish it undone. Since you heap such great praises upon me with a full mouth: love is the cause. But yet I interpret it thus: that this one praise is the greatest of all praises to me: that I deserved to be praised by you, even falsely. If there is anything else you wish to handle in person: there is no delay in your Poliziano. Farewell.

**FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS.**

*They represent* <note>original: "Referunt"</note>, that is, they portray. Virgil in the 4th book of the *Aeneid*: *If only some little Aeneas were playing in my hall, who might represent you in face alone.* *I with flowers* etc. These are Virgil's words from the second Eclogue, which are used as a proverb against one who wishes or brings evil upon himself. <margin>To return to the path.</margin> *To return to the path.* This is a proverb from Terence's *Andria* regarding those who, when they recognize their errors, leave them behind. *In the house of Maro* <note>Virgil</note> etc. These are the words of Anchises telling Aeneas in the 6th book of the *Aeneid* what brave deeds the Romans will do, or what excellent arts they will practice. *You, Roman, remember to rule the peoples with authority* (he says). *These shall be your arts: to impose the custom of peace, to spare the subjected, and to war down the proud.* *Years have not subdued* etc. This is a Virgilian verse from the 2nd book of the *Aeneid*. *By his own Mars,* that is, by his own labor, his own study, his own genius. Moreover, it is a proverb whenever <margin>By his own Mars (proverb).</margin> we say something was done without outside help. Cicero, in the third book of *On Duties*, says: *We shall fill this remaining part with the help of no one, but (as they say) by our own Mars.*
ASCENSIUS. *Much less should they have approached with arms* etc. Lorenzo Valla seems to think that "not" ought to be added, so that it is "Much less should they *not* have approached with arms," which I think is almost necessary in "not only," "not just," and similar phrases; but in "much less" <note>original: "nedum"</note>, if it is resolved as "lest I say," it is not at all necessary. For you would rightly say, "lest I say they approached with arms." But I doubt whether "much less" can be explained as "lest I say."

# **Book V of the Letters, Folio 46**

-> Bartolomeo Scala gives greetings to Angelo Poliziano. <margin>Letter VIII</margin> <-

Just as those who have first tasted bitter things seem to find a sweeter flavor if they then happen upon milder ones, so have I myself just now been refreshed by your "sugar" and that nectar of your letter. To confess the truth, I do not know how it happened, but everything written by you tastes of your particular wit <note>original: "salem," literally "salt," a common Latin metaphor for wit or intellectual sharpness</note> and reflects your character. This gift which you sent to me most recently is even more uniquely yours. I see that I provoked you a little too much, and I was the cause of the change in my own style. To use a Virgilian proverb: "Wretch that I am, I have let the south wind blow on my flowers, and let the wild boars into my clear springs" <note>A quote from Virgil's Eclogues, signifying self-inflicted ruin or a mistake in judgment</note>; I have mixed oil into my clear lye-water. But I have returned to the path, and believe me, those things which have less agitation and passion are more serious—though perhaps poets would deny this, whose trumpet, often more inflated, fills the ears better.

You have already granted pardon for my error, which was worthy of you; we have heard that the great-hearted heroes of old used to act in this way. And to you also that passage in Virgil <note>original: "Maronem," referring to Publius Vergilius Maro</note> is addressed: "But you, Roman, remember..." and so forth. You know the poem <note>A reference to the Aeneid, Book VI, regarding the Roman virtues of mercy and governance</note>. It is truly a noble mind that is either not moved by injuries or forgets those received, even if unavenged. 

As for what I said about you "triumphing over literature," it did not have the meaning that I wished to call you an enemy of letters—for nothing is more hospitable to professors of learning than your home or yourself—but letters are placed in a high and rugged location. "And he who desires to reach the longed-for goal in the race: has endured and done much as a boy, has sweated and shivered" <note>A quote from Horace's Ars Poetica on the labor required for artistic mastery</note>. Nothing deterred you, nothing called you back; "ten years did not subdue you, nor a thousand ships" <note>A playful adaptation of Virgil's description of the Trojan War</note>. You have achieved a triumph over literature; that is, you have held within your power those things which are immortal...

Diomedes wounds Venus.

# Of Illustrious Men

Ancus Martius <note>The fourth legendary King of Rome</note> dedicated a temple to Fortune under the name "Patchwork": as he himself records: because in achieving a victory bravely, the primary role belongs to Fortune. Regarding the armed Venus, there is that most charming epigram by Ausonius <note>A 4th-century Roman poet</note>:
Pallas <note>Athena</note> saw Venus armed in Lacedaemon <note>Sparta</note>,
"Now let us compete," she said, "even with Paris as judge."
To whom Venus replied: "Rash woman, do you despise me when I am armed?
When I defeated you, I was naked."
"Warlike works are not given to you," etc. In the fifth book of Homer's *Iliad*, Pallas removes the cloud from the eyes of Diomedes, so that while fighting he might discern between gods and men, lest he unknowingly fight against the gods. Pallas forbids this battle with the gods. However, if Venus should descend into the fight on behalf of the Trojans: she exhorts him not to hesitate to wound her. Therefore, a little later, Diomedes rushes with a hostile spear against Venus as she protects Aeneas:
<margin>Diomedes wounds Venus.</margin>
not unaware that she was not of the number of those goddesses who preside over wars—insofar as victory is situated in the judgment of men—such as Minerva and Bellona <note>The Roman goddess of war</note>: but rather a goddess unwarlike and without strength. He pursues her with these words: "Is it not enough," he says, "to conquer the weak and soft female sex with your corruptions: unless you also attempt to move among the arms of fighting men? If you attempt to do this again: I believe it will come to pass that, taught by your own misfortune, you will regret having been present." Likewise, Jupiter addresses the wounded Venus with these words: "It is not, my daughter, your gift to handle the affairs of war..."

# Book V of the Letters. Folio 47.

I have competed with the ancient Greeks (unless this is too bold a claim). Nevertheless, compare them yourself: and in whatever way I might displease you, believe that the themes by which I could have pleased were already snatched away by others. But first, read what I have composed regarding the Venus of Apelles <note>Apelles of Kos (4th century BCE) was the most renowned painter of ancient Greece; his "Venus Anadyomene" was his most famous masterpiece.</note> after so many of the ancients. Our own Pliny <note>Referring to Pliny the Elder, who describes this painting in his *Natural History*.</note> also calls her *Anadyomene* <note>original: "Anadyomenen" (Greek: "Rising from the sea").</note> and says she was surpassed by Greek verses, by which she was nonetheless made famous—praise which does not belong to me, as I had not yet been born at that time.

**On Venus Anadyomene, that is, emerging from the sea.**

When I saw the Venus, the work of Apelles' hand, I stood still:
Long astonished, I said, "Venus Rising from the Sea."
Now of a maiden, now even of one indulging in jests, modesty
Claimed her face, mingled with laughter.
And with her right hand indeed she was squeezing the drops
Of her salt-drenched head, and the foam was splashing.
There was indeed a certain shivering at the moisture. But with her left hand
She was covering her groin, which was still submerged.
For she was in the sea as far as her hips, and there was still a certain ripple.
From the labor pains of her mother <note>Referring to the sea foam from which Venus was born.</note> she had a sharp breast.
If Mars, when bound, had once held such a woman,
He would not have wished to be freed even from Vulcan’s shackles. <note>In mythology, the blacksmith god Vulcan caught his wife Venus and her lover Mars in a magical net; the poet suggests the trap would be worth it for such beauty.</note>

But I also played in this way regarding the Armed Venus, so long after others.

**On the Armed Venus.**

For what purpose do you hold a shield, Lady of Paphos <note>Paphos, a city in Cyprus, was a major center for the worship of Venus/Aphrodite.</note>, and why do you brandish a spear,
And why have you put on a breastplate and a crested helmet?
Remember that the works of war were not given to you,
The delicate one; rather, you have the care of sweet marriages.
"But I am not armed for battle; instead, I put on the arms
Of Mars, so that Mars might forget the fight (that is, cease from battle)."
For having found both weapons and Venus in me alone,
He will never sleep away from my bedchamber.

Also on a Spartan mother: a theme well-worn by the Greeks, in this manner.

**On the Spartan Woman.**

When the Spartan mother recognized her son
Fleeing from battle, she met him with a sword.

# Letters, Book V. Folio XLVIII.

-> His foot caught in the branches; his head fell in the stream; and he was borne by <-
-> Woman, man, neither; by rivers, weapons, and a cross. <-
<note>This is a famous medieval riddle about a person of ambiguous gender (a hermaphrodite) who dies a triple death (hanging, drowning, and piercing). The author provides a Greek version below.</note>
Now hear our Greek version, if it pleases you.
She knew she was a woman, having given birth; to Apollo, to Mars,
And to Juno at the same time she questioned the three gods.
She asked the three gods so many things at once.
Apollo said a male, Mars a female, and you, Juno, said neither.
Juno, all were truly correct. For a hermaphrodite was born.
But seeking her fate, Juno told her death would be by the sword,
Mars by the cross, Apollo by the waves: all these things came to pass.
He stood upon a tree, but his sword fell; he himself upon it
Fell into the river face down, but by his feet
He was caught up by the branches. Thus died female and male,
And neither, by the cross, by the waves, and by the sword.

But perhaps I am being too troublesome to you; therefore, I shall now finish. First, however, I will testify to this: I have not competed with such illustrious talents, which antiquity has long approved—especially in their own arena—because I hoped for or sought victory from it. Rather, it seemed to me that I would understand those works better the less I succeeded in the attempt. Nevertheless, whatever these trifles of mine may be, I would wish you to explore them diligently; you will recognize in my other works of this kind, which I have either already written or am still itching to write, exactly the same flavor. Farewell.

F.S. <note>Likely "Feliciter Salve" or a similar closing</note> *Socors* [sluggish] and *secors* [senseless], just as *iocinora* and *iecinora* [livers] are commonly said. Apuleius in his first *Apology* says: "Among the most sluggish <term>Scythas</term><note>An ancient nomadic people often stereotyped as unlearned</note> the wise Anacharsis was born; among the shrewd Athenians, the foolish Melecides." The letters *o* and *e* have a great kinship between them; and as Priscian says in Book I, *o* passes into *e*, as *bonus* [good] becomes *bene* [well], and <note>original: "γομυ"</note> *gonu* becomes *genu* [knee]. The ancients said *compos compodis* instead of *compes compedis* [shackled]. Moreover, *socors* is said as if "without a heart" <note>Latin: *sine corde*</note>. For we note that the particle *se* was used by the ancient Latins for *sine* [without] even by apposition. A. Gellius in the last chapter of his book, calling forth words from the laws of the Twelve Tables, says: "On the third market day they are cut into parts; if they have done more or less, let it be <term>se fraude</term> <note>without harm/fraud</note>." Likewise, *se fraude esto*. Cicero in his book *On the Laws* says the same from the Twelve Tables. Therefore, *secors* is said as if "without a heart," that is, without a mind, without prudence. For they believe the seat of prudence to be in the heart. Whence they call the prudent "hearty" <note>Latin: *cordatos*</note>. "Washed with biting vinegar," that is, purified, prudent, learned. Persius in Satire V: "Here, the ear washed with biting vinegar." Either because vinegar has no small power for purifying and washing a thing—as Pliny is the authority in Chapter 1 of Book 24 that gum is easily washed away with vinegar—or because the sluggish senses of men are excited by vinegar and receive greater vigor. Hence "to have vinegar in the breast" is a proverb of Plautus used for men of the highest prudence. *Gradensis* from *Grecia*, as *Sardiniensis* and *Hispaniensis* from Sardinia and Spain. "Perpetual epithets" are those which always suit their substantives, such as "hot fire" or "wicked usury." <note>original: "Ομφακα μασομ"</note> "Chewing unripe grapes" in the first epigram. <note>original: "μορομ μοροδ"</note> "Fate, fate" in the last epigram. "You will hear well," that is, you will be praised. "To see the back and the breast," that is, you will precede and surpass. "That his flanks may burst," etc. These are the words of the Virgilian shepherd Thyrsis from the seventh Eclogue: "Arcadian shepherds," he says, "adorn the rising poet, so that Codrus's flanks may burst with envy." But he understands Codrus as another shepherd. Do not think it was said of the King of Athens. <note>original: "Σειριοσ"</note> Sirius is a star in the mouth of the Dog, which rises around the eighth day before the Kalends of July <note>Late June</note>; once risen, it often causes pestilence for the whole year, often for a few days, and sometimes it is born harmless. For according to the power of the adjacent stars, it is either overcome or its strength is diminished, as Servius says. Virgil in *Aeneid* Book X: "Or the heat of Sirius. That star, bringing thirst and diseases to weary mortals, is born and saddens the sky with its sinister light." The same in Book III: "Then Sirius began to scorch the sterile fields. The grass withered and the sickly crop denied sustenance." The same in the fourth book of the *Georgics*: "Now rapid Sirius, parching the thirsty Indians, was burning in the sky; and the fiery sun had consumed the middle of the world; the grass withered, and the hollow rivers, warmed in their dry beds, were cooked to mud." These are the "Sirian days," which the common people call the "dog days." For the Dog of Orion (which some call Sirius) is placed among the stars; it has one star on its tongue, which is called the Dog. On its head is another, which Isis is thought to have established in her own name and called *Sirion* because of the brightness of its flame, which is such that it seems to shine beyond the others. Hyginus is the authority. For <note>original: "σειριαω"</note> *seiriao* means "I shine." <note>original: "γουνατα"</note> *Gounata*, that is, knees. For in firm and strong knees there is no small firmness of strength. Hesiod: These are the words of Hesiod from the second book titled *Works and Days*. <margin>It is in Book I of *On the Laws*.</margin> <margin>Sluggish.</margin> <margin>The particle *se* taken by apposition.</margin> <margin>Washed with biting vinegar, etc.</margin> <margin>Sirius.</margin>

ASCENSIUS: In great matters. This has been sufficiently explained by Sylvius. However, when he says that *se* was in use by the ancients through apposition, understand this as "without composition" <note>meaning as a standalone word rather than a prefix</note>; although Donatus places it as inseparable. For he does not place a distinction between a preposition and an apposition, though it is manifest. One should look not so much at the meaning of the cited verses as at their composition; nevertheless, the interpretation is placed in the margin.

Antonius Codrus Urceus to Angelo Poliziano. Health and Greetings.
Letter X.

# .IIII. Of Illustrious Men

<margin>i.e., Let it not be, or let it be absent.</margin>
<margin>The first is a poem of Hesiod, Book 2, titled *Works and Days*.</margin>
<margin>i.e., The Pleiades, born of Atlas, rising.</margin>
<margin>i.e., Tell me, Muse, of the man of many devices, who wandered very much, etc. <note>original: "ἄνδρα μοὶ ἔννεπε μοῦσα πολύτροπον: ὃς μάλα πολλά" - the opening of Homer's Odyssey.</note></margin>

**I**n the great heats of July, your letter was delivered to me, most learned Angelo: in which you did not find it burdensome to send me a few Greek epigrams out of the many you had composed, which vie with both Greek and Latin ones. I cannot find words to thank you for such a prompt and liberal spirit toward me. For you have given to me, in my old age, something to compare and something to learn by comparing. And certainly, you seemed to me both a most polished Latin man and a most eloquent Greek. But as for what you wrote—that you had thought of publishing the little book of epigrams itself, provided I did not disagree—what is there that could be done, or said, or thought by Poliziano, in which Codrus <note>The author, Francesco Silvio, often referred to himself by the academic nickname "Codrus."</note> would disagree? Indeed, I am not so sluggish, nor do I so please myself, that I would step forward only when enticed by your words, or exult like a crested cock at those singing. Shall I, endowed with very little learning and mediocre talent, give advice to you, a man most skilled in every kind of doctrine? **May it not be.** <note>original: "μὴ γένοιτο" (me genoito) - a strong Greek negation often translated as "God forbid."</note> And certainly I wondered not a little what reason exhorted you to write this: unless perhaps my singular love toward you and the somewhat numerous years of my life moved you. If that is so, I will gladly write what I feel, yet on this condition: that if anything unpolished or unpleasant here should offend your ears (which are washed with biting vinegar <note>A metaphor for a sharp, critical, and refined palate or ear.</note>), you should accuse not me, but yourself, who awakened one who was silent and almost asleep. I have therefore compared, as you commanded, your epigrams with the Greek ones. And I am so far from wishing to find fault with the Greek ones that I approve of them greatly. Truly, in your verses, I know not what more of grace and sweetness seems to be present to me: which can be felt more than it can be demonstrated. Furthermore, I do not deny that hexameter verses composed of few but rather long parts preserve their own authority in their time: such as is found in Hesiod, **the Pleiades born of Atlas rising**, <note>original: "πλικιάδων ἀτλαγενέων ἐπιτελομενάων"</note> and in Virgil, *The Muse of the shepherds Damon and Alphesiboeus*, and many others of that kind among both Greek and our own [Latin] poets. But surely little verses compacted of many words, overflowing with dactyls <note>A metrical foot consisting of one long syllable followed by two short ones, creating a "galloping" rhythm.</note>, are in my judgment to be considered more elegant, more rounded, and running more smoothly, such as: **Tell me, Muse, of the man of many devices, who wandered very much**, and *If anyone among this people does not know the art of loving, let him read me, and having read the poem, let him love as one learned.* And this appears especially in elegies or epigrams. In pentameters, indeed, I gladly hear long words: such as **the one rising from the sea**, and **as the Spartan**. For they have, I know not how, the manner of Greek custom. Finally, how much ornament and grace epithets provide to verses—not only the perpetual ones, but also those newly devised—and sharp sentiments, no one who is unlearned fails to understand. In your verses, to return to you, all these things are found. For they are read and scanned with many parts fittingly cohering and with frequent dactyls, and they are concluded with sentiments perhaps sharper than the Greek verses. How much do you think that epithet **unripe breast** <note>original: "ὄμφακα μασόν" (omphaka mason)</note> moved me? And that varied likeness **death of death** <note>original: "μόρον μόρου" (moron morou)</note> and many other things of that kind! Which contain within themselves manifold learning and pleasure. But with what words shall I praise that sentiment which you used at the end of the *Venus Rising from the Sea*, where you wrote: *if Mars, when bound, had possessed such a Venus, he would never have wished to be loosed from the chains of Vulcan?* My venerable Angelo, I do not flatter you: but I speak from my heart. In other things indeed you are not inferior to the Greeks; in this truly you are even (as I feel) superior. Therefore, I do not only exhort you to publish what you have written: but I ask and entreat you. Publish, publish as quickly as possible: so that both you may enjoy glory and the students of letters may enjoy your learning. For whether you summon or provoke to writing those whom you know, or do not, you will be well spoken of by all and praised exceedingly. But it will be permitted to those running with you in this race (believe me) to see your back rather than your chest. And if no other cause moved you to this edition, even this ought to impel you: *that the flanks may be burst*—I do not say of Codrus, who is yours—but of those whom I certainly do not see, but whom you perhaps know are not your friends; so that they may understand that what you have already done in Latin, you are no less able to do in Greek: both to benefit the unlearned and to delight the learned exceedingly. And finally, if you do not wish to bring them forth for others: bring them forth for me, who am, as I always shall be, a diligent reader and promoter of your affairs. But let these things suffice, especially in these heats: which, I know not how, deal harshly with you, and certainly with us: **since Sirius parches the head and the knees**, <note>original: "ἐπεὶ κεφαλὴν καὶ γούνατα σείριος ἄζει" - a reference to the "Dog Days" of summer when the star Sirius rises.</note> as Hesiod writes. Farewell: and remember that we expect an entire volume of Greek epigrams. I commend myself to you: and if Pico, our prince <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous Renaissance philosopher.</note>, is there: intimate to him that I am his servant. At Bologna. The fifth day of July. 1484.
FRANCESCO SILVIO.

There are, moreover, those who say that Justinian himself wrote elegantly on the incarnation of the Lord; he also took care to have built at his own expense and by his command in Constantinople a temple in honor of God the Father (for the Son of the Father is Wisdom), namely Saint Sophia, than which there is none greater in the world. ->[Marginal note: The Temple of Sophia.]<- These things are from Platina <note>Bartolomeo Platina, a Renaissance humanist and papal librarian.</note>. But since he says that Justinian was outstanding in learning, I should not regret adding here what our friend Budé <note>Guillaume Budé, a famous French humanist scholar of law.</note> says in opposition to this opinion. His words are from his annotations on the books of the Pandects. Justinian (he says), Emperor of the Romans, was above all orthodox. ->[Marginal note: Memory of Justinian's expertise in letters.]<- He was devoid of all literature, and even (as they say) illiterate. Those who do not even know their elementary letters are called "analphabeti" by the Greeks, which Fulgentius calls "abecedarian" in the third book of his *Mythologies*. Yet this is the man who is believed to have had all laws stored in his breast: and also to have had all antiquity in a sort of storehouse, so that nothing in the volumes of civil law should differ even by a tiny bit. These are his words. Regarding Tribonian, the architect of the laws (as we were saying), the same Budé writes there on the authority of Suidas. Tribonian (he says), a Greek by nation, was a despiser of all religion, and truly was especially averse to the Christian faith. ->[Marginal note: Tribonian the jurisconsult.]<- A flatterer and fraudulent, as one who persuaded Justinian that he would not face death, but would be taken up into heaven with his flesh. He was Justinian's Quaestor, endowed with such force of intellect that he emerged most outstanding in learning, and was second to none in his age. However, he indulged in avarice to such an extent that he always thought the law should be held for sale for profit. For he had established the practice of annulling and proposing laws almost daily through foul selling, according as it was convenient for anyone. Although he survived a long time after attaining honor, he finally died of disease, having suffered no trouble from anyone. For he was charming in speech and otherwise sweet, and could easily overshadow the disease of avarice with the excellence of his learning.

In the preface of the *Institutions*, it is recorded how Tribonian, Theophilus, and Dorotheus received the mandate from Justinian. Paulus Diaconus, in the seventeenth chapter of the first book of the *History of the Lombards*, enumerates how many books of laws Justinian had written. ->[Marginal note: How many books of laws Justinian published.]<- He contracted (he says) the constitutions of the Princes into twelve books. He wanted that volume to be called the *Justinian Code*. Then he reduced the laws of individual magistrates, judges, and jurisconsults within the number of fifty books, and called that code the *Digests* or *Pandects*. He composed a new work, the four books of the *Institutions*, in which he briefly comprised the text of all the laws, and reduced the new laws which he himself had established into one volume, and decreed that same code be called the *Novels*. Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano, an Italian humanist scholar.</note>, in the eighty-fourth chapter of his *Miscellanies*, left it written that Justinian's *Institutions* were translated into the Greek tongue as *Centones*. ->[Marginal note: Centones.]<- What the Greeks write as *kentrōnas* are garments stitched together from various scraps and sometimes even different colors. By a certain similarity, they are spoken of regarding many other things. As "stuffed patchwork" is a proverb against those who sew lies upon lies. Plautus in *Epidicus*: "Look for someone else for whom you may stuff your patchwork." Likewise, those poems which are composed from fragments of different poems summoned from here and there are called *Centones*. Such is the *Nuptial Cento* of Ausonius to Paulinus. Such are the *Centones* of Proba Falconia on the New and Old Testament made from Virgil's poems. Therefore, Poliziano calls the books of the *Digests* "Centones," in which not only the opinions but the very words of the authors are stitched together.

Ancient and... Pomponius the jurisconsult enumerates many others before this Mucius, son of Publius, who were famous for their knowledge of civil law, as his words are cited in the first book of the *Digests*. First was Papyrius in the age of Tarquin the Proud, who collected the royal laws, which had been passed without order, into one. ->[Marginal note: Why Civil Law was called Papyrian.]<- From him, the civil law was called "Papyrian." Then Appius Claudius, one of the Decemvirs, whose counsel was greatest in writing the Twelve Tables. After him, Appius Claudius of the same family, who dissuaded the city from receiving Pyrrhus. After him, Sempronius, whom the Roman people first called "the Wise." After him, C. Scipio Nasica, who, having been called "the Best" by the Senate, was given a house publicly on the Sacred Way so that he could be consulted more easily. Then Q. Mucius, he who as a legate offered the Carthaginians two tokens: one of peace and the other of war. Likewise Tiberius Coruncanius, who first began to profess law publicly. After him Sextus Caecilius, and his brother P. Aelius, whom Ennius praises; and P. Attilius, son of Caesius, who was first called "the Wise" by the people. Then M. Cato, the leader of the Porcian family. Afterward P. Mucius, the Chief Pontiff, Brutus, Manilius, P. Rutilius Rufus, Paulus Virginius, Q. Tubero, Sextus Pompeius (uncle of Gnaeus Pompeius), and Caelius Antipater, who devoted more effort to eloquence than to the knowledge of civil law. L. Crassus, brother of P. Mucius, who was likewise called Mucius, whom Cicero says was the most eloquent of the jurisconsults. After these, Q. Mucius, son of Publius, Chief Pontiff. For as Marsus says in the commentaries on Cicero's *Offices*, the family of the Mucii held civil law as if by inheritance. "P. F." means "Son of Publius," as Valerius Probus says in his book on interpreting Roman names. Otherwise, "P. F." is said to mean "Pious and Fortunate" by the same author. Mention of him and of the other Mucius is not infrequent in Cicero's *Topics*, *Laelius*, and other books. And in the first book of *Offices*: "Those whose fathers (he says) or ancestors excelled in some glory, most of them strive to excel in that kind of praise. As Q. Mucius, son of Publius, in civil law." These are Cicero's words, from which you may easily understand that this Mucius was not the most ancient of the jurisconsults. Only one book, etc. Pomponius Laetus and Volaterranus were persuaded that Mucius, son of Publius, reduced civil law into eighteen books. Then Aquilius Gallus. He was a disciple of Mucius Scaevola, son of Publius, as Pomponius records. "Intimate friend"—the words are Cicero's from the *Topics*. "Aquilius, my colleague and intimate friend (he says), when dealing with shores—all of which you wish to be public—because it pertained to what a shore was, used to define it thus: where the wave plays." This is as if one wished to define youth as the flower of age, and old age as the setting of life. ->[Marginal note: Pithanon.]<- *Pithanon*, etc. <note>original: "πιανοῦ"</note>—that is, "probable" or "likely." The interpreters of St. Augustine, in the eleventh chapter of the second book of *The City of God*, recorded that Labeo wrote other books—that is, forty volumes. Aulus Gellius, in the twelfth chapter of the first book, is the authority that he wrote commentaries on the Twelve Tables. Labeo divided the year so that he taught in Rome for six months and withdrew from the city for the remaining six to devote his effort to writing books. Pomponius the jurisconsult is the authority. Horace calls him "insane." Horace's words are from the first book of *Satires*: "If anyone should crucify a slave who, ordered to remove a dish, licked up the half-eaten fish and warm sauce, he would be called more insane than Labeo among the sane." ->[Marginal note: Antistius Labeo.]<- Antistius Labeo (as Acron and Porphyrio mention), not unmindful of the ancient liberty in which he was born, inveighed against Augustus Caesar as the oppressor of that liberty during the triumvirate. Wherefore Horace, flattering Augustus, calls Labeo insane. But it would not be absurd for Labeo to have been called insane by Horace because of that defiant response. For when Augustus had chosen Marcus Lepidus, an exile, as a triumvir, he asked Antistius Labeo whether there were others more worthy; to which he replied that every man has his own judgment, as Suetonius is the authority in the *Life of Augustus Caesar*. Appian, in the fourth book of the *Civil Wars*, records that the name of this Labeo was famous for his experience, and that his father Labeo was illustrious for the name of wisdom. Aulus Gellius writes many things. The words of Aulus Gellius are from the tenth chapter of the thirteenth book. Labeo (he says), Antistius, practiced the discipline of civil law with primary zeal and gave public responses to those consulting on the law. He was not devoid of other good arts; he had penetrated into grammar and dialectic, and more ancient and profound literature; and he had mastered the origins and reasons of Latin words. He used that knowledge especially for unraveling many snares of the law. There are even books published after his death which are inscribed as *Posthumous*. Of these, I have held three books—the thirty-eighth, thirty-ninth, and fortieth—which are full of that kind of matter leading to the narration and illustration of the Latin language. These are Gellius's words. Also of Salvius Julianus, etc. Poliziano says this Julian was the brother of the Emperor Didius or (as others say) Didymus. However, Eusebius in his *Annals* records that the Emperor Pertinax was killed in the palace by the faction of Julian the jurisconsult, and Julian himself was killed by Severus...

<meta>This page continues the commentary on legal history and the origins of the Pandects (Digest), specifically focusing on the jurists whose works were compiled under Emperor Justinian.</meta>

**Book of Letters. V. Folio L.**

[Marginal notes, printed:]
<term>Twelve Tables</term><note>original: Dodecadeltos</note>.
<term>Symbol</term><note>original: Symbolũ</note>.
<term>Nomenclator</term>.
<term>Givers</term><note>original: Munifices</note>.

The Emperor <note>likely Alexander Severus, based on the mention of Ulpian and Paul</note>, having been created for the purpose of restoring the republic, applied his mind to fixing the state which had been weakened by the vice of previous princes. He had as assistants in this matter Julius Frontinus, a most learned man, and Ulpian and Paul, men most outstanding in civil law, as Platina is the author. The advocacy of the jurisconsult <term>Massurius Sabinus</term> is frequent in the books of Gellius; Pomponius Laetus records that he succeeded Atteius Capito. Volaterranus mentions the jurisconsult Pomponius. Boethius, in the third book of his commentaries on Cicero’s *Topics*, summons the jurisconsult Gaius when he describes what a "nexus" <note>a legal bond or obligation</note> is. Likewise, he mentions the "cession in court" <note>in iure cessio</note> citing Gaius as the authority. <term>Dodecadelti</term> means the Twelve Tables, for *deltos* means a tablet in Greek. *Symbole* or *symbolon* is called a "mark" or "sign" in Latin, as Cicero mentions in the *Topics*. A <term>Symbolum</term> is also a contribution, that is, that which many people bring together into one. For example, the common people call a contribution to a dinner a "scot" <note>a payment or tax</note>. We call the <term>Apostles' Creed</term> that very contribution of the Apostles in which the articles of our faith are contained. By the same reasoning, these founders of the laws are said to have contributed a "symbol" to Justinian’s *Pandects*. For from each individual, several parts were taken, from which the book of the *Pandects* was made as if sewn together. From the author comes <term>nomenclatura</term>, that is, a very exact calling out of the names from which the *Pandects* consist. The Romans who had a large multitude of slaves used to have <term>Nomenclators</term> who would *calare*, that is, call out the names of individual slaves so that none might escape. You would call him a "Nomenclator" in Latin rather than a "roll-bearer" <note>rotuligerum</note> who calls out the names of fellow students in classes. "Those who are entirely immune etc." means that the names of many besides those mentioned above are cited, but in corrupted and faulty manuscripts, the names are counterfeit. A <term>Munificus</term> or <term>Munifex</term> is one who provides a gift or service. Therefore, they are not "Givers" <note>Munifices</note> of the *Pandects* whose false names have been substituted for true ones in faulty manuscripts.

**CASCEN.**
*You asked.* The first words of the letter indicate the subject matter. *Since I have put you off longer.* A novel but scholarly way of saying "I have put you off," that is: your expectation, or you from the things expected. *With a little interest* <note>foenufculo</note>, that is, a small accessory gain, because he is going to give more than he had promised. *Centrones* <note>patchwork garments</note>: I found it written thus. However, Sylvius seems to have read it as *Centones*. <term>Munifices</term> are those who perform *munia*, that is, duties, and contribute services to the republic.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giacomo Modesto of Prato. Greetings.** [Marginal note, handwritten: Legal seasonings for studies]
**Letter XI.**

[Large initial R] You have asked me quite often to collect for you the names of the ancient founders of the law—not those who are cited by others, but those whose own words stand as laws in the *Digests* of the Prince Justinian, [Marginal note, handwritten: pandects] which we also call the *Pandects*. Indeed, because I have put you off longer than perhaps your singular love toward me deserved, [Marginal note, handwritten: Books of the Digests] lest that delay be without a little interest, I shall also write out for you the titles and the number of books from which the fifty volumes of the *Digests* are patched together. For I want to add this for you as well, as if it were a seasoning for your studies. I am uniquely glad that you are putting much effort into these and making much progress, as your teachers often tell me. For since you have been nourished in our home from boyhood, and I have always approved of your talent, character, mind, and loyalty, I think of almost nothing of yours as separate from me, and I embrace your praises just as my own. But to return to the matter: there were thirty-seven founders of the law in total, [Marginal note, printed: 37 Founders of law.] from whose words the laws of the *Digests* are sewn together like certain patchwork garments <note>centrones</note>. And mention of some of these is in the title "On the Origin of Law," which I do not give to you as payment, because it is already "in your bronze" <note>a Latin idiom meaning 'on your account' or already known to you</note>. The oldest of all, as it seems to me, is Quintus Mucius Scaevola, [Marginal note, printed: Q. Mucius.] the Pontifex Maximus. There is very frequent mention of him in Cicero as well. Only one of his books, *On Definitions*, is summoned here. Then comes Gallus Aquilius, [Marginal note, printed: Gallus Aquilius.] who heard Cicero pleading as a judge, and whom the same Cicero calls his intimate friend in the *Topics*. The *Digests* are watered only by his "responses." From Labeo, however, eight books of *Pithanon* [Marginal note, printed: Pithanon Labeo. Gellius book 14: chapter 10] are adopted—that is, of "probables" or "verisimilitudes"—and likewise ten of his *Posthumous Works*. This was the Labeo whom Horace calls "insane," about whose talent, nature, studies, and learning Gellius writes much in *Attic Nights*. There are also ninety books of the *Digests* by Salvius Julianus; [Marginal note, printed: Salvius Julianus.] one on ambiguities; six to Minutius; four to Urseius. He flourished in the times of Hadrian and was on the council for judging; a man of great authority, and also the uncle of Didius Julianus, who was later prince. They also summon fifteen books of "Rules" by Neratius Priscus, [Marginal note, printed: Neratius Priscus.] seven of "Parchments," and three of "Responses." Trajan is thought to have intended him as his successor by the consensus of his friends, so much so that he said to him once: "I commend the provinces to you, if anything fatal should happen to me"; and the Emperor Hadrian soon after held the same man on his council. Volusius Maetianus was also held as a famous jurisconsult, [Marginal note, printed: Volusius Maetianus.] whom the same Hadrian used much, and who taught the Prince Marcus Antoninus, surnamed the Philosopher. Therefore, sixteen of his books on "Trusts" [Marginal note, handwritten: the place is corrected] and fourteen on "Public Matters" come here. But the name of Maetianus is corrupted into "Martianus" by the scribes. For [Marginal note, printed: Martianus. Monobiblos] Martianus himself was also an author of law, ordered to be killed by the Prince Didius Julianus; he contributed sixteen books of "Institutes" here, five of "Rules," two "On Appeals," and two of "Public Matters." Likewise, single volumes, which the Greeks call *monobiblos*, under these titles: *On Informers*, *On Mortgages*, and *On the Turpilian Decree of the Senate*. Julius Celsus was also on the council for Hadrian; [Marginal note, printed: Julius Celsus.] he composed thirty-nine books of *Digests*. Also Valens, who wrote seven on "Trusts." Also Marcellus, [Marginal note, printed: Valens Marcellus.] who wrote thirty-one of *Digests*, one of "Responses," and six on "Laws." Likewise Javolenus, [Marginal note, printed: Javolenus.] whose books summoned here are...

**The Commentaries of Franciscus Sylvius on the Sixth Letter of Angelo Poliziano.**

**A**utographs: that is, one's own copies. For in Greek, *autographois* <note>original: "αυτογραφοις"</note> is said of that which is written by one's own hand. They "excepted": <margin>Autograph.</margin> that is, they wrote down. Note that *excipere* <note>to except/receive/take down</note> is a polysemous word—that is, a word signifying many things; <margin>Excipere.</margin> it signifies "to receive" what is falling. Virgil in the third book of the *Aeneid*: "Alas, what chance receives you, deprived of so great a husband?" But writing "receives" the falling voice. "We deny that by Virgil," etc. These are the words of Statius. But we also read the *Cultex* <note>The Gnat</note>. Domitius says: the *Cultex* is a work of Virgil, where he laments the death of a shepherd's gnat, which he composed while young and unrefined. In the commentaries on Virgil, Domitius feels otherwise. Domitius doubted concerning the Homeric hymns. He says: we read the hymns of Homer to the gods, of which Pausanias often uses the testimony. I, <margin>Whether the hymns commonly circulated are by Homer.</margin> however, would affirm by the certain authority of Greek monuments that the work is not by Homer the poet whom we venerate, but by another who is called Homer Sellius the grammarian. For he wrote the hymns. Thus far Domitius. Volaterranus and Archilochus in the eighth book *On Times* remember that there were two Homers. Diodorus Siculus in the fifth book of his *Library* calls upon Homer in the hymns: whom he thinks to be that most famous one among the Greeks. Therefore we do not depart from the opinion of Poliziano. But Plutarch pulls us back to the opinion of Domitius, for in the *Life of Homer* he hands down that Homer wrote two poems, the *Iliad* and the *Odyssey*. And he affirms that those are in error who say the *Battle of the Frogs and Mice* <margin>Batracomyomachia.</margin> and the *Margites* were composed by him for the sake of exercise. Statius: "The steep house of the Daci saw him astonished." Domitius: "The astonished Dacians." For he was struck dumb when conquered, though he thought himself safe. Which interpretation I <margin>The expeditions of Domitian.</margin> think should not be entirely exploded. For Eutropius writes in the seventh book of *Roman Deeds* that there were two expeditions by Domitian against the Dacians, from which he received very heavy calamities. For Appius Sabinus and Cornelius Fuscus the prefect were killed with great and numerous armies. And so Diurpaneus, king of the Dacians, thought himself safe by a double victory, but in the end he was overcome. Or "astonished": that is, marvelling stupidly. "Cato about to go to the camps." Statius: "With you bearing the standards, both the lesser son-in-law and Cato would go into the laws of the camp." Domitius: "With you bearing the standards." If you had been the leader in the camp, the Caesarian son-in-law—that is, Pompey—would go into the laws: that is, would come into your treaties. "Cato from the camp." Cato (he says) would depart from the camp, which he did not do when Pompey was defeated. For he attempted to collect the Pompeian remnants and <margin>A passage of Statius.</margin> prepare them against Caesar. These are the words of Domitius. In which, if he erred, the error detected is very small. But without doubt you may interpret more coherently with poetic locution: "Cato goes to the camps": that is, into your camps, and into your jurisdiction, as "a shout goes to heaven." "Pellean waxes," etc. Statius: "Enjoy the perpetual gift of the people and the great senate: the Apellean waxes would desire to paint you." Domitius says: "The Apellean waxes would desire": Apelles would have had so glorious a subject for his art—

Taras was the son of Neptune, who first founded Tarentum, which was named after him. Laetus <note>Pomponius Laetus, a 15th-century Italian humanist</note> reads this in my codex. Beroaldus <note>Filippo Beroaldo, a famous scholar of the 1400s</note> records in his wedding oration that five torches made of white-thorn were used for brides. But we are coming to the matter at hand. This is the first "problem" of Plutarch: "Why is it," he asks, "that when a new bride is given in marriage, she is commanded to touch fire and water?"

**FRANC. SYL.** <note>Likely the commentator Franciscus Sylvius</note>
On Authority. Cicero writes not a few things regarding authority that are not unworthy of being known. One should not regret having transcribed his words here. <margin>Authority:</margin> These are from the book *Topica*. To create belief (he says), authority is sought. But authority is brought about by either nature or time. The authority of nature is greatest in virtue. In time, however, there are many things that bring authority: genius, wealth, age, fortune, art, experience, necessity, and even sometimes a concurrence of fortuitous events. For they think that the gifted, the wealthy, and those proven by the span of age are worthy of being believed. Perhaps not rightly, but the opinion of the common folk can hardly be changed, and both those who judge and those who form opinions direct everything toward it. For those who excel in these things I have mentioned seem to excel in virtue itself—that is, in the testimony of those things I just enumerated. Although there is no appearance of virtue in them, nevertheless, belief is sometimes confirmed if a certain art is applied. For knowledge or experience has great power for persuasion. For mostly, those who are experienced are believed. Necessity also creates belief, which arises both from bodies and from minds. For those exhausted by lashes, tortures, and fire—what they say, truth itself seems to say. And those things also caused by disturbances of the mind: pain, desire, anger, fear; because they have the force of necessity, they bring authority and belief. To this class also belong those states from which truth is sometimes found: childhood, sleep, imprudence, drunkenness, insanity. For the small often judge something while ignorant of what it pertains to. And through sleep, wine, and insanity, many things have often been revealed. Many have also blundered imprudently into hateful matters, as happened recently to Staterio <margin>Others say Stagerius.</margin>, who spoke certain things while good men were listening behind a partition; when these things were revealed and brought into judgment, he was rightly condemned for a capital crime. We have heard a similar thing regarding Pausanias the Spartan. A concurrence of fortuitous events is such as if someone happened to intervene by chance when something was being done or said that should not have been brought forth. In this category is also that multitude of suspicions of treason cast upon Palamedes. Truth can sometimes hardly refute this kind of thing. To this category also belongs "common report," which is a kind of testimony of the multitude. But those things which create belief through virtue are two-fold: one of which prevails by nature, the other by industry. For the virtue of the Gods excels by nature, but that of men by industry. These are the words of Cicero. The words of Augustine are from a certain letter to Saint Jerome. <margin>What reverence Augustine paid to the Canonical scriptures.</margin> I have learned (he says) to defer this honor only to the books of the scriptures which are called "canonical": that I most firmly believe no author of them erred in anything while writing. Others, however, I read in such a way that, no matter how much they may excel in holiness and doctrine, I do not therefore think a thing is true because they themselves felt or wrote it so. "The rising sun," etc. More people worship the rising sun than the setting sun. This is a proverbial sentiment used regarding the beginnings of honorable things, which are to be preferred over ancient and falling things. <margin>Cn. Pompey. More worship the rising sun.</margin> When Gnaeus Pompey returned to Rome after bravely defeating Domitius in Libya, he was pleasantly received with several honors by Lucius Sulla, and was first called "The Great" by him. Nevertheless, because he was not yet a senator, a triumph was denied to him. Pompey is said to have said to those who were present: "Sulla does not know that more people worship the rising sun than the set..."

.III.I.O Of Illustrious Men

### Philip Beroaldo sends greetings to his friend Angelo Poliziano.

<note>Philip Beroaldo (1453–1505) was a leading humanist scholar in Bologna. Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was the preeminent poet and scholar of the Medici circle in Florence.</note>

See, my most refined Poliziano, how I regard you in our shared studies—and indeed, most deservedly so. Whatever is brought forth from that brilliant workshop of yours, I am fully persuaded that it is all upright, polished, and free of blemish. Indeed (such is your curiosity and excellence in letters), even if something slightly unrefined had slipped out through oversight while you were still a youth, it would nevertheless be considered most perfect by me and others who judge well, for the very reason that it came from Poliziano. For your fame and reputation have long been so great that you are able to give brilliance to the obsolete, grace to the loathed, and authority to the new. To conclude: such is my reverence for your studies that I am accustomed to grant you the same honor that Saint Augustine <note>Augustine of Hippo, who argued for the infallible authority of the canonical scriptures.</note> claims to have paid to the canonical writers: I would never dare believe your work to be anywhere near error. This judgment does not spring from love; rather, love springs from judgment. Six hundred students are my witnesses; that pulpit from which I profess daily is my witness: I am repeatedly the herald and trumpeter of your singular erudition. Why say more? Publicly, privately, at home, abroad, in the literary gymnasium <note>term: gymnasium (a university or place of higher learning)</note>, outside the gymnasium, in every place, among every people, at all times: Poliziano is extolled and celebrated by Beroaldo with most deserved praise. Your virtue has made me your friend.

I read with pleasure what you wrote to me so affectionately and dutifully. I read with even greater pleasure what you composed so eloquently and wisely against Merula <note>Giorgio Merula (c. 1430–1494), a rival scholar known for his bitter feuds with other humanists.</note>. 

<margin>A taunt against Merula.</margin>

He had already adopted for himself a nickname like Zoilus <note>term: Zoilus (an ancient critic known as the "scourge of Homer," used here to mean a spiteful, nitpicking critic)</note>; he who sharpened against all the learned men of our age—not his teeth, for he was toothless—but his vibrating, poisonous tongue. He was a man who could not bear to see virtue blossoming in the young. He, who was most skillfully formed for speaking evil, used to groan—or rather, to speak more truly, he used to burst with rage—because the rising sun <note>A reference to the younger Poliziano.</note> was already being adored by almost everyone more than the setting sun <note>A reference to the aging Merula.</note>. The death of the man declared how pleasing he was to all. Indeed, it seems Merula was "born of joy," for all mortals rejoice at his passing. 

As far as I am concerned, I wish he were still alive; I wish he had brought forth those most criminal "annotations" which he is said to have been in labor with for a long time against me. Then, the battle between the veteran and the recruit would have been a sight to see! Perhaps, just perhaps, he would have learned that he had provoked a horned beast, that he had bitten one who would bite back, and that "blood follows from our wound" <note>A poetic way of saying that Beroaldo is capable of drawing blood in a literary fight.</note>. For my sword is not blunt, nor is my pen dull. But if his writings against us are published now that he is dead, we shall be forced to take up the contest against a dead man and strike back in retaliation—though it does not escape me...

The Living Voice

# Book of Letters. VI. Folio 54.

CASCEN.
**He would have perished, had he not perished.** <note>Latin: *Perierat nisi perijsset.* A famous paradox regarding the preservation of a reputation through a timely death or a strategic loss.</note> Sylvius explains this learnedly and as if from the very source. But if anyone still seeks the meaning: it seems to me to be unique and clear in the saying of Poliziano: Merula <note>Giorgio Merula (1430–1494), a rival humanist scholar.</note> is overwhelmed, namely by shame and confusion, when he recognized his errors pointed out by Poliziano; "had he not perished," that is, by death. In the saying of Themistocles, however, it can be seen as twofold. One: we would have perished by death or captivity, since the wealth of Xerxes is so great, had we not "perished" as if by the exile imposed by the citizens. The other: since the splendor of Xerxes' tables is so great, we would have surely perished in want and hunger among our own people, had we not "perished," that is, unless we had betaken ourselves here as if lost men.

Angelo Poliziano to his friend Filippo Beroaldo, greetings. May 3rd.
**A**s God is my witness, your love toward me needs no proof: it was won by a similarity of studies and strengthened by many kindnesses. So much so, that those who come from Bologna to Florence immediately, as if by a solemn rite, count themselves among your cohort so that they may better prove themselves to me. I wish, however, that you could praise me as truly as you are accustomed to do so fully. Although this very thing—to be praised by you—is a praise (as it seems to me at least) not only ample but also true. I am glad, moreover, that what I wrote to Merula pleased you; I wish he had not been snatched from us so suddenly. We would have tested to the touchstone <note>original: *ad obrusam* — a technical term for testing the purity of gold.</note> whatever he had ever committed to letters. And I think (let this be said with modesty) **Merula would have perished, had he not perished.** Now it is not pleasing to pursue his ashes and bones, even if it were permitted. Nor is there any reason for us to expect any of his writings as if they were posthumous: "He deluded the gaping crows" <note>A reference to Horace, meaning he cheated those waiting for an inheritance.</note>; for neither his *Centuries* nor his *Plautine Questions* appear anywhere. Thus did that charming man impose upon posterity. He was entirely worthy, nevertheless, of us professors not despising him, had he himself not despised all professors. Furthermore, as for the notes which a certain necessity extorted from us while we were almost holding them back: it will be handled quite famously with me if they seem to savor of boyhood <note>original: *pueritiam*</note> but not also of puerility <note>original: *puerilitatem*</note>. Farewell. Florence, April 23, 1494.

F.S. **Oracles** (as Cicero says in the book of *Topics*) are so called from this very fact: that the speech of the gods is in them. Gellius writes: When Alexander (who had been his disciple), having learned that the books of Aristotle had been published by him to the common people—and at that time he held nearly all of Asia with his arms and army, and was pressing King Darius himself with battles and victories—nevertheless, in the midst of such great affairs, he sent a letter to Aristotle. He said that Aristotle had not done rightly because he had made public the **acroamatic** <note>original: *ακροαματικασ* — referring to "esoteric" or "oral" teachings meant for a private audience.</note> disciplines (for so he calls the "listening" books) in which he himself had been instructed by him, by publishing the books abroad. "For in what other thing," he said, "shall we be able to excel the rest, if those things which we received from you become common to all?" Indeed, I would prefer to excel in learning than in resources and wealth. Aristotle wrote back to him to this effect: "Know that the acroamatic books, which you complain were published, and not hidden away like secrets, are neither published nor not published. Since they will be recognizable only to those who hear us." These things are from Aulus Gellius, chapter 4 of the twentieth book. **The living voice** <note>original: *ζωσα φωνη* / *viua vox*</note>. "The living voice" is a proverb signifying that the voice and the very pronunciation of the teacher have much more liveliness and energy than the writing of another or of oneself. Quintilian, in the second book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: "For although reading supplies enough examples for imitation, nevertheless that **living voice** (as he says) nourishes more fully, especially that of the teacher, whom the students, if they are rightly instructed, both love and revere." Pliny the Younger in a certain letter to his nephew: "Besides, the living voice (as is commonly said) affects one more." Saint Jerome in his general preface: "The living voice has I know not what hidden energy, and sounding more strongly when poured from the mouth of the teacher into the ears of the disciple." These and other things are from Erasmus. **Vermiculated works** <note>original: *Vermiculata opera*</note> are those which are variegated with very tiny pieces. He calls it a "vermiculated interweaving" because it is colored with a variety of elegance. **A woman's world** <note>original: *Mundus muliebris*</note> is all the adornment of a woman, which is called *kosmos* <note>original: *κοσμοσ*</note> by the Greeks. **The Coronis** <note>original: *Coronidem*</note>, that is, the end. For a *koronis* <note>original: *κορωνισ*</note> is the prow of a ship, a curved horn, an extremity, an end, a peak. Therefore, "from the preface to that final coronis," that is, from the beginning to the end. For Poliziano mentions the *coronis* at the end of his *Miscellanies*. "But as this book," he says, "although thus also too long, let it nevertheless be crowned with some sort of coronis." **Like that Africa.** In Africa there is a very great lack of water; for that reason many wild beasts gather at the few rivers. Therefore, the males mingle with females of every kind, either by force or for pleasure. Whence also the common Greek saying: **Africa always brings forth something new.** The author is Pliny, chapter 16 of the eighth book. **Corollary**, that is, an addition. A corollary (as Marcus Varro writes in the fourth book of *On the Latin Language*) is that which is added beyond what is due. The word was made from *corollas* (little crowns), because these were accustomed to be given to actors on the stage when they had pleased the audience. The unlearned call it an "antipodium," which you could call a "corollarium" in Latin. **In your storehouse**, that is, your hidden learning. **As much as between an eagle and etc.** To compare an eagle with an owl is a proverb for things that are compared which are unlike. Martial in a scazon: "You seek to make owls similar to eagles." For the eagle is of the sharpest sight, but the owl flees the light of the sun in every way. The author is Erasmus. **A giant's little brother.** Of which Poliziano mentions in chapter 18 of the *Miscellanies*. **With cinnabar and wax.** Poliziano discusses this in chapter 57. **Cacoethes** <note>An "evil habit" or "malignant itch," often used for an uncontrollable urge to write.</note>. Poliziano discourses on this in chapter 46. **Cornelius Celsus.** Cornelius Celsus in book 5, when he speaks of a carcinoma: "That kind is the worst," he says, "and it usually first becomes that which is called *cacoethes* by the Greeks." A little later the same man says: "Nothing can be removed except a *cacoethes*; the rest are irritated by treatments." The same man a little later: "But no one can know when a *cacoethes*, which receives treatment, departs from a carcinoma, which does not." Pliny often counts *cacoethes* among ulcers. For in chapter 22 of the 25th book: "For ulcers," he says, "which they call *cacoethe*." And in chapter 4 of the 24th book: "A ground acorn heals the hardnesses which they call *cacoethe* with stale lard." In chapter 10 of the same book, he smears a decoction in wine on all kinds of ulcers, even if they are *cacoethe*. **To the Satirist**, that is, Juvenal. **Vomica** <note>An abscess or "sore."</note>, as Nonius Marcellus says: they are hollow places, swollen with age, so called because they "vomit out" gore. **Those three.** Augustus Caesar had two Julias, a daughter and a granddaughter, contaminated by every vice, and a grandson Agrippa whose mind was insane, base, and fierce. All of whom he was not accustomed to call otherwise than his **three vomicas** or his **three carcinomas**. The author is Suetonius. A **carcinoma**, however, is a defect of the body which, according to Cornelius Celsus in book 5, occurs mostly in the upper parts around the face: nostrils, ears, lips, the breasts of women; and it is born in the liver or spleen. They say a carcinoma is of the genus of cancers. **Added "incurable."** The words of Juvenal are: "An incurable *cacoethes* of writing holds many and grows old in the sick heart." **I shall add a white pebble**, that is, I will favor it, and I will think the cause is approved and to be acquitted. For the Romans were accustomed to acquit with white pebbles and condemn with black ones. Ovid testifies to that: "With white and black stones, with these to condemn the accused, with those to absolve the fault." **How much Thersites differs from Ajax.** It signifies the same as that: "how much difference there is between an eagle and an owl." For Ajax, son of Telamon, was the most handsome and strongest of all the Greeks except Achilles, as Homer relates in the seventeenth book of the *Iliad*. We have mentioned elsewhere that Thersites was the most deformed and most cowardly. **Regarding the "Abundance" etc.** Some envious people were prattling and making a noise that Poliziano had stolen from the *Cornucopia* of Perotti, as Poliziano writes in that *coronis* of the *Miscellanies*. He seems to allude to the **nature of the Rhinoceros**. For the Rhinoceros, as Pliny writes in chapter 20 of book 8, when he is about to fight with the elephant (to whom he is a natural enemy), prepares himself for the fight by sharpening his horn against rocks; in the struggle he aims for the belly...

...since he knows it to be softer. As you yourself wrote in the conclusion of your *Miscellany*: "The wall between you is thicker than that between Pyramus and <margin>The story of Pyramus and Thisbe.</margin> Thisbe." He uses this as a proverbial expression, which signifies that there is a great difference, or that they are far apart, even though you might be compared and joined with another. 

A certain Babylonian youth named Pyramus, of a beauty surpassing all others, ardently loved a neighbor of his named Thisbe, who was of a similar age and perfect beauty; she loved him no less in return. Over time their love grew, but their parents forbade their marriage. With all witnesses and judges removed, they spoke through nods and signs. The more the fire of their love was covered, the more it burned. 

A wall stood between their two houses, divided by a certain thin crack. Through this fissure they spoke to one another. Since the opportunity to join their bodies was denied to them as they did this so often, they would say: "Envious wall, why do you stand in the way of lovers? How much would it cost for you to allow us to be joined in our whole bodies? Or, if that is too much, at least to open wide enough for us to give kisses?" <note>The author is quoting and explaining the myth of Pyramus and Thisbe, famously told by Ovid, to illustrate a metaphor used in a letter.</note>
