**Book of Letters. VI. Folio LV.**

...you think: when we see something brought forth from your own storehouse, it is as if we ourselves had acquired it in our own affairs by our own <term>martial effort<note>original: "nostro marte" - a Latin idiom meaning by one's own skill or strength</note></term>. For although I clearly perceive how great a difference there is between an eagle and an owl, nevertheless, that our reasonings should arrive at the same point and agree with yours—that truly pleases me; it makes me seem, at last, to be someone of worth in my own eyes. I shall omit certain other things: that "little brother of a giant" in Juvenal <margin>Son of the Earth</margin> and the "Son of the Earth" in Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>; how learnedly and aptly has it been explained by you? That we had explained it in the same sense nearly two years ago in public, and before a crowded auditorium, is known by that most excellent youth and most dear friend to us both, Niccolò Valori, who happened to be present then. Also, regarding the "vermilion wax" <note>original: "miniatula cera" - referring to a philological dispute over a passage in Cicero's letters</note> in the letters of Cicero: our reading was not very different. Although I had found no corrected manuscript (due to a wonderful scarcity of good books in these parts), moved only by conjectures, I had thought that "vermilion and wax" should be placed there.

But I should also like to ask your opinion on that "malignant habit" <note>original: "cacoethes" - a Greek term used by Juvenal to describe an incurable itch or compulsion to write</note> of Juvenal, for the sake of testing your judgment; I will not remain silent on the fact that your word is like a Delphic oracle to me. For since I have read in Cornelius Celsus <note>A famous Roman medical writer</note> that a *cacoethes* is a certain type of carcinoma, and indeed a most troublesome and long-lasting one, I believed that from there, through a certain metaphor, the Satirist <note>Juvenal</note> used this name to signify the constant, nagging plague of writing poems. This is especially so since he added the words "incurable" and "in the sick heart," and the very word "grows old" <note>original: "senescit"</note>, which aptly falls upon a recurring ulcer; then...

# **Of Illustrious Men**

**ASCENSIUS** <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, was a famous printer and commentator. These are his introductory notes on the text.</note>
*Was accustomed.* Therefore, the word "sowed" [seui] also pertains to trees or plants. *The ancient judgment of studies, etc.* I doubt whether it should be read as "of the studious who"; if it is "of studies," let it be said instead of "of the studious whose judgment it is." Certainly, even in Virgil’s century, the Neapolitan Gymnasium <note>The University of Naples</note> was noble. *Similar to the unlabored.* Those writing should take primary care that the natural vein flows rather than a channel sought by art. *Nay, imitate.* A holy and memorable admonition. For very many always remain disciples and, as it were, boys, because they do not dare to depart from the writings of their elders; they are so sworn to them that they would sooner believe they do not understand them than that they were not written correctly—a pious and religious observance that is owed only to divine letters. *Enjoy as much as you can; for my sake and yours, my Baccio.* "Baccio" is the proper case following "enjoy" [fruere]; "for my sake" [vicem meam] is common, having almost the force of an adverb or governed by a silent preposition, as if it were "at the turn" or "according to the turn" of me and you; or it is positioned like "to rage a rage" or "to play a game." *Salt.* That is, the sharpness of judgment and wisdom; this is what good literature tastes like. *Cautiously* and *Reluctantly* are fine adverbs. *From the horn of plenty, etc.* From this response, it seems Puccio hinted that there were those who contended that the *Cornucopia* of Perotti <note>Niccolò Perotti, author of a massive commentary on Martial</note> could contend equally for praise with the *Miscellanea* of Poliziano. To which Puccio responded: "Clearly a thicker wall stands between you than between Pyramus and Thisbe" <note>A reference to Ovid's lovers who spoke through a crack in a wall; here implying a vast difference in quality</note>—a judgment Poliziano does not reject. *What most foul beast, etc.* The little verse of Ennius is known to him: "The monkey, how like us, that most foul beast."

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Francesco Puccio, many greetings.**

[I]Ncredible pleasure your letters have brought me: not so much, I believe, because they praise our *Miscellanea* (though that too), but because they profess a certain singular erudition or eloquence of yours, to whom I once happened to be a teacher. For just as a farmer exults vehemently when he gathers noble offspring from the very tree which he once was accustomed to tend with his own hands and had led forth with long and much care; so you should know that we were greatly delighted by that letter of yours, which exhibited to us the wonderful fruits of that genius of yours, cultivated by our labor. I had indeed often heard before—and not without my own great joy—that you were teaching the youth at Naples with great renown and great glory. But this letter of yours has now clearly declared that that ancient judgment of studies—which once chose for itself a proper seat and, as it were, a fixed domicile among them—is not absent from the Neapolitans whom you so please. For the style of that letter is not only Latin and pure (which I am accustomed to demand above all), but truly carries before it a certain elegant character: it is elaborate, yet similar to the unlabored; that is, it is cultivated so hiddenly and dissemblingly that beauty, not the effort of cultivation, shows itself in it. It is likewise easy, flowing, rhythmic without anxiety, not painfully diligent; rather, it is similar to the negligent, but in such a way that it possesses more grace by that very means, just as the color is in the paintings of Apelles. What wonder is it then if, just as in the breast of Latona, silent joys thrill me when I see such disciples come forth from our shadows, such as I perhaps would not now disdain even as masters? For I am not more learned than you now simply because I was your master then. For even those who taught me sometimes later failed in our school along with the other learners. Such are the turns of things, and most beautiful they are. Certainly nothing is more pleasing to me than to send out disciples more learned than I am myself. Especially if they are grateful, if they are mindful, and if they do not kick back against the teacher himself as colts do against a parent.

But what shall I say of your verses, my Puccio? That there are many new things there, or rather ancient things; what a thread, what color, what cultivation, what allurements, what softness, what a kind of tenderness! You have expressed there many figures and many outlines of the Greek Callimachus—I know not whether by deliberate effort, but you have expressed them. For as to your praising me in these also, girding me with triple eloquence, and saying that envy has no right over us—whether you believe it so or whether you imagine it as a poet—I nevertheless give thanks entirely; since to have this happen to me, to be praised by a learned man (even if falsely), is surely a great praise, and for that reason, true. But this, I think, you say in jest: that you demand redress for a great injury because what I previously taught in school, I have now published in the *Miscellanea*. But what is this to you? Do you still need dictations, you who can fulfill all measures by yourself and can now prescribe to others? Nay, you too should imitate the lion cubs who, when their teeth and claws have grown enough, scorning the mother's teats, capture prey for themselves far off in the woods.

But you say you spend your time with Baccio Ugolino, <margin>Praises of Baccio Ugolino.</margin> and that our book was a pleasure to him. Do you then spend time with my Baccio, Puccio? Do you share jests and serious matters with Baccio? I almost said (which would be a sin) that I am envious. But who would not envy you the company of that man, than whom no one is more charming, more refined, or sweeter! I would swear I have seen nothing more lovable than him, yet also nothing more loving. And so he seems to me to have achieved what almost no one ever has: to be dear to all, pleasant to all. He is loved by princes, but without the detraction of courtiers; he is celebrated by the learned, but without the offense of rivals. He lives with others in such a way that he gathers the goodwill of all ranks equally, yet does not confuse their distinctions. How great is his prudence, how great his faith, how great his loftiness of mind in administering the greatest affairs; what force, what eloquence, what sharpness! Then how much love, duty, zeal, and diligence; furthermore, what courtesy, ease, and simplicity in social life! How everywhere he is sincere, witty, and ingenious; how also erudite and lettered! Finally, what is sweeter, cleaner, more polished, or more charming than those songs of his, whether those he sings to the lyre extemporaneously or those he composes at leisure! But why do I wander further? Enjoy as much as you can, for my sake and yours, my Baccio. Enjoy Baccio, my leisure and my delight. And indeed, he is not so much mine as everyone's—at least those who have any "salt" <note>Wit or wisdom</note> at all. Do take care (so that I may bear the longing for you more lightly) that there be frequent talk of me between you.

**Book of Letters. VI. Folio LVI.**

The same things (as the saying goes) very often ring in my ears. Regarding the "little brother of the giant": what wonder is it if you brought forth almost the same things two years ago that we did almost four years ago? Do not two puppies often discover the lair of the same hare, if by chance they both followed the same tracks? *Cacoethes* <margin>Cacoethes</margin> <note>Greek: an incurable habit or "malignant disease," often used by ancient authors to describe a compulsion to write.</note> is truly not just an ulcer, but also a kind of slow fever in the definitions found in Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note>, which we have also recorded in writing elsewhere. However, in Juvenal <note>A Roman satiric poet.</note>, it signifies a bad habit in both cases. But what is this, that you approach us so timidly and diffidently—so slowly, so suspiciously, so cautiously, so much as if on tiptoe? Do you fear that you might offend me with those things? As if your praises do not overflow onto us, just as ours do onto you; and as if you do not know that I favor the praises of my friends somewhat more than my own. I would certainly admit you into the partnership of my praises (if indeed any praises are mine) so far from being burdened <margin>Burdened</margin> by it, that I would rather consider this one praise the greatest of all: that you do not despise them. Regarding the "horn of plenty" and our *Miscellanea* <note>Poliziano's famous work of philological "Miscellanies."</note> (though you too can slip through love), I do not, to tell the truth, greatly disagree with you. Nevertheless, I remember in the meantime that even the Ape itself—which Ennius <note>An early Roman poet.</note> calls the "foulest beast"—believes its own offspring to be the most beautiful of all. Farewell.

**F. S.** *Excribi* <note>To be copied out.</note>, that is, what they commonly call to be duplicated or copied. For to *excribere*, as Agraetius says, is to transfer what has been written by others; just as to *conscribere* <margin>Excribere</margin> is to write many things together, that is, to commit various traditions of learning to memory in the same book. <margin>Conscribere</margin> But to *transcribere* <margin>Transcribere</margin> is when our right passes to another. Virgil in the seventh book of the *Aeneid*: "Will you suffer so many labors poured out in vain, and your kingdoms to be *transcribed* <note>original: "transcribi"; here meaning transferred or assigned.</note> to Dardanian colonists?" *With blinking eyes*, that is, by looking at something with too little attention. <margin>Blinking and Borrowed times.</margin> "With blinking eyes" is a proverb used when we look into a matter with too little attention and diligence, or when we intentionally pretend not to see or understand something. The translator of Plutarch, in the book titled *On Tranquillity of Mind*, says: "In order to maintain constancy of mind in adversity, it is worthwhile not to pass over with 'blinking eyes,' as they say, those things which once turned out excellently for us and according to our heart's desire." The same author a little later: "Why, you most malevolent man, do you see the faults of others with the eyes of a kite, but pass over your own with the eyes of an owl and blinking eyes?" To *hallucinate* <margin>Hallucinate</margin> is therefore to be imprudent; but we *blink* out of industry. We *prophesy* <note>original: "Ominamur"</note>, that is, we augur. They call *borrowed times* <note>original: "Succisiua tpa"</note> those which we cut off and, as it were, steal away while heavily occupied in another matter, and apply to something else; as when one very busy in the study of letters intercepts a tiny bit of time in which to write to a friend. Although we have said enough and more about what *postliminium* <margin>Postliminium</margin> <note>A legal term regarding the restoration of rights to a person returning from captivity.</note> is, let it not be a cause for regret to have said this: with Boethius as the authority in the third book of his commentaries on Cicero's *Topics*: "Whoever has been captured by enemies and returns to his fatherland returns by *postliminium*." For while he suffers captivity by the enemy, he loses the right of a citizen, but he recovers all rights if he returns by *postliminium*. Likewise, with Cicero as the authority in the book of *Topics*: "A man, a ship, a pack-mule, a horse, or a mare that is accustomed to take the bit, return by *postliminium*." Where the word *postliminium* comes from is not agreed upon by everyone. For Servius (as Cicero says in that place) thinks the word was made from the particle *post* (which, with Boethius as authority, means "back"), and the rest, *liminium*, is an extension of the word, as in *finitimo*, *legitimo*, *aeditimo*, where there is no more meaning in *-timus* than there is in *tullium* in the word *meditullio*. <margin>Where Postliminium comes from.</margin> Scaevola, the son of Publius, however, thinks it is a joined word, so that it contains *post* and *limen* [threshold]; so that things which were alienated from us, when they reached the enemy, exited as if from their own threshold. Hence, when they later return to the same threshold, they are seen to have returned by *Postliminium*.

**ASCENSIUS.**
*Antiquius*, that is, dearer: because those things which are dear to us, the older [*antiquiora*] they are, the dearer they tend to be, such as wines, friends, servants, beasts of burden, furniture, and other things of that kind. "As if it consists of a legitimate contest"—this is a verse in full meter.

**Augustinus Maffeus to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. VI.**

Since you were with us at Rome last summer, most learned man, and I had received word not many days before that you had translated the histories of Herodian—a truly most illustrious man—from Greek into our language with no less genius and learning than care, clearly for the common favor and utility of all scholars: I was indeed moved with such great pleasure of mind that I think nothing more precious or more desirable could have been brought to my ears at that time. From this, I believe, it happened that, moved and stirred by a fresh desire to see that work, I did not hesitate to ask you somewhat inquisitively for a copy. Which, out of your singular kindness toward everyone, you not only did not deny me, but even promised with more ample words that you would send it to us all the way from Florence, so that we should no longer lack the fruit and pleasure of such flowery and pleasant reading. When I had greedily expected this book for many days, and could no longer sustain that huge desire of mine (for my mind already seemed to be held back by a certain doubtful and uncertain hope), I labored with all zeal, care, and industry to bring it about that I should no longer have to long for such a work. And so, having found a certain copy in the possession of I know not whom—of truly doubtful reliability—I first ordered the volume itself to be copied out and transcribed just as it was. Which indeed I believe to be corrupted and debased in many places, partly by the carelessness of the scribe and partly by the fault of the model, and it clearly does not consist of all its integral parts. I might seem to have noted this fact not improperly, while recently I surveyed that brilliant history itself, not carelessly, nor with "blinking eyes." It so filled my ears that I have placed all my study and leisure during these continuous days into that reading. In which, besides the elegance and harmony of the Roman speech and the variety of sentiments, I observed this especially as being most worthy not only of chief praise but of singular admiration: that it abounds in speeches so frequent and so sublime, that in that part the distinguished historian Herodian himself seems not to have yielded even the first place to our Cornelius Tacitus. In which truly your praise and good fortune ought to be no less, since in translating that work you clearly achieved this: that while the majesty of true history was preserved everywhere, nothing pertaining to clarity...

**F.S.** *To fight for* <note>original: "Propugnate"</note> is to defend; *to fight against* <note>original: "oppugnare"</note> is to attack. *He would not yet wish, etc.*—that is, he has not even lightly attacked another. **Sedentary learning** <margin>Sedentary learning.</margin> is trivial and common, the kind found in idle and lazy men; it is also called "sitting" learning. **Of Marcus Cato.** Quintilian, in the twelfth book of the *Institutes of Oratory*, says: "In a speech, if you wish to look at the types, you will find almost as many forms of intellect as there are forms of bodies." But there were certain styles of speaking that were somewhat rougher due to the conditions of the times, though otherwise displaying great intellectual power. From this era come the Laelii, the Africani, the Catos, and the Gracchi. <margin>The eloquence of Cato.</margin> Plutarch also writes in his *Life of Cato* regarding his supreme eloquence, acquired through much use and labor, to nearly this effect: "He composed his speeches," he says, "like a second persona, with great zeal and care; as if, in dealing with weighty matters, it were a necessary instrument—not to be handled through sloth, but with dignity." Therefore, he practiced speaking everywhere throughout the neighboring villages and towns; he failed no one who needed his help. In this matter he was so effective that he was judged first a most ready advocate, and later a most eloquent orator. Pliny, in chapters 8 and 20 of his seventh book, is the authority that Cato was the best orator, just as he was the best general and the best senator. Cicero was not silent regarding this oratory faculty of Cato. These are his words from the fourth book *On Famous Orators*: "Who," he asks, "is more weighty in praising? More stinging in censuring? More clever in his maxims? More subtle in teaching and explaining? More than a hundred and fifty of his speeches have been recorded—at least those I have found and read so far—illustrious in both words and matter. Though people may select from these what is worthy of note and praise, all the virtues of an orator will be found in them." Cicero pursues other immoderate commendations of this kind regarding the excellence of Cato. **He had come to the Triarii.** <margin>To the Triarii.</margin> That is, to the most imminent danger. <note>The Triarii were the third and most veteran line of the Roman legion, only called upon in desperate situations; hence the proverb "it has come to the Triarii" means a crisis has been reached.</note> We write the reasoning for this proverb in *Griphon*. **The Caesarians.** Favorinus, in Aulus Gellius (Book 1, Chapter 10), rebuking a young man speaking in an excessively archaic style, says: "That which was written by Gaius Caesar, a man of excellent intellect and prudence, in his first book *On Analogy*: keep it always in your memory and in your heart—that you should avoid an unheard-of and unusual word just as you would a reef." **They will go into labor, etc.** Horace, in his book *On the Art of Poetry*, dissuading one from beginning with heavy and lofty words, says: "Nor shall you begin like the Cyclic writer of old: 'I shall sing the fate of Priam and the noble war.' What will this promiser bring forth worthy of such a wide-open mouth? The mountains will go into labor; a ridiculous mouse will be born." <margin>Aesop's fable of the mouse born from the earth.</margin> There is a fable in Aesop to this effect: "The swelling earth," he says, "gives great groans of one in labor. Everyone fears it will bring forth monsters. The fear turns to laughter, for the pregnant earth brings forth a mouse. It is a joke, what was before a fear. Often men who threaten much do less harm. Often a tiny cause carries excessive fears." **Just as, etc.** These are the words of Quintilian from the second book of the *Institutes of Oratory*: "Having spoken much of the duty of teachers, I meanwhile advise students of this one thing: that they love their tutors no less than their studies, and believe them to be parents—not indeed of their bodies, but of their minds. This piety contributes much to study. For thus they will listen willingly, believe what is said, and desire to be like them." He also teaches in the same book that the teacher must play the role of a parent: "Let them take up, above all, the mind of a parent toward their students, and consider that they are succeeding to the place of those by whom the children were entrusted to them." **I would doubt becoming a second Niobe.** <margin>Niobe.</margin> Niobe bore six sons and as many daughters to her husband Amphion; proud of this offspring, she dared to prefer herself to Latona, who had borne only two <note>Apollo and Diana</note>. Apollo and Diana, avenging the insult to their mother, killed the sons and daughters with arrows. Consumed by grief, Niobe was changed into a marble statue and still suffers the scourges of the gods. Homer is the authority in the last book of the *Iliad*. Ovid, making a story of it in the sixth book of the *Metamorphoses*, says that Amphion committed suicide upon hearing of the death of his sons. Aulus Gellius, in the last book (Chapter 6), recorded that writers do not agree on how many children Niobe had. Therefore, "a second Niobe" means "made of stone," and as Plato says in the *Symposium*: "I would be turned from a man into a stone." **By the bond of the Academics.** Pausanias, addressing Socrates in the *Phaedrus*, says: "But tell the truth, by friendly Jove: do you think any of the Greeks could say more or greater things on this very matter?" Those whom Plato introduces speaking almost always swear or entreat "by Jove."

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Marsilio Ficino, Greetings.**
**Letter XVII.**

[Decorative initial H] You call me Hercules in your book *On Life*, because I tame monsters. I suppose you are looking at those monsters which so excessively besiege the books of the ancients, in the purging of which I labor long and hard. This is magnificent praise, especially from that philosopher who is a leader in the leading sect. But I am unable to sustain the weight of such a great name, no more than I could the heavens—which Hercules himself nevertheless sustained. Call me Iolaus instead, if you delight in beautiful names; for I am ready with a torch for antiquity, which is almost oppressed by the Hydra, just as I was for the shouting Hercules. You, however, indulging in love (as other parents are wont to do), have given your son a name that is not the most fitting, but the most beautiful. Farewell.

**Commentaries of F. Sylvius on Book VII of the Letters of Angelo Poliziano.**

[Decorative initial C] Centurion: Mutius briefly reviews Poliziano’s *Centuria* <note>The "Centuria" refers to Poliziano's *Miscellanea*, a collection of 100 philological observations</note>. He calls Cicero a "Centurion" because in the first chapter he vindicates him from slander. He notes these topics in the *Miscellanea*: *Philotheoron* in chapters 7 and 80; *Sciamachia* <note>Shadow-fighting</note> in the 34th; *Carpatinas* in the 2nd; *Chomodis* and *Hiomis* in the 19th; *Oano* in the 69th; *Harpocrates* in the 82nd; *Camelopard* <note>Giraffe</note> in the 3rd; the *Wooden Horse* in the 5th; *Compare to a mule* in the 23rd; *Navia* in the 14th; *Echo* in the 22nd; *The color of Venus's rose* in the 11th; *Cotytto* in the 10th; *Cacoethes* <note>A bad habit or itch</note> in the 46th; *Laconicum* and *Pitylisinate* in the 38th; *Augury of Safety* in the 12th; *Ascopera* <note>A traveler's bag</note> in the 20th; *Tetraones* <note>Grouse</note> in the 57th; *Automaton* in the 97th; *Sybaritidos* in the 15th; *The books of Aristides* in the 16th; *The song of Priapus* in the 59th; *The Teuthrantian crowd* in the 29th; *Ceratinas* <note>Horned syllogisms</note> in the 54th; *Crocodilitas* <note>Crocodile paradoxes</note> in the 55th; *Ocnum* in the 81st; *Duria night* in the 5th; *Causarios* in the 92nd. <margin>The Civic Crown.</margin> The "Civic Crown," as Aulus Gellius records in the sixth chapter of his fifth book, is that which a citizen gives to another by whom he was saved in battle, as a witness to his life and safety preserved. It is made of oak leaves, because the oak was the most ancient source of food and sustenance. It is also made from the holm-oak, which is very similar. <margin>Vindex.</margin> A "Vindex" (as Boethius says in the first book of his commentaries on Cicero’s *Topics*) is one who takes up the cause of another to be defended; like those we now call proxies or attorneys. Aulus Gellius in chapter six of his twelfth book writes that very charming riddle: "Whether once less or twice less, I do not know. Or both of them; as I once heard it said, he refused to yield to King Jupiter himself." Which (says Gellius) we have left unexplained to sharpen the conjectures of readers in seeking it. He who does not wish to search for it long will find what it is in the second book of Marcus Varro’s *On the Latin Language* addressed to Marcellus. Thus says Gellius. Therefore, he does not call it Varro’s riddle, but says its explanation can be found in Varro’s second book. In chapter 36 of the *Miscellanea*, Poliziano solves this riddle. <margin>The Law of the Sphinx.</margin> Ausonius: Poliziano explains a certain Ausonian riddle in chapter 39. "Fearing the law of the Sphinx." The law of the Sphinx was that if her riddle were solved, she would throw herself headlong from a cliff and perish by that kind of death. Whether riddles should be called *scirpi* or *sirpi*, we discuss at some length in our commentaries on the *Gryphon* of Ausonius. "Domitius with a noble brow": because he is mocked by Poliziano in chapters 9 and 77. "With fetched pigments": that is, interpretations which Domitius did not know. "Attegias" <note>Huts</note>: Poliziano writes of these in chapter nine. Pliny’s "poppyfmi" <note>clucking/smacking sounds</note> at lightning bolts in chapter 32. The Nemean Lion in the 17th. The Dog of Hercules in the 12th; these are discussed by Poliziano. "Inustas": that is, "made." "Other Centuries": Poliziano is remembered to have made another *Centuria*, as Crinitus testifies with many words in his twelfth book. <margin>To mutter. (Handwritten: To mutter.)</margin> "Let envy mutter." To mutter (*mussare*), as Pompeius says, is to murmur. Ennius: "They muttered in secret." Commonly, however, it is used for "to be silent." The same Ennius: "It does not befit the good to mutter." The word *mussare* is familiar to our households for "to hide." "To mutter" and "to murmur" have this distinction between them, as Nonius Marcellus prefers: that *mussare* belongs to men speaking secretly and with a low voice what they wish to be concealed. <margin>To murmur.</margin> Virgil in the tenth book: "What the fortune of the people may bring: but they mutter to say it." Murmuring, however, is of a louder sound, close to a tumult. Virgil in the first *Georgic*: "The murmur of the groves begins to increase." <margin>To dally. To make a 'mu' sound.</margin> To dally (*muginari*) and "to make a 'mu' sound" (*my facere*) are the same as "to mutter," as Crinitus maintains in the fifth chapter of his eighteenth book. Sextus Pompeius, however, says that *muginari* is to trifle and to attempt something slowly. Baptista Pius thinks one should say "to make a 'mu' sound." The ancient Greeks (he says) called the letter *mu* (μυ) the letter of silence, because it is of the slightest voice. Whence that line of Ennius: "Which is the least; nor (as they say) do they dare to make a 'mu'." From this he thinks *mussare*, *mussitare*, *mutire*, and *muginari* are derived. For we have said elsewhere that *u* and *v* can easily be exchanged among the Latins. "More freely": that is, more boldly. "He substituted": He alludes to hens under which eggs other than their own are placed. "Rhinoceroses": that is, the snub-nosed; the reasoning is in our commentaries on the *Gryphon* of Ausonius. <margin>Mastiges.</margin> "Mastiges": that is, scoundrels who deserve a beating, who are also called *mastigiae*. But *mastiges* in the sense used by Plautus as "a heap of elm-rods" <note>referring to the rods used for whipping</note>. For *mastix* (μαστιξ) is a whip or scourge. "The die": that is, dangerous volatility. "Of Papinius": that is, of Statius. <margin>Apoplexy. Paralysis.</margin> Apoplexy is a disease when all the nerves have lost the power of both feeling and moving. But where this happens to one of the sides, either right or left, it is called *paralysis* (παραλυσις), that is, a loosening. Galen is the authority in the third book of *On the Affected Parts*. Cornelius Celsus in his third book mentions that now both are called paralysis. According to the same Celsus, those who are violently loosened in all their limbs are usually snatched away quickly. But if they are not snatched away, they live longer, yet rarely reach health; and for the most part, they drag out a miserable spirit, with their memory also lost. In certain parts, however, it is never acute; often long-lasting; and almost always a curable disease. "Thunderstruck," as Cornelius Celsus recorded in his third book, are those whose body and mind are stunned. It happens sometimes by a lightning strike, sometimes by disease. The Greeks call this apoplexy. <margin>Sideratio (Star-struck/Blight).</margin> "Sideratus": *Sideratio* is a disease sometimes suddenly corrupting and drying out the whole body, sometimes a part of it, and sometimes killing it. It is thought to occur with a certain sudden impulse and, as it were, the force of a star. This is wont to happen not only in men, but in trees. Pliny, in the twenty-fourth chapter of his seventeenth book, says: "*Sideratio* depends entirely on the heavens." Budé commemorates more concerning the *sideratio* of trees in his *Annotations*.

**ASCENSIUS.**
"He was, he was," says Macarius. He speaks of himself as of a noble man both in the perspicacity of his senses and judgment, and in the abundance of his sciences; such as he had been when whole and untouched by apoplexy. Whence also at the end: "I do not yet recognize the Macarius who was with me."

# .X.I. Of Illustrious Men

**Money-changer.** <note>original: "Colybista"</note> **F.S.** <note>F.S. likely refers to the commentator Fabritius Septimulius.</note> Money-changers, that is, bankers. For a *kollybistēs* <note>original Greek: κολυβιστὴς</note> is what a banker is called. **I will count out.** That is, I will pay. **Acting as a stepmother.** That is, acting as an enemy, or opposing me. **I profess.** That is, I publicly interpret literature <note>meaning he holds a public teaching chair</note>.
**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Josse Bade, also known as Ascensius, a famous printer and commentator.</note> **They fell into, etc.** These matters were explained in the letter to Filippo Beroaldo. **As an auspicious sign.** As if to say, a happy beginning; for as of yet, he has contributed nothing to the friendship beyond his goodwill. **Entering into.** That is, beginning a friendship. **Lest your authority be diminished:** because among friends, all things are held in common; yet authority does not seem lesser because of that. Hence I doubt whether the text should read **be fortified** <note>original: "muniatur" instead of "imminuatur"</note>; especially since he adds: "if you require anything of me, command it." For that is not the speech of one whose authority has been diminished—unless perhaps you wish the word to have an intensifying force, as in "unchanged" <note>original: "immuto"</note>; and according to some, in that phrase of Pilate: "I am innocent," meaning "greatly guilty" <note>original: "multum nocens"</note>; which was indeed the case in reality, though far from the mind of the speaker. **A school.** <note>original: "Ludum"</note> Specifically a literary one; **I have opened,** that is, for those wishing to learn for a fee.

### Tydeus Acciarinus to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter III.

[Decorative initial I] **There have fallen into our hands,** like mutilated scraps, certain fragments of your interpretations of the *Silvae* of Papinius <note>Publius Papinius Statius, a 1st-century Roman poet</note>; in which you either explain things left untouched by Domitio <note>Domizio Calderini, an earlier commentator</note> or render better those things he did explain, O Angelo, most learned of men. Having weighed these most diligently, I could not help but vehemently approve of them. I am compelled both to look up to your genius and to pursue your singular learning with wonderful praise. Although men who are most brilliant in their own light have little need for the small sparks of others, nevertheless, even if I have not deserved well of you and no services of mine toward you exist, yet by your peculiar humanity—in which I hear by the one and constant voice of all that you excel everyone else—I ask, nay, I beseech and entreat you, that you signify to me by letter whether you have published anything else, either on the same Papinius or on other Latin authors, which differs from other interpreters. For one may divine <note>original: "Ariolari"</note> that many things, both noble and worthy of knowledge, have been collected by you, a man of sharp genius. If you are willing to impart these to me, I shall profess myself to be in no small debt to you. I am not unaware that you do not lack scribes. I will count out the money to you through **money-changers.** Come then, and do not despise my goodwill as the **auspicious sign** of my friendship, lest **your authority be diminished** with me as a new friend. Truly, if you require anything of me, command it. I promise I shall do what is commanded. I am a native of the Picene territory; but by the will of the fates and with **fortune acting as a stepmother**, I **profess** <note>teach</note> in Cosenza among the Bruttii; and I, who until now have enjoyed the intimacy of Princes, have now, with the stars opposing me, **opened a school.** Farewell, and love me, as I revere and observe you. From Cosenza, the 4th of the Nones of June.

<margin>See Seneca</margin>

#### The Fable of Atreus and Thyestes.

**F.S. Not so averted, etc.** Virgil’s Dido, in the first book of the *Aeneid*, responding to Ilioneus as he prayed that the unspeakable fires be kept away from his ships, says: "We Carthaginians do not carry hearts that are so blunt, nor does the Sun yoke his horses so **averted** from the Tyrian city."
He alludes to the fable. For when the brothers Atreus and Thyestes were at odds with a capital hatred for one another, Thyestes lay with his brother's wife, by whom he had three sons. Atreus, having invited his brother to a banquet under the pretense of a simulated reconciliation, set before him his own sons to be eaten, and their blood mixed with wine to be drunk. Thyestes, having learned the truth, lay with his daughter according to a response from a god, so that one might be born who [would avenge] the injury...

**Letters, Book VII, Folio LXII**

->All of Tuscany is distinguished and joyful because of so great and grave a teacher.<- And so, the volumes have been printed: and in a single birth, as it were, more than six hundred volumes have been issued into the light. We are sending one of these to you, so that you may have something of ours in your hands. Whenever you read it (if you have not done so before), having spurned the bitter sweetness of all earthly things and their vain and false joy, seek happiness with a high and most firm mind. Follow that certain and direct path, my Robert, which leads you to where the greatest goods and everlasting joys are found. Since this little book sets out to you without any added ornaments, but pure and naked exactly as it emerged from the <term>art<note>Refers to the "art of printing," a common Renaissance term for the new technology of the press.</note></term>, you, Robert, will take care to both decorate it with merit and clothe it with a cover, for you are liberal and wealthy. Farewell.

...are generally reconciled. The authority is Servius in his commentaries on the first book of the *Aeneid*. According to Servius in that same place, Idalium is a grove in Cyprus where there is a small town. From that place, she is called Idalian Venus. Permessus: as Strabo is the authority in his ninth book, is a river flowing down from Mount Helicon. The goddess Hora is the goddess of youth, whom some wish to be the wife of Quirinus <note>An early Roman god associated with the state and Romulus.</note>. Likewise, Homer records in the fifth book of the *Iliad* that the Hours are the guardians of the gates of heaven. Macrobius, in the first book of the *Saturnalia*, is pleased to state that they were named after the Sun, who is called "Horus" in the language of the Egyptians. We gather from the words of Apuleius that roses are held by the Hours; his words from the sixth book are these: "The Hours," he says, "made all things purple with roses and other flowers." Grace <note>One of the Graces, specifically Charis.</note> is the wife of Vulcan on Lemnos, just as Venus is in heaven; the authority is Lucian in his *Dialogues of the Gods*. We have written more elsewhere concerning the three Graces. Aurora <note>The Dawn.</note> announces the rising of the sun to the gods, as Homer relates in the second book of the *Iliad*: she is called *rhododaktylos* <note>original: "ροδοδακτυλος"</note>, that is, having rosy rays which are like fingers. Violet-beds, that is, gardens. Regarding Chloris: we have already remembered sufficiently when we spoke of the *Floralia* <note>The festival of Flora.</note> that Chloris is the same goddess who is called Flora. However, on the authority of Homer in the eleventh book of the *Odyssey*, Chloris the daughter of Pandareus was turned into a nightingale; sitting among the thick leaves of the trees in the new spring, she continually moans for her beloved son Itylus with varying cries, whom the son of King Zethus once rashly slew with a blade.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>The printer/commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius.</note>
To correct is too difficult. He asserts this shrewdly, so that what the elder man restored should not be judged as the work of a boy.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Antonio Zeno. Greetings.**
**Letter XIV.**

**A**long-awaited "Fugitive Love"—which I translated from Greek into Latin when I was almost still a boy, preserving not only the sentiments but even the meters and nearly all the outlines—I finally send to you, who have been desiring and demanding it for a long time. The reason I sent it so late was that I deliberated with myself for a while first whether I should send it at all. For many things displeased me as I reconsidered them after a long interval, which perhaps seemed excellent at the time I wrote them. To correct them is too difficult, because they had already become so long-established. I am also sending the elegy about Violets: another plaything of that age. For you indicated that you desired that too much as well. To me, certainly, there seems to be nothing in these that you should approve of, except perhaps the natural talent. I would ask you not to show these trifles to anyone, if I did not know that I would be asking entirely in vain. For I think you seek our works for no other reason than to show them to as many people as possible: since (such is your love toward us) you are entirely confident they will please immediately because they are ours. I am not sending the Epigrams to you because I intend to publish them immediately along with the Greek ones. Farewell.

**Fugitive Love, from the Greek of Moschus.**
[Small illustration of a bird's head and wing]
When Venus called her son with an intent cry:
"If anyone has seen Love wandering in the crossroads,
This fugitive," she says, "is mine; the informer shall bear a reward:
A little kiss from Venus. But if you lead him to me,
I will not give just a little kiss; you, stranger, shall have more.
The boy is distinguished; behold, learn all his signs:
He is not fair-skinned, but imitates fire; his eyes
Are sharp and flaming; a wicked mind, but sweetest words.
What he speaks, he does not feel; his voice is like honey, but when
He is inflamed with anger, then his mind is harsh, deceptive,
A cheater, a liar: the boy plays cruelly.
His crown of hair is curly, and his face is bold;
His hands are tiny, yet he hurls his darts far—
He hurls them even into shadowy Acheron <note>The river of the Underworld.</note> and the realms of the silent.
He is naked of limb, but his mind is veiled; and like a bird
He shakes his wings: and now he seeks these people, now those,
Often pressing upon the heart of a man, often a girl's.
He has a tiny bow, and an arrow is set upon the bow;
A small arrow indeed, but it is carried even unto heaven.
A small golden quiver hangs from his back;
And within are bitter shafts, with which that bold boy
Often strikes even me, his mother. All things about him are savage.
Everything: and he torments himself much more savagely.
He has a tiny torch, yet it burns even the Sun itself.
If you catch him, come, lead him away, do not pity the boy.
If you see him weeping, take care not to be deceived.
But if he laughs: drag him more; if by chance he offers kisses..."

O beautiful violets, the little gifts of our Venus, <margin>Violets</margin> in which the sweet pledge of such great love resides, <margin>Gifts of Venus</margin> what earth produced you? With what nectar did the soft West Winds <margin>Pledge of love</margin> and the breeze scatter your scented hair? Those which she shall have moved with rosy fingers to her beautiful mouth—she, from whom Love hurls his arrows into me. Perhaps this grace comes to you from that source; such great honor breathes from the mouth of my mistress. See how this one charms with its milky color; see how that one reddens with purple petals. This is the color of my mistress: when a pleasing purple paints her milky cheeks with a rosy modesty. Because it breathes a sweet scent from its lips far and wide, behold, violets, that scent has passed into you. O fortunate violets, my life and my delight, O harbor and breeze of my soul! From you at least, violets, I shall pluck grateful kisses. I shall touch you three and four times with a greedy hand. I shall saturate you with my tears, which go through my mourning face and over my bosom like a living river. Drink up these tears, which cruel Love squeezes from my eyes as fuel for the slow flame. Live forever, violets: let neither the summer with its suns nor the winter with its biting cold pluck you away. Live forever, the solace of a wretched love, O violets, O grateful rest for our soul. You shall be with me always, I shall always love you, while I, a wretch, am tormented by my beautiful mistress: and while the flames of Cupid pluck at my breast: while both tears and groans remain with me.

**FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS:** A *Scomma* <note>A taunt or a "scoff."</note> is a gibe and, I might almost say, a figurative bite: which is covered by a certain sophistication or trickery, so that it sounds like one thing, but you understand another. <margin>**Scomma**</margin> Yet it is not always bitter: but sometimes it is even sweet to those at whom it is thrown. This is the kind of thing that either a wise man or a sophisticated man especially practices. *Loedoria* <note>From the Greek "loidoria," meaning reproach or verbal abuse.</note> however, is that which is openly an object of reproach and upbraiding. For example: "Have you forgotten when you used to sell salted fish?" That is *Loedoria*. "We remember when you used to wipe your nose on your sleeve"—this is called a *Scomma*, which signifies the same thing as that *Loedoria*, but covers it figuratively. To Cicero, while he was reciting, Octavius said: "I do not hear what you are saying." Cicero replied: <margin>**Loedoria**</margin> <note>The text cuts off here; historically, Cicero's retort alluded to Octavius's supposed pierced ears, implying he was of servile or foreign origin.</note>

**Book VII of the Letters. Folio 64.**

This speech is truly Roman: Roman wit:
Nothing here is ungraceful, or foolish, or "Greekish" <note>original: "græculum" - a derogatory term for trivial or overly-ornate Greek style</note>:
The sort of trifles other builders of plays usually produce:
Whose comedies consist of no real verses:
Nor do they hold together with a coherent plot:
Nor do they have anything of comedy except the titles.
The parts do not fit together, nor is there any credibility
In the actions, nor any natural character in the roles:
And if there is anything good, it is stolen,
For such a man lies in wait to prey upon the labors of others.
These young men will surely perform much more worthwhile work
In the future, provided they have become accustomed
To the pure, native speech of the city of Rome:
But if, relying on common <term>trivial</term> <note>referring to the "Trivium" or basic grammar school education</note> teachers,
They pollute their tender tongues with solecisms.
Indeed, it has been handed down by praised men:
That if the Muses themselves wished to speak in Latin,
They would use no words but those of Plautus <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), the famous Roman playwright known for his vigorous, colloquial Latin</note>.
And if any should cry out that we are practicing the actor's art,
And should find fault with it: we shall by no means deny it:
As long as they know we follow the ancient discipline.
For the ancients used to give noble-born boys
To comic actors to be trained, so that they might learn delivery.
But those who condemn us are the greatest actors of all.
For they pretend to be like Curius <note>Manius Curius Dentatus, a model of ancient Roman austerity</note>, but they live like revelers at a Bacchanal.
These are especially certain loud-mouthed, frivolous men:
Hooded, wooden-shoed, girt with ropes <note>A scathing description of certain friars or monks</note>:
A haughty, wry-necked herd,
Who differ from others in their dress and habit:
And with a gloomy face they sell their "holiness":
They seize for themselves a kind of censorship and tyranny:
And terrify the fearful common folk with threats.
But now, farewell spectators: and favor
Our troupe: may it turn out well for you.

ASCENSIUS <note>The commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note>: *To be despised.* A sharp little letter and an ingenious invention as in the others: for the sake of which they are placed here. But this first one also possesses this bit of erudition: that one should only write to learned men in an erudite and learned manner; but to the unlearned, not in a barbarous way, but yet so that they can grasp it. One may also notice that the names of those praised are expressed, while those of the wicked are suppressed.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Caesar Carmentus. Greetings. Letter XVI.**
You think you are being despised because I do not write back. I would despise you if I *did* write back. For those whom I despise, I venture to answer even when I am busy. To you, I do not write even when at leisure. Farewell.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Jacobus Modestus. Greetings. Letter XVII.**
You grieve because I do not write back. Cease to grieve; I am writing back now. Farewell.

**Angelo Poliziano to a Certain Person. Greetings. Letter XVIII.**
You do not perform what you promised. I complain if you have forgotten, but even more if you have not forgotten. To have forgotten is hardly the mark of a friend; not to perform when you remember is truly the mark of an enemy. Farewell.

**Angelo Poliziano to Pico della Mirandola. Greetings. Letter XIX.**
The things I wish you would correct, you praise. But you do this easily, because you always do it. Farewell.

**Angelo Poliziano to a Friend. Greetings. Letter XX.**
You are angry because that "Ape" <note>original: "Simius" - likely a specific rival scholar</note> carps at me. He does not carp at me for the sake of carping, but so that he, a starving man, may seek a living among certain people who take great joy in flatterers—but even more in detractors. Farewell.

**Angelo Poliziano to a Friend. Greetings. Letter XXI.**
If I had begun to love you on account of your riches, I would have ceased to be your friend now that you have ceased to be rich. But if I had ceased now, it would show that even when you were rich, I was not your friend, but a flatterer. He who is a flatterer cannot be a free man. Farewell.

[Handwritten at top: Swans]

.14. Of Illustrious Men

Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to his Friends. Letter 22.
**M**any of you ask for letters at the same time; behold, I send one to many, but it is a single letter. A single one is suitable for many whom I love singularly; yet it will be as if it were many, since many of you will read it. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to an Envious Man.
Letter 23.
**Y**ou envy everyone everything, except for envy itself. But you even envy this in your peer, who is even more envious than you. Thus he does not envy you your envy, though you envy him his. So, in turn, he is the less envious one. I will not say who you are, lest I make you more miserable than you already are. For if I were to bring forth your name, you would envy even the name itself; and not just each of you the other, but each of you yourself.

Angelo Poliziano to a Slanderer. Letter 24.
**I** do not speak ill in return to one who speaks ill of me, lest you perhaps stop speaking ill of me—which is to say, lest you stop praising me. For who is more truly praised than he who is slandered by a wicked man? Indeed, to call you a "wicked man" is so far from being a slander that nothing better could be said of you.

<margin>Swan.</margin>
FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS. <note>Francis Sylvius (1481–1539) was a Flemish humanist and commentator.</note>
Cygnus was a certain Ligurian; he was so sorrowful at the fall of Phaethon, whom he loved, that he was eventually changed into the bird of his own name <note>The swan</note>. The author is Virgil in the tenth book of the *Aeneid*: *“Nor does he believe in the second fires of Jove, as if mindful of the fire unjustly sent from on high, he seeks the pools and wide lakes; hating fire, he chose rivers contrary to flames.”* <note>original: "Nec secūdoꝝ Iouis q̃ Credit..." Virgil, Aeneid 10.189-193. The passage describes Cygnus's grief and transformation.</note> Ovid devises this in the second book of the *Metamorphoses*. Concerning the song of swans before death, I wish to mention in passing what Plato writes in the *Phaedo* to roughly this effect: *“Swans,”* he says, *“when they perceive they are soon to die, then sing much more and more sweetly than they were accustomed to before, rejoicing that they are about to depart to the god whose servants they were.”* <note>original: "Cygni, inqt, quando se breui..." Plato, Phaedo 84e-85b.</note> Men, however, because they themselves dread death, falsely accuse swans as well, claiming they emit a song mourning death out of grief. Surely they do not notice that there is no bird that sings when it is hungry, or cold, or affected by any other distress. Not the nightingale itself, nor the swallow, nor the hoopoe, which they say sing through lamentation while mourning. But to me, neither do those birds seem to sing out of grief, nor do the swans; but because they are sacred to Apollo, as I believe, being endowed with divination, they foresee the blessings of the other life, and therefore they sing more briskly and exult on that day more than in the time before. Thus far Plato.

ASCENSIUS. <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535), a famous printer and scholar.</note>
On the Swan. Whence also they call poets "swans." For Horace sang thus of Pindar: *“A great breeze lifts the Dircaean swan.”* <note>original: "Multa dircæuʒ leuat aura cygnū." Horace, Odes 4.2.25.</note> For which reason, in the *Bucolics* of Virgil, I would prefer to take "goose" as a discordant bird rather than as a poet; except that allegorically it indicates a bad poet just as the swan <term>holor<gloss>swan</gloss></term> indicates a good one when it is said: *“To cackle like a goose among the swans.”* <note>original: "Strepere anser vt inter holores." Virgil, Eclogues 9.36.</note>

Angelo Poliziano to Lorenzo de' Medici. Greetings.
Letter 25.
**A** poet is like a swan: both are white; both are tuneful; both love rivers; both are pleasing to Apollo. But it is denied that the swan sings unless the west wind <term>zephyrus<gloss>the gentle west wind</gloss></term> blows. What wonder is it then if I, your poet, am silent for so long, when you, my west wind, do not blow for so long? Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to Pico della Mirandola. Greetings.
Letter 26.
**I** used to be surpassed by you in learning; I was surpassed in genius; but I rejoiced to be surpassed; and indeed I rejoice because I love you—rather, I love you for this very reason: that I am surpassed by these things. But now you surpass me even in kindness. This indeed I cannot bear, because it is shameful. But now I do bear it. For nothing is shameful to me which is honorable to you. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to a Friend. Greetings. Letter 27.
**Y**ou are grieving because I, your friend, defeated you in a debate. You ought not to grieve. For if all things are common among friends, I am no more the victor than you, nor are you less the victor than I. But perhaps you grieve for this: that by this law of friends, even I am not clearly the victor who defeated you. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to a Friend. Greetings. Letter 28.
**I** was silently rebuking you for delighting yourself in the countryside for so long, when a basket full of flowers was delivered to me from you: and indeed still dewy, multicolored, and sweet-smelling. I confess I wanted to envy you the field that brought forth such beautiful flowers. But when I then read your letter, heaped with other flowers much more beautiful than the basket had been, I began instead to envy the field which (as it seems to me) had flourished from your letters. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to a Friend. Greetings.
Letter 29.
**I** grieved vehemently; I rejoiced vehemently: that you were sick, and that you have recovered. Farewell.

Angelo Poliziano to Someone. Greetings. Letter 30.
**I** send lilies: not to do a favor for you—though for you too—but for the lilies themselves: that is, so they do not wither. Farewell.

FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS.

**Book of Letters. VII. Folio LXV.**

<margin>The death of Servius Sulpicius</margin>

F. S. The translator of Hesiod, Nicolaus Valla, sings of these most humble matters in the second book of the *Georgics* <note>Valla was a 15th-century scholar who translated Hesiod's "Works and Days" into Latin hexameters; the author here refers to them as "Georgics" or agricultural poems</note> with these words: "In cutting through the deep seas, do not carry everything with you; reserve the greater part. The raft must not be over-burdened. Let whatever is in it be of equal weight, for it is a hard thing to run headlong into an adverse fate." Servius Sulpicius, a most renowned orator and most learned in the law, was sent by the Roman Senate as an ambassador to the camp of Mark Antony. He undertook this embassy though he was suffering from the inconvenience of ill health. Therefore, neither the violence of winter, nor the snows, nor the length of the journey, nor the roughness of the roads, nor his worsening disease delayed him. And when he had arrived for the meeting and conference with the man to whom he had been sent, he departed from this life in the very midst of his care and meditation on performing his duty. But while Publius Servilius was of the opinion that a tomb should be publicly decreed for Sulpicius, he did not think a statue should be granted, for the reason that he believed this honor of a statue should be granted to no one unless they had been killed by the sword while on an embassy. As was the case with Lars Tolum— <note>The text cuts off mid-name, referring to Lars Tolumnius, King of Veii, who killed Roman ambassadors</note>

[Handwritten at top: Why he was called Nero]

### XV.I.O On Illustrious Men

**Nero.** He was called Nero because of his fortitude <note>The name "Nero" is of Sabine origin, meaning "strong" or "valiant."</note>. But the Sabines seem to have adopted this from the Greeks, who call the ligaments and supports of the limbs *neura* <note>original: "νευρα" (neura) - nerves or sinews</note>. From this, we also call them *nervos* in Latin. Cicero calls the soldiers, fleets, and taxes the "sinews of the republic" <note>A metaphor for the essential strength or infrastructure of the state.</note>.

**In front of the Rostra.** That is, on the Rostra. For a platform was built in the Hostilian Court in the Forum, which the Romans adorned with the beaks <note>term: *rostra* - the bronze prows or "beaks" of captured enemy ships used to decorate the speaker's platform</note> of the ships of the Antiates: and for that reason, they called that place the Rostra. From this place, orators were accustomed to deliver speeches. The beaks of the ships fixed to the tribunal were a mark of honor, as Pliny records in the fourth chapter of his sixteenth book.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Referring to the commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius.</note> "You have done a most pleasing thing," etc. The power of such Cudweed <note>original: "Gnaphalij"</note> and of French Spikenard <note>original: "gallicæ nardi"</note> growing wild—and for that reason called "of the woods"—is seen to be of no small strength in the deserted fields of Flanders which lie between Ghent and Bruges; whence I would easily believe he collected them, so that he might even ascribe Flanders to Germany. For the Venetians and Florentines make frequent journeys through that area, though they did so more frequently in the past. At Bruges, moreover, Hermolao Barbaro greeted Maximilian, the designated King of the Romans, in the name of the Venetians. **Specimen.** An example; the French call it a *monstre* <note>In the sense of a "showing" or demonstration.</note>. **Forgotten.** Used as an adjective, meaning things given over to oblivion. **Trichae.** Occupations that entangle and impede you, like the "trichae" <note>hairs or tangles</note> that bind the feet of chickens. Iacobus Tusanus rendered this Idyll of Theocritus in verse thus: "Running about everywhere through these ridges, she destroys one." Where he says "through these ridges" instead of "through these porches." For porches are shaded areas seen before the doors of the wealthy, made either of planks, or vines, or other topiary work, behind which Apelles hid himself to catch the criticism of his works. **And I wish.** <note>original: "και βουλομαι" (kai boulomai)</note> That is, "and I want": or as Poliziano interprets it, "and it pleases": for what we want pleases us. This will be discussed again in the last letter of this book. **Denaria.** Because in Greek they are called *denaria* <note>original: "δηνάρια"</note>. But some change either the gender or the word itself among us; they are of a different gender: as in *-es*, which are masculine for the Greeks but are mostly feminine for us when they end in *-a*, except for *planeta* and *cometa*. Or perhaps because the noun they silently refer to is of a different gender among the Greeks than among us—as perhaps *denarion* if they understand it as "coinage" <note>neuter</note> and we as "coin" <note>masculine</note>. However, it does not seem to be derived from *deca* or *decem* <note>ten</note> since it lengthens the first syllable and is written with an *e*, and shortens the second, which is usually lengthened in words ending in *-arius* derived from numbers, such as *ternarius* <note>triple</note>, *senarius* <note>sixfold</note>, etc.

### Angelo Poliziano to his friend Pandolfo Collenuccio. Greetings. Letter XXXII.

**Y**ou have done a most pleasing thing by sending me a specimen of the herbs Cudweed and French Spikenard, which you recently found in Germany. Nor can it be doubted that they are (as Plautus says) the very things themselves. For this Spikenard does not differ much in appearance or color from that of Assyria and Cilicia. And in the Cudweed, the signs agree: the whiteness and softness of the leaves, for which reason it was used as stuffing by the ancients. Artemidorus also shows this in the fifth book of *On the Interpretation of Dreams*, writing that he who seemed to himself to have wheat instead of Cudweed in his mattress would have a male son. But more on this elsewhere. Truly, your diligence and skill...

# On Thymele and Latinus

Greetings, Pico: I understand that you greatly desire for me to make more clear to you what I briefly touched upon regarding **Thymele** and **Latinus** <note>Thymele and Latinus were famous mimes/performers in ancient Rome, often mentioned by the satirist Juvenal.</note> against the opinion of Merula. <note>Giorgio Merula (c. 1430–1494), a contemporary humanist scholar known for his commentaries on classical texts.</note> I will gladly comply with your request, as you are a man most outstanding in both letters and character, and one who has deserved the very best from me.

Merula claims, therefore, that **Thymele** was the wife of **Latinus**, and that he was even accustomed to "prostitute" her—as he puts it—so that she was sometimes beaten by her adulterers. He suggests that Thymele's adultery and the disgrace of Latinus himself were so well known that a new character based on them was introduced onto the stage by the writers of Mimes. <note>Mimes were a form of popular, often ribald, Roman theatrical entertainment.</note>

But, while first professing my respect for an otherwise learned man, I say that what he hands down in this passage is partly demonstrably false, and partly can be proven by neither authority nor reason. Although the burden of proof lies more with Merula himself—or whoever might defend Merula—than with me, I will nevertheless set forth the suspicions by which I believe he was led to devise these things. He was, evidently, reading from **Juvenal**, whom he was then interpreting. And...

--- Page 148 ---
<meta>This page continues the scholarly defense of the Roman mime Latinus, refuting claims of his immorality or a supposed marriage to the mime Thymele. The author continues to analyze classical poetry to reconstruct the actual stage practices of the 1st century AD.</meta>

->.IVX. Of Illustrious Men<-

As I myself have said: what good will it do to gnaw tooth with tooth? One needs meat if one wishes to be satisfied. <note>A metaphorical way of saying that petty criticism is unsatisfying; one needs substantial facts.</note>

[Marginal note: Thymele.] Finally, the very Epitaph which I have set forth favors his character. Nowhere, therefore, did Merula <note>Gaudenzio Merula, a contemporary scholar</note> read this: that Thymele was the wife of Latinus. Nor, because she is said to be "sent" by Latinus, will it immediately signify that she was prostituted [Marginal note: In his place] but rather employed by Latinus so that she might stroke the informer with a gift in his place, whom Carus <note>A notorious informer under Emperor Domitian</note> was also stroking. Nor is it absurd that a male mime should use the services of a female mime, even if she were not his wife. For that Thymele was also a mime is persuaded by the very etymology of her name <note>From the Greek 'thymele', an altar or stage platform</note>: because she, just like Latinus, was watched by Domitian himself. Furthermore, female mimes (as much as we read) were generally of that reputation where they made their bodies common; such as those who were celebrated in the age of Augustus: [Marginal note: Arbuscula. Cytheris. Origo. The chest of Latinus.] Arbuscula, Cytheris, and Origo. Whereby it happens that there is almost no room for "adultery" in the case of a female mime <note>Meaning: since they were already considered promiscuous, the legal or moral concept of adultery hardly applied to them</note>. For that "chest of Latinus" <note>A famous stage prop</note> which was to be the death of him has nothing to do with Thymele. Just as, for example, the "Jealous Husband of Thymele" has nothing to do with Latinus. But "Latinus’s chest," in which an adulterer is hidden, can be understood such that the hiding places of adulterers in general are designated by that chest under which some adulterer used to hide on stage (perhaps as the plot required), a role which this most noble mime was accustomed to play. For I think he is called "about to perish" not because Latinus actually perished by the work of informers—whom Martial indicates remained dear to the Prince even in death—but because in the plot of a Mimic play the caught adulterer is killed, or at least seems entirely about to perish unless he immediately hides under the chest. [Marginal note: The Jealous Husband of Thymele.] There is a similar conjecture regarding the "Jealous Husband of Thymele." For just as I believe: the mime Thymele sustained the persona of someone's wife on stage who would deceive her jealous husband; and because that noble youth played the husband, he is called by Juvenal "the Jealous Husband of Thymele." [Marginal note: Whosoever.] That adulteries were the primary "harvest" of the Mimes is declared by the poet Ovid in these verses to Augustus, in the second book of the *Tristia*:
*What if I had written Mimes jesting with obscenities,*
*Which always have the song of joined love?*
*In which the elegant adulterer constantly proceeds,*
*And the fair bride deceives her foolish husband.* And a little after:
*And when the lover has deceived the husband with some novelty,*
*There is applause, and the palm of victory is given with great favor.* And again:
*And with your eyes, which the whole world uses,*
*You have happily watched stage-play adulteries.*
Is it now clear to you, Baptista, that it has nowhere yet been proven either that Thymele was the wife of Latinus, or that adulterers were accustomed to be procured by him, or finally that a new persona was introduced by the mime-writers for such an adultery? Because no author has said these things, and those empty ideas are like mists—not of arguments, but of the lightest suspicions, or rather of some dream—blown away by a mere breath. [Marginal note: Panniculus being beaten by Latinus.] It remains for us to show that Latinus was not beaten by adulterers. For what he cites from Martial regarding the slaps of Latinus, and also regarding Panniculus, ought rather to be understood as Latinus himself beating Panniculus, rather than him offering his face to Panniculus. That this is true is also declared by the same Martial in the second book of *Epigrams* in these words:
*It is told, Posthumus, what happened at yesterday's dinner,*
*Which I would wish had not: for who would approve such deeds?*
*Your face was smitten, with as much sound as Latinus himself*
[Marginal note: To smite the face.] *Does not strike the cheap face of Panniculus.*
You see: that the face was smitten not *to* Latinus by adulterers, but rather *to* Panniculus himself by Latinus. For the face is said to be "smitten" when it is well-struck. Certainly Seneca uses it this way in the third book of *Natural Questions* (which however is commonly inscribed as the fourth, and subjoined to the tenth). Seneca's words are these: "I show myself credulous to those who lead me all the way to these lighter lies in which the face is usually smitten, not the eyes plucked out." [Marginal note: Panniculus the Mime.] That Panniculus himself was also a mime is taught by that same Martial in book three:
*Lest you should read a part of a wanton little book, chaste lady,*
*I forewarned and advised; yet look, you read it anyway.*
*But if you watch Panniculus, if you watch Latinus, chaste lady,*
*These things are no more wicked than mimes; read on.*
But Panniculus was (as it seems) a mime of a cheaper sort: for which reason the Poet called his face "cheap." Therefore, I think he always sustained that persona which would receive slaps according to the plot. Because, as a witty man, Latinus was accustomed to do this with a huge sound, so that the spectators might raise a laugh at the louder cracking of Panniculus's cheeks. [Marginal note: A passage of Juvenal.] For that those slaps were in the plot of some play (as we said), Juvenal indicates, saying:
*He can laugh, who [watches] the slaps of the Mamercus family.*
For he censures the citizens because they took delight in the nobility performing gestures on stage, such that some of them even offered their faces to slaps, or gave them. But this also could be asked: what reason would there be why Latinus should be beaten by adulterers, if he himself was prostituting his wife to the adulterers? Or what need, finally, for the adulterers to be covered by the chest of Latinus, if the spouse was being provided at Latinus's command? Therefore (as I said before), these things are frivolous and false, and utterly clashing with themselves, and supported by no reason.

# On the Pairing of Books

If one should bring forth a collection of **books** <note>original: "librorum"</note> from the **Florentine Pandects** <note>The Pandects, or Digest, is a vast collection of Roman legal writings compiled under Emperor Justinian I in the 6th century; the Florentine manuscript is its most famous witness</note>, they would provide a clear **example** <note>original: "exemplum"</note> of the craft. These volumes were often **silvered** <note>original: "inargentati"; referring to the practice of decorating or binding books with silver</note> with great care and according to a specific **method** <note>original: "ratione"</note>.

**According to** <note>original: "secundum"</note> the records of **Illustrious Men** <note>original: "Virozum Illustrium"; likely referring to a biographical compendium such as that by Jerome or Gennadius</note>, there is a notable **conjunction** <note>original: "piunctio"</note> of texts found thereafter.

**Letters, Book VIII. Folio LXIX.**

ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, was the printer and commentator for this edition.</note>. *Although shame [restrains] me.* He gives magnificent thanks and prays for the best for Pope Innocent VIII because he had adopted Giovanni, the son of Lorenzo de' Medici, into the College of Cardinals. At the same time, to justify the Pope's action, he extols Giovanni’s natural talent and his wisdom, which exceeds his years. He says beautifully: *the reason for the cast vote will be evident to the colleagues*—that is, they will prove they adopted him for a just reason when he proves himself worthy of such great honor. He referred to the "Medici" either in the third declension or as an adjective.

**Angelo Poliziano to Pope Innocent VIII, Supreme Pontiff, sends greetings.**
**Letter V.**

[Large decorative initial E] Although shame prevents me—a man of slender fortune and almost no authority—from sending letters to you, the Vicar of the Most High God and the Prince of the human race; nevertheless, in such great joy, both my own private joy and the public joy of our entire city, I cannot help but testify before you, Supreme Pontiff Innocent, to this sudden gladness of soul. I profess my joy and give thanks also in my own private name to your Holiness, because you have adopted our youth Giovanni, the son of Lorenzo—the delight of the Florentine Republic—into the number of your brothers and the college of the supreme senate. Through this most flourishing city and most noble family, you have heaped such a distinguished gift and such eminent dignity. Then I also congratulate you, because by this most constant faith of your sharpest judgment, you have secured a glory almost immortal alongside your other extraordinary virtues. For even if I remain silent about Lorenzo himself—whom you have bound to you forever, Holy Father, by this so great a benefit—what, finally, is more perfect than our Cardinal Giovanni himself? Or what is more complete in every respect? I will not indulge my own love, nor will I flatter your judgment, O Pontiff; I shall speak of things known to all and witnessed. He was so born and made, so raised and educated, and finally so learned and instructed, that he yields to no one in genius, nor to his equals in industry, nor to his teachers in literature, nor to the elders in gravity. A native and genuine integrity is in him; the diligence of his parent was also so expensively cultivated that from his mouth, not only has no foul word ever fallen, but not even anything slight or even too licentious. No action, no gesture, no gait in him has been criticized; in short, nothing else was seen that could be interpreted in a worse light. There is such a gray maturity in his green age that the elders who hear him speaking recognize in him the ancestral—and we certainly recognize the paternal—disposition. He sucked in the cultivation of piety and religion almost with his nurse's milk; even then, from his cradle, he meditated on sacred offices, when his most provident father had already destined him for the Church even before he was born. Immediately, however, as he was received into the light of day, he began to be educated for this hope with many magnificent omens. And since he gave such a specimen of himself as to provide proof even then of that virtue, the most wise and most holy King Louis of the French <note>Louis XI of France</note>, compelled by his fame, judged that this same person, while clearly still a boy, was not unworthy even of the height of a supreme Archbishopric. You have, therefore, that King as a supporter of this conferred dignity. The greatest King began the web which the Supreme Pontiff might finish. Would that you could hear the voices of the Florentine people now boding well and prosperously for you; would that you could see the multitude of citizens everywhere exulting and rushing together in our courtyards, unable to contain their gladness, and the common people themselves scarcely able to hold the joy in their souls. Neither the gravity of the old men, nor the modesty of the matrons, nor the weakness of the boys holds them back from their duty. Every sex and every age, every rank flows together to the Medici house (as if to their own private relations); each for himself hastens to be the first to drink in with his eyes the sight of the new Cardinal; they exult, they shout, they stretch their hands to heaven, praying to God to be propitious to you and for all things to be prosperous and favorable. Vows are undertaken by absolutely everyone for either your health or your dignity. Nor is it right that you should count our Cardinal by his years or his birthdays; virtue reached him before his day. Do not doubt, O Pontiff: he will surely fill the August purple. He will not pant under the weight of the hat; he will not be dazzled by too much splendor; you will not receive him unsuitably for such a great senate, nor unequal to such a great height. Even now there is an ample majesty; even now a presence greater than usual. The reason for the cast vote will be evident to the colleagues, and you, Supreme Pontiff, will never repent of your judgment. In this name (which is the only thing I am able to do), I congratulate you and give thanks. Those most blessed feet which I once kissed in person, I now prostrate myself before them in absence, full of joy, and I pray to God that we may long enjoy your benefit, and that the most prosperous outcomes may follow your prosperous undertakings. As for what pertains to me (since there is no other faculty according to my soul), I will certainly take care, as long as my strength lasts, that your benefits of this kind, Holy Father, are propagated into all posterity by the eternal memory of letters.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of classical metaphors and the inherent qualities of nature, specifically focusing on the term 'Ingenium' (innate character).</meta>

[Handwritten: The natural character of the Rhine]

# XIX. Of Illustrious Men

**Character.** For snakes do not flee from those born of wild blood <note>original: "ferino sanguine natos." A reference to the belief that certain lineages possessed a natural power over animals.</note>. **Character** <note>original: "Ingenium"</note> is that which is implanted in us by nature, which they call a natural inclination. Terence says in *The Girl from Andros*: "It is the character of all men to be inclined from labor toward lust." Aulus Gellius calls the nature of the palm tree its "character." His words are from the sixth chapter of the third book. "For that reason," says Plutarch, "it was decided that the palm should be the sign of victory in contests: because the character of such wood is this: that it does not yield to those things pressing down or crushing it." <note>The palm tree was a symbol of resilience because its wood was thought to grow upward against a weight.</note> Either to Thetis—that is, to water or the sea—or to the husband of Venus—that is, to Vulcan and fire. Ausonius says much the same in his letter to Symmachus regarding the number three: "This trifling little book," he says, "long kept secret but now torn apart by common reading, will finally reach your hands. You will either restore it to life like Asclepius, or like Plato—with the help of Vulcan <note>meaning: by burning the manuscript</note>—you will liberate it from infamy, if it is not meant to reach fame." We say more on this in the *Gryphon* of Ausonius.

ASCENSIUS. From the heart: from the mouth:
