<meta>This page continues the commentary on a letter from Cardinal Jacopo Ammanati Piccolomini (the Papiensian) to the scholars Angelo Poliziano and Niccolò Michelozzi regarding Poliziano's Latin translation of Homer.</meta>

# Book of Letters. VIII. Folio LXX.

In this phrasing, because he inserts many things before he reaches the principal verb, he repeats that upon which the verb depends, saying:
*I say, I fear lest he respond* etc. In the middle of the phrasing he also uses a graceful ellipsis <note>original: "eclipsi"; a rhetorical omission of words</note>: because the words that are missing are easily understood; and yet, so that you may recognize a hesitant mind, the speech is intricate and somewhat obscure, especially to me. Lest it perhaps be more obscure to others, I shall explain it thus. *I fear lest Homer, seeing many things from across the sea*—such as Latin things, which to the Greeks are from across the sea—*are perceived* (the particle "that" <note>original: "ut"</note> is missing, I believe by design, so as not to appear to side with the Greeks; and yet it can be understood) *either better or more sharply or more aptly among the Greeks than our own*, i.e., the Latins: *furthermore*, i.e., because it is certainly established that each language has its own, i.e., peculiar excellence: which, namely excellence: *it is given* or *it happens*: *scarcely to attain in a foreign* language: *finally*, i.e., to say it in one word: they say or it is established: *a beard on the chin*, i.e., which is only on the chin (unless you construe it as "referring to the mind" <note>A play on the Latin words "menti" (to the chin) and "menti" (to the mind)</note> of those seeing it) *neither proves*, i.e., demonstrates: *plainly*, i.e., clearly enough that he is a Latin man: *nor represents*, i.e., presents a Greek. This means if someone grows a beard on or under the chin as long as possible, as Italians sometimes do: yet neither an Italian nor a Greek will be proven by this. Not an Italian, because many Italians do not grow a beard; nor a Greek: because for them the beard also stands out on the upper lip. And therefore if someone translating Greek simulates a "beard on the chin": that is, expresses some figures and some Greek-style wit: yet because he does not express all of them, he will be judged plainly as neither Latin nor Greek: *I say, I fear lest* Homer *should respond that he prefers to be considered Colophonian* <note>Colophon was one of the cities claiming to be Homer's birthplace</note> etc. Concerning this, as Aulus Gellius recites, there is a controversy among the Greeks: for seven cities claim him as their citizen. *Equal to your Phaethon*. I would doubt whether to read "equal" <note>Latin: "aequalem"</note>: unless I understand "equal" <note>Latin: "aequalis"</note> as being of equal age with you: that is, a youth as you are: although born many centuries after him. Moreover, Phaethon is praised because he attempted to attain the golden chariot of his father, even if things turned out badly for him. It is a proverb: he who proposes a golden chariot for himself will attain either a golden wheel or at least a spoke. Indeed, the effort is praised for great things: provided, however, it is not entirely in vain. *A dexterous manner*. A Virgilian saying beautifully adopted. *To have pleased leading men* etc. That is from Horace in his Epistles. *To grant even to the Papiensian thus far*: repeat "beware": so that it is "beware even to grant to the Papiensian" (he speaks beautifully of himself as if of another) *thus far*, i.e., to the point that you think his benevolence is an honor to you out of his dignity, not out of merits to be conferred upon you.

### Cardinal Jacopo of Pavia to Angelo Poliziano and Niccolò Michelozzi. Health and Greetings.
### Letter VII.

You will both bear it with a calm mind if, rarely having any free time, I respond late and with only one letter to both of you. I have read your translation, Angelo, diligently enough for the amount of leisure I had. To you asking what I think: it is easier for me to respond than for me to be confident that a response can be well-given by an unlearned man. You believe me to be something; I am much below your opinion. If I once brought any light to this place, it has been darkened by the shadows of the Court. Poverty long ago, and now dignity, have compelled me to handle matters different from my first studies. Endive has succeeded ambrosia, and gluttony has succeeded taste: I am now as poorly able to judge oratory and poetry as those with blocked ears judge music. Lest I fail your expectation, however, receive this, which is a sign of benevolence rather than of retained learning. Your oratory, as far as I measure past things, is Latin and illustrious, so that it can be added to this commendation. The verses are also full: and magnificently serving the ears with their rhythms. In such a fresh age, these are things of praise and admiration. Nor do I think the labor undertaken is useless. It pertains to learning Homer thoroughly: to nourishing the spirit by degrees: to finally undertaking those things in which we may walk by our own step, not in the footsteps of others. Yet if anyone should ask Homer whether he wishes to be made Latin, and rendered verse for verse: I fear lest, seeing many things from across the sea are perceived among the Greeks than our own, and furthermore that each language has its own excellence, which it is scarcely possible to attain in another: finally, that a beard on the chin neither plainly proves a Latin nor represents a Greek, I say, I fear lest he respond: that he prefers to be held as a Colophonian than a Florentine, and that the cloak <note>The Greek *pallium*</note> fits Greek limbs more aptly than the toga. Then he might praise the judgment of those who, endowed with great genius: since they distrusted that the same quality he has among his own could be rendered in ours, preferred to imitate rather than to translate. I judge, however (as I said), that the work begun should not be abandoned, and this study of exercising the style should be cultivated with diligence, praised indeed by the ancients, and most necessary for filling the heart. If you do not attain what you wish, it is no more due to the nature of the thing than to the poverty of our eloquence:

To Alfredo, my friend.

# Of Illustrious Men

Complete the remaining tasks with diligence: and love me: and know that you are recorded in the account-book of my friends, not among the last: but fixed to my heart as if with <term>foundation nails</term> <note>original: "trabalibus clauis"; a metaphor for an unbreakable bond, famously used by Horace</note>. Farewell. Rome. On the Calends of January.

**To strike.** F.S. <note>likely Franciscus Sylvius, the commentator</note> **To graze.** that is, to disturb. For to strike is to hit. Moreover, those whose noses are struck find the sharpness of their jests disturbed.
**Lord.** ASCEN. <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer and scholar</note> **Prince and Lord.** The frequent use of writers, or rather the abuse, has grown so strong that one calls another "Lord," even though to the ancients it smacked of tyranny: and aside from that, it is appropriate to God alone. But he fortified himself by first saying "Prince," who is the first in a free city, as if the first of the fathers. **Yourself.** <note>original: "Tute"</note> that is, you yourself. One does not say "tumet" in the nominative case to avoid a coincidence with the verb "tumet" (to swell). **Author of daring.** The Virgilian Juno. *I am the author of daring.* Therefore, boys should learn to adopt Virgilian words, provided they do so sparingly and aptly. **Of us.** the memory which you held of us. **You remember coming.** So Agretius prescribes that one should say "coming" rather than "to have come." Valla, however, feels the opposite. **Because from ignorance of greatness.** There is a missing particle (which he ascribes to elegance) having the force of a comparative, such as "more," "rather," "more evidently," "more confidently," or similar: as in the letter of Papiensis. He also speaks beautifully of himself as if of another: for we do this when we think or speak magnificently of ourselves: as in the *Aeneid*, book 5: *What gifts will you give worthy of Nisus? I who earned the first crown by praise?* Where perhaps it is more correctly read "he earned": although in the "Nisus" pointed out, the demonstrative pronoun "to me" can be understood, which "who" refers back to. For Papiensis wrote: "To grant thus far to Papiensis, so that his (not my) benevolence etc." He ingratiates himself into the friendship of the Cardinal so that by his recommendation to the <term>Supreme Pontiff</term> <note>The Pope</note> he may be made so dear that the Pope stands by his promises.

### Angelo Poliziano to Ascanio Sforza Visconti, Cardinal. Greetings.
### Letter VIII.

[Decorative initial P] Much and often, I confess, I hesitated: whether I, a man of the lowest strength and humble fortune, should send letters to you, an excellent prince and lord. Indeed, your greatness deterred me from writing: and as if by certain rays, it grazed the edge of our mind. On the other hand, your experienced humanity and clemency encouraged me to write at last. Moreover, it seemed too foolish, since you yourself were the author of my daring, to allow—whether through a certain untimely fear or a rustic shame—the memory of us to fade away in your mind. You remember, I believe, that someone once seemed to come to you and greet you along with the young son of Lorenzo de' Medici: a certain Angelo Poliziano, the teacher of the boy himself. Whom some said was considered a man not entirely unlearned: He, having taken up a sudden boldness in your presence, chatted for a while about the ancient works and foundations of the city. I am that man, of course. And the same confidence or boldness toward you remains in my absence which was not lacking then in my presence. But yet, there is no reason why anyone should turn that into a fault in me. Naturally, it proceeds from the knowledge of your humanity rather than from ignorance of your greatness. You may ask what these letters seek for themselves. Truly nothing else: except that they renew the memory of me with you: that they declare me to be a man most devoted to you: hoping greatly in your patronage: and that I will give effort (if the matter allows) so that I may one day prove my soul, faith, and goodwill to you. Moreover, I pray (unless it is improper) that if any mention of us arises before the Supreme Pontiff (it will arise, I know, when you wish it), you show that I am a man not ungrateful to him. For I easily understand how much your authority will avail with him: since I am not ignorant of how much it ought to avail by right. Farewell. Florence. 1485.

**By paying.** F.S. **I am not for paying.** i.e., not even my life could satisfy you. Moreover, "paying" is a gerund in the dative case. i.e., for paying, like a man "of heart" and "of fruit." i.e., for the heart, and for the fruit. As Cicero says. Moreover, those words of Cicero are from the second book of *On Duties*. "Conveniently," he says, "whoever said that he who has the money has not repaid it: and he who has repaid it does not have it: **Grace/Gratitude.** but he who has repaid gratitude both has it, and he who has it has returned it." He writes almost the same sentiment elsewhere. The words are from the oration for Gnaeus Plancius. "Because," he says, "the owing of money and of gratitude are different. For he who pays off money immediately does not have that which he returned. But he who owes it retains the property of another. However, he who returns gratitude, has it: and he who has it, in that very fact that he has it, returns it." Regarding which, Aulus Gellius in chapter 4 of the first book records a clever sentiment of Antonius Julianus. **We shall have loosened.** i.e., we have begun. **There shall be Alcedonia.** i.e., there shall be tranquility. For *Alcedo* was said by the ancients for *Halcyon* (the kingfisher), as *Catamytus* for *Ganymede*, and *Melo* for the *Nile*. Pompeius is the authority. Moreover, the *Alcedo* is a certain bird larger than a sparrow, distinguished by a color sometimes blue, sometimes green, and sometimes even lightly purple: not indeed distinct in color part by part: but reflecting variously from the whole body and wings and neck without distinction: the beak is greenish, long, and thin. The nest is closest in shape to medicinal gourds, those which have a more extended neck. The size is larger than the largest sponges. Some are larger, others smaller. It is visible and crowded on all sides: it can hardly be cut by a sharp iron, unless you both strike with the iron and crush it with the hand at once. The entrance is so small that if it is turned, water cannot flow in. From what material it is composed is ambiguous. It seems, however, to be constructed rather from the spines of the needlefish. For the kingfisher lives on fish. Five of its young are consumed by it. These things are in the fourteenth chapter of the ninth book of *On the Nature of Animals* by Aristotle. Pliny in chapter 32 of the tenth book relates that Halcyons make nests seven days before the winter solstice: and give birth in as many following days: which days are called Halcyon days, at which time the Sicilian sea is especially navigable, on account of its extreme tranquility. Ovid in the eleventh book of *Metamorphoses*, where he writes the fable: *And through seven placid days in winter time Halcyone broods upon her nests hanging on the sea. Then the way of the sea is safe, Aeolus guards the winds and keeps them from departing, and provides a calm sea for his grandsons.* Therefore, "Alcedonia" are called tranquilities. Plautus in the prologue of *Casina*: *Lest anyone fear his debt-collector. It is a game, a game has been given to the bankers, it is calm, there are Alcedonia around the forum.* i.e., tranquility and silence. Halcyon days are tranquil and idle.
**Word.** **Word.** i.e., a proverb. Terence: *This is an old word, that all things are common among friends.* The same in the *Andria*: *That is a true word which is commonly said: that all wish better for themselves than for another.* **Thrice beautiful.** **Thrice beautiful because it pleases thrice.** That is a Greek proverb: <note>original: "Δις και τρις το καλον"</note> that is, "twice and thrice the beautiful," it must be understood as "to be said." It is used by Plato in the last book of *Laws*. "Concerning these things," he says, "although we touched on them somewhat above, yet those things which are excellent, as it is said in the proverb, can be rightly repeated twice and thrice." Bordering on this is that of Seneca: *That which is well said is never said enough.* Also that of Horace: *Ten times repeated, it will please.* Yet there is that of Terence: *It wearies me now to hear the same things a thousand times.*

**Book of Letters. VIII. Folio LXXI.**

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer and commentator.</note> *We have set sail.* <note>original: "Oram soluerimus"</note> This is well used in Quintilian: and we are well described as "loosening the cable." *Having found a favorable wind.* "To loosen the cable" is also from Virgil. *Lest any delay happen to the favorable wind.* For a ship is carried by the blowing wind upon the sea. Whence "favorable" <note>original: "ferenti"</note> is usually explained as "blowing." *By the divine power:* by a nod, or by favor: otherwise, if one were to be a substitute for a deity, the praise would exceed all measure. *The more I read.* Furthermore, in this he imitates Virgil: *The more that trembling thing, etc.* Concerning things either badly recited or unworthy of being recited: about which Terence speaks: if Sylvius cites him at the end, there is also what Poliziano cites while correcting Juvenal: *Twice-served cabbage is death* <note>original: "Δὶς κράμβη θάνατος"</note>. Whence Juvenal says: *Repeated cabbage kills the wretched teachers.* Now, cabbage is a species of cheap vegetable: which, when served frequently, tortures those eating it with loathing: just as the repeated reading or writing of unrefined boys tortures their teachers.

->**Angelo Poliziano to Francesco Piccolomini, Cardinal of Siena. Greetings.**<-
**Letter IX.**

**E**ven though I know, most distinguished Father, that I owe so much to your kindness—which you showed me so excellently and singularly when I was there—that I seem unable to satisfy it by any duties, work, labor, or industry of mine: nevertheless, considering that nothing is so ungrateful as to conceal what you owe when you cannot repay it, I decided to send you some letters by which my feeling toward you and my conscience might be witnessed. If a contest of giving and returning thanks were pressed upon me with you, I would certainly have yielded my hands to you immediately, as one in whose very house the Graces themselves dwell. But since you are greater than our attempts can reach, we reward you with certain imaginary duties, as befits the matter and our means: namely, by thinking and speaking well of you, favoring you, and wishing you all good things. But if duties are weighed only by services, and not rather by will and spirit, I confess I am not solvent. But if (as Cicero thinks) even when thanks are felt, they are returned in the very act of being felt: I do not fear but that I shall be what I ought to be, at least repaying you with my spirit itself. Since that spirit is entirely owed to you by the merit of your kindness, I now dedicate it all to you, on the condition that it never be set free from your service. We have approached the writing of a history of the Roman Emperors with great spirit and courage. And although we have only very recently *set sail* and have moved only a little way from the harbor, nevertheless, *having found a favorable wind*, we are carried forward with a steady foot. Nor do we doubt that, with the prosperous favor of the divine power of Innocent <note>Pope Innocent VIII</note>—under whose auspices we set out—there will be for us a perpetual *Halcyon calm*. <margin>Halcyon days.</margin> But I beseech you: if ever mention of us should happen before his Holiness (and it will happen as often as you wish), commend me, if it seems right, with these words: "This Angelo Poliziano is neither a bad man, nor entirely unlearned. Indeed, Holy Father, he is so devoted to you that he is perhaps not unworthy of your occasional regard." This is enough for him; the rest I entrust to God. As for that golden oration on the circumcision by your friend Antonio Lollio, I read it recently again and again; the more I read it, the more it pleased me. There is a Greek proverb: *A thing is thrice beautiful which pleases when read three times.* I would commend that man to you, were it not absurd and backward for him to be commended by us to you, whom you hold so dear that I rather desire to be vehemently commended to you by him. Farewell. 1485.

**F.S.** <note>The commentator Franciscus Sylvius.</note> *Those who sew pillows under the head.* That is, those who stroke and flatter. For just as pillows, which are called *oraria* <note>from 'os', mouth/face</note> from the face, are placed under the head so that the head or the ears themselves are not hurt: so flatterers, lest the ears of those they wish to flatter be offended, tickle and delight them with a certain softness of words. The ears of men who rejoice in flatteries are said to be "soft." <margin>To sew pillows. Face-cloths.</margin>

**ASCENSIUS.** *We had conceived.* The letter is polished and clean: adorned with chosen words without deceit, and no less full of thought: for that reason, it is worthy of imitation. Death envied us this Roman history. Sabellicus—not to be regretted indeed, but inferior, I think, to that which Angelo was toiling upon—brought the history down to our times in a continuous thread.

->**Francesco Piccolomini, Cardinal of Siena, to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings.**<-
**Letter X.**

**W**e had conceived such an opinion of Poliziano that we thought it could by no means be increased; for it had reached the summit. Yet he increased it by his most ornate and weighty letters. And he increased it so much that we, who thought before that we had grasped everything about him, seemed not even to have touched how much he is worth. We praise the dexterity of your genius, we are delighted by the elegance, we admire the gravity. But all these things must be approached with silence rather than weak speech. Nor should you think us to be in the number of those who *sew pillows under the head*. For true love knows not how to flatter. God is witness: our conscience is witness. As for the work you have undertaken on the Roman Emperors: it will be, I think, perfect, because it will be yours. We await its final touch, which we do not doubt will be most consummate. Because we owe much to virtue, we owe much to you. To whom we shall never be lacking in service or industry. Rome. April 6, 1485.

**F.S.** *Nutricia* <note>Nurture-poems</note> is the name of a book by Poliziano in the plural number, just as Statius calls a certain *Silva* <note>Forest/Collection</note> of his first book *Soteria* <note>Health-wishes</note>: in which he prays for the health of Rutilius Gallicus. <margin>Nutricia.</margin> Names of books made of only one word, which is like an adjective, are often declined in the plural number: as *grammatica, logica, physica, ethica, politica, buccolica*, and six hundred others of this kind. They say the *Biblia* <note>The Bible</note> is spoken of by the same figure.

**Angelo Poliziano to Giovanni Pietro Arrivabene, Bishop of Urbino. Greetings.**
**Letter XIV.**

ALthough it had never been in doubt that to you, a man excelling in every praise, all honors and dignities were long ago owed; nevertheless, after it was heard that you were made the Bishop of Urbino, we were affected by such great joy—everyone indeed, but especially we who venerate the sacred rites of letters—that this joy seems to have happened to us almost unexpectedly, and not, so to speak, even touched by any hope. For since we were already beginning to fear—all of us who are uniquely devoted to you—lest you, who had been delayed by fortune, might even have been plainly passed over; the more heavy and unworthy that fear had been, the greater and more just is the joy that has now arisen after the fear vanished. To this almost public cause of such great joy, a private and peculiar reason is also added for me: that I see a man promoted to great titles whose authority and kindness, even in my hardest times, so supported me that my hope and confidence ought to grow as much as your fortune or dignity deservedly should. Wherefore, in this particular pleasure of my mind, I would desire a particular way of congratulating you, were I not dealing with you—that is, with a most experienced man—whose distinguished prudence (as we believe) looks into the very hearts of men as if with lynx-like eyes. However, I should by no means omit that Pope Innocent VIII seems to me to strive toward immortal glory as if by a "royal way," because he increases the honors of men who are both learned and grave, and does not allow the bright light of virtue to hide under a bushel (as the saying goes). For to omit the others: I mention here Hermolao Barbaro, whom the Pope undertook first to adorn with such zeal for himself, and soon also to protect and defend; even lately I hear that Hieronymus Balbi himself, a man outstanding in learning and character, has been made a bishop along with you, from which a huge heap, as it were, is added to this excellent joy and pleasure of ours. I would wish you to congratulate him (if you allow it) in my name as well. Farewell.

F.S. With Clement as the author of the *Stromata*. Poliziano in the preface of the *Miscellanea*. Which (he says) lest you should call the commentaries of Clement of Alexandria, [Margin: Clement of Alexandria.] a pontiff and apostolic man, which you might call *Stromateis* <note>Greek: "Patchwork" or "Miscellanies"</note> like "painted coverlets." I think Leonello read "Romans" not "Alexandrians" in the printed books. He thought Poliziano had therefore hallucinated because he said Clement of Rome composed the *Stromata*, when it was he who was of Alexandria. Eusebiuses or Jeromes. Eusebius in his books on the *Preparation for the Gospel* cites Clement of Alexandria; and in the sixth book of *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 11, he says this Clement composed eight books of *Stromata*: which we can understand as a work woven together from various things. Likewise, Saint Jerome in his book *On Illustrious Men* mentions those same things. Both mention Clement of Rome as the third or, as others are persuaded, the fourth Pope.
ASCEN. To your very self. He could have said "To his own," but "himself" is believed to apply to all three persons and has a reciprocal force. *Stromateon* is a Greek genitive. I found it written in Latin characters: either because it was so in Leonello's letter, or because we treat all Greek neuters in "a" as Latin. Introduced or deleted. Great authors hold "introduced" and "deleted" as the same, asserting [Margin: Introduced. For "to delete" (handwritten)] that "to introduce" also signifies in the *Pandects* <note>A compendium of Roman law</note> to strike out and delete; the reasoning being drawn from wax, onto which while the deleting part of the stylus or a fingernail is "introduced" (pressed in), what was written is erased. However, in this place, however "to introduce" is taken elsewhere by Poliziano, "introduced" and "deleted" seem to some to be different. For while we find our writings and delete what had pleased us, they say we "introduce" new things. And although to introduce the stylus or nail may be to delete in a way, yet "introduced" things seem to them to be those placed more correctly over deleted ones. But I, because he adds "badly," which he had received word-for-word as "I add to," do not see how they could have received things utterly deleted, since I see that "introduced" (that is, more correctly imposed) things could have. I would not, however, wish to contend too stubbornly as if "for one's altars" <note>A proverb meaning to fight for what is most sacred</note>; when shall I say things written on paper are then deleted? When, pierced through with lines, although they can still be read, we have marked them to be deleted. Eusebiuses or Jeromes. That is, passages cited from Eusebius and Jerome, by which Clement of Alexandria, not of Rome, was proven.

**Angelo Poliziano to Leonello, Bishop of Concordia. Greetings. Letter XV.**

FRancesco Soderini of Volterra, the Prelate, recently showed me your letter to him regarding our *Miscellanea*, in which learning and kindness seemed to me to compete with a doubtful palm <note>An uncertain victory</note> between them. And indeed, not only did the style itself—elegant, ornate, and grave—exhibit learning, but even more so those things which were objected to me by you concerning Clement, the author of the *Stromata*. Moreover, those seemed the most certain signs of kindness: that a man of both the greatest authority and most ample fortune, occupied with many and great affairs, thought it pertained even slightly to you what I, a little man of humble fortune, had reported in my books. I pass over how kindly, how blandly, how modestly, how lovingly, and even how slowly and hesitantly you brought forth that error of ours—for so it seemed. I pass over that you overwhelmed me first with many praises, even if far more eloquently than truly...

<meta>This page continues a discussion on the principles of rhetoric and the imitation of classical models, specifically focusing on the theories of Quintilian regarding Cicero and Demosthenes.</meta>

->...they seemed to themselves to have expressed the style of that heavenly man in their speaking, if they could only end a sentence with the phrase: "it would seem to be." <note>original: "esse videatur." This was a famous rhythmic cliché used by Cicero; the author is mocking those who think imitating a single phrase makes them equal to the master.</note> Therefore, the first point is this: that whoever is about to imitate someone must understand what they are imitating and know why it is considered good. Then, in taking up the burden, he should consult his own strengths. Thus says that author <note>referring to Quintilian, a Roman educator of the 1st century AD</note>. A little later, the same Quintilian writes that even the most perfect example in an art should not always be imitated. He says: "By far the most perfect of all the Greeks was Demosthenes; nevertheless, others did certain things better in certain places. He did most things best, but he is not the only one to be imitated, nor is he the most to be imitated in every single instance." What then? Is it not enough to say everything just as Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note> said it? For my part, it would be enough if I could attain all his qualities. Yet, what harm would it do to adopt, in certain places, the force of Caesar, the sharpness of Caelius, the diligence of Pollio, or the judgment of Calvus? <note>These are all famous Roman orators known for specific stylistic strengths.</note> For besides the fact that it is the mark of a wise man to make his own whatever is best in each person (if he can), it is also true that in such a difficult matter, if we look only at one model, we will scarcely succeed in following even a small part of it. Therefore, since it is almost impossible for a human being to express the whole of whichever model you have chosen, let us place the good qualities of many before our eyes...</p>

<summary>This passage discusses the philosophy of rhetorical imitation, arguing that students should not blindly mimic a single master like Cicero or Demosthenes, but should instead incorporate the diverse strengths of various classical orators.</summary>

->Various foods that are harmful.<- <note>This heading appears to be a misplaced topical marker or a reference to a different section of the volume, as the text below concerns rhetoric.</note>

# Book of Letters VIII. Folio 73.

Those who are believed to have held the leadership in eloquence are similar to one another, as Seneca has passed down. They are mocked by Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus, a celebrated Roman rhetorician</note>—those who thought themselves to be the brothers of Cicero simply because they closed their sentences with these words: "it would seem to be." <note>original: "esse videatur" — a common rhythmic ending in Cicero's oratory that became a cliché for poor imitators.</note> Horace cries out against imitators, and those who are nothing other than imitators. To me, certainly, whoever composes solely from imitation seems to be like either a parrot or a magpie, producing what they do not even understand. For the writings of such men lack strength and life; they lack movement; they lack passion; they lack natural character. They lie there; they sleep; they snore. There is nothing true there, nothing solid, nothing effective. "You do not express Cicero," someone says. What of it? For I am not Cicero; yet I express myself (as I believe). There are some, moreover, my dear Paul, who beg for their style in scraps, like bread; they do not only live from day to day, but for the sake of the day. Then, unless that book is at hand from which they may extract something, they cannot pull together three words. But these very things also...

# .XIII. Of Illustrious Men

or are said to have been collected by me: except for I know not what few men. I, however, remit all of this to you: nor will I clearly interpose my own judgment, since it is in a way a sacrilege to dissent from you: and I am he who (as <term>M. Tullius<note>Marcus Tullius Cicero, the Roman orator and statesman who served as the primary model for Latin prose.</note></term> says) would neither wish to judge another if I could, nor could I if I would. But I shall come to that point in which you say you disagree with me most greatly. For you write that you have heard that I approve of no one unless they seem to follow the features of Cicero. Truly, as far as I can recall in my memory: I neither remember ever having said that, nor do I wish it to have been said. For what folly would it be: that since the talents of men are so varied: their natures so manifold: their wills so diverse among themselves: to wish to bind them within the narrow limits of a single genius and, as it were, to set a predefined boundary? But since you call me into this disputation: it will perhaps not be an inappropriate time for clearing my judgment: and for defending myself: so that I may clearly recognize the truth

Dinocrates the Architect
Letters Book VIII. Folio LXXIIII.

sometimes base and uncultivated, at other times splendid and flourishing; and thus, in the whole genre, it is as if many most hostile seeds were scattered in a single field. For it cannot be otherwise than that various kinds of food are poorly digested, and that from such a dregs-filled mixture, words of the most dissimilar kind collide with one another. Nor does the harsh clash of this corrupt speech strike the ears any less than the crash or noise of falling stones, or chariots racing past. For what pleasure can ambiguous meanings of words bring, or twisted words, abrupt sentences, a rugged structure, bold—and unhappy—metaphor, and rhythms intentionally cut short? This must necessarily happen to all those who unearth meanings and words from individual instances and imitate no one. Truly, the entire speech of these men is like the house of the Hebrews, in which the goods of various men are pledged for a certain time. <margin>The house of the Hebrews.</margin> <note>A reference to a pawnbroker's shop, where many different styles of clothing would be seen hanging together.</note> For there, a cloak, a mantle, a hooded cape, and often the robes of many people are seen hanging and distinguished from one another. 

But I think there is as much difference between him who imitates no one and him who follows a certain leader, as there is between him who wanders aimlessly and him who sets out on a straight path. The former rolls about out of the way among thorns; the latter, however, hastens from his intended journey to the appointed place without a slip or trouble. Furthermore, Poliziano, hold this to be true: no one has achieved the praise of eloquence who has not been practiced in some kind of imitation. Among the Greeks, not only the orators—Demosthenes, Hyperides, Lycurgus, Aeschines, and Demarchus—but even those very philosophers, the masters of virtues, wished to be imitators of someone. I am silent about our own writers in this place, lest I seem to you, the most learned of all, to be explaining a sort of school lesson. Nor do I think anything needs to be said about Marcus Tullius <note>Cicero</note>. It is now well established by everyone that he who applies himself to modeling himself after Marcus Tullius, even if he achieves less glory in imitating him, is nevertheless honored in that he chose him as his model to express; so that the former might seem to be a matter of nature and talent, and the latter a matter of judgment. Farewell.

CASCEN. <note>Likely a commentator's abbreviation.</note>
Nor do I doubt. He responds to the letter of Battista Mantovano; however, he did not care to have it printed with the others, either because it did not seem elegant enough, or because it had been lost, or because it contained certain secrets and he did not wish to publish it mutilated, or for some other reason. In it, Mantovano seems to have written that he loves Poliziano exceptionally, about which he says he has no doubt. However, he says it is inconvenient for him to write often since he is occupied with various things; but he says he does not demand that. He congratulates him for devoting effort to philosophy; he says he will give greater effort himself. He had commended a young man—as I think, a brother—and says that he refused to use his advice, and thinks for that reason he would not want to use his help either. Unless the omen is in vain. One must add "religion" as is most known to poets: "Vain parents taught," which is read in the first book of the Aeneid. He therefore rebukes the young man for rashness and disobedience.

Angelo Poliziano to his friend Battista Mantovano, Carmelite Theologian, sends greetings.
I do not doubt that I am loved by you, nor do I demand what might be inconvenient; but neither do I measure friends by the duty of letters, since that is usually provided even by enemies. Regarding your congratulation that I am dedicated to philosophy, I myself, by Hercules, so congratulate myself, intending to give such effort that you may be able to congratulate me more deservedly day by day. But if this young man of yours had used our advice, he would perhaps have consulted his own interests better. Now, since he refused advice (unless the omen is in vain), I believe he will not want to use my help now either. Nevertheless, I desire you to write to him that he should expect everything from me, certainly for your sake. For nothing is more annoying than that this man was commended to me by you in vain. Farewell.

F. Sylvius on the Ninth Book of Letters of Illustrious Men.

<margin>Dinocrates</margin> Dinocrates the architect, relying on his thoughts and skill when Alexander was gaining power, set out from Macedonia to the army, desiring royal commendation. He was of very large stature, with a grand face, and the highest beauty and dignity. Trusting in these gifts of nature, he laid aside his clothes at his lodging, anointed his body with oil, crowned his head with poplar leaves, covered his left shoulder with a lion's skin, and held a club in his right hand. Thus equipped, he walked to the tribunal of the king who was administering justice. The novelty turned the people's attention. Alexander, seeing him, wondered at him; he ordered a path to be made for him to approach and asked who he was. He replied: "I am Dinocrates, a Macedonian architect, who brings to you thoughts and designs not unworthy of your fame. For I have shaped Mount Athos into the figure of a man's statue, in whose left hand I have designed the walls of a very large city, and in his right a bowl to receive the water of all the rivers that flow from that mountain, so that it might be poured from there into the sea." Alexander, delighted by the logic of the design, immediately asked if there were fields nearby that could sustain that city with grain. Hearing that it could not be done except by overseas transport, he said: "Dinocrates, I observe the excellent composition of the design and am delighted by it. But I notice that if someone were to lead a colony there, his judgment would be blamed. For just as a newborn infant cannot be nourished without the nurse's milk, nor be led to the stages of growing life, so a city without fields and their fruits flowing into the city cannot grow, nor have a large population without an abundance of food, nor maintain a people without plenty. Therefore, just as I think the design should be approved, so I judge the location should be disapproved; and I want you to be with me, because I shall use your work." From then on, Dinocrates did not leave the king. This is from Vitruvius's preface to the second book on architecture. One or another. <margin>Stagyra.</margin> Alexander rebuilt Stagyra, the city of Aristotle, which had been destroyed by him, and restored the citizens who were then scattered or enslaved. Plutarch is the authority in the life of Aristotle. "Sell that to yourself," that is, I do not proclaim these things to you so that I may ask for some reward from you. For criers used to commend a thing for sale. "Behold the poem." He understands the "Nutricia" <note>A poem by Poliziano</note>.

CASCEN.
That the strengths of the mind sometimes prevailed no less than those of talent. "Of the mind," that is, of an eager will or assumed spirit; "than of talent," that is, of natural disposition or innate virtue bestowed on us by nature. **Letter III.**

[Decorative initial N] I cannot help but seem plainly "Barbarous" <note>A pun on his own surname, *Barbarus*, and the concept of being unrefined or ungrateful.</note> and ungrateful to you: I, who have so often delayed giving thanks to you, who write and proclaim so many things about me—and not only write them, but truly feel them. For no letters have ever come here from you, since I first became known to you, in which you did not make an illustrious and honorable mention of me. But see how much I value your testimony of me, whether you do it by judgment or by an inclination of will. I, who am otherwise modest—indeed, timid and lacking confidence in myself—seem to be something significant because you praise me; because you approve of my works; because, as you write, you often rest in our *Themistius* <note>Hermolaus Barbarus published a famous translation and commentary on the Greek philosopher Themistius in 1481.</note> as if in a most pleasant lodging-house. What of the fact that in your letters I frequently recognize myself? Do you think anything could be more pleasant to us than when I perceive that you have not merely noted, but actually imitated, some phrase, period, or figure of speech of ours? And were it not for the fact that you do not seem to do this feignedly or by design when writing to many people, great reasons would suggest themselves to me why I might think this was devised by you for the sake of favor. For I could not see why you would break that flowing and florid style of yours and descend to me: I who, following a dry and very thin thread of oratory, creep upon the ground; I never rise up; I do not inspire; I do not use rounded periods; I do not elevate; I do not cast down—assuredly because my nature is unwilling and resistant. Take away from me a certain amount of labor and diligence, and otherwise I am nothing, except when I am commended by you or those very few like you, or when I find that my works please you even to the point of imitation. O your remarkable and plainly divine genius, Pico! Though the things you write are the best, you nevertheless express and mold the things of others—which are the worst—so that they seem to be your own, which are the best. For to lower oneself and descend, I reckon to be of more value than to strive for the heights. For though the latter may be more honorable, the former is certainly more laborious and of greater effort. Therefore, whether you believe our works to be such that you should spend effort in imitating them, or whether you do this for the sake of putting me in your debt, in both ways I owe you very much. I will return the favor some day; I do not want to say "when I am able" (for I shall never be able), but when you yourself, or your people, think I am able. For so great is the goodness and humanity of your whole family that you are accustomed to count as a benefit that which is not one. Wherefore I shall act for my own benefit if I leave both the manner and the time of repaying the favor to you, so that in the settling of accounts, every false calculation <note>term: *paralogismus* (a piece of illogical reasoning)</note> and deception may proceed entirely from you, not from me. Truly, those things which you wrote to the Scythian <note>Likely a reference to Pico's famous 1485 letter to Ermolao Barbaro defending the "barbarous" medieval philosophers against the polished style of the humanists.</note> concerning the method of your studies, and which you wished to be shared with me, affected me with the greatest pleasure. I congratulated this age for a man of such great learning that he knows almost everything, and of such great care that he seems to know nothing at all [by his humility]. I see that you are an excellent poet and a most eminent orator. I observe that you, formerly an Aristotelian philosopher, have now also become a Platonist. I see that Greek literature—which alone could be found wanting in you <margin>The value of Greek literature.</margin> and without which you would have been nothing—you have not only learned, but have drunk deeply; and that with such great ease and speed that you neither remember, nor could you persuade others, that you were ever ignorant of Greek letters. This is something I proclaim about my friend Hieronymus Donatus no less gladly than truly. I would exhort you to these letters, so that you might use them as clearly...

O men, the essence of a banquet guest is purity and integrity. For he values neither the beauty of anyone’s body, nor riches, nor honors, nor the other things which the common crowd admires; rather, he despises all those things as being beyond the grasp of true faith, and considers them as nothing. Therefore, I assert that we are of no account in his eyes; yet he feigns otherwise with irony, and does not cease to joke openly about these matters. However, when he acts outwardly while remaining open inwardly, I do not know whether any of you has ever glimpsed the divine images that lie hidden within. I, certainly, have glimpsed them at other times.

Regarding the orations of Pericles: Alcibiades, in Plato's *Symposium*, speaking of the oration of Socrates, says: "My heart is stirred within me because of his words; I shed tears; and I see this same thing happening to many others. And when I heard Pericles and other good orators, they indeed seemed to me to speak excellently; but nothing of the sort happened to me: neither was my mind stirred, nor did it condemn itself as if living like a slave." Alcibiades says in the same Plato that the words of Socrates were naked and ->**What the speeches of Socrates were like. Images of Sileni.**<- <margin>What the speeches of Socrates were like. For if anyone listens to his speeches, they seem at first glance, as they say, to be exceedingly absurd. For the names and words, in their exterior aspect, bear the habit of some insulting satyr. For he always has asses and smiths, plowmen and shoemakers, and tanners in his mouth, and he always seems to say the same things about the same things: so that almost all who are less skilled mock his words. But if one looks into his speeches, first he will find that they alone of all men have a depth of meaning; moreover, they are most divine, and contain many most beautiful images of virtues, and extend themselves to many things: finally, they comprehend all the precepts by which he ought to be instructed who is to live honestly and well." *Manifest*, that is, clear. *Exotic*, that is, foreign, adventitious, not native. Plautus in *Mostellaria*: "I cannot smell exotic ointments." ->**Exotic. Trope.**<- <margin>Exotic. Trope.</margin> For *exotikos* <note>original: "εξωτικοσ"</note> is called foreign. *Tropes*, that is, by the figurative meanings of words. A trope is, as defined by Quintilian in the tenth book of *Institutes*, a speech transferred from its natural and principal meaning to another for the sake of adorning the oration: or as most grammarians define it, a word transferred from that place in which it is proper to that in which it is not proper. *You fail us*, that is, having left your opinion you concede to ours. *Our people*, the philosophers. *Immediately*, on the spot. *The argument errs*, that is, the consequence is improper, to speak with them. For either the meaning of names was made by the will of some authority prevailing in that matter, ->**How names were imposed on things.**<- <margin>How names were imposed on things.</margin> or by the community, or by some natural reason. Vitruvius writes that the names of things were made by the common and fortuitous will of all. Whose words I subscribe from the first chapter of the second book. "Men," he says, "in the ancient manner, were born like wild beasts in woods and caves and groves, and passed their lives by eating rustic food. Meanwhile, in a certain place, trees agitated by the density of storms and winds ->**The invention of speech not to be accepted.**<- <margin>The invention of speech not to be accepted.</margin> and rubbing their branches together, excited fire. Terrified by the vehement flame, those who were around that place fled; afterwards, when things were quiet, approaching closer and having noticed that there was great comfort for their bodies, adding wood to the warmth of the fire and preserving it, they brought others: and showing by gesture, they demonstrated what utilities they had from it. In that gathering of men, when they poured forth voices differently from their breath: by daily custom they established words as they had happened. Then, by signifying things more often in use, they began to speak by fortuitous event: and thus they procreated speech among themselves." Thus he spoke. Lactantius also, in the tenth chapter of the sixth book of *Divine Institutes*, writes toward this opinion from the tradition of some. "Men," he says, "who were first born from the earth, when they wandered in fields and woods, were held together by no bond of kinship or speech; they had leaves and grass for beds, caves and dens for homes, and were prey for stronger beasts. Those who fled after being mangled, or saw their neighbors mangled, warned of their danger, ran to others and implored protection: at first they signified their will by gestures. Then they tempered the beginnings of speech: and by imprinting names on each individual thing, they gradually perfected the system of speaking." But this opinion, as being hostile to our religion, Lactantius refutes in that place. However, Herodotus writes in his second book that speech was first made by nature, toward almost this opinion. "Psammetichus," he says, "the king of the Egyptians, inquiring with diligent care who the first of men ->**The device of Psammetichus in discovering the antiquity of languages.**<- <margin>The device of Psammetichus in discovering the antiquity of languages.</margin> had been, and finding no end to that matter, devised a thing of this sort. He handed over two recently born children of humble parents to a shepherd to be brought up among the flocks in this manner: ordering that no one should emit any voice in their presence: both in a solitary hut by themselves, and that goats should be brought to them when there was need: when they were filled with milk, other things should be administered. The king did and ordered these things because he desired to hear from the children, when they had ceased to wail inarticulately, if any first voice would break forth, as happened later. For when the time of two years was finished, to the shepherd who administered these things, as he opened the door and entered, both infants, with hands stretched out, falling down, cry *bekos*. The shepherd, approaching more frequently, observes the same voice being repeated. He reports the matter he heard to the king. When the king hears the children, ordered to be brought, repeating the same voice, he inquires which men say *bekos*. When he hears that in the Phrygian language bread is called *bekos*, then he declares that the Phrygians were prior to the Egyptians." Battista Piso writes that *bek* <note>original: "βεκ"</note> was the first voice of infants of this kind, and adds that someone wittily mocked this, ->**Bek.**<- <margin>Bek.</margin> saying it was no wonder to him if one raised by goats emitted the voice of goats. Yet among philosophers the question is agitated whether words signify by nature or by imposition. P. Nigidius teaches that words were made and signify not by fortuitous imposition, but by a certain force and reason of nature. ->**Words as an invention of nature.**<- <margin>Words as an invention of nature.</margin> As when we say *nos* (we), we draw our lips and breath toward ourselves; when we say *vos* (you), in a certain way we emit breath outside ourselves and extend our lips outward. The words of that Nigidius are in Aulus Gellius, chapter four of the tenth book. "When we say *vos*," he says, "we use a certain motion of the mouth agreeing with the demonstration of the word itself: and we move the tips of our lips forward by degrees: and we direct our breath and soul forward and toward those with whom we are speaking. But on the contrary, when we say *nos*, we pronounce it neither with a profuse and intent blast of voice, nor with projected lips: but we restrain both breath and lips as if within ourselves. Moreover, Lucretius followed the opinion of Epicurus in his book *On the Nature of Things*. *Periclitaretur*—that is, "he might experience." For just as the origin of the word *periculum* <note>danger/trial</note> is twofold, so its meaning is twofold. For if it comes from *peteundo* <note>to seek or attack</note>, it signifies a crisis; hence *periclitari* means to be engaged in danger. But if it proceeds from the ancient word *periendo* <note>to go through—the root of "experience"</note> (from which the words *peritus* <term>skilled/expert</term> and *experior* <term>to try/test</term> are made), then *periculum* signifies experience, and *periclitari* is almost the same as "to experience." There are also many words of this twofold origin, such as *patibulum* <note>a yoke or gibbet</note> from *patiendo* <note>suffering</note> or *patendo* <note>lying open</note>; and *commentum* <note>a fabrication or thought</note> from *comminiscendo* <note>devising</note> or *comeminisse* <note>remembering</note>.

**Letters, Book IX. Folio LXXIX.**

<meta>This page continues a defense of the "barbaric" or plain style of medieval scholastic philosophers against the criticisms of Italian humanists who prize elegance and rhetoric. The speaker argues that truth needs no embellishment.</meta>

->not on the tongue, but in the heart of Mercury <note>original: "non in lingua: sed in pectore Mercurii." A proverbial expression meaning that wisdom resides in the intellect, not in mere speech.</note>: that wisdom was not lacking in those men, even if eloquence was. To have failed to join eloquence with wisdom is perhaps so far from being a fault that to have joined them would be a sacrilege. For who would not condemn curls and makeup on an honest maiden? Who would not detest them on a Vestal Virgin? So great is the conflict between the duty of the orator and the philosopher that they could not be more opposed to one another. For what is the other duty of the rhetorician except to lie, to deceive, to circumvent, and to juggle? For it is in your power (as you say) to turn black into white and white into black at your whim. You are able, by speaking, to raise up, cast down, amplify, or diminish whatever you wish. Finally, you boast that you can transform the things themselves, by the almost magical powers of eloquence, into whatever face or habit you please; so that things become—not as they are by their own nature—but as you have willed them; or rather, they do not actually become so, but since they are not, they nevertheless appear so to the listeners. Is this whole business anything other than pure lying, pure imposture, pure trickery? Since it always departs from the nature of the thing, either exceeding it by exaggeration or falling short by minimization, and by holding out a deceptive harmony of words—like masks and phantoms—it mocks the minds of the listeners with flattery. Shall there be any affinity between such a man and the philosopher, whose entire study is occupied in learning and demonstrating the truth to others? Add to this that we shall have no trust in those who affect a richness of vocabulary and charms of style, as if they lacked confidence in the facts; nor, relying on the truth, do we seek to draw men into our opinion by these seductive lures. It is for this reason that one should read sacred matters written in a rustic rather than an elegant style, because nothing is more unseemly or harmful in any matter where the goal is the knowledge of truth than this whole elaborate genre of speaking. This, this belongs to the disputes of the law courts, not to the study of nature and the heavens. It belongs not to those in the Academy <note>The school of philosophers</note>, but to those engaged in that republic where what is done and what is said is weighed on the popular scale, where flowers far outweigh the fruit. Do you not know this: that not all things suit all people with the same thread? Eloquence is an elegant thing (we admit this), full of enticement and pleasure; but in a philosopher it is neither becoming nor welcome. Who would not approve of a soft gait, expressive hands, and playful eyes in an actor or a dancer? But in a citizen or a philosopher, who would not disapprove, rebuke, and abominate them? If we see a girl who is charming and witty in her manners, we will praise and kiss her. These same things in a matron we shall condemn and prosecute. Therefore, it is not we who are inept, but those who would hold a drunken festival <note>original: "bacchanalia"</note> at the feet of Vesta <note>The goddess of the hearth and purity</note>; those who would dishonor the gravity of philosophical matters and their chastity with playthings and curling irons. Truly, what Synesius <note>A 4th-century philosopher-bishop</note> said of a youth can be aptly said of a speech: "A well-groomed speech is always a lewd one." <note>original: "comatam orationem semper cinedam." A harsh critique suggesting that overly polished prose is effeminate or immoral.</note> Therefore, we prefer our speech to be shaggy-haired, knotty, and unencumbered, rather than beautifully groomed with the mark or suspicion of impurity. Otherwise, it would not reveal the robe of Pallas Athena, but would be driven away from sacred rites as something profane. And even if there were nothing else, this is most true: nothing is more foreign to the purpose of a philosopher in any matter than that which tastes of luxury or pride in some part. Socrates used to say that Sicyonian shoes were comfortable and well-fitted to the foot, but they did not suit Socrates. In general, the rule for civic dress and philosophical dress is not the same, just as it is not the same for the table or for speech. The philosopher uses these things only for necessity; the civic man uses them also for grace. If the latter neglects grace, he is not a "civil" man; if the former affects it, he will not be a philosopher. If Pythagoras could live without food, he would even spare the vegetables; if he could explain his thoughts by a look, or at least with less effort than speech requires, he would not speak at all—so far is he from polishing and adorning his tongue. We must beware of this even for this reason: lest the reader, enticed by the "medicated skin" <note>i.e., the artificial surface of the text</note>, linger there and not penetrate to the marrow and the blood, which we have often seen to be infected beneath a face painted with white lead. We have seen it, I say, in all these people, for whom it has become a habit—since there is nothing inside that is not empty and vain—to detain the reader on the surface with various melodies and harmonies. If a philosopher does this, Musonius <note>A Stoic philosopher</note> will cry out that it is not a philosopher speaking, but a flute-player piping. Therefore, let it not be held against us as a vice that we have not done that which it was a vice to do. We seek *what* we should write, not *how*. Or rather, we do seek the *how*: namely, that it be without pomp or any flower of oratory. We do not want it to be delightful, charming, or witty, but to be useful, grave, and reverend; so that it attains majesty through a certain ruggedness rather than grace through softness. We do not expect the applause of the theater, where a smooth or rhythmic closing clause might stroke the ears, or where one might say "this is clever" or "that is charming." Instead, we expect the silence of the few in deep admiration, looking deeply into something either dug out from the inner sanctuaries of nature or brought down to men from the court of Jove. Then, let there be something so sharp that there is no room for defense, or so well-defended that there is no room for attack. Let them admire us, moreover, as being keen in inquiring, circumspect in exploring, subtle in contemplation, grave in judging, intricate in binding an argument, and easy in unraveling it. Let them admire in us a brevity of style, pregnant with many great things; beneath plain words, the most profound meanings, full of questions and full of solutions. How fit we are, how well-equipped to remove ambiguities, to smooth away difficulties, to unfold the involved, and with soul-bending syllogisms both to weaken the false and confirm the true. By these titles, O Hermolaus <note>Hermolao Barbaro, the humanist scholar to whom this letter is addressed</note>, we have hitherto defended our memory from oblivion, and we do not doubt we shall continue to do so. And if by the common crowd (as you say) we are considered filthy, rude, and uncultivated: this is to our glory, not to our shame. We did not write for the crowd, but for you and those like you...

# **Of Illustrious Men**

and similar things. Nor was it any different for the ancients, who by their enigmas and the wrappings of fables kept ignorant men away from the mysteries. We, too, are accustomed to frighten such people away from our feasts—which they could not help but pollute—by using a slightly bitter crust of words. Those who wish to hide treasures, if they cannot put them away in a secret place, usually cover them with trash or rubble so that passers-by do not discover them, unless they are those whom the owners have judged worthy of such a gift. Philosophers have a similar desire to hide their affairs from the common people; since it is not fitting for them to be merely approved by the masses, nor even understood by them, it would be disgraceful for their writings to have anything theatrical, plausible, or popular about them—anything, in short, that seems to accommodate itself to the judgment of the multitude.

But do you want me to fashion an image of our style of speech? It is the very same as that of our Sileni of Alcibiades. <margin>The Sileni of Alcibiades</margin> <note>original: "Sileni Alcibiadis." Thus, if you look from the outside, you see a wild beast; if you look within, you recognize a divinity. 

But you will say, "Modern ears cannot endure a texture of prose that is now harsh, now gaping, and always dissonant. They cannot endure barbarian names, terrifying even in their very sound." O delicate listener! When you approach dancers and lute-players, place yourself in your ears; but when you approach philosophers, call yourself away from the senses. Return to yourself, into the inner chambers of the soul and the retreats of the mind. Assume those ears of Apollonius of Tyana <margin>The ears of Apollonius of Tyana</margin> <note>Apollonius was a 1st-century Pythagorean philosopher said to possess supernatural perception.</note> which he used when he was not in his body at all—not to hear the earthly Marsyas <note>A satyr in mythology who challenged Apollo to a musical contest and lost.</note>, but to hear the heavenly Apollo tuning the melody of the universe on his divine lyre in ineffable ways.

# XXXI. On Illustrious Men

<margin>Glaucon</margin>
In this matter, which is as if it were infamous—like those who praise a quartan fever <note>A recurring fever associated with malaria; praising it was a common rhetorical exercise in irony.</note>—I have spoken both to test my own wit and with this specific intent: just as that famous Glaucon in Plato’s work praises injustice, not out of conviction, but to stimulate Socrates to praise justice, so too have I attacked eloquence. I have done so somewhat freely, pushing against common sense and nature for a short while, so that I might hear the cause of eloquence pleaded by you. If I truly thought that eloquence should be neglected or held in lower esteem than the "barbarians" <note>The "barbarians" here refers to the unpolished scholastic thinkers or those lacking classical refinement.</note> hold it, I would never have almost entirely abandoned them for it—as I recently did—turning toward Greek literature and toward your never-sufficiently-praised Themistius <note>A 4th-century statesman and philosopher known for reconciling Aristotle with public eloquence.</note>.

To speak my mind freely: certain petty grammarians turn my stomach. When they have mastered the origins of a mere two words, they show themselves off so much, they sell themselves so much, and they carry themselves about so boastfully, that they think philosophers should be considered as nothing compared to themselves. "We do not want," they say, "these philosophies of yours." And is that any wonder? Neither do dogs care for Falernian wine <note>A high-quality vintage from ancient Rome; the author implies the grammarians lack the refined palate to appreciate philosophy.</note>. But let us close this letter with this conclusion: if the barbarians have earned any honor or reputation for themselves...

It seems, therefore, to be a matter of repugnancies: it is permitted to worship the gods, but a wickedness to adorn philosophy with mere words.

two cases in speaking. I would not wish anything to be said unless it can be expressed in Latin: to say *specierum* and *speciebus* <note>original: "of species" and "for species"</note>; and seven cases must be used for the three. But I would prefer *formis* and *formarum* <note>original: "for forms" and "of forms"</note>, since both words signify the same thing. I do not think convenience in speaking should be neglected.
He thinks a *petasus* <note>A broad-brimmed hat</note> is a covering for the feet. No one calls a tunic a covering for the feet: that is, no one calls a tunic a foot-covering; nor likewise a *petasus* something with which the sides are clothed. Maecenas the poet was received among the principal friends of Augustus Caesar on account of his singular loyalty <margin>Maecenas.</margin> and the pleasantness of his character; but just as he was of a softer mind, with loose garments, excessively voluminous and flowing, so he was accustomed to use a softer style of speech, flowing with too many delicacies. Beroaldus <note>Filippo Beroaldo, a famous Italian humanist scholar</note> cites those words of Maecenas in his commentary on Suetonius: "What is more beautiful than a river and banks with leafy woods? What if one curls a woman's ringlets and kisses her lips? They barely demand the genius as a witness for his weary self, or the threads of a thin cart; and the mother or wife clothes the hearth with a crackling millstone." For this reason, they say that Maecenas was a *Cacozelus* <note>A Greek term for a "bad imitator" or someone with an affected, distorted style</note>, that is, an excessive affecter of eloquence. *Cacozelia* is a sentiment corrupted by affectation, whereby the speech is disgraced by the very thing with which the author wished to adorn it. Macrobius writes concerning the excessively dissolved and flowing speech of Maecenas.
His words are from the second book of the *Saturnalia*. Augustus (he says), because he knew his Maecenas had a relaxed, soft, and dissolved style, often showed himself to be such in the letters he wrote to him; and contrary to the restraint of speaking which he otherwise observed in writing, in a familiar letter to Maecenas he wove in many things poured out in jest: "Farewell, honey of the people, my little fear, ivory from Etruria; laser of Arezzo; diamond of the upper world; pearl of the Tiber; emerald of the Cilnii; jasper of the Potters; beryl of Porsenna." With Suetonius also as the authority, Augustus sometimes harassed his Maecenas, whose "perfume-dripping" curls, as he says, he pursues everywhere, and mocks by imitating them in jest. *Myrobrechis*, as Beroaldus says, is a word of Maecenas signifying as if "dripping with ointment." For the Greeks call ointment *myron*, and *brecho* signifies to drench or water.
Hence those who are anointed with hair ointment are called *Myrobrecharii* by Plautus in the *Aulularia*. <margin>Myrobrecharii.</margin> From which words I would think *brechatum* not *brachatum* ought to be read there according to this sense: that Maecenas had a *brechatum* mouth—that is, watered and sprinkled with certain soft and flowing words—so that like some barbarian he could scarcely be understood. **To give the grass.** <margin>To give the grass.</margin> That is, I have confessed myself to be conquered, says the Paduan. **To give hands.** <note>To surrender</note> To be bound, i.e., to be conquered. **They attack.** That is, they argue, they pursue. The Paduan says: **To move the Anagyris** is a proverb used for those men who bring evil upon themselves; <margin>To move the Anagyris.</margin> who are the authors of their own evils; and who provoke someone to their own destruction. For the *Anagyris* (others call it *Anagyron*) is a shrub of a foul and ungentlemanly odor, to be rejected, especially if it is rubbed by hand; its fruit, if tasted, provokes violent vomiting, as found in Dioscorides and Pliny, chapter 3 of the twenty-seventh book. You may read more about this proverb in Erasmus. **To fall from the whole cause.** That is, to be overcome and to lose the lawsuit. <margin>To fall from the cause.</margin> **To whiten an Ethiopian.** This is a sufficiently common proverb, <margin>To whiten an Ethiopian.</margin> used when labor is signified to be wasted on some matter, or when an honest thing is poorly disguised with words, or the unpraiseworthy is praised, or the unteachable is taught. For that native Ethiopian color is washed away by no water, nor does it become white by any means. Therefore, in Aesop, a certain man who bought an Ethiopian thought that color had happened through the negligence of the previous master, not by nature. He therefore omitted nothing of those things with which clothes are accustomed to be whitened; and he so harassed the wretched man with perpetual washings that, with the color unchanged, he drove him into sickness. Erasmus is the authority. **To nourish a whetstone.** This is to expect gratitude from those who are ungrateful and have no <margin>To nourish a whetstone.</margin> gratitude at all, which seems to have proceeded from their hard rusticity. Erasmus, however, in his collection of proverbs, turns this toward gluttonous men who consume a great deal of food, yet are rendered no more fit or fat by it. **For the word...** According to Aristotle in the first book of the *Rhetoric*: there are three kinds of persuasion provided by speech. Some are in the character of the speaker; others in the listener being affected in a certain way; others in the speech itself, when we demonstrate or seem to demonstrate. Therefore, they believe on account of character when the speech is so delivered that the speaker appears worthy of trust. For we believe honest men more easily about everything, and character creates the principal trust. The philosophers, therefore, think they are betrayed by Pico <note>Likely Giovanni Pico della Mirandola</note>; they say, therefore, that he is unworthy of being trusted. **A human...** that is, **man is a god to man.** <margin>Man is a god to man.</margin> This proverb is usually said of one who has brought sudden or unhoped-for safety, or immoderate utility. For antiquity thought God was nothing else than to be of use to men.
For according to Cicero in the second book of *On the Nature of the Gods*: whatever brought great utility to the human race, they thought that did not happen without divine goodness toward men. And so they then called that which was born of a god by the name of the god himself. As when we call grain Ceres, and wine Liber. From which comes that line of Terence: "Without Ceres and Liber, Venus grows cold." <note>Meaning: Without food and wine, love withers.</note> Then, however, the thing itself in which some greater power exists is so called, so that the power of those very things is named a god: such as Faith, Mind, Virtue, Honor, Safety, Concord, Liberty, Victory. Because the power of all these things was so great that they could not be ruled without a god, the thing itself obtained the name of the gods. Therefore, gods were established for him by the magnitude of their utilities, who produced each utility. Moreover, the life of men and common custom undertook to raise men excellent in benefits to heaven by fame and goodwill. Hence Hercules; hence Castor and Pollux; hence Aesculapius. These things are from Cicero. Plutarch, in the first book of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*, numbering seven institutions of the gods, says the last is of those who, conducting themselves in a human manner, earned divine honors on account of their beneficence toward men. Such as Hercules, Castor, Pollux, Father Liber. They claim these gods are in human form because, of all things that exist, the divine power is undoubtedly the most powerful, and the nature of man is the most honorable of all living beings. Plato also, in the second book of the *Republic*, says a proverb is present to the man: "Brother (he says), stand by the man," as the proverb has it. That saying of Chremes is well known: "I am a man; I think nothing human is alien to me." <margin>To stand by a man (proverb).</margin> Contrary to this is that saying of Plautus: "Man is a wolf to man, not a man." For according to Cicero in the second book of *On Duties*: just as next to and after God there is nothing from which you may take greater utility than from another man, so from no thing may you experience more grievous detriment than from another man. Plato (as found in Eusebius, chapter 4 of the eleventh book of the *Preparation for the Gospel*) thinks *anthropos* <note>Greek for "man"</note> is said in Greek from the word *anathrein*, that is, to see and reconsider; so that he is an *anthropos* who reconsiders what he has seen. **The line itself drew nothing.** That is, it caught nothing: from that proverb, it fished out nothing. The metaphor is made from fishermen who catch fish with lines. **You have chased the winds with nets.** That is, you have labored in vain. It is a proverb. For "to chase" is to wish to catch with traps set. <margin>To chase the winds with nets.</margin> **Since you are of the earth, do not seek the sea.** <margin>Of the earth.</margin> A proverb signifying that one's nature and established way of life <margin>since you are... do not seek the sea.</margin> must not be changed, which the whole school of philosophers forbids. In Erasmus, there is something not so dissimilar: "Since you are of the sea, do not wish to become of the earth." It is adapted from Aesop's fable, which is of this kind: A certain crab, having left the sea, began to feed in a field. There, by chance, having been seen by a fox, it was immediately seized and devoured. **Since you are not a Syrian, do not act the Syrian woman.** <margin>Since you are not a Syrian, do not act the Syrian woman.</margin> That is, do not take on an unseemly persona. Do not wish to seem other than you are. Or, since you were born free, do not act with the manners of a slave and a barbarian. For the Syrians were ill-reputed on account of the softness of their manners. It is, moreover, a witty jest from the ambiguity of this word *syrizein*, which signifies both "to act the Syrian" and "to play the pipe." These things are from Erasmus. **New friends, etc.** Erasmus cites this proverb from <margin>New friend.</margin> Hermolaus. In Cicero's *Laelius*, a certain difficult question arises, as he says: whether new friends worthy of friendship are ever to be preferred to old ones, as we are accustomed to prefer tender horses to old ones. A doubt unworthy of a man. <margin>Others read "satiety."</margin> For friendships ought not to be like associations of other things. All the oldest things, like those wines which endure age, ought to be the sweetest. That common saying is true: many bushels of salt must be eaten together so that the duty of friendship may be fulfilled. But if novelties offer hope, so that fruit appears as if in non-deceptive blades of grain, they are indeed not to be rejected; yet antiquity is to be preserved in its place. For the power of antiquity and custom is very great. He also says other immoderate things, by which he judges that old friendship is to be preferred to new.
