If these things are true, into what misery have we fallen? Has the matter really come to this, that we must maintain our rights through fables and apologues <note>moral fables or allegories</note>? But indeed, there are places where one must deal in hypotheticals, inductions, and enthymemes <note>term: *enthymeme*; a rhetorical syllogism where one premise is unstated</note>. Why not? I am a philosopher: I desire a demonstration <note>original: *apodixin*; a certain, logical proof</note>: the rest I leave to the orators. You will say that not everything can be taught through demonstration, and that in the meantime there is a place for probabilities. The matter is thus returned to a game of chance; there are many probabilities against us, and likewise many for us—who shall judge? Imagine it has been said by that man that philosophy consists of things and requires no pomp of words. For I believe this is the sum of all that is said on our behalf. Against this, they argue that philosophy, which is a divine, holy, and religious gift, ought to be approached religiously; it should be handled not with unwashed hands, but with pure and clean ones, in speech that is chaste, not filthy or muddy. Both are probable: as much the former—that things which prevail by their own strength do not need external aids—as the latter—that a noble, extraordinary, and sight-worthy thing ought not to be defiled, contaminated, or polluted by sordid and ignoble words. This latter view is perhaps more "salable," not because philosophy ceases to be the highest good without a choice of translucent and shining words, but just as the deities, although they need nothing of human wealth, nevertheless wish to be given gifts and to be worshiped: so philosophy, they say, not only allows itself to be adorned, but loves and strives for it. Nothing is more perfect or absolute than God; yet nowhere is more gold, more silver, more marble, more precious clothing, or more gems to be seen than in temples and on altars. Therefore, if it is permitted to worship the gods, it cannot be a crime to adorn philosophy. For even orators know the "argument from contraries," and they use it most frequently; it is, as they themselves proclaim, the most pressing and sharpest of all. However, they teach nothing about what "pressing and sharp speech" actually is, but instead refer us to Aristotle, whom we have never read and never intend to read. Now, they do not even rank philosophers below the eloquent. For they are not so shameless; rather, they prefer eloquent philosophers to "infant" <note>original: *infantibus*; here meaning "speechless" or "unschooled in speaking"</note> ones. Naturally, because it is better to be endowed with two goods than one, they say this argument is drawn "from the whole": that Themistius taught them this, whom they boast to have translated from Greek into Latin. For they make "the whole" a matter of quantity: and quantity they further divide into number and measure. Because we were responding to the argument (for I often clash with that band of grammarians and rascals) that either eloquence is not a good, or it is indeed a good but has no more to do with philosophy than with shoemaking, statue-making, or metal-casting, they brush aside both parts of the disjunction with the longest and most profuse laughter, and they dilute it in this manner: First, they contend that almost all Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle</note> testify that all philosophy is a good, and furthermore that Rhetoric is a part of philosophy. For Rhetoric is a species of civil science; one must believe Aristotle, who says this. They affirm that this type of interruption is called by Aristotle those things which declare generally and pertain only to the first figure of syllogisms; just as that which is conceived particularly cannot be placed otherwise than in the highest figure. Whether this be true or the opposite, I do not know, for I do not find where Aristotle said this: but it is well enough understood that the argument is taken "from the genus." Whether Aristotle says these portents or not, we ourselves labor little over it. Since almost all his books on philosophy have been deserted by us on account of excessive obscurity, they have been occupied by those men as if by right. Therefore we, who eat beef and pork, and who have easily allowed these delicate and idle men to steal these "delicacies" from us, avoid a confrontation here in Aristotle as if it were a reef; in other matters, we are persistent and undaunted. Furthermore, in the other part of the disjunction, we are eluded thus: If philosophy has nothing to do with rhetoric, then "animal" has nothing to do with "man." But "animal" does pertain to "man"—who does not see this? Therefore, philosophy pertains to rhetoric, either as a part or as a form and species, which they approve of more. I responded that it is a part of that philosophy which we call "practical," not that which we call "theoretical." They say, "We were eager to squeeze this out of you. You wish to be half-philosophers, semi-perfect, mutilated; you concede that rhetoric is a part of philosophy, and yet you consider it foul and shameful for a philosopher to possess rhetoric, without which philosophy..."

**Letters, Book IX. Folio LXXXV.**

I have not received the end: that you should use the laws of the Greeks. To confirm this, I appoint for you a period of four months from now.

The Milesians <note>Inhabitants of Miletus, an ancient Greek city in Ionia</note>, having suffered the loss, departed as if they had been defrauded of their money. Glaucus betook himself to Delphi to consult the oracle. To him, as he consulted whether he should seize the money by means of an oath <note>original: "orco," referring here to a solemn oath or the god of the underworld</note>, the Pythia <note>The priestess of Apollo at Delphi</note> responded with these verses: "Glaucus, son of Epicydides, it is indeed profitable for a short time to conquer thus by an oath and to embezzle the funds. Swear the oath and roll the dice: since the same end awaits everyone. But the Oath has a son, who has no name, no hands, and no feet, yet he arrives swiftly, until he rolls together and destroys the entire offspring and the house. It is better to be overturned with one's progeny; later it will be dealt with." Having heard these things, Glaucus beseeched the god to grant him pardon for what he had said. To him the Pythia said: to tempt the god and to do the deed have the same power. Then Glaucus, having summoned his Milesian guests, returned the money. Afterwards, no house and no offspring of Glaucus remained.

## **Jacobo Antiquarius to his friend Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter XI.**

I had already folded my letter to Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous Renaissance philosopher</note>, Poliziano; but as I was about to write the address and add his title, I could not decide which one to choose above all others from the entire heap of his fortunes and even his most perfected virtues. For if I had assigned him something specific, I seemed to have failed to take account of the rest of his many qualities. Therefore, having carefully weighed the matter in the balance, nothing pleased me more than to call him "The Fortunate One": he upon whom the gods have utterly poured out the very bosom of their gifts.

<meta>This page continues the correspondence of the Italian humanists, specifically a letter from Angelo Poliziano to Marsilio Ficino regarding their shared intellectual circle in Florence.</meta>

**Letters, Book IX. Folio LXXXVI.**

[Decorative initial Q] With how much pleasure and with how much joy do you think I am affected, Marsilio Ficino, when I see you and my dear Pico <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), the famous philosopher and polymath.</note> so much in agreement? You are united not only in what you desire in life, but also in what you think in your studies. I rejoice further when I perceive that I am no less dear to you both than you are to each other. Why is it that we all apply ourselves to this: that we may assist right studies to the best of our ability, and not for any reward, but for the love of the work and for happiness? We always act thus, with our duties so distributed among us that no part of our studies is ever idle. For Pico della Mirandola himself interprets all sacred literature; he fights with a direct front against the seven enemies of the Church; and he walks as a herald of peace <note>original: "caduceator"</note> between my Aristotle and your Plato. You, meanwhile, teach Plato—and others of the ancients, but especially Plato himself and all the Platonists—to speak Latin, and you enrich them with most abundant commentaries. As for me (who for a long time have been a novice <note>original: "catechumenos," a term for a student or beginner in the faith, here applied to philosophy</note> in your philosophy), this variety of literature has certainly fallen to my lot, which possesses no less delight, even if it has less authority.

For as pertains to the astrologers, concerning whom you wrote me a most beautiful letter, I am exceedingly glad that you also now stand with our Pico, or perhaps have stood with him for some time. For I do not think it matters whether you once saw things differently, or whether you sometimes wrote according to the opinion of others. For it is not shameful for a philosopher to change his opinion, since he sees more every day; and he often accommodates himself, not uselessly, to the opinion of the common people. This is what Aristotle did in his *Exoteric* books and Plato in his *Dialogues*, which the dogmatic writers do not do. Indeed, even the laws of the Emperor Justinian—in which it is against the law for anything to be contradictory—decree one thing in the *Institutes* and another in the *Pandects* <note>The primary collections of Roman Law</note>; this is (as it seems to me) because they give instructions one way to the unrefined and another way to the learned.

I truly give you immense thanks that you have deemed me worthy of such great honor as to share your opinion with me especially. But as for that other matter, I do not know if I quite approve: that you continue to call me "Hercules." You are joking, I suppose; but still, I fear you may provide an opportunity for carping and laughter to the malevolent and envious, whom no good and learned man has ever lacked. For what you attribute to me—if not deceived by love (which is more likely), then certainly led by a slight resemblance by which we often compare small things to great—these malignant interpreters will, I believe, assign to flattery instead, and they will laugh at me as if I took great pleasure in that nickname. Nevertheless, this proof of your love for me is of far more value to me than anything those people may feel or say. For I despise false and trivial things, relying on my own conscience and fortified by your authority.

But we can discuss these things more conveniently in person. I would wish that when your villa at Careggi becomes too hot in the month of August, you would not disdain this little country estate of ours at Fiesole. For here we have much water, as is common in a valley; we have very little sun, and we are not lacking in a constant breeze. Then the little villa itself is out of the way, hiding almost in the middle of a wood, yet it can see all of Florence. And although there is a great crowd nearby, with me there is always pure solitude, such as a retreat truly loves. You will be able to enjoy a double hope. For Pico often visits me from his place at Querceto, creeping in unexpectedly, and leads me out of my hiding place with him to a little dinner—the kind you know: frugal indeed, but also clever and always full of pleasant conversation and jokes. You, however, should come to me instead. For you will not dine worse here; perhaps you will even drink better. For as to the prize for wine, I would strongly contend even with Pico himself. Farewell.

**F. Sylvius on the Tenth Book of Illustrious Men's Letters.**

[Decorative initial E] Neither laurels nor gilded chariots, that is, triumphs. For the triumphal crown was of laurel, as Pliny writes in the last chapter <margin>Triumphal crown.</margin> of the fifteenth book. And as Aulus Gellius says in the sixth chapter of the fifth book, they later began to be made of gold. This is commonly called "coronary gold." <margin>Coronary gold.</margin> Appian, in the book titled *Libycus*, is the authority that those triumphing were accustomed to be carried to the Capitol in a gilded chariot drawn by white horses. *Facies*, that is, form and appearance. *When large shortcuts*, that is, many advantages. For "shortcut" <note>original: "compendium"</note> is usually accepted in that sense which is contrary to "expense" <note>original: "dispendio"</note>; <margin>Shortcut / Advantage.</margin> as we say a thrifty man uses a shortcut of his resources. But since, just as expense produces loss, so a shortcut produces utility, it has come to pass that *compendium* signifies utility. *Scarcely credible*. Many, among whom is Lactantius in the tenth chapter of the sixth book, deny that men originally lived in a wild manner, though it must not be denied. Poliziano says this will gain belief because the King of Portugal found such people in these new islands. *Still other worlds*. Alexander, when he heard Anaxarchus arguing that there were infinite worlds, is said to have wept; and when his friends asked if anything worthy of tears had happened to him, he said, "Is it not unworthy for us to weep if, when infinite worlds are said to exist, we have not yet become master of one?" The author is Plutarch in the book *On Tranquility of Mind*. Yet this Alexander, having conquered the greatest part of the lands, is said to have doubted what he would do for the rest of his life. When this was told to Augustus Caesar, he wondered that Alexander had not thought it a greater task to govern a produced empire than to have acquired a large one, as is found in the same Plutarch in the *Apophthegms*. However, there were those who believed that worlds were infinite. <margin>Many worlds.</margin> For Democritus, Epicurus, and their disciple Metrodorus thought there were innumerable worlds in the infinite, spreading out immensely through its whole embrace. Heraclitus and the Pythagoreans said each star was a world surrounding its own earth, air, and ether in the infinite ether. The Pythagoreans believed the moon was inhabited like our earth, in which there are very large animals and more pleasant plants, as Plutarch mentions in the second book of *On the Opinions of the Philosophers*. Plato writes in the *Phaedo* that a pure earth lies in a pure heaven in which men dwell. *After the likeness* <note>original: "Ad instar"</note>. There are those who deny this is said in Latin. <margin>After the likeness.</margin> Which is not entirely true. Aulus Gellius says in the first chapter of the last book: "Indeed, in exercising and cultivating all kinds of virtues, the Roman people shone forth from their native origin to the likeness of such great amplitude." *That noble one*. Alexander the Great, coming to Ilium <note>Troy</note>, having performed a sacrifice to Minerva, made offerings to the demigods. Then at the statue of Achilles, anointed with oil along with his companions and running around it naked according to custom, he adorned it with crowns, calling him happy because he happened to have such a faithful friend while alive, and such a great herald after death. Then, as he was surveying and visiting the city, someone asked him if he desired to see the lyre of Paris. He replied that it was of no concern to him, but that he had sought the lyre of Achilles, with which he used to sing of the deeds of the bravest men and famous things. From Plutarch in the *Lives*.

For "girded" <note>original: "procincti"</note> soldiers fought either so that they might be more unencumbered, or because, according to Servius in his commentary on the seventh book of the *Aeneid*, when the city of Gabii in Campania was performing sacred rites, war was suddenly announced. Then, having girded their togas, they set out from the fields toward the enemy and obtained the victory. Gaius Caesar <note>Julius Caesar</note> wrote the commentaries of his deeds which are found everywhere. Regarding these, Quintilian in his tenth book mentions them in these words: "Gaius Caesar," he says, "if he had devoted himself only to the forum <note>the law courts and public speaking</note>, no other of our men would be named as a rival to Cicero. There is such force in him, such sharpness, such excitement, that it appears he spoke with the same spirit with which he waged war. Yet he adorns all these things with a wonderful elegance of speech, of which he was particularly studious." Appian also records in the book titled *Libycus* <note>The Punic Wars</note> that Augustus Caesar wrote commentaries. Likewise, Lucius Cornelius Sulla left behind an unfinished book concerning his own deeds, which Cornelius Epicadus, Sulla's [freedman]...

# Book X of the Letters, Folio 87

->We sing of legality granted to crime, and of a powerful people turned against their own vitals by their own victorious right hand, and of kin-strife.<-
<note>original: "Iusq; datum sceleri canimus..." These are the opening lines of Lucan’s "Pharsalia," an epic poem about the Roman Civil War.</note>

He speaks of "kin-strife" <note>original: "cognatas acies"</note> because in both armies, kinsmen—that is, those related by blood—were fighting against one another.

Our colleague Budé, in his annotations on the *Pandects* <note>The *Pandects* or *Digest* is a massive compendium of Roman law compiled under Justinian</note>, asserts that the word "Chancellor" <margin>Chancellor</margin> is hardly proper Latin. Commentaries <margin>Commentaries</margin> and notebooks <margin>Notebooks</margin> are books in which history is written in a very brief style, serving as a sort of monument to deeds performed. "Of that"—meaning, of yours.

<meta>This page continues the dedicatory preface addressed to King Manuel I of Portugal, following the initial salutation. The author is positioning the King's maritime and military achievements above those of classical heroes like Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar.</meta>

->**Of Illustrious Men**<-

That noble exclamation of Alexander <note>original: "rius" likely referring to Alexander the Great</note> at the tomb of Achilles is well known, calling him a fortunate youth for having found a Homer to herald his praises. Another leader <note>Julius Caesar</note>, even while on the march and almost in the heat of battle itself, composed the commentaries of his deeds so diligently that nothing is thought to have been written by anyone with such accuracy that it is not surpassed by their pure elegance. These, therefore, are the men you must follow, O best of Kings—you who already excel them in all other matters by a vast distance. And you will understand that this is said by me truly, and not from a desire for flattery, when you, O King, reflect the sharp gaze of your divine mind upon yourself; when you behold with intent eyes (as the saying goes) the most beautiful titles of such great honor, such majesty, and finally of that empire of yours; and when you consider, while deeply moved, what a pinnacle you hold in human affairs.

For indeed, you will see yourself as the King of Lusitania <note>The Roman name for the region comprising most of modern Portugal</note>: that is (to put it simply) the King of a Roman multitude, whose region was once most densely populated by so many colonies, as we have been told. You will see yourself as the avenger of Africa: a third part of the world, a great portion of which has already been stripped of its barbarian chains by you, and which triumphs daily in the expectation of full liberty. You will see yourself as the tamer of that vast and raging ocean, at whose first onset even Hercules, the tamer of the world, trembled. You will encounter yourself as the champion of the holy Christian faith and true religion: the greatest arbiter of peace and arms against Muhammadan <note>original: "Maumeticam"</note> treachery, prostrating that most foul madness by your majesty alone, and settling the gravest wars by your name alone and the miracle of your virtue.

You are likewise the mediator and gatekeeper of another world, enclosing in a single fist (as it were) so many bays, so many promontories, so many shores, so many islands, so many ports, so many towns, and so many maritime cities; holding under your hand numerous nations to which, previously, not even the swiftest wings of Fame herself had flown. What of those things? How great they are, I ask, that kings unknown to us yearn to visit you and adore your footsteps: that they hasten to prostrate themselves at your knees, and strive to be washed in the saving fountain <note>A reference to Christian baptism</note> by your right hand, which is as powerful in faith as it is in arms! What of the fact that, stirred by the love of virtue, even the furthest of men—unheard of in ancient centuries—flock to you in crowds? The entire South, torn almost completely from its foundations, runs to you in veneration, so that they may contemplate from nearby that countenance equal to the dwellers of heaven, the grace of your royal brow, and your utterly divine majesty.

Let someone now compare to these things the capture of Babylon, proud of its brick walls, or the routed barbarians of the East, who are by their very nature most prone to flight. Let him compare the Scythians of the plains and the wanderers, who were not even bravely provoked—provided he does not attribute to praise the killing of one's dearest friends amidst wine cups, or the shameful adoption of foreign customs and unseemly flatteries. Let him also compare the Gauls, scarcely subdued in an entire decade, or other lesser deeds—provided he does not deem worthy of heraldry the cruel shedding of kindred and civil blood throughout the world.

You, therefore, you especially (though envy may burst with rage), you alone, O King, are uniquely worthy of eternal honors. It is fitting above all others that our nightly labors—that is, the labors of all of us who venerate the sacred rites of the Muses—keep watch for you. Therefore (if any trust is placed in me by you, though I am an unknown man, yet most devoted to you), I pray, Great King, that the duty of committing these matters to writing be delegated to suitable men—in the meantime, in whatever style or language—to provide the material and harvest of the things done by you and yours. In the more laborious cultivation of this material hereafter, both others who have the same ardor of mind and we ourselves shall exert whatever strength we possess.

Indeed, I recently asked those young men of your dominion, outstanding in talent and character—the children of João Teixeira, your High Chancellor—to have the records of your deeds described for me there (if any commentaries currently exist). Although they promised to take the greatest care in this duty, out of what they owe to their teacher, I did not wish to be wanting to myself. Instead, I decided to send this letter of my own to you, the most indulgent and merciful King, preferring to undergo the charge of an audacious spirit by writing, rather than a small one by remaining silent.

As for what pertains to my person: I am indeed a man of no modest fortune, yet in the profession of letters, some believe me to be of no mean reputation. I have been nurtured almost from boyhood (if this is relevant) in the most chaste inner chambers of that great man and Prince in his most flourishing republic, Lorenzo de' Medici. Since he himself is most desirous of you, he has also at times so inflamed me with his words into a love of your virtue, that I do not cease to think of your praises day and night. Nor do I now desire anything more than that the strength, the faculty, and finally the opportunity be given to me, whereby your name—most worthy of heavenly proclamation—and the testimonies of your piety, integrity, innocence, religion, restraint, prudence, judgment, justice, fortitude, foresight, liberality, and greatness of soul, and finally of so many of your works and illustrious deeds, may be consecrated through me in faithful monuments of either the Greek or Latin tongue. Thus, by no vicissitude of human affairs, by no incursion of shifting fortune, and by no wasting of squalid old age, shall they ever be erased. Farewell.

# Book 10 of the Letters. Folio 88.

**ASCENSIUS** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the scholar-printer and commentator.</note> **On the phrase "From your sweetest."** This letter from King John seems to have been set down exactly as it was received from the messenger, without any editing. This was done perhaps (as seems likely to me) to persuade the reader that it is truly the King’s own work by showing a certain lack of care in the wording; or perhaps to show how much foreigners freeze up compared to Italians when it comes to literary refinement; or (as I most strongly believe) because that is simply how he sent it. For since it is a true sign of skill to recognize each person's particular style, and since Poliziano published these letters while most of the authors were still living, it is not right to believe he changed them much. The King uses the common term "Chancellor" <note>original: *Cancellarium*</note> for his chief secretary or the head of judicial and royal affairs. **"Into our memory."** <note>original: *Nostram in memoriam*</note> Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Latin stylist.</note> would have said *nostri*, as would Poliziano himself. Where it says **"with your feasting,"** <note>original: *conuiuante*</note> I read it as **"with your helping,"** <note>original: *coniuuante*</note> that is, assisting. However, this letter—judging by the recommendation of the Chancellor’s sons and the official nature of the writing (since it is the Chancellor's job to write for the King)—was likely composed by the skill of the Chancellor himself. **"From Lisbon."** <note>original: *Ex Vlixbona*</note> They did not even wish to change this spelling, though it is spoken differently by the learned.

-> **John, by the grace of God King of Portugal and the Algarves on this side and beyond the sea in Africa, and Lord of Guinea, to Angelo Poliziano, a most learned man and his friend, sends heartiest greetings.** <-

### Letter II.

**[E]**Xceedingly sweet were your letters, most learned man, which I have long since read thoroughly. Especially from the frequent reports of our beloved João Teixeira, our Grand Chancellor, we have most abundantly understood that you are very eager for our glory (if any exists in human affairs). We understand you wish to rescue our name and our deeds from the rust of oblivion through your literary gift. Although these things testify to a great enough argument of your supreme goodwill and respect toward us, we believe they have emanated even more from the integrity of your soul, the sharpness of your genius, and your abundance of learning, which aspire to far greater things. For these we give you great thanks, which we shall return more fully when time and circumstances demand; and we hope you shall not repent of your affection toward us.

To respond briefly to your proposal: know that your service and the pious labor which you so frequently promise for the "redemption of our mortality" <note>i.e., granting immortality through writing</note> are very pleasing to us, and we embrace and vehemently praise them. Toward the execution of this, we shall diligently see to it that our annals—which we have ordered to be handed down to posterity in our common native tongue according to the custom of the realm—be composed in the Tuscan language, or at least in familiar Latin. These shall be brought to you as soon as possible, so that, according to the tenor of the truth, you may sprinkle our memory with your wit, gravity, and learning. You shall polish them with your file so that, at least with your helping eloquence, you may make them worthy of reading. For it matters much (as you know better than anyone) in what style a thing is related, however remarkable it may be. Just as we see in daily life that the best natural foods are rightly rejected when they are prepared too filthily, so too we think history, which lacks its own ornament and luster, should be despised and rejected. But there is little to fear from these errors when a man as praised as you, endowed with every kind of discipline, takes care to look after our affairs.

You have, therefore, our thoughts on the matter. It remains, our dear Angelo, that you hold the sons of the aforementioned Chancellor—nobles of our Royal household—as most highly commended to you. Even if you were going to do this of your own accord and humanity, we ask you earnestly that some extra measure be added for our sake. For these are the men to whom you should believe yourself indebted in every kind of gratitude. For in turn, the father and the sons—the one by his merits and praises, the others by the most approved testimonies of your learning—do not cease to extol you often in our presence and to spread your name to these ends of the earth, which conduces not a little to your glory and reputation. But we congratulate the youths themselves most of all for having fallen into this age and time when they can happily drink some learning from your fountain of letters. Serving God first and us thereafter with this learning, they may deserve and claim for themselves the happiness of both the heavenly and earthly kingdoms. Farewell.
From Lisbon, the 23rd day of October, 1491.

<margin>The word "nowhere" <note>original: *nullibi*</note>.</margin> **F.S. They give work to the masters.** That is, they listen attentively to the teachers and make progress. Note that I would not want to assert with many others that the particle *nullibi* is truly Latin. For "nowhere" <note>original: *nusquam*</note>, not *nullibi*, is what we remember always being said by men of pure Latinity (as far as our memory goes). **They dedicate seasonable hours to good health.** That is, they refresh themselves at the proper and opportune time, following the needs of their soul. **Travel-money, etc.** Bias of Priene used to say: "Prepare wisdom as travel-money for yourself from youth to old age." For that alone is a certain and true possession, as Laertius records in his first book.

-> **Angelo Poliziano to João Teixeira, Grand Royal Chancellor, sends greetings.** <-

### Letter III.

**[C]**onstantly I have attempted to write something to you, most illustrious man, by which my soul, zeal, and goodwill might become known to you. But I know not what—should I call it a natural or a rustic shame?—always stood in the way. I knew I was not well enough known to you, and I was deterred, as it were, by the lightning-flash of your virtue and fortune. But at last, either the requirement of my duty or the reputation of your humanity has wrung these letters from me, such as they are. What argument for this letter could I hope would be more suitable for me or more acceptable to you than if I wrote what I truly feel about your children, who are also my disciples? You sent them to Italy, excellent man, so that they might be formed in character, in letters, and finally in all the liberal arts for the cultivation of the highest fortune. But I believe they brought their father’s character with them from home; they do not so much receive examples as provide them to others. There is nothing silly in them, nothing wicked, nothing immodest, nothing harsh. No shameless face, no arrogant brow.

# XVIII. On Illustrious Men

Their eyes are not wandering, their tongues are not bold, and their expressions are not fickle. In short, there is nothing in their entire countenance, nor in their gestures, nor in their posture, nor in their gait that might give offense, cause annoyance, appear foul, or be hateful. They frequent the sacred temples daily; they devote themselves to their teachers, not only with diligence but also with eagerness. They win over their more learned classmates through kindness and obedience; however, they completely abstain from the company of those whom they believe might harm their character or their reputation. There is no competition among them except regarding their studies and their excellence. Nowhere are they found more often or more willingly than before the eyes of their instructors or in the company of their fellow students. They also dedicate appropriate hours to maintaining good health, and for that reason, they preserve it most successfully. Furthermore, they excel in their natural talents to such an extent that they easily prove themselves (to say the least) to be your true children. They quickly grasp what is taught, express themselves with elegance, and retain <note>The text cuts off here at "retinent," meaning "they retain" or "they remember."</note>

**Book X of the Letters. Folio LXXXIX.**

which letter: and compare. A Greek epigram on the front, Greek prefaces: an index of authors and books, from whose sources these laws emanated. Indeed, there are many arguments everywhere, which I omit for the sake of brevity: by which I would not doubt that the book was even written in the age of Justinian <note>Emperor Justinian I, who codified Roman Law in the 6th century</note>: and especially the venerable appearance of the volume itself: which displays that holy antiquity from afar. It was permitted to me, therefore, to inspect this more closely: to search through everything: to "scent" it out: and to diligently excerpt whatever I wished: and to compare it with the commonly circulated copies. For the great Lorenzo de' Medici, that most excellent and wise man, granted this to me alone, judging that at some point, through our work, labor, and industry, great utility might be drawn from it. I discovered, therefore, many faults in the new codices, and many in the translators, because, having been born in an unlearned age, they were both unskilled in Latin itself and entirely ignorant of the Greek language. Indeed, there are many laws there published in Greek words, which the younger scholars either omitted or translated most poorly into the Latin tongue. For which reason I believed I would be doing something worthwhile if I were to work tirelessly on some commentaries, by which the long-corrupted reading might be restored to its integrity, and the force of the Latin language, which is almost entirely contained within the laws, might be explained. That I may accomplish this according to my intention: it also helps me much that I have obtained those books of his, which the same Justinian took care to have translated from Latin into the Greek language. There is only one thing which does not so much impede as delay me, because through my public lectures, while I profess both languages and philosophy, much of my effort is withdrawn from me, and much time is snatched away. For indeed, that matter which required the principal labor, we confer upon it only secondary studies. But these night-watches of ours shall nevertheless be protected by the authority of your Maximilian, the most invincible King of the Romans: who, since he is already the designated Emperor (as we hope), whose majesty ought to be armed with laws, will, I think, favor the study of one who is so greatly occupied in either polishing or refitting his arms. Farewell. Florence. February 4, 1494.

F.S. <note>Likely Franciscus Sylvius, the commentator</note> Franciscus Philelphus, in the twenty-fifth book of his letters, denies that *praevidere* <note>to foresee</note> was ever in use among the Latins. <margin>To foresee.</margin> We are very far from agreeing with his opinion. For we observe that many most learned in the Latin tongue did not scorn the use of this word. From many, we shall call upon a few. Macrobius, in the first book on the *Dream of Scipio*: "Those are given over to be distracted by the spokes of the wheels, who, foreseeing nothing by counsel, moderating nothing by reason, explaining nothing by virtues, permit themselves and all their acts to the falls and chances of fortune." Virgil, *Aeneid* book V: "He, swift, foresaw the blow coming from above." *Campus* <note>Field</note>: i.e., the material for speaking. Cicero, *On Duties* book I: "Hence the field of the rhetoricians concerning Marathon." <margin>Field.</margin>

ASCENSIUS <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer/commentator</note>: *From the letters.* The letter is grave and full of thought: and for that reason more esteemed than for the elegance or sharp invention applied to others. *Health (Valitudinem).* There are those who, following Horace, write *valitudo*: and in my judgment, more correctly. For from *validus* comes *validitudo*, but from *valeo* comes *valetudo*. And *valetudo* is a neutral word: for it is both good and bad: but here it seems to signify bad health, although it seems it ought rather to note good health: for *validus* is taken in a good sense. Nevertheless, although *valere* sounds rather like something good, it is yet common; whence we say both to be "well well" and "badly well" <note>i.e., to be in good or bad health</note>. <margin>Health.</margin> But a *valetudinarius* <note>an invalid</note> implies something bad because it implies a variable health, which if it were always good would not be variable. Certainly what he adds: "But I have experienced fate whenever," I think is not correctly written: and instead of "whenever" (*quandoque*), one should read "sometimes" (*quandoque*), or rather, "also however" (*quoque utcumque*) I have experienced. So that it is: "but I have also experienced however," i.e., in whatever way, although not properly in my children: but in one no less dear: "fate," i.e., the death of children in the death of a father. *And for exercise.* For those less experienced sometimes write so that they may be exercised and become experienced; and so it is in the Aldine edition, not "for excitation."

->**Lorenzo de' Medici to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter V.**<-

**F**ROM the letters which you gave to Michelotius: I have been made more certain that our little sons are being vexed by adverse health. As becomes a humane parent, I took this heavily and with distress. Which distress, indeed, you, **foreseeing**: tried to strengthen our mind with so many words and reasons, that you seem to have fallen into a very great doubt concerning our constancy. Which, although I am certain it proceeds from your love toward us, nevertheless affected us with much greater distress than any indication of the adverse health of the children. For although children are said to be the substance of a parent, yet the sickness of the mind is much more one's own than that of the children. For those whose mind is whole and safe: easily attain the safety of other things: but for those whose mind is weak, no harbor is ever safe from the waves of fortune: no sea is so placid: no military service so quiet: that they are not vexed by perturbation. Do you think me so weak by nature: that I would be moved by so small a thing? If indeed our nature is of such a kind: that it is easily driven here and there by perturbations: yet a mind confirmed by the experience of many things: has learned to be consistent with itself. I have experienced not only the health of my children, but their fate whenever. My father, snatched away by an immature death when I was in my twenty-first year, so exposed me to the blows of fortune, that sometimes I was weary of my life. For which reason you ought to think that experience has brought us the virtue which nature denied. But, since you in the letter to Michelotius: seem not a little to distrust the weakness of our mind, and yet in your letters to us you extol the virtue and gifts of our genius to the highest degree, and since these things seem to conflict at the same time, either one is false, or you are not of that greatness of mind which you seem to desire in me: since you pass over in silence in your letters to us those things which were written to Michelotius, as if your letters were not to be received by me, seeing as you judge that the news would bring me much more distress than the health of the children. But I do not wish to be longer on small matters, lest I run into the same fault which I blame in you: nor in the same letters seem both to despise small things and to pursue them with more prolix words. If there is anything in the letter that bites you: forgive it all to our love, and to exercise, for which I think it supplies material more abundantly if we inveigh against someone than if we praise, and the field of blame is much wider in everyone than that of praise. I rejoice in a wonderful way that our Julian [gives] himself entirely to letters...
**M**

**F.S.** <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Frater Suus" or "Your Brother"</note> **Almost another.** A brother is so called as if he were "almost another" self: as Publius Nigidius <note>Publius Nigidius Figulus, a Roman scholar and contemporary of Cicero</note>, a man of immense learning, interprets it, and Aulus Gellius is the authority for this in the tenth chapter of his thirteenth book <note>original: "Noctes Atticae," 13.10</note>. **Book of Letters X. Folio 90.**

Finally, I shall spare no effort to satisfy that will of yours and your most honorable desire. However, it is troublesome that I have nothing certain as of yet to write to you. Indeed, I have not had the opportunity of meeting with Piero de' Medici <note>Piero "the Unfortunate" (1472–1503), son of Lorenzo the Magnificent</note> these past few days, as he is still staying in the country for the sake of his spirits. Certainly, a vain rumor has increased among you regarding preparations for war and the recruitment of soldiers. For on the contrary, things look more toward peace—may it turn out well—and concord. <margin>Insects.</margin> F.S. <note>Likely the commentator's initials</note> Animals are called "insects" from their incisions <note>Latin: *incisura*</note>, which separate the members—sometimes at the neck, sometimes at the chest and belly—connected only by a thin tube, as Pliny is the authority in the first chapter of the eleventh book. Moreover, in the genus of insects are bees, gnats, cicadas, wasps, hornets, ants, spiders, beetles, locusts, and others of this kind. Those which they call *ephemera* <note>Greek: "lasting a day"</note>. <margin>The River Hypanis.</margin> The river Hypanis <note>The Southern Bug river in Ukraine</note> brings down little sacs larger than grape-seeds into the Cimmerian Bosphorus at the summer solstice, from which four-legged winged creatures break out. <margin>Ephemera.</margin> This kind of animal lives and flies until the afternoon; soon, as the sun descends, it withers and grows faint, and finally dies at sunset; its life is extended no further than one day. Whence it is called *ephemeron*, that is, a "daily." Aristotle is the authority in the nineteenth chapter of the fifth book of *The History of Animals*; he also mentions the same animal in the fifth chapter of the first book. Pliny calls it *ephemerobion* in the thirty-sixth chapter of the eleventh book. <margin>Gardens of Adonis.</margin> "As if the Garden of Adonis." The "Gardens of Adonis" is a proverb found in Erasmus regarding trivial things that bear little fruit, suitable only for brief and present pleasure. For with Pausanias as the authority, he writes that the Gardens of Adonis were once among the luxuries, filled mostly with lettuce and fennel. Although these were dedicated to Venus, they were called by that name because of Adonis, her lover, who was snatched away in the first flower of his youth by Mars (changed into a boar) and transformed into a flower. <margin>Gardens of Tantalus.</margin> The "Gardens of Tantalus" in Philostratus, in the fourth book of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, signify almost the same thing. "You see the gardens of Tantalus," says Apollonius, "which, as written by Homer, appear to be something when they are not." Or as it seems, it is rather said of those things which seem to be something when they are not. <margin>Words are the daughters of cypresses.</margin> The words "daughters of cypresses"—so that we do not speak "the bronze pot" <note>A proverb for something irrelevant</note> away from the purpose—are those which, although they are beautiful, have no efficacy or meaning. For with Plutarch as the authority in his *Apophthegms*, cypresses, though they are beautiful and lofty, have no fruit. <margin>Garden and gardens.</margin> Therefore, the meaning is not foreign to the Gardens of Adonis. Many distinguish "garden" from "gardens" such that a "garden" is for vegetables, but "gardens" are for delights.
ASCENSIUS. <note>Josse Bade, the printer/commentator</note> "You compel," etc. He writes to Lorenzo de' Medici, not to that famous patron of his, but to the son of Pierfrancesco; for he calls him a youth, which does not fit Lorenzo the father. Moreover, he dedicates his *Manto* to him; whence it is placed before it.

**Angelo Poliziano to Lorenzo, son of Pierfrancesco de' Medici, sends greetings.**
**Letter IX.**

[Large initial C] You indeed compel me, Lorenzo, to publish a poem that is unpolished, uncorrected, and which, having been recited once in public, seemed too impudent. It would certainly have been enough for it to have lived for one day, because it was such an imperfect creature, and could even be numbered among those insects which they call *Ephemera*. For I had fashioned it only for a present celebration, like a Garden of Adonis. You desire not so much to prolong the life of our *Manto* (for so we entitle it) as its disgrace. I would be made of iron if I denied you anything—you, such a noble youth, so upright, so fond of me, and finally, demanding this thing with such great zeal. Therefore, have for yourself whatever this little book is, and you also, relieve our longing sometime; and those songs which the amorous Muses suggest to you in the vernacular <note>Italian, rather than Latin</note>, I pray do not allow them to be expected by us any longer. Farewell. Florence. November 2, 1482.

ASCENSIUS. Here is the *Rusticus* for you. This letter is also a dedicatory letter for the *Rusticus*, that is, a small poem titled *Rusticus*; whence it will also be placed at its front. <margin>Rusticus.</margin> Truly, here it is expressed in the masculine gender, whereas above he wrote of his *Eunuchus* and his *Rusticus* [as feminine]; for he says "he will impute." *Ascitus*: summoned, called to, moved toward. It is written thus for the sake of sonority instead of *adcitus*, just as *asporto* is used for *abporto*.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giacomo Salviati, sends greetings.**
**Letter X.**

[Large initial E] Here is the *Rusticus* for you. That name, of course, was given from the subject matter. By your compulsion it goes out to the public; it is you who will have to answer for whatever happens to it. Do you not already feel how it must be defended by you, either in your own name or in mine? For your credit is at stake in it, and my honor; care for which has indeed always kept watch with you since childhood. Yet you ought to protect it now even more expensively for this very reason: that you are recently the son-in-law of Lorenzo de' Medici, a leading man, whose client and foster-son I am—the one son-in-law chosen from all the Florentine youth. Bring forth, therefore, in such a patronage all your authority and grace, which the affinity of that excellent man, your own extraordinary nature, and the sweetness of your manners clearly win for you. Farewell. And love me, as you do.
F.S. *Poemation*: a small poem. *Nuncupamus*: we dedicate. *Perrexeris*: you shall have continued.
ASCENSIUS. "He owes," etc. With this short letter, he dedicates his *Ambra* to Lorenzo Tornabuoni—that is, a *Sylva* <note>A "forest" or collection of poems</note> named from the name of the estate at Poggio a Caiano, which was a delight to Lorenzo de' Medici. Or from the subject matter, which is in praise of Homer; whence near the beginning: "Why should I not release my whole heart to the great son of Maeon <note>Homer</note>, from whose living stream the whole crowd of bards drinks in secret furies," etc.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Lorenzo Tornabuoni, sends greetings. Letter XI.**

[Large initial D] This *Sylva* is owed to you, either by its subject or its title. For you are a student of Homer, and as it were our fellow-follower and a relative of the most high and excellent man Lorenzo de' Medici, who chose for himself Ambra at Poggio a Caiano—an all-bearing estate (if I may say so)—as a relaxation from his civil labors. To you, therefore, we dedicate this small poem, such as it is, so that it may be a monument of our love, and an incitement to you for the study of letters, especially Greek, in which you have nevertheless proceeded so far that you seem likely to reach the summit shortly, if only you continue. Farewell. Florence. November 4, 1485.

F.S. <note>Likely an abbreviation for "Factum Scilicet" or a similar scholarly shorthand</note> *That would befit such a tender age.* Aulus Gellius, in the twenty-second chapter of his tenth book, cites Plato’s *Gorgias* to roughly this effect: "When," he says, "I see a little boy, for whom it is still becoming, babbling with his tongue and playing, I am charmed; the thing seems to me indeed festive and gentlemanly, and suitable to a boyish age. ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, the commentator</note>: *To do, etc.* He commends Matteo Franco for his integrity, urbanity, and wit; on account of which gifts he praises Piero de' Medici, who saw to it that his father’s companion, his sister’s attendant, and a sort of tutor <term>pedonomus</term> <note>A Greek-derived term for one who directs or trains children</note> and private secretary, was elected into the college of canons. *To whom he might refer in a doubtful matter*, that is, whom he might consult, or from whom he might seek advice, or to whose judgment he might refer. *What use requires*—this is indeed the "tail" of a poem, but borrowed from a poet. *To prescribe*, that is, to define as if by giving a law, what, how, and to what extent: because he himself knows how to attend to everything.

**Angelo Poliziano to his dear Piero de' Medici. Greetings. Letter XII.**

**I** cannot help but give thanks to you, my Piero, that by your authority and effort you have seen to it that Matteo Franco—a man (as you know) most dear to me—was elected into our college. He is, moreover, most worthy not only of that honor (though certain envious men may burst with rage) but of any honor whatsoever. His first commendation occurred with your father, a most wise man, on account of his jokes and urbanity, when he wrote those witty poems in the native tongue <note>Italian/Tuscan, as opposed to Latin</note> which are now celebrated throughout all Italy. Indeed, that same parent of yours, while you were still almost an infant, used to teach you some of the more humorous parts of them for the sake of a laugh, which you would then babble among gathered friends, commending them with a certain elegant gesture which would indeed befit that tender age. Nor is Franco any less pleasant in conversation and domestic habit, whether you seek witty remarks, or storytelling, or other amusements of that kind, in which his prudence shines no less than his genius. For he never says anything scurrilously, nothing immodestly, nothing out of place, nothing beside the point, nothing incautiously, and nothing without discernment. Therefore, whether your father Lorenzo was staying in the country at the villa <note>original: "caula," literally a sheepfold or enclosure, here referring to a rural retreat</note> or attending the baths, he used to bring Franco along as a companion (which I do not doubt you remember), so that he might be refreshed, as it were, by his charm. He then employed him as a counselor to your sister Maddalena when she was setting out for Rome to join her husband; namely, so that a girl still inexperienced, who had never before left her mother’s bosom, might have some fatherly friend near her to whom she could refer in a doubtful matter. Here Franco (as he is a man of extraordinary patience, but also dexterity) so accommodated himself in some way to diverse and unknown customs that he gathered the goodwill of everyone, and to your sister herself...

### Letter I.

**E**ven if the matters about which I now write to you, best of Princes, might perhaps seem of minor importance, and hardly worthy of your attention and care, I nevertheless trust that you will bear them with a calm mind—given that quality which is called your humanity. he wrote with great hope for posterity, and they were received with the favor of those now living; now, if by some fate he threatens the reputation of another, he will be as ill-spoken of as he has spoken ill of the other—forgetful of praise, or prodigal of his own. **Ludovico Maria Sforza to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter IV.**

[Large initial D] Due to nature and the institution of our ancestors, it is innate in us toward the learned—as you desire to happen—that we love them and, when the occasion arises, also gladly honor them. Moreover, we deal with you all the more zealously because, in addition to your learning, you have lived until now among the Medici family, who are most friendly to us, and you are held dear by them. Therefore, with very little reluctance, we have done with Giorgio Merula what you requested; not only so that you may understand more clearly what you say is being carried there through the obscure talk of men regarding his accusation against you, but also because we do not at all approve of learned men either exercising mutual hatreds or turning what ought to be done fraternally and by friendly warning into bitterness by acting harshly. He is writing back to you; we have given the letter to the secretary of the ambassador acting here for us. Therefore, we think he will satisfy you and show who it was that took it poorly that things he considers his own were being usurped by others as if they were theirs; yet he does not forget what he owes to an old friend and a man of letters. Farewell. Vigevano. The second day of March, 1494.

<gloss>He may profess: i.e., he may teach publicly, whether in circles, in assemblies of men, or in society.</gloss> <gloss>That matter moved my stomach: i.e., it stirred me up, and as Plautus says, it sharpened my heart.</gloss> <gloss>Designated: i.e., those from which my mark was taken away, so they would not recognize them as mine.</gloss> <gloss>Good names: i.e., good debtors, who, if the will to pay their debt is not lacking, certainly lack the means.</gloss> <gloss>We have vindicated: that is, we have set free.</gloss>

ASCENSIUS <note>The commentator Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note>: You complain, etc. The response is clever, as if made by a veteran caviler; who, since he does not dare to pluck at things individually and by name, plucks at them generally. *Beyond anger*: to say, "short of anger," as in letter VII of this book, "short of insult." *And reproach*: it is well known from where the name "reproach" is derived, but perhaps he wanted to invent a repetition. *Partly stolen*: He accuses Politian of theft, but of a literary kind; because certain things which he himself had delivered openly, Politian allegedly snatched away—that is, published as his own and as his own inventions. Certain things which he had marked secretly and signified he would point out elsewhere, Politian "designated"—that is, having removed the mark of secret significance, he made them manifest as his own. *In notebooks*: i.e., in papers for memory, in which opposing things and notes are usually recorded, so that at some time they may be written more diligently. *Good names*: i.e., good debtors, because in the books of accounts and taxes and those who owe us, we have as many debtors as there are names written. Good debtors, however, even if they are not able to pay, nevertheless acknowledge and confess the debt. *They exult*: i.e., they leap for joy, and display immoderate happiness through a certain gesture.

**Giorgio Merula to Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter V.**

[Large initial Q] You complain, Angelo, through letters, that I pursue you with insults, whether I am teaching or speaking in circles against the learned, and that I have moreover composed a most criminal pamphlet, which, although I have not yet published it, I nevertheless recite to whomever I happen upon; and you wonder not a little why I should devise these things against you, since you have cultivated me, praised me, and affected me with no injury. My dear Angelo, before I knew you, led by the fame of your name, I followed you with whatever services I could; I sent Greek books to you in Florence, in which ample and recondite erudition is contained, fearing nothing less than that you would be a rival and imitator of my studies. What of the fact that I have always spoken honorably of you? I deferred to you so much that those who heard me thought I attributed more to friendship than to truth. You remember, I believe, that in a crowded auditorium in Venice, when you had come to me, I said openly that you were the one whom I promised myself would be the restorer of ancient and Roman learning. I have never spoken anything more insulting, nor has anyone heard Merula bring forth anything against your writings (I except the *Miscellanea*) which ought to offend you. Others have noted syllables incorrectly placed in meters; others have touched upon solecisms. I thought these and such things in Politian ought neither to be required nor blamed. As for the *Miscellanea*, as soon as they were offered to me, moved by the title itself, I read them snatchingly. When I had fallen upon that place where you make mention of me with an honorable preface, I could not help but rejoice in your testimony. For who would not seek to be praised by a learned man? But certain friends and disciples noticed...

<meta>This page continues the heated intellectual dispute between the scholars Giorgio Merula and Angelo Poliziano, mediated or commented upon by Franciscus Sylvius and Jodocus Badius Ascensius. The tone is one of sharp academic rivalry typical of the 15th-century Italian Renaissance.</meta>

# On Illustrious Men

professors seem to me not particularly learned: I beg you, refrain from anger and indignation. For it is well enough established from our *Commentaries*, which are in circulation, what Merula is capable of achieving in Latin matters. Our painstakingly composed *Centuries* <note>original: "Centuriæ," referring to a collection of a hundred scholarly observations</note> will come out into the public and into the battle-line. Who will withstand their force and onset? They will immediately turn their backs and scatter. But to return to the books which, under the auspices of the most excellent Prince Ludovico <note>Ludovico Sforza, Duke of Milan</note>, we rescued from decay and imminent destruction: why do you accuse me of false charges? As if I wished to suppress a benefit. I have published the names of the authors and the titles of the works. I believe the shade and the spirits of the writers rejoice; I think the diligence and loyalty of Merula have already reached them. Or do you think I am of the same character—if not yours, then certainly that of many others—who, if they had found these treasures, would have buried them again? You reproach me for my gray hairs; they are not troublesome, for there remains vigor of mind, strength of body, and swift movements of intellect; there remains, moreover, that tenacious and ample memory of both facts and literature. And this is enough regarding our Poliziano. Farewell. From Milan. The sixth day before the Kalends of March [February 24], 1494.
FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS.

<margin>Plagiarist.</margin> Minute and puny. He says this in reproach, as if they were half-men: having nothing human except the body, and lacking reason, by which alone we differ from the beasts. They filled me with suspicion. Plautus in *Amphitryon*: "He filled me with suspicion most unworthily." He is called a "plagiarist" <note>original: "plagiarius"</note> who sells another's property as his own, or one whom he knows to be free as a slave. So called because by the Fannian Law (which was also called the Plagiarian Law) a penalty was inflicted upon the plagiarist. He calls "plagiary" a crime just as he does "bribery." Evil <margin>Deceit.</margin> deceit. Deceit <note>original: "dolus"</note> was sometimes used in either a good or bad sense. Therefore they often say "evil deceit": just as Sallust says "evil poison" when speaking of avarice. It, he says, as if imbued with evil poisons, makes the body and the manly soul effeminate. Concerning words of this kind, once ambiguous but now of only one meaning, Aulus Gellius writes in chapter nine of the twelfth book. "Begun," that is, "imperfect." *Pitylisma* <note>A Greek term for a rhythmic movement or spitting</note>. In the thirty-eighth chapter of the *Miscellanea*, Poliziano asserts that in Juvenal one should read *pitylisma* and not *pytisma*: which passage he retracts here. <margin>Laconicum.</margin> The *Laconicum* was a steam room or sweating-room in the city. "Whether from the race of the <margin>Parthians.</margin> Parthians." The Parthians frequently abandon battles in the very heat of the contest, and a little later resume the fight from flight: so that when you think you have most certainly conquered, then you must undergo the greatest danger. Justin is the authority in book forty-one. "Expressing." When Merula says "they will immediately turn their backs and scatter," he understands this to refer to those who are about to experience the force of the *Centuries*, or who will not wait for it: whereas in truth, as the words are written, it ought to be understood as the flight of the *Centuries* themselves.

ASCENSIUS. "Introduced for accepted." Here he clearly placed "introduced" for "erased" and what they call "canceled" or "marked with a spit" <note>a critical mark used by scholars to denote suspect text</note>. In the last foot of the former verse, Merula wrongly lengthens the first syllable in *pati*; in the latter, he wrongly shortened it in *panes*. He indicates cleverly what he now thinks about the *pytisma*, lest he be forced to acknowledge an error if it is objected to by that man. Certainly Poliziano teaches in *Miscellanea* chapter 38 that the *Laconic* circle was in the city—not in Lacedaemon [Sparta] but in Rome—though he confesses it was an invention of the Lacedaemonians.

Angelo Poliziano to his friend Giorgio Merula, Greetings. Letter VI.
Your letter was altogether pleasing to me, yet it would have been more pleasing if—as I especially hoped and requested of you—it had also brought with it the notes on our *Miscellanea*. For that method of writing of yours has given me neither the power of clearing myself of a charge, nor of acknowledging one. But since it was not in my hand how you would finally write back, I will respond briefly to these specific heads of your letter. You recount favors which you performed for me while I was still unknown. For you say you sent Greek books to me at Florence, full of recondite erudition, fearing nothing though I might be a rival and imitator of your studies. I am not accustomed, Merula, nor do I easily forget or willingly hide it, if anyone has ever conferred a benefit upon me. However, you indeed sent no books to me; and if any were brought to Florence from Venice, the Venetian Senate always made a supply of them available to our Lorenzo de' Medici. But neither am I a rival or imitator of your studies. For although you are altogether a great man in literature, you are not quite so great that I ever proposed you to myself for imitation. For as to your saying that you have always spoken honorably of us: I prefer to believe you rather than your associates. For certain minute and puny men are accustomed to disparage even the fame of their masters; the malice and ungrateful spirit of such men we also sometimes experience, even more than we wish. Clearly they have striven to set me against you, and for that reason filled you with false suspicions. But you say you detected faulty syllables in our verses. I ask, which ones? Will you perhaps name those which we ourselves collected right at the very front, just like other errors of the librarians? But this is most unfair. For I ought not to be responsible for another's fault, especially one which I have corrected. Do you not know how often those half-learned men who work for the printers of books are accustomed to explain themselves so that in whatever they have hesitated, they either substitute <margin>Introduced.</margin> "introduced" for "accepted" readings, or they themselves invent some falsehood on the spot for their own convenience? Especially if the copies were written in a confused and disordered way, as those which we first strike off usually are. For it also sometimes happens in practice that we ourselves do not easily re-read our own writings. But if there is room for this calumny, how, I ask, will you defend those lines of yours: "Not a bed, nor any coverings are able to endure [*pati*]"? And likewise: "To whom the barking crowd gives meted bread [*panes*]"? For you cannot at least produce ancient manuscripts that support a corrupt reading, as we do in that verse of Catullus, which some attack in vain: "That tongue of yours, if use should come to you." <margin>Errors from the first printer.</margin> It happens sometimes, certainly, that while re-reading we do not detect a blemish, if there is any there from the librarians. For behold how many things escaped me, which no good and fair man would object to: *Eulabia* for *Ablabia*; *Sabadius* for *Sabazius*; *Theodoritus* for *Theodoretus*...

**Book XI of Letters. Folio XCIII.**

They gave, in the same eighteenth chapter: Pedianus instead of Pompeius; Umbricius instead of Juvenal. Again in the forty-eighth chapter, they cited the twenty-fifth volume of Pliny instead of the thirty-fifth. In the eighty-sixth, they cited the seventh book of Martial instead of the eleventh. Elsewhere, they preferred *Mustelaria* instead of *Mostellaria* <note>original: "Mustelariam quoq alibi q̄ Mostelariā"; referring to the title of a play by Plautus</note>, and the *Caecilian Annals* instead of the *Caelian*. Furthermore, no one among the more learned has yet charged me with solecisms <note>grammatical mistakes or improprieties in speech</note>. For as to what certain vile triflers were chattering about in narrow corners, we have publicly refuted those things by citing the original authors. But these things, and such as these (you say), I considered ought neither to be demanded nor blamed in Poliziano. You are indeed correct: since these are not our errors. For if any fault of ours were there, it would have been somewhat more necessary to demand and rebuke it in us than in those for whom no loss would be incurred, in whatever manner they might eventually speak or write. I come now to the *Miscellanea* <note>Poliziano's major work of philological "miscellanies" or varied scholarly observations</note>. In which you write that you are offended because I have stolen certain things of yours; and certain things—for so you say—I have marked "with a low shoe" <note>original: "subfole," a metaphorical expression for treating something with contempt or treading upon it</note>. Thus you charge us both with plagiarism, Merula, and with malicious deceit: both are grave crimes, but both are false. For there is nothing in my work which you can say was stolen from you; since what I have written partly has nothing to do with your commentaries, and partly differs greatly from them. There is only a little regarding the *Baptae* <note>original: "Baptis," referring to a lost play by the Greek poet Eupolis</note> in your work; but it is still rough and incomplete, concerning which I thought I should remain silent, lest I be forced to rebuke you by name immediately in the same place regarding Cotyto <note>a Thracian goddess associated with the play Baptae</note>. For as to the fact that you also cited an Ovidian verse about the *Naulia* <note>likely referring to a type of stringed instrument or vessel</note> in certain small commentaries (which I indeed had not yet seen), it is so tiny and minute, so much of nothing, that perhaps you are even ashamed of it. Where I might have marked your things "with a low shoe," I truly do not yet understand. Indeed, twice in the whole work I have praised you: first for your learning, and later for your character. But perhaps you believe an injury was done to you because I did not publish the same views as you regarding the same matters; as if, forsooth, I should have had greater regard for you than for myself. I think we have given enough to friendship, in that we praised you whenever there was an occasion and never rebuked you. Now those errors of ours, which you boast of having pointed out to others: I ask that you also eventually point them out to us ourselves. I will bring it about, I believe—I will bring it about, Merula—that you immediately abandon your opinion. Nevertheless, if you show that I have sinned anywhere, I will not defend it, but will immediately acknowledge it and give you deserved thanks. For I myself, in later writings, do not hesitate to sometimes retract things from earlier ones, following the example of the most learned men. Just as with that *Pytilisma* in Juvenal; since I seem to be able to beautifully defend <margin>Spitting.</margin> *Pytisma* <note>original: "Pytisma," a Greek-derived word for spitting out wine after tasting it</note> also: by which the poet may imply those who scatter the mouthfuls of water they have taken into their mouths through a Spartan marble floor. For the word itself, *diapytizein* <note>original: "διαπυτίζειν"</note>, is found even in Clement of Alexandria, who is called *Stromateus* <margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>. Whose simple and grammatical meaning someone declares—as we have mentioned before—and the common language of the Greeks still uses. From which I would believe that Terentian term *pytissare* <margin>To spit.</margin> was formed. But if you have the same feeling and mind, that you either desire your own errors to be pointed out to you by us in turn, or at least that you do not take it badly: I profess that I too will perform this duty elegantly. For as to the fact that you also make *Centuries* <note>collections of a hundred scholarly notes</note>, and do not even abstain from our titles, I bear it easily. But what is it that you say will happen—that they will immediately turn their backs and flee <margin>A sharp joke.</margin>! Are those *Centuries* of yours from the Parthian nation, so that they evidently fight while fleeing? But I have joked about this. Nor does it escape me that you clearly meant something else than what you expressed entirely in your words. If you publish the recently discovered books, you will have performed the duty of a very good man. Thus we indeed have rescued many Greek authors from the darkness, of whom we daily provide a supply not only to our rivals but even to our detractors. I marvel at this: that you think gray hairs are thrown at you as a fault; would that they might eventually be thrown at me in the same way. For gray hair is not disgraceful to a man, especially a learned one such as you are, who is always engaged (as you yourself do) in the study of letters. Farewell.

***

**F. S.** <note>Franciscus Sylvius</note> *Postulat*: that is, he accuses and, as it were, calls into court. From which comes the title of the law "on petitioning" <note>original: "de postulando"</note>. *Causam dicere*: that is, to defend oneself. Just as *sententiam dicere* is to judge; for this belongs to the judge, just as the former belongs to the defendant. *He makes principal from interest* <margin>To make principal from interest.</margin>: he is said to make principal from interest who gives out money again which was received as interest, in the hope of profit. For the principal <note>original: "Sors"</note>, as we have said, is the sum of the money given as a loan—the capital, so to speak. Saint Jerome, in his letter to Marcellus: "What you have received must be returned with interest, and the delay of the principal gives birth to interest." But here "fictitious interest" is spoken of metaphorically. However, properly, principal is made from interest when as much is added to the capital sum from profit as had been there before.

->**ASCENSIUS.**<-

*Or I shall dash charges against him* <note>original: "Aut crimina impingam"</note>. I think it should be written: *But charges* etc. *Against Poliziano*: I believe "against" <note>original: "in"</note> is redundant. *Born again rather than restored* etc. Roman letters are reborn while from the same sources—namely the Greek ones, as if from the same mother—new things, but similar to the old ones, are drawn forth. They are restored, however, when once born and found, they are replaced in their original state, with errors and faults driven out. Since he threatens, therefore, that he will send forth Greek authors, he reckons that Latin literature will arise from them.

->**Giorgio Merula to Duke Ludovico Sforza. Greeting. Letter VII.**<-

Angelo Poliziano petitions you, most excellent Prince, against Merula on a charge of injuries, and presses quite sharply: that I have attacked his writings, nor do I spare him whenever it concerns literature, and therefore that I am unjust and ungrateful, who, although he has cherished me and defended me against detractors, do not return any favor, but dash charges against him. Finally, he petitions: that I desist from detraction, and why I do not eventually publish what I keep at home and closed in boxes, so that he might be able to defend his cause. I, most clement Prince: if I have spoken anything regarding Poliziano a little too freely: it was without insult...

We interpret poets and orators; and if there is anything in them that requires interpretation, we reveal it openly, even if it causes offense to the grammarians of our own time, whom we vigorously oppose.
