->**Of Illustrious Men**<-

Even if I remain silent for now, I cannot be persuaded that I have ever received any benefit from you—except perhaps this one thing: that you arrogantly mention my name in the presence of the prince. For it will finally be permitted for me, now corrected (since my age for learning has not yet passed), to be taught modesty and humanity by you. You, who are (as you wish to be seen) the most learned of all men, yet lower yourself so much and carry yourself so submissively that you do not allow yourself to be compared with other professors. You rightly praise Hermolaus <note>Hermolaus Barbarus (1454–1493), a famous Venetian scholar and diplomat</note> as a learned and upright man; yet, if he were still alive, you would not have praised him, just to keep to your usual habit. Nevertheless, he always stood with us against you in some way, though I know not how; so do not flatter yourself too much based on his judgment. 

It is entirely false that you say, once and again, that I repeatedly begged those books from you; I certainly did not do so, nor, if I had, would I have trusted your "generosity" <note>Poliziano is being sarcastic here about Merula’s willingness to share resources</note> to grant them. Furthermore, regarding your claim that I cannot bear to have anything brought forward against what I feel or have written—have you so forgotten my messengers and letters? In those, I urged you to publish what you had written against me, professing that I would be greatly indebted to you if you would present something for me to defend or something I might correct! 

Since you could not be moved to do this by my prayers or by the authority of the most illustrious prince, and yet you admit to having written against us for three years to him (which you had almost denied in your letters to me), I will now attack you, Merula, by another path. I will lead you out at last, if I can, from the shadows into the sun. I will not imitate you by attacking your writings within the university—though I could do so quite easily—but I will instead approach the specific parts where we find your talent, your learning, and that "ample memory" you boast of to be lacking. However, since I am writing a letter and not a book, and I am playing with you gently rather than seriously for now, I will touch briefly on only a few points out of many. 

<margin>Errors of Merula</margin> 

You do not have a good understanding of <term>satire</term> <note>A genre of Roman poetry that critiqued vice and folly</note>; you confuse the types and you confuse the authors. If you do not admit this immediately, I declare I will prove it with arguments. You err likewise when you say the poet first gives his reasons for why he took up satire after leaving behind the common material of poets. For he does not do this first, but rather explains why he composes poetry at all—and then, why he chooses satires specifically. At that point, he adds: "Why I choose to run across this field instead." <note>Poliziano is likely quoting Juvenal’s Satires, Satire I, line 19: "Cur tamen hoc potius libeat decurrere campo"</note> 

Regarding Rhinthone <note>Rhinthon of Tarentum, a 3rd-century BC playwright known for mixing tragedy with comedy</note>, you err twice: both in that you pollute rustic authors here as well, and in that you falsely believe he was a most worthless trifler, even though his poems are celebrated by a Greek <term>Epigram</term>. 

I deny that it is read anywhere, as you assert, that it was first devised that "rust" should be applied to wounds when Achilles cured Telephus <note>Telephus was a mythological king whose wound from Achilles' spear would only heal by being scraped with the same spear (the "rust" or filings)</note>; in this matter, your beloved Pliny does not help you at all. 

You also believe that it was customary for wives to be married by <term>Eunuchs</term> <note>original: "Spadonibus"</note>, as noted in an epigram by Martial; but in that passage, Egle seems no more a wife than a prostitute, and no more the eunuch’s than the old man’s. 

<margin>The cure of Telephus</margin> 

You believe the *lacerna* <note>A type of open cloak worn by Romans</note> is always a military garment, failing to remember examples that contradict this everywhere—such as the one that now comes to mind: "How much laughter will it move when our <term>lacerna</term> is seen alongside the palace toga." <note>Poliziano is arguing that the cloak was also civilian or courtly attire, not just for soldiers</note> 

Regarding Latinus and Thymele <note>A famous pair of mimes (actors) in Rome often associated with scandal</note>, everything you say is most false; she was never the wife of Latinus, nor was her adultery famous, nor do the "slaps" signify that Latinus was struck by adulterers; nor was a new character of his ever introduced by the writers of mimes. If I am lying, refute me. 

<margin>A passage of Ovid</margin> 

There follows, as if out of order, a verse of Naso <note>Publius Ovidius Naso, known as Ovid</note> corrupted by you: where instead of the "Teuthrantian crowd" <note>referring to a region in Mysia</note> (about which we wrote in the *Miscellanea*), you substituted "Thestitian." Thus, so that you may recognize your error and my kindness alike, I who even on such an occasion, despite the loss...

<meta>This page continues Angelo Poliziano’s (Politian) relentless critique of Giorgio Merula’s scholarship. While the previous page addressed Merula’s personal conduct and his relationship with other scholars like Hermolao Barbaro, this page dives into a technical, line-by-line demolition of Merula’s interpretations of the Roman satirist Juvenal. **Book 11 of the Letters. Folio 95.**

You see how concisely, how strictly, and how briefly I proceed, and yet I have not even exhausted a single satire; nonetheless, this letter is being extended too far. Therefore, lest it grow into a little book, I will only touch upon a few points piece by piece in the following parts, namely whatever catches my eye.

Thus, regarding the second satire, you want the word *vulva* <note>the womb or female reproductive organs</note> to be used for other animals, and *uterus* for women. <margin>Vulva.</margin> On the contrary, we read *vulva* in reference to a woman in that same passage; and truly we find *uterus* used for a stag and a horse in Virgil <note>Poliziano is pointing out that Merula’s rigid distinction between "human" and "animal" terms doesn't hold up in classical literature</note>. Defend this too, then, if you can. Defend that point also, that the *Creticus* <note>a metrical foot consisting of a short syllable between two long ones</note> is derived from a Greek judge, even though—I believe—both orthography and syllable length protest against it. Then teach us, master, where that place is from which this "clear" Cocytos <note>a river in the Underworld</note> is named, despite the syllable length fighting against it. For regarding Lyde, I believe enough was said in my *Miscellanea*.

Truly, that reasoning of yours in the third Satire is such that you have clearly found a prize-winning argument: for you conclude (as I see) quite sharply that this Umbricius in Juvenal is one person, and the one Pliny mentions as a soothsayer is another. <margin>Umbricius.</margin> Because, you say, this man calls himself unskilled in soothsaying. But I should like you to show in what passage Umbricius says this. For you also transfer "the entrails of frogs" to the art of poisoning, and rightly so; for I do not believe frogs were slaughtered for sacrifices.

Now for the *palliolum* <note>a small Greek-style cloak</note>: you think it is made of linen. I might perhaps believe it, if you yourself had not summoned this verse from Martial against yourself: *He seeks five fleeces of greasy wool for his small cloak* <note>original: "Succida palliolo vellera quinq; petit." Poliziano’s point is that you can’t make wool fleeces into a linen cloak</note>. <margin>Palliolum.</margin>

Furthermore, you take the *Opici* <note>an ancient Italian people, often used as a slur for "uncultured"</note> to mean "gnashing" and "barbarous," but reliable authors persuade us that *Opici* are those who are ignorant of Greek, even if they are not unlearned in Latin. <margin>Opici.</margin> Thus, mice are jokingly called *Opici* when they gnaw on Greek poems which they do not understand; and that woman, like an "Opic woman," corrected the faults of her poorly "Greeky" friend. 

Moreover, you read of "Phæcasian gods" in Appian; we read of "Phæcasian shoes" <note>white shoes worn by priests or gymnasts</note> there, not gods. <margin>Phæcasian.</margin> But you also present the word *strigiles* <note>skin-scrapers used in baths</note> corruptly, and you summon Persius as a witness, though he resists you on the quantity of the syllable.

Now, if it pleases you, let us descend to the fourth satire, unless you are too fatigued; truly, rest a little while, but soon we shall resume the work. I deny that "Arician axles" <note>chariots from the town of Aricia</note> have anything to do with Bovillae. <margin>Arician axles</margin> I deny that you wrote the truth regarding the etymology of *pegma* <note>a theatrical stage-machine</note>. For you read the word *Chironomonta* <note>referring to a carver who gestures with his hands</note> as corruptly in the fifth satire as you explain it ignorantly. <margin>Chironomonta.</margin> For the things you have brought forward regarding those three names are foreign to the truth; they are sufficiently refuted, as I judge, in my *Miscellanea*.

Nor could you defend that point in the sixth satire from laughter: *And I yield the paternal little field,* where you equally forget your Latinity and confuse the understanding. Truly, regarding Glaphyra—who is "Glaphyrus" in your work—you would certainly never have believed her to be a comedian or a cithara-player <margin>Glaphyra.</margin> if you possessed the Greek epigrams of Antipater and Philip. Nor is a "Greek style of intercourse" found anywhere among the figures of Venus; you found it necessary to flee to these absurdities when women are being taxed there for using flattering Greek speech even during sex.

Certainly, how the "Capitoline Oak" <margin>Capitoline oak.</margin> might signify a consulship or a triumph, I do not understand. Nor do you show that there was an oak on the Capitoline hill, but rather (which is irrelevant) on the Palatine. Here I pass over a large crowd of errors, serving brevity; yet I call you to the "Columns of the Dolphins," and may you eventually see, if you can, what Dio the historian recorded about Agrippa in his forty-ninth book. You will surely understand how poorly you understood that.

Shall we also run through the seventh satire? Or will you defend your *Cacethes*? For which we use *Cacoethes* <note>a "malignant habit" or medical sore</note>, which, whether it is an ulcer as many say, or even a fever as Galen relates, certainly signifies a "bad habit." <margin>Cacoethes.</margin> Indeed, regarding the peaks of Parnassus, your Helicon and Cithaeron, Beroaldus <note>Filippo Beroaldo, a contemporary rival scholar</note> has relieved us of the burden; by him, together with Servius, you are refuted. <margin>Peaks of Parnassus.</margin> Beroaldus, I say, that learned and famous man, who, being himself provoked by your insults, has sharpened teeth to be feared, so that he may fall upon you with bites. He, I believe, will not grant you that the "snakes about to fall from the hair" refer to the helmet of Turnus; just as our friend Hermolao did not allow it, by whom you falsely believed yourself to be praised. <margin>Satus Lacerta.</margin> You believe that Satus Lacerta <margin>Lacerta.</margin> was the wealthiest of lawyers, who, when he praised our "Crambe" <note>referring to a repetitive or "hashed-over" argument</note>, praised it, I believe, not without great disgrace to you. You also believe Chrysogonus and Pollio were rhetoricians, forgetting what you had read above and what you had cited.

The eighth satire now calls us: where we perceive your "Numantine origins" and your famous discussion of the rising of Lucifer <note>the morning star</note> to be insufficient in astronomy; although we hold this completely: since the earth is round, the stars rise later for some nations than for others. <margin>Before the Numantines.</margin> In my interpretation, "the die is played all night before the Numantines"; that is, in an atrium full of the wax images of ancestors, whom the poet indicated as men of triumph and famous renown specifically before the Numantine [ancestors]. Then I would read "at the rising of Lucifer," not "risings," so that it means "while Lucifer is rising." I wish to say nothing of the "laureated Mime." I only promise that I will indicate whenever you wish: that you have written things not only vain, but contradictory. 

Furthermore, you do not have a suitable witness to teach that those who conquered at Nemea were crowned with pine. <margin>Crowned with celery.</margin> For Lucian testifies to celery. Nor do those things escape me which Plutarch writes regarding the pine and celery in the fourth book of the *Symposiacon*: where he crowns the victors at the Isthmian games with both. He also found some Greek thing in the ninth satire: which if anyone reads it as you still read it, I will not say they have no ears, but rather too long ones <note>a joke implying Merula is an ass</note>. You put a "librarian" <margin>Librarius.</margin> in charge of dividing tasks, while Ulpian himself, whom you summon, is annoyed by it. 

But you assign a *struma* <note>a tumor or scrofulous swelling</note> to the back and a *gibbus* <note>hump</note> to the chest in the tenth satire; <margin>Struma. Hump.</margin> by what authors, I ask? For Celsus says this nowhere. But also in the eleventh, that trainer of gladiators denies that he is a cook and a butcher. For I think you believe our "Pytisma" <note>the spitting out of tasted wine</note>, and you mock your "Lacedaemonian dance." Just as you mock the craftsman Parthenius in the twelfth. Then, if the "half-head" <note>finciput</note> were sane: it would not always be what you yourself estimate in the thirteenth, a "cooked half-head." I return the "span" and the "pleurisy" to you, because the fourteenth satire presses upon us: which...

<meta>This page concludes Poliziano’s biting technical critique of Giorgio Merula’s commentary on Juvenal and Plautus. It then transitions into a more somber and diplomatic tone as Poliziano reacts to the sudden news of Merula’s death, writing to their mutual patron, Ludovico Sforza, to offer his services in completing Merula’s unfinished works.</meta>

**Of Illustrious Men**

...you say a life is requested by a little book: but he does not say "after the books." Rather, a prince is petitioned by such a book. For concerning the "Huts" <note>original: *Attegiis*; referring to primitive dwellings mentioned in Juvenal’s Satire 14</note>, and the "Festivals of Ceres," I believe you have discovered nothing, nor regarding the "Stage-Machine" <note>original: *Petauro*; a device used in ancient theaters for acrobatic leaps</note>. For we do not know from where you fished out the idea that it was a game in which men were tossed through the air by the pulses of wheels. Two Satires remain: of which the former by no means hints at those who would hold a torch while running; the latter does not agree concerning the "Soldier’s Boot" <note>original: *Bardaico*; a reference to a coarse Gallic boot</note>. And the verse of Martial, deformed by you with three strikes, groans heavily. These things and many others in those famous commentaries of yours on Plautus—in which you make yourself out to be a Hercules—must be investigated. For what kind of scholar do you promise yourself to be in other matters, when you read *emusitata* <note>a nonsensical reading</note> in the *Soldier-Braggart* <margin>A passage of Plautus</margin> instead of *amusitata* <note>meaning "accurately done" or "refined," from the mason's level</note>? No one could be ignorant of this who had even once taken into his hands the very common writer Nonius Marcellus! But truly, regarding this, and likewise regarding the rustic authors, I shall speak more at length elsewhere. Now, however, I ask you, Merula, that you either concede these points or defend them: since in the one you may be considered honorable, and in the other, even learned. May you also grant pardon for our ignorance, if this thick and rustic truth of an unlearned man seems a bit harsh to you, to whom those embellishments of words are not known; those with which, evidently, the letters of the most erudite men, and those similar to you, are seasoned. Farewell.

**ASCENSIUS:** "So may it be to me," etc. This is a golden letter: for you would not know whether it excels more in its weighty sentiments or in its charms of speaking. For what is weightier than that: "I do not see what prevents," etc. "To disagree" <note>original: *dissidere*</note>: to dissent, and that firmly: a term drawn from those who, while they persevere in an opinion, are not moved from their place, while others depart toward those with whom they agree. <margin>I disagree.</margin> For "to sit" <note>original: *sedere*</note> for this reason signifies to be firmly pleased: as in *Aeneid* book 2: "And it sits fixed in this mind: it pleases to add you and yours to the ruins of Troy." And in book 4: "If it did not sit fixed and immovable in my mind," etc. "To the same stone": a term drawn from the blind and the stupid <note>referring to the proverb "to stumble twice against the same stone"</note>. "Like a good poet": that is, a skilled one: who strives to hold the listener right to the end, and to please him most in that. Whence "Farewell and applaud" <note>original: *Valete et plaudite*</note> is accustomed to be said to those departing.

**Angelo Poliziano to the most illustrious Prince Ludovico Sforza. Greetings. Letter XI.**

[Large decorative initial I] So may it happen to me, most illustrious Prince, to grow old softly in leisure and letters: that I am no less moved by this so sudden and so unexpected death of our Merula than if I had been his pupil, or otherwise a most intimate friend. This will perhaps be little believed by those who will unkindly interpret this contest between us that arose regarding our shared studies. But yet, as I have very often testified, I do not see what prevents us from being able to disagree among ourselves about literature, while the law of friendship remains safe. Moreover, this opinion has been contracted through the immodesty of certain men: who think themselves mortally wounded by those who have refuted their speech or writing, even regarding the most trivial matters. I certainly have always both professed and demonstrated that I would place it in the position of the greatest benefit if our Merula had at some time pointed out to me marks on my own writings. I would have truly given my hand at once and given great thanks, because by his warning I would have achieved this: that I would not, as they say, stumble again against the same stone. Finally, this contest between us seemed destined to be of such a kind: that I could neither be shamefully conquered by so learned a man, nor conquer him in turn, except with my great glory. Truly, all students must grieve for his loss: in which the Latin cause has suffered a public forfeiture. But since he finished his life just as a good poet finishes a play—with great praise and the great approval of all—his passing is not to be followed with tears, but rather with sweet and grateful mention. This I indeed promise, as far as the reason of my studies will allow: I shall do so gladly and abundantly on whatever occasion. Moreover, since death prevented him from publishing that history of your family, brilliantly written, and likewise certain very ancient books discovered under your patronage, we—as many of us as are engaged in the study of letters—ask you, Prince, that you no longer allow those works to lie hidden. But if you, although you abound in most learned men, have any use for our mediocrity to contribute something to either edition: use, I pray, boldly—I will not say our genius and learning—but our labor and industry. For not only do I desire to perform this so honorable duty of my own accord, but I truly wish to gratify you, whom I deservedly value most highly; and I profess that, if you wish, I will add prefaces either to the history or to the ancient codices to be published, with your illustrious glory (which comes first): yet in such a way that we do not defraud even our Merula of the testimony due to his learning and diligence. Farewell.

**ASCENSIUS.**
**The Advice.** This letter also is full of good and humane counsel and the best method of speaking: it is worthy that we imitate it both in matter and in speech. "Do not turn away from the intercessor" <note>original: *deprecatorem*</note>: that is, do not despise me as a mediator and reconciler. For "to deprecate" <margin>To deprecate. To turn away.</margin> is either to pray that something happen, or that it not happen: whence we deprecate death lest it be brought upon us, and fault lest it be imputed. "To turn away" <note>original: *aversari*</note>, however, is to despise, because we turn away from those whom we do not wish to look upon.

**Jacopo Antiquari to his Angelo Poliziano. Greetings. Letter XII.**

[Large decorative initial C] I have always, and strongly, approved of your counsel: you who neither yield anything against an opponent, nor, when the adversary has given up his ground, think any victory more honorable than simply to have been able to conquer. But Merula was nonetheless the provocateur, whom, when he was repenting of his undertaking, death withdrew from us. Therefore, against him who has ceased to be among men, there is nothing more for you to forge: if you will have imitated yourself, who are accustomed to go with great strides toward all duties of humanity. For what could you achieve...

**Book XI of Letters. Page 96.**

...you have shown clearly and sufficiently from his various commentaries on Juvenal. But because he wished me to be the intermediary of his great goodwill toward you: I now ask you again and again that you do not take away the advocate of reconciling his former benevolence with the fates: I will take care diligently that no trace of any sting is seen to have remained between you. Farewell. Milan. April 5th, 1494.

ASCEN. <note>The scholar Josse Bade, known as Badius Ascensius</note> As it pertains to both matters. Thus the Aldine edition. There are those who substitute "this"; I [refer] to both, namely to the edition of histories and books. "There was the power of establishing." Let it be "he will have been," or "let it be," or "it will happen." "If from elsewhere than here," that is, from our people: whom he implies are learned.

**Ludovico Maria Sforza to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. Letter XIII.**

**F** we easily believe you, most learned man, that the death of our Merula—excellent in doctrine and the learning of many things—was heavy. For what is less fitting for one who desires to be and be considered good than to take up literary strife in such a way as to exercise it toward hatred rather than the investigation of truth? You act rightly then: you who confess you loved Merula while he lived, who was so deserving in literary studies, although you both disagreed in some things; and now that he is lost, you follow him with a mention full of love. Regarding those monuments of his which you advise us not to let perish, and offer your help—whether we desire it in history or in the ancient codices found by Merula's diligence—we recognize your goodness in this. It is a great pleasure to us that a most literary man seems to care so much for the fame of our name and the cause of literature. Indeed, although we will by no means neglect what pertains to both matters, yet because the recent loss of Merula and greater cares turn us from this thought, until there is the power of deciding what we wish to be done. Whatever happens to be done, if we think we must seek help from scholars elsewhere than here, we will show that our consideration for Poliziano's virtue, learning, and especially love for us will be not at all hidden among us, and that it was very pleasing that you so studiously and lovingly offered your work to us. Farewell. Viglevano.

F.S. <note>Likely Franciscus Sylvius, a commentator</note> "You will brand" <note>original: *Inuretis*</note>, that is, you will make. "A handle" <note>original: *Ansam*</note>, that is, an opportunity. "Truth is submerged in Democritus's well." This is a proverbial sentence by which we signify that truth is obscure and difficult to find. We think this is the reason for it: obscure things are said to be in a well. Hence our people say proverbially that something is "done in a well" when they say a thing is done secretly from others. Democritus, however, plainly denies that there is truth: because he says the senses are not obscure or dark, as is found in Cicero’s book *To Hortensius*. It is unknown to no one that Augustus Caesar forbade the Virgilian *Aeneid* to be burned. We say that in passing. Caligula, Emperor of the Roman People, wished to abolish the writings of Virgil from human memory; I therefore append the words of Suetonius from the life of the same Caligula. "He thought," (he says) "about abolishing the poems of Homer; for why should it not be permitted to him, saying it had pleased Plato, who threw him out of the city he was establishing. But he was also close to removing the writings and images of Virgil and Titus Livius from all libraries, carping at one as having no talent and minimal learning, and the other as verbose in history and negligent." We said before what the Lydian stone is. Gold or silver is called "sub-coppered" <note>original: *subaeratum*; plated or debased</note> when, although it appears solid, copper is nevertheless placed inside; they call it counterfeit money. "Apellean Venus." Apelles had begun a Venus for the Coans, intending to surpass even his own previous one. Death occurred when part was finished: nor was anyone found who could succeed the work according to the prescribed outlines. Pliny is the author in Chapter 10 of Book 35.

<margin>To be submerged in Democritus's well.</margin>

<margin>Caligula's perfidy toward the poets.</margin>

<margin>Sub-coppered gold. Apellean Venus.</margin>

ASCEN. "You will brand marks" <note>original: *notas inuretis*</note>. A term drawn from those disgraced for a public crime, upon whom a mark is branded with a cautery iron, either for blasphemy or perjury or some other violation of faith and for treason in a significant matter. A "handle" <note>original: *ansa*</note> is that by which you take a vessel, attached like ears. Virgil: "And the heavy jug hung by its worn handle." Hence a *Diota* is a jar with two ears; without it, unless the neck is narrow, it could be taken with difficulty: therefore it is used for the opportunity of taking and the power of doing.

<margin>Handle.</margin>

**Angelo Poliziano to his Bartolomeo Chalco, Greetings. Letter XIV.**

**O** I beseech you, Chalco: do not allow the marks <note>a play on the word *nota*, meaning both a scholarly note and a brand of shame</note> of my writings to be removed from Merula’s commentaries. For you will brand much heavier marks upon me. The envious will seize this handle, always believing—rather, they will be like those who believe—that I obtained this from you by many prayers because I was conscious of my own weakness. If he critiques me justly, why do you envy his praise? If unjustly, why mine? You might perhaps respond to the two-headed argument: "If he critiques you unjustly, we spare him; if justly, we spare you." Certainly, therefore, by that indulgence of yours, truth is again submerged in Democritus’s well. But he provided in his will that they be removed. Let it be. I know what kind of will that was: overcome by a heavy illness, and already troubled by present death, he could not say no to Antiquario <note>Jacopo Antiquari, a scholar and colleague</note> who was asking and insisting much. I wish that had never come into the mind of our Antiquario! For this duty of his—which I know was undertaken diligently and piously—I fear has greatly harmed me. But they are few and trivial things (so I hear) which Merula threw against me: why then do you delete them as if they were many, as if they were heavy? "Prince Ludovico orders it," he says. Indeed, he orders it because he thinks he is doing me a benefit, not an injury. For it is known how much he favors me, how well he thinks of me, and speaks honorably. Ask him in my words, I pray—in my words, I say—rather in the words of all scholars: that he does not allow the lucubrations of a most learned man to be defiled by a most shameful erasure. Let him imitate Augustus Caesar, who through his reverence vindicated Virgil’s *Aeneid* from the flames against his own will. Oh, if it were permitted to run there [to Milan], how I would humbly roll myself at the prince’s knees, with what words, with what (so may God love me) even tears I would beseech him: that he does not permit such a disgrace to be done, nor permit Merula to be extinguished again: that he does not defraud our age and posterity of the fruit of his vigils: that he does not knock the Lydian stone <note>A touchstone used to test the purity of gold; here, the criticism that tests Poliziano's skill</note> as if from my hands...

**Of Illustrious Men**

...not so that I may distinguish pure gold from that which is debased, <note>The original Latin *subaratum* likely refers to ancient coins with a copper core plated in precious metal, or "plowed-under" metal.</note> but so that I may judge truth from falsehood in my own writings. By the fortunes of Chalcus <note>Bartolomeo Calco, the influential secretary to the Duke of Milan.</note> who surrounds you all, plead with the Prince [the Duke] that nothing there be changed, nor any deletions allowed. Let them be published as soon as possible, and certainly not tampered with—not only those works he left finished, but even the rough drafts. For we hope those works of a great artist are best which are his last, just as the final touch was in vain desired for the Venus of Apelles; <note>Apelles was the most famous painter of ancient Greece; his "Venus Anadyomene" was left unfinished at his death, and no one dared to complete it because of its perfection.</note> for even though it was only just begun, it immediately held the eyes. Farewell.

<margin>Dares and Entellus.</margin>

F. S. <note>Likely "Formal Summary" or a scholar’s initials.</note> Lest he should refer to the Virgilian Entellus. In Virgil's *Aeneid*, Book 5, Aeneas celebrates games in Sicily in honor of his deceased father. When it is time to fight with boxing gloves, Dares the Trojan—towering above the others in bodily mass and strength—offers himself for the fight. No one is found who dares to encounter him. Entellus the Sicilian was once the bravest of heroes, but now exhausted of strength in his old age; persuaded by Acestes, he girds himself for the fight. During the struggle, Entellus rises up and lifts his hand to strike Dares. Dares, seeing the blow coming, escapes it. Entellus pours out his strength into the wind, and being heavy himself, falls heavily to the ground with his vast weight. Acestes lifts Entellus from the ground. Entellus returns to the fight more fiercely, and his anger rouses his power. Then shame and conscious virtue set his strength on fire. Burning, he drives Dares headlong over the whole plain, now redoubling his blows with his right hand, now with his left. There is no delay, no rest: just as clouds rattle with heavy hail upon the rooftops, so the hero with thick blows repeatedly beats and spins Dares with each hand. Aeneas finally put an end to the fight and rescued the exhausted Dares. <note>This story is used as a metaphor for the intellectual "boxing match" between the elderly Merula and the younger Poliziano.</note> He is said "to drive flies to someone else's luxuries" who does something worthy of no praise, to which, naturally, no flies—that is, no envious people—come; instead, they seek other things more refined and more praiseworthy. For the envious are compared to flies (which foul all bright things with their touch).

<margin>Driving away flies (a proverb). Comparing a gnat to an elephant.</margin>

To "drive away flies" is otherwise said proverbially of one who performs an idle and useless duty, as Erasmus says. "Evanished," that is, very vain; the word is formed from the act of vanishing. "Indian gnats to an elephant," that is, the smallest things compared to the greatest. This means just as a gnat can neither harm nor be compared to an elephant, so it is with you, Merula. "To compare a gnat to an elephant" is a proverbial sentiment in Erasmus signifying the comparison of the smallest thing to the greatest. Indian elephants are as much larger than African ones as the African elephant is larger than the Nystian horse, as Philostratus says in the second book of the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*.

**Jacopo Antiquari to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. Letter XV.**

[Large decorative initial R] I see that a matter that is ambiguous and full of uncertain counsel has come to you from the death of Giorgio Merula. For it is neither permitted to retreat while he was alive, nor is it decent to wound him now that he is fallen and "unarmored." <note>The original *deloricatum* refers to a soldier whose breastplate (lorica) has been removed.</note> Yet no thing was ever so difficult or troublesome that, if you calm your mind, you will not find a way to gain praise. He used to say he had written certain "Centuries" <note>A "Century" in this context is a collection of 100 philological or grammatical observations, often used to critique another scholar’s work.</note> against you. You took it poorly that he would not publish them. We, indeed, because we thought there was something he judged worth refining—as we have a sweet concern for your reputation—began to act so that the disagreement between you would not be fed by the rumors of young men, and that you might return to mutual favor. I also, often jokingly approaching a man of that age, urged him not to refer to himself as the Virgilian Entellus. Now he had yielded entirely to the prayers of friends; now he loved you as before, when suddenly he fell into that illness from which he could no longer be seen by us. However, before he departed from life, you know well enough what concord he had established with you. But you still seem to want to look with a patient brow at what he had prepared—quite sluggishly—as a contest regarding letters. We would certainly comply with your wish, except that by the decree of the most wise Prince Ludovico, the excellent and rare man Chalcus has gathered everything Merula ever wrote and put it "in chains" [under seal]. The "Centuries" in particular are not resisting, for they are not of the sort that can bear the light. There are scarcely thirty notes, in which he seemed as much to "drive flies to someone else's luxuries" as to "drive them away" from there—things which were nowhere else anyway—so that I grieve with shame for the sake of such a learned man. He repeats (as I hear) a few things from your *Miscellanies* <note>Poliziano's major work of philological criticism, published in 1489.</note> as if they were his own, and again sleepily complains about not many things accepted by others through you which you wished to be your own. Therefore, that "evanished" and "toothless" biting of his, we believe, pertains to you as much as "Indian gnats to an elephant." Nor would it be of any further use to you to summon his ghost to repentance, because the history he had begun concerning the deeds of the Visconti <note>The ruling family of Milan before the Sforzas.</note> from the very origin of that clan requires the author's authority to remain intact. Farewell.

**ASCENSIUS.**
"I will want what can [be done]." This is taken from Terence's *Andria*. "But what do you say?" This is also Terentian; I say this so that boys may imitate the elegance of the playwright Terence. "So formidable," because Merula himself in earlier letters judged that no one could resist them. "To the shades," to the underworld.

**Angelo Poliziano to his friend Jacopo Antiquari, Best Greetings. Letter XVI.**

[Large decorative initial I] And so, therefore, following your counsel as a wise man and a friend, since what I want cannot be done, I will want what can be done. But what do you say? Did our Merula leave so few things, and so unorganized, that they are even suppressed by the prince’s order? Where then are those "Centuries," so prepared, so equipped, so formidable? Where are the "Plautine Questions" we expected for so long and which were promised so often? Or did he perhaps take them with him to the shades, and judge that none of us who survived—utterly unlearned men—were worthy of reading such great things? But joking aside, I will always spare Merula since he has escaped us; I was never truly angry with him, lest you think I am pursuing a feud against a shadow. I gladly defer this honor to the most wise Prince Ludovico Sforza, whose authority ought to protect the deceased now no less than it once protected him while living. Farewell.

**ASCENSIUS.**
"To be desired by you," that is, for you to lack it, or for it to be missing from you, because we "desire" [miss] those things which are not here or do not exist.

**Book 11 of the Letters. Folio 97.**

[Stamp: Bavarian State Library, Munich]

**Bartolomeo Calco sends greetings to Angelo Poliziano. XVII.**

[Large initial E] From the letters you recently sent me, I understood that you are possessed by a great desire: that the works Giorgio Merula wrote long ago against your *Miscellanea* <note>Poliziano's most famous work of classical philology.</note> should finally come to light. To show your intent more clearly, you contend for this not only with many reasons, but even with many prayers: asking that I plead with Prince Ludovico <note>Ludovico Sforza, the Duke of Milan.</note> to agree, and that he should wish that Giorgio’s writings—the destruction of which would do an injustice both to you and to him—should not be destroyed by erasure. This petition of yours is indeed not only honorable, but also noble: since you profess you are led to wish for this not so much to clear yourself of offense or ill-repute, as to ensure that studious men do not suffer the loss of the "harvest" they hope for from Merula's writings.

Truly, I would not have allowed this to be requested from you, had not Prince Ludovico—who, upon receiving your letters, noticed that you were somewhat bothered by this matter—concluded that they ought not to be published so that you would not be offended. He had discovered, through a proxy, that you were acting anxiously to prevent them from being brought to light. Furthermore, Antiquari <note>Jacopo Antiquari, the Duke's secretary and a friend to both men.</note> had (as you write) wrung the same sentiment from Merula, as if it were his own wish. <margin>Antiquari</margin> But since both things were done for your sake, and you seem to want nothing less than that, and you seek most greatly to be given access to these writings, we will make every effort so that the Prince’s opinion (who entirely wishes to deserve your favor) and his "violent" decree (if we may call it that) shall not stand in the way of your wish. Instead, what you seek shall be abundantly supplied to you. However, since those works are still barely marked in their first draft, <margin>Antiquari</margin> and Giorgio, overtaken by death, could not polish them or transcribe them with a better hand, we will first take care that they are reviewed before they are published, and reduced into that order which Giorgio seems to have intended. Soon, thus finished, they will be sent to you. Farewell.

F.S. <note>Likely "Formal Summary" or scholar's initials; these sections define difficult vocabulary from the letters.</note> *Every machine* means all one's strength, all one's industry. For with machines, men tear out stones and other things of this kind. <margin>Away!</margin> *I shall protest the injury* means I shall complain about the injustice. *Away!* <note>original: "Apage"</note> means drive away, remove, lead away. It is a Greek word, *apago*, meaning I lead away, drive away, or remove. Plautus says in the *Amphitryon*: "Bah! Away with you from me!" The same author in *Curculio*: "Away with this little dog!"

**Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to his friend Bartolomeo Calco. XVIII.**

[Large initial A] I give you immense thanks for having settled the matter of publishing Merula’s writings according to our heart's desire. I cannot explain how much I feel I owe to Ludovico, a prince equally wise and most kind, on this very account: for he has granted me as much as I hardly ever dared to hope. For both previously by suppressing them, and now by releasing them, he wished to consult my honor above all. But what is this you say—that he noticed from my letters that I would take it poorly if they were published? Did I ever pray for anything else than that the opportunity be given to hear the accusation? Finally, what "proxies" do I have there in Milan? Or what did I ever mandate to anyone, except that they use *every machine* <note>original: "omnis machinas"</note> to unearth those notes from their hiding places! Or perhaps some friend there, believing he saw more in my business than I saw myself, and looking at my mind through the lens of his own, either did or said something without my knowledge that I would not want? I shall protest the injury if I find out who did it so zealously, so "amicably," or so "dutifully." But who is more to be believed than my many published, attested letters, written (as I think) in Latin and with clarity? Therefore, I beg you, drive *away* from me that slander; for no one was ever more ready for both confession and defense. For this, I am even more grateful to you now: that you have cared, through your effort and authority, that the power of doing both should be mine. Farewell.

**ASCENSIUS** <note>The scholar Jodocus Badius Ascensius, who often added commentary to these editions.</note>
*Besides the histories, etc.* I read "beyond the histories," so that the order is as above: so that we leave him surviving, that is, in the memory of men as if still living through histories and certain letters, without other monuments. That is, by destroying everything else.

**Jacopo Antiquari sends greetings to his friend Angelo Poliziano. XIX.**

[Large initial I] I now feel nothing is better in the matter of Merula than to leave him surviving exactly as he fashioned himself: beyond his histories and certain letters, without other monuments. No *Plautine Questions* appear; <note>A lost or unfinished work by Merula on the playwright Plautus.</note> one would hardly believe the commentaries on Juvenal were his, unless he himself had affirmed it by publishing them. You indeed do rightly in deciding to restrain yourself regarding his name; to disparage him now would not escape the charge of impiety, even if the authority of the most noble Prince Ludovico had not intervened. Those who love you greatly desire that you turn your study toward literature and the common good, according to your custom. For that which is yours shall be such that nothing will be found wanting after you. Farewell.

F.S. *Disturbed* means confused. *Smeared* <note>original: "interlita"</note> means written between the lines. *Corycean* <note>original: "Coryceo"</note> means a curious person or a spy. <margin>Corycean.</margin> For according to Strabo in book 14, the entire navigation past Mount Corycus was full of robbers called Coryceans. They devised a new kind of ambush. For, dispersed through the ports, they would approach merchants who had landed, listening to what goods they carried and where they were sailing. Afterward, when the merchants set sail and reached the deep sea, the gathered robbers would attack and plunder them. From this, we call all curious people who try to listen to hidden and secret things "Coryceans," and we say in the proverb: "A Corycean heard this," when someone thinks they are saying or doing something in secret, which is nevertheless heard or seen because of those who watch and strive to know what does not concern them. Erasmus has more on this proverb. <margin>Corycus.</margin> Corycus is also a town, a port, and a cave near the sea in Cilicia, as Pliny testifies in the 27th chapter of his fifth book. They say that city was very harbor-rich and convenient. <margin>With a suspended hand.</margin> *With a suspended hand* means lightly, without effort, without labor. Aulus Gellius translated this as "a white line." <margin>to do something... a white line.</margin> The words of Aulus Gellius are from the last chapter of his book: "Those men," he says, "especially the Greeks, reading many varied things, whatever they happened upon, would overturn them with (as they say) a *white line* <margin>Proverb.</margin> without care for discrimination, pursuing only abundance." In reading them, the mind will languish with old age or weariness, finding only one or two things that are a pleasure to read, an ornament to have read, or a use to remember. *Amussis* (as Budé says in his annotations) <margin>Amussis.</margin> is a string which carpenters smear with red ochre or another color; it is called *stathme* by the Greeks. Whence the proverb was born: "a white line" <note>original: "leuke stathme"</note> according to Suidas. In Latin, it is called *alba linea*. This proverb applies to those who do something without discrimination, as if one were to make a white line on a white wall. To be a white li... <note>Text cuts off; refers to the "white line" proverb for lack of distinction.</note>

Of Illustrious Men

...and so on. Socrates, in Plato's *Charmides* (which Poliziano translated), says: "As far as handsome people are concerned, I am simply a carpenter's rule. For almost all who are of age seem handsome to me." *Ex æquo*, that is, equally. In the *Cedalion* of Sophocles—Erasmus, following the author Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia often referred to as "Suidas" in the Renaissance.</note>, records that Sophocles wrote this proverb in full in his play *Cedalion* (for that is the name of the book). He renders the Latin words thus: "Your speech indicates nothing more to me than a white line marks on a white stone."
ASCENSIUS: <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, was the printer and commentator for this edition.</note> "If therefore," etc. The order is seen: "If only you have ever heard," etc., who this Suidas was; because at that time he was still known to few, as were the other Greek authors.

**Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to his friend Bernardo Riccio. XX.**
[Large initial S] You indicate to me that I should clearly despair of the publication of Giorgio Merula's writings: how frivolous, how few, how imperfect, how disturbed, and how blotted they are. But you say it was whispered into your ears by a certain "Corycaean" <note>A proverbial term for a spy or eavesdropper.</note> that I am being rebuked by him in a certain passage, because I understood the proverb of the "white line" differently than I ought to have—namely, in a positive sense. I shall reply lightly and, as they say, with a "suspended hand" <note>A metaphor for acting cautiously or tentatively.</note>. For a defense need not be heavy where the attack is light. The Greek proverb, *leukē stathmē* <note>original: "λευκὴ στάθμη"</note>, is well-known; Aulus Gellius translated it as "white line." You might also call it a mason's rule <margin>i.e., A white mason's rule.</margin>, or a "sillus," the tool of craftsmen which is smeared with red ochre. Therefore, the proverb applies to those who say or do something without distinction. Just as I might rightly say that all evil men should be hated without distinction, so conversely, all good men should be loved. 

<margin>Socrates' white line.</margin> Certainly Socrates in Plato’s *Charmides*—he who claims no knowledge of anything except the power of love—says that he is a "white line" toward handsome people, because he loved them all equally. I translated this very thing toward a man who was not particularly learned, but a lover of the learned nonetheless; from whose love I modestly (as I see it) removed judgment, choice, and distinction, lest I be said to attribute too much to him as if he were already fully learned. Nor did I do an injury to a friend. For we commonly say to our praisers that those who love are deceived. However, the proverb is complete, as some report it: *leukō lithō leukē stathmē* <note>original: "λευκῷ λίθῳ λευκὴ στάθμη"</note>, which you may conveniently translate as: "A white line on a white stone"—namely, one that makes no distinction. That this is the full form in Sophocles' *Cedalion*, both the Greek interpreters of Plato and Suidas himself (if anyone here has ever heard of Suidas), a not altogether bad authority, have testified.

ASCENSIUS:
"It is not," etc. Not because of elegance, but because of the authority of the man asserting it, by which he thought his reputation would be protected, he inserted this letter. Yet it is in Latin and not unworthy of the person writing; lest by chance we demand the same elegance from a Prince as from a declaimer or a professor of letters.

**Ludovico Maria Sforza, Duke, to Angelo Poliziano.**
**LETTER XXI.**
[Large initial N] There is no reason for you to fear, Angelo, that any mark of shame should be burned upon you if the writings are suppressed which Merula was said to have prepared against you. For it should by no means be thought that this happened through your effort, since you did not seek for them to be hidden; rather, you did not cease to plead with us through many prayers and through our representatives that we should allow them to come to light. We wished to write this to you so that these letters of ours could testify to everyone that you wrote saying it would not only not be burdensome to you if the writings of that most learned man came into the hands of men, but even affirming that, if we allowed it, you would owe us immense thanks. Farewell.

ASCENSIUS:
"Not so much," etc. He responds most beautifully and most appropriately; among which that common sentiment ("everyone feels this") is expressed in no vulgar way. "If however you estimate," etc. Let the boy mark it and imitate it, though with a few words changed.

**Angelo Poliziano to his Prince, Ludovico Sforza, sends greetings. XXII.**
[Large initial N] You consult not so much for my glory as for your own: you who both support the truth and vindicate a professor of letters from injury. "Thus one journeys to the stars" <note>A quote from Virgil's *Aeneid*, meaning this is the path to immortality/fame.</note>, my Prince. For vain proclamations do not procure such solid, such true praise as his own right actions procure for each man. But even the memory of right actions is itself little reliable on its own, unless it be strengthened by the testimony of literature. Indeed, how much I owe you, I myself am not ignorant, nor do you allow it to be ignored by others. If however you estimate how much I wish to provide for you, I am solvent; if how much I am able, I am not. Farewell.

ASCENSIUS:
"Angelo, if." The response is accurate and no less festive. "And a desire," etc. That is, we desire to labor for you often in this way.

**Ludovico Maria Sforza to Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. XXIII.**
[Large initial A] Angelo, if, while we give our effort to you so that truth may have its place, we consult our own glory, our labor is a gain to us; and the desire to labor often for you is left to us. Moreover, this fruit is all the more pleasing because it happens even beyond expectation. For we thought it enough if, while we mutually fulfilled our duty, our custom of dealing kindly with everyone was not interrupted; although that was done even more willingly with you, whose virtue and learning have long been known to us, and upon whom we have always desired our benefit to be bestowed. Therefore, it is now more than what we were looking for, if our benefit is joined with yours as well. We consider that you are solvent with us, both as long as you wish to be and while you do what you can; and we see that more will remain to you when you have paid than those things will be which you spent in paying what you owe. Farewell.

F.S. <note>Probably a sub-commentator or the editor's initials.</note> He would have committed an imposition upon posterity—that is, he would have deceived those to come—having [delivered] nothing or very few things out of the many he promised...

...had left behind in his writings. Merula had previously threatened that he would compose "Centuries" (the force of which no one could withstand). The Antiquarian <note>Jacopo Antiquari (1444–1523), a prominent scholar and secretary to the Dukes of Milan.</note> wrote to Poliziano that after Merula's death, barely thirty notes were found. Therefore, Beroaldus plays upon this matter. Those soldiers of the middle battle line were called **Spearmen** <note>original: *Hastati*</note>, who were best arranged with javelins and spears. In the first line [Marginal note: Spearmen.] were the experienced and veteran soldiers, whom they called the **Foremost** <note>original: *Principes*</note>. In the third line, however, were the **Third-rankers** <note>original: *Triarii*</note>, [Marginal note: Foremost.] who were accustomed to sink down behind their shields on bended knees, so that while standing they would not be wounded by incoming missiles; often, after the first lines were killed, victory was achieved by these men. The **Skirmishers** [Marginal note: Third-rankers.] (that is, the *rorarii*) were light-armed soldiers. Concerning all of these, we have written in our commentary on the *Gryphus* of Ausonius. He uses the term **Supporters** <note>original: *Fauissores*</note> [Marginal note: Supporters.] in place of "favorers." If this name is derived from *favissae* <note>Underground cellars or pits in temples used for storing sacred objects.</note> (about which there is a discussion in Aulus Gellius, book 2, chapter 10, and in Sextus Pompeius), the reasoning behind the meaning does not match the word. Nonius Marcellus writes that "supporters" was once said for "favorers," as in Lucilius: "You may consider me your supporter, friend, and lover."

**Filippo Beroaldo sends greetings to his friend Angelo Poliziano. 24.**

[Decorative initial Q] I am not at all surprised that Merula has played a trick on posterity. For so "boastful soldiers" <note>A reference to the *Miles Gloriosus*, a stock character in Roman comedy who brags of military feats he never performed.</note> are accustomed to do: those who are vigorous in the noise of words, but go limp in action. Clearly, this distinguished "general" of ours, while threatening the unbearable force of his "Centuries," had not yet even stationed a "decury" <note>A group of ten; a much smaller unit than a century (a group of 100).</note> in the battle line; and while we waited with anxiety for his terrifying "spearmen" and "third-rankers," he had scarcely organized his "skirmishers" and "auxiliaries" into centuries. But let Merula now live and be well among the spirits of the dead with his "dog-like eloquence" <note>original: *canina facundia*. A term used to describe a snarling or biting style of criticism.</note>; as you wrote most beautifully and truly: he would have already perished if he had not died; just as he had sown, so he was clearly going to reap. As for what concerns us: know, my Poliziano, that you have more "supporters" and "trumpeters" of your most polished learning here than there; which, like a most fragrant shrub, breathes out a certain unspeakable sweetness. I write what I feel; I feel what I write; my pen accords with my heart, and my tongue with my mind. Farewell.

*Libystidos*: that is, African. Although it has a patronymic name as an adjective rather than a noun, as in Virgil’s *Aeneid*, book five: "Rough with javelins and the hide of a Libystis bear," that is, an African bear.

...if I have entered into a formal agreement <term>stipulation<gloss>A formal Roman legal contract made by question and answer.</gloss></term> and either the person making the promise <note>original: *promissor*</note> or the person receiving the promise <note>original: *stipulator*</note> dies leaving several heirs, Cato <note>Referring to the Roman jurist Marcus Porcius Cato Licinianus or his father, Cato the Censor.</note> writes in his fifteenth book that when a penalty of a specific sum of money has been promised if something is done otherwise than agreed: if, after the death of the promisor, one of the several heirs acts against the provision, the penalty is incurred either by all the heirs according to their inherited share, or by that one individual for their own portion. <margin>**Continuous motion.** <note>original: *Endelechia*</note></margin>

**I**n this section, the commentary addresses the nuanced linguistic debates that occupied Renaissance humanists. One of the primary disputes involves the terms *Endelechia* and *Entelechia*. Cicero famously used the former to describe the soul as a kind of "continuous motion," while others argued that Aristotle’s original term was the latter, meaning a state of "completeness" or "actuality." The commentator here provides a defense of Cicero’s usage against his critics. Furthermore, the text examines the poetic meter and "melody" <note>original: *Melos*</note> found in the works of the poet Persius, and tracks the history of the translations of Dionysius, whose geographical survey of the world was a staple of classical education.

**Book XII of Letters. Folio 100.**

...[showed the skills] of this boy. Fabio was riding a horse, in which he takes the greatest pleasure; a very beautiful animal indeed, but one that resists the bit too much. On this horse he is accustomed to gallop across the field and to charge down. He spurs it on and turns it, as skillfully as he does boldly. 

He was going along with me, then, captivated by our conversation and hungering for literary tales; he had given his ears and his mind entirely to me, when suddenly the horse, having stumbled on a path, fell backwards upon the rider himself. The boy cries out and shrieks, as if in extreme danger. Servants run from every direction, each for his own part trying to lift him up; one of them, poor soul, even broke his own leg while leaping too incautiously. All was full of tumult; terror and horror had numbed me. 

The father <note>Paolo Orsini</note> is present; he encourages him to be of good heart. When the boy saw his father—so that you might easily perceive the character <note>original: *idolem*. Referring to his innate disposition or natural quality.</note> of a noble spirit—he uttered no further cry and no groans. He only urged that they act slowly and cautiously, lest by chance the horse should strike him more severely while it attempted to rise. 

Therefore, the cinches <term>cingula: the girths or straps used to fasten a saddle to a horse. Poliziano previously noted the distinction between these and a man's belt (cingulum).</term> were cut while the horse lay there, and so Fabio was pulled out and restored to us—who were much terrified—unharmed, although he was somewhat shaken, and for that reason he was then left in the house. I, hardly in control of myself, abandoned the spectacle; not yet fully believing myself regarding the boy's safety, I returned home almost thunderstruck, and faint with the fear of such a great danger, as if it were still present.

You have the story of one day concerning the Orsini family.

<margin>Contesting in a strange arena</margin>
F.S. <note>Likely the commentator Franciscus Sylvius.</note> To "contest in a strange arena" is to fight or to exert oneself in a place where the adversary is accustomed to train, where he has many supporters, and where he knows more thoroughly how the struggle must be maintained. This means nearly the same thing as the phrase of Erasmus: "to litigate in a foreign forum." For different forums have different formulas for lawsuits and various methods of handling disputes. Either phrase can be used for someone who is engaged in a new matter to which they are not yet accustomed. Wherever gladiatorial contests were held, much sand was scattered there. From this, the "arena" <note>original: *arena*, literally meaning sand.</note> is taken to mean the contest itself. "To descend into the arena" is to enter the contest, and "to yield the arena" is to admit that one has been defeated.

**Angelo Poliziano sends greetings to his friend Pico della Mirandola. VII.**

<margin>The cavalry contest called the "Name of Troy"</margin>
[Decorative initial C] Today our youth celebrated a contest of knights clashing with spears. It was a spectacle I could hardly miss—and certainly did not wish to. For indeed, most of the contestants were products of our own school. You might think that I only produce poets or orators, but I make warriors no less. And those whom I favored won everything: Piero de' Medici and Lorenzo Tornabuoni, both of whom are not just my students, but my foster-sons. There was a double prize there; Piero took the first, and Lorenzo took the second. Yet this was met with the remarkable acclaim and manifold applause of the whole people. A certain admiration was working in their favor: that these youths of the highest nobility, usually seen in the civilian toga and the forum, had clashed with highly practiced soldiers and surpassed them in their own—as they say—arena.

You know, however, how dear our Piero is to the multitude and the citizens, no less for his own glory now than for that of his family. In him, the genius of his father <note>Lorenzo the Magnificent.</note>, the virtue of his uncle <note>Giuliano de' Medici.</note>, the humanity of his great-uncle, the integrity of his grandfather <note>Piero the Gouty.</note>, the prudence of his great-grandfather <note>Cosimo the Elder.</note>, and the piety of his great-great-grandfather <note>Giovanni di Bicci.</note> live again—indeed, the generosity and the spirit of all his ancestors. But Lorenzo is also wonderfully favored, not only for his wealth and nobility (though for those too), but much more because he is constant with Piero, as his kinsman, as one educated alongside him, and as his most faithful friend. Thus, just as he manages Piero's financial affairs diligently, cautiously, and faithfully, so he loves him vehemently—yet in such a way that he honors and imitates him.

For Lorenzo is also very learned in both languages <note>Latin and Greek.</note> and is a poet, even an extemporaneous one. He applies himself to music and trains his physical strength, doing all things successfully; yet he yields by far to Piero alone—which he also does happily, as one who favors Piero even more than himself. Finally, when you step away from Piero, you will find nothing more placid, gentle, or sweet than Lorenzo; nothing more charming, kind, or benign; and lastly, nothing more modest, sincere, or lovable. By these arts, therefore, these most celebrated young men gather favor, stir up applause, and draw out acclamations. I certainly wish you had been there with us, although you great philosophers despise these popular things. You, certainly—whose invitation I failed today—will, I know, grant this easily. For (if I know you) you receive this letter from me no less gladly than you would have received me at your table. **Of Illustrious Men**

...for there is both God and marriage <note>original: *γαμοσ* (*gamos*)</note>. However, I do not recall reading which marriages of the gods the Athenians celebrated. Yet Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author and natural philosopher.</note>, in the seventh chapter of his second book, expresses a dislike for the marriages of the gods. He says that it is almost the stuff of childish delusions to believe in marriages among the gods, and that in such a long span of time no one is born from them; that some are elderly and always gray-haired, while others are youths and boys of a dark color; some are winged, some lame, some born from an egg, and some living and dying on alternating days. Seventeenth [day]. Hesiod <note>An ancient Greek poet; the author is quoting from Hesiod's *Works and Days*.</note>: "Let the seventeenth be set apart as sacred for others to thresh; and it is permitted to cut down a vast forest with the axe, and to fit various beams, with which you might build lofty roofs and drive a well-constructed ship." A husk <margin>Husk.</margin> (as Marcus Varro <note>A Roman scholar and writer on agriculture.</note> says in the first book of *On Agriculture*) is the little pod in which the grain is wrapped in the ear; from this comes the verb "to peel" <note>original: *deglubere*</note>, because the grain, as he says, is "peeled" from that pod. When Tiberius Caesar <margin>The saying of Tiberius Caesar.</margin> was urged by his friends to increase the taxes on the provinces, he wrote back: "It is the part of a good shepherd to shear his flock, not to skin it," as is found in Suetonius <note>A Roman historian.</note>. This later passed into common use as a proverb. For "to peel" <note>original: *deglubere*</note> the grain is to strip it of its pod. From this, "to skin" a beast is to pull the hide off the animal. He who shears a beast hopes for more wool from it; he who skins it takes a greater profit once, but there is nothing left for him to hope for further. Nineteenth [day]. Hesiod: "The nineteenth is lucky after the tenth; when the Saffron Goddess <note>Refers to Eos, the Dawn.</note> rises: but when she comes into the middle circle of the sky, it becomes heavy; from the middle to the end, it shines most joyfully." Twentieth [day]. Hesiod: "The next light thrives with the divine duty of creating a wise man; nor should one grieve on this light." Twenty-fourth [day]. Hesiod: "And the fourth after that is sacred; then let them draw forth happy joys. The fifth day after this places curved yokes on the oxen, and on the mules, and works the necks of horses, and leads the tall, sail-flying ships down to the deep sea; how few know this and call it by its right name." They attributed this to Justice. Macrobius <note>A 5th-century Roman provincial and philosopher.</note> reports in the first book of his commentary on *The Dream of Scipio* that the number eight <margin>The number eight is sacred to Justice.</margin> was called "Justice" by the Pythagoreans. Because, he says, it is the first of all numbers to be resolved into "even-even" parts—that is, into two fours—and that division itself is likewise resolved into "even-even" parts, into two twos. It is woven together by the same quality. That is, two times two, twice. But since the number eight tripled generates twenty-four, it is not unsuitably attributed to Justice here. The thirtieth [day] is also praised. Hesiod: "The last of the month shall be spent in no labor. But one must indulge the spirit: that day leads festivals through all the cities; it closes the forum, nor does it resolve laws." A ration <margin>Ration.</margin>, says Donatus <note>A 4th-century Roman grammarian.</note> in his commentary on Terence’s *Phormio*, was formerly the four-measure portion of grain which slaves were accustomed to receive from their masters every month; and this was called a *demensum* <note>A monthly allowance or ration.</note>. It is uncertain whether it comes from "month" <note>original: *mense*</note> or from "measuring" <note>original: *metiendo*</note>. Plautus in *Stichus*: "You remember on which Calends <note>The first day of the month.</note> to seek your ration of food; you remember less what work needs doing in the house." Budé <note>Guillaume Budé (1467–1540), a leading French humanist.</note>, in his *Annotations*, thinks that passage of Scripture—"That he may give them their measure of wheat in due time"—should be understood as this *demensum*. From this, perhaps, arose that common superstition: that those who look at the new moon with an empty purse think they will be in need of money for the whole month. ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, also known as Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535), the printer and scholar.</note>.

Mockery also by lies. One should read "by jests." And a little later, what is read in the Aldine edition as "and by those who damage" <note>original: *dannilarijs*</note>: I read as "and by those who act in secret" <note>original: *dancularijs*</note>. *Theogamia* are the marriages of the gods. Twentieth. I found it written this way: and it pleases me more than "vicesimus," since it is derived from twenty. Morning and evening: is better understood.

<margin>Our *Rusticus*.</margin> When in recent days I was explaining to the Florentine youth our poem *Rusticus*—to which you also grant some merit—and I had come to that place where, following Hesiod, I attributed certain lunar days to certain observations or works, I began to wonder within myself, most learned Pico: whether such ancient observations of this kind proceeded from the causes of nature, or rather from the credulity of the common people. <margin>Hesiodic days.</margin> Therefore, since you are now especially composing a book against astrologers <note>Referring to Pico's *Disputationes adversus astrologiam divinatricem* (Disputations Against Divinatory Astrology).</note>, built with manifold learning and great arguments—to which these matters might seem either specifically relevant or certainly related—I must especially approach you: so that you may prescribe to what extent we should obey the laws of this ancient seer <note>Hesiod.</note>, which we have now made our own through imitation. And lest I impose upon you, occupied as you are with weightier and, as it were, more sacred letters, the burden of searching for and re-reading the rustic poet, I will briefly encompass in this letter both what he handed down and what reasons or causes I might seem able to bring forward, partly from my reading of Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> and others, and partly from my own conjecture. The sum of Hesiod's division, then, is this: that he admits some days either for observation or for action; and again, that he passes over others as if they were dead. However, he calls three "the days of Jove": such as the first day of the month, the fourth, and the seventh. The first <margin>First.</margin>, I think, because unity is the prince of numbers and every divine principle (as Plato teaches), from which the month is called "the one-horned calf" <margin>That is, the one-horned calf.</margin> <note>original: *μονοκερωσ μόσχοσ* (*monokerōs moschos*)</note> in the works of Orpheus. The fourth <margin>Fourth.</margin>, however, because in it are contained all the musical ratios which are summoned from the proportions of numbers, which previously lay hidden as feminine in unity; whence the ancients called it Pan <margin>Pan.</margin>. The seventh <margin>Seventh.</margin>, finally, because unity alone produces this number, which nevertheless also agrees with the number four because of the quadruple proportion, which is clearly found in one, two, and four; and altogether between these numbers there is an Arithmetic proportion. But he accommodates the number four to marriages, because it is born from the number two, whether you add it together or multiply it by itself. Furthermore, the number two is called "fruitful," and the bond of marriage exists only between two; yet that harmony which we mentioned requires it above all others. But the number four also constitutes the number ten—if only you join the parts themselves together—which closes the first limit and is held to be most perfect. The seer also commands ships to be built on the fourth day; perhaps because the nature of a solid is owed to the number four, under which three things—surface, line, and point—are comprehended. <margin>Harmonides.</margin> And the same is the first "even-even" number. Nor is harmony <margin>The number seven.</margin> <note>original: *septenarius*</note> inconsistent with building ships, so much so that Homer is thought to have named a certain Harmonides for that reason. Yet Hesiod also calls the number seven sacred, as being that on which Apollo was born, as he himself says; and for that reason I think the lyre of Apollo consists of seven strings. He claims the sixth <margin>Sixth.</margin> is useless for girls but useful for generating males. I believe this is because it is born from two and three, that is, from the female and the male. In it, however, the male prevails, as it results from its parts. Therefore, he then especially commands the gelding of lambs, so that they may clearly be emasculated; but also the penning...

# Letters, Book XII. Folio 102.

...to drive the livestock from the pens; it is because this is a "perfect number" <note>In early mathematics, a perfect number is a positive integer that equals the sum of its divisors. For 6, the divisors are 1, 2, and 3, which sum to 6.</note> (for such is the number six, being equal to its own parts), so that the number itself might, as it were, reflect back upon itself. He [Hesiod] also dedicates this day to mockery, lies, flatteries, and altogether secret whispers, because the face of the moon itself also "lies" at that time; for instance, she appears divided in half, even though she does not actually possess light and shadow in equal measure <note>This refers to the moon near its first quarter, when it looks half-illuminated to the eye but is not geometrically balanced.</note>. The Ninth.</margin> He calls the ninth day harmless, fit for planting trees and for begetting children...

In this epigram, Battista Pius <note>Battista Giovanni Pio (c. 1460–1543), an Italian humanist and scholar.</note> modestly suggests that Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494), a brilliant Renaissance scholar and poet.</note> was in error. It stands as if the *s* sounds were removed and the final vowel shortened. This is because the ancients used such forms more freely, as if speaking with a novelty that was not yet fully refined. Martianus Capella also, in his third book, is the authority for the idea that some believed "s" was not truly a letter; Messala <note>Marcus Valerius Messalla Corvinus, a Roman statesman and grammarian.</note> called it a mere "hissing." For snakes are twisted and winding, and hissing is their particular sound. "Men had come together among themselves." <meta>This page continues the correspondence between the Florentine Chancellor Bartolomeo Scala and the renowned scholar Angelo Poliziano.
