**Letters, Book XII. Folio CIII.**

->**Bartolomeo Scala to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. X.**<-

[Decorative woodcut initial A] I now give thanks for that error of mine—by which I referred to the Gnat <note>original: *Culicem*</note> in the feminine gender—since it gave you, most elegant man, the occasion to warn me with that hendecasyllable distich <note>A two-line poem consisting of eleven-syllable lines.</note>, and gave me the chance to respond as best I could. I confess, I hardly thought anything would turn out well for one so unpracticed and so ignorant of that kind of poetry. But I have pursued these trifles, perhaps being no less ridiculous myself. Farewell.

**F.S.** <note>Likely the initials of a commentator, possibly Franciscus Sylvius.</note> A man "of a wiped nose" [original: *Emunctæ naris*] is said to be of sharp and exact judgment, as if the nostrils were cleared; conversely, a man "of a thick nose" [original: *obesæ naris*] is said to be one who is rather stupid. <margin>A man of a wiped nose.</margin>
**Precocious** [original: *Præcox*], that is, premature and too hasty. According to Aulus Gellius in the eleventh chapter of the tenth book, when something must be signified as being done more forcedly and hastily, it is more correctly called "prematurely" than "maturely." <margin>Precocious.</margin> Just as Afranius said in his Roman comedy <note>original: *Togata*</note> titled *The Name*: "You madly seek a precocious dominion prematurely." In which verse Gellius says it must be noted that he says *præcocem*, not *præcoquem*. For its nominative case is not *præcoquis*, but *præcox*. Thus says he. **"Quiet through the limbs"** etc. is a Virgilian phrase from the first book of the *Aeneid*. We have already spoken of the **Sturgeon** <note>original: *Acipensere*</note> and of **Persius** <note>The Roman satirist.</note>. **Insipid** [original: *Fatuus*], that is, tasteless. For there is a mutual metaphor between physical taste and character [original: *ingenii*]. <margin>Insipid</margin> For "to be wise" [original: *sapere*] is a matter of taste. Therefore, there are thirteen kinds of flavors according to Pliny in the twenty-seventh chapter of the fifteenth book: <margin>13 kinds of flavors.</margin> sweet, pleasant, fatty, bitter, harsh, pungent, sharp, tart, sour, salty, etc. <note>original: *dulcis, suavis, pinguis, amarus, auſterus, acer, acutus, acerbus, acidus, ſalſus*</note>. We have already said what it means "to sing a recantation" [original: *Palinodiam cantare*]. We have likewise spoken of the multitude of Cupids.
**ASCENSIUS** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535), a famous printer and commentator.</note>
**"Lest you sing blindly."** The order is: and see that you do not sing blindly [original: *cæcus cantites*], that is, do not praise in song what you do not know or have not thoroughly examined.

->**Bartolomeo Scala to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings. XI.**<-

[Decorative woodcut initial N] You have far too sharp a nose, Poliziano. Believe me, these local writings of ours are not written for you, who have clearly approached antiquity more closely. We write these things for our fellow citizens and those who are content with our mediocre efforts at refining what we write. For what can suit those most learned ears of yours? What, I ask, can satisfy your judgment? Yet watch yourself, lest at some time you seem to be a too-sharp accuser of others' writings, perhaps by the habit of teaching with which you have instructed the Florentine youth for so many years, making them better to the best of your ability. In my hendecasyllables on your *Gnat* <note>Referring back to the poem mentioned in the previous letter.</note>, which I have not yet published, you seize upon certain things of mine too hastily, in my opinion, for what befits a serious man. Not that I shun or disdain your "file" <note>A common metaphor for the process of polishing and correcting a literary work.</note>—nothing could be more desirable for such matters—but I know not how that precocious severity (if I may call it that) seems to become so cheap. I pass over other things which you may read later, perhaps more corrected; but that point was punished by you more rigidly than was profitable. Mutual love usually excuses and protects even those things which are placed less firmly, as sometimes happens. You, on the contrary, twist what is correct (as it seems to me, at least).

To "summon" [original: *citare*] is certainly to move; the word (as I think) is made from *cio* <note>A Latin verb meaning to move, stir, or shake.</note> by frequency of meaning, from which comes "excite," "incite," "gape," "arouse," and others of this kind. In all of these there is the power of stirring up, than which nothing is more contrary to sleep—if indeed sleep is accustomed to be nourished by leisure and quiet, which is itself sleep according to Virgil, in whose work Venus "waters a placid quiet through the limbs." I do not see clearly why "to summon sleep" [original: *citare somnum*] is not "to stir and disturb" it. Add that, as far as I know, no one speaks of inducing sleep in the way you wish to be an interpreter. Nevertheless, if it displeases you, I would have you change it: let it be "to put to flight" [original: *fugare*] instead of "to summon." Sometimes a change is difficult if you take something away, so that you may find what fits; here it was no trouble. It does not please you? I "feed my own flesh," and I do not wish to strike such good skin. I do not wonder; your taste is more delicate; you would hardly put forward anything that tastes good. Even a sturgeon will be insipid if it falls upon your palate. 

But I prepare these things for the less learned, not for a Persius—whom Gaius Lucilius does not care to read his own works, according to Marcus Tullius [Cicero]. I also want a "Lucius Decimus" <note>A reference to a person of moderate learning mentioned by Cicero.</note> who would not entirely despise these things. Though I may laugh thus with friends in these summer heats when there is leisure, I do not forge these things so that posterity may preserve and admire them, or that they might enrich these "formers of books" <note>Likely referring to printers or publishers.</note> whose help some people so greedily implore. As for the Greek epigram you sent me, such is the poverty of my Greek language that I can barely interpret the words, let alone perceive the elegance of the poem; but I am sure it is yours. Farewell.

Something came into my mind regarding the Greek epigram after I had written these things: I fear you have offended Venus and her son "who flits through the air" [original: *ἀεροπότητον*], as you call him. <margin>i.e., flying in the air.</margin> Is a gnat born from water as Venus was from the sea? Unless you speak like Thales <note>The Greek philosopher who believed water was the primary substance of all things.</note>, you will hardly persuade anyone; by nature its birth ought rather to have happened in the storms of winter or the watery times of spring. It is born and rages more in the burning heats of summer. Or do you compare the god of Love, such a terrifying power, to a gnat? See that you do not also need a recantation, and do not sing blindly. What business does a gnat have with women—that is, with human beings? That is the play of Love, not of a most foul little insect born in dung heaps. The fictions of poets imitate nature better. For if poems become so free, what will not be a poem? A fish seems to me more similar to Venus, if you seek a similarity of origin. If you seek flight: an eagle. Indeed, for the sucking of blood, the Leech takes the prize. For bats and owls and that kind of bird flying in the darkness see through the shadows of night—I believe even less obscurely than gnats. <margin>Obscurely</margin> Perhaps you might more appropriately bring in a blind man if you think he should be compared to Cupid. For since you say he is an arouser of women, you may also take note here, lest you become another Comus <note>The Greek god of festivity, revelry, and nocturnal dalliance.</note>... <margin>Comus.</margin>

**Of Illustrious Men**

An army is summoned for that reason. But look here: what envy is this, that because you have condemned your own works, we should not trust in our own sleepless labors? Such works are sought after, celebrated, and praised by the learned—and perhaps no less desirably, they are criticized by the ignorant! For it is not as you think: we do not beg for the work of the booksellers; rather, they implore us for ours while they pursue their own profit.

I come now to the *Epigram*, the elegance of which you say you cannot perceive (being a modest man) due to your lack of Greek. Yet you say you think it is mine; I do not see in which way I should take that. For I do not yet know what you truly think of my talent. Nevertheless, you mock and pluck at the whole argument, fearing that I have offended Venus or Cupid by comparing a gnat to them. If that were so, then Virgil must have equally offended the Trojans, and Homer the Greeks, by comparing them to flies! You do not think the gnat is born from moisture, yet that same Virgil calls it "the nursling of moisture." For the sake of this gnat, he reproaches the Egyptian soldiers with their mosquito nets, as they live in marshes. Furthermore, just because they appear more in summer, it does not mean they are not born from water—unless you believe the ponds are so completely drunk up.

Those points of yours are surely too frivolous and irrelevant: the things you heap up concerning fish, eagles, owls, and leeches. A gnat is not "not from water" just because a fish is also from water; nor does it "not fly" just because an eagle flies higher. An eagle is not called "one who flies in the air" <margin>i.e., flying in the air.</margin> by Hesiod, but the spider is. Likewise, the gnat is not exempt from sucking blood just because that is more the trait of a leech. <margin>Leech.</margin> Indeed, Theocritus compares Love to a leech, and he does not believe he offends Love.

Finally, the same applies to what you added about the owl and about Comus <margin>Comus: The Greek god of festivity and revelry.</margin>. We were not treating a fish, an eagle, a leech, nor bats or owls, nor finally that god of revelry, but entirely your gnat itself. Likewise, if a certain shepherd in that same Theocritus said that Love is blind, we shall not therefore pluck out his eyes; for his eyes are (as Moschus says) "sparks and flaming" <margin>i.e., sharp and flaming eyes.</margin> <note>original Greek: ὄμματα μὲν φλόγα καὶ φλογόεντα</note>. Truly, it is not absurd for us to prefer a gnat to a man, once we have undertaken this theme in a matter of love—seeing as Love also yields to doves, leverets, chickens, rabbits, and sparrows. Even if a poet's argument is taken up against what nature allows, he will not have any less art for it, provided he answers to the theme once it is undertaken; this is shown by Virgil’s *Gnat* and Homer’s *Battle of the Frogs and Mice* <margin>Batrachomyomachia.</margin>.

But enough of these things. They do not seem worthy enough for me to spend my labor on them any longer, lest an "elephant be made out of a gnat" <note>A proverbial expression meaning to make a mountain out of a molehill.</note>. I will only add this: I have nothing hidden, nothing manufactured, nothing secret <margin>Secret.</margin>; nor am I captured by the flatteries of those who easily disparage one who is absent. For that saying of Homer pleases me: "For that man is as hateful to me as the gates of the underworld..." Jacobus Tufanus translates it thus:

*He is as heavy to me as the thresholds of black Pluto,* <note>original Greek: Ἐχθρὸς γάρ μοι κεῖνος ὁμῶς ἀΐδαο πύλῃσιν</note>
*Who hides one thing in his heart, but says another.*
*The one who carries one thing on his lips, but hides another in his breast.* <note>original Greek: ὅσχ’ ἕτερον μὲν κεύθῃ ἐνὶ φρεσὶν, ἄλλο δὲ εἴπῃ.</note>

Farewell.

**Bartolomeo Scala to his friend Angelo Poliziano, Greetings.**
**LETTER XIII.**

I can hardly be led to believe that this last letter you sent me about the gnat is yours. It is too light; it is too peevish; it is too suspicious; and finally, it is too vain. Ah, I believe some one of your disciples—while you are occupied in those inner shrines of philosophy and look down upon these lighter matters—took it upon himself to answer me. It does not taste of your wit; it mixes many things, confuses everything, and proves nothing. Or I am mistaken. It is unworthy of your name. Your writings usually carry something of "yourself"—that is, something polished, frank, brilliant, and elegant; in short, they are *yours*. You, too, if you stumble upon hendecasyllabics with an extra syllable or two, will know they are mine, so that I too may have something of my own. Farewell.

**FRANCISCUS SYLVIUS**
**To scratch one another.** "Mules scratch one another" <margin>Mutual scratching.</margin> is a proverb used when the unlearned praise the unlearned, the deformed praise the deformed, or the wicked praise the wicked. More on this elsewhere. "One hand rubs the other" <margin>Hand rubs hand.</margin> is a similar proverb, which, when used in a good sense, means to share duties and business together. Things are said to be "of the same flour" <margin>To be of the same flour.</margin> when they are of the same lot or condition, between which hardly any distinction can be marked. Persius in his fifth Satire says: "But if you, who were just now of our flour, retain your old skin." The reason is well enough known. "Milk is not more like milk, nor water more like water." These are proverbs from Plautus regarding things that are entirely similar to one another. That saying of Cicero to Hortensius likewise means exactly the same: "Those things between which there is a likeness."

**Book XII of the Epistles. Folio 109.**

Antimachus loved Lyde; and he wrote a poem about her death. Suidas <note>The *Suda*, a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of the ancient Mediterranean world.</note> says many things on this matter. Plutarch also agrees: who, in his *Consolation to Apollonius*, says that Antimachus <note>Antimachus of Colophon (c. 400 BC), a Greek poet and scholar.</note> wrote an Elegy under the title of his wife Lyde, whom he loved passionately, in order to console himself. But there is also frequent mention of Antimachus’s Lyde among the Greek grammarians, such as among the commentators of Apollonius himself, as well as Lucillus of Tarrhae, Sophocleus, and Theon. But, Alexander, I have written more extensively about these things elsewhere.

I come now to that part of the letter in which you demand my [work on] poets, since I had written in my previous letters that I am pressing on with this work: so that both the labor and the love of the labor grow day by day. You act as a true friend: you who take an interest in my sleepless nights <note>original: "vigiliis," referring to the common humanist trope of "lucubration," or scholarly work conducted by candlelight late into the night</note>. I will soon send the book to you first, in which I have embraced the more ancient authors. These include, specifically, all those among the Latin authors who wrote before the time of Virgil. From that, given your own great learning, you will easily be able to make conjectures about the rest. Give my warmest greetings to our friend Aldus <note>Aldus Manutius (1449–1515), the famous Venetian printer and publisher of Greek and Latin classics.</note> again and again. Farewell. The Calends of April <note>April 1st.</note>.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on classical figures and transitions into a personal letter from the scholar Scipio Carteromachus to his teacher, Angelo Poliziano. ...deeds: you should set out these "sweetmeats," <note>original: "bellaria," referring to dessert or treats, here used metaphorically for a collection of polished letters</note> that is, you should publish your letters. Currently, they lie like individual and severed limbs, as if without spirit; let them finally revive, gathered into a single body. In this way, the Florentine Academy may at last possess what it desires, and it may boldly compare you in every kind of refinement even with antiquity itself. Indeed, if the old books and testimonies of literature should all perish by the incursion of barbarians, let it hold you alone in place of them all—secure as if it had lost nothing—as the one it most gladly reads, imitates, and honors. [Marginal notes: <margin>Descendants of Neleus / Nestor.</margin> <margin>Alcibiades’ versatile nature.</margin> <margin>Lysander the Spartan.</margin> <margin>Oebalia.</margin> <margin>Rhodes, the Island of the Sun.</margin> <margin>The Tagus river.</margin> <margin>Homer’s uncertain birthplace.</margin> <margin>Tiresias.</margin>]

**The Descendants of Neleus.** That is, of Nestor, who was the son of Neleus and Chloris. *His own if twice five,* etc. <note>A reference to Nestor’s legendary long life, spanning three generations.</note> We mentioned this matter before. **The twin son of Clinias.** Alcibiades, the son of Clinias, was an Athenian. In him, nature seems to have tested what it was capable of producing. For it is agreed among all who have handed down memories of him that nothing was more excellent than he, whether in his vices or his virtues. In a very great city and born of the highest noble line, he was by far the most handsome of all in his age, fit for all things, and far-sighted in his counsel. He was a supreme commander on land and sea, and so eloquent that he was foremost in speaking. Such was the charm of his face and his speech that no one could resist him when he spoke. Then, when the time required it, he was hardworking, patient, generous, and splendid no less in his public life than in his private habits; he was affable, charming, and most shrewdly adapted to the circumstances. Yet this same man, as soon as he relaxed and there was no reason for him to endure the labor of the mind, was found to be luxurious, dissolute, lustful, and intemperate—so much so that everyone wondered how there could be such great inconsistency and such a diverse nature in a single man. These details are from Aemilius Probus <note>Now known as Cornelius Nepos, a Roman biographer.</note>, who writes more on this Alcibiades; but Plutarch writes the most. **Nor do you have Lysander.** Lysander the Spartan left behind a great reputation for himself, though it was prepared by good fortune rather than virtue, as the same Aemilius Probus records. Plutarch wrote his life more extensively. Plutarch also mentions him in his *Laconian Sayings*. **The land of Oebalus.** That is, Laconia <note>The region surrounding Sparta.</note>. For they say Oebalus was a king of Laconia, from whom Laconia was called Oebalia. Lactantius, in his commentary on the fifth book of the *Thebaid*, says that Oebalia is the city of Sparta. From this comes "Oebalis." **The Island of the Sun.** That is, Rhodes. Why it is called the island of the sun we write in our notes on Ausonius's *Gryphon*. He calls it "the goldsmith" because Pindar sang that it rained gold there, as is found in Beroaldo’s commentaries on Suetonius. **The Tagus.** A river of Lusitania <note>Modern-day Portugal.</note> having golden sands. **Concerning the birthplace, etc.** According to Aulus Gellius in the eleventh chapter of his third book: "Seven cities contend for the origin of the noble Homer: Smyrna, Rhodes, Colophon, Salamis, Ios, Argos, and Athens." However, whether "Ius" or "Chios" should be said, as pleases some, we trust we shall discuss elsewhere. **Beyond the life of Tiresias the Theban.** That is, beyond the span that Tiresias lived. Tiresias was made long-lived by Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena.</note>, as Poliziano says in the eightieth chapter of his *Miscellanea*. He says that when the nymph Chariclo, the mother of Tiresias, was washing herself naked during the heat of the day in the Hippocrene spring on Mount Helicon with Minerva (to whom she was dear), the hunter Tiresias happened to arrive at the same spring, thirsty. Unintentionally catching sight of the naked Minerva, his eyes were seized. For it was cautioned by the laws of Saturn that whoever beholds a god against their will shall behold at a great price. Pallas [Minerva], moved by Chariclo’s tears, made Tiresias a prophet, long-lived, and wise and discerning even after death. Therefore, Lucian, in his *Necromancy*, makes him the most consulted counselor among those in the underworld.

# Scipio Carteromachus to Angelo Poliziano.
### Greetings. Epistle XXV.

[Marginal notes: <margin>That is, you have entered this contest.</margin> <margin>Friendship does not admit an excuse.</margin> <margin>But if not.</margin>]

Indeed, Poliziano, my best teacher, I am ashamed to have waited for this particular occasion to write to you, from which the reason for our bond appears to be necessity rather than will or duty. For although I ought to have written to you immediately at the beginning when I set out for here, as is the duty of a friend and much more of a student, I neglected it then when I could have done it most honorably. Thus now, I do it not by my own will (as it seems), but as if compelled. But if you consider why or by what reasoning I avoided that duty, you will find it was done for no other cause than a profound awe of you, or rather, reverence. For as often as I thought to myself to whom I would be writing if I wrote to you, immediately my spirit failed; it took away all my plan for writing. I confess my weakness: whether it is timidity, or reverence, or both, it certainly never allowed me before this day—otherwise always ready and eager—to write to you. And in this (unless I am mistaken), I seem worthy of pardon rather than accusation, because I so greatly dreaded the judgment of that man who, on account of the excellence of his genius and his manifold knowledge of all doctrines, alone turned the minds of everyone toward admiration of himself. 

But why, you will ask, have you now finally **entered the contest?** <note>original Greek: "εἰς τὸ τομὶ τὸν ἀγῶνα εἰσῆλθες"</note> Because, as you know, **friendship does not wait for an excuse.** <note>original Greek: "φιλία πρόφασιν οὐ περιμένει"</note> For since it was a matter of either a friend losing his safety or me having to write to you, I thought it most shameful not to risk a very small thing rather than lose the greatest. Especially since, if I wrote to you, I would act as both a friend and a student; **but if not,** <note>original Greek: "εἴ δὲ μή"</note> besides losing a friend and never fulfilling the duty of a student, I would also seem to have very little confidence in you, by whom I know myself to be loved as much as a student can be by a teacher. 

Why then should I fear to commend the safety of a friend to you? For if you love my own self, as you certainly do, without doubt you will not neglect one who is most dear to me. For he is the one about whom I have decided to write to you: no one in this city is more familiar to us; we have known him since our tender years in Rome, when we were both being educated in the same studies under the same teachers. And (to tell the truth), nothing kept me here so long, even against my will, as the fear of being torn away from his company. Indeed, although I had immediately regretted our departure, I congratulated myself on coming here for this one thing: that I had recovered a friend long since lost. For concerning him, I had learned nothing for ten years, and he was certainly believed lost by me. He who is now lost a second time must be recovered again through you—and more honorably than before. For then he was restored to us not from misfortunes, but only from absence and a kind of forgetfulness; now he must be restored from the greatest miseries and calamities. For what can be more miserable for a man than to die daily while living and willing (as the saying goes)? That, however, is prison. To which punishment our friend here has been condemned, because he wounded a monk of the same order to which he himself belongs...

# Of Illustrious Men

Furthermore, this Tuscan mixture <note>original: "miscella haec ethrusca"</note> made from almonds, sugar, flour, and rosewater seems most exquisite; today, it is called **Marzipan** <note>original: "Mazapanis"</note> by way of excellence <note>original: "exochen"</note>: just as "the Poet" refers to Homer or Virgil. I called it Tuscan: not because it isn't kneaded or shaped elsewhere, but because among your people it is made exceptionally well. Its chief grace is that it does not dry out, but stays fresh and soft for a long time; it is not so refined that it smells like **yesterday’s cheese of Xenocrates** <note>referencing the previous page's discussion of the philosopher's extreme frugality and his habit of keeping food until it grew moldy</note>. We have played with these matters with you as if with a great censor of letters. Set aside the mask of a prince and take up that of a grammarian, for you are supreme in both—as kings have occasionally done. Elsewhere, as you know, I have commented much on **Sugar**; but good gods, what a difference: I write about Sugar, you give it. Farewell.

<margin>To be in ferment.</margin>
**F.S.** <note>likely the initials of a commentator or editor</note> So that it may be in ferment longer—that is, better and more aptly and, as it were, more sweetly composed for the taste—so that it becomes a reasoning made from bread: which, when fermented, is no small delight to the palate. Otherwise, "to be in ferment" <note>original: "in fermento esse"</note> means to swell and be puffed up with anger or pride. **Plautus** <note>Roman comic playwright</note> in *The Merchant*: "Your wife lies in ferment." **Persius** <note>Roman satirist</note> in his first Satire: "Why learn anything, unless this ferment and the wild fig-tree, which has once sprouted within, should break out from the burst liver." Here, Persius compares the knowledge of a show-off to ferment: which, due to a kind of swelling in the breast, cannot be contained.

<margin>Butchery.</margin>
He practiced **butchery** <note>original: "Carnificina"</note>: that is, he mutilated, lopped off, ruined, and removed letters, words, clauses, and sentences from the midst. For "butchery" is the torture of the executioner. **Plautus** in *The Captives*: "I can endure this man doing butchery." It is also "carnificina," a public place where, by order of a magistrate, guilty men are punished with death by the executioner.

**Hermolaus Barbarus, Ambassador and Patriarch of Aquileia. To the most illustrious man Antonius Calvus, Venetian Patrician. Greetings. Letter XXIX.**

[Decorative initial A] My sweetest Antonius, I did not reply to your most loving letters because I hoped shortly to put the final hand to the **Corrections of Pliny** <note>Barbarus's famous *Castigationes Plinianae*, in which he identified thousands of errors in Pliny the Elder’s "Natural History"</note>. But the work and the labor grew, and so did the love of the labor. Who would believe it? There exists almost no author in either language <note>Greek or Latin</note> whom I have not read, so that this midnight-toil of ours might be fortified—and all this in a space of no more than six months. We discovered five thousand errors made by scribes in that work—not errors made yesterday or the day before, but those customary and accepted by readers for many centuries past. The matter has indeed reached the final stage <note>original: "ad umbilicum," literally "to the navel," an ancient idiom for the end of a scroll</note>, but yet there is no day on which some addition is not made. Now I have begun to deal with the printers, intentionally delaying the matter slowly, so that it may **be in ferment longer**; fear nothing. We shall apply such diligence as you have often complained to me was omitted in the other edition. Our order will be as follows: first, we place the corrupt words of **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, author of the first-century Roman encyclopedia</note> according to the individual chapters of each book. Then, we add how they are to be corrected, citing the authors from whom what we want can be easily proven. This will be done with all prefaces removed and without any pomp of words; lest, as many do while they admire their own labors too much, I detain the reader with an ambitious speech before he hears the end of some matter. Thus the mind is exhausted before it is fed, and otherwise good things are loathed before they are learned. However, I undertook much more work and labor than I thought, because it is necessary to be knowledgeable of all things in heaven and under heaven if one professes to understand Pliny—all the more so to correct him. Truly nothing tortured me as much as the layout of the lands <note>geography</note>: in which part especially the negligence of the scribes practiced **butchery** <note>referencing the earlier definition of mutilating text</note>. 

<margin>The learning of Pliny.</margin>
Indeed, I have often wished that the excellent man **Antonius Leonardus**, our friend, were present; assisted by his counsel and confirmed by his authority, I would have solved the difficulties and knots in that genre, which were inextricable with so much business. We have restored more than fifteen hundred places clearly depraved in that part alone, so that we seem to have healed as many wounds—or rather, to have tamed monsters, smaller indeed, but far more numerous than those of **Hercules**. For why should I not joke with you? Especially at this time, when certain minute philosophers of a thin soul think I should be allowed to grieve. Others proclaim that a festive face little becomes a less happy fortune. Others are hurt and burned by our constancy and this nature of ours. They seethe much more than they harm those who are harmed. But I have never experienced anything in myself more excellent than this strength of mind with which God has fortified me, nothing more pleasant; so that (as I wrote to you elsewhere) I not only bear what I suffer moderately, but even much more often feel fruit and pleasure in bearing it. I complain of nothing, I seek nothing, I am hostile to no one, I accuse no one; peace, cheerfulness, and the giving of thanks comfort me while awake and cherish me while sleeping. Those who pursue me are not of such a composed mind—I do not say those who pursue me, but those whom no one pursues. This is not idleness or stupor, nor is it contempt or pride, but a weighing of the human lot and a meditation on death. If the things for which life struggles are great, they are to be esteemed as small because they will last a short time; if they are small, you know what follows. Farewell. December 13, 1491. Just now, just now, I received your other letter, to which I will respond as soon as possible; I hope these will satisfy you in some part. **Didymus** <note>likely a nickname for a friend or assistant</note> commends himself to you greatly.

**Hermolaus Barbarus, Ambassador and Patriarch of Aquileia. To Antonius Calvus, Venetian Patrician. Greetings. Letter XXX.**

[Decorative initial V] Just as it was new to you to hear that I had been made a soldier of Christ from a pagan soldier of the world <note>referring to his transition from a secular political career to being named Patriarch of Aquileia</note>, so it is an old thing for me to understand that my Calvus has taken solid pleasure from the honor of his Hermolaus. Whatever this is, whatever status has fallen to me, whatever fortune I use or shall use, my sweetest Antonius, it serves and shall serve you and your interests just as it does mine. I recognize your piety toward me, your zeal, charity, and faith; I clearly see and feel it so much that I could not do so more. I give thanks, and I intend to return the favor as soon as possible. It has always been my goal to be grateful toward all. Having been chosen for the lot of the Lord <note>entering the clergy</note> by this virtue, I intend to increase it, not lose it. Pour out prayers to God with me, that this dignity may profit me not toward vain glory, which is the image of death, but toward life and salvation; so that, even if we are taught by **Augustine** <note>St. Augustine of Hippo</note> to trample upon earthly things and thirst for heavenly ones. Farewell. Rome. April 6, 1491.

**Book XII of Letters. Folio CXII.**

<margin>On the address at the beginning of an oration.</margin>

**F.S.** <note>likely the initials of the commentator/editor Franciscus Sylvius</note> Antonius, etc. Note that the vocative <note>the grammatical case used when addressing someone directly</note> is placed at the very beginning of the speech. **Hermolaus Barbarus, orator and Patriarch of Aquileia, to Antonius Calvus, Venetian Noble. Health and Greetings.**
**Letter XXXI.**

**A**ntony, most excellent man, be of good cheer. He who called me to the priesthood while I was sleeping—and indeed even while I was reluctant—has also willed that I be constant and brave. I bear these adversities with a calmer mind than I bore those favorable times. I call God to witness my justice and innocence: I am so free from all anxiety, so liberated from cares, that I fear such great security might be argued by the spiteful as proof of either rashness or negligence. **The Lord has sent me help from the sanctuary, and he will protect me from Zion; some trust in chariots, and some in horses, but we will call upon the name of our God.** <note>A paraphrase of Psalm 20:2-7</note> Again I say, be of good cheer; we have risen and stand upright. **Wonderful are the surges of the sea, wonderful is the Lord on high.** <note>Psalm 93:4</note> I, who have spent so many years playing the philosopher for others, believe it will come to pass that I may seem able to play the philosopher for myself as well. You will say: "You are brave because you hope it will soon happen that this storm will grow calm, and that those who hated you will love and embrace you." I think nothing of this; no hope directed toward a happier outcome sustains me. He is not brave who is brave through hope; he is brave who feels and endures present evils, and endures them in such a way that even if he sees they will last, he despises them and looks not to the future. Otherwise, if he tolerates present inconveniences in expectation of future comforts, it is a compensation, not fortitude—or if it is fortitude, it is certainly not that noble and absolute kind, but plainly mercenary and mangled. When I remove hope from fortitude, I do not mean that hope of which it is said: *It is good to hope in the Lord*, but that of which it is written: *Cursed is the man who trusts in man.* <note>Jeremiah 17:5</note> Furthermore, my sweetest Antony, how much I owe you, and how much I wish to always owe you, you may weigh by the magnitude and purity of your love toward me. Your letters are so full of piety and charity that they are able to bring both pleasure in prosperity and solace in adversity to all those whom you love. Greet Nicolaus Foscarinus, who is no less a friend to me than to you, in my name. Would that it were permitted to me at some time, as it once was, to take part in your most refined and most cheerful debates. Farewell. Rome. The Ides of April <note>April 13th</note>, 1491.

<margin>What a brave man is.</margin>

**F.S.** **The executioner of glory.** <note>original: "Gloriae carnifex"</note> That is, one who kills glory. The ancients used *carnufex* for *carnifex* <note>executioner</note>, just as *lubens* was used for *libens* <note>willingly</note> and *pessumus* for *pessimus* <note>worst</note>, as Priscian records in his first book. **To roam** <note>original: "grassari"</note> and **to fatten** <note>original: "crassari"</note> have this distinction between them, as Agretus mentions: *crassari* pertains to things of the body and blood, but *grassari* belongs to the mind or to cruelty. **Much more, etc.** On the authority of Diogenes Laertius in his first book, Bias used to call that man unhappy who could not bear misfortune.

<margin>To fatten / To roam</margin>

**Hermolaus Barbarus, Orator and Patriarch of Aquileia, to Antonius Calvus, Venetian Noble. Health and Greetings. Letter XXXII.**

**D**istracted and still distracting me is my correction of Pliny <note>original: "Pliniana castigatio"</note>, which has been brought almost to the "navel" <note>a metaphor for the end of a scroll or project</note>, preventing me from writing anything to you about matters—I will not say my own, but our common affairs, or rather yours entirely. Others may think this is done out of some pain or grief; but you, who know me, beware of such suspicion. I see the game of Fortune. I understand the violence of the storm. I am aware of the stings of detractors. I hear what is being said and what can be said, and I follow it in my thoughts. I realize how great an injury would be done to me, were it not done by my fatherland, by whom nothing done against a citizen can seem cruel or injurious. I do not lack grief because I fail to perceive these things or because I feel them too little. I recognize all these things, Antony, and I estimate their weight perhaps more subtly than others, because they come into my mind much more often than into the minds of strangers. Nevertheless, there are many things which ensure that I do not allow myself to be broken, or even tempted, by grief. First is the conscience of having accepted a priesthood not only without filth, but without any suspicion of greed or ambition; how hesitantly I admitted the command, what a struggle of the mind it was, with how much shame I fought. I call upon God quickly; I name him my advocate, witness, and avenger. What innocence would not tremble before such a judge? Conversely, what child, what woman, what slave would fear with such a patron and protector? Indeed, far from yielding my flank to grief, I even can and ought to rejoice, since fortune—the executioner of glory, as that man says—attacks so sparingly that there is much more benefit in patience than there is loss in the wound itself. See how far I am from complaining or lamenting my lot, I who even defend Fortune herself. In what way, I ask, could she have opposed me more lightly than by raging against a small portion of accidental honor, while the Republic is flourishing, my family survives, my domestic affairs are safe, and my health of body and mind is most prosperous? Why do I say honor? Is it not rather a burden? <note>a pun on the Latin words "honoris" and "oneris"</note> Which is surely so great and so widely felt that he who does not see this, or pretends not to see it, cannot be anything but most dull-witted. I do not attack you, Fortune; I lose nothing. If you thought this would be a great disaster for me, you are deceived; if you intended to exercise me, I rejoice; if you wished to test a fortitude that was perhaps lying hidden, I give thanks. Nothing is more excellent than this virtue of the soul, nothing more upright; none shines brighter, none is a greater maker of peace and pleasure; and while all things yield to impotent Fortune, fortitude alone goes out to meet her hand-to-hand and binds Fortune in chains. But imagine that I have received some great and notable wound: how much protection do you think remains for me, and how much solace survives from those little letters <note>his classical studies</note> which I have drunk in since I was a boy? What calamity could happen to me, sound in mind and body, so great that it would shake my studies from me? While these are preserved and excepted, my life cannot be anything but tranquil, pleasant, and splendid. Born for letters, dedicated to letters, I cannot exist without letters. I can exist without those things which hinder, interrupt, or remove letters. I have held many and great honors in the Republic; I shall not say with what faith, reputation, or grace. It is indeed pleasing to have spent twelve full years...

<margin>Fortune, the executioner of glory.</margin>

**Illustrious Men**

...but eight continuous years in the service of the republic: yet almost all that time was lost to literature. Those studies indeed called out to me, and repeatedly commanded me to restore myself to them. I, on the contrary, dragged things out day by day and procrastinated—not indeed because of the sweetness of honors and magistracies, but to obey my father, brothers, and friends, who thought my efforts in the republic would be useful; I myself did not see it. Since, therefore, having been so often reminded of my profession and my vow, I was unwilling or unable to return home <note>original: "postliminio reuerti," a legal term for returning to one's original status or country</note>, I was dragged back from my flight by force. I do not see from where that force was inflicted on me, except by literature itself, which wanted to claim me for itself—me, who was already raising my horns and watching over my liberty—back into its service. This was achieved by a devised plan so that, through a leisure not without dignity, I might be excluded from public affairs. These are my "miseries," as many call them; this is that "disaster," that "calamity" by which most think I am ruined and dismayed. This is that bitterness of fortune, which my friends fear I will be unequal to, and which my enemies proclaim. O happy calamity! which restored literature to me and me to literature—nay, which restored myself to me! O blessed disaster! which gave me back my peace. O bright storm, which brought forth security for me. O sweet bitterness, which brought me back into a most pleasant harbor after a long tossing, not to say shipwreck. If tranquility is sought, literature will provide it; if glory, literature; if the rest—part of which is already available to me, part of which I despise—literature. Living, I experience with such modest learning as much as literary men might hope for in death, if by the will of God any name of ours remains. No one credits this to the embassies or magistracies I held, but to literature; far more love Hermolaus <note>referring to himself as the scholar</note> than the "candidate" version of me. Perhaps they are mistaken, but so it is: only fellow citizens admire honors in the republic, but the whole world emulates the glory of letters. Farewell. I knew that Quintilian <note>The Roman educator and rhetorician; Barbarus is likely referring to a manuscript or edition of his work</note> had been restored to your father by you—though he does not truly restore who restores his own; for I wish all my things to be yours. Rome, July 22, 1491.

<margin>A message.</margin> ASCENSIUS <note>The scholar Jodocus Badius Ascensius, providing commentary</note>: And a very sad message. It is also said this way in Tibullus: "The gods, true messengers, warn of the coming fate." And yet Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, the famous humanist grammarian</note> truly advises that for the thing announced as well as for the one who announces it, "messenger" [*nuncius*] is said in the masculine gender. However, I think the thing itself is properly signified by the neuter gender [*nuncium*], and the one announcing by the masculine [*nuncius*]. Figuratively, however, "a sad message" is said of the thing announced, because he who brings a sad message is himself a sad messenger.

**Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarch, to his friend Antonius Calvus. Greetings.**
**Letter XXXIII.**

**W**e received your letter, in which you wished to soothe our intense and just grief over the death of my father Zacharias, and we found it most welcome. It cannot be denied—especially to you, Antony, the most faithful of friends—that this was a hard and very sad message for us. For what, I ask you, could have happened at a more inconvenient time, either for him or for me? And to pass over other things which are as well known to you as to me, do you think it was more painful for him that he was dying, or that he was dying while I was absent? You knew what affection he had for me—not common or ordinary, but beyond what fathers are accustomed to. I have it certain and proven: if it was heavy for him to die, it was not for his own sake, but only for mine. I know for certain that this also tormented him: he did not know with what composure I would bear such a great disaster. He who was going securely toward death was anxious only about my grief. If I had been present, and he could have seen that strength of ours—with which not virtue, not learning, not any experience of affairs, but God alone has protected me—I have no doubt that he would have departed life, if not cheerfully, then certainly with no pain. Yet, as I understand from your letters and those of others, such was the man’s constancy in facing death that he showed no signs of a dismayed mind, nor even of the slightest sorrow. He was so intrepid throughout that he seemed to be migrating into some other home from home, rather than departing from life. For three continuous days he either heard others discussing or himself discussed God, religion, and the immortality of souls. Those extreme sacraments, which everyone dreads and about which the sick are usually interrupted by their relatives with fear and hesitation, he not only did not shrink from but was the first to ask for them of his own accord. All the senses of his mind and body—in which few mortals surpassed him—he showed to the very end to be not only intact but even far more subtle than ever before. Finally, having gathered two small <margin>Small images or icons.</margin> images—one of Christ and the other of the Virgin—into his lap with his own hand and applied them to his chest, he breathed out his soul while embracing and kissing them most tightly. This kind of death—I will not call it death, but a glorious death—nay, rather, salvation and a better life—cannot be sufficiently explained for how much power it has to temper grief. Add to this that he had entered his seventieth year—a length of life no one in our family has reached—and that, having performed all honors while the republic was sound and his children were placed in honorable positions, he departed with the incredible longing and love of the city. The attendance at his funeral was so great (as I hear) as never before for a citizen. It remains for me to commend my brothers to you; since you cannot be with me, attend to them for me, not only as a comforter with diligence but as a father with love. Farewell. Rome, December 13, 1492.

<margin>White. Bright. The silence of the Pythagoreans.</margin> **P.S.** *Villa*: that is, small wines most pleasing to the taste. *Candor* [Brightness/Purity] is almost the opposite of envy. Agretius distinguishes *candidum* [shining white] from *album* [plain white], in that *album* is merely by nature. *Candidum* pertains to application or zeal. For it is sometimes assigned to both the body and the soul. Thus we say "white hairs" [*albos*] but a "bright poem" [*candidum*]. Regarding the silence of the Pythagoreans, etc.: Aulus Gellius discusses the silence of the Pythagoreans in the ninth chapter of his first book. <meta>This page continues the scholarly reflections and correspondence of Hermolaus Barbarus. Having previously discussed his forced retirement from Venetian politics into the Patriarchate of Aquileia, he now turns to philosophical definitions and a specific defense of his monumental work, the "Castigatio Pliniana," in which he corrected thousands of errors in Pliny the Elder’s Natural History. **Letters, Book XII. Folio CXIII.**

...they would spend time, during which they heard what was said by others; it was not permitted to ask questions if they understood little, nor to comment on what they had heard. Indeed, no one was silent for less than two years. Philostratus mentions this silence in the first book of his *Life of Apollonius*. He says that silence <note>original: "Silentium"</note> instituted by Pythagoras was thought to have drawn its origin from the gods. For many divine and secret things were spoken by him, which could not be understood except by those who had learned them thoroughly. From this, they believe the reason for silence was introduced by him. **Of the Academics.** The Academy was threefold: the Old, the New, [Marginal note: The triple Academy.] and the Middle. The Old was instituted by Plato and his disciples Speusippus and Xenocrates. The philosophers of this Academy affirmed many things and denied many things. The Middle was that which Arcesilaus introduced; he asserted that nothing should be affirmed, since nothing could be comprehended, and because the reasons on both sides are of equal strength, the senses are also deceptive, and no reason can be made firm. The third was instituted by Carneades, who affirmed that nothing could be known for certain, and he opposed the Stoics who stubbornly affirmed everything. These things are from Peter Marsus in his commentaries on the second book of Cicero’s *Offices*. Therefore, the New and Middle Academics, affirming no certain thing, held back their judgment. **Under whatever omen.** <note>original: "Quocunq[ue] alite," literally "by whatever bird"</note> That is, by whatever bird, whether lucky or unlucky. "By prosperous birds" is a common proverbial way of saying a thing is done successfully, as we might say now.

ASCENSIUS: It is never enough to **attack arrogance**. That is, to rail against arrogance: to pluck at it, taunt it, and pursue it. It is also said: [Marginal note: To attack/creep in.] the desire for things **has crept into** you. That is, as if it crept or creeps in and is born within you. **Otherwise**: <note>original: "Alioquin"</note> in other places it is now written as *alioqui*: which means "if in any other way," [Marginal note: Otherwise.] and that seems to be the true meaning. Here, however, a new way of signifying this appears: so that it is what we call "but" or "besides." **As it might happen to me**: which has also happened to many others—namely, that these were not errors. That is, Pliny's errors. For what he noted was as if little was opposed to Pliny. He attributes this, therefore, to Plinian learning, which we all ought to attribute to holy things: so that when he does not seem to speak well, we believe that we do not understand him well. However, this modest and friendly choice has no place in the errors of scribes, which he was able to restore without harming the majesty of Pliny.

**Hermolaus Barbarus, Patriarch of Aquileia, to M. L. Phos. Pont. Signinus. Health and Greetings.**
**Letter XXXIIII.**

I used to think that only the villa of Signia and its pears were celebrated; but I see that Signian letters also have their own glory. All your things always please me, but those you wrote recently along with the pears, we approved of wonderfully—so much so that compared to them, the pears, which were otherwise most excellent, seemed worthless. I follow your interpretation of Gellius so clearly that I could not do so more; I am truly delighted, moreover, that you judge Pliny to be justly praised by us, for there are some who—either because they do not understand his books, or because they are imbued with backward learning—bear it with an unjust mind that as much is attributed to one man as they themselves cannot foresee or reach by conjecture. So it is: and it has always been the same. Everyone condemns what he is ignorant of. We generally grieve that anyone appears wise in that in which we ourselves can in no way be wise. Nor is this a vice of the common people alone: it often entangles great minds as well. This fault creeps up on many and sticks to them, otherwise under an honorable appearance, as if they wish to speak freely what they feel; but no one can feel rightly about something of which he is ignorant. Thus it happens that those who ought to have known themselves, and suspended judgment about another's profession, pronounce petulantly and rashly: and what follows is that they are greatly laughed at and taunted. The virtue contrary to this plague is **candor**, [Marginal note: Candor.] which is accustomed to be present in good and simple minds, even if they are not cultivated by that highest and eminent learning; [Marginal note: The duty of the candid.] to know their own faults, to extol the virtues of others, to consider the things they themselves know as small, and at least not to despise what another knows; to weigh their own strength by the labors of others, not to estimate others' labors by their own: how much they have profited their own age, how much they are worth, that they breathe, that they move in the assembly of men; how much labor they have spent on letters, how much of the day and night they have consumed in jokes and trifles, how much they have read, and how many things they have not read. "White" souls do this, and (as the Greeks say) well-born minds, whose highest and certain property is never to teach, but always to want to be taught, to hate judgment, and to love silence, in which two things the whole instruction of the Pythagoreans and Academics is contained. This is that virtue, or one not greatly different, celebrated by Christians under the name of **humility**: [Marginal note: Humility.] which, as it is the most certain way to salvation and the glory of eternity, so in all of life, especially for a man of letters, it is a necessary companion, without which we will be neither teachable in discovering nor prudent in judging. But boldness and pride snatch men away. His own ignorance is an evil to each; but it is a plague when unrecognized. The **beginning of wisdom** (as Plato writes) [Marginal note: The beginning of wisdom.] is the recognition of one's own ignorance; neglecting this makes men over-confident and miserable. I have been carried away—I do not say railed—further than I intended: but it is never enough to attack arrogance: otherwise, if you spare names, we cause reproach to no kind of men with less danger, because those who attribute everything to themselves never think it is said about them. The *Plinian Correction*, since you so wish—or rather command, urge, and rebuke—will go forth under whatever omen; it is wonderful to say how much I desire these works of ours to be tested by learned men, so that what happened to many others might happen to me: that these things might not be errors, but things poorly understood which seemed like errors to me. For whether the unlearned receive or reject our works matters little; for to be praised by them, even for things that deserve praise, is no praise at all. Either your authority, or certainly these Signian pears, have given me this stomach. Farewell. The sixth day before the Kalends of November, 1492. <note>October 27, 1492.</note>

F. S. D. While he praises meanly. A. Certainly Gellius does not praise Pliny so meanly—from what I have read—that he would deter students from reading him. [Marginal note: Gellius on Pliny.] These are the words of that Gellius in commendation of Pliny from the fourth chapter of the ninth book: "Pliny Secundus," he says, "was a man in the times of his own age endowed with great authority because of the dignity of his talent." And in the sixteenth chapter of the same book: "Pliny Secundus," he says, "was considered to be the most learned of his age." But in the same chapter he modestly reproves Pliny because the vice of an argument—which the Greeks call *antistrephon* <note>original: "αντιστρεφον," a reversible or circular argument</note>—was hidden from him. **Meanly.** That is, thinly and sterilely: as we call a sterile field a **malignant field**. [Marginal note: A malignant field.] Virgil in the second book of the *Georgics*: "First, difficult lands and mean [sterile] hills." The author is Marcellus. Those are said to be **reduced to the ranks** who, [Marginal note: To be reduced to the ranks.] when they were superior to others, are made equal to others by the lessening of their dignity. The reasoning is made from army commanders: who, when they have fallen from command, are reduced to the ranks. Macrobius, in his third book, writing about the sturgeon: "Nor do I deny," he says, "that in the times of Trajan this fish was not at great price, as Pliny Secundus testifies, who in his *Natural History*, when speaking of this fish, says: 'It is in no way held in honor.' Which I truly wonder at, since it is rare to find." But...

# Of Illustrious Men

->It is Pliny who wonders, not Macrobius; whether he wonders elsewhere, I do not know.<- **After Quintus Fabius, etc.** The words of Fabius <note>The author is referring to Quintilian (Marcus Fabius Quintilianus), the famous Roman educator and rhetorician.</note> are from the eleventh book. "The ancients," he says, "let the **toga** down as far as the shoes, just as the Greeks did with their cloak <note>original: "pallium"</note>." And so that this might be done, those who wrote about gesture around those times, Plotius and Nigidius, give instructions. Therefore, I wonder all the more at the belief of **Pliny the Elder** <note>original: "Plinii Secundi"</note>, a learned man—and in this book especially, almost excessively curious—who records that **Cicero** was accustomed to do this for the sake of veiling his varicose veins: since this kind of dress also appears in the statues of those who lived after Cicero. **The pontifical dinners** <note>The "Cœnas pontificias" were legendary, lavish banquets held by the high priests of Rome.</note> which he describes in the third book of the *Saturnalia*, as well as the dessert courses <term>second tables (mensas secundas)</term> and the tree-orchard. 

<margin>The Egyptian Dog.</margin> **The Egyptian dog, to lap while running.** That is, to touch and taste very gently. "It is certain," says Pliny in the fortieth chapter of the eighth book when he speaks of the nature of the dog, "that near the Nile river, it laps while running, so as not to provide an opportunity for the greed of crocodiles." 

<margin>To beat the water.</margin> **To beat the water.** <note>This Latin idiom "Tundere aquam" typically refers to performing a useless or repetitive task, similar to "flogging a dead horse."</note>

<summary>This page features a scholarly critique of Pliny the Elder’s observations on Roman fashion—specifically Cicero’s use of the toga to hide varicose veins—and explains the "Egyptian dog" metaphor regarding the Nile.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the general scholarly commentary on Pliny to a specific exchange of letters between two of the most famous Renaissance humanists: Hermolaus Barbarus and Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. The page begins with a philological commentary by Jodocus Badius Ascensius (indicated by "ASCEN."), who provides linguistic and philosophical context for the letter that follows.</meta>

**Book XII of the Letters. Folio CXIIII.**

ASCENSIUS: **Who pleads for my negligence in place of yours.** This means: since I have been no less, or rather more, negligent than you: <margin>I plead against.</margin> you pray that I might forgive your negligence, or that I do not hold it against you as a fault. **You recognize the fault of another.** That is, you attribute my fault to yourself. However, he alludes to that famous saying: "It is the mark of a modest mind to acknowledge a fault where there is none." Since you could have avoided it by denying you were at fault, or shared it by attributing a part of the fault to me. **Who could have been secure.** That is, set apart from care, weighing my accusation as nothing: and **simultaneously with recrimination** <note>original: "anticategoria"</note>, and even with a better cause: because if I were to find fault with your silence, you would be able <margin>Recrimination.</margin> to find fault with mine, and indeed more justly: because by writing, I ought to have accommodated you, rather than you accommodating me. Beware of reading "antecategoria": because it is a single word and it is Greek. **Otherwise.** That is, for the rest, or "but because." **And instruments.** For this is what the Peripatetics <note>Followers of Aristotle’s philosophy.</note> almost always call logic, as will be held in the following letter. **Dogmatic.** That is, prescriptive. **Parænetic.** That is, advisory or hortatory. **How great a name.** That is, how great a debtor he is: namely, to God. **Nor will you be for paying.** That is, as they say, you will not be sufficient to pay <margin>Paying.</margin> or to return the equivalent: nor **by blotting out.** That is, by deleting the marks <note>original: "puncta"</note> which are usually written next to names every year, so that as many years of taxes or assessments are owed as there are marks written: these, however, are easily blotted out from the parchments. **How much you are.** <margin>The grace of the neuter gender.</margin> The neuter gender here has something more pleasing and abundant than the others: hence he said "How much you are" <note>original: "Quantum es"</note> rather than if he had said "How great you are" <note>original: "Quantus es"</note>. As Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous humanist and linguist.</note> noted, it is sometimes more pleasing even when not more abundant: as in "nothing is more learned than your father," where he says no more than "no one is more learned than him." **Preconceived.** Or taken and perceived beforehand. He uses the word properly: but those who ineptly call a boastful person "presumptuous" <margin>Preconceived.</margin> are mistaken: since perhaps "presuming" can be said of one who takes for himself what is given by no one.

**Hermolaus Barbarus to Giovanni Pico della Mirandola. Greetings.**
**Letter XXXVII.**

[T] Truly, Pico, you owe me nothing, whether on account of silence or any service of mine toward you; indeed, your own letters have brought me great shame, in which you plead for my negligence as if it were your own, when both of us should have first redeemed ourselves to you at any price. This is the goodness, the candor, and the fairness of your character. **You recognize the fault of another**, when you could either avoid it or certainly share it. In a mutual crime, you are anxious: you who, with both **recrimination** <note>original: "anticategoria"</note> <margin>Recrimination.</margin> and an even better cause, could have been secure. Either both are guilty, or you are not. Otherwise, as far as you are concerned, you have already cleared yourself. It remains that I myself should give satisfaction. But what can I possibly write to you? Shall I exhort you to continue to love letters, in which you are most eminent? Shall I advise you to devote yourself to virtue and good morals, in which you have made such progress that it is difficult to know to which part of philosophy you have applied the greater effort: the one containing the **speculative and the instruments** <margin>The division of philosophy.</margin> <note>Meaning logic and theoretical study.</note>, or the one which embraces **dogmatic and parænetic** <note>Meaning moral instruction and practical advice.</note> matters? Altogether, it is a supreme thing, greater than human capacity, which you owe either to your own genius or certainly to your Maker, having attained at such a tender age what would be most impudent to even hope for in extreme old age. These things are not yours, Pico; they belong to nature, they belong to God—though if anything is yours, these are yours most of all. See how much less your nobility, fortune, health, and beauty can be called "yours," though in these goods you yield to no one, just as you do not yield in those things which are more truly yours. I exhort you to turn yourself here; ponder this day and night: **how great a debt you owe** to Him who has enriched you to such an extent that you will never be capable of either paying it back or blotting it out. Think how much He can do, who willed that you should be capable of these things; how much you are loved by Him, who chose you for Himself out of so many thousands: you who, almost a boy, surpassed old men, and who, not yet a young man, turned the circles of learned men into admiration of your learning. Unless you see this, unless you value it, I affirm to you right now, and I proclaim with a free voice: **you are not as much as you are.** <note>A rhetorical way of saying Pico is even greater than he realizes, or that his potential is infinite.</note> What I promised myself about you long ago, and continue to promise, is immense and infinite: but neither speech nor proclamation can reach this **preconceived opinion**. I act as people usually do: the more they admire someone and wish to explain what they feel, the less they achieve what they desire; though they conceive something great in their mind, words fail them, and they seem to be struggling rather than speaking. Therefore, do not listen to these things which I now write and put forth, but rather understand those things which I speak about you, alone and silent, within myself—which are as much greater than this speech as thought is greater than words. Greet Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino.</note> and your friend Salviati. There is no need to labor over Poliziano <note>Angelo Poliziano.</note>, who (as I hear) will be with me shortly; nothing more pleasant could have happened to me in this whole embassy. I am so glad that a library is being built there every day, larger and more ornate, that nothing could be more so. Letters owe much to the Florentines, and among the Florentines to the Medici, and among the Medici to **Lorenzo**, who fosters this ancestral glory of his family with no less care than the Republic, which he has the right of governing and establishing. Farewell. Milan. The Kalends of January, 1487.

P.S. **Redemption.** That is, excuse. **Common.** <margin>A common soldier.</margin> That is, vulgar, as if "from the herd" <note>original: "ex grege"</note>, and therefore not very reliable, just as we call soldiers "common" when they are not chosen, but come from everywhere.

## Hermolaus Barbarus to Roberto Salviati, Health and Greetings. Letter 38.

[Large initial E] You are mistaken, Salviati, if you suspected anything other than my busy schedule as the reason why I have not yet replied to you. Especially in that work, than which nothing is more subtle, more forceful, or more acute. Concerning which...

They worshipped Truth as the daughter of Saturn; this is because Saturn represents Time, and Truth is discovered through Time. <margin>Truth the daughter of Saturn.</margin> This was the reason why, whereas one sacrifices to almost all other gods with the head covered, one performed divine rites to Saturn with the head uncovered. For Truth cannot be hidden or obscured. The authority for this is Plutarch in his *Roman Questions* <note>original: "in problematibus." Plutarch's *Quaestiones Romanae* (Roman Questions) explains various Roman customs, including why Saturn was worshipped with an uncovered head (capite aperto)</note>. The philosopher Peregrinus <note>Peregrinus Proteus (c. 95–165 AD), a Cynic philosopher who famously immolated himself at the Olympic Games</note>, who was later nicknamed Proteus, used to say (according to Aulus Gellius in chapter 11 of his twelfth book): "If men knew that nothing at all can be hidden for long, they would sin more quietly and prudently." For this reason, he said the words of Sophocles, the wisest of poets, should be kept on the lips. They have been rendered into Latin thus: "Nothing is secret; for the day, seeing all things and hearing all things, will reveal everything." <note>original: "Nihil occulte: quoniam cuncta tuens et cuncta audiens omnia revelabit dies." This is a Latin translation of a Greek fragment attributed to Sophocles, emphasizing the omniscience of Time.</note> Plato, in the second book of his *Republic*, records that it is not easy for a wicked man to remain hidden forever. Among the Fables of Aesop, we read that famous story: A certain man, carrying a large sum of money and fearing bandits, did not dare to cross through a forest. He asked the king for a guide. The king chose the butler <note>original: "pincernam," referring to a cup-bearer or high-ranking household official</note> whom he considered his most faithful servant...

<margin>Precarium</margin>

That which is momentary is called *precarium*, as in "borrowed beauty" <note>original: "precaria forma."</note>. They are named from *juniores* <note>The Latin word for "younger."</note>, from which comes the comparative form "younger" (*junior*): because they are younger than the youths. Lemonade in a drinking vessel <margin>Lemon-water.</margin>. I would think that *lymoniaca* is the same as what is called "Limonade" by the Spanish. For lemons <margin>A drinking vessel.</margin> are a sharper kind of fruit, almost similar to "golden apples" <note>original: "aureis malis." In classical and Renaissance Latin, this could refer to citrons or oranges.</note>, from which they squeeze a juice, which is called *lymonate* by them. *Capidas*, that is, platters. Swimming olives <margin>Swimming olives.</margin>. These olives are gathered while green and placed into a vessel full of water, in which, along with the water, are laurel leaves, salt, and a little vinegar. From all these, an excellent broth is made, which is poured with the olives into a dish; and it pleases the palate in no ordinary way. On the other hand, if any of you have come here completely unrefined <note>original: *rudes*. In this context, it refers to students who have not yet been "shaped" or biased by other philosophical schools.</note>, you should not despair for that reason; rather, you should rejoice that it has fallen to you to learn the foundations <note>original: *incunabula*, literally "swaddling clothes" or "cradle," referring to the very beginnings of a subject.</note> of philosophy directly from Aristotle himself, and to immediately enter upon that path which only his most famous and purest followers knew.

Otherwise, those who think this entrance is open to no one who has never entered those [scholastic] schools of philosophy are in great error. For neither Marcus Varro, nor Brutus, nor Plantius, nor Calcidius, nor Boethius <note>Barbaro lists major Roman intellectuals and translators who lived before the rise of the medieval university system to prove one can be a master of philosophy without "modern" schooling.</note> ever entered such schools; nor did Alexander <note>Likely Alexander of Aphrodisias, the most famous ancient commentator on Aristotle.</note>, nor Themistius, nor Porphyry, nor Iamblichus, nor Simplicius—who were nonetheless most eminent philosophers and the most devoted interpreters of Aristotle. But I return to where I left off: I believe I can promise you two things. One, that I will interpret for you within a three-year period, or...

**Book 12 of the Letters, Folio 120**

...they desire to have those things which are absent. For example, a priest of the lowest rank can wish for the highest office of the papacy <note>original: *summum pontificatum*</note>; and yet, if he is of sound mind, he neither devises a plan for it (for he does not occupy himself with such thoughts) nor does he truly crave it. # **Of Illustrious Men**

If you had immediately agreed to everyone’s wishes, it would have been judged as either a father's love for his son or a matter of ambition. It seemed to you insufficient for the Emperor <note>original: *Cæsarem*</note> to excel over others, unless you had also excelled over yourself. Indeed, you who are most merciful, humane, and easy-going toward others—and I speak this not from hearsay but from experience—have chosen to be somewhat less than fair and even a bit harsh toward yourself. There was nothing in your flight from pleasure and your self-restraint (virtues which no one before you has commended more than you do by your example) that would matter, unless you had also restrained and suppressed that paternal affection, than which nothing in a powerful man is more constant, and nothing more lawful. For it was not within the Emperor's power to desire that his own children—who are themselves "Caesars" from the moment they are born—should immediately be kings, since it is no more honorable to be called a king than to be the son of the Emperor. Now, a father's indulgence toward his sons is usually popular and even applauded; it is certainly not an object of envy or reproach. In an Emperor, it has always been commendable; in your case, it is even sought after as if it were a debt. It no longer bears the name of "indulgence," but of justice and equity.

For who is more famous than your son <note>Maximilian I, son of Frederick III</note>, whether in war or in peace? Whom have adverse circumstances exercised more thoroughly? Who has been less puffed up by prosperity and success? Who is more constant in either fortune! Who is more persistent in labor! Who is more diligent and prepared in times of relaxation! I pass over his military virtues, which, though they are excellent and distinguished in him, are not for all times or all places. Let us touch upon the arts of peace, which are of use always and everywhere: wisdom, temperance, placability, innocence, religion, and frugality. These are seen to be so noble and eminent in this one young man that it seems impossible to desire anything greater even in an elderly commander. They would be utterly incredible, were it not that we remember he comes from the most celebrated Austrian lineage <note>original: *Austria gente*</note> and is your son. Since these things are so, immortal thanks are given to you by every province and town, and shall always be given, O most learned Emperor, because for the sake of the common good you allowed your shame and modesty to be overcome. Therefore, you have conquered yourself twice, most invincible Emperor <note>original: *Cæsar invictissime*</note>. First, when you turned away from and prayed against the kingdom offered to your son, showing no pretense, and you surpassed the natural piety of a father for his sons with a virtue more than heroic—indeed, with a certain divine greatness of mind and soul. Second, when the consideration of public utility overcame this very virtue by which you had just conquered yourself, and obtained from the Emperor what could not have been obtained from the father.

But the Emperor has just signaled to me: Maximilian, most noble August Prince, he suggests that I should turn my speech from him to you. I shall obey gladly and joyfully, both because a father listens to your praises with a more tranquil mind than his own, and because in this way I shall better and more abundantly satisfy the command of the Senate and the desire of the Republic. Therefore, the name of your Majesty has always been so celebrated among us that it has impelled us not only to be inclined to love and cherish you, but also to worship and observe you. It is a very ancient and sacred custom of our republic to hate destructive and wicked tyrants to the death, but not only to favor good and brave Princes, but also to obey them, and to help, protect, and defend their dignity and greatness by every means. Furthermore, in our age, there is no one among the number of kings and princes whom we judge can be compared or even ranked with you; you are altogether such a person, and so great among us, that it would be a shame to wish for, devise, or desire more or greater qualities than those you display. Thus, no one should wonder if we can in no way represent in speech the immortal happiness, the incredible joy, and the incomparable pleasure we conceived when you were declared King of the Romans <note>The title given to the heir-apparent of the Holy Roman Empire</note>. All the imperial virtues shine and stand out in you alone, even as a young man—a wonder to say: justice, liberality, greatness of soul, clemency, placability, and abstinence from all pleasures. To embrace many things in a single word: as much as we see you are of an immature age <margin>Charles of Burgundy <note>Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy (1433–1477)</note></margin>, we recognize you are of a mature command. Charles, King of the Belgians <note>original: *Carolus Rex Belgarum*; referring to Charles the Bold's dominion over the Low Countries</note>, a most experienced leader in war and a man of the sharpest intellect, foresaw this depth of character. He was so inflamed by it that he seemed to hold nothing more important than that he might betroth his only daughter <note>Mary of Burgundy</note>—a maiden of great hope, a most select woman, the future heir of many races and nations, and one whom many kings sought, observed, and courted—to you alone, when you were almost a boy, neither seeking a wife nor asking for one. Wherefore, in the twentieth year of his age, that prince whose <margin>His slaughter <note>Charles the Bold was killed at the Battle of Nancy in 1477</note></margin> son-in-law you were soon to become, was cut off by the Leuci <note>The people of Toul/Lorraine</note> and the Helvetians <note>The Swiss</note>...

<meta>This page continues a laudatory address to Maximilian I, shifting from a discussion of his father Frederick III's restraint to Maximilian's own merits as a military leader and a philosopher-king.
