# **Book 12 of Letters, Folio 121**

Indeed, leaders are not understood to be illustrious simply because things go well for them in war or peace, but because it has been their lot to shine through labors, through hardships, and through inconveniences. For while favorable circumstances make a man happy, adverse ones certainly make him great. There are those who claim that Alexander the Great of Macedon was a less remarkable military leader because he never experienced a battle that did not go his way; for, in the very height of his successes, he departed this life before he could experience a turn of fortune. 

But in your case—you whom the fixed decrees of the stars had destined for your father’s scepter and throne—is it any wonder if some have worked to ensure that more somber times befell you? This was so that your virtue would not languish in idleness, nor would you seem to have been unworthy of the empire simply because you were destined to be Emperor. And so, spending nine continuous years in the camps, you brought five very difficult wars to a conclusion: the **Gallic** (or Frankish), the **Eburonian** <note>original: *Eburonicum*; referring to the region of Liège</note>, the **Sicambrian** <note>original: *Sicambricum*; referring to the Gelderland region</note>, the **Batavian** <note>original: *Batauicum*; referring to Holland</note>, and the **Morinian** <note>original: *Morinicum*; referring to Flanders and Artois</note>. Regarding this last one, it is not easy to judge for which thing you earned more glory: that you received back your son <note>Philip the Handsome</note> who had been taken and torn from you for so long, or that you compelled the most noble races, peoples most skilled in warfare, and the wealthiest cities to surrender and repentance. This is something that neither your father-in-law **Charles** <note>Charles the Bold, Duke of Burgundy</note> nor his father **Philip** <note>Philip the Good</note>—both excellent leaders, the latter in wisdom and the former in war—are remembered as being able to achieve. 

I am not contemplating a formal Panegyric <note>a speech of high praise</note>, most illustrious King; I do not labor over flowery phrasing; I amplify nothing, and I diminish nothing. Instead, I run through the main points and touch upon the bare summaries of your deeds. Yet everyone marvels at these things; they marvel even at what is stated without embellishment or thrown out casually. They would marvel more if they could look into you more closely and behold those virtues by whose protection you have achieved so many distinguished victories and so many honors of war. 

That countenance of yours would seem so honorable, so eloquent; that appearance as if drawn from heaven; that strength of your arms and chest; that vigor of your whole body; that imperial fire in your eyes. Furthermore, consider how fierce you are in battle, yet mild in the company of your men; lavish toward others, but frugal toward yourself; in the camp, distinguished neither by your clothing nor your table. Winters are spent with the rest of the soldiers under skins <note>tents</note>; summers are sweated through equally. Your feasts are content with modest and soldierly food. Now, who could choose a site for a camp more skillfully than you? Who could secure provisions more quickly, mock the enemy, choose the time for battle, draw up the line of march, or surround cities with a siege? 

Nor do you merely fulfill the roles of a general and an excellent leader while failing to fulfill those of a soldier. No soldierly task is too lowly for you: whether standing before the standards, keeping watch by chance, carrying the rampart <note>original: *vallum*; a defensive stake</note>, or going out to scout. You are the first to enter battle and the last to leave; equally skilled in both the work [Marginal note: Equally.] of a soldier and the counsel of a leader. Neither your princely fortune nor the majesty of your empire excuses you from any duty. You spare yourself nothing; you flatter yourself in nothing. Most indulgent toward others, you are hardly cheerful toward yourself; in all ways, you have nothing more than a common soldier, except that you labor more. 

You have judged it to be as it truly is: that your reign is not so much an honor as a burden. You believe it is the duty of an Emperor to turn his wealth and greatness not toward private [Marginal note: † anyone's] ambition, but toward the safety and benefit of the state; in short, he should not make the empire subject to himself, but himself subject to the empire. 

But other things are also said to be peculiar to you: that you indeed love all people, but you especially love your friends—not those offered to you or encountered everywhere at the gym, the ball-court, or the dice-table, but those whom you have tested often for their innocence, patience, restraint, and for their endurance of cold, heat, and military labors. For those who follow you are not all friends (otherwise they would be as numerous as the "flies in the kitchen" mentioned by **Plutarch**, who flock together at the scent of food and then depart); rather, those whom you have judged worthy of friendship are those you ought to seek out yourself. And so, with those who have at some point recommended themselves to you by their virtue, delighted you with their company, or earned your gratitude by their usefulness, you descend into all the duties of familiarity and forget you are Caesar <note>the Emperor</note> so that you may act as a friend. 

Nor would I place it last among your praises that you love letters and genius (as I hear) so intensely; that you do not merely cherish the liberal arts, but you nourish and promote them. This too is an imperial glory, since this brilliance and light of learning shines in no one more than in kings. From this comes that saying of **Plato** (interpreting **Homer**): that the "disciples of the gods" are none other than kings. Moreover, the precepts of wisdom are most useful because they do not only benefit those who possess them, but they overflow (I might even say more so) onto others. Who is ignorant that **Anaxagoras** instructed many through **Pericles**, or **Plato** through **Dion**? **Cato** would not have sailed from the army to Rhodes to hear **Athenodorus**, nor would **Scipio** have desired to see **Panaetius**, unless they had judged there to be so much ornament or fruit in that pursuit.

Furthermore, being wise and conscious of many things, nothing escapes me: how religiously, innocently, and holily you spend your blossoming youth is clear to everyone. There is not, nor has there ever been, a son more obedient to his father. I know how noble and magnificent all your thoughts are. I am not ignorant of the vows you conceived long ago, worthy of a Christian prince, worthy of your ancestors, worthy of Caesar, and worthy of yourself. 

These virtues of yours, O unique Emperor, are the reason why the **Belgians**—the most warlike part of the land of Gaul—not only do not disdain you as their leader, despite being a foreigner and a German (peoples toward whom they are otherwise so hostile, as they are neighbors separated by language, climate, and customs), but they seek you out as a native, revere you as a prince, and love you as a parent. These are your immense merits, on account of which your father **Frederick**—a most innocent and grave Emperor—could be led and persuaded to allow you to be declared **King of the Romans** <note>the title for the successor to the Holy Roman Emperor</note> during his own lifetime. And indeed he was deferring...
Q.

**Illustrious Men**

He hesitated at first, so that he might maintain his modesty and restraint—as we have said before—free from every stain of suspicion; at the same time, he wished to discover whether those who had worked so strenuously on behalf of the son were merely agreeing with the father, or whether they truly desired to look out for his own safety. But it immediately became clear that those acclamations and prayers had not been the voices of flatterers, but of those truly devoted to him. <margin>Flattery</margin> For flattery, once it is rejected, is immediately broken and withers away. <margin>Devotion</margin> Devotion, the more it is restrained, the more it spreads and blazes forth.

...ca, or near Attica: but I sing of things known. *Little Sirens.* <note>original: *Sirenulæ*</note> A charmingly said phrase; for the diminutive word carries some kind of pleasant flattery. Moreover, the sirens are most seductive; their song is extremely alluring in Homer, as we can recognize from this first line found in Cicero: "O glory of the Greeks, why do you not turn your ship, Ulysses?" <note>original: *O decus argolicum quin puppem flectis Ulysse*; a Latin translation of a line from Homer’s *Odyssey*</note> By these sirens, our Jerome <note>Saint Jerome, the 4th-century scholar</note> and Angelo Poliziano <note>1454–1494; a leading scholar of the Italian Renaissance</note> seem to understand in this passage the allurements of pleasures; Horace, however, even understands them as laziness, saying: "One must avoid that wicked siren, Laziness." <note>original: *Vitanda est improba siren Desidia*</note> *Be happy* <note>original: εὐτύχει (*eutychei*)</note>, that is, "be fortunate" or "fare well." *Leader of the Muses* <note>original: μουσηγέται (*mousagetai*)</note>; Apollo is addressed by this title in the works of Macrobius <note>a 5th-century Roman writer and grammarian</note>.

# **Plato’s Charmides.**

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Josse Bade, or Ascensius, was a renowned humanist printer and commentator who often added explanatory notes to classical editions.</note>

"I have indeed come," etc. If anyone desires to see this little work of Plato regarding temperance <note>The *Charmides* is a Socratic dialogue traditionally centered on the definition of *sophrosyne*, often translated as temperance or self-control</note> in its entirety, let them consult the works of Plato as translated by Marsilio Ficino <note>Ficino was the primary translator of Plato's works into Latin in the 15th century, making them accessible to the Renaissance world</note>. "I indeed" <note>original: *Equidem*</note>: that is, I for my part, because the others were already in Athens. "The day before yesterday" <note>original: *Nudiustertius*; an idiom literally meaning "now is the third day"</note>: that is, it is now the third day; therefore, it preceded yesterday. Marsilio did not translate this quite right. "From Potidaea": Marsilio removed the preposition; there was no need for it since it is the proper name of a place. However, there are two such places: one in Thrace; the other, of which I believe he speaks here, is in Macedonia and is called Cassandrea, which Demosthenes <note>The famous Athenian orator</note> often mentions. Indeed, Socrates did not only exercise his mind in philosophy, but also his body in war. For he also took up Xenophon <note>The historian and soldier, a student of Socrates</note> after he was thrown from his horse in a battle near Delos, looking after him and returning him to safety. He was also victorious in a naval battle while others were fleeing, and he secured the victory for Alcibiades <note>A prominent Athenian statesman and general</note>. I say this so that no one wonders why such a philosopher is introduced as having recently returned from war. For it would not be fitting to fashion dialogues that are not plausible, which this would be if Socrates had devoted himself solely to ethics. Immediately, everyone from a distance and from elsewhere...

He also critiques Marsilio Ficino's Latin translation regarding specific grammatical and prepositional choices.</summary>

# **Plato’s Charmides. Folio 124.**

...the youngest <note>original: *minimus*; referring to the younger boys in the wrestling school who were following Charmides</note>: but they all gazed at him as if at a statue of a god. Then Chaerephon, calling out to me, said: "What do you think of this youth, Socrates? Is he not of a handsome countenance?" "Beyond measure," I replied. "Yet," he said, "if he should wish to strip <note>original: *exuere*; in Ancient Greece, athletes exercised and wrestled naked, and Chaerephon suggests that Charmides’ body is even more beautiful than his face</note> now, he would surely seem to you to have even a deformed face, so entirely beautiful is he in every other part of his body." And with these very words which were spoken by Chaerephon, the others also agreed. 

And I said, "O Hercules! What an unconquerable excellence <note>original: *virtutem*; here used to describe the overwhelming power of Charmides' physical beauty</note> you describe to me, if only one thing might be added to these." "What is that?" asked Critias. "If he has a soul not unsuited for virtue. Surely, O Critias, it is right for him to be of such a kind, since he draws his origin from your family." "But indeed," he said, "in this very respect he is as excellent as he is beautiful." "Why then," I said, "do we not first strip <note>Socrates uses the metaphor of "stripping" to move the conversation from physical beauty to the character of the soul</note> this very part of him? Even before we contemplate the appearance of his body...

# **Plato’s Charmides. Folio 125.**

## **The Examination of the Soul**

"Indeed," said Critias, "you speak quite rightly. For he is a lover of wisdom <note>original: *philosophiae amator*; the literal meaning of 'philosopher.' Socrates is testing if Charmides' inner life matches his outer grace</note> and, as it seems to others as well as to himself, he is a very fine poet."

"This excellence, my dear Critias," I replied, "is an ancient inheritance in your house, derived from your kinship with Solon <note>Solon (c. 630–560 BCE) was a famous Athenian lawmaker and poet; his presence in the family tree suggests a natural talent for both politics and literature</note>. But why do you not call the youth here and present him to me? For even if he were younger than he is, there would be no shame in his speaking with us in your presence, since you are his guardian as well as his cousin."

"You speak well," he said, "and we shall call him." 

Turning then to an attendant, Critias said: "Boy, call Charmides, and tell him that I wish to introduce him to a physician <note>original: *medicum*; Critias uses Socrates' supposed medical knowledge as a pretext to lure the shy youth into the conversation</note> who says he possesses a remedy for that heaviness in the head <note>original: *gravitate capitis*; likely a recurring headache or migraine Charmides had been complaining about</note> of which he recently spoke."

<column-break/>

Then Critias turned back to me and explained: "He has been complaining lately of a dull weight in his head when he rises in the morning. It is a fine excuse to bring him over."

"Only let him come," I said, "and I promise to provide the remedy."

And so he came. It was a sight to behold, for as he approached, the rest of us who were already seated were forced to move aside. Each man pushed his neighbor so that he might make a space for the boy to sit next to him, until those who were sitting at the ends of the bench were forced to stand up, and one was even pushed off sideways <note>This humorous detail illustrates the celebrity-like status of beautiful youths in the Athenian wrestling schools (palaestrae)</note>. 

But he came and sat down between me and Critias. At that moment, I must confess, I began to feel a great confusion <note>original: *perturbatio*; Socrates often admits to being physically overwhelmed by beauty, though he uses this as a starting point for philosophical inquiry</note>. The confidence I had felt only a moment before—thinking I could easily converse with him—vanished entirely. And when Critias told him that I was the man who knew the cure, he looked me directly in the eyes with an expression I cannot describe, as if he were about to ask a question. 

At that moment, everyone in the wrestling school began to circle around us. I caught a glimpse inside his cloak <note>original: *intra vestem*; a moment of physical intimacy that Socrates describes as a "fire" or a "stinging" sensation, shifting the tone from casual banter to intense focus</note>, and I was overcome. I felt as though I were a lion who had been mastered by its prey...

<meta>While the previous page featured a translation of Plato’s "Charmides," this page transitions to a Latin preface (Præfatio) for a different scholarly or humanist work. The text shifts from a philosophical dialogue to a defense of a new literary style and a critique of the "crimes" committed by contemporary editors and writers. # **Preface. Folio 125.**

The law of this new work is such that it should have nothing uniform: nowhere should it be equal to itself: let it always limp with dissimilarity: let it maintain this one rule: that nothing is done by the rule, nothing by the plumb line, nor recalled to the level <note>The author is arguing for a varied, organic style rather than a rigid, perfectly "square" or academic one</note>. If a freer style is judged to be of an insolent nature: perhaps a kinder interpreter will attribute it instead to a simplicity that does not disgrace a well-born man. Furthermore, wherever custom <margin>Custom.</margin> fights back: then truth—which does not deal in trifles—or custom’s deputy, a better custom, will offer patronage. For that which is received against authority is also said to be taken up by custom: and the error of custom is often cast as a reproach by the learned. Then, as a certain man beautifully said: Custom without truth is the antiquity of error <note>A famous maxim attributed to St. Cyprian of Carthage, often used by reformers and humanists to challenge long-standing but incorrect traditions</note>. Finally, if we have occasionally sprinkled in a few thorny and anxious points—or more truly, "sub-acidic" ones—either from philosophy (whose smoke we candidates have long breathed) or from that circle of disciplines which serve the study of wisdom: nonetheless, these will perhaps refresh and sharpen the reader’s stomach, which might otherwise grow faint from too many sweets.

For so that all these things might harmonize by their very variety, and be joined together like opposing figures, we have run (as the saying goes) almost from the lime-kiln into the coal-pit <margin>Proverb.</margin> <note>original: *de calcaria in carbonariam*; a Latin proverb similar to "out of the frying pan into the fire," though here used to mean moving rapidly from one extreme topic to another</note>: and we have taken pains that opposites should follow one after another in turn, which might exempt us from complaints of that sort. Indeed, we do not allow ourselves to lack those things which are more pleasant and delightful—I might even say alluring—rather than merely useful or necessary: since it is (as Varro says) one thing to satisfy a man, another to satisfy humanity <margin>Man and Humanity.</margin> <note>Marcus Terentius Varro was an ancient Roman scholar; the quote suggests that while a "man" has basic needs, "humanity" or "culture" requires beauty and refinement</note>, even beyond any practical gain. Meanwhile, beautiful things are sought after, by Hercules, no less than a profit without beauty. Therefore, just as some unpolished and raw parts of this work—roughly hewn rather than finely planed, having felt neither the file, nor the plane, nor the scraper—will delight those rustic and "shaggy" readers: so, on the other hand, a style that is occasionally intricate and variegated with multi-colored mosaics will capture those more delicate readers, the smooth and polished ones. Thus, I may not be raised to the heavens by a unified shout of praise, nor cast down to the ground by a hiss, by voices coming from both sides. But for those in the middle, who should be marked by neither extreme, a certain *Cinnus* <note>original: *Cinnus*; a Roman term for a mixed drink or a "medley," used here to describe a balanced, varied style</note> of diverse elements (as Cicero says) will satisfy: not excelling in any one thing, yet participating in all. 

For the same taste is not in all men, but each has his own palate. Then I believe some will even spit out at a banquet, as if it were distasteful and meager, that which they would soon greedily lick up in the kitchen as sweet and rich. We have prepared these things certainly not for the marketplace or the senate-house, but for the bedroom and the school: and for that reason we have striven—I know not if we have succeeded—that if anything were here, it should be entirely easy and of a simple elegance; not laborious and painted allurements; true and natural color and luster, not a summoned look from a cosmetic box, but a fitting and ready habit, not burdensome or tattered. Finally, in whatever manner these things go forth <margin>In whatever manner.</margin>, in whatever way they are received: we certainly do not refuse, nor do I think we shall escape, that common lot of writers: to be ill-spoken of, provided it is to the readers' liking. On the contrary, we expose our head to this roll of the dice, nor do we seek patronage, which we have voluntarily stripped from ourselves by our own judgment. Let judgment be passed against us; let us be traduced and harassed, rather than let there be a public fraud against literature—the honor of which is more ancient to us than our own interests—even at the cost of some of our reputation or leisure. For why, I ask, is this profession of shared studies, if it has come to this: that the duty we owe to the university of studies should be allowed to cease entirely because of a base suspicion? In what way can the integrity of honorable letters last or even exist now, if judgment is entirely loosened, while we all equally dread ill-will? <margin>Ill-will.</margin> As for me, I wish that my labor were owed envy rather than contempt. For that is almost my prayer: if indeed, as Livy says, Envy seeks the heights like fire. 

But come now, best cultivators of studies: let each be eager for his part; pull up this invincible grass by which the good fruits of humanity are choked; and as for the deadly ivy creeping up the sacred stems and sucking all their juice with its wandering glides, break it off entirely and cut it down. There is no lack of those who alter the truth; let there not be a lack of those who restore it as well. Let some champion, I pray, and patron of the endangered disciplines arise. For I, as one of the crowd, will certainly try what is permitted to me. Whether I shall achieve anything worthwhile, I shall see later. Yet wherever it flows, or however the matter falls out, I shall take it in good part. I will not only swallow the poison of all malice and detraction, but (such is my stomach) I will even digest it, certain that this is the very "genius" of truth: that as soon as it appears in public, it is hateful and an enemy to the common crowd. Therefore, others may blink if they wish and mutter the truth in silence <margin>"Mussent" [to mutter] means they dare not mutter openly. From Persius.</margin>; I alone (whatever it shall be) will certainly not hide my judgment, I will not suppress what I feel: I will no longer indulge such things with patience, but will whisper at least semi-freely to this little book of mine. 

I have seen, I have seen with my own eyes, little book, and I see daily, many capital crimes committed in literature: someone else's work stealthily compiled, things made up according to whim, and whatever is convenient being ascribed even to suitable authors who would not recognize them; authors being cited who do not exist; works being quoted as ancient when the manuscripts appear nowhere; all books being filled with the most laborious vanities; false things substituted for true ones, adopted things for native ones, and novelties for the vernacular; everything being substituted, polluted, adulterated, smeared, encrusted, distorted, confounded, thrown headlong, and diverted, with no faith, no shame, and no judgment—and what is more pestilential than all these, by the opportunity of recent art...

This page shifts to a defense of his scholarly method, his reliance on primary sources (including those provided by Lorenzo de' Medici), and a preemptive strike against the critics—both pedantic grammarians and "rusticated" theologians—who might attack his work.</meta>

[Centered Title]
**Miscellanies**

[Main Text]
...of the papacy: how any of the most foolish opinions are propagated in an instant through a thousand volumes of descendants. Finally (to say it once and for all), even now many still have the ears of an ass. <note>A reference to the myth of King Midas, used here to describe those who lack the refinement to judge good literature or art.</note> Here someone might say: "But what about you?" I certainly admit that I can be mistaken, as I am human. But I certainly deceive no one knowingly; and though I might perhaps say a falsehood, I certainly do not lie. <margin>To tell a lie and to be a liar, from Augustine.</margin> As the character Mevius says, "Then I forgive myself." <note>Mevius was a famously bad poet; Poliziano is using him ironically to show he is his own harshest critic.</note> On the contrary (joking aside), I do not even forgive myself; and if I bring forth anything too unlearned or careless, I desire to be refuted by anyone, being refuted by my own self once I have been warned. For I do not love myself so perversely that I would prefer others to wander in error rather than let it be known that I have erred. But I am among the number of those who write by making progress, and make progress by writing. 

As for that matter, let fate see to it. This much is very true: if I had kept these commentaries at home and in my hands for a longer time, and if it had been permitted to taste them again after an interval, they would have come forth far better instructed, richer, and more supported. Clearly, this is that particular kind of study which grows through late-night vigils; just as a river gains from its downward course, so this study grows little by little from reading, becoming more abundant. Even now, much remains unarranged, unrefined, undiscussed, not rounded, and not yet turned on the lathe; <note>Poliziano uses metaphors of woodworking and pottery to describe his editing process.</note> but these things have essentially bypassed the ear, since they were thought out in a restricted way and from the moment, rather than with the care that almost excessively looks after the business of the pen and polishes the elocution—a care that white-haired truth and faith especially demand. 

Indeed, lest idle men think that we have drawn these things, whatever they are, from the dregs, or that we have overstepped the boundaries of the grammarians, we have immediately followed Pliny’s example and bypassed the names of authors—except for those who are honorable and ancient. It is from them that these things take their authority, and from whom we have "borrowed." <margin>Whatever: that is, of whatever sort.</margin> <margin>We have borrowed: we have taken on loan.</margin> Nor have we used those whom others have only cited while their own works have perished over time; rather, we have used those whose treasures we ourselves have handled, whose "smoke" we have traveled through in literature. <note>Poliziano insists on reading primary sources rather than relying on medieval summaries.</note> Furthermore, the antiquity of manuscripts, the reliability of coins, and antiquities carved in bronze or marble—which you, Lorenzo, supplied to us—support our commentaries greatly, beyond even the variety of books. <margin>In bronze or marble: Valla listens.</margin> <note>A nod to Lorenzo de' Medici's vast collection of artifacts and a reference to the scholar Lorenzo Valla.</note> 

However, so that we might teach by example that the tricks of charlatans <margin>Impostures: deceptions.</margin> and all impostures must be removed, and that the wantonness of certain people must be restrained—which now creeps widely like a cancer <margin>Cancer: a disease.</margin> through the empty and licensed departing from what is prescribed—we have never cited a testimony of ancient writing unless we could represent it in its own form. We did this so that nothing substitute or superimposed might prevail, and we have applied those marks from which the authority can be sought out deeply, right from the root. 

And so that no appendices to this duty of ours should be lacking, we have organized the chapters of things—enclosed in very brief titles, but in which the utility is greater than their number—into "centuries" (groups of one hundred). <note>Poliziano organized his *Miscellanea* into one hundred distinct philological essays.</note> Like a calculator, we have collected huge sums as if on brief wax tablets, so that we might personally sign off on the negligence of the fastidious reader. Therefore, just as the Homeric Teucer hid under the shield of Ajax, so we, lurking under the shadow of your name, will make an attack <margin>Attack: an assault in the military fashion.</margin> upon the barbarians in groups of a hundred. Thus, by this edition, the whim of both the fair and the unfair will be satisfied. In a sort of turnabout, just as we provide the former with something to kiss, we shall provide the latter with plenty to bite. 

But I think certain rabid men will bite our work—men whom Cato elegantly calls "vignette-scrapers" <note>Original: *vitiligatores*. These are critics who find small faults in others to distract from their own lack of talent.</note>—suffering from that vice of litigiousness as if from a disease; a brainy and irritable race who, without cause, without discrimination, and with (as they say) eyes closed, bark at whatever name they see. <margin>Pliny in his preface: There will be many who find fault (vitiligant), that is, who bind themselves to a fault or disparage.</margin> Or there are those who, by mercenary advocacy and a venal opinion, once they have hired themselves out and been enslaved to someone, as if they were a piece of property given over, resolve to protect that person tenaciously and pugnaciously, whether by right or by wrong. <margin>Whether by right or by wrong: regarding things from above and below.</margin> Or there are those little boasters and peddlers of trifles, full of swollen but foolish conjecture, who love only themselves and their own works without rivals; they favor themselves and disparage others. Or finally, there are those shunners of the light of truth—or to speak more plainly, "cockroach-men"—literary types who, with leaking and truly nocturnal eyes, cannot bear even a clear day, much less a faint shadow. 

For no one doubts those who are eaten by the moth of spite, whom the rust of envy gnaws; those who make the glory of another their own punishment, and another's happiness their own executioner; those who waste away at another's progress, whom malevolence—sickened by the success of others—constantly tortures like an internal executioner. But likewise, the "pulpit censors" <margin>Pulpit-censors: those who lecture.</margin> (though we are not speaking now of the learned and the good) are often accustomed to prod us and clamor against these studies. Full of fasting, they defame the study of the humanities before the ignorant common people with puffed-out cheeks, almost solemnly. Fierce in their thick rusticity <margin>Fierce (feroculi): diminutive of fierce.</margin>—which is the only thing (as Jerome says) they hold as holiness—they rage against these studies and those who study them with bombastic proclamations, gnashing their teeth and foaming. Thus they easily declare that they even disapprove of, and almost hate, those Greeks—truly holy souls such as Basil, Chrysostom, and the Gregorys—and even the Latins: Cyprian, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome himself, and other leaders of our religion of that kind, who were stuffed <margin>Stuffed (suffarcinatos): he did not say this out of dignity.</margin> <note>Meaning they were enriched by pagan learning, which Poliziano compares to the Israelites taking the "spoils of the Egyptians."</note> with the disciplines of all nations and languages as if with the wealth of the Egyptians. 

Because of this, your favorite, Marianus of Genazzano, <margin>Marianus.</margin> <note>A famous Augustinian preacher in Florence and a friend of Poliziano and Lorenzo.</note> seems to me even more admirable; he is second to none in theology, and of all those whom I have heard preaching in the church...

Following his defense against critics, he now shifts to discussing the preparation required for true wisdom, his refusal to cater to the whims of the present age, and his intention to defend his intellectual property from "plagiarists." **Preface. Folio 126.**

...we have heard: not only the most prudent, but also the most eloquent; whose eloquence is not suspicious to people striving for good fruit, since it is commended by an incredible severity of life—nor, on the other hand, is his austerity gloomy or formidable, since he does not despise poetic delights and this beautiful variety of literature, its brilliance, and its charms. Therefore, just as wool, intended to drink the purple dye <note>original: "purpuram bona fide potura"</note> in good faith, is first treated with certain medicinal preparations, so I believe the mind ought to be cultivated by such letters and teachings (as Cicero says in his *Hortensius*) and imbued and prepared to receive wisdom. And yet, it will not be a source of regret to demand from my pen whatever this product of my midnight labors may be, or to test what may be allowed against those who conceive capital frauds in the business of literature. <margin>Imitation of Juvenal.</margin> For I also forgive Philoxenus <note>A Greek poet who famously preferred to return to the stone quarries (prison) rather than praise the bad poetry of the tyrant Dionysius.</note>—just as the same Cicero does when writing to Atticus—for preferring to return to prison rather than to surrender his judgment; especially if it is fitting for writers to serve not the present age, but rather eternity, just as was said by Thucydides. <margin>Monuments.</margin> And for this reason, I think books themselves are called "monuments," <margin>Why they are called books.</margin> because they ought to look more toward the memory of posterity, which will judge more incorruptibly, than toward the foolish favor of the present time. Therefore, so that this wickedness of those who corrupt everything far and wide might not only be extinguished (if it be permitted) but even crushed, and so that such a worn-down and prostituted face—and such hardness of mouth—might not become an example, I now promise the following centuries nothing at all in terms of a taste of this first offering, in favor of the healthy effort I have undertaken. For those whom we now handle with a soft finger, whom we touch with a light and joyful arm, we shall, I think, press and urge more strongly later. Content for a little while in the meantime with a preliminary skirmish and a light-armed battle <note>original: "velitarique pugna" - referring to the *velites*, the light infantry of the Roman army who skirmished before the main battle.</note>, we shall soon, having collected our strength, fight with the full power of the army. Furthermore—since "the tunic is closer than the cloak" <note>A Latin proverb meaning one's own interests or family must come first.</note>—we shall boldly and diligently reclaim our things from plagiarists and petty thieves, and we shall lay a hand of "liberal cause" <note>term: *Liberalis causa* — a legal procedure in Roman law to determine if a person was free or a slave; here used metaphorically to claim ownership of his intellectual work.</note> upon them. For we wish only those things to be accepted as ours which we ourselves, as leaders, push out with great labor and industry; and we will never allow them to be coaxed or extorted from us as long as it is permitted—ours, I say: not discarded scraps, but pledges. For just as we leave these things in the open like missiles to be snatched up and trampled, so we take back and defend those others; these we expose, those we both acknowledge and uphold—yet in such a way that we do not wish to imitate monkeys, who are said to admire their own offspring, however deformed, as if they were the most beautiful. <margin>On the monkeys' [admiration] for their young.</margin> Nor, I think, will these studies of ours, though they are of lighter effort or even playful, be a disgrace to you, Lorenzo de' Medici, to whom they are now ascribed. <margin>Lorenzo.</margin> They are ascribed, however, not so much to prove me grateful for your benefits or to repay a favor, as because they have had you as a helper and even an advisor; and so that they may proceed under good auspices, and that your memory may be frequented in them, from which the book, taking authority, may be commended by the fame of a great name. Then, since the whole sum of my studies is owed to him, that portion will also rightly begin from him. And by Hercules, let these be like the "desserts" <note>term: *bellaria* — sweetmeats or desserts served at the end of a Roman banquet.</note> received at the second course; since those weightier matters occupy the place and appearance of the proper dinner—many of which either Marsilio Ficino, <margin>Ficino.</margin> the interpreter of Plato, or John Argyropoulos of Byzantium, <margin>Argyropoulos.</margin> the interpreter of Aristotle, have gathered for you from the storehouse of philosophy. Concerning that man who is to be admired above all others—not just Pico now, but (as I myself am accustomed to call him) rather a Phoenix <margin>Pico della Mirandola.</margin> <note>The Phoenix was a mythical bird that was unique and reborn from its own ashes; Poliziano uses it to describe the singular genius of Pico della Mirandola.</note> who now nests in your laurel—my expectation is indeed so great that I would dare to sing along with Propertius: "Give way, Roman writers; give way, Greeks!" <note>Poliziano quotes Propertius's famous praise of Virgil's *Aeneid*, applying it here to Pico.</note> Fare you well, most pleasant patron; and (as you are doing) continue to favor the learned; continue to stir up literature; continue to rescue the Latin interest from neglect and the Greek from destruction, so that the memory of your name may be claimed from the injury of total oblivion.

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary by Jodocus Badius Ascensius. While the previous page discussed contemporary humanists like Argyropoulos and Budé, this section shifts to a defense of Marcus Tullius Cicero’s philosophical authority, citing the reverence shown to him by later classical and late-antique authors like Boethius and Macrobius.</meta>

It is established that he flourished with such quickness of talent that he grasped whatever is taught concerning the art of speaking and debating, whatever regarding dimensions and figures <note>A reference to Geometry.</note>, and whatever regarding music and numbers <note>A reference to Arithmetic.</note>, even without great difficulty and with no human person teaching him. He then stood out with such sharpness of disputation that the defense of the whole truth seems, by right, to rest upon this one man especially. Let us therefore consider what these individuals at least thought of Cicero, and how much they credited to him in philosophy; then let us boldly believe that it is not for just anyone to stir up a slander against a man who was so uniquely praised by the most highly regarded men. 

Boethius <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 AD), a Roman senator and philosopher whose works were fundamental to medieval education.</note>, therefore, not only uses the testimonies of Marcus Tullius [Cicero] repeatedly, presenting them as the firmest and most unshakeable arguments, but he is also not ashamed to undertake a commentary—which is the greatest honor—on Cicero's *Topics* <note>original: "Topica"; Cicero's work on the "topoi" or "seats" of logical arguments.</note> itself. 

Macrobius <note>Ambrosius Theodosius Macrobius (fl. c. 400 AD), a Roman provincial and Neoplatonist writer.</note>, moreover, is so engaged with even a tiny portion of one and the same book <margin>Macrobius’s *Dream* <note>original: "Somniū Macrobij"; referring to his famous *Commentary on the Dream of Scipio*, which was originally the final part of Cicero's *On the Republic*.</note></margin> that he does not hesitate to make him equal to Plato, nor to distinguish him with the hallmarks of all branches of knowledge...

...to have called it by that name? Which also Alexander of Aphrodisias <note>A celebrated commentator on Aristotle (active c. 200 AD) often called "the second Aristotle."</note>, the most highly praised of all the Peripatetics <note>The "Peripatetics" were followers of Aristotle's philosophy.</note>, even by Averroes <note>Ibn Rushd (1126–1198), the Andalusian philosopher whose commentaries on Aristotle were foundational to medieval European thought.</note>, showed in those exceptionally subtle books of *Natural Questions*, which Saint Jerome boasts were read by him; and Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 234–305 AD).</note> in the commentary which he published on Aristotle’s *Ten Categories* <note>original: "decem genera"; referring to the *Categories*, a work on the classification of all possible things.</note> through questions and answers; and Themistius <note>A 4th-century statesman and philosopher known for his paraphrases of Aristotle.</note> regarding these, in his second paraphrase *On the Soul* <note>original: "de anima"</note>; and Simplicius <note>One of the last great Neoplatonist philosophers (c. 490–560 AD).</note> where he interprets Aristotle’s volume of similar argument; and Quintilianus Aristides in the third book *On Music*; and finally Saint Ambrose in a certain letter of his (to pass over others for now) have almost unanimously indicated. 

And concerning this matter, there is no doubt in either case, not even in the words of Aristotle himself. Or is he <note>Referring to Cicero.</note> rather blamed for the fact that he neither noted the word <term>Endelecheia</term> <note>original: "Endelechiæ"; a term meaning "continuity" or "constant motion," which Cicero used to describe the soul.</note> with its own letters, and adapted a meaning other than Aristotle intended (as we said above)? In the first place, therefore, I ask of those critics, by what argument especially they gathered that it was written <term>Entelecheia</term> <note>original: "entelechian"; Aristotle's term for "actuality" or "perfection." --- Page 275 ---
<meta>This page continues the defense of Cicero's philosophical terminology, specifically his use of the term "Endelecheia." The author is arguing that Cicero had access to earlier, more accurate versions of Aristotle's texts than later Greek critics realized. This section transitions from a defense of Cicero to a philological investigation into an obscure term for footwear found in the poet Catullus.</meta>

**First Century. Folio CXXX.**

Even denies that the work *On Interpretation* <note>original: "Peri hermenias"; a foundational Aristotelian text on logic and language.</note> belongs to Aristotle, though he published a great abundance of that philosopher’s books, even some from obscure catalogs I know not what. Therefore, there is no reason why we should now doubt the original integrity of that reading, especially given such a small distinction: either suspicion may be free to lean in either direction, or (if one must side with one or the other) it is safer for Cicero to be preferred. He lived long before Alexander <note>Alexander of Aphrodisias, a famous 2nd-century commentator.</note>, who was the first of that group we mentioned—the interpreters of Aristotle. Alexander flourished in the times of the Emperor Severus, and was nearly a contemporary, or perhaps slightly older, than those supreme Academics, Origen and Plotinus. What, then, prevents Cicero himself from being able to see the very source-copy <margin>A source-copy <gloss>compiled</gloss>.</margin> of Aristotle’s books that were published in his own age? Even if it was not entirely uncorrupted, it was certainly (as we said) compiled. Then, I would believe it was done deliberately by a most learned man: so that, protected by the free wall of his own heart, he dared to rightfully apply that interpretation to this new term of Aristotle's. This interpretation agreed with Plato’s sentiment in the *Phaedrus* regarding the eternal motion of the soul, and (as Varro says) its divine nature—something Cicero himself mentions either in the *Tusculan Disputations* or in the sixth volume of the *Republic*. For Philoponus in his *Life of Aristotle*, Simplicius in his commentaries *On the Soul*, and Boethius himself in the last book of *On Interpretation*, all assert that the sentiments of both philosophers are twin and comparable. It is even recorded that Porphyry composed seven books in which this argument was chiefly gathered: that the school of thought <note>original: "haeresin"; here used in the classical sense of a philosophical school rather than a religious crime.</note> of Plato and Aristotle is entirely the same. My friend Pico della Mirandola <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola (1463–1494), a brilliant Renaissance polymath and friend of the author.</note> also treated this in the preface of one of his disputations. He will prove it to be truer than truth itself in a most copious and (I believe) most beautiful work (unless my taste fails me), which he is laboring on and forging night and day regarding this very "concord" between Plato and Aristotle. Thus, it will be understood that our Cicero not only did not err in that term, but understood it somewhat more eruditely than others, or more appropriately for his own school. Thus, the doctrine of a most illustrious man, which such suitable authors as we have shown above have vouched for, he himself has fulfilled most generously and abundantly, even in the very point where he suffers most from slander. Nor is it new or unusual for Cicero to suffer slander from the Greeks, since even Didymus composed six books against him, imitating the "Sillographi" <note>Writers of "Silli," which were satirical or abusive poems.</note>—those foul-mouthed writers—whose books, however, have been rejected by the judgment of learned ears. Thus, against a most noble lion, certain "lamp-lighting" dogs <note>A metaphor for scholars who stay up late only to bark at their betters.</note> often bark with their voices echoing from afar. <margin>Sillographi <note>Greek term for satirical writers.</note></margin>

ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, a famous printer and commentator.</note>: Valerius, etc. Because the arguments are clear from the titles, I will not repeat them, nor those things that seem obvious, except for a few things in a few words. <margin>Deceiver.</margin>
**Deceivers.** <note>original: "Plani"</note> That is, vain impostors of errors, who dared to overturn what they did not understand. It is a Greek word and the first syllable is short, as in "planet," named from wandering. Horace in the first book of *Epistles* says: "Nor once mocked, does he care to pick up the deceiver <note>original: "planum"</note> with a broken leg at the crossroads." **Darkness-dwellers** <note>original: "Tenebrones"</note> and **scoundrels** <note>original: "nebulones"</note> are those shrouded in darkness. **From the pigsty.** <note>original: "Ex hara"</note> That is, from the bed of pigs. **Pastoral.** <note>original: "Poemenicon"</note> **False prophet.** <note>original: "Pseudomantis"</note>

**What the Carpatine sandals in Catullus are, and how a correctly written word is wrongly changed. Chapter II.**

[Woodcut: A hand holding a pair of dividers over a scroll, symbolizing intellectual precision and measurement.]

Valerius Catullus in a certain Epigram speaks thus:
"Yet with that tongue of yours: if the use should come to you,
You could lick backsides and Carpatine sandals." <note>Catullus, Poem 98. A vulgar insult directed at a man named Victius.</note>
It has been asked by many, but explained as yet by no one, what "Carpatine" or "Carbatine" sandals are. <margin>Carpatine / Carbatina / Sandals.</margin> For both are correct: but it is also called "Carbasine." Some deceivers and darkness-dwellers in literature, having erased the old word, substitute I know not what, either "Cercopithecae" <note>Long-tailed monkeys.</note> or "Coprotinae" produced from a pigsty, not a school—naked words, empty names, and voices of nothing. From the Greek tool-chest, as if from a storage cellar, we shall bring forth authorities that are neither despicable nor of doubtful faith. By these, the reading may be restored unharmed and the cloud of interpretation discussed. First, then, Julius Pollux himself, in his ninth book to Caesar Commodus, says that **Carbatinae** are a rustic shoe, so named from the Carians. <margin>Carbatina.</margin> Aristotle, moreover, in the second book of the *History of Animals*, writes that camels are shod with **Carbatinae** so that they do not grow weary on a long march with the army. <margin>Handwritten: camel footwear</margin> There also exist four elegant little Greek books titled *Pastoral* <note>original: "Poemenicon"</note>; in the second of these, a certain old man with a pouch and **Carbatine** shoes is introduced. Lucian, too, in the dialogue titled either *Alexander* or *The False Prophet* <margin>Handwritten: False prophet</margin>, says certain orators from Paphlagonia were shod in **Carbatinae**. Finally, even Xenophon the Socratic in the third book of the *Anabasis* says: "When their old shoes failed, they had **Carbatinae** made from fresh ox-hides." <margin>Handwritten: barbarian footwear</margin> Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedia.</note> also cites this passage, though concealing the author. Indeed, some interpreter of that same Xenophon adds that **Carbatinae** are a barbarian footwear.

ASCENSIUS: **Little horns.** <note>original: "Cornicula"</note> Small horns. Moreover, he says wonderfully that the thing itself was male; for in "Epicenes" <note>Nouns that have only one grammatical gender regardless of the sex of the animal.</note>, where the word used distinguishes the sex, the genus of that thing is usually expressed: as a "pregnant elephant" or "pregnant camel." **A goose having brought forth young.** **Not diluted.** That is, clear. **They crouched on the ground.** That is, they lowered themselves to the ground. **The Ostrich** <note>original: "Struthis"</note> is a well-known bird that digests iron. **Libyan:** usually born or found in Libya; commonly called "Struthio" [Ostrich].

¶ How many things must be read by interpreters of poets; and how Persius fashioned his Satire on Alcibiades [Marginal note: How many things] from Plato. Chapter IIII.

**O**ne who undertakes the interpretation of poets must have worked by night, not only (as the saying goes) by the lamp of Aristophanes <note>Aristophanes of Byzantium was a famous librarian and critic at Alexandria; his "lamp" symbolizes meticulous editing and scholarship.</note> [Marginal note: The Lamp] but also by that of Cleanthes. [Marginal note: Of Cleanthes] <note>Cleanthes was a Stoic philosopher who supposedly worked as a water-carrier by night so he could study philosophy by day.</note> He must look not only toward the schools of the philosophers, but also those of the jurists, the physicians, the logicians, and all those who comprise that circle of learning which we call the "Encyclopedia" <note>original: "Encyclia." He must not (as they say) greet them only from the threshold and the entryway [Marginal note: From the threshold etc.], but rather invite them into his inner chambers and into the most intimate familiarity, if we are eager to help the cause of Latin letters and put to flight the ignorance that grows stronger every day. Otherwise, a half-educated diligence, accompanied by great self-persuasion, is a detriment rather than a benefit. You may find very many things, especially in the works of philosophers, which have been adopted into the books of our poets. For instance, as we were pointing out a few years ago while lecturing publicly on the poet Persius: his fourth Satire <note>The text says "fifth," but describes the fourth.</note>, which begins *You handle the people’s business*, <note>original: "Rem populi tractas." Persius did not merely modestly sample those topics—concerning the just and unjust, and the knowledge of oneself—which Socrates discusses therein with Alcibiades, but he also clearly drew certain passages from it which, if not of great weight, are certainly full of charm and wit. Of this kind is the phrase: *Say this, you ward of the great Pericles* <note>Persius 4.3.</note> [Marginal note: Of this kind], since Socrates also shows that Alcibiades appeared the greatest of all because Pericles, the son of Xanthippus, was left as his guardian by his father. Likewise, the phrase *I am the son of Dinomache* <note>Persius 4.20.</note> is drawn from the passage in Plato which says: *O dear child of Cleinias and Dinomache.* <note>original: "ω φιλε παι κλενίου και δινομάχης" (ō phile pai kleiniou kai dinomachēs). Indeed (as the commentator Proclus affirms), Plato had nothing else in mind here but the Delphic letter, which warns that everyone should know himself. [Marginal note: The Delphic letter] This was also most beautifully touched upon by Pico della Mirandola, our dear friend, [Marginal note: Heptaplus] in his *Heptaplus*—which he is soon to publish—concerning the sevenfold explanation of the six days of Genesis. Therefore, to have discovered these things, or even to have compared them in turn, will produce not only a benefit for scholars but also a pleasure that is by no means common.

**L**ucretius, in the first book of *On the Nature of Things*, writes: *Nor yet had the Duratean horse, by its nocturnal birth of Greeks, set the heights of Troy on fire.* [Marginal note: The Duratean horse] <note>Lucretius, *De Rerum Natura* 1.476. *which Epeius made with the help of Athena.* And likewise a little later:
*the great wooden horse, where all the best men sat.* <note>original: "δουρατεον μέγαν ίππον, όθ' ειαθ' πάντες άρισοι." Odyssey 8.512.</note>
In common speech, the same thing is called not *durateon* but *durion* in the more ordinary tongue, as used also by the poet Aristophanes. But ignorant men <note>original: "opici homines."</note> [Marginal note: The ignorant], beginning to strike out a word unknown to them, replaced it with various trifles like *dura tuens* <note>"looking at harsh things"</note> or *dira tenens* <note>"holding dire things"</note> instead of *Durateus*. Furthermore, Thaddeus Ugoletus of Parma, [Marginal note: Valerius Flaccus] a most learned man and courtier to Matthias, the wisest and most invincible King of the Hungarians, showed us a very ancient manuscript of the *Argonautica* of Valerius Flaccus. [Marginal note: a passage] From this manuscript, I believe, the others now in circulation have flowed. In the second book, it reads: *The Duric night remains by fixed fates*, not *Doric night* <note>"Dorian/Greek night."</note> as is commonly read. This is certainly either the true and corrected reading, or (as I strongly suspect) very close to it, as both usage and the sound of the words suggest: it becomes "Duric night" [Marginal note: Duric night] in his work—the night, that is, when that "Duric" (that is, wooden) horse, having been opened, returned the Greeks hidden in its belly to the open air. Nor should the diphthong stand in the way. For just as it is *dourios* in Greek, so also is it *dourios*...

Of Catullus: Oh girl, after kisses I shall give a sparrow.

# Miscellanies

<margin>Obscene. Obscene.</margin>
ASCENSIUS: *More obscene*: that is, more filthy and more base than is fitting. The word is derived from the "Osci," <note>An ancient people of Central Italy, often stereotyped by later Romans as being crude or foul-mouthed.</note> a people considered foul. Others write *obscenior* as coming from *ob* and *coenum* (mud), with the letter *s* inserted as in *obscuro* (obscure) or *abstineo* (abstain). The nature of the preposition does not entirely oppose this, for in *offusco* (to darken) it increases the strength of the word it precedes. I would rather derive the term *obscicium* from the Osci. But in these matters, everyone is free to choose their own derivation. What should be understood by the "sparrow," since the author does not wish to say—nor would I, even if I knew—I shall not say.

### In what sense Catullus's sparrow is to be understood, and the place indicated in Martial. Chapter VI.

<margin>Sparrow. Obscene.</margin>
**P**hat sparrow of Catullus: I believe it hiddenly allegorizes, through a figure of speech, some more obscene meaning which, for the sake of modesty, we cannot speak aloud. I am persuaded to believe this by that Epigram of Martial, the final verses of which are:
*Give me kisses: but such as those of Catullus.*
*If they are as many as he said:*
*I will give you the sparrow of Catullus.*

<margin>Dull</margin>
For the poet would be excessively dull (which it is a sin to believe) if he were to say he would finally give a literal sparrow of Catullus, and not something else which I suspect, to the boy after kisses. What this is, indeed, for the sake of the modesty of my style, I leave to each person's own conjecture, based on the natural lewdness of the sparrow.

ASCENSIUS: A *pathic* <note>original: "pathicus" — a passive partner in male-male sexual acts, frequently used as a derogatory term for effeminacy in Roman satire.</note> is one who, though he is a man, seeks another man to endure Sodomitic filth. *There was someone* etc. Although he speaks of a specific person, he says *there was someone* most fittingly: for it answers a silent question of the mind: "will there be someone?" No (he says), *there was someone* who, by the license of poetry, despised three golden chariots—that is, the three triumphs of Pompey—referencing the *pathic* by this: because his head, tickled by lust, itches as if bitten by a flea, so that he likes to scratch it with a single finger.

### That Juvenal alludes to pathic men who scratch their heads with one finger, and this from the verses of the poet Calvus. Chapter VII.

<margin>Those scratching their head with one finger.</margin>
<margin>Calvus Pompey</margin>
**W**ho scratch their head with one finger. Certainly, it is a doubt to no one that an effeminate man is signified by this in Juvenal’s ninth Satire. But Plutarch also indicates in his *Life of Pompey* that Pompey was thus marked by Clodius; I will omit for now that he also touched upon this mark of Pompey in the book titled *How one may benefit from enemies.* Moreover, Ammianus Marcellinus in the 17th book of his History notes that Pompey's detractors observed this ridiculous and vain habit in him: that by a certain natural habit he scratched his head with one finger. However, it is not just a "soft" man designed by these words, but clearly a *pathic* and a *draucus* <note>original: "draucus" — a term for a physically strong or well-endowed male lover or prostitute.</note>. Juvenal attacks this kind of men throughout his entire Satire. Otherwise, this poet would be a faint attacker and a pimp-like, or rather (if I may say so) a "Ficulnean" <note>original: "Ficulneus" — literally "of a fig tree." Fig wood was considered weak and useless for building, so the term implies something worthless or ineffective.</note> poet, if he were now attacking merely the effeminate after having raged against the *pathic*. For he alludes, as it seems to me, to the verses of the poet Calvus against Pompey, regarding which Seneca says in the books of the *Orators and Rhetoricians*: "His poems too," he says, "though they are humorous, are full of great spirit." He says of Pompey: *He scratches his head with one finger, by which you would believe this man wants a man for himself.* Thus far Seneca regarding Calvus. Therefore, since the poet Juvenal was trying to indicate that all the *pathics* were flocking to Rome—that is, those who wanted a man for themselves—he wittily alludes to it from the snippet of Calvus's verses: both because (as is likely) they were very well known, and so the consequence would be recognized. And regarding these aforementioned verses of Calvus, I think Porcius Latro feels the same in a certain declamation in that same Seneca, who says: *Against Gnaeus Pompey, victor on land and sea, there was one who composed a poem, scratching his head (as he says) with one finger: There was someone who, by the license of poetry, despised three golden chariots.* Thus Porcius Latro. Since, however, this book of Seneca which we cite is still very rare to find, we have therefore thought this passage worthy of our commentaries as if it were new, lest anyone think we have reported things that are perhaps too common, trite, or "lying in the open."

<margin>Mid-day [Wednesday]. The Lord's Day. The Sabbath Day.</margin>
ASCENSIUS: He used the word *Planetes* (Planets) as if it were of the third declension. Indeed, it is known that this custom of naming the days by the names of the Planets was very ancient among the Germanic peoples, who even now call them thus. But the "upper" Germans differ from the "lower" in this: the upper call the day of Mercury the "middle day of the week" [Wednesday]; which I think they did piously, having received the Christian faith. For the lower Germans call the same the Lord’s Day, or God’s day, because Mercury was held as a god by the Gauls and all Germans—at least the lower ones—and particularly the Goths, who fashioned themselves as gods because they were called the progeny of Mercury. They differ from the Romans, however, in that they call the day of Mars by the name of Dis [Pluto], perhaps believing Mars and Dis to be the same. They still call the Sabbath the day of Saturn, and the following day the day of the Sun. Sheep-herders have also noted that the position of the planets in the sky follows the order of the days, if starting from the Moon we skip every other one in an intercalary way; by what mystery, they themselves shall see. In descending from Saturn, it is necessary to skip four full days. For, omitting four, after Saturn is Jupiter; and by similar reasoning, after Jupiter is Mars; after Mars, the Sun; after which is Venus; after her, Mercury; and finally the Moon.

...if anyone should report these things: some people, even those who are mischievously clever and deceptive, present things that have the outward appearance of truth at first glance. Yet, they entangle the reader in obscure opinions to the great cost of those who believe them, and (as the saying goes) throw dust in their eyes. Or, wherever a greater difficulty arises, by neither refraining from the topic nor truly engaging with it, such a writer eludes the reader’s hope for clarity. Thus, while he strives to prove that he is ignorant of nothing, he is found at times to be even more deceptive than the Parthians or the Cretans <note>In the ancient world, the Parthians and Cretans were proverbial for their dishonesty; "to act the Cretan" was a common idiom for lying.</note>. 

Because others have followed his example, this bloody gangrene of evil has now permeated every "joint of literature"—to use the words of Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), considered Rome's greatest scholar.</note>. This corruption must be cut away eagerly by all learned men using the erasing part of the stylus <note>Roman writing styli were sharp at one end for inscribing wax and flat at the other for smoothing the wax over to delete text.</note>, lest it creep all the way to the vital organs. Indeed, there are several grammatical commentaries published by him, such as those on the poets Martial and Juvenal...

# Book XXXX of the Miscellany (continued)

<margin>Rufinus, in the seventh book.</margin>
<margin>Shades and parasols.</margin> <note>original: *umbracula*. In ancient Rome, these were types of sunshades or parasols used by women or effeminate men, often mentioned in satires to denote luxury or weakness.</note>
<margin>Then in Juvenal and Horace.</margin>
As for the shades and the accompanying explanation, as we find in Rufinus <note>Tyrannius Rufinus (c. 345–410 AD), a monk and historian known for translating Greek works into Latin.</note> in his seventh book, as well as in the works of Juvenal and Horace, there is much to be said. However, when we turn our attention to the specific mention of the "Baptists," we see how far a scholar can stray when they prefer their own inventions over careful reading.

<margin>The Baptists.</margin>
<margin>Drowned in the sea.</margin>
<margin>Domitius's suspicions.</margin>
Concerning the "Baptists" <note>original: *Baptæ*</note>, whom some mistakenly associate with the Cocytus <note>a river in the underworld, often called the "river of wailing."</note>, Domitius presents various suspicions. He falsely claims they were priests of certain Ionian gods or of the goddess Cotytto <note>a Thracian goddess whose secret night-time festivals were notorious for their indecency.</note>. But the truth is far simpler and found in the history of the theater. The comic poet Eupolis <note>an influential playwright of Old Comedy in Athens, a contemporary of Aristophanes.</note> wrote a play titled *The Baptists* to lampoon the effeminate and debauched rites of certain citizens.

Indeed, the ancient records tell us that Eupolis himself was "the one who was drowned in the sea by those against whom he produced *The Baptists*" <note>original Greek: "τοὺς βάπτας, ἀποπνιγέντα εἰς τὴν θάλατταν ὑπ’ ἐκείνων εἰς οὓς κάθηκε τοὺς βάπτας." Legend says that Alcibiades, the Athenian general, was so enraged by being mocked in the play that he had the poet thrown overboard during a voyage.</note>. Thus, the "Baptists" were not some obscure priesthood discovered by Domitius's imagination, but the very subjects of a famous Greek comedy who took a literal, murderous revenge on their creator.

The goddess had already gathered lilies and violets; yet meanwhile, that scent charmed her more and more. She proceeded to follow the trail of the fragrant breeze; she saw a rose, <margin>The Rose.</margin> and having seen it, she brought it to her nostrils and recognized it as the mother of that sweet fragrance. There, she cast the other flowers she had scorned to the ground; and crowned only with roses, she returned again to Mount Ida. Nor did the flower seem to win more favor for Venus than Venus did for the flower. And so immediately Juno and Minerva were so overcome that they did not even wait for the shepherd's vote; but both running forward, they pulled the garland from her hair, kissed the flower itself, and placed it back upon Venus's head. Thus far Libanius concerning the rose; however, I do not know if our hasty Latinity has represented to the letter that most polished plasterwork of his tongue, painted as it is with Greek colors.

**How purple was discovered, together with an explanation of a passage by Nonnus, the Greek poet.**
**Chapter XII.**

It will not be out of place to relate here in what manner purple was discovered, both so that a passage of the Greek poet Nonnus may be understood, and so that a very charming little story, untouched by Latin authors, may be known. <margin>Very charming.</margin>
It is found in Pollux's <note>Julius Pollux (2nd century AD), author of the *Onomasticon*, a Greek thesaurus and encyclopedia dedicated to Emperor Commodus.</note> first book *On Terms Suitable for Commodus*, to this effect. The Tyrians say (he says) that Hercules <note>Referring to the Tyrian Hercules, also known as Melqart.</note> was seized with love for a native nymph whose name was TYRO, <margin>Tyro.</margin> and a dog followed him (they say) according to the ancient custom by which dogs used to accompany men even to the public assembly. Therefore, this Herculean dog, having spotted a purple-shell <note>The murex snail, from which Tyrian purple dye was extracted.</note> creeping among the rocks, attacked the fleshy part and stained his own lips with Phoenician blood. When Hercules therefore went to the girl, she was delighted by that unusual dye which she had seen as if blooming on the dog's lips, and she declared that she would have nothing to do with him thereafter unless he brought her a garment even more splendid than the lips of that dog. Wherefore, Hercules having discovered the creature and collected the blood, brought the gift to the girl; he was the first author (as the Tyrians constantly say) of the Phoenician dyeing process. We ourselves, therefore, in our *Rusticus*, finally called the Shell "Herculean" for this very reason when we were signifying purple. <margin>The Herculean Shell.</margin> Furthermore, the verses of the poet Nonnus concerning this very fable are found thus in the fortieth book of the *Dionysiaca*:

And behold the Tyrian garments dyed by the shell,
Flashing with the purple splendors of the sea,
Where the sea-wandering dog, running on the shores, snatching
An amazing fish hidden deep in its gleaming jaws,
Reddened its snowy cheeks; inside the shell,
Staining the lips with dewy fire, with which once alone
The pleasant robe of purple-clad kings was reddened.

Others who derive it from *dius* write it with a double *i*. But in this chapter there are things which you might think are written wrongly: such as *pernitiosa* should be written with a *c*. Because before many causes: I would doubt whether it should be read *annis*. You might rightly say *Clusum* or *Clausum*.

# **Miscellanies**

[Left margin]
<margin>The Augury of Safety.</margin>

[Main text]
**S**uetonius Tranquillus <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD) was a Roman historian best known for his biographies of the first twelve emperors.</note>, in his *Life of Augustus*, speaks thus: "He restored several of the ancient ceremonies that had gradually fallen into disuse, such as the Augury of Safety <note>original: "Salutis augurium." A ritual to determine if it was an auspicious time to pray for the well-being of the Roman state.</note>, and so forth." But as to what the Augury of Safety might be, I see that even some learned men are ignorant. We have found an account of this matter in the thirty-seventh book of the histories of Dio Cassius <note>Cassius Dio (c. 155–235 AD) was a Roman statesman and historian of Greek origin who wrote a massive 80-volume history of Rome.</note>, to this effect: "Then indeed they also performed the Augury of Safety, as they call it, after a long interval. It is a certain method of augury whereby, if God permits, they may ask for safety for the people, as if it were not even lawful to seek safety from the gods unless the gods themselves first granted permission for this very request. It was observed, moreover, on one particular day each year, on which no army went out to war, no one prepared himself against an enemy, and no one fought. For this reason, in times of constant danger, and especially during civil wars, it was by no means performed. For it was particularly difficult to keep a day pure from all these activities, and it could seem quite absurd to voluntarily bring incredible harm upon themselves <note>i.e., by ceasing military defense on a specific day</note> through civil strife..."

As to who this Aristides was, or what material he used for his books, there is great hesitation; however, we refer the studious youth to the author Plutarch, whose words in the *Life of Marcus Crassus* are to this effect: "Therefore, having assembled the senate of the Seleucians, he displayed the Milesian books of Aristides, which were extremely obscene; in this he told no lie, since they had truly been found among the baggage of Roscius." The Milesians were also notable for their luxuries and excess, from which a proverb is carried in Greek: *oikoi ta milēsia, mē gar enthade* <note>original: "οἴκοι τὰ μιλήσια, μὴ γὰρ ἐνάδε"</note>. **A passage in a tragedy of Seneca corrected and explained from a more remote Greek fable: regarding the Nemean Lion. Chapter XVII.**

<margin>A passage of Seneca</margin>
In the tragedy of Seneca titled *Hercules Furens*, this iambic verse is read: "May the high Moon conceive lofty beasts." <margin>Dwellings of the Moon</margin>

"Cools the Neronean baths": i.e., it cools down very hot and boiling things; they should keep away from the heat of reading or believing. For while an ingeniously invented thing is read, the work "seethes"; when it is dull, it "freezes." Moreover, the baths of Nero, which the Barbarians call *stuba* or *stuva* <note>heated rooms or stoves</note>, were famous in Rome. # First Century. Folio 136.

**E**veryone who has interpreted this verse of the poet Juvenal, from his fourth Satire, has up until now found themselves on rough ground <note>original: "in salebra," a Latin idiom for a bumpy or difficult road, meaning they are struggling with the text</note>, as far as I can see. They do not seem to me to explain the passage, but rather to hunt for a laugh with old wives' tales, or more accurately, they seem to deserve mockery. Indeed, some invent stories of giants turned into monkeys; others imagine a monkey produced by the Earth after the giants to show contempt for the gods. Other explanations are even "colder" <note>In classical literary criticism, a "cold" (frigid) argument is one that is dull, forced, or lacks wit</note> than these, which—just like the rhetorician mentioned by Martial—would "cool down the Neronian baths." <margin>To cool the Neronian baths</margin> <note>A reference to Martial’s Epigrams 3.25, where a boring speaker is so "cold" he could lower the temperature of Nero's famously hot steam baths</note> Truly, as far as I can grasp, these men are said to hand down these trifles with no logic and (as far as I know) no supporting author. 

To me, <term>a giant's little brother</term> <note>original: "fraterculus gigantis"</note> <margin>A giant's little brother</margin> seems to signify a man born from no great ancestors, of an unknown and obscure lineage. This is because the ancients were accustomed to calling those whose parents were unknown "sons of the Earth" <note>original: "Terræ filium"</note>. From this usage, Persius writes:

"Manius is ready as my heir,
A child of the earth..." <note>A quote from Persius, Satire 6. Manius was a common name for a beggar or person of low status</note>

<summary>The author critiques previous commentators on Juvenal's Fourth Satire for using ridiculous myths to explain the phrase "a giant's little brother." He argues the term is actually a metaphor for a person of obscure or lowly birth, commonly referred to as a "son of the earth."</summary>
