**Of Miscellaneous Matters**

-> And after that they did not fear such words for themselves, <-
-> When suddenly a horrible messenger arrives: <-
-> The Ionian waves, after Arrius had gone there, <-
-> Were no longer Ionian: but "Hionian." <-
<note>This is a quote from Catullus, Poem 84. The poet mocks a man named Arrius for "hyper-correction"—adding the 'h' sound (aspiration) where it doesn't belong to sound more sophisticated. He turned "Ionian" into "Hionian."</note>

It should truly be observed that even in pronunciation, one should breathe upon the words just as one does in writing, a practice which the Greeks now retain only in consonants, and the Latins have not retained even in consonants. On the other hand, the ancient Latins used to breathe upon vowels even in speech. On this subject, Cicero writes in his *The Orator*, addressed to Brutus, as follows: "Indeed, although I myself knew that our ancestors spoke in such a way that they never used aspiration except on a vowel, I used to speak in such a way as to say *pulcros* [beautiful], *Cetegos*, *triumphs*, and *Cartage* [Carthage]. At some point—and quite late at that—when my ears were finally convinced and the truth was wrung from me, <margin>The habit of speaking belongs to the people, etc.</margin> I yielded the common way of speaking to the people, but I reserved the proper knowledge for myself." So says Cicero. But I myself recently saw a golden coin in the possession of Lorenzo de' Medici <note>A reference to Lorenzo "the Magnificent," the famous patron of the arts in Florence</note> with the inscription: *TRIVMPVS*. And likewise another silver one with the more common spelling: *TRIVMPHVS*. <margin>Triumph</margin>

Furthermore, Aulus Gellius also testifies in the second book of his *Attic Nights* that the ancients inserted this letter 'h' (or breathing) for the sake of strengthening and (as he says) "firmed up" many words, so that their sound might be fresher and more vigorous. Moreover, Priscian <note>A famous Latin grammarian from around 500 AD</note> says: Aspiration is added to vowels externally, so that it sounds as little as possible, but to consonants internally, so that it sounds the most. Therefore, if you wish to appreciate the wit of Catullus’s epigram, you will pronounce that breathing in its proper place as much as you can.

But I see that these things have now become so well known that they might perhaps seem to belong to someone else. Nevertheless, when I was still almost a youth, in the presence of several learned men (whom I think also remember this), I reported on this very passage to Domitio in Florence. He immediately applauded it so much that he frankly confessed he had learned more that day from a single student than in many years from any of the professors. Aurelius of Rimini knows this (to omit others), who now lives in Padua—a young man of outstanding talent and literature—who received this explanation from us many years ago while I was active in Florence. He later recounted in Padua that it seemed entirely new and unknown to everyone to whom he spoke of it.

As for the works of Catullus as a whole: in Verona (Baccius Ugolinus, a man of the most liberal mind, knows this), while inside a certain workshop where the rain had driven us, I explained them to several learned men who were almost forcing me to do so. At that time, there was also present a relative of Guarino, named Giovanni Battista (if I am not mistaken), and along with him a certain <margin>Dante.</margin> **Dante Alighieri**, the fifth descendant (as he said) from the Florentine poet Dante. There were also two men who were then teaching in Verona, not unlearned men, and a large group of students, who received those words of ours, such as they were, with such eager ears that they repeatedly cried out that an Angel had been sent down to them from heaven (for so they said) to interpret their fellow countryman, the poet.

I do not mention these things so that I might claim my discoveries for myself alone, admitting no one to a share of them (for I am not so arrogant), but lest someone should perhaps think that I, like a crow or a vulture, am feeding on the labors of others, like carcasses left behind by an eagle.

ASCENSIUS. *In all the above.* This is read or held as σακκοπάθιομ [*sakkopathion*], that is, a small sack. This word is also used by the Germans for a *crumena* [purse/money-pouch]. For "saccus" [sack] is common to almost all modern languages.

**Chapter XX. This word *Ascopera* is amended and explained in the works of Suetonius.**

[Decorative initial V]
**T**he manuscripts of Suetonius are found to be corrupted in the *Life of Nero*. For so it is read in all of them: "With a broom [*scopa*] tied to the neck of the other, and a title alongside it: 'I have done what I could, but you have deserved the sack [*culleum*].'" For the word *scopa* is not used in the singular in Latin, and even if it were, a broom has no connection to a sack. But in the ancient copies, a trace of the uncorrupted and true reading remains, in my opinion, in this way: "With an *ascopa* tied to the neck of the other." Therefore, if you write the second to last letter as a 'p', it becomes *Ascopera*, <margin>Ascopera, that is, a pouch or small sack. The Sack [Culleus].</margin> which I think is most correct. Indeed, an *Ascopera* is a small leather sack, and the name is composed in Greek from "leather bottle" [*askos*] and "pouch" [*pera*]. Regarding this word, Suidas writes: ἀσκοπήρα τὸ μαρσύπιομ ἤτοι σακκοπάθιομ [*askopera to marsypion etoi sakkopathion*]. Suidas teaches that *Ascopera* signifies a purse. This, therefore, was the *Ascopera* tied to the neck of Nero's statue—a symbol of the "sack," because he was a matricide <note>Nero killed his mother, Agrippina</note>. For since parricides are sewn into a "sack" [*culleo*] made of ox-hide, the person who tied the *ascopera* to the statue represented a sort of likeness of that sack. Juvenal says of the parricide and the sack:

"And to be lowered into the sea in an ox-hide, with which
Is enclosed, by an adverse fate, the innocent monkey."
<note>In Roman law, those who killed their parents (parricides) were punished by the *Poena Cullei*: being sewn into a leather sack with a live dog, rooster, viper, and monkey, then thrown into the water.</note>

ASCENSIUS. *Writing "on" [in] the epistle of Paul.* It is pleasing to remind the boys of a common rule. One writes *in* [into] a work as if in explanation of it; whereas the author himself is *in* [inside] the work. For example: Paul is *in* the Epistle to the Ephesians; Jerome writes *on* [in] the Epistle of Paul. Virgil is *in* the Aeneid; Servius writes *on* [in] the Aeneid of Virgil, etc.

**Chapter XXI. What either a "Minerval" or a "Minerval gift" is; and from that, the opinions of Juvenal and Varro are explained.**

**First Century. Folio 137.**

**Whoever still worships Minerva, gained with a single penny,** <margin>Juvenal passage.</margin>
This is from the tenth Satire of the poet Juvenal. Domitius <note>Domitius Calderinus, a 15th-century Italian humanist and commentator</note> explains it in such a way that he does not seem to have fully grasped its meaning. He interprets "Minerva gained" as referring to the Quinquatria <note>A five-day festival in honor of Minerva, the goddess of wisdom and weaving, held in March</note> games, which one might attend after having competed for them. What could be more absurd or awkward? I ask you, could anyone, with a single penny, achieve enough to compete publicly in eloquence? Rather, Juvenal seems to have alluded to the **Minerva-gift**, <margin>The Minerva-gift.</margin> which is also called a *Minerval*—specifically, the small fee for teaching usually given by students to their masters, most likely, I believe, before the Quinquatria, during which days the boys were on holiday. Hence, Horace says in his final epistle: <margin>No school during the Quinquatria.</note>
*And rather, as the boy once did during the festive Quinquatria:*
*May you enjoy your brief and pleasant time in haste.*
This was the custom, just as it was during the Saturnalia <note>A mid-winter festival of role-reversal and gift-giving</note> and the Kalends. Therefore, Ovid, discussing the Quinquatria in his *Fasti* <note>A poetic calendar of Roman festivals</note>, says:
*Nor should you, the crowd cheated of your fierce master’s fee,*
*Despise her; she will attract new students.* <margin>The Minerva-gift.</margin>
Saint Jerome also mentions this Minerva-gift in his letter to the Ephesians <note>St. Jerome, a 4th-century scholar famous for translating the Bible into Latin, often criticized the integration of pagan culture into Christian life</note>, which you may also find in the canonical Decrees. He says: "Let the bishops and priests read it, those who educate their sons in secular literature and make them read comedies and sing the shameful writings of mimes—men perhaps educated at the expense of the churches. And that which a virgin, a widow, or any poor person pouring out their entire substance had offered to the treasury for their sins, the grammarian and the rhetorician converts into a New Year's gift, a Saturnalia handout, and a **Minerva-gift**, either for household expenses or for temple offerings, or turns it into a sordid profit." What Jerome calls "Saturnalia handouts," Tertullian <note>An early Christian author from Carthage</note> simply calls "Saturnalia." Varro also, in the third book of his *On Agriculture*, speaks thus <margin>Saturnalia.</margin> regarding the Minerva-gift through the character Axius: "Merula," he says, "take me back as a student of villa-pasturing." Merula replies: "As soon as you have sent ahead the **Minerva-fee** <margin>Minerva-fee.</margin> (*Minerval*), I will begin," meaning a dinner. For Merula is joking here in Varro’s text; because Axius had said he wanted to be received as a student, Merula demands a Minerva-fee be sent to him beforehand, as if he were the master. But he jokingly called a dinner a "Minerva-fee" because it is the reward for teaching. Therefore, might not the poet's meaning here be this: even he who has once offered a Minerva-fee to a teacher—which he signifies by a "penny"—that is, one who has spent only a few days with a rhetorician or grammarian, desires throughout the Quinquatria (which were festivals for Minerva, the patron of genius) no small thing, but the eloquence and fame of Demosthenes or Cicero.

ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, also known as Ascensius, was a famous printer and commentator. Here he adds notes on specific terms</note>: Regarding **supine poems**, <margin>Supine.</margin> that is, poems that are turned away from the matter and are thus vain and empty. We know that those intent on labor and business are called "prone" (leaning forward) because they lean into their work; conversely, those who are idle and turned away from the matter are "supine" (lying on their back), as they walk with their necks held high. Thus, "supine" is taken by some for "proud," and by others for "self-indulgent" and "least busy," as in that passage: *And bringing back much of the supine Maecenas.* Moreover, the final sound of this Greek poem is most fitting for the business at hand: for Echo (which the Greeks call *Acho*) responds that it is best to enjoy one's loves. These are the kind of verses in which (as Martial says) a little Greek Echo sings back.

### Chapter XXII.

**M**artial, in the second book of his *Epigrams*, <margin>Domitius is corrected.</margin> discussing certain "supine" and superfluous poems in which there is much labor but very little praise for the making, writes this among other things:
*Nowhere does a little Greek Echo sing back.*
Domitius, however, takes "little Greek Echo" to mean a Greek word inserted into the text, as if Martial were denying that he ever used Greek words in his epigrams—which is proven to be false. Either our conjecture deceives us, or certain verses suggest this: they are composed so that the responses at the ends are spoken by the character of Echo, completing the meaning and observing her habit of throwing back the final words. We ourselves have made some such verses in our native tongue, which are now celebrated by musicians, having been commended by the melodies of **Henricus** <note>Likely Heinrich Isaac, a famous Renaissance composer</note>, and which we also gave nearly ten years ago to Pietro Contarini, a Venetian patrician and a man of no small genius who desired them greatly, as well as to several other students of literature. But there also exist Greek verses by a certain ancient poet, Gauradas, which I shall set down here.

Dear Echo, agree with me on something. <gloss>What?</gloss> <note>original: τί</note>
I love a girl, but she does not love me. <gloss>She loves.</gloss> <note>original: φιλεῖ</note>
But the time for action brings no opportunity. <gloss>It brings.</gloss> <note>original: φέρει</note>
So tell her yourself that I love her. <gloss>I love.</gloss> <note>original: ἐρῶ</note>
And give her a pledge of coins. <gloss>Give.</gloss> <note>original: τὺ δός</note>
Echo, what remains? To obtain my desire? <gloss>Obtain.</gloss> <note>original: τυχεῖμ</note>

**First Century. Folio 138.**

[Large decorative initial V] These verses are from the *Priapeian Epigrams*, through which—unless I am mistaken—the old woman **Hecale** <margin>Hecale.</margin> is shown. Theseus, while a youth, was once kindly received by her in hospitality. From this event, the sacred **Hecalesium** <margin>Hecalesium</margin> also became celebrated throughout the villages in honor of Zeus Hecalus, not without honors for **Hecale** <margin>sacred.</margin> herself. They also used to call her *Hecalene* in the diminutive form, because she, in her elderly way, was accustomed to greet Theseus while he was still a youth and to receive him with such endearing diminutive terms. However, since she had vowed a sacrifice to Zeus for Theseus's return as he set out for battle, and she died before he returned, she received this honor in turn by the command of Theseus for her hospitality, as **Philochorus** recorded. **Plutarch** mentions this matter in his *Life of Theseus*. Furthermore, **Callimachus** composed a proper poem about her titled *Hecale*, as indicated by a verse from a very well-known epigram:

"I sing of the ways of the hospitable old woman." <note>original: "Μέλπω δὲ γραὸς τῆς φιλοξένου τρόπους."</note>

Many authors are found everywhere citing Callimachus's *Hecale*. Indeed, **Pliny** sometimes lists edible herbs that the rustic Hecale serves in Callimachus's work, such as samphire <term>Crethmon; a salty, aromatic plant found on rocks by the sea</term> in Book 26, and also sow-thistle <term>Sonchum; a wild green similar to a dandelion</term> in Book 22—although in newer manuscripts it says "Hecate" there instead of "Hecale." However, a trace of the true reading still remains in those ancient manuscripts kept in the public library of the **Medici** family. Moreover, where Callimachus says in his *Hymn to Apollo*:

"Envy spoke secretly into the ears of Apollo," <note>original: "ὁ φθόνος ἀπόλλωνος ἐπ᾽ οὔατα λάθριος εἶπεν."</note>
"I do not admire the singer who does not sing as much as the sea." <note>original: "οὐκ ἄγαμαι τὸν ἀοιδόν, ὃς οὐδ᾽ ὅσα πόντος ἀᾴδει."</note>

In that place, the interpreter says roughly as follows: "Through these words," he says, "he accuses those who mocked him as if he were unable to compose a long poem. Because of this, he was forced to write the *Hecale*." The interpreter's words are:
"He accuses through these [words] those mocking him for not being able to make a long poem, whence he was forced to make the Hecale." <note>original: "ἐγκαλεῖ διὰ τούτων τοὺς σκώπτοντας αὐτὸν μὴ δύνασθαι ποιῆσαι μέγα ποίημα, ὅθεν ἠναγκάσθη ποιῆσαι τὴν ἑκάλην."</note>
That is: He accuses his envious mockers through this of being unable to compose a great poem; hence he was forced to compose the *Hecale*.

From this, we wrote in the *Nurse* <note>A reference to the *Nutricia*, a poem by the scholar Angelo Poliziano</note>:
"The son of Battus <note>original: "Battiades"; a common name for the poet Callimachus</note> resounds with Hecale: and the Marathonian deeds are loftier than his usual style."

And **Statius** also writes of her at the end of the *Thebaid*:
"Nor did the old hostess pour out vain tears."

And **Suidas** <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> says that Hecale is a certain heroine in Callimachus's work. Finally, **Apuleius** in the first book of the *Metamorphoses* <note>Also known as *The Golden Ass*</note> says of her, I believe: "If, content with a tiny hearth, you would emulate the virtues of your father of that same name, Theseus, who did not spurn the meager hospitality of the old woman Hecale." I am not unaware, however, that the writing is corrupted almost everywhere; for indeed, you will often find written "Ales the old woman" <note>original: "Ales anus"</note> rather than "Hecale the old woman" <note>original: "Hecales anus"</note>, with several letters having been cut off at the beginning. Thus, in passing, let us cleanse the manuscripts of Apuleius and send the reader away laden, as it were, with **excess weight** <note>A reference to the scholar's note on the previous page regarding the word "superpondio"</note>.

### ASCENSIUS
Regarding "How many" etc.: if "to be" is understood, he used "how" for "very," as elsewhere with a positive adjective; if they are present, he takes "how" for "how much." **Just as.** That is, in the same way. **It was pronounced.** That is, the sentence of acquittal was brought forth publicly and in an express voice. **Or you will induce.** <margin>To induce.</margin> That is, you will erase, as if from a wax tablet. **In that [letter] of Caelius.** For "Caelius": for this is how the genitives of proper names...

# Miscellanea

So you say, Hircisius: read it to that point, until you stumble upon these words: "If you see any hope, as soon as you find it, you shall delete all of this." Or if there is a fault in the roof, the rest will prove it to me. "All of this," I say, "you shall delete or strike out," for these things are clearly foreign to this place. Soon you will return again to those things which were placed incorrectly, in that [section] of the Sky <note>Caeli</note> of which we spoke earlier, and thus you will continue the reading. If you show any hope in letters: you will read it at such a stretch that you will arrive at the twenty-third letter from this one, which begins as follows: "I shall respond to two of his letters, and with this I will conclude the matter." For if there is nothing wrong in the walls or in the roof, the rest will prove it to me. After that, the letter which ought to follow immediately is the one now numbered eleventh, which you should arrange thus: "Your letters have delighted me." This order which we have established is confirmed not only by both codices—the ancient one and this one immediately derived from it—from which it is clear all others have been corrupted by the fault of the booksellers, but also by the intellect and sense itself, which is clearer than light. Thus, to one looking more sharply, whatever was previously obscure or ambiguous is removed.

**ASCENSIUS:** <note>Josse Badius Ascensius, the 16th-century printer and commentator.</note> For when he says "someone mentions those things," he means when Ovid mentions that someone spoke those words which are in the distich <term>distich: a pair of poetic lines</term> of Evenus. For he said: "Someone looking at him," etc. In which sense, if the precept of Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous Renaissance humanist</note> is true, he ought to have said "a certain person looking at him," for he speaks of a specific person. **Addition** <term>auctarium</term>: an increase or surplus from profit. **Price** <term>merce</term>: for the sake of which business was done in this Ovidian passage. **Most beautiful Hercules**: an adverb for swearing an oath <note>original: "pulcherrima Hercules"</note>; or "so may Hercules keep me." **Parody**: an allusion.

### Verses in the *Fasti* from the Greek concerning the vine and the goat, and also a somewhat obscure Parody in Suetonius, Chapter 26.

[margin] A passage of Ovid [/margin]

[Decorative woodcut initial V containing a portrait of a man]
**Ovid** in the first book of the *Fasti*:
"The sow had paid the penalty: terrified by their example,
O goat, you should have abstained from the vine-shoot.
Someone, watching him pressing his teeth into the vine,
Gave vent to these words with no silent grief:
'Gnaw the vine, goat! Yet when you stand at the altar,
There will still be enough from here to sprinkle on your horns.'"

Certainly these two verses were made from a very famous and witty distich by a Greek poet, which is celebrated among the foremost and "flies through the learned mouths of men." For when Ovid mentions that "someone" said those things, he surely pointed his finger at the author of the poem itself, **Evenus**. In the Greek verses, the vine itself speaks, as follows:

"Even if you eat me to the root, I will still bear fruit <note>original: "Κήν με φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν, ὅμως ἔτι καρποφορήσω"</note>
Enough to pour a libation over you, O goat, when you are sacrificed." <note>original: "ὅσσον ἐπισπεῖσαί σοι τράγε θυομένῳ"</note>

The most talented poet translated these as closely as he could; yet there are some things in the Greek which our poet expressed with less detail. Indeed, if we must admit the truth, our poet did not even touch upon that "overseas Charm" <note>original: "transmarinam illam... Venerem"</note> of the Greek. This is perhaps a fault of a language that is less playful, rather than one that lacks abundance. But since we have stumbled into the mention of this Greek distich, let us also bring forward what is in **Suetonius** in his *Life of Domitian*, so that we may bring the light of interpretation to that passage—which is also not obscure—and give it as an addition to a commodity by no means cheap. The words are thus:

[margin] A passage of Suetonius [/margin]

"To induce him to grant a pardon regarding the edict proposed for cutting down the vineyards, it is believed he was compelled by no other thing more than that pamphlets were scattered with these verses:
'Even if you eat me to the root, I will still bear fruit <note>original: "Κήν με φάγῃς ἐπὶ ῥίζαν, ὅμως ἔτι καρποφορήσω"</note>
Enough to pour over Caesar when he is sacrificed.'" <note>original: "ὅσσον ἐπισπεῖσαι καίσαρι θυομένῳ"</note>

For what the vine previously threatened against the goat, the same thing now—by a most beautiful "By Hercules!" Parody—it threatens against Caesar: "Even if you eat me to the root, I will still produce enough wine to be poured over Caesar as he is being sacrificed." For it was the custom of the ancients that wine should be poured over the heads of victims standing under the blow and the knife. Thus, for example, in the works of Maro <note>Virgil</note>:
"The most beautiful Dido herself, holding the bowl in her right hand,
Pours it between the horns of a white cow."
Therefore, they were marking the Emperor Domitian for death through these verses in the pamphlets. For as the same Suetonius writes: "Due to a once-great abundance of wine but a scarcity of grain, thinking that the fields were being neglected through too much devotion to vineyards, he issued an edict that no one in Italy should plant new vines, and that in the provinces the vineyards should be cut down, leaving at most half; but he did not persist in executing the matter." Let students remember that in this discovery, we have consulted the common good in more than one way, since in most manuscripts of Suetonius still, and even in some ancient ones, you would not only fail to find these Greek verses, but not even a trace or a place for them to be received. But since we have held them for a long time as most charming, we have thoroughly tracked them down from obsolete and faulty copies by weighing each part, gradually recognizing them and restoring the letters.

**ASCENSIUS:** That comic line is in the *Andria* of Terence. Similarly, he says "to be silent" in the *Eunuchus*. However, regarding the verses of Euripides: he previously spoke of "Euripides" in the same case so that he might teach how to decline it in both ways. [margin] Cyanean rocks [/margin] The **Cyanean rocks**, which Euripides and Flaccus in the *Argonautica* mention, are in the Hellespontine sea; to those looking from afar, they seem to crash into each other. No one dared to sail to them before the Argonauts made the attempt. They are called by Theocritus the **Symplegades**, the **Syndromades**, and the **Choerades** from the thing itself. [margin] Iolcos [/margin] **Iolcos** is a city of Thessaly; from which comes "Iolcas," a patronymic term, but used to refer to one's fatherland.

**First Century. Folio 139.**

Words in a Letter of Cicero from the *Medea* of Ennius, derived from the Greek of Euripides. Chapter 27.

[Decorative initial C] Cicero, in a letter to Trebatius <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a prominent Roman jurist and friend of Cicero</note>: "We, your friends, will forgive you for this, just as the goddesses who held the high citadel of Corinth—the wealthy and noble matrons—forgave Medea <margin>A passage from Cicero.</margin>, whom she persuaded with her most whitened hands <note>original: 'manibus gypsatissimis'. This obscure phrase likely refers to the powdered or whitened hands of the noblewomen, or perhaps the gestures of the actors on stage</note> that they should not count it as a fault against her that she was away from her fatherland.
For many have managed their own affairs well, and the public’s too, while far from their fatherland.
Many who spent their lives at home were disapproved of for that very reason."
No one among those whose opinions have been published has yet suspected that these are not entirely Cicero's own words, but rather belong to some poet who would be permitted to use such expressions and figures of speech. Such examples include: *who held the high citadel of Corinth* and *wealthy, noble matrons*. Nor have they seen that at least two whole Iambic verses <term>iambic verse: a poetic meter common in ancient drama</term> still stand out in these lines, and the torn-apart limbs of others can, as it were, be recognized. We have concluded that these words are from the *Medea* of Ennius <note>Quintus Ennius, an early Roman poet who adapted the Greek tragedy by Euripides</note>, and certainly not...

**First Century. Folio 140.**

...and certainly not <insert>as some might think</insert> a mere coincidence of prose. For Euripides, whose tracks Ennius followed <note>Quintus Ennius was a pioneering Roman poet known for "Romanizing" Greek tragedies</note>, expresses the same sentiment in this way: "Women of Corinth, I have come out from the house, lest you find some fault in me. For I know many people have become arrogant, some out of sight and others in the public eye; but those who have lived a quiet life have gained a reputation for idleness and a lack of spirit." <note>original Greek: "Κορίνθιαι γυναῖκες, ἐξῆλθον δόμων, μή μοί τι μέμψησθ'· οἶδα γὰρ πολλοὺς βροτῶν σεμνοὺς γεγῶτας, τοὺς μὲν ὀμμάτων ἄπο, τοὺς δ' ἐν θυραίοις· οἱ δ' ἀφ' ἡσύχου ποδὸς δύσκλειαν ἐκτήσαντο καὶ ῥᾳθυμίαν."</note>

So, what the orator <note>Cicero</note> says <note>original: "inquit"</note>—"that they should not count it as a fault against her that she was away from her fatherland"—is exactly what the Greek poet meant by "lest you find some fault in me." Furthermore, when he says "with most whitened hands," <note>original: "manibus gypsatissimis"</note> he <margin>The custom of ancient actors.</margin> is referring to the ancient practice of the stage. For those who played the parts of noble women in theater would whiten their hands and faces with gypsum <note>a white mineral powder</note> to represent the pale, sheltered complexion expected of "wealthy and noble matrons" <term>matrons: high-status married women</term> who lived their lives indoors.

Thus, the reconstructed verses of Ennius would be:
->*I have come out from the house, wealthy and noble matrons,*<-
->*Lest you count it a fault against me that I am away.*<-

We see then how the orator has used <note>original: "utuntur"</note> the old poet’s verses in his own familiar letter, preserving the spirit while adapting the words. Since <note>original: "Quoniam"</note> many have managed their affairs well while abroad, it is said <note>original: "dicitur"</note> that one's reputation should not be diminished by absence. This is how the characters were being driven <note>original: "agebantur"</note> in the play, and how Cicero's friend should not be affected <note>original: "afficiatur"</note> by the judgment of others. It is clear that this whole passage is named <note>original: "denominatur"</note> after the *Medea* of Ennius, and it is a certain <note>original: "quodam"</note> remarkable thing that these verses have survived hidden through all <note>original: "per omnia"</note> these years. Even in the seventh <note>original: "septimus"</note> book of his *Annals*, Ennius does not exceed this level of dignity.

<summary>Poliziano proves that a passage in Cicero's letters is actually a rhythmic adaptation of Ennius’s lost play Medea. He explains the "whitened hands" reference as a theatrical convention where actors used makeup to portray noble women.</summary>

**First Century. Folio 140.**

[Margin: Pan the warrior]
But also Sozimus <note>Zosimus, a 5th-century Greek historian</note>, an author of Greek history, says in his third book that someone of a monstrous appearance, dressed in skins, appeared during the battles between the Albans and the Romans. Indeed, we know that the god Pan was warlike, either from the arguments of Nonnus <note>Nonnus of Panopolis, author of the *Dionysiaca*</note> or from the *Syrinx* <note>original: "fistula"</note> of Theocritus, for in that poem are these words concerning the god Pan: "Whose spirit the boss of the shield once inflamed." <note>original Greek: "ὃν ἄϊθε πάρος φρέμασ τέρμα σάκους"</note> We read elsewhere that he also came to the aid of the Athenians against the Persians, as well as in that very poem we mentioned, in these words: "Who extinguished the god-like arrogance of the assembly" <note>original Greek: "ὃσ σβέσεν ἀγορέαμ ἰσαϊθέα"</note> and "with the grandfather-slayer, he took away from the Tyrian." <note>original Greek: "παπποφόρου τυρίκστ’ ἀφείλετο"</note>

**Why the "Teuthrantian crowd" in Ovid refers to the daughters of Thespius. Chapter XXIX.**

Ovid writes in the letter from Deianira to Hercules:
*Nor shall the Teuthrantian crowd of sisters be a reproach to you:*
*Of whose people none was left behind by you.*
The story is very well known, even recorded by Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>, concerning the many children fathered by [Margin: The Teuthrantian crowd.] Hercules upon the daughters of Thespius. However, why they are called the "Teuthrantian crowd" is so unknown and misunderstood by most that certain scholars <term>literatores: teachers or grammarians of lesser rank</term> dare to replace the word "Teuthrantia" with "Thespeia"—a move that is both wicked and ignorant. I have found the explanation for this in Eustathius, the commentator on Homer, specifically [Margin: The author explains sufficiently.] where he discusses the "Catalogue of Ships." He says: "The writer of epics says that the city is not 'Thespeia' from Thespiades, but according to some it is from Thespius, the son of Teuthras, who was the son of Pandion." <note>original Greek: "φησὶ δὲ ὁ τῶν ἐπικῶν συγγραφεὺσ ὅτι κτίσμα ἐστὶ μὴ θέσπεια θεσπιάδου κατὰ δέ τινασ θεσπίου, υἱοῦ τεύθραντοσ τοῦ πανδίονοσ."</note> Based on this authority, who wrote [Margin: Thespia. Teuthras.] about various nations, he records that Thespia was founded by a Thespiades; however, others write it was by Thespius, the son of Teuthras and grandson of Pandion. Therefore, the daughters of Thespius are called the "Teuthrantian crowd" after their grandfather, Teuthras. Finally, even Aeschylus, in his tragedy *Agamemnon*, called the city of Thespia the city of Teuthras.

ASCENSIUS <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, was the printer and commentator</note>: A *cucuma* is a cooking vessel, a name still used by the people of Lyon; it is usually made of bronze. Thus Ambrose said: "Your gods are made of bronze; from them, kettles are better made for the use of men."

**Words rare to find, yet not unique: *Cucuma*, *Proseucha*, and *Scruta*. Chapter XXX.**

**C**ertain words are so rare to find that if we stumble upon them a second time, we feel our labor has been worthwhile, as they were previously thought to be unique. Such is the word *Cucuma* <term>cucuma: a kettle or cooking pot</term> found in Martial in a half-verse: "Otacilius made a kettle." We also read it in the *Satyricon* of Petronius Arbiter: "Then she even tasted a little of the meat, and while she was using a fork to put a pig's head—as old as her own birthdays—back into the meat-rack, her rotten stool, which had added to her height, broke, and threw the old woman down by her own weight onto the hearth. Thus, the neck of the **Kettle** [Margin: A little kettle.] broke, and extinguished the growing fire, covering her whole face in stirred-up ash." From this, I find the diminutive *cucumion* in Arrian’s books on Epictetus, specifically in the chapter "On the Cynic Profession," where he speaks of the Cynic lifestyle; I will provide Arrian’s words here: "He must have a **little kettle** where he can make warm water for the child to wash him." <note>original Greek: "μεῖ αὐτὸν κουκούμιον ἔχῃμ ὅπου θερμὸν ποιήσῃ τῷ παιδίῳ ἵπ’ αὐτὸ λούσῃ."</note> He used the Greek-inflected *cucumion*, which we might not inelegantly call a *cucumula*.

[Margin: Proseucha.]
Furthermore, many think the word *Proseucha* <term>proseucha: a place of prayer, often used disparagingly to mean a beggars' haunt</term> is found only in Juvenal to describe a place for beggars. However, Cleomedes, in his second book of *Circular Inspection* arguing against Epicurus, speaks almost in this way: "Some of these things are taken from brothels, others are very similar to what women say at the festivals of Ceres; still others come from the middle of the **prayer-house**, taken from those very people who beg there, plainly Jewish and worn-out, and far lower than even crawling things."

[Margin: Scruta.]
Additionally, Horace used the word *Scruta* <term>scruta: second-hand goods, junk, or rags</term> once in this little verse: "Selling cheap **junk** to the tuniced commoners." Sidonius Apollinaris used it again, as far as I can see, in his seventh book of letters: "Now he gave some trifles, now **bits of junk** fit for a young girl’s game."

ASCENSIUS: And "to put outside." I read "outdoors," meaning you are expelled. The middle syllable is long because it is future tense, as the meter shows. Regarding what are called "Suidas": they doubt whether there ever was a person named Suidas <note>The *Suda* is a massive 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia, once thought to be authored by a man named Suidas</note>.

**What that passage in Juvenal means: "As if he had three names," concerning those manumitted by patrons who took their names, and adoption by will. Chapter XXXI.**

To mutter, as if you had **three names**.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535), the scholar-printer.</note>

**Certain faults in a letter of Cicero, and concerning the word "Sciamachia" (Shadow-boxing). Chapter XXXIV.**

[Large decorated initial R] A word far too rustic, unrefined, and clearly foul has occupied a letter of Cicero; specifically the one to Brutus, with the beginning: "I rejoice marvelously, my Brute." For thus we read in it: *And those intense struggles of mine seem as if they were annihilated by knowledge.* <note>original Latin: "tanquam scientia adnihilatæ"</note> Some, however, have corrected this so far as to say: *as if they were already annihilated.* I ask the learned and those skilled in suitable ancient words and readings to consult their own judgment and sense, and only then dare to believe that "annihilated struggles" was actually written by Cicero. In two manuscripts of the Medici family—whose reliability we have appealed to above—we found it also in error, but in such a way that the trace of the mistake has not yet been abolished; we found it thus: *As if Sciamachalae.* Therefore, we suspect the reading should be "Sciamachiae." <margin>Shadow-boxing.</margin> <note>original Greek: "Sciamachiæ," literally "shadow-fighting."</note> For "sciamachiae" are nothing other than "shadow-boxings" or mock-battles. Cicero means this: that he is now clearly losing influence <note>original: "frigere," literally "to grow cold."</note> in the Senate since things are not succeeding for Brutus, and those intense struggles of his seem like mere shadow-boxings. The word itself is very elegant among the Greeks and widely used. Indeed, Galen the physician, in the second book of *On Health*, <note>original Greek: "ὑγιεινῶν" (Hygieinon)</note> says thus: "It is time to pass to quick movements without tension or violence; these are races and shadow-boxings." <note>original Greek: "δρόμοι δι’εἰσὶ ταῦτα καὶ σκιαμαχίαι" (dromoi di'eisi tauta kai skiamachiai)</note> Among the fast exercises which are nevertheless not strained or violent, he numbers both running and shadow-boxing. Finally, even Eustathius, in his commentary on the third book of the *Odyssey*, mentions the word thus: "Similarly, the phrase 'we fight under the shade' indicates nothing bad, nor indeed does the compound word 'to shadow-box'." And Marcus Varro inscribed one of his Menippean satires *Sciamachia*. For this is the true reading found in Gellius <margin>Passage in Gellius.</margin> from ancient copies, not as some write, *Criomachia* (Ram-fighting). Moreover, a little earlier in that same letter of Cicero, another word, *organon*, <margin>Organon (Instrument).</margin> <note>original Greek: "ὄργανον"</note> having been corrupted from the Greek script, migrated into the Latin. For in place of what was *organon*, it had become *optanon*. No one until now has noticed this either. Therefore, you should read it thus: "I am clearly cooling off now, Brutus, for the Senate was my instrument." <note>original: "Organon enim erat meum senatus."</note> He used it as an "organon" or a tool.

**ASCENSIUS.** "Atheon," <note>original Greek: "ἄθεον"</note> that is, without god, or one who denies God. "Cretans are liars": <note>original: "Cretes mendaces"</note> a term used by him. It declines as "Cres, Cretis," etc.

**A passage in Marcus Varro, and likewise another in the books of Columella on rural affairs, defended from fault; and certain things added therein concerning Euhemerus, the tomb of Jupiter, and the Cretans, and a passage in Statius explained. Chapter XXXV.**

[Large decorated initial I] In Marcus Varro’s first book of *On Agriculture*, <note>original: "rerum rusticarum"</note> there is a faulty reading: "The ear of corn and the grain are known to almost everyone, the husk to few. The words of Lactantius from the first book of *Divine Institutes* are as follows: "The ancient author Euhemerus, who was from the city of Messana, collected the deeds of Jupiter and the others who are thought to be gods, and wove together a history from the titles and sacred inscriptions which were held in the most ancient temples, and especially in the shrine of Jupiter Triphylius, where a title indicated that a golden column had been placed by Jupiter himself. On this column, he wrote down his deeds so that they might be monuments of his affairs for posterity. Ennius translated and followed this history, whose words are these: 'Where Jupiter gives the empire of the sea to Neptune, so that he might reign in all the islands and all places along the sea.'" Then the same Lactantius brings forward several passages of Ennius concerning this same history again and again, which I, desiring brevity, shall pass over. Indeed, Sextus Empiricus also alleges the words of Euhemerus himself, especially in the fourth volume of his *Pyrrhonian Outlines*, and says he was called "Atheon" (the Atheist), <margin>Atheists.</margin> just as were Diagoras of Melos, Prodicus of Ceos, Theodorus of Cyrene, and several others. And Timon of Phlius (I believe) says of him thus: "Euhemerus, an arrogant old man, writing wicked books." <note>original Greek: "Εὐήμερος γέρων ἀλαζὼν ἄδικα βιβλία ψύχων."</note>
But setting these aside, that point in Columella <margin>Passage in Columella.</margin> must be inspected more keenly in Book X, Chapter 3, where he deals with bees: Homer is cited twice instead of Euhemerus in the common copies. This last part was translated by Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> in this way—I believe he was Varro Atacinus, the interpreter of another’s work:

**ASCENSIUS.** He reconsidered this passage regarding "pitylism" <note>A rhythmic exercise or a medical term for spitting/spraying.</note> in his letters, as you will find through the index.
An exposition of a poem by Juvenal, contrary to all opinions held until now, concerning the Laconian [bath] and Pitylism.

## **Chapter XXXVIII.**

[Decorative initial Q] Who makes the Lacedaemonian circle slippery with splashing. <note>original: "Qui Lacedæmonium Pityſmate lubricat orbem." A line from Juvenal's Satire 11, line 173.</note>
This verse from Juvenal's eleventh Satire has been interpreted in various ways until now, and (as I believe) quite carelessly. For Domitius says that *Pitysma* is a sprinkling of light spit, derived from the word *Pityo*. However, he takes "Lacedaemonian circle" to mean a ring, because he says the use of rings originated with the Lacedaemonians <note>The Spartans.</note>, so that senators and knights might be signified by the mention of a ring. 

<margin>
The Lacedaemonian Circle.
The Lacedaemonians use an iron ring.
Pityzo.
</margin>

Furthermore, another very learned man—whom we shall refrain from naming out of respect, even though we disagree with him—thinks it refers to a Lacedaemonian dance. But he honestly confesses that he has read nothing about it so far, except for a mention of a Lacedaemonian dance in the works of Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian.</note>. Finally, a third man, also very learned, understands it to be a hoop made from a pine tree, because a pine is called *Pitys* in Greek, from which comes *pitysma*. Out of these three opinions, though we respect the authors, we approve of none.

First, we deny that "Lacedaemonian circle" can signify a ring, because it is nowhere read that the origin of the ring came from the Lacedaemonians. Indeed, Pliny, whom Domitius cites, reports that even then the Lacedaemonians used only an iron ring. If this is removed, it becomes impossible for the "Lacedaemonian circle" to be understood as a ring—as indeed it is removed—and that fictitious "sprinkling of spit" will certainly carry no weight. Moreover, you will never find the word *Pityo*; rather, *pitysma* is derived from *pityzo*, which is explained in the works of the grammarian Nicander. 

<margin>
Pine.
Pitylisma, i.e., healthful.
</margin>

As for the one who thinks it is a Lacedaemonian dance called *pitysma*, since he finds nothing about it, he will likely yield (as he is a man of integrity) to a stronger opinion. I believe the same will be true of the one who thinks it is a hoop made of pine; for such a thing is never read of, nor does it fit the context, and the rules of syllable length argue against it, since the first syllable of *pitys* <note>original Greek: "πίτυς"</note> is short, as is clear from the very first verse of Theocritus. 

Therefore, let us believe the text should read *pityliſma*, and that through the ignorance of scribes, a syllable was dropped from the middle. This is hardly surprising in such darkness. By *Pityliſma*, we understand an exercise about which the excellent physician Galen <note>A famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire.</note> writes in his second book *On Health* <note>original Greek: "ὑγιεινῶν" (Hygieinon).</note>. In his work, the word is used more as a verb, *pitylizin* <note>original Greek: "πιτυλίζειν" (pitylizein)</note>, than as a noun, *pityliſma*. However, *pityliſma* is correctly formed from it by a very common grammatical proportion. It is not inappropriate to first write down Galen's Greek words, and then translate them according to our ability. 

<margin>
Explained by the author.
</margin>

Thus, when he notes various types of exercises and teaches about those which are fast but without extreme tension or violence—among which is the very one we are discussing—he writes word for word: 
"To perform *pitylizin* <note>original Greek: "τὸ δὲ πιτυλίζειν"</note> is to stand very much on the tips of the feet, extending both hands and moving them very quickly, bringing one backward and the other forward; they especially exercise this while leaning against a wall. This exercise is such that if they should ever stumble, they can easily steady themselves by touching the wall, and thus the stumbles of those exercising are hidden and the exercise remains safe." 

It means, he says, to *pitylizin*—or if you prefer, *pitylize*—when someone walking on their tiptoes extends their hands and moves them very rapidly: one backward and the other forward. This type of gymnastic exercise is mostly done against walls so that if they slip, they can quickly recover by grabbing the wall; thus the slips of the exercisers are deceptive, and the exercise itself becomes less taxing. 

<margin>
Lacedaemonian circle.
Sweating room.
</margin>

Furthermore, I would take the "Lacedaemonian circle" to mean the *Laconicum* <note>A dry-heat sweating room, similar to a sauna.</note> itself, in which they used to exercise in that manner. Dio <note>Cassius Dio, a Roman historian.</note> records in the fifty-third book of his histories that a Laconian steam-room or sweating-room (for thus we seem able to translate what he calls a *Pyriaterium* <note>original Greek: "Πυριατήριον"</note>) was built by Agrippa in the city. He then says it was called "Laconian" because during those times the Lacedaemonians, more than all others, exercised naked and anointed with oil. Martial also hints at this Laconian practice, saying: 
"If the rites of the Laconians please you, you can be content with dry steam and be plunged into the raw virgin water of Mars." <note>Martial, Epigrams 6.42. The "virgin water" refers to the Aqua Virgo aqueduct in Rome.</note>

But also Columella, in his first book on agriculture, says: "And we, astonished, marvel at the gestures of effeminate men, because they mimic with feminine movement the sex denied to men by nature, and deceive the eyes of the spectators." Shortly after, he adds: "Then, so that we may come to the gluttonous feasts with an appetite, we boil away our daily indigestion in the Laconian baths, and having dried up our sweat, we seek a thirst." 

Now, therefore, even from these words of Columella, it can be clear to anyone which people the poet <note>Juvenal.</note> chiefly signifies. Doubtless it is those who waste the whole day in those Laconian baths and gymnasiums, anointed and naked. This is also why he says "makes slippery" (*lubricat*), on account of the oil and ointment with which they were rubbed down for exercise.

<summary>This page provides a philological correction of a verse in Juvenal’s Satires, arguing that the "Lacedaemonian circle" refers to a Spartan-style dry-heat bath (Laconicum) where men performed a specific rhythmic exercise called pitylism.</summary>

# First Century. Leaf 143.

Seneca also, in the seventh book of his letters to Lucilius, suggests nothing other than the Laconian [bath], stating it thus: "What do I care for those steaming pools? Why those sweat-rooms, in which dry vapor is trapped to exhaust our bodies, so that every bit of sweat might be driven out through effort!" <note>original Latin: "Quid mihi cum istis calentibus stagnis..." Seneca, *Epistles to Lucilius*, 67 (often numbered differently in modern editions).</note> It remains for us, since he spoke of a "circle," to also show that these Laconian rooms were constructed in a circle. This is evident from the fifth book on Architecture by Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio (c. 80–15 BC), a Roman architect whose work *De Architectura* is the primary source for Roman building techniques.</note>, in these words: <margin>The shape of the Laconicon.</margin> "The Laconian sweat-rooms, which are to be joined to the warm-room <term>tepidarium|The moderately warm room in a Roman bath complex, used for transitioning between hot and cold areas</term>: let them have a height equal to their width, up to the bottom curve of the hemisphere. Let a central opening be left in the hemisphere, and from it, let a bronze shield <note>original Latin: "clypeum æneum." This was a disc used as a damper to control the escape of steam.</note> hang by chains. By raising and lowering this shield, the temperature of the sweat-room will be regulated. It appears that it should be made perfectly circular <note>original: "ad circinum," literally "by the compass."</note> so that the force of the flame and vapor may spread equally from the center through the curves of the rounded structure."

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535), a renowned grammarian and printer.</note> On the rush <note>original: "Scirpum," referring to a common water-rush. This relates to the proverb "nodum in scirpo quaerere"—to look for a knot in a rush—meaning to find difficulty where none exists.</note> etc. There are those who think "scrupus" <note>A sharp stone or a source of anxiety/difficulty.</note> should be said instead of "scirpus." However, the explanation of this "scirpus" or "scrupus"—that is, a difficult passage—is contained in the context. Nevertheless, lest it be too long for anyone to read through, let him explain Ausonius's <note>Decimus Magnus Ausonius (c. 310–395 AD), a Roman poet and teacher.</note> poem thus: "Either let it be present"—that is, let it help—"your interpreter"—that is, the one you are accustomed to use, who is the one who understands my riddles—"when he has brought forth"—that is, revealed to you—"the daughters of Cadmus" <note>original: "filias Cadmi." A poetic metaphor for the letters of the alphabet, which the mythical Phoenician prince Cadmus was said to have brought to Greece.</note>—that is, the letter marks brought into Greece by Cadmus—"tiny black ones"—that is, black but very small, because larger ones are usually painted in another color—"and the white page of the melon"—that is, of the Nile. This refers to the thin skin of the papyrus born near the Nile, upon which the ancients used to write; they still call paper "papyrus" for this reason.

# Miscellany

In the *Menaechmi* <note>A famous comedy by the Roman playwright Plautus, often used by scholars to study early Latin forms.</note>, it will correspond, as is the case everywhere, that a diphthong <note>A sound formed by the combination of two vowels in a single syllable.</note> exists there. Moreover, we read *Fouri*, not *Furi*, on another coin, so that the first syllable is lengthened by a diphthong. This is also how it appears among the Greeks. What should I say about that which Quintilian <note>Marcus Fabius Quintilianus (c. 35–c. 100 AD), a Roman rhetorician who discussed the evolution of the Latin language in his "Education of the Orator."</note> points out, <margin>Doubled vowels, an obsolete practice.</margin> and which we ourselves have observed at times: that they used to double a vowel to indicate it should be lengthened? For instance, on a gold coin one finds *Feelix* <note>The Latin word for "happy" or "lucky," usually spelled "Felix."</note> spelled with a double "e," and on a bronze coin from the reign of Emperor Galba, *viirtus* <note>The Latin word for "virtue" or "valor."</note> is found with a double "i." 

Now, as for those "improper" <note>original Greek: "ἄκυρος" (akyros); here referring to irregular linguistic forms that do not follow standard rules.</note> sounds: are they not also found among us, at least in Greek names such as *Harpyia*, *Orithyia*, and *Thyia*? It seems, then, that the ancients might be seen to have had not just seven diphthongs, but as many as ten.

# Chapter 46

In the seventh Satire of the poet Juvenal, it is written thus: <margin>Juvenal, Satire 7</margin>
An incurable 
itch for writing <note>original: "cacoethes"</note> holds many, and grows old in their sick hearts.
Now, as for the word *cacethos*, it is used neither by the Greeks nor the Latins anywhere; nor does the meter of the poem allow it. Therefore, we suspect it should be read as *cacoethes*, so that it is what is called among the Greeks *to kacoethes*. <margin>Cacoethes</margin> Indeed, by that very word, a most frequent and common one, a "bad habit" is signified. We found this same reading in an ancient manuscript written in Lombardic letters <note>A medieval script used in Italy before the Carolingian reform.</note>, which Francesco Gaddi of Florence—a secretary of the highest magistracy, a prudent and refined man, and not unlearned in letters—gave me the opportunity to read. Furthermore, that verse appears in the same manuscript as follows:
"Nor does bloated Lyde help with her stored-away jar." <margin>Juvenal</margin>
Elsewhere, this is incorrectly rendered as: "Lyde stored in a jar." You should understand this "Lyde" to be an old woman who sells medicines of that sort; she is thick and (as Plautus says) "barrel-like." <margin>Lyde. Barrel-like.</margin> Perhaps looking at this, and most wittily playing upon the drunken Silenus <note>The tutor of Bacchus, usually depicted as fat and intoxicated.</note>, Martianus Capella says: "And while he desires to move his step, Lyde calling him away." For just as if you were to hear the names of Canthara, Pyrrhia, or Baucis, you would immediately imagine them to be stuffed, winy, and wrinkled by a certain selection of traits; so, having heard the name of Lyde, you soon recall this "bloated" woman of Juvenal's. Thus, the characters are wonderfully brought in to provoke laughter: Silenus, his veins swollen with wine, and the pot-bellied Lyde, who (if it pleases the gods) calls the staggering and slipping man away from mockery.

# Chapter 47

What Pliny recorded concerning the "hanging titles" of ancient artists, recognized from ancient monuments in Rome; likewise, the appearance of the Vergilian Aegis.

Recently in Rome, in the courtyard of the Mellini house, we observed a certain marble base, as it were, on which it was written in Greek: *Seleukos basileus, Lysippos epoiei*. <note>original: "σέλευκος βασιλεὺς,λύσιππος ἐποίει"</note> In Latin, this means: "King Seleucus; Lysippus was making [this]." At that time, Giovanni Lorenzo of Venice was there with us, a secretary to the Supreme Pontiff; he is a man most learned in both languages <note>Latin and Greek.</note> and most studious of all such "luxuries" of knowledge. He, therefore, reminded us—which we immediately seized upon—and we recognized that it was not by chance that *epoiei* <note>Imperfect tense: "was making."</note> was used there rather than *epoiesen* <note>Aorist/Perfect tense: "made."</note>; that is, "was making" rather than "made." <margin>Was making</margin> Indeed, as Pliny says in the preface to his *Natural History*, those greatest artists inscribed even their finished works with a "hanging title," such as "Apelles was making [this]" or "Polyclitus," as if the art were always just begun and imperfect. This was so that against the varieties of judgments, the artist would have a recourse to forgiveness, as if he were about to correct whatever was found wanting, had he not been interrupted. Therefore, he says, it is full of modesty that they inscribed all their works as if they were their most recent, and as if something had been snatched away from each one by fate. However, only three works (not more, as he thinks) are handed down as inscribed absolutely—"He made it"—which he records in their proper places. From this, it appeared that a total confidence in their art pleased those authors. And for that reason, all those works were held in great envy. Moreover, the same Giovanni Lorenzo of Venice asserted that similar titles are found elsewhere in Rome.

We also saw—which we thought should be included in these *Miscellanies* of ours—a certain marble statue of Pallas in that same city, wearing the Aegis <note>The magical breastplate or shield of Athena/Pallas, often fringed with serpents.</note> covered with the scaly skin of dragons, so that small snakes likewise enclosed its outermost edge in place of a border or fringe. <margin>The Aegis of Pallas.</margin> There was with us then Giuliano of Bologna, whose surname has now become "Antiquarius" from his profession, along with Giorgio "Italianus" of Genoa, a most experienced investigator of hidden things. We immediately recalled the Vergilian verses, in which that incomparable poet seemed to have wonderfully expressed that very carving of the Palladian shield, writing thus in the eighth book of the *Aeneid*:
"And the horrific Aegis, the arms of agitated Pallas,
They busily polished with the scales of serpents and gold,
And the connected snakes, and on the breast of the goddess
The Gorgon itself, turning its eyes from its severed neck."

### That others wrote concerning Megabyzus what Pliny wrote concerning Alexander: that he was accustomed to frequent Apelles' workshop. Chapter 48.

<margin>Pliny's words</margin>
<margin>Megabyzus</margin>

Pliny the Elder <note>Pliny the Elder (23–79 AD) was a Roman author and naturalist whose *Natural History* is a primary source for ancient art history.</note>, in the thirty-fifth volume of his *Natural History*, states that Alexander the Great of Macedon was accustomed to frequenting the workshop of the most excellent painter, Apelles. Alexander was delighted not only by the artist's skill but also by the man’s pleasant company. Pliny says that when Alexander was in the workshop discussing many things quite ignorantly, Apelles would politely urge him to be silent, telling him that he was being laughed at by the boys who were grinding the pigments.

This story, which Pliny writes concerning Alexander, Plutarch relates instead regarding Megabyzus <note>Megabyzus was a high-ranking Persian priest of Artemis at Ephesus; the shift in the subject of the anecdote is a typical point of philological investigation for Poliziano.</note>, in that volume where he discusses the differences between a flatterer and a friend. "Apelles the painter," he says, "said to Megabyzus, who was sitting beside him and attempting to say something about line and shadow: 'See how those boys grinding the Melian earth <note>original: "melida"; a fine yellow-white earth pigment from the island of Melos</note>—a type of color—were just now paying attention to you while you were silent, admiring your purple robes and gold jewelry. But now...'"

<meta>The previous page concluded Chapter 48 of the *Miscellanea*, which discussed an anecdote about the painter Apelles and his interactions with Alexander the Great and Megabyzus. **First Century. Folio 146.**

The *Library* <note>original: "bibliotheca"; this refers to the *Bibliotheca* of Pseudo-Apollodorus, a primary source for Greek myths.</note> (for so his book is named) refers the purification of the daughters of Proetus to the seer Melampus rather than to a shepherd. It states that the daughters born of Proetus and Stheneboea were Lysippe, Iphinoe, and Iphianassa. <margin>The madness of the daughters of Proetus.</margin> As soon as they reached adulthood, they were afflicted with madness—either because (as Hesiod writes) they did not accept the rites of Father Liber <note>original: "Liberi patris"; the Roman name for the Greek god Dionysus.</note>, or (as is found in the writings of Acusilaus <note>Acusilaus of Argos was a Greek historian and mythographer from the 6th century BC.</note>) because they looked with contempt upon the statue of Juno <note>original: "Iunonis"; the Roman name for Hera.</note>. 

After they began to rave, they first wandered through the entire territory of the Argives, and then indeed through Arcadia and the whole Peloponnese. Forgetting their own dignity, they ran through lonely places. <margin>Running out.</margin> This continued until Melampus—the son of Amythaon and Idothea, who was the daughter of Abas—a seer, of course, and the first who had discovered how to heal through medicines and purifications, <margin>Melampus.</margin> promised he would cure the young women if a third part of the kingdom were transferred to him. When Proetus by no means agreed to this, clearly deterred by such an enormous price, the madness of the girls began to grow more and more daily. The contagion even migrated to the other women, so that they commonly abandoned their own homes, killed their sons, and wandered through the wilderness. 

Therefore, as the calamity spread further and further, when Proetus finally agreed that he would give the requested payment, Melampus now said he would not perform the cure unless another equal portion of the land were awarded to his brother Bias. At this point, Proetus, fearing that if he rejected the current condition he might subsequently demand even more, consented to that price. And only then did Melampus take the strongest of the young men as companions for himself, and with shouting and a certain "inspired dance" <note>original: "enthea... chorea"; *enthea* implies a state of being possessed by a god or divine frenzy.</note> (for so he says), he drove them from the mountains as far as Sicyon. <margin>The purification of the daughters of Proetus.</margin> However, in the pursuit, Iphinoe, the eldest by birth, perished.

**Of the Miscellanea**

<margin>A castrated priest.</margin>

### That the name of Agamemnon in Marcus Tullius Cicero’s *On Divination* is put for Ulysses: then, in passing, a passage in the *Letters to Atticus* is elegantly corrected and explained concerning little red wax marks. **Chapter LIII.**

<margin>Cicero’s little errors.</margin>
**A**ulus Gellius, in those *Attic Nights* of his—which are most brilliant—notes a manifest error of Cicero’s. It is not a matter of great importance, nor is it surprising that he erred; rather, Gellius wonders that the error was not noticed later, either by Cicero himself or by his secretary Tiro. For when Cicero translates certain verses of Homer into Latin, he writes that Ajax says them in that poet's work, when in truth they are spoken by Hector. This boldness of Aulus Gellius makes me not fear to report in these books a small matter comparable to that one regarding the same Cicero, almost a close relative to that previous error—and indeed a twin—unless by chance (which I would more greedily believe given such a long span of time) the error was in the manuscript copies. However, we find it written no differently even in the oldest books, nor is the slip from one name to the other easily explained by any similarity in the letters. 

The words are Cicero’s in the second book of *On Divination*: "For I would wonder if I believed what you said regarding Calchas in Homer, that he prophesied the years of the Trojan War from the number of sparrows; regarding whose conjecture, Agamemnon speaks thus in Homer, as we have translated at our leisure:
*Endure, O men, and tolerate hard labors in your soul,*
*So that we may know the fates of our augur Calchas:*
*Whether they be fixed, or truly the predictions of his breast.*" <note>Poliziano is quoting Cicero's Latin translation of Homer, *Iliad* 2.299–301.</note>
And then he sets out the rest of the Homeric verses translated by himself. Therefore, that Cicero relates that Agamemnon speaks these things in Homer—if indeed Cicero left it written so—is in no way true. For in Homer himself, in the second book <note>original: "Rhapsodia"</note> of the *Iliad*, it is not Agamemnon, but Ulysses who utters the verses of that sentiment. Nor is there any reason for anyone to be annoyed that such things are found in Cicero, or to wonder at it, since it appears from his own letters that errors of memory of this kind were sometimes found in Cicero's books, noticed and attended to by either Atticus or Brutus. Just as that error in the *Speech for Ligarius* regarding Lucius Corfidius, which Cicero confesses was his own mistake; but (as they say) he calls it a "slip of memory" <note>original: "mnemonikon hamartema"</note>. Likewise, in *The Orator*, I believe Cicero had placed Eupolis instead of Aristophanes.
<margin>That is, a fault or vice of memory.</margin>
Then Atticus put back Aristophanes for Eupolis. Therefore, Cicero even says he sometimes fears that his "compositions" <note>original: "syntaxeis"</note> must be marked in many places by little red wax marks. 

<margin>Little red wax marks.</margin>
But since it happens that we mentioned the "little red wax mark" <note>term: "miniatula cerula" refers to the red wax used by ancient and Renaissance editors to mark errors in a manuscript.</note>, this passage in the penultimate book of the *Letters to Atticus* must be corrected and interpreted by us in passing, in which it is found wrongly written as follows: *With these letters written, I gave myself to my compositions; which indeed I fear must be marked by your excessive [nimia] marks in many places: I am so distracted [meteoros] and hindered by great thoughts.* 

I think it should be read: *lest they be marked in many places by your little red wax* <note>original: "miniatula cera"</note>, so that the meaning is that Cicero gave himself to the composing of books (for that is *syntaxis* in Greek). But he feared nevertheless that they must be marked in many places by the little red wax of Atticus himself, to whom he was writing, whom he often used as an editor; for Cicero was "distracted" <note>original: "meteoros"; term: "meteoros" in Greek means 'suspended' or 'up in the air,' referring to a mind that is anxious or unfocused.</note>, that is, suspended in mind and (as he says) hindered by great thoughts.
<margin>Compositions.</margin>
<margin>Distracted.</margin>
Atticus was accustomed, I believe, if a passage was treated with insufficient perfection by Cicero, to affix red wax to that place, which we also do now. Moreover, in the manuscript which they say belonged first to Francesco Petrarch, then certainly belonged to Coluccio Salutati, and after him to Leonardo Aretino, and soon to Donato Acciaioli—the most learned men of each of their ages—it still stands thus: *lest by your little red white-lead [cerusa]* <note>Poliziano is noting a corruption in the text where "cera" (wax) became "cerusa" (white lead pigment).</note>. But if you extend the second-to-last letter of the second-to-last word a little bit from the top—that is, if you make an *l* out of the letter *i*—you will undoubtedly remove the whole error. But also in the common manuscripts, it is still read thus at the very end of that same volume of letters: *For I was dreading those little red marks of yours*; so that now all previous ambiguity is abolished by this testimony.

**ASCENSIUS** <note>This is a note by the printer, Jodocus Badius Ascensius.</note>
As to what the *Ceratinae* are: I read "what they are" and write it without a diphthong; for it is not derived from *cera* (wax) but from *ceras* (horn). It could, however, be read: "what the *ceratine* [thing] is."

->### What the "Ceratinae" are in Quintilian. **Chapter LIIII.**<-

<margin>Quintilian. Horned syllogisms.</margin>
**Y**ou would not easily find someone to explain to you what the *Ceratinae* <note>term: "Ceratinae" refers to the "Horned Syllogism" or "The Horns," a classic logical paradox.</note> are in the first book of Quintilian. However, those who want Greek and Latin commentaries will clearly understand that it is a species of inexplicable reasoning, which introduces I know not what handles and hooks by the art of dialectical perplexity. I believe it was so named from the very subject matter of the words they used; just as it is in Seneca’s fifth book of *Letters to Lucilius*: "I might sit idle," he says, "and pose little questions of this sort: *What you have not lost, you have; you have not lost horns; therefore you have horns*"; and other things fashioned after the example of this sharp delirium. But you may find more on this likewise in the *Attic Nights*. For who does not know that "Horns" are called *cerata* in Greek? Lucian also mentions this in the *Symposium of Philosophers*, as well as the "Sorites" and the "Therizon". But also in the *Dialogue of the Dead* between Castor and Pollux, he says roughly this: "And the horns..."
**T.iiij.** <note>The printer's signature mark for the page.</note>

# Miscellanea

...they bring forth among themselves: and they create "Crocodiles" <note>The "Crocodile" is a famous ancient paradox: a crocodile steals a child and promises to return him if the parent correctly guesses whether he will do so. If the parent guesses "you will not return him," the crocodile is stuck in a logical loop.</note>: and they teach how to ask such intricate questions: namely, from "horns": this reasoning which we have called the <term>Ceratine</term> <note>From the Greek *keratínē*, meaning "horned." Moreover, in another dialogue, the name of which is either *The Dream* or *The Cock* <note>A satirical work by the Greek writer Lucian of Samosata.</note>, he says, while teaching, that an affirmation is constructed from two negations, and that "it is not night, if it is day." <note>original: "Noctemq̃ non esse: si dies sit." Poliziano is illustrating the basic logical principle that two negatives make a positive, or the law of the excluded middle.</note> Sometimes he even said that I had horns, and other things of that sort. 

Eubulides of Miletus <note>A 4th-century BCE philosopher of the Megarian school, famous for inventing several logical paradoxes.</note> also made extensive use of these kinds of dialectical puzzles in questioning, such as the sharpness of human wits frequently devises, as recorded by Diogenes Laertius in his *Life of Euclid of Megara*. Let us attempt to translate these into English: 
*   **The Liar** <note>A paradox: "This sentence is a lie." If it is true, it is false; if it is false, it is true.</note>
*   **The Deceiver** 
*   **The Electra** <note>A paradox of recognition: Electra knows her brother Orestes, but does not recognize the man standing before her who is Orestes.</note>
*   **The Veiled Man** <note>Similar to the Electra: "Do you know this veiled man?" "No." "But he is your father; therefore you do not know your father."</note>
*   **The Heap** <note>The *Sorites* paradox: At what point does a collection of grains of sand become a "heap"?</note>
*   **The Horned One** (or Cornea) 
*   **The Bald-head** <note>The *Phalakros* paradox: At what point does a man with hair become "bald" if you pull out one hair at a time?</note>
