...that you feel yourself struck and cast down by that single horn: you shall find him heavy with a double horn—that is, he will be heavy for the bull, which has twin horns. In this sense, "horn" should be in the dative case rather than the ablative <note>Poliziano is discussing a grammatical nuance in a Latin verse. In Latin, *cornu* can be various cases. He argues that while bulls toss things to the stars with their horns, they could not lift a bear "heavy with a double horn" (meaning the bear is a match for the bull), whereas the Rhinoceros famously lifted things with a single horn.</note>.

**What "Tetraones" are in Suetonius, and a correction of an error in the copies of Pliny. Chapter 57.** <margin>Grouse.</margin>

[Decorative initial E] Most people are entirely ignorant of what kind of birds the *Tetraones* are, mentioned in Suetonius’s *Life of Caligula*. His words are these: "The sacrificial victims were flamingoes, peacocks, grouse <note>original: "tetraones"</note>, Numidian hens, guinea fowls, and pheasants, which were sacrificed specifically each day." However, finding the truth of the matter would not be difficult, if only we did not have such uncorrected copies of Pliny. For what we read in him, in the tenth book of his *Natural History* where he treats geese: "A particular luster and absolute blackness befits the *Erythrotaonas*." <margin>A passage from Pliny.</margin> But in that most ancient manuscript of Pliny from the public library of the Medici family, it is read almost correctly—save for a single letter being changed, just as many words are interpolated in all old volumes. For although these manuscripts are themselves very faulty in many places, they still preserve clear traces for tracking down the true reading, which are often completely erased from newer copies by incompetent scribes. In that manuscript, therefore, it is written: "It befits the *et traonas*"; so that if you swap the order of the first two letters, "Tetraonas" <note>The grouse.</note> leaps out. Therefore, following Poliziano’s authority, you should read the passage in Pliny as: "A particular luster and absolute blackness befits the grouse. They have a scarlet redness on their eyebrows. Another kind of them exceeds the size of vultures, whose color they also mimic; nor does any bird, except the ostrich <margin>Ostrich.</margin>, fill a greater weight of body, becoming so enlarged that they are caught even on the ground because they are unable to move. The Alps and the northern regions produce them." Thus far Pliny on the grouse.

**ASCENSIUS** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius (1462–1535) was a scholar and printer who often provided commentary on Poliziano's work. His notes here focus on grammar and the pronunciation of names.</note>
"He emerged" <note>original: *extitit*</note>, he arose, he appeared with a monstrous appearance. So too the poet speaks of "monstrous births of men." Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist scholar.</note> approves of "monstrous" <note>original: *monstruosum*</note> as the form, contrary to the rule of others. "Valesius"—now "Valerius"—following the custom of Parisian women, who often pronounce an "r" for an "s" and vice versa. Truly, whereas he frequently writes "Tatentus" here, I think it should be written "Tetentus," and I have noted it written so in other books. The origin which Poliziano brings forward also approves that it should be written with an "e," whether it is derived from "earth" <note>Latin: *terra*</note> or from "stretching" <note>Latin: *tetendo*</note>. Nevertheless, there is one reason why I would not deny it was called "Tatentus": having heard the oracle, Valesius decided to seek the city of Tarentum. But a rustic man could easily be deceived by the sound of "a" and "e," since the Gauls <note>The French.</note> still pronounce them almost indifferently, to the point that many, even when trying, cannot show the difference between "than" and "then" <note>original: *quā* and *quē*</note> unless they say one is written with "a" and the other with "e." However, a little later in Martial, it is read as "Tarentus" three times. "Of the same color" <note>original: *concolorem*</note>, that is, equally black. <term>Lectisternia</term> <note>A Roman religious ritual where images of gods were placed on couches and served a meal.</note>: draped couches upon which, as some wish, the images of the gods were laid out; or, as others say, those seeking help lay down upon them, just as we see people today lying down at the tombs and relics of the saints. "For the sake of health" <note>original: *salutis ergo*</note>, that is, for the cause of health. "Moreover the sixth," meaning the sixth games, "which occurred," meaning they were distant from each other by eighty-three years; perhaps you might more correctly read it as eighty-three years. But it is strange that the same man "danced" twice with such a long interval, since boys did not dance. "Without any peaks" <note>original: *citra vlla fastigia*</note>, that is, without the marks of accentuation.

**The origin and rites of the Secular Games; and other things related to them: the oracle of the Sibyl cited therein: and soon, certain things explained in passing, and others refuted not without profit. Chapter 58.** <margin>Origin of the Secular Games.</margin>

[Decorative initial R] I think it is worth the effort to collect here also the origin of the Secular Games <note>The *Ludi Saeculares*, a major Roman festival meant to happen once in a "saeculum" or long lifetime (roughly 100-110 years).</note>, the cause of their name, the span of years between them, how often they were held, by what rite, and for which gods they were celebrated. For the matter is itself not unworthy of being known—provided one has any passion for antiquity—and it brings great help to understanding many passages in the poets. When, therefore, a war was being waged between the Romans and the Albans, and both battle lines stood ready for action, <margin>Illusions of demons.</margin> there suddenly appeared a certain figure of monstrous appearance, clothed in a dark skin, shouting that Father Dis <note>Pluto, god of the Underworld.</note> and the goddess Proserpina commanded a sacrifice to be made to them before the battle was joined. Terrified by this sight, the Romans immediately built an altar under the earth, and as soon as the sacrifice was performed, they covered it with a mound of twenty feet, so that it would be unknown to everyone except the Romans themselves. But it happened that Valesius <margin>Valesus Valesius.</margin> (whence comes the name and origin of the Valerian family), a most distinguished man of the Sabine people and a wealthy man of rustic life, found this altar we have mentioned through divine intervention. He had a grove in front of his farmhouse with very tall trees, which were suddenly struck by a lightning bolt and burned. Not long after, his two sons and a daughter were seized by a pestilential disease and were suffering to the point that the doctors despaired. When, therefore, the father threw himself down before the household gods <note>original: *laribus familiaribus*</note> for the health of his children, offering his own life and the lives of the children's mother as a vow, a voice was suddenly heard from the grove that had been struck from heaven. It promised they would be saved if, having been carried on the Tiber to Tarentum, they drank water from the river itself, heated at the hearth of Dis and Proserpina. Since he knew that Tarentum was very far away (namely, in the farthest part of Iapygia <note>The heel of Italy.</note>) and that no River Tiber was found near that city, he began to imagine the worst for his hopes, being further terrified that the voice had mentioned the powers of the underworld. Nevertheless, having placed his children in a boat, he set out for Ostia <note>The port of Rome.</note> and soon drifted down to the region of the Campus Martius. There, desiring to refresh those who were thirsty and suffering from heat and fever, he set the sick children on the bank where the river flows most calmly. While he was putting together a makeshift mat for himself, and his small fire had gone out, he was advised by the pilot that he should rather seek Tarentum <margin>Tarentum.</margin> (for that was the name of a nearby place), as he saw smoke there. Then, indeed, having heard the name of Tarentum, he was more joyful...

# **Of the Miscellanies**

Valesius, praying to the gods and now almost in good faith promising himself the recovery of his children, ordered the ship to be driven forward and to put in at that very spot. When he had arrived there, he hastily drew water from the river. Relying on the omen he had firmly seized, he coaxed the smoking earth into a flame by blowing on it, and soon offered the warmed water to the boys in a cup. After the drink, sleep followed. In their rest, they saw their illness being wiped away with a sponge by someone unknown. They were then commanded that dark-colored <note>original: "furvae". In Roman religion, black or dark-colored animals were specifically sacrificed to deities of the underworld.</note> sacrificial victims should be offered there to Father Dis and Proserpina <note>The Roman deities of the underworld, equivalent to the Greek Hades and Persephone.</note>, and that three consecutive nights <term>trinoctium | a three-night festival</term> should be celebrated with dances and songs. 

They rose, therefore, with their health restored, and reported the vision to their father. As he was a wealthy man, he ordered the ground to be dug deep for the laying of foundations. In this way, the altar we mentioned was discovered, bearing an inscription to Dis and Proserpina. He immediately sacrificed the dark victims (as he had been commanded) and observed the three nights of sacred rites; for he had received back that many sons from the very jaws of death. <meta>This page continues Poliziano’s exploration of the Secular Games (Ludi Saeculares), moving from the legendary origins of the Valerian family to the historical instances of these games under the Roman emperors and the specific rituals performed during the three-day festival.</meta>

**First Century. Folio 149.**

[Marginal note: Stephanio lived <unclear>X</unclear> years.]
We have learned that Stephanio, who was the first to institute dancing in the *toga* <note>original: "togatis saltare". The *toga* was the formal garment of a Roman citizen; dancing in it was a notable innovation in Roman theater.</note>, performed at both sets of Secular Games: those of Augustus and those of Claudius. These games took place no more than eighty-four years apart, although Stephanio lived for a long time afterward. Domitian celebrated the seventh occurrence of the games in his own fourteenth consulship, with Lucius Minutius Russus as his colleague. He calculated the timing not from when Claudius had last held them, but from the earlier era of Augustus. Indeed, on various coins in the collection of our patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, we have seen this very inscription: ->HE CELEBRATED THE SECULAR GAMES IN HIS FOURTEENTH CONSULSHIP.<- <note>original: "LVD. SAEC. FEC. COS. XIIII"</note> I was already pointing out to my students that Papinius <note>The poet Statius.</note> refers to these games in his short poem to Gallicus, the Prefect of the City, titled *Soteria*, back when I was publicly lecturing on that volume nine years ago. The words are as follows:

*Nor have the new ages brought such a reproach upon the fates,*
*Or the restored altar of Tarentum committed a fault.*

In this passage, our friend Domitius <note>Domizio Calderini, a contemporary rival scholar of Poliziano.</note>, while mentioning the altar of Tarentum and the gods of the underworld themselves, nevertheless suspects nothing at all regarding these Secular Games. Furthermore, in the works of Martial—who is almost of the same literary era—he forgets his own talent, so to speak. I clearly refuted him (if I am not mistaken) both then and a year later when I was explaining the *Fasti* <note>Ovid’s "Calendar" of Roman festivals.</note>. There is an epigram by Martial about a matron who, I believe, had been present at two games—those of Claudius and Domitian—and in it is this verse:

*Twice has my life beheld the Roman Tarentum.* <note>The "Tarentum" or "Terentum" was a specific site in the Campus Martius in Rome associated with these games, not the city in southern Italy.</note>

In this place, a man of little sense <note>A jab at the rival scholar mentioned above.</note> says that it was customary for the sacred rites at Tarentum to be celebrated every thirty years—a thing no one has ever heard of, even by rumor. Indeed, while discussing those verses from the fourth book of the same poet:

*May he worship the ages returning in a great five-year cycle,*
*And the sacred rites held by Romulean Tarentum.*

He even separates the latter part from the former; and just as he thinks the "Secular Games" are in the first part, he imagines some fictional "thirty-year" rites are hinted at in the second. However, Varro mentions this Tarentum in his commentary on the Latin language, and Ovid mentions it again in the *Fasti*. But I return to where I Digressed. One hundred and ten years after Domitian’s games, the Emperor Septimius Severus restored them. Even now, his beautiful triumphal arch is seen in Rome <margin>The Arch of Septimius Severus.</margin>, built with his sons, Antoninus and Geta, when Chilo and Libo were consuls. Herodian records that he saw these games, and Dio handed down to memory that they occurred in his own time. After Severus, Zosimus denies they were restored. This is because the cycle of one hundred and ten years, which had been accepted as the authoritative span, would have fallen during the third consulship of Constantine, the Christian prince, and Licinius (whom Constantine later defeated in war). However, we read in the chronicles of Eusebius and in the ninth book of Eutropius's history that during the reign of Emperor Philip <margin>Emperor Philip, the first Christian.</margin> (who is believed to have been the first Christian emperor), the thousandth year of the city of Rome was celebrated with a massive display of games and spectacles. Countless beasts were killed in the circus, and theatrical plays were celebrated in the Campus Martius for three days and nights with the people keeping watch. Regarding these Secular Games, it is said that Philip the Younger—who is believed never to have laughed—noted with a turned-away face that his father, Philip the Elder, was laughing a bit too wantonly. It remains for us to touch upon a few details of the ritual.

As the games approached, heralds were sent throughout all of Italy <margin>The ritual of the Secular [Games].</margin> to summon people to "games which no one had seen, nor would ever see again." Then, in the summertime, a few days before the spectacles were presented, the Fifteen Men <term>Quindecimviri | The college of priests in charge of the Sibylline Books and these games</term>, sitting upon a platform in the temples of the Capitol and the Palatine, distributed means of purification to the people <margin>Purifications.</margin>. These were sulfur and bitumen. However, slaves had no right to receive them. The people would gather not only in the places I mentioned above, but also at the Temple of Diana on the Aventine; it was the custom to give each person wheat, beans, and barley. Then, in the manner of <margin>In the manner of.</margin> the initiations of Ceres, night-watches were held. When the festival day finally arrived, they occupied themselves with sacred rites for three days and three nights, especially upon the very bank of the Tiber. Sacrifices were undertaken for Jupiter, Juno, Apollo, Latona, and Diana, and additionally for the Fates, and those goddesses called the Ilithyiae <note>Goddesses of childbirth.</note>, and then for Ceres, Dis, and Proserpina. Therefore, at the second hour of the first night, the Prince himself, at three altars built on the riverbank, would sacrifice three lambs, and the Fifteen Men would do the same. Once the altars were soaked with blood, they would burn the bodies of the slain victims. A stage having been constructed in the manner of a theater, lights and fires were kindled, and hymns were sung, composed specifically for this purpose. Solemn spectacles were also customary, with a reward given to those celebrating: the wheat, beans, and barley which we showed above were distributed among the whole populace. In the morning, they would ascend the Capitol, perform the customary sacred rites there, and then gather in the theater for games held in honor of Apollo and Diana. On the following day, at the hour prescribed by the oracle, noble matrons would gather on the Capitol to pray to the god, attend the ritual banquets <term>lectisternia | a ritual meal offered to statues of the gods</term>, and sing hymns according to the rite. Finally, on the third day, in the Temple of Palatine Apollo, thrice-nine <note>Twenty-seven.</note> boys and as many girls, all with both parents living <note>original: "patrimi matrimique". A ritual requirement that the children's parents must still be alive for them to be considered ritually "pure" or lucky.</note>, sang songs and hymns of praise in both the Greek and Latin tongues, by which they commended their empire and the safety of the people to the immortal gods. If anyone should ask what kind of games or sacrifices were held then, let him know that games were celebrated in all the theaters...

# First Century. Folio 150.

"I think it is." For that which is written "it is as I think": otherwise Servius <note>Servius was a famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil; Poliziano is likely debating his grammatical interpretations.</note> would have said "I think it to be." On the word "more obscene": as I have said elsewhere, it comes from the "Osci" <note>The Oscans were an ancient people of Italy, often associated in the Roman mind with rustic or lewd behavior.</note>, rather than the derivation suggested by Ascensius <margin>Ascensius</margin> which I find less convincing.

**That Ovid, not Virgil, seems to be the author of the *Priapeia* poems. Then that the little verse which is found thus in Martial: *Laugh, if you are wise, O girl, laugh*, is without doubt by Naso [Ovid]: but it seems to be cited from his epigrams rather than from his *Art of Love* or from the tragedy *Medea*: and soon something new and wonderful regarding Ovid's *Medea* is added. Chapter LIX.**

[Q] Most people attribute those epigrams called the *Priapeia* <note>The *Priapeia* is a collection of eighty-some poems dedicated to Priapus, the god of fertility, known for their explicit and humorous sexual content.</note> to Virgil; among these (I believe) is also Servius. <margin>Priapeia.</margin> However, in those books of Seneca <note>Seneca the Elder, a rhetorician whose works were rediscovered during the Renaissance.</note>—which had long been hidden and have recently been brought into the light, even if they appeared in a form not entirely pure—which encompass the opinions, divisions, and rhetorical "colors" of the orators and rhetoricians in their persuasive speeches: (unless by chance we believe the text is faulty, as there is only a single copy) I detect that these poems are spurious, and belong not to Virgil, but to Ovid. Indeed, in Seneca's second volume, the words are as follows: "I remember a certain man of praetorian rank saying this kind of sentiment when he was declaiming a legal controversy concerning a woman who sued her husband for ill-treatment because she was still a virgin and had been condemned. Afterward, he sought the priests. We know, he said, that abstinence of husbands: who, even if they grant the first night to fearful virgins, nevertheless play in neighboring places." Scaurus was listening to him—not only a most eloquent man, but most charming, who never allowed anyone's stupidity to pass unpunished—and he immediately quoted that line of Ovid:

> *While the foolish woman fears a wound in another place.* <note>original: "Dum timet alterius vulnus inepta loci." This line contains a sexual double-entendre regarding anatomy.</note>

And that man faltered, and said no more. Thus far Seneca. We know, moreover, that this very verse is in a *Priapeia* epigram, the beginning of which is:

> *I could speak to you obscurely.* <note>original: "Obscure poteram tibi dicere."</note>

But even the style itself (unless I am mistaken) and a certain genuine Ovidian "playfulness" <note>original: "lasciuia"</note> is present in those verses. However, the extent to which this authority should be trusted must be left to the judgment of the readers. Just as I have not written this as a baseless claim, neither do I present it as an established fact. Certainly, such obscenity suits Ovid as it does in his other works; conversely, it is unbecoming of Virgil, who was called "Parthenias" <margin>Virgil the "Maiden."</margin> <note>The nickname "Parthenias" (from the Greek for "maiden") was given to Virgil because of his legendary modesty and shy demeanor.</note> on account of his maidenly modesty. The very title of this work—though it might make even an unsworn and suspicious witness blush—makes it truly difficult not to believe my point. It is certainly established that Naso [Ovid] wrote other epigrams as well, from which Priscian cites this verse:

> *With Lars slain, the fierce Cossus brought back the spoils of honor.* <note>original: "Larte ferox cæso Cossus opima tulit."</note>

And Quintilian had surely read this line in his playful works:

> *Why should I not call you a fury, you fury?*

And I would not believe that the Phalaecian hendecasyllable <note>A specific meter of eleven syllables, often used for light, witty, or erotic poetry.</note> cited by Martial was found anywhere else but in Ovid's epigrams:

> *Laugh, if you are wise, O girl, laugh.* <note>original: "Ride si sapis o puella ride."</note>

As for Domitius, who thinks this precept refers to one of the *Arts of Love*, he is refuted by the authority of Martianus Capella, who in his *Satire* recognizes it as a verse of Naso [Ovid], not Martial. I have even heard those who believed it was from the tragedy *Medea*, <margin>Ovid's *Medea*.</margin> which Tacitus and Quintilian praise, and which the author Tertullian says was—to my surprise—sewn together almost entirely from Virgilian words; we also mentioned this in *The Nurse*. But this does not seem likely to me. For who has ever read Phalaecian verses in either a Greek or a Latin tragedy? Or what about this verse tastes of tragedy at all? It recoils and shrinks away entirely from that terrifying gravity! Or does Martianus himself not almost clearly deny that this is from a tragedy, if only his words are faithfully recited and diligently weighed? Does he not, in his *Satire*—which is austere and censorial—having chastised the plays of the tragic brow with too much severity, turn back as if inviting a softening of the face? He says: "As for the rest, grow wise by the verse of the Pelignian youth <note>Ovid was born in Sulmo, in the territory of the Peligni.</note>; and (unless you are wrinkled by tragedy):"

> *Laugh, if you are wise, O girl, laugh.*

He says, "Unless you are wrinkled by tragedy," which means "unless you wrinkle your brow with tragic severity." This refers to the sadness of wrinkles and the roughness of a frown. <margin>To wrinkle the brow.</margin> Therefore, if the verse itself were from a tragedy, the poet would be trying to recall his *Satire* from that very tragic austerity using a tragic line; surely this joke would be (as I think) "Coldly spitting white snow upon the winter Alps." <note>A quote from Horace, used here to suggest a joke that falls flat or is nonsensical.</note> Now if anyone doubts the sincerity of this reading, let him inspect the most ancient books of Martianus from the public Medicean library <note>The Laurentian Library in Florence, founded by the Medici family.</note> of the Florentine people; for I believe his diligence will surely support our good faith.

"Substuler" [he took away]. I shall read "Sustuler"; for in a compound where it signifies "upward" or "from below," the "b" has no place: as in "susque deque" [up and down] or "fero" [I carry]. "Surgo" [I rise]: "surrigo" [I lift up], etc. <margin>Ascensius</margin>

Poliziano is noting that this was the ritual question asked by a sacrificial official before striking a victim.</note> which is what is usually done with sacrificial victims." **First Century. Folio 151.**

## That the words of Terence are cited differently by Varro than they are found in the manuscripts or recognized by Donatus. Chapter 63.

**M**arcus Varro, in his books *On the Latin Language*, speaks thus: In Terence, "He whores, he drinks, <margin>Passage in Terence: Whore.</margin> he smells of perfumes at my expense." <note>original: "Scortatur, potat, olet vnguenta de meo."</note> To "whore" (*scortari*) is to take a little prostitute quite often. So says Varro, and then other things to that effect. However, all the manuscripts of Terence to a single man do not have "he whores" as Varro reads, but "he buys provisions" <note>original: "obsonat"</note>. Now, the passage is in *The Brothers* <note>original: "Adelphis," a comedy by Terence (c. 195–158 BC).</note>. "He buys provisions, he drinks, he smells of perfumes at my expense." This reading is also recognized by Donatus <note>Aelius Donatus, a 4th-century grammarian and commentator on Terence.</note>. What then shall we say here? Is there an error in all the manuscripts of Terence? Or (which I would hardly dare believe) did the memory of Varro himself waver—Varro, who was called the "most prolific writer" <note>original: "polygraphōtaton"</note> <margin>i.e., one who wrote many things. Praise of diligence.</margin> by Cicero? Just as Gellius <note>Aulus Gellius, a 2nd-century author known for his "Attic Nights."</note> detected the same in Cicero? We must admit that even the greatest geniuses are sometimes hindered by negligence, while diligence is beneficial in every way.

## Explanation of the verses of Ausonius, as well as Ovid, regarding the Choliamb or Scazon. Chapter 64.

**A**usonius the poet has trimeter verses that go like this: <margin>Passage in Ausonius.</margin>
"To whom shall I yoke from the turnings of the mill-stones:
Who roll the stones with mechanical weight
Three-footed Nags: their backs broken by the whip."
What should we think he means here? Surely, as I think, those verses which are called Choliambs <margin>Choliambs, Scazons.</margin> or Scazons—as if you were to say "limping" ones. Such as those found in Persius at the beginning, or like those of Martial, cited by him by name:
"Meet my Scazon, Apollinaris."
For a Scazon is an iambic trimeter, consisting of six feet itself, just like a straight iambic. It is different in this one way: as Hephaestion <note>A Greek grammarian of the 2nd century AD who wrote on meters.</note> writes, while the straight one occupies the last position with an iamb or a pyrrhic foot, and in the antepenultimate accepts all feet (of which that meter is capable regarding the quantities of the syllables), this limping iambic requires a spondaic or trochaic ending. As for the penultimate foot: it is not just any two-syllable foot, but clearly an iamb or a spondee. As to what Hephaestion says—that a spondee is received in the fifth seat of the choliamb—I do not recall ever finding this among the Latin poets, though he himself brings forward this Greek verse:
"Dragging to the top just as cooling a sausage." <note>original: "ἐπ’ ἄκρον ἕλκων ὥσπερ ἄλλαντα ψύχων."</note>
And Quintilianus Aristides, the Greek author, in his book *On Music*, speaking on the iambic trimeter: says it becomes "limping" when it receives a spondee at the end. Finally, Ovid also, in his first book on the *Remedies for Love*, writes of both types of iamb thus:
"Let the free iamb be drawn against opposing enemies,
Whether it be swift, or whether it drags its final foot."
Both, however, are made for slander and freedom of speech; they are fierce and bloody. For this reason, Ovid says they should be "drawn against opposing enemies." Dionysius of Halicarnassus also, in his book *On Composition*, says the Choliamb is a forceful or sharp meter. <margin>Choliambs.</margin> And he says soon after that Hipponax, when he wanted to provoke his enemies with insults, broke the meter on purpose and made it limping and unrhythmical instead of straight—that is, a meter suitable for bitterness and insult. For just as a loose figure of speech prepares the way for bitterness, so (as he says) does a loose composition. Therefore, Ausonius <margin>Nags.</margin> names those Choliambs "Nags" (*Caballos*), a metaphor he drew from a carriage or vehicle to which Nags are hitched. And to show they are slow, he says they are "taken from the turnings of the mill-stones," and furthermore, "their backs broken by the whip." Then he called them "three-footed," because in Greek they are called "trimeters," although they have six feet; <margin>Trimeters.</margin> for in iambics, two feet are seen to be taken as one. "Who roll the stones with mechanical weight": he said this either as if describing the mill-stones he had indicated they were turning, or to show they are violent and fierce allegorically, as if they hurl and roll huge stones at the enemy. Regarding both types of trimeter, the same Ausonius says elsewhere in a Greek verse:
"The club-footed Scazon and the non-scazon trimeter." <note>original: "ἐλιπόβιω σκάζοντα καὶ οὐ σκάζοντα trimetron."</note> Which you may translate into Latin thus:
"The club-footed Scazon and the non-scazon trimeter."
Regarding these same Scazons, it says in a certain letter from the fifth book of the younger Pliny: <margin>Scazons.</margin> "Therefore either break off delays, or beware lest those same booklets, which my hendecasyllables could not draw out from you with flatteries, the Scazons extort with insult."

ASCENSIUS <note>likely Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer/scholar who often added notes to such editions.</note>: The "Peacemaker" pose is placed in statues as a disposition, not a garment, signifying one who is peaceful.

## Who this Peacemaker in statues might be, and the passage in the first book of the *Silvae* concerning him. Chapter 65. <margin>Passage in Statius.</margin>

**S**tatius, in the first *Silvae*, which was written about the Great Horse <note>Referring to the massive equestrian statue of the Emperor Domitian in the Roman Forum.</note>: "It is a joy to look upon the face mixed with the marks of war, and bearing calm peace." Then the same: "The right hand forbids battles." Which passage Domitius <note>Domizio Calderini, a rival Renaissance humanist whose commentaries Poliziano often critiqued.</note> explains thus: "'The right hand forbids battles,' that is, it is unarmed in the statue, or to the right is the Temple of Peace: which he says he does not like."

# Miscellanies

**The Linden Tree.** Pliny, in the sixteenth book of his *Natural History*, relates things that you will surely recognize quite easily: that what we call the **Linden** <note>Latin: *Tilia*</note> is the same as what the Greeks call the **Philyra**. <note>The Greek term *philyra* refers specifically to the inner bark of the linden tree, used in antiquity as a writing surface.</note> And indeed, Theodorus Gaza <note>A 15th-century Greek scholar and translator of Aristotle and Theophrastus.</note>, despite being a man of great learning and diligence, translates it this way.

**Ribbons.** Furthermore, there are certain thin membranes or "little tunics" made from the inner bark of the Linden tree itself, or made in imitation of it, from which either **Ribbons** <note>Latin: *lemnisci*</note>—that is, small bandages or fillets hanging from crowns—or little books were made. These were specifically called *philyrae* using the Greek word. Pliny testifies to a part of this in the same book with these lines: "Between the outer bark and the wood are thin membranes, a manifold skin, from which Linden bonds are drawn; the thinnest of these are the *philyrae*, famous for the ribbons of crowns, an honor among the ancients." And again, in the twenty-first book, he mentions Ribbons and *Philyrae* as follows: "Crassus the Rich was the first to give crowns at his games with leaves imitating silver and gold; then Ribbons were added, which was an extra honor for the crowns because of the Etruscans, to whom only golden ribbons should be joined. For a long time, these remained plain."

<margin>**The Linden Tree.**</margin>
<margin>**Ribbons.**</margin>
<margin>**To Caesar.**</margin>
<margin>**Ribbons.**</margin>
<margin>**Ribboned Crowns.**</margin>
<margin>**Philyra.**</margin>

**To Caesar.** Caesar was the first to institute them. P. Claudius Pulcher also gave gold-leaf <note>Latin: *bracteas*</note> to the *Philyra*. Furthermore, we repeatedly see **Ribboned crowns** (if I am not mistaken) on the coins of Lorenzo de' Medici; mention of these is also found in Suetonius. Likewise, Pompeius Festus diligently explains the word "Ribbon." Tertullian also says something about Ribbons in his book *On the Soldier's Crown*. Nicas, however, in the commentary he arranged in alphabetical order—writing in Greek, but understood in this sense in our language—interprets **Philyra** as follows: "The Philyra," he says, "is a plant having a bark similar to papyrus, from which even ropes are twisted." That the *Philyra* is pliable like wool, or rather spinnable, is also suggested by the same Tertullian in the little book titled *On the Mantle*. Moreover, the Greek author Herodian, whom I long ago translated into Latin and dedicated to Pope Innocent VIII, mentions in the first book of his history a little book made of the thinnest *Philyra*, which could be folded back on both sides. But also Martianus Capella, in the sixth book of *The Marriage of Philology and Mercury*, says: "One could see what books, how many volumes, and works in how many languages flowed from the mouth of the maiden. Some were seen to be made of papyrus, which had been smeared with cedar oil. Other books were wrapped in linen volumes, and some were even made from the skins of sheep. Rarely, however, were they noted down on the bark of the *Philyra*." Then you may also find these words of Ulpian in the title of the *Digest* concerning legacies and trusts: "The designation of 'books' includes all volumes, whether they are on paper, or on parchment, or on any other material. But even if they are on *Philyra*, or Linden—as some imagine—or on some other hide, the same must be said." Finally, even Eustathius, in his commentary on the second book of Homer’s *Odyssey*, having previously mentioned nautical ropes, says the bark of the Linden—which he calls *philyra* in Greek—supplies abundant material for that kind of rope. It seems to have been accepted from this that they call individual hides, or membranes of material different from the Linden, *philyras* or *philuras*—the Greek letter *y* being changed to *u* by an old and common custom of the Latins. Thus Pliny, dealing with papyrus in Book 13, says: "From it they prepare papers divided with a needle into very thin, but as wide as possible, *philuras*." For that other point which Pliny mentions in Book 18 certainly does not pertain to this explanation: that the **Philyra** removes the excessive saltiness for cooks from their porridge. 
<margin>**Philurae.**</margin>
<margin>**Removal of salt.**</margin>
**Ascensius.** <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, a famous printer and commentator.</note> Regarding the word *supernati* [having grown above], I think it should be written *suppernati* [hamstrung], so that they are those whose haunches [pernae] have been cut from below.

***

**That the word *Expernata* should be restored to the manuscripts of Catullus. Chapter 73.**

<margin>**The work of Pompeius Festus.**</margin>
<margin>**Pomponius Leto.**</margin>
<margin>**Catullus.**</margin>
<margin>**Suppernati.**</margin>
<margin>**Expernata.**</margin>

[Decorative initial Q] What we are about to hand down now will perhaps be derided and hissed at by some as uncertain, wavering, and not yet sufficiently explored. But I thought I must speak of it, lest this trace of antiquity, already almost abolished, be extinguished, whatever it may be. Four years ago in Rome, Manilius Rallus—a Greek man, but excellently refined in Latin literature—showed me a certain fragment of Sextus Pompeius Festus (for so it was titled), truly ancient but for the most part mutilated and eaten away by mice. This held my attention greatly, since those remains, such as they were, survived from the original complete volume which the author Festus had composed. It was not from this abridgment <note>The epitome of Festus made by Paul the Deacon in the 8th century, which Poliziano disparages.</note> which is now violently compressed and shortened in our hands, namely by some ignoble and unlearned man who, even by that name, did not deserve well enough of literature. Pomponius Leto, a man most learned in antiquity and good letters, had also kept for himself some pages from the same fragment, which he likewise gave to me to read and transcribe. From that reading, I certainly suspected that I would restore a word of Catullus to its proper home, as if by "right of return" <note>Latin: *postliminio*, a legal term for the restoration of rights to a person returning from exile.</note>. For where this abridgment explains the word **Suppernati**, showing that it signifies those whose thighs are cut through in the manner of swine's haunches [pernae], a verse is cited from Ennius:
*Against these men, the unjust pride of the Carthaginian cut through their haunches.* <note>original Latin: "His pernas succidit iniqua superbia Poeni."</note>
In this very place, the old manuscript has an explanation that is clearly gnawed all around; however, it appears from the remaining, poorly coherent letters that Catullus is also brought in after Ennius, and that verse is cited which is now erroneously read as: *He lies in a Ligurian ditch, separated by an axe.* <note>original: "In fossa Liguri iacet separata securi." This is from Catullus 17.19.</note> 
For while I would not rashly claim anything regarding the rest of the poem, I seemed then, sniffing out every syllable, to be able to offer as certain that we should read **expernata** [hamstrung/cut at the thigh] in it, not *separata* [separated]. This is as much as I could gather from those few "scraps" or "shavings," and as much as I could divine even from the almost obliterated traces. If the truth of this still seems to hang in the balance for anyone, I would rather it hang than fall.

**First Century. Folio 153.**

...or it may lie fallow. We certainly place some firm foundation in it, and I do not think we do so unjustly.

-> A not-unpleasant story concerning Zeuxis the painter and Helen. Chapter 74. <-

<margin>Zeuxis. Helen.</margin> **E**veryone knows that Zeuxis, the painter from Heraclea, was exceptionally noble. He even painted an image of Helen for the people of Croton, which was praised beyond measure. Cicero wrote most brilliantly about this in his works on rhetoric against Hermagoras. <note>Cicero discusses Zeuxis choosing the five most beautiful virgins of Croton as models for his Helen in *De Inventione*.</note> However, I happened to read something in passing in Aelian’s books of *Miscellaneous History* <note>Latin: *omnifariae historiae*; a reference to Claudius Aelianus’s *Varia Historia*.</note> a few years ago at the home of Giovanni Lorenzi of Venice—a man of great authority in the papal court and of no less erudition in literature, but also a man of keen judgment <note>original: *emunctae naris*; literally "of a wiped nose," a Latin idiom for someone with sharp, discerning taste</note> whom we read in Rome. What I found there did not seem at all unworthy of being read here as well. He says that Zeuxis would admit no one to view the painting unless they had paid a fee in hand. <margin>Why Helen was called a harlot.</margin> Because of this, the painting was even then commonly called "Helen the Harlot," since she was "for profit." <note>original: *quaestuaria*; suggesting the painting, like a prostitute, was only accessible for money.</note>

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the scholar-printer, adding a grammatical and biographical note.</note> Regarding *Ibis*: He does not observe the precept of Servius, who teaches that words which do not always increase in the genitive and dative should not increase [in syllable count] in that way. But the ablative seems to agree mostly with the dative. Hence what Servius noted: "with a pregnant tiger" <note>original: *tigride foeta*</note> as said by the poet. In which—that is, in what—unless the writing is flawed, he writes concerning the capture of Troy <note>original: *Ilio capta*</note>. Here the word *Ilio* is derived from the nominative *Ilios*, which Horace also uses: "Troubled Ilios." And Ovid in the 14th book of the *Metamorphoses*: "After high Ilios was burned," etc. If only [Poliziano] had not ceased to dwell among the living <note>original: *apud superos*; "among those above," i.e., the living</note> while still a young man. This tastes of either envy or paganism, or rather both. Envy, because he thinks he would have admitted new errors rather than correcting old ones; and because it implies he migrated to the underworld rather than to the heavens. Paganism, because along with Macrobius and other Pagans, he places the "living" here; where, in respect to the dead, we are indeed "above," but in respect to the heavenly beings to whom the souls of the good migrate, we are "below."

-> A corrected passage in the *Ibis*, together with an explanation of a meaning hitherto unknown. Chapter 75. <-

<margin>The distance from the forehead to the tongue.</margin> **N**arravit Domitius <note>Domitius Calderinus, a rival scholar of Poliziano</note>, in his commentary on Ovid’s *Ibis*, prefixed his work by saying he wrote things accepted from Apollodorus, Lycophron, Pausanias, Strabo, Apollonius, and other Greek and Latin authors. In that commentary, he invents many vain and ridiculous things, and devises them according to the occasion and his own convenience. By these, he proves either that he has completely lost his shame <note>original: *frontem*; literally "forehead," the seat of shame in Latin idiom</note> or that there was such a great gap between his forehead and his tongue (as someone once said) that the forehead could not restrain the tongue. It is madness that some lovers of this man are still found so blind that they do not yet open their eyes—such as they are—to these things. It is madness, indeed madness, to give an occasion for impudence to others by fostering the errors of someone just because his opinions were occasionally not to be regretted. <margin>Masters of elementary schooling.</margin> But what can you do with these masters of "lettering" rather than literature, who lift their eyebrows at nothing more than such trifles, like the horns of snails? Their leaden wits, the more they are polished, the more they become dull. But lest we waste our labor entirely, disregarding those whose own worthlessness makes them contemptible, let us pursue the rest of our purpose. For me, that one passage among the others usually stirs my stomach, which is now read so incorrectly:

*And as the talkative one was crushed in the throat on the horse [Agenor],*
*So may the path of your voice be closed by a thumb.*

<margin>A passage in Ovid's *Ibis*.</margin> On this, Domitius says: "Agenor was killed by a hand inserted into his mouth during a fall from a horse." Is that so, most learned man? But I pray you, my dear Domitius, produce a Greek author if you can, or at least a suitable Latin one for this story. If you do, I will not refuse to be condemned as most unlearned and even most impudent by your followers and admirers—or even by any man of letters for whom this work is produced—and that by unanimous vote, since I disagree with you. To me, the writing seems quite correct and sound if one allows for a free conjecture based on reason: not **Agenor**, but **acerno** <note>Meaning "of maple wood," referring to the Trojan Horse.</note>, so that we take it as being said of **Anticlus**. <margin>Anticlus. Related to Helen.</margin> There is an account of him in Homer, in the fourth book of the *Odyssey*. For when Helen had approached that Trojan horse, woven of beams and heavy with soldiers, by the impulse of a deity, she began to imitate the voices of the wives of each man, so that she might evoke the desires of those hiding within, rub their memories raw, and try to elicit a response. But while the others maintained patience and silence, only Anticlus was on the slippery edge of responding. <margin>Ortygides. Laodamia.</margin> He was immediately prevented by Ulysses and suffocated by hands pressed upon him. Thus, by intercepting or rather blocking the evidence, the danger was driven away. Furthermore, Tryphiodorus, a Greek author, in his poem on the capture of Troy, calls this man Anticlus "Ortygides" and names his wife Laodamia, saying thus:

ὀρτυγίδης δ' ἀντίκλος ὁμ' αὐτῶι τεθνεῶτα $\quad$ *Ortygides Anticlus, whom there, dead*
ἵππωι δακρύσαντες ἐνεκτερείξαμ' ἀχαιοί. $\quad$ *In the horse, the weeping Achaeans buried.*

And likewise elsewhere:

ἀντίκλος δ' ὅτε κέντρον ἐλέξατο λαοδαμείης $\quad$ *Anticlus indeed, when he received the sting of Laodamia*
Μενὸς ἀμοιβαιίω ἀνεβάλλετο γῆρυν ἀνοίξας $\quad$ *Began to raise his responding voice alone, opening [his mouth]:*
ἀλλ' ὀδυσσεὺς κατέπαυσε. $\quad$ *But Odysseus rushed upon him [and stopped him].*

And he adds other things thereafter, through which the whole story is explained similarly by Homer in many words. <margin>Ambra.</margin> But we also touched upon this in our *Ambra*: <note>Poliziano's own poem, part of the *Sylvae*.</note>

*And for fear of discovery, the throat of Anticlus Ortygides*
*Was closed by a thumb.*

There are many things similar to these in Domitius's work which easily prove to what extent his license would have proceeded—especially invited as it was by the favors of the unskillful—had he not ceased to dwell among the living while still a young man.

**V iii**

<meta>This page continues Poliziano’s "Miscellanies," moving from his discussion of art history and anecdotes about Zeuxis into the realm of textual criticism (philology). He begins a series of chapters dedicated to correcting errors in classical manuscripts and debating the correct spelling of the poet Virgil’s name based on ancient inscriptions.</meta>

**Of the Miscellanies**

-> That it was not Antilochus who was conquered by Hector: but that it should be read differently in the first of the *Heroides*. Chapter 76. <-

<margin>Ovid in the *Heroides*, Book 1.</margin>

<margin>The slaughter of Amphimachus.</margin>

<margin>The slaughter of Antilochus.</margin>

[Large decorative initial I]n the first epistle of Naso’s <note>Ovid’s full name was Publius Ovidius Naso.</note> *Heroides*, it is read as follows:
*Whether someone was telling of Antilochus conquered by Hector.* <note>original: "Siue quis Antilochum narrabat ab Hectore victum."</note>
But that Antilochus was conquered and killed by Hector will certainly not be found anywhere. Therefore, I would believe either that "Amphimachus" should be read, or that it was not by Hector, but by Memnon. For it is established from the thirteenth "Rhapsody" <note>A common Renaissance term for a "Book" of Homer’s epic.</note> of Homer that Amphimachus, the son of Creatus, was killed by Hector; he is one of the Greek leaders also numbered in the Catalogue of Ships. It is likewise established that Antilochus, the son of Nestor, was killed by Memnon. Therefore, just as a manifest error is detected in the version that has prevailed until now, I would hope that you, reader, might look kindly upon these corrections we have substituted for the time being; for if they do not possess the absolute grace of truth, they certainly lay claim to the grace of probability.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, the printer and commentator whose notes often accompany Poliziano's text.</note> Lodovico Celio <note>Caelius Rhodiginus, a contemporary scholar.</note> contends in the fourth book, chapter four of his *Ancient Lessons* that both *Vergilius* and *Virgilius* can be written on the authority of several authors. **Shameless ones** <note>original: *Propudiosi*</note> refers to those who should be greatly and openly ashamed, because shame is far from them, or because there are many shameful things in them; the word is derived from "shameful act" <note>original: *propudium*</note>. **Rust** <note>original: *Erugo*</note> is written by many with an "Ae" as if from "bronze" <note>original: *aes*</note>; some also think it means "red-rust" <note>original: *rubigo*</note>, but it is rather a defect of bronze or silver. Hence it is used by the Satirists for money that has contracted rust. Vitruvius <note>A famous Roman architect and engineer.</note> judges that the "caterpillar" <note>original: *eruca*</note> is called by another name; here I think those who are hallucinating are signified, because there is much use of "rust" in eye-salves. **To claim** <note>original: *Vindicare*</note>: which many say as *vendicare*, but this is less approved; for it is derived from *Vindicius*, from which also comes *Vindiciae* (legal claims); the distinction sought between *vindico* and *vendico* based on spelling is in vain. **Contemptuously**: they rebuke with contempt. **We expend**: we pay out. **But only these**: let it be repeated so that it reads: "but if I pursue only these things." **We must stand by ancient custom**: that is, we must fight for it, just as soldiers fight for the side on which they stand. **Whence this medley**: This is from Persius. <note>original: *Vnde hęc fartago*; referring to a "hash" or "hodgepodge" of ideas.</note> **The greater part of the youth**: that is, we young men for the most part; this is an imitation of Horace from his *Art of Poetry*: "The greatest part of poets... father and sons worthy of the father... we are deceived by the appearance of right." The authority of inscriptions leaves me cold, because the common crowd of stone-cutters follows the masses, who use 'e' instead of 'i'.

-> By what argument we should say *Vergilius*, not *Virgilius*. Chapter 77. <-

<margin>Vergilius.</margin>

<margin>Shameless ones. Rust. I claim.</margin>

<margin>Illustrators of letters.</margin>

<margin>Trifles and toys.</margin>

<margin>Christopher Landino.</margin>

[Large decorative initial V]hether one should say *Vergilius* or *Virgilius*—as is now commonly spoken, that is, with the second vowel <note>'e'</note> or rather the third <note>'i'</note> in the first syllable—I see is still a matter of doubt among the learned. However, as for why I would say *Vergilius* with an 'e' (which is already beginning to please some who have been taught by us) rather than *Virgilius* with an 'i' (which has too much prevailed among the common people), the reason lies in several very ancient monuments that patronize our observation. These I will gladly put forward on account of certain "shameless" and "rust-filled" men, worthy of all hatred and loathing, who, although they are forever mere alphabet-teachers, nevertheless dare to claim for themselves the censorship of literature among unlearned supporters. They do this so that they might not only quibble with our diligence and zeal for detecting and restoring antiquity (if it be permitted), but even rebuke it so sharply as if they thought it a crime that we delight in such leisure—or (as they say more contemptuously) that we "begrudge our own leisure" for these things, while we take up work in such frivolous and light matters, as if we were expending that most precious thing, time, on the superfluous. Yet if they had read that the greatest men once composed entire volumes on single letters, and that even Caesar himself did not fear to descend into such subtleties, they would perhaps grant me pardon—though I am not a man of much leisure—if at times, between higher studies, I also treat matters of this sort: small indeed, but by which even great things are aided. Nor do I think I am rightly rebuked if I pursue these things—but only these—to which I refer myself not as if moving from leisure to study, but as if from study to leisure. I am not so much driven to this by profession as I fall into it by chance, as if walking for convenience along the shores, I safely gather shells in the meantime. Nor do I raise my eyebrows so high, nor would I easily allow myself to be judged thereby, as if I did not know that these things are not only "trifles and toys" <note>original: *Apinas & tricas*; a Latin proverb for things of no value.</note> as the playful proverb goes, but even almost nothing—and this I confess. But nonetheless, it is better to do this very "nothing" than to draw out long yawns perhaps after their example, and to grunt shamefully in the mud, or to do nothing at all, lest by doing absolutely nothing, we learn to do poorly.

Evidence must therefore be rendered by us, so that our credit does not limp anywhere, and so that nothing is not ready for those wishing to know. You will find at Bolsena <note>Latin: *Volsinii*</note> a certain marble table in very ancient, almost obsolete characters within the Church of St. Christina (which is near the Church of St. Peter the Apostle), where one reads *VERGILI*. You will also find this name noted as *Vergilius* at Sutri on a stone table which they use as an altar inside the church of the Virgin. We inspected both of these from close up, not without several witnesses. For we desired to be not only "hearing" witnesses of ancient inspections, but "seeing" ones as well. Furthermore, in those *Pandects* <note>The *Digest*, a collection of Roman law compiled under Justinian.</note> which are now publicly preserved at Florence, in the very Archetype book of the Emperor Justinian, that name is noted in no other way than with an 'e'. It is the same in the volume of Maro <note>Virgil's full name was Publius Vergilius Maro.</note> prepared in larger letters, which appears wonderfully ancient in the inner Vatican library at Rome. Moreover, Cristoforo Landino <note>Poliziano's teacher and a famous Florentine humanist.</note>—an eloquent and learned man, for a long time now a most celebrated teacher of fine literature at Florence—now has in his hands the commentary of Tiberius Donatus. My own youthful beginnings owe much to him as a teacher, and he now favors us as a colleague (as I might call it) in the profession; with his own fame already secured, he favors us while we are still laboring most hard in the stadium, so that whatever praise we acquire for ourselves, he seems to embrace and acknowledge as his own. He, therefore (as we said), has in his hands the commentary of Tiberius Donatus, which is itself marked with larger ancient characters, the authority of which leaves this matter beyond doubt.

<summary>Poliziano argues that a line in Ovid's Heroides contains a factual error regarding Antilochus' death and makes a pioneering case for spelling "Vergilius" with an 'e' based on ancient marble inscriptions and early manuscripts.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Poliziano’s philological investigation into the correct spelling of the poet Virgil's name, moving from literary arguments to physical evidence found in ancient manuscripts and stone inscriptions. It then transitions into corrections of legal texts and explanations of classical iconography and mythology.</meta>

**First Century. Folio 154.**

Just as in the manuscript of Saint Augustine’s *The City of God* from the public library of the Medici family, and likewise in a manuscript of Columella from the private collection of that same family—both of which are written in Lombardic script <note>A style of medieval handwriting used before the revival of "antique" or humanistic script.</note>—and also in an ancient book of Seneca’s epistles, which was made available to me by Niccolò Michelozzi (secretary to Lorenzo de' Medici and a man of elegant wit), and in many other volumes venerable for their antiquity: I have repeatedly compared these findings, sometimes with our close associate and assistant in studies, Jacopo Modesto of Prato, and at other times with my other students, as the situation required or demanded. Furthermore, in the collection of ancient inscriptions and monuments that Iucundus <margin>Iucundus of Verona <note>Fra Giocondo, a famous architect and scholar who collected ancient inscriptions for Lorenzo de' Medici.</note></margin> of Verona recently sent to Lorenzo de' Medici—a man who is, in my opinion, not only the most diligent but also the most indisputably expert of all mortals regarding such things—I find two epitaphs recorded that were found in Rome (as he indicates) carved in marble: **TIBERIUS VERGILIUS DONATUS**. And again: **GAIUS PAPIRIUS CESTUS TO VERGILIA OPTATA, HIS WELL-DESERVING WIFE.** Even if these monuments, strengthened by the antiquity of so many ages, were not enough of a defense for me, the matter itself and reason also agree. For just as I would believe this name is derived from the stars truly called the "Vergiliae" <margin>The Vergiliae <note>The Latin name for the Pleiades star cluster, associated with the coming of spring.</note></margin> or from spring (*ver*) itself, it is certainly more likely than being derived from "virga" (a wand or laurel branch), as some triflers suggest. For not only is that found in a less reliable author, but it is refuted by the fact that many people were called by this same name long before this poet published his work. Therefore, since no testimony is more weighty and no reason more powerful, we must certainly stand by ancient custom rather than modern ignorance. From where this "hodge-podge" of speaking <note>Poliziano is mocking the corruption of the Latin language over time.</note> entered into our tongues is unclear, for many of us younger scholars are blind to the sight of the truth. Indeed, to follow up on the rest, we noticed in Rome the name "Verginius"—a name closely related to this—not "Virginius," inscribed on a marble basin in front of the Church of Saint Mary Major.

**ASCENSIUS.** Archetypes: meaning the principal and first types from which all others were copied. An archetype is what is commonly called an "original."

### A false negation added to the first volume of the *Digests*, in the chapter concerning the office of proconsuls and legates. Chapter 78.

[Large initial A]ulus the legal consultant writes as follows in the second book *On the Edict*: <margin>A passage from the *Digest*.</margin> "A legate, when jurisdiction has been mandated to him, has the right to grant a judge." But you will find these words in the first volume of the *Digests* <note>The *Digest* or *Pandects* was a massive compilation of Roman law authorized by Emperor Justinian.</note>, in the chapter where the office of proconsul and legate is treated, with a negation rashly added in most manuscripts, like this: "A legate... does *not* have the right to grant a judge." However, in those Florentine Pandects <margin>Archetype <note>Poliziano refers to the famous 6th-century manuscript of Roman law kept in Florence, which humanists considered the "original" source.</note></margin>, which we also believe to be the archetype, there is absolutely no negation. Because of this, the Florentine interpreter of laws, Accursius <note>The primary medieval commentator on Roman law.</note>, having himself encountered a faulty manuscript, tortured himself (I might almost say miserably) trying to explain it.

### Why the face of King Lysimachus on coins has horns. Chapter 79.

[Large initial L]ysimachus the king has a horned face on coins. The reason for this is found in Appian’s *Syriac Wars*. For he says that a wild bull escaped its bonds during a sacrifice by Alexander the Great, and Lysimachus held it back with both hands and killed it. <margin>Why Lysimachus's face is horned.</margin> And because of this, he says: "They add horns to his statues because of this." <note>original: "πϱοσιέασι ἐπὶ τοὺς ἀμφιϱάπτασ ἐπὶ τῷ δὲ τὰ κέρατα"</note>

### A lesser-known fable of Tiresias and Pallas, which clarifies Propertius’s meaning. Chapter 80.

[Large initial P]ropertius says the following in his fourth book of elegies: <margin>A passage from Propertius.</margin>
*The prophet Tiresias saw great Pallas,*
*While she bathed her strong limbs, her Gorgon shield set aside.*
There still exists a hymn by the poet Callimachus titled "On the Baths of Pallas." <margin>i.e., The Washing of Minerva.</margin> In this poem, the story of Tiresias is treated in many elegiac verses to this effect: there was a certain nymph in Thebes named Chariclo, the mother of Tiresias, who was dear to Pallas <note>Athena/Minerva.</note> above all others. <margin>Chariclo. Why Tiresias was deprived of his sight.</margin> But when Pallas and Chariclo were once bathing naked in the Hippocrene fountain on Mount Helicon during the summer heat, the hunter Tiresias happened to approach the same spring to quench his thirst. He unintentionally saw Minerva naked, and he was immediately struck with blindness. For he says it was decreed by the laws of Saturn that "whoever looks upon a god against their will shall do so at a great price." Abammon the Egyptian <margin>Abammon</margin> also writes something similar about the sight of the gods in his letter to Porphyry, though Proclus thinks that work belongs to Iamblichus rather than Abammon. From this, Virgil... <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence at the page break.</note>

<meta>This page continues the author's exploration of silence and the Egyptian deity Harpocrates, transitioning from the previous page's discussion of Roman sexual terminology into a scholarly philological and mythological analysis of why Harpocrates (the god of silence) is invoked in the poems of Catullus.</meta>

# **Miscellanies**

<margin>A passage of Catullus.</margin>

## On Harpocrates. Chapter 83.

**E**pigram of Catullus: <note>This refers to Catullus 74. The name "Lelius" in the text is a common Renaissance misreading or variant for "Gellius."</note> Gellius had heard that his uncle was accustomed to scolding anyone who spoke of or indulged in "delights" <note>original: *delicias*, referring to sexual pleasures or affairs.</note>. To prevent this from happening to himself, he seduced the uncle's own wife, and thus turned his uncle into Harpocrates. He did exactly what he wanted: for who would now "shame" <note>original: *irrumet*; see the previous page for the technical sexual definition of this term.</note> the uncle himself? The uncle will not say a single word.

It has long been asked who this Harpocrates was, whom Catullus mentions in this passage and also in another epigram, saying:

> If anything was ever committed in silence to a faithful friend,
> Whose soul's loyalty is deeply known:
> You will find me, Cornelius, to be one of those initiated into that law,
> And you may consider me to have become Harpocrates. <note>Catullus 102.</note>

However, I myself publicly answered students regarding this matter both in Venice and in Verona (as I have mentioned) about eight years ago. I now call upon their faith and conscience as witnesses, lest I seem to be claiming the discoveries of another as my own. 

Plutarch, therefore, in the book he wrote *On Isis and Osiris*, writes that Harpocrates was born from Isis and Osiris, conceived by her after Osiris was already dead. <margin>Harpocrates.</margin> He was born, however, as a premature birth, with weak legs. Furthermore, he was brought forth around the time of the Winter Solstice <note>original: *Brumen tempus*.</note>, incomplete and unformed—at the time, one might say, when the earth's offspring are just beginning to bud and turn green. For this reason, the first fruits of the harvest are offered to him during joyful times. <margin>His significance.</margin> Yet Plutarch says we should not think of him as an imperfect god, or an infant, or even as a type of legume; rather, he is the presiding protector and moderator of unrefined, imperfect, and inarticulate speech. This is why he presses his finger to his lips, a sign of taciturnity and silence. Indeed, in the month they call Mesore, when offering the first fruits of legumes, they say: "The tongue is fortune, the tongue is a spirit <note>original: *daemon*.</note>." Regarding Egyptian trees, they say the Peach tree is primarily sacred to him, <margin>Symbolism of the Peach tree.</margin> because its fruit is like a heart and its leaf is like a tongue. Thus far from Plutarch on Harpocrates, gathered here and there from various sections. 

Lucilius, the Greek poet, also mentions him in an epigram to Dionysius, warning that if one has an enemy, one should not pray for Isis or Harpocrates to strike them, nor for the god who makes those he angers go blind; instead, one will learn what God and what Simon are capable of. Furthermore, Tertullian in his *Apology* says: 

> The consuls Piso and Gabinius—who were certainly not Christians—prohibited Serapis, Isis, and Harpocrates, along with their dog-headed companion <note>Anubis.</note>, from being brought into the Capitol; that is, they were expelled from the assembly of the gods. Their altars were overturned and they were renounced, as the consuls sought to restrain the vices of shameful and idle superstitions. Yet you have restored them and bestowed the highest majesty upon them.

<margin>Serapis and Isis.</margin> Marcus Varro, in his book *On the Latin Language*, writes: "Sky and Earth: these are the same gods as the Egyptian Serapis and Isis, although Harpocrates signifies with his finger that you should remain silent." Ovid also understood this in the ninth book of his *Metamorphoses*:

> Holy Bubastis, and Apis of varied colors,
> And he who suppresses his voice, and urges silence with his finger.

And likewise Augustine, in the nineteenth book of *The City of God*: "And since," he says, "in almost all temples where Isis and Serapis were worshipped, there was also an image that seemed to advise silence by a finger pressed to the lips, Varro thinks this signifies the same thing: that men should remain silent about the fact that those gods had once been human." Thus far Augustine. 

But in the *Letter of Abammon the Egyptian to Porphyry* (which the Platonist Iamblichus is thought to have either translated into Greek or composed himself), <margin>Icheon.</margin> mention is made of a certain "second god" whose name in the Egyptian language is *Icheon*; he shows that this god ought to be worshipped in silence. Porphyry says the same thing at length regarding the worship of the Supreme God *On Abstinence from Animal Food* <note>original: *ἐν τῷ περὶ ζώων ἀποχῆς*.</note>.

Moreover, the prophet David begins a certain psalm in this way:
*leha dumia tehila elohim bezion* <note>original Hebrew: לך דומיה תהלה אלהים ב ציון. From Psalm 65:1.</note>
In Latin this means: "To you, silence is praise, O God, in Zion." However, the Septuagint translators rendered this differently, as: "A hymn becomes you, O God, in Zion."

I believe, therefore, the Egyptians employed Harpocrates in their rites to show that the Supreme God of the gods must be worshipped in silence. Pliny also mentions Harpocrates in the thirty-third book of his *Natural History*: "Now men are even beginning to wear Harpocrates and the statues of Egyptian deities on their fingers." 

To return to the "Lelius" of Catullus: he acted quite cleverly indeed. To avoid being scolded by his uncle, he set aside the wife he was embracing and began to "shame" <note>original: *irrumare*.</note> the uncle himself, and by that pact forced him to be silent—for one who is performing a lewd act with his mouth <note>original: *fellator*.</note> cannot speak.

<summary>This page provides a scholarly identification of Harpocrates, the Egyptian god of silence, by synthesizing classical, patristic, and biblical sources. It concludes by using these mythological insights to explain a crude pun in a poem by Catullus.</summary>
<keywords>Harpocrates, Catullus, Plutarch, silence, Isis, Osiris, Tertullian, Varro, Augustine, Psalm 65, philology, Egyptian mythology</keywords>

**First Century. Folio 157.**

**ASCENSIUS:** <note>Josse Bade, known as Ascensius, was a famous Renaissance printer and scholar who provided these commentaries.</note> "More strictly and briefly in our Roman instructions" <note>original: *Romanis institutionibus*</note>—this refers to what has been written or handed down above. We now know that "institutions" <note>original: *institutiones*</note> are precepts, doctrines, or books by which the unlearned are instructed and educated. "Institutes" <note>original: *instituta*</note>, however, refer to customs and the things for which people are being trained. Therefore, as Valla <note>Lorenzo Valla, a famous 15th-century humanist and critic</note> advised, Justinian would have more correctly titled this work *Institutions* rather than *Institutes*. Where it reads "if anyone for a long time" <note>original: *si quisq̄ diu*</note>, I read "if anyone as long as" <note>original: *siquis q̄ diu*</note>; and a little later, where it says "they had given themselves to the victors" <note>original: *se uictoribus dedissent*</note>, I read "they had surrendered themselves" <note>original: *dedidissent*</note>. For "to surrender" <note>original: *dedere*</note> is to hand oneself over to the power of another so that one receives nothing back except one's life. "To devote" <note>original: *deuouere*</note>, however, is to even give up one's life.

<margin>Institute</margin>

**On Freedmen, who are called the Surrendered,**
**Chapter 84.**

**T**hese *Institutes*, as they are called in civil law, were published under the name of the Emperor Justinian but were actually composed by <term>Tribonian</term> <note>Justinian's chief legal advisor</note> and other learned men. They are also found written in Greek with exactly the same meaning. However, certain rituals and ancient customs of the Romans are reported somewhat more fully and loosely in the Greek text than in the Latin codex, so that the whole matter might become thoroughly known to foreigners and those unfamiliar with Roman character and custom. But because the matter of those <term>freedmen</term> <note>original: *libertinis*; former slaves who have been granted freedom</note> who were called <term>dediticii</term> <note>literally "the surrendered"; the lowest class of freedmen</note> is treated more strictly and briefly in our Latin *Institutes*, it seemed appropriate to explain it here more extensively—and thus more clearly—according to the sentiment of the Greek volume.

Therefore, among the ancients, those who were <term>manumitted</term> <note>legally released from slavery</note> sometimes obtained a greater and "just" liberty and became Roman citizens. Other times they obtained a lesser liberty and became <term>Junian Latins</term> <note>freedmen with limited rights, named after the Junian law</note> under the <term>Lex Iunia Norbana</term>, which was the law that established their status. Sometimes, however, they obtained an even inferior status and became "the surrendered" <note>original: *dediticiū*</note> under the <term>Lex Aelia Sentia</term>. For if anyone, while serving as a slave for a long time, had suffered a punishment for a crime—such as being "inscribed" (meaning they received marks or brands <note>original: *stigmata*</note> burned into their forehead), or being thrown into a public prison, or being whipped for a crime and confessing to the offense—and was later manumitted by the grace of their master, they were called a **Surrendered Freedman** <note>original: *Libertinus Dediticius*</note>. This was modeled after the example of "surrendered foreigners." For when certain foreigners, who were once taxpayers to Rome, suddenly took up war against them with proud spirits, and were then conquered by force, they threw down their arms and surrendered themselves to the victors. They were treated humanely by the Romans to the extent that they obtained their lives, but they were marked with this mark of ignominy: they were henceforth called "the surrendered" because they had surrendered themselves. For this reason, this class of freedmen was also named "the surrendered" by the Aelian Sentian law, so that since they were like those foreigners in committing a crime, they should also be called by the same name.

<margin>A passage in the Institutes</margin>
<margin>Freedmen</margin>
<margin>The surrendered</margin>
<margin>Junian Latins</margin>
<margin>The surrendered status</margin>
<margin>A surrendered freedman</margin>

**ASCENSIUS.**

"With a double title, Quirinus etc." That is, the two titles were Quirinus and C. Memmius. Thus "Quirinus" and "C. Memmi" (for Memmius) are placed here as <term>indeclinable</term> words; as grammarians would say, they are used "materially"—that is, referring to the words themselves. Otherwise, he would have said "of Quirinus and of C. [Memmius]." "On the other side" <note>original: *altrinsecus*</note>: that is, from the other face. "Carrying [her] with dragons" <note>original: *draconibus uehentē*</note>: this is a remarkable expression. Usually, you would say "carried" <note>original: *uectā*</note>, as Virgil does: "And where he was carried" <note>original: *qua uectus*</note>, as Servius says. Properly speaking, a thing is said "to be carried" when it is changing location or sitting on something that moves. Therefore, because (in terms of time) the little image of Ceres on the coin appeared to be in the process of being carried and had not yet arrived, he perhaps preferred to use the present tense ["carrying"]. But regarding the grammatical voice, it is surprising that he said "carrying" in the active sense. Truly, I think this was done because the word "carrier" <note>original: *uector*</note> commonly signifies both the one who carries and the one who is carried, which is derived from the verb "to carry" <note>original: *ueho*</note>. Thus the verb itself seems to signify both; just as both the horse and the rider are said "to ride" <note>original: *equitare*</note>. Lucilius says: "Truly we see this horse run and ride." Certainly, we say that a ship carries the person who is being carried by it, and the things that are in it; especially if he is the leader or the captain. Thus Aeneas says of himself: "I carry with me in my fleet the household gods snatched from the enemy." He was therefore both carrying and being carried in the same ship. We almost never say "carrying" otherwise: for one who is not on the ship does not carry, even if he sees to the carrying. "With the rest of the worn-out ones" <note>original: *exoletis*</note>: those who have endured womanly things <note>a reference to male prostitutes or those who took a passive role in sex</note>. Hence it was tossed at Caesar during his triumph after he subdued Gaul: "Nicomedes does not triumph, who subdued Caesar." <note>A famous Roman joke suggesting Caesar had been the passive partner of King Nicomedes of Bithynia.</note>

**What sort of Games of Ceres are understood in Juvenal, and on Memmius, the founder of the Cerialia.**
**Chapter 85.**

**J**uvenal, in his fourteenth Satire, speaks thus:
> "Therefore you may leave all the tapestries of Flora,
> And of Ceres, and of Cybele."

None of the interpreters of this poet have said anything about these "Games of Ceres"—not by what name they were called, nor what was done in them, nor by whom they were first celebrated, nor where mention is made of them. Each of these things, however, is not foreign to the duty of a good and learned interpreter. Therefore, we must fill in all of that, lest the meticulousness of this care of ours be found wanting even in small moments. The Games of Ceres, therefore, mentioned here, were called the **Cerialia**. In these games, horse races were celebrated in the Circus. Gaius Memmius, a <term>Curule Aedile</term>, was the first to hold them. Cornelius Tacitus, in the sixteenth book of his *Histories*, speaking of the Emperor Nero, says: "At last they decided to carry out their plans on the day of the Circus games which is celebrated for Ceres, because the Emperor, who rarely went out and stayed closed in his house or gardens, used to come to the spectacles of the Circus." And a little later: "So that the spectacle of the Cerialia in the Circus might be celebrated with more horse races." Ovid says in the fourth book of the *Fasti*:
> "The Circus will be crowded with a procession and a multitude of gods,
> And the first prize will be sought by wind-swift horses.
> These are the Games of Ceres; there is no need to point out the cause."
