# Of the Miscellanies

<margin>The Aediles of Ceres.</margin> Dio <note>Dio Cassius, a Roman historian of Greek origin (c. 155–235 AD)</note> also, the writer of history, narrates in his forty-second book: once Caesar had gained control of affairs, two <term>aediles</term> <note>magistrates responsible for public buildings and festivals</note> were then for the first time created from the patricians, and four from the plebeians. But those two higher ones, he writes, were named from Ceres <note>original: *a Cerere*</note>, and that practice remained from that beginning until his own age. The same Dio also says, in his forty-seventh book, that before the defeat of Brutus it happened that the plebeian aediles exhibited gladiator contests for Ceres in place of horse races. 

Furthermore, Lorenzo de' Medici <note>Lorenzo "the Magnificent," Poliziano's patron</note>, a man excelling in every praise, showed us several coins which have the face of a bearded and unshaven man with a double title: "Quirinus" and "C. Memmius." <margin>Memmius first carrying dragons.</margin> On the other side is a small image of Ceres being carried by dragons, with a title of this sort: "Memmius, Curule Aedile, first performed the Cerealia" <note>original: *Memmius.Aed.Cur.Cerialia Preimus fecit*</note>. Here we also observed that "First" <note>original: *Preimus*</note> was noted not as "primus," but with a diphthong in the first syllable. 

We think this was that same Gaius Memmius who was <term>praetor</term> <note>a high-ranking Roman magistrate</note> with Lucius Domitius; who also accused Caesar of having stood at the cup and wine of Nicomedes <note>a reference to a scandalous rumor about Caesar and the King of Bithynia</note> along with the other catamites; and who tore into the same Caesar with the harshest speeches. Later, having been reconciled, he even had Caesar as a supporter in his petition for the consulship. Cicero writes of him thus in the fourth book of his *Letters to Atticus*: "O what a man, what a citizen is Memmius." All Caesar’s resources support him, and they have joined Domitius to him as consul—by what bargain, I do not dare commit to a letter. I think the poem of Lucretius, *On the Nature of Things* <note>original: *de rerum natura*</note>, was written to him, or certainly to his son. Indeed, both the dignity of the man and the times agree, unless we prefer to think it was instead the son of the same Gaius Memmius, named after his father, who was then made Curule Aedile by Caesar.

**ASCENSIUS:**
Ovid <note>the Roman poet</note> often contracted the genitive case of proper names ending in *-ius* to *-i*, or removed the latter part, as in the cases of Memmius (*Memmi*) and Lucretius (*Lucreti*), etc. Truly the Roman Church, indeed the whole church militant for Christ, now has Leo X <note>Giovanni de' Medici, son of Lorenzo the Magnificent, reigned as Pope 1513–1521</note> as its bishop and Supreme Pontiff <note>original: *pontificem maximum*</note>, from whom we have long expected and hoped for all things best and greatest. Poliziano himself would surely have done the same with us, if the "decuman" <note>fateful or large</note> fates had preserved him to this age.

## On the Tenth or "Decuman" Wave, which very many poets have mentioned.
## Chapter 86.

<margin>The passage in Ovid on the Tenth or Decuman.</margin> The verses of the poet Ovid are in the first volume of the *Tristia* <note>original: *Tristium*</note>:

> The wave that comes from here towers above all waves;
> It is after the ninth, and before the eleventh.

By this he understands the "decuman" wave, which is said to be the largest, just as "decuman" eggs <note>original: *oua decumana*</note> are those which are the biggest. For the tenth egg <note>original: *ouum decimum*</note> is born larger. From this, "decuman" shields <note>original: *scuta decumana*</note>, which were the most ample, were also named. And the "Decuman Gate" <note>original: *Decumana porta*</note> in a military camp, turned away from the enemy. And just as the "decuman" boundary <note>original: *decumanus limes*</note> in a field runs from east to west, it does not seem to me to be so named because it is "twice-handed" <note>original: *duocimanus*</note>, as Marcus Iunius Nypsus <note>a Roman land surveyor (gromaticus)</note> thinks; for that is too harsh, and...

**First Century. Folio 158.**

In Cicero’s letter to Trebatius <note>Gaius Trebatius Testa, a prominent Roman jurist and friend of Cicero</note>, which begins: "You know it is in the Trojan horse," <note>Cicero, *Ad Familiares* 7.16</note> near the end, where it is written "they grow wise too late," the text is found in almost all copies as follows: "Then, as for the fact that in Britain you showed yourself no less than a **Philoctetes**, I certainly do not find fault." <margin>A passage of Cicero.</margin> I had long tortured and tormented myself trying to draw out a meaning from these words, yet it did not make sense. For to what purpose would Cicero speak of Philoctetes here? <note>Philoctetes was a Greek hero famous for his archery but also for being marooned on an island; the comparison makes little sense in the context of a friend visiting Britain.</note> 

But then afterwards, through the efforts of Lorenzo de' Medici, I obtained that very ancient manuscript which I also cited above, which was much less deformed, defiled, perverted, and confused than the others. For in that manuscript, it was written thus: "Then, as for the fact that in Britain you showed yourself no less a **Philotheorus**, I certainly do not find fault." 

For a **Philotheorus** <margin>Philotheorus.</margin> <note>original: *Philotheorus*, from the Greek *philotheoros*, meaning a "lover of spectacles" or a "curious observer"</note> is one who is fond of spectacles. This is exactly how Trebatius had shown himself in Britain; while fleeing battle, he devoted himself to leisure in the midst of arms...

<meta>This page continues Poliziano’s philological investigations, shifting from the correction of Cicero’s letters to a defense of the poet Virgil against the interpretations of the 4th-century commentator Servius. The discussion focuses on the famous "Messianic" Fourth Eclogue and the Roman religious customs surrounding childbirth.</meta>

**158. Miscellanies**

...in the ninth book, declaring this to be a figure of speech in number, such that he joins a singular to a plural. For he says, "From those who did not smile, she did not deem him worthy." <note>referring to Quintilian, *Institutio Oratoria* 9.3.8, discussing the final lines of Virgil’s Fourth Eclogue: *cui non risere parentes*.</note> But who could doubt that one should trust Quintilian regarding the integrity of a Virgilian reading rather than Servius, especially since Quintilian occasionally cites the actual handwriting of Virgil and Cicero? Therefore, what we have said is manifest: the passage is cited erroneously by Servius. <margin>Vulcan: why he was cast down, and that he was born of Jove.</margin> For who does not see that Servius invented a story for himself on purpose and for convenience? Nowhere do we read that **Vulcan** was cast down for the reason that he was born deformed, or because **Juno** did not smile at him. Indeed, the poet **Homer** says it was because he brought help to his mother against his father **Jove**. For according to Homer, Vulcan was born from Jove and Juno, although **Hesiod** in the *Theogony* feigns he was from Juno alone, just as **Minerva** is said to be from Jove alone. Whence she is called **fatherless** <note>original: *ἀπάτωρ* (apator)</note> by **Theocritus** in the little riddle whose inscription is **The Altar**. <note>original: *βωμὸς* (bomos)</note> Therefore, the parents can hardly even be properly referred to Jove and Juno. 

But it is also surely cold how that same Servius says that Vulcan was neither admitted to the banquets of the gods nor earned divine honors, he whom **Varro** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, the great Roman polymath</note> actually numbers as the seventh among the "select gods." <margin>A select god: Vulcan.</margin> Then it would not even follow by the very logic Servius strives for, since he does not say he was cast down because *he* did not smile, but because *he was not smiled upon*. We shall see whether he himself later suspects more credible things; certainly, Servius is now refuted by the truest facts. 

And indeed, I would read it thus and explain it thus: The parents of the boy **Saloninus** <note>The child mentioned in Virgil's 4th Eclogue, often identified as the son of Asinius Pollio</note>, who is now under discussion—so that "parents" is the vocative case—"him on whom they have not smiled, neither has a god deemed worthy of his table, nor a goddess of her bed." <margin>Explanation of the passage.</margin> That is, neither the **Genius** nor **Juno** thought him worthy of the vital breaths among those who did not smile. Thus it is spoken figuratively, by Quintilian’s testimony, for "him who did not smile," or "who is of the number of those who did not smile." For it was believed that everyone had their own god and their own goddess, that is, their own **Genius** and their own **Juno** as presiding over life. <margin>Genius. Juno.</margin> These, therefore, Virgil indicated by way of excellence. For a **Table** is appropriate for a Genius, as in "Pour the wine for the Genius"; a **Bed** for Juno. This is also what **Junius Philargyrius** <note>A commentator on Virgil</note> teaches, interpreting this very passage thus: "When noble boys are born," he says, "a bed for **Juno Lucina** is placed in the hall, and a table of **Hercules'** measure." 

But it is also read in **Varro** that boys are initiated to **Educa**, **Potina**, and **Cuba** <margin>Superstition of initiating children.</margin>—the deities of eating, drinking, and lying down—when they are first transferred from milk and the cradle. Donatus, bringing this authority of Varro into his commentary on Terence’s *Phormio*, also cited this very verse of Virgil, and reported that **Probus** <note>Marcus Valerius Probus, a famous Roman grammarian</note> had noted the same. Therefore, the Table and the Bed are proofs of vitality, which were applied at the very beginnings of life. 

Otherwise, man has his own unique property of laughing. <margin>Laughter as the human principle.</margin> But for one who does not laugh, "what life can be vital afterwards?" as **Ennius** says. You could not, however, refer the "god" and "goddess" to Varro’s Educa, Potina, and Cuba, because these are all female, as **Augustine** also declared in the sixth book of *The City of God*. Nor by equal reason could you refer them to **Pilumnus** and **Pitumnus**, the conjugal gods, for whom (as **Martianus Capella** says Varro wrote in the second book) if the newborn was vital, he was immediately lifted by the midwife and laid on the ground so that he might be omened to be upright, and they were also accustomed to spread a bed in the house. It remains, therefore, that what we said regarding the **Genius** and **Juno** is supported by the pillars of authority. 

Thus **Pliny** in the first book of *Natural History*: "Since individuals," he says, "make as many gods out of themselves, by adopting Geniuses and Junos for themselves." **Seneca** in the nineteenth letter to Lucilius: "However," he says, "I want you to place this so that you remember our ancestors, who believed there were Stoics; for they gave to individuals both a Genius and a Juno." Whence I believe is that line of **Juvenal**: <margin>A passage of Juvenal.</margin>
"And by the Juno," he says, "of the master, the servant swearing."
For the satiric poet censures this: that the master’s servant would swear not by the Genius, but by the Juno—clearly in the womanly fashion. 

Wherefore **Quartilla** in **Petronius Arbiter** speaks thus: "May I have my Juno angry at me, if I ever remember being a virgin. For as an infant I was defiled with my peers, and thereafter as the years went by, I applied myself to older boys, until I reached this age." Here also I think that proverb was born, that it might be said: "He can lift the bull †who has carried the calf." <margin>Proverb. †Who.</margin> <note>A reference to the athlete Milo of Croton, who grew strong by carrying a calf every day until it was a bull.</note> Otherwise, if only he allows it, a not entirely unfair censure is carried out by us, and that Servian commentary, which had held as indubitable before we brought such things forward, now begins to fail. We shall leave the rest to be judged by those who will think freely (lest we flatter ourselves).

**ASCENSIUS** <note>Glosses by the printer/editor Jodocus Badius Ascensius</note> **Amusoteros:** seems to be said of one more unrefined and more foreign to the Muses. The people of Tarentum and Consentia were held to be soft and inept judges and readers of literature. **Opie:** rustic and boorish. **To be named:** i.e., named, to be selected by me. But most learned of all, **Persius**. Cicero repeated those words. **Macti:** i.e., great and more increased or august. **Those who have not looked deeply:** above, as they themselves—i.e., we ourselves—looked within. If I had found it written "as he himself," I would explain: "those who were not entirely," i.e., altogether, such as he himself. For just as no one knows God entirely, because no one is like Him, so no one knows the wisdom of a man who is not like him, i.e., equally wise; and then "entirely" would be explained as "altogether," but now it is for that which is "inwardly," as if "almost inside" (whence come "more deeply" and "most deeply"). **Terget:** present tense from *tergeo*, second conjugation; i.e., he polishes the old or forges new things on the anvil; where "forges" is a deponent verb with active meaning. The **weapons of philosophy** are words. **Holy man:** Jerome. **When he shall pronounce:** which will never be. **While our dignity is unharmed:** i.e., while our dignity may yet be intact. **Viticulas:** i.e., small strengths.

What a man **Theodore Gaza** was, and yet how much he slipped in translating the *Problems* of Aristotle.

**First Century. Folio 159.**

**[Decorative initial N]** I do not refuse, nor do I shrink from the risk, that this work of mine—whatever it may turn out to be—should come under the scrutiny of critics and the roll of the dice <note>original: *sub aleamque*, a metaphor for the unpredictability of public reception</note>. I hope that no judge happens upon me who is unlearned <note>original: *ἀμουσότερος* (amousoteros), literally "unmusical" or "untouched by the Muses," a term Poliziano borrows from the Roman statesman Symmachus</note>, nor one who is a boor <note>original: *opicus*, an archaic term for the Oscan people, used by Romans to mean uncultured or provincial</note>, nor one who is harsh and stubborn—a man sworn to the words of another man rather than to the truth itself. 

Indeed, if judges are to be named, I do not wish for the Tarentines <margin>Tarentines</margin>, nor the Consentines <margin>Consentines</margin>, nor the Sicilians <note>These groups represent the "half-Greek" or provincial audiences that the early Roman satirist Lucilius famously claimed to avoid</note> to read these writings of mine, as Lucilius said of certain works of his. I do not want a Junius Congius <note>A minor Roman legal writer mentioned by Lucilius as a mediocre reader</note>, but a Scipio, or a Persius—the most learned of all—or a Rutilius. By this I mean those who are their equals: men blessed with prudence, genius, and learning, for whose judgment one should rightly labor. Such a man, for instance—if I may say so—is he himself <note>Likely referring to Poliziano’s patron, Lorenzo de' Medici, "the Magnificent"</note> who provides me with so many tools for my studies and such deep leisure; whose ancestors, great-great-grandfathers...

<margin>Peter of Abano</margin>
Yet, this same passage was also poorly translated by Peter of Abano <note>A 13th-century physician and philosopher</note>, who was given the surname "The Conciliator" <note>original: *Conciliatori*; he was famous for his work *Conciliator Differentiarum*, which sought to resolve contradictions between medicine and philosophy</note> because of his work. I would grant him that point only if some word from that etymology were actually pronounced there. But indeed, anyone may now know that Theodore’s case is already pushed over, prostrate, and bound, even if I add nothing more.

...ed, so that they seemed to do something of their own accord, even though they appeared to lack a conscious cause.

Such as the clocks we have now, or certain revolving machines: in which we marvel at little figures <note>original: *imagunculas*</note> running about and playing through a hidden force. Such are also either fountains or fires which, by some ingenious tempering and in a novel appearance, shoot forth water or flames at certain intervals. For we can interpret the word **Automaton** in Latin as "voluntary" and "spontaneous."

Thus Homer, in the second Rhapsody <note>Book 2 of the *Iliad*</note>, says that Menelaus came to the feast **of his own accord** <note>original: *automaton*</note>, meaning by his own will and not by anyone's summons—as if by his own power. Eustathius <note>A 12th-century Byzantine scholar known for his extensive commentaries on Homer</note> also explains it this way, later saying that more recent authors use the term **automata** <note>original: *αὐτόματα*</note> for things that happen by a certain chance: as if from the word *mato* <note>original: *μάτω*</note>, which means "rashly," and **just as it happens** <note>original: *καὶ ὥσ ἔτυχεν*</note>. <margin>that is, and as it occurred or happened</margin>

And a little later, he adds almost the same: "Such a definition also gave the name to the **Automata** of the engineers." Furthermore, Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician and engineer who wrote *Pneumatica*</note> in his *Pneumatics* says that water is forced upward in a sublime **Automaton**...

...perhaps to show that it was now permitted for them, according to their own judgment, to move in whichever direction they wished, which Persius also said above:
*Let his master turn him around; in the moment of a spinning top, Marcus Dama comes out [a free man].* <note>original: "Verterit hunc dominus, momento turbinis exit Marcus Dama." From Persius, Satire 5.75-76, describing the ritual of manumission where a slave was spun around to symbolize their new freedom.</note>
And they were often freed by the official rod <note>original: *vindicta*</note> of the praetor; for this reason, he mentions both the "shaking" and the "lictor." For lictors <note>officials who cleared the way for Roman magistrates</note> attended to the senior officials. Seneca also teaches that it was customary for those being freed to be turned around, in the eighth letter of his first book to Lucilius. "You must serve philosophy," he says, "so that true liberty may befall you. He who has submitted and surrendered himself to her is not put off from day to day; he is immediately turned around <note>original: *circumagitur*</note>. For this very service to philosophy is liberty." <margin>Turning around makes one free.</margin> "Turned around" here means being manumitted and set free.

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, a renowned 16th-century printer and scholar</note> On those riding in a carriage: used here in the same way as the common expression for those "carried in a carriage." It is also customary for part of the city walls to be scattered or torn down by someone who wishes for the city to be safe, and the significance of this act is what the author explains: sometimes it is a sign of a conquered city, as a mark of subjugation.

[Marginal note: Suetonius on the Hieronicae. Riding. Tearing down walls. Pests/Apples.]

**Why they were accustomed to tear down part of the walls, as Suetonius says the Hieronicae did. Chapter XCIX.**

[Large decorative woodcut initial S depicting a figure in a landscape]
**S**uetonius, in his life of Nero, says: "Having returned from Greece to Naples, because he had first performed his art in that city, he entered with white horses through a breached part of the wall, as is the custom of the Hieronicae." <note>original: *Hieronicarun*. These were victors in the sacred Panhellenic games (like the Olympics).</note> There is no doubt that the winners of sacred contests are called Hieronicae. But thus far, I find the reason for this custom only in Plutarch, in the second book of his *Symposiacon* <note>Table Talk</note>, to this effect: "Because," he says, "it was permitted for victors riding in a carriage to divide and throw down part of the wall, it truly has this meaning: that a city has no great need for a wall when it possesses men who can fight and conquer."

**ASCENSIUS.** Pests and apples <note>original: *Mala. pyros.*</note>. It should be noted that the names of fruits are also used for the trees themselves, as with "apples" in Cato and "fruits" in Tibullus. *The silent virgin*: ordered to be silent about things that were secrets; as it is still understood today, just as the little hedge <note>original: *sepicula*</note> usually is.

**What the "silences of the Moon" are in Virgil, or the "Silent Virgin" in Horace, and the refutation of the opinions of Servius and Acron on these matters. Chapter C.**

[Marginal note: A passage in Virgil.]

[Large decorative woodcut initial V depicting two figures with a cross-like structure]
**V**irgil says in the second book of the *Aeneid*: "Through the friendly silence of the silent Moon." <note>original: *Tacitæ per amica silentia Lunæ*. Aeneid 2.255, describing the Greek fleet returning to Troy under the cover of night.</note>
Servius <note>A famous 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note> says: "It should be known that Troy was captured on the seventh day of the moon, an image of which was established at Argos. This is why he says: 'revealed by the moon.' And elsewhere: 'Through the blind night.' By 'silent moon,' he either means the night in a poetic manner, or he spoke with physical reasoning. For there are seven spheres: Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. The first, which is Saturn, sounds loudly; the others less so according to their order. Just as we have heard in a lyre, whose last string sounds the least."
Thus far Servius. I would gladly ask him why he refers the "friendly Moon"—to those attempting to hide and deceive—to the same harmony of the planets, as well as the "silent Moon" found in Marcus Cato and likewise in Pliny.
Because he says the last string of the lyre sounds less: this would only follow if he takes "last" not as "first," but as the "highest" <note>original: *summa*</note>, which is called the *hypate* <note>original: *ὑπάτη*</note> in Greek, from which a deeper sound is produced. Just as from the outermost and thinnest string—which I would more gladly call the "last"—a sharp voice is brought forth, which seems to sound more for that reason because it is stretched tight; as Porphyry says Theophrastus writes in his second book *On Music*, in those commentaries he left on Ptolemy’s *Harmonics*. For this reason, he says it is heard less: because it is diffused around. <margin>The *Hypate*. The sound of the strings.</margin>

[Marginal note: A passage in Macrobius. The course of Saturn.] As for what we read in Macrobius and others, that the sphere of Saturn (whose revolution is more rapid) emits the sharpest sound, I think this would hardly be approved by Plato, either in the *Timaeus* or the *Republic*, who writes that the sphere of Saturn is the slowest—though perhaps he refers this to the longer circuit of its path. But Aristotle certainly says in the second book of *On the Heavens* that the upper spheres are slower for this reason: they are more retarded by the force of the eighth, star-bearing sphere. So, to pass over the opinions of Alexander, Simplicius, or the more recent scholars, if you wish to clearly grasp Macrobius's true meaning, you should refer it to the diurnal <note>daily</note> motion, which is undoubtedly found to be fastest in the highest parts and most rapid. 

But having dismissed this (as I believe) artificial and entirely unnecessary subtlety of Servius, we rather accept the "silences of the silent moon" as the moon itself when it is called "silent"—that is, not shining at all at that time—so that an ambush could better remain hidden. This is surely a beautiful and elegant metaphor, moving from the ears to the eyes. <margin>The silence of the silent moon.</margin> For just as nothing is heard in silence, so nothing is seen in darkness. Pliny, therefore, says in the sixteenth book of his *Natural History*: "The day of the moon's conjunction is called by some the 'silent moon,' and by others the 'interlunium' <note>the period between the old and new moon</note>." Likewise, in his eighteenth book, he says: "They order this to be sown during the silent moon." Marcus Cato also says in his book *On Agriculture*: "Now haul out manure during the silent moon; now likewise during the silent moon, graft figs, olives, apples, and pears." <margin>Silent Moon.</margin> Finally, he even orders meadows to be manured in early spring during the same silent moon. <margin>Apples.</margin> It would be ridiculous to refer these passages of Cato or Pliny to the music of the spheres, or to seek such evasions in an ancient and widely accepted expression. 

Indeed, I would take the "silent moon" here, as I said, to mean not shining at all, which was a time the Greeks had to observe. I do not, however, interpret it so strictly as to mean only the exact moment of the moon's conjunction <note>the new moon</note> when the whole night is dark—for this is certainly refuted, since the poet soon says: "Revealed by the moon." Therefore, the moon was not yet shining when they were sailing from Tenedos toward evening, but it began to shine when they had already occupied the city. Therefore, it was either a late moon or a moon that lasted all night; I think it refers not to the total conjunction of the moon, but rather to the time during which it was not shining. For...

**ASCENSIUS.** <note>Jodocus Badius Ascensius, a prominent Renaissance scholar and printer, often provided "familial" commentaries on complex texts.</note> **The Finishing Touch.** <margin>Coronis</margin> <note>original: *Coronis*. In Greek manuscript tradition, a *coronis* was a flourish or symbol placed in the margin to mark the end of a section or a book; here it refers to Ascensius adding a final concluding thought.</note> I have placed this flourish here so that I might add something from the commentary of other scholars, for there are those who believe that the tearing down of the walls signifies that the city is open and safe for the victor.

[Decorative initial S] **Since** many people often mention the "friendly silence of the moon," <margin>Poliziano in his poem *The Countryman*. Friendly silence of the moon. Silence during the observation of omens. Horace speaks.</margin> <note>original: "Amica silentia Lunae" from Virgil’s *Aeneid*, Book 2, line 255. Poliziano is here cross-referencing his own work *Rusticus* and the Roman concept of *silentium* in ritual.</note> although <note>original: *quamquam*</note> there are nonetheless <note>original: *tamen*</note> various interpretations of what this "silence" actually means, it is often taken to refer to the dead of night when the moon has not yet risen. However, in the ritual of the auspices <note>the Roman practice of interpreting the will of the gods through the flight of birds or other natural signs</note>, "silence" did not mean a total lack of sound, but rather the absence of any faulty or ill-omened occurrence. As Horace says, even the moon can be called a "silent maiden" <margin>The silent maiden.</margin> when she is hidden or in her dark phase.

But indeed, because <note>original: *At enim quod... quoniam*</note> I have frequently observed that this point is misinterpreted, I must explain it more clearly. Just as a "divine wand" <margin>† letters. The divine wand.</margin> <note>original: *virgula divina*; a reference to a dowsing rod or a metaphorical tool for uncovering truth</note> might reveal hidden treasure, we must look to the ancient sources to understand why a "white line" <margin>A white line.</margin> <note>original: *Alba linea*. A Greek and Latin proverb referring to a line drawn with white chalk on a white stone, used to describe things that are indistinguishable or a lack of clear judgment.</note> is sometimes drawn between different meanings. 

In this regard, I must offer praise to Marsilio Ficino <margin>Praise of Marsilio Ficino.</margin> <note>Ficino was the head of the Platonic Academy in Florence and a mentor to Poliziano.</note> and to Johannes Argyropoulos, <margin>Argyropoulos.</margin> <note>A Greek scholar who fled to Italy and taught Greek philosophy to the leading minds of the Renaissance.</note> whose learning has illuminated these mysteries. Furthermore, there is a proverb concerning the dog that drinks from the Nile while running away <margin>Proverb: The dog drinks from the Nile while running away.</margin> <note>original: "de Nilo canis fugiens bibit." This proverb describes a person who does something with extreme haste or caution to avoid danger—specifically, the dogs of Egypt were said to lap water from the Nile quickly to avoid being caught by crocodiles.</note>, which serves as a metaphor for those who skim the surface of knowledge without pausing to drink deeply. Finally, I must also give praise to Pico <margin>Praise of Pico.</margin> <note>Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, the famous philosopher and close friend of the author.</note>, whose intellect is as vast as the subjects we discuss here.

# **Miscellanies**

...with honorable arts, fortified and equipped beyond what is credible. Finally, to put it briefly, he is greater than any praise. He, therefore, who is accustomed to share with me his sweetest concerns and sometimes to joke pleasantly, and who has chosen me as a nearly constant companion in his studies (which is the greatest honor): he urged me toward philosophy. It was to be explored not with sleepy eyes as before, but with vigorous and watchful ones, as if he were animating me with a certain military trumpet-call of his voice. Therefore, having found such a great author or leader, I did not miss the opportunity, but rather ran to meet it and seized it, so that through nearly constant study of the greatest authors, as if by frequently striking flint, I seem to have struck out at least a few sparks of truth. I have caught so much flame in the kindling that in the dark and moonless night, a certain brightness now begins to shine for me.

-> <margin>Cornucopia</margin> <-
But look, meanwhile, while I was entirely focused on this, suddenly that *Horn* <note>original: *Cornu*. This refers to the *Cornu Copiae* (The Horn of Plenty), a major reference work by the scholar Niccolò Perotti, published posthumously in 1489.</note> was released to the public. There is a rush. It is in everyone's hands. It is poured out. It is examined. Why say more? It frees me from calumny. You would have seen immediately the faces of some, silently brooding over something mournful, and in a way never seen before, I know not how (like Thrasymachus in Plato’s *Republic*), they were blushing. But regarding that *Horn*, which is certainly not empty, what I might have seen within it is not a judgment for this time. Let it suffice for the present that I did not aim for the same goal as the author of that volume, nor was an equal summit destined or prescribed for both of us. If by chance we both treated the same passages as the occasion arose (and it was necessary for that to happen somewhere), there is nevertheless a thicker wall between us than there was between Pyramus and Thisbe. <note>In Ovid's myth, the lovers Pyramus and Thisbe spoke through a thin crack in a wall; the author here claims his work and Perotti's are entirely separate despite covering the same topics.</note> Let that Cotytto of Juvenal serve as proof, which however in his work is Cocytus <note>A river in the underworld; the author is pointing out a philological error in the other scholar's work</note>, about which he fights with Domitio as if over a poor kingdom, or likewise the Altar of Martial, crowded with horns, or Philyra, or any other such thing which you might wish to entrust to my companions and -> <margin>Attendants.</margin> <- attendants.

Indeed, it happened that during this very interval while the *Miscellanies* were at a standstill, some hundred learned and—by Hercules (who would deny it?)—laborious notes were published by a man most friendly to us, who was not unaware of our purpose, and who is well-lettered, not without a benevolent and grateful mention of us. In these, I believe by chance one or two notes have almost the same argument as ours, and certainly several are nearly related to those things which we had dictated in the public auditorium with great attendance—either when we were interpreting Ovid’s *Fasti* nearly nine years ago, or later Horace’s *Satires*. Most sacredly (if need be) I would swear, holding the altar, that I immediately thought to yield entirely to a friend—if not concerning my own right, certainly concerning a common right—and not to recognize anything from those things for which he had claimed the title for himself, not, I think, unjustly. For I am not so swollen with pride, nor so favorable to myself, that I would wish to be seen as more learned than such a learned man in anything, lest that saying be thrown in my face: "A pig teaching Minerva." <note>original: *Sus Mineruam*. An ancient proverb describing an ignorant person trying to instruct an expert.</note> 

But since he related that he had finally discovered these things as the first to do so, as if they had been completely unknown (so I believe he thought) and untold to others until that day: I am forced to confess, which he himself will easily tolerate out of the kindness he professes, to simply and candidly clear my profession from those suspicions of common ignorance. For just as I might rightly be considered either uncivil or arrogant if I did not think that both these things and better ones could be born at home for him who is so diligent and erudite (Since God has placed all things in the middle of the field), so, on the other hand, to abandon the defense of one's reputation could seem not only the act of a dissolute man, but also (if I am not mistaken) almost cruel toward oneself. -> <margin>Donatus’s harsh saying.</margin> <- "And may they perish," Donatus <note>A 4th-century grammarian; this famous quote complains about people who come up with one's ideas before one can.</note> used to say, "who said our things before us!" We pray for and desire prosperous and fortunate things for him who either found or certainly said our things after us. We only ask that he not be reluctant to admit us also as a partner into the company of those things which so many have received under our teaching so long ago, and in which we have labored to the best of our ability, lest all things (as Euripides says) be not common among friends.

**THE END.**

<meta>This page transitions from the author’s general defense of his scholarship in the "Miscellanies" to a specific dedicatory preface for his translation of Herodian’s history. **In Herodian’s History. Preface. Folio 1.**

**PREFACE OF ANGELO POLIZIANO TO POPE INNOCENT VIII, SUPREME PONTIFF, ON THE HISTORY OF HERODIAN TRANSLATED FROM GREEK INTO LATIN.**

[Large decorative initial letter 'C' inside a square frame of interlaced knotwork]
When I was at Rome almost three years ago in the company of the Florentine embassy—which had come to congratulate you, Holy Father Innocent, Supreme Pontiff, upon your recent elevation to the summit of that highest dignity—I remember that with great ceremony a task was delegated to me by you: to translate <note>original: *verrendi*, likely a transcription error for *vertendi*</note> into Latin speech the deeds of the Roman emperors, if any were still to be found among the Greek monuments untouched by our countrymen. Therefore, when I perceived that by the judgment of your heavenly mind no more honor was added to me than a burden enjoined, as soon as I returned to Florence, I began to look around with the deepest concern for whom most of all from the whole abundance of the Greeks I should undertake to translate.

Herodian occurred to me first, this excellent writer of history, who, having spent a long time in the imperial palace and being already of advanced age <margin>Advanced Age</margin>, set out to compose a history of his own times; he lacked neither the praise of eloquence nor, above all, did he fail to maintain truthfulness and freedom. When this work was composed by us—with not much labor indeed, nor, as I believe, against the grain <note>original: *invita Minerva*, literally "with Minerva unwilling," a classical idiom meaning to act against one's natural talent or without divine inspiration</note>—those times soon occurred which hindered our studies and drove out almost all the alacrity that is most powerful in writing.

But after you, through your providence, restored the peace Italy desired, and privately contracted an alliance <note>referring to the marriage alliance between the Pope’s son and Lorenzo de' Medici’s daughter</note> with my patron Lorenzo de' Medici—a man of most ample fortune but even ampler genius and prudence—that cloud, as it were, departed, and its serenity was returned to the world, so that we may now collect ourselves again. Like flowers weighed down by rain and almost falling, we are raised up by the rays of new light. Therefore, I now delight both to publish old works and to forge new ones, so that in some way either celebrity may be born for your most sacred name, or clarity for our times, or utility even for studious men.

But as for this Herodian of ours, until we have prepared greater and perhaps better things for you, we ask, Supreme Pontiff, that you receive it with a joyful face as a sort of prelude to true and just labor. You will find in it a great variety of affairs and persons, much novelty of events, frequent examples of fortune wavering in both directions, admirable counsels and unexpected outcomes of those counsels, weighty opinions suited to the time, and a speech full of dignity and sweetness everywhere. It is a copious supply for instructing morals and is like a mirror of humanity into which all life may look, and from which it may draw those lessons through which either public or private interests may be consulted.

These indeed were our parts: we have certainly attempted—and would that we have also achieved—that all things should correspond faithfully, lest an inept foreignness <margin>Here is long-standing skill in translating</margin> or little Greek figures of speech (unless they are already accepted) should pollute Latin purity. *We aimed for the clarity of both languages to be almost the same, with the same elegance, the same sense and character in both, with no stubbornness of words and no anxiety.* Since you have raised for us a signal for good hope from that citadel of your Pontificate, proceed, I beseech you, Most Holy Father; proceed, I say, to cherish and illuminate the liberal arts. They roll themselves as suppliants at those most holy feet and implore your divinity against rude ignorance and foul barbarism, so that from the one by whom peace was restored to Italy and indeed to the world, letters—the foster-children of peace—may also be vindicated from injury and indignity.

[At the bottom left, there are faint columns of text, possibly bleed-through or erased notes, containing Roman numerals such as IVXXI, IXXXI, etc.]

He emphasizes his commitment to a translation style that preserves Latin purity while remaining faithful to the Greek original.</summary>

<meta>This page transitions from the formal dedication to Pope Innocent VIII to a more personal letter from Angelo Poliziano to his friend and collaborator, Andrea Magnanimo. While the previous page established the scholarly and official motivation for translating Herodian’s history, this letter deals with the practicalities of publication and Poliziano’s editorial anxieties as the text moves to the printing press.</meta>

Angelo Poliziano to his dear Andrea Magnanimo, greetings.

[Decorative woodcut initial E] You write that the printers there are demanding my Herodian. I call it "mine" by right, as if I have gifted the author with Latinity <note>Poliziano refers to his translation as "giving the text Latinity," a common humanist trope where the translator "naturalizes" a Greek author into the Latin world</note>. Then you ask that I finally return your own manuscript to you, corrected by my own hand (which you say the printers desire). I am returning it; but to tell the truth, it has been corrected gently rather than strictly. Indeed, you may find more of my own errors in it than those of the scribe.

I should believe, however, that somewhat more indulgence is owed to my style as a translator than to that of an author. For what one writes flows much better when the work is like an open racecourse, compared to what one translates, where nothing is permitted outside what is prescribed. There is also the fact that this task of translation was for me a lighter effort, as it were; I dictated it in just a few days while walking about. Thus, I am so far from seeking praise for it that I think it will be quite fine if I merely avoid serious blame. For this reason, I do not only leave the defense of this work to you and our other friends, but I almost forbid you from it, saving your full strength for other works that will be published later.

But although there are very many among you who favor me even more than is proper, you alone, Andrea Magnanimo—most worthy of that family name of yours <note>Poliziano puns on *Magnanimo*, which means "Magnanimous" or "Great-Souled"</note>—are the one I value most highly. This is not only because you are of noble birth and flourish in wealth and honors, but especially because you possess a most elegant talent and the sweetest manners. You conquer people through a certain unique grace in whatever you do or say—indeed, even if you do nothing and say nothing—and finally, by your very countenance, as the saying goes. Therefore, I fear no one as long as you are devoted to me. For no one who understands that Poliziano pleases Magnanimo will ever think ill of him.

There is only one thing I now ask of you: ensure, with your usual diligence in my affairs, that the volumes soon to be printed deviate as little as possible from the original. See to it that even those little marginal notes <margin>Marginal Notes</margin> which I have written in the margins are not omitted. Among those, you will find perhaps three or four places at most where I had to offer an excuse because the Greek manuscript was corrupt. To handle these matters easily, you could have no one more suitable or more useful to you than Alexander Sartius <note>Alessandro Sarti, a fellow scholar and friend of Poliziano</note>, your fellow citizen, a man of letters and a student of my work. Furthermore (which I consider most important in this matter), he is by no means one to fall asleep when a friend’s business is at hand.

Farewell, from my little villa at Fiesole <note>Rusculo Fesulano: Poliziano’s beloved retreat near Florence</note>. The day before the Nones of May. In the Year of Salvation 1493.

# Herodian’s Book I. Folio II.

HERODIAN’S HISTORY OF THE EMPIRE AFTER MARCUS, OR
OF HIS OWN TIMES, BOOK ONE, TRANSLATED FROM THE
GREEK BY ANGELO POLITIANO, <note>Angelo Poliziano (1454–1494) was a preeminent Italian humanist scholar and poet of the Florentine Renaissance.</note> INTERPRETER,
FOR INNOCENT VIII, SUPREME
PONTIFF.

## PREFACE.

<margin>[unclear]</margin>
[Decorative initial Q] Those who have recorded ancient deeds for posterity and have studied to renew the memory of old history through letters have, for the most part, done so while desiring the fame of learning and attempting to rescue their own names from the injustice of oblivion. They have certainly applied less diligence to the investigation of truth than to the decoration and composition of their speech; thinking, of course, that if any falsehood were produced regarding matters very remote from their own age, it could not be refuted—and yet they would receive the greatest fruit of their labor and talent through the sweetness of the narration. Others, however, driven by private enmities and hatred of tyrants, or overflowing with immoderate flattery in the praises of princes, cities, and private men, have—through the artifice of writing—elevated matters that were thin and humble in themselves far beyond the truth.

<margin>From the time of Augustus / up to Marcus</margin>
<margin>Many small / and various princes</margin>
But I, on the contrary, have undertaken to write a history—not one received from others, nor unknown, nor lacking witnesses—but one still clinging to the senses and memory of those who will read it, collected with the highest faith and diligence. I hope that the knowledge of these things, which truly great and many occurred in not so long a time, will not be unpleasant to posterity. For if anyone considers in his mind the whole age from Prince Augustus <note>The first Roman Emperor, Augustus Caesar (r. 27 BC – 14 AD)</note>—when, clearly, the power of the Romans devolved to the will of one man—not even in those roughly two hundred years (for about that many are counted until the time of Marcus) will he find such diverse successions of empires, or such various cases and outcomes of wars, whether civil or foreign, among so many stirred-up nations, so many of our cities and barbarian ones captured, and besides, earthquakes and plagues, and also the lives of princes and tyrants so new and unheard of, that no similar examples among the ancients, or certainly very few, may be found. Some of these held power for a long time, others for a brief period; some, however, having scarcely entered into the honor and being called emperors only on that very day they received it, lost the empire. For since the city of Rome endured more princes in sixty years than was usual for the time, it resulted from this that many varied things worthy of admiration arose. Indeed, the Princes advanced in age, being skilled in affairs and business, ruled themselves and their people more diligently; conversely, the youths, having been held softly and indulgently, designed many new things, whereby it happened that from disparate age and license, disparate pursuits and customs followed. We shall write down how these things were done, preserving the order of the times and the princes themselves.

<margin>Marcus’s / offspring.</margin>
<margin>Marcus’s / probity.</margin>
[Decorative initial I] Emperor Marcus <note>Marcus Aurelius, the famous "Philosopher King" who ruled from 161 to 180 AD.</note> had several daughters but two males. The younger of these, still a very young boy, died; his name was Verissimus <note>Marcus Annius Verus Caesar, who died at age seven.</note>. The other, Commodus, the father educated with great diligence and care, summoning from everywhere men famous for learning and offering the greatest rewards, so that each might cultivate the character and talent of his son. Furthermore, when his daughters had grown, he married them to the best men of the senatorial order. Nor did he think those should be chosen for him who could display a long lineage of ancestry or who showed off excessive wealth, but those who excelled in the probity and modesty of their character and the innocence of their lives. For he considered these alone to be the certain and stable goods of the soul. There was no virtue he did not greatly practice. He was so studious of ancient literature that he was second to no one of that kind among the Greeks or Romans. Evidence of this are the many things said and written by him <note>Original: *conscripta*; likely referring to Marcus Aurelius's *Meditations*.</note> that have come down to us. Truly, he showed himself so civil and agreeable a prince to all that he would calmly give his right hand to anyone approaching and would permit no one to be barred from entry by his guards. He alone of emperors practiced the study of wisdom <note>Original: *sapientiae studium*, a standard term for philosophy.</note> not with words or knowledge of decrees, but with the gravity of his character and the restraint of his life.

<margin>men are usually accustomed / to imitate a good prince</margin>
Thus it happened that that age produced a great harvest of wise men. For men are usually accustomed to emulate the life of the prince. Whatever, therefore, was done by him modestly and bravely at home and abroad, and how he conducted himself against the barbarian nations subjected to the north and toward the east, these things are contained in the monuments of many most learned men. But those things which have been seen and heard by me throughout my entire life after the death of Marcus—and some things also known through experience, as I was engaged in public and imperial offices—these I have now undertaken to write.

**a ii**

<summary>Herodian introduces his history by critiquing historians who prioritize style over truth, arguing that the sixty years following Marcus Aurelius were more chaotic and remarkable than the preceding two centuries. He praises Marcus Aurelius’s character and philosophical governance as a baseline for the history to follow.</summary>

# II. Herodian

<margin>The wicked character of young princes.
Dionysius
Ptolemy
Antigonus
Nero
Domitian</margin>

[Decorative initial S] Now Marcus was an old man, worn out not only by age but by many labors and cares. While he was staying in Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans, where Marcus Aurelius spent years campaigning against Germanic tribes.</note>, a very grave illness suddenly struck him. When he clearly perceived that his health was beyond hope, he was visibly anxious, fearing that his son—who had then just entered early youth—might abandon honorable arts and studies to give himself over to drunkenness and excess, whether through the excessive heat of his age or the absolute liberty he would have in his position. Indeed, the minds of young men easily slip away from upright and honest discipline toward luxury and pleasures. 

Furthermore, the situation terrified a man of no small experience, as he remembered many princes who had taken up power as youths: such as Dionysius, the tyrant of Sicily, whose excess in living was so great that he bestowed the highest rewards upon those who invented new pleasures; and likewise those who succeeded Alexander. For they ruled so insolently and violently that they brought grave disgrace upon his legacy. Specifically, Ptolemy fell into such baseness that, contrary to the laws of the Macedonians and even all Greeks, he involved himself in the love of his own sisters. Antigonus, moreover, so that he might represent Father Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus or Dionysus, the god of wine and theater.</note>, was accustomed to circle his head with ivy instead of the Macedonian *causia* <note>A flat felt hat worn by Macedonian royalty.</note> and diadem, and to carry a *thyrsus* <note>A staff topped with a pinecone, associated with Dionysian rituals.</note> instead of a scepter. 

Recent examples also troubled the old man’s mind, such as that of Nero himself, who did not even abstain from the murder of his own mother and offered himself as a ridiculous spectacle to the people. Likewise Domitian, who left nothing undone in the way of extreme cruelty. Turning these images of tyrannies over in his mind, he was tossed between hope and fear. He was additionally terrified by the neighboring tribes of Germany, whom he had not yet fully subdued; some he had accepted into alliance, others he had tamed by arms and war. Some of them had even escaped and were only restrained for the present by fear of the Emperor. Therefore, he doubted whether they might soon resume their arms out of contempt for his son's youth. Indeed, it is the custom of barbarians to be driven by any slight momentum or cause. 

Tossing, therefore, on these waves of care, he ordered all his friends and kinsmen who were present to be summoned. After they had gathered, with his young son standing in their sight, he raised himself slightly from his cot and delivered a speech of this kind:

<margin>The Speech of Marcus to the nobles.</margin>

*In the salt-sea and tide of life* <note>original: "In salo et fluctu vitæ". This is a handwritten marginal addition emphasizing the metaphor of the sea used in the text.</note>

[Decorative initial D] It is not at all surprising that you grieve and are distressed when you see me thus afflicted. Indeed, it is human to groan at human misfortunes, and those things which are witnessed by the eyes provoke much more mercy. However, our relationship with you is of a special nature. For, out of the consciousness of my own mind toward you, I hope for a mutual benevolence from you as if by my own right. But now this moment has arrived, when I must judge whether I have held you in honor for so long in vain, and whether I have devoted all my zeal to you to no purpose; and you must show your gratitude by proving you are not unmindful of what you have received. 

You see my son, whom you yourselves have educated, now entering the first boundaries of youth, standing as if in the salt-sea and tide of life, needing pilots lest, through inexperience of affairs, he be carried away from the right course and strike against evil arts. Be you, therefore, many parents to him in my place, by cultivating him and suggesting the best path. For neither the power of money can satisfy the luxury of a tyranny, nor can huddling ranks of bodyguards protect a prince, unless those very people whom you rule grant their goodwill and spirit to the one commanding. Indeed, those alone rule for a long time and in safety who instill not fear through cruelty, but love through goodness in the souls of their citizens. For those whom necessity has forced to serve are not the same as those whom their own will has driven to obey; the latter are free from all suspicion and flattery in their actions and endurance, and they never reject commands unless they are treated violently and insolently. 

It is difficult, however, to moderate oneself in the greatest liberty, and to place bridles, as it were, upon one's desires. But if you will be the authors of his living well, and if you will repeatedly remind him of the things he hears now in person, you will at once render him the best possible prince for yourselves and the rest of the world, and you will earn our memory—which you can make immortal by this one means alone. 

As Marcus was saying such things, his spirit suddenly failed him, so that he immediately fell silent and fell back supine upon his bed from excessive weakness. Such a great pity then seized all who were present that some of them, losing their composure through grief, raised a great cry.

<margin>The death of Marcus.</margin>

*Epithets of the Best Prince* <note>original: "Optimi Principis Epitheta". Handwritten note likely referring to the virtues of Marcus Aurelius described in the following lines.</note>

But he, having survived only one day and night, met his fate, leaving a great longing for himself among the mortals of that age, and an eternal memory of his virtue for posterity. After rumors spread his death abroad, an incredible grief suddenly occupied the army and even all the common people. Indeed, there were no mortals within the Roman dominion who did not receive such news with many tears; and all, as if with one voice, called him some a noble parent...

**Book I. Folio III.**

[Large decorative initial 'C']
**C**ommon to me and you is the grief of this calamity: nor am I less persuaded that you are affected in the same way as I myself. For while my father was alive, I never conducted myself as your superior, but as one of you. For he loved us all as if we were a single person: and he more gladly called me his fellow-soldier <note>original: "commilitonem"</note> than his son. Indeed, he considered the latter a title of nature, but the former a sharing of virtue. Why, he often carried me as an infant in his arms and placed me into your hands, as if entrusting me to your loyalty. <margin>Speech of Commodus to the soldiers.</margin> <insert>Son [and] Fellow-soldier</insert> Therefore, I have no doubt that you will show me all goodwill: since the elders among you ought to regard me as their foster-child, while those of my own age I might rightly call my fellow-students in the law of arms. Indeed, my father loved us all as one, and he took care that we were instructed in every pursuit of virtue and the liberal arts. Now, after him, fortune has given me to you as your Prince: not indeed an adopted one, as those who came before me were, nor as one boasting of an acquired empire. For I alone was born and raised for you in the palace; untouched by private cradles, the imperial purple <note>The "purple" refers to the dye and fabric reserved strictly for the Roman Emperor; to be "born to the purple" meant being born while one's father was the reigning monarch.</note> received me as soon as I had issued from the womb, and the sun saw me as both man and Prince at the same moment. <insert>Born a Prince</insert> Reflecting on these things in your minds, rightly cherish a Prince who was not merely given to you, but born for you. For my father, having now been raised into heaven, is a companion and witness of the gods. Upon us, however, falls the governance of the world and the care of human affairs. What success these things shall have, and how much strength they shall maintain, is in your hands. For if you bravely destroy the remnants of the war and extend the boundaries of the Roman Empire as far as the ocean, you will not only win great glory for yourselves, but you will return the gratitude owed to the memory of our common parent. Believe that he hears what we say and watches what we do here in person. We are most happy to have such a witness of our good deeds. Those things, therefore, which you have done most bravely and prosperously until this day are attributed to his wisdom and governance. But those things which you shall do with me—that is, with your young Emperor—shall win for you a peculiar fame, both for loyalty and for virtue. By this, you will win authority for my age by performing deeds energetically, and the barbarian tribes, repressed at the start of a new reign, will not now arrogantly exalt themselves in contempt of my youth; rather, taught by their current dangers, they will be restrained by perpetual fear. Having said these things and distributed a great sum of money to ensure the soldiers' minds remained faithful to him, he returned to the palace. Therefore, for a short time indeed, all things were managed on the advice of his father's friends. They were never lacking in diligence or prudent counsel, allowing him only as much leisure as they judged sufficient to maintain his physical health. Gradually, however, some of the court attendants crept in, who left nothing undone to corrupt the character of the young Emperor. <margin>Table-flatterers.</note> Indeed, these "table-flatterers" <note>original: "mensarii adulatores" — literally parasites who live off the Emperor's table.</note>, who measured happiness by their bellies and obscene pleasures, repeatedly reminded him of the delights of the city. Now they recounted what things there would be pleasant to see and hear; now they praised the abundance and affluence of all things. In contrast, they disparaged the banks of the Ister <note>The ancient name for the Danube River.</note> as being at all times inconvenient, lacking fruit-bearing trees and gripped by perpetual cold and clouds. "Will you never cease, Emperor," they would say, "to drink water dug out of frozen ice? While others enjoy the warm springs, the cool of flowing streams, and that air and sky peculiar to Italy?" By mentioning such allurements, they easily inflamed the mind of the youth with a desire for pleasures. Therefore, having immediately summoned his friends, he did not hide that he was gripped by a longing for his fatherland. Yet, fearing to admit the causes of such a sudden change, he said he was anxious lest some wealthy man from the nobility might seize the House of the Prince, and then, having gathered forces as if from a most fortified citadel, claim supreme power for himself—arguing that a large enough force of select youth could be raised from the people. While he made such excuses, the rest remained fixed in fear, looking at the ground with silent and mournful faces, until Pompeianus rose. <margin>Pompeianus's speech to Commodus.</margin> He surpassed the others in age and was married to Commodus's eldest sister. "It is not at all surprising, O son and master," he said, "that you are held by a longing for your fatherland. For that same desire for our domestic affairs troubles us as well. But we resist it, because those things which remain to be finished here take priority and weigh more heavily upon us. For you will enjoy those city delights for a longer time in the future. Moreover, Rome is there, wherever the Emperor is. <insert>Rome is where the Emperor is</insert> But to leave a war unfinished seems not only unbecoming but also dangerous. For we would inspire audacity in the barbarians; they will not think we departed out of a desire to return home, but that we fled, struck by fear. How much more beautiful would it be for you to return to the city in triumph after conquering the enemies and extending the borders of the empire to the ocean, driving before you bound and captive kings and barbarian governors? For by these arts in previous ages, Roman men emerged great and illustrious. There is nothing to fear that your affairs there will be endangered. For every best senator is here with you, and the entire army defends your empire in person. Why, the whole treasury of imperial money is also with you. Furthermore, the eternal memory of your father has strengthened loyalty and goodwill toward you among all powers." When Pompeianus had spoken in this manner, urging the better course, he momentarily restrained the impulse of the youth.

<meta>Continuity: Following Commodus's speech to the legions where he emphasized his "birth to the purple," the narrative now shifts to the internal politics of the imperial family and the growing resentment of his sister, Lucilla.</meta>

...[possessing] the honors of the principate <note>original: "principatus insignibus"; these were the symbols and privileges of imperial rank</note> even after her father had betrothed her to Pompeianus. Nevertheless, Commodus allowed her to continue enjoying her former honors. For he permitted her both to sit in the imperial chair <note>original: "sella imperatoria"</note> at the theater and to have the sacred fire carried before her according to custom <note>The "sacred fire" was a ritual honor usually reserved for the Emperor and his immediate family as a sign of their divine protection</note>. 

But afterward, because Commodus married Crispina, it became necessary for Lucilla to yield the first place to the Prince's wife. Lucilla bore this with a resentful mind, viewing the other woman's honor as her own insult. Since she knew that Commodus was loved by her husband Pompeianus, she did not dare to mention anything to him regarding the seizure of the empire. 

Instead, she tested the mind of Quadratus, a most noble and wealthy young man, with whom she was also believed to be having an illicit affair <note>original: "stupri consuetudinem"; implies a scandalous relationship outside of marriage</note>. Complaining most bitterly to him about the injury she had received, she gradually drove the young man to a point where he plotted most ruinously against the Emperor and the entire Senate. Indeed, among others of the senatorial order who conspired with her in this crime, she also brought to her side a certain young man named Quintianus, a man of a ready and daring spirit...

<meta>Continuity: Following the failed assassination attempt by Quintianus and the subsequent exile and execution of Lucilla, the political landscape of Rome shifted. The Emperor Commodus, now deeply suspicious of the Senate, turned his favor toward the Praetorian Prefect Perennius, leading to a period of concentrated power and new threats to the throne.</meta>

# The Rise and Fall of Perennius

As Commodus withdrew from public business, abandoning himself to pleasures and the spectacles of the arena, the administration of the Empire fell entirely into the hands of Perennius.

<margin>The extortion of Perennius</margin>
Perennius, fueled by an insatiable desire for wealth and power, began to systematically eliminate anyone of noble birth or significant fortune. By leveling false accusations against the wealthy, he confiscated their estates to enrich his own private treasury. 

<margin>An ambush prepared for Commodus is betrayed</margin>
His ambition did not stop at wealth; he secretly plotted to seize the imperial throne for his own family. He appointed his sons to high military commands in Illyricum, intending to use their legions to overthrow Commodus. However, his designs were brought to light when certain soldiers, arriving from Britain, informed the Emperor of the Prefect's treachery.

<margin>The slaughter of Perennius</margin>
Realizing the danger, Commodus abandoned his usual apathy. He ordered the immediate execution of Perennius. The man who had once ruled Rome with a word was handed over to the very soldiers he had sought to command, who tore him apart in a fit of rage. 

<margin>The son of Perennius falls</margin>
The purge did not end with the father. Messengers were dispatched with haste to the provinces to ensure that his sons were executed before they could rally their troops to revolt. With the house of Perennius extinguished, a brief period of uneasy peace returned to the palace.

<margin>New plots</margin>
### The Conspiracy of Maternus

However, a new and different kind of threat soon emerged from the borders of the Empire. A common soldier named Maternus, possessing a spirit far above his rank, deserted the army and gathered a massive band of outlaws and other deserters. 

...having planned <note>original: "rati"; implying they had calculated or resolved upon this course of action</note> to leave those regions, they traveled secretly through certain pathless shortcuts <note>original: "per auia quedam compensadia"; these were "compendia" or remote tracks used to bypass the main Roman highways and military checkpoints to avoid detection</note>. Moving separately from one another so as not to draw suspicion, they arrived in Italy. And now Maternus, along with his companions, began to deliberate on the seizure of the throne <note>original: "de regno"; literally "concerning the kingdom," here referring to the imperial office</note> and even greater matters...

<summary>This page details the tyranny and eventual execution of the Prefect Perennius, followed by the emergence of Maternus, a charismatic deserter who led a band of outlaws into Italy to challenge Commodus.</summary>
<keywords>Perennius, Maternus, conspiracy, Illyricum, Praetorian Prefect, deserters, Roman roads, shortcuts, imperial power</keywords>

<meta>Continuity: Following the downfall of the ambitious prefect Perennius, a new threat arises from a former soldier turned bandit leader named Maternus. Having escaped the army and gathered a large force of outlaws, Maternus now sets his sights on the highest prize: the imperial throne.</meta>

### III. 6 On the History of Herodian

...was deliberating with his men. For as his affairs had so far proceeded beyond his every hope, he believed that he should either attempt some great enterprise or, since he had fallen into such a precarious position, ensure he did not die in obscurity or cowardice. But because he realized he did not possess enough strength to resist Commodus in an open battle—as the goodwill of both the Roman commoners and the Praetorian soldiers <term>Praetorians<note>The elite unit of the Imperial Roman army who served as personal bodyguards to the emperors.</note></term> was believed to favor the Emperor—he decided he must proceed by craft and cunning. Therefore, he devised the following plan.

<margin>Solemnities of the Mother of the Gods</margin>
At the set and solemn day at the beginning of spring, the Romans celebrate a procession for the Mother of the Gods <note>The goddess Cybele, an ancient Phrygian deity whose cult was central to Roman state religion.</note>. During this festival, the most precious treasures of every person, and most of the Imperial furniture—notable for their material or craftsmanship—are traditionally carried before the goddess. A general license to play and revel is granted to everyone; people may put on whatever masks or costumes they please, and there is no magistrate so high that someone might not represent his likeness according to their own whim. Thus, one cannot easily distinguish the true person from the false. Maternus thought this would be a suitable time to hide his plot, believing that if he donned the mask of an Imperial bodyguard and equipped his men in the same likeness, they could mingle with the spear-bearers. In this way, they would be believed to be part of the Emperor's own retinue, and with no one on their guard, they could suddenly rush upon Commodus and strike him down.

<margin>The slaughter of Maternus</margin>
But he was betrayed to the Emperor by some of his own companions who had come with him into the city. They were indignant that they might soon have to regard him not as a fellow bandit, but as a prince. Before the feast day arrived, he was seized and beheaded, and those who were part of his faction were subjected to their deserved punishments. Commodus, having performed the sacred rites, celebrated the festival in gratitude to the goddess, joyfully attending the procession. Indeed, all the people celebrated the day with gladness for the safety of the Emperor.

Now, as for the reason why the Romans hold this goddess in such high honor, it seems not out of place to recount what we have learned from history, especially since these matters appear to be unknown to many of the Greeks.

<margin>The image of the Mother of the Gods</margin>
The statue itself is said to have been sent down from heaven. It is not entirely clear what material it is made of, nor which craftsman fashioned it; it is not believed to have been made by human hands at all. They say it fell from the sky into a certain field in Phrygia called Pessinus, and they believe the place received its name from the fall <note>original: "a casu" — a wordplay on the Greek 'pesein,' meaning 'to fall.'</note> of the statue. I find in other sources, however, that a battle was fought there between Ilus the Phrygian and Tantalus the Lydian, either arising over a right of way or, more likely, because of the abduction of Ganymede. 

<margin>The battle of Ilus and Tantalus. Ganymede</margin>
After they had fought for a long time with equal strength and many had fallen on both sides, the name was given to the place from that slaughter. Fame also reports that Ganymede himself was deprived of life here, as the hands of his brother and his lover pulled him in opposite directions. He was taken away from their midst to provide solace for the calamity, and the story was told that he had been carried off to Jupiter <note>The king of the gods, known as Zeus in Greek.</note> and endowed with divine honors. 

In this Pessinus we have mentioned, the Phrygians anciently performed secret rites near the river Gallus, from which the castrated priests of the goddess also take their name <note>The Galli priests.</note>. But when the Roman state grew, they received an oracle stating that their Empire would endure and grow to its greatest height if they transferred the Pessinuntian goddess to themselves. Ambassadors were sent to Phrygia to request the statue of the goddess. This was easily granted, as the Phrygians claimed they were kinsmen of the Romans, descended from Aeneas the Phrygian. 

When the statue was brought by ship and arrived at the mouth of the Tiber, which the Romans then used as a port, the ship suddenly stood still by some divine power. It could not be moved by any strength of the Roman people who were pulling it in competition, until a Vestal Virgin <note>A priestess of Vesta, sworn to celibacy.</note> stepped forward. 

<margin>The prayer of the Vestal</margin>
She had been falsely accused of violating her vow of perpetual virginity. Fearing her sentence, she knelt as a suppliant and asked the people to leave the judgment of her character to the Pessinuntian goddess. When this was granted, she loosened her girdle <note>original: "Zonam" — a belt or sash symbolic of her status.</note> and prayed aloud that if the goddess knew her to be untainted and a virgin, she should command the ship to move forward. As soon as she spoke, she took the tied sash in her hand, and the ship began to follow her. Thus, the Romans admired both the manifest divinity of the goddess and the innocence of the virgin. But enough of this regarding the Pessinuntian goddess; perhaps I have been more long-winded than is proper, yet it may bring some pleasant knowledge to those who are less familiar with Roman affairs.

However, after the plot of Maternus, Commodus fortified himself with a larger guard. He rarely appeared in public, spending most of his time in the suburbs or on his imperial estates far from the city. He withdrew entirely from the administration of justice and all imperial duties.

<margin>A great plague</margin>
Around this same time, it happened that a massive plague occupied the whole of Italy, but it raged most violently in the city of Rome, as the city was both overcrowded with people and received travelers flocking from the whole world. Consequently, a great slaughter of both livestock and humans followed. Then Commodus (for so certain medical experts had persuaded him) retreated to Laurentum, because that region is cooler and shaded by many laurel trees, from which the region takes its name. For they said that the scent of the laurels and the pleasantness of their shade were very effective at avoiding the contagion of the air. Therefore, following the doctors' advice, many in the city also filled their nostrils and ears with the sweetest ointments, and constantly used incense and perfumes. This was because the passages of the senses (as some say) would be occupied by those scents and thus would not admit the pestilential air; or even if they did admit it, the bad air would be overcome by a greater force. Nevertheless, the disease grew no less heavy, and humans died everywhere, along with the cattle that lived among them.
