**Book I. Folio V.**

Cleander was a certain man of Phrygian <note>An ancient region in what is now central Turkey; Phrygians were often stereotyped as subservient in Roman literature.</note> origin, belonging to that class of men who are sold publicly by a crier at auction. [Margin: Cleander.] When he was brought into the imperial household as a slave, he grew up alongside Commodus himself. He was eventually promoted to such a height of honor and authority that he alone held the command of the bodyguard, the care of the imperial bedchamber <note>The position of "Cubicularius" or Chamberlain, which granted intimate and influential access to the Emperor.</note>, and even the prefecture of the soldiers. However, wealth and luxury soon incited him to hope for the empire itself. Therefore, having amassed a vast sum of money, he bought up a great deal of grain and kept it locked away. He hoped to secure the goodwill of the Roman people and the army for himself if he first made them suffer through a shortage of basic necessities, and then suddenly won them over with massive distributions. He had also built a massive gymnasium and opened public baths for the citizens, attempting to bait the people in this manner. But the Romans had long been resentful, blaming him for the entire pestilence <note>The Latin "pestilentia" here refers to both a literal plague and the man-made famine caused by Cleander's hoarding.</note>. Hating this man of insatiable greed, they first began to mock and denounce him repeatedly in the theaters. Later, while Commodus was staying in the suburbs, the entire city suddenly rushed together with great shouts, demanding Cleander’s execution. As the suburbs were filled with the riot and Commodus himself was indulging in pleasures in his deep retreat—unaware of what was happening because Cleander had hidden the truth from him—the prince’s armed cavalry suddenly burst out beyond everyone’s expectation. At Cleander’s command, they charged forward, wounding everyone in their path. [Margin: Slaughter of the unarmed.] The unarmed people were unable to withstand the assault of the armed men, nor the crowd on foot against the cavalry; thus, they were driven back into the city in flight. There, many were put to death—not only those the soldiers cut down with the sword, but also those trampled by the horses or crushed in the dense crowd or the cavalry’s charge.

The soldiers pursued them to the city gates without any hindrance and killed a great part of the people. However, those who had remained in the city, realizing the calamity of their fellows, closed their houses and climbed onto the roofs and battlements, attacking the cavalry from above with stones and roof tiles. Thus, fortune was immediately reversed; no one dared to fight the soldiers hand-to-hand, but the entire multitude fought from above as if from safety. Consequently, many of the cavalry were wounded; unable to endure further, they turned their backs and fled. Many fell under the frequent throw of missiles. Many were thrown from their horses, their footing failing as the animals slipped on the fallen stones. Furthermore, the infantry <note>The urban cohorts or city police, who often rivaled the elite cavalry guards.</note> who were stationed in the city quickly brought aid to the people against the cavalry, whom they detested. Thus, while it was effectively a civil war, no one dared to report what was happening to Commodus for fear of Cleander’s power. Finally, his eldest sister, named Fadilla, ran to the emperor (for a sister had easy access). With her hair disheveled and throwing herself on the ground in a clear state of mourning, she said: "You, O Prince, live in leisure and are ignorant of all that is happening, yet you are in extreme danger. We, your own blood, are nearly destroyed. It is over for the Roman people; it is over for a great part of the army. What we did not expect to suffer even from barbarians, our own household does to us. Those upon whom you bestowed the greatest benefits are your primary enemies. Cleander has armed the people and the army against you; though he is hated by one and dear to the other, both are in arms, committing slaughter among themselves and filling Rome with civil blood. But the calamity of both sides will surely fall upon us unless you immediately put to death this most wicked servant, who has already caused such slaughter for them and will soon do the same to us."

Speaking these words, she tore her garment; many others who were present, taking courage from the woman’s words, began to terrify Commodus. Struck with fear—dreading the danger not as something impending, but as something already present—he ordered Cleander to be summoned in haste. Cleander, knowing nothing for certain but suspecting something had been reported to the Emperor, approached. [Margin: The killing of Cleander.] As he arrived, the Emperor ordered him to be seized; his head was cut off and fixed on a pole to be carried around, providing a delightful and longed-for spectacle for the people. Thus the evil was settled and the fighting on both sides was broken off. When the soldiers saw that the man for whom they were fighting had been killed, they feared the anger of the emperor, realizing they had been deceived and had acted against his will. The people, on the other hand, felt satisfied by the punishment of the man responsible. Furthermore, Cleander’s children (for he had two sons) and all those who had been his friends were slaughtered to a man. Their bodies were dragged through the city, treated most shamefully, and finally thrown into the sewers. This was the end of Cleander’s fate; as if in that one man, nature more ambitiously displayed (if I may say so) that a human could be raised from the lowest place to the highest summit, and then, once raised, be cast down again by any small and unexpected moment of fortune. 

However, although Commodus feared the people might attempt some new action against him, he returned to the city at the persuasion of his friends. He was received with joyful acclamations and a great entourage as he went to the imperial palace. Yet, from that time on, having encountered so many dangers, he began to trust no one. He began to kill one man after another, giving credit to every slander. To this, he joined no friend who possessed any virtue, but turned his mind away from all upright pursuits. Indeed, day and night, various unbridled physical pleasures pressed upon him in the heaviest servitude; he removed everyone from his threshold as if they were traitors—anyone distinguished by integrity or even mediocre discipline. # **Herodian**

Indeed, the flatterers of Commodus represented even his most shameful acts as virtues, treating him as if he were their personal champion. He practiced chariot-driving and the slaying of wild beasts beyond all measure. Because of these pursuits, his sycophants celebrated him with the glory of "fortitude," even though he handled these matters with far less dignity than was appropriate for a modest prince. At that time, there also appeared <margin>Prodigies.</margin> certain prodigies in the sky; for stars were visible continuously throughout the day, and some of them appeared elongated, as if suspended in mid-air. Furthermore, animals of every kind were born that did not preserve their natural forms, having both monstrous body shapes and limbs that were entirely mismatched. But the greatest disaster caused immediate sorrow and terrified everyone with the worst of omens for the future. For although there had been no rain or clouds—only a slight earthquake preceding it—whether by a stroke of lightning at night or by some fire struck out during the earthquake itself, the entire <margin>The Temple of Peace burned down.</margin> Temple of Peace was suddenly consumed by fire. This was, of course, the largest and most beautiful of all works in the entire city. It was also the wealthiest of all temples, exceptionally well-fortified and adorned with much gold and silver. Indeed, nearly everyone used to deposit their riches there as if in a treasury; therefore, the fire, which raged through the night, reduced many of the wealthy to poverty. For this reason, all the people mourned the common loss publicly, while each individual wept for his own private loss. But when the entire temple was consumed by the fires, many other beautiful buildings in the city also caught fire. Among these was even the Temple of Vesta, so that <margin>The Palladium.</margin> the Palladium <note>The Palladium was an ancient wooden statue of Pallas Athena, believed to have been brought from Troy by Aeneas; its safety was thought to ensure the safety of Rome itself.</note> was seen by all. This object is primarily revered and kept in secret by the Romans, having been brought from Troy (as they say); it was then seen by men for the first time since it had arrived in Italy. Indeed, the Vestal Virgins snatched it up and carried it through the middle of the Sacred Way into the Emperor’s palace. Many other beautiful parts of the city were burned, and the fire, having spread for several days, was not settled until it was extinguished by sudden rains. Thus, the mortals of that age attributed the whole matter to the Gods, by whose will they believed the fire had both begun and ceased; they interpreted the destruction of the Temple of Peace as a portent of the wars that followed thereafter. The eventual outcome of events confirmed this famous interpretation. Indeed, while the city labored under many great inconveniences, the multitude no longer looked upon Commodus with goodwill as before, but everyone attributed the cause of that calamity to his unjust acts and the other crimes of his life. For his crimes were not hidden from the people, nor did he wish them to be hidden; rather, the things he perpetrated at home, not without infamy, he did not fear to show even in public. He proceeded to such a point <margin>The insolence of Commodus.</margin> of madness and impudence that he repudiated his father's surname; and instead of "Commodus, son of Marcus," he ordered himself to be called "Hercules, son of Jupiter." Laying aside the traditional attire of Roman princes, he would spread out a lion's skin beneath him and carry a club in his hand, while simultaneously wrapping himself in purple garments interwoven with gold, much to the ridicule of everyone; for in the same costume, he represented both effeminate luxury and heroic virtue. Such was the way he presented himself daily. He also changed the names of the months, and in place of the ancient names, he imposed new ones from his own titles, most of which referred to Hercules as the strongest of beings. Furthermore, he ordered statues of himself to be placed throughout the entire city, including one in front of the Senate House <note>original: "curia"</note> depicted as an archer drawing a bow, so that even the images themselves might display terror and threats; this statue, however, the Senate removed after his death and replaced with an image of Liberty. But when Commodus could no longer restrain himself, he publicly announced he would host spectacles, promising that he would kill all the wild beasts with his own hand and fight in single combat with the strongest of the young men. As these rumors were celebrated, people from all over Italy and the neighboring nations flocked to the spectacle—something they had never seen with their own eyes nor ever heard of in stories. Indeed, <margin>Commodus's skill in throwing.</margin> his hand was said to be so steady that whatever he aimed at, he hit with a javelin or an arrow. He was constantly accompanied by the most select Parthian archers and Numidian javelin throwers, yet he far surpassed them all in skill. When the day of the spectacle arrived, a <term>peridromus</term> <note>A raised, circular gallery or walkway that allowed the Emperor to move around the arena while remaining safely separated from the animals.</note> had been built for Commodus in the crowded amphitheater, through which he could run in a circle so that he would not be in danger by fighting the beasts at close quarters. Instead, by throwing weapons from above and from a safe place, he displayed his knowledge of throwing rather than his courage. Therefore, he would strike stags and does, and other horned animals except for bulls, while running himself and following them; he would lay them low with the most certain strikes, preventing their flight. But lions and panthers, and other most noble animals of that kind, he would pierce with javelins from above while running in a circle, so that no one saw a second weapon used, nor any wound except a lethal one. For as soon as the beast had stirred itself, he would immediately wound it either in the forehead or in the heart; he used no other target, nor was his weapon aimed at any other part of the body, so that the beast was finished simultaneously with the wound itself. Moreover, beasts were collected from everywhere; and then for the first time we saw things that we previously admired only in paintings. Whatever had been unknown to prior ages—from India, Ethiopia, the South, and the North—he both killed and displayed, leaving everyone astonished by such a steady hand and by weapons that never missed. Sometimes he would also shoot arrows with a crescent-shaped head <note>original: "lunatæ cuspidis"</note> at Maurusian ostriches, which moved most swiftly by the speed of their feet and the sail-like use of their wings; he would strike the very top of the neck, and thus cut off their heads...

### IV. Herodian

<note>original: "tudinem credebatur" — This page begins mid-sentence, concluding the thought that the list found by the young boy was believed to be a record of those marked for death.</note> ...and after the tablet had been handed over into his hands, Electus said: "Look, see what kind of feast we are to celebrate tonight." Upon reading it, he was struck with terror (for he was Egyptian by birth: a bold man, quick to act and easily moved to anger). He immediately sent the sealed tablet by a man faithful to him to be read by Laetus. He likewise was terrified and hurried to Marcia, pretending to go to her to consult about the things that pertained to the preparation of the gladiatorial games by order of the prince. Using this pretext, they decided that they must either act immediately or suffer the consequences, as there was no room for delay or procrastination. It was decided, therefore, that the matter should be carried out by poison <margin>Poisonous Draught</margin>, which Marcia promised she would easily administer. Indeed, she was accustomed to being the first to mix and offer him the cup, so that it might be drunk more pleasantly when offered by a mistress. Therefore, as he returned from the baths, she offered him a cup of poison mixed with the most fragrant wine. Having gathered a great thirst from long bathing and hunting, he drank it down greedily, as was his custom. For this reason, he was immediately seized by a heavy head and fell into a deep sleep; since he thought this had happened from exhaustion, he gave himself over to rest. Electus and Marcia, however, ordered everyone to depart immediately and for each to return to their own home, lest they wake Commodus who was in need of sleep. He was accustomed to doing this at other times as well from excessive drunkenness; for whether he was attending to baths or banquets, he truly had no set time for rest. Indeed, one pleasure followed another, and these being most diverse among themselves, they compelled the man to serve them, even against his will, at any time.

Therefore, when he had rested a little, and the power of the poison had already insinuated itself into his stomach and bowels, a dizziness arose, followed by a great deal of vomiting—either because the heavy food he had taken before and the large amount of unmixed wine expelled the venom, or because it is the custom of princes to use a medicine <note>This refers to "Mithridatium," a universal antidote used by Roman elites to build immunity to poisons.</note> to prevent poisoning before they take food. However, when he had vomited much, the conspirators feared that if all the poison were ejected, he would recover himself and order them all to be killed at once. They persuaded a certain Narcissus <margin>The death of Commodus</margin>, a bold and vigorous young man, with a great reward to strangle him in his bedchamber. This was the end of the life of Commodus: he ruled the empire for thirteen years after his father's death, the most noble of all emperors before him, and the most handsome of all men of that age. But if one must speak of his bravery as well, he was second to none, especially in his skill with aimed strikes. Yet, he contaminated his entire way of life with the foulest pursuits (as has been said).

# BOOK TWO

[Large decorative initial O]
**C**OMMODUS HAVING BEEN KILLED, as we demonstrated in the previous book: since the killers wished to hide the deed and deceive the palace guards, they wrapped the small body in a cheap rug and bound it. They then ordered two servants of proven loyalty to carry it out of the house as if it were some superfluous piece of bedroom furniture. Those who were carrying it out escaped through the midst of the guards—some of whom were drunk and dozing, holding their spears with limp hands, while others were indifferent to things they thought did not concern them. Thus the body of the prince was carried out by stealth, placed on a vehicle during the night, and sent to Aritium. 

Laetus, Electus, and Marcia, having deliberated for a long time on what should be done, finally decided to spread rumors of his death as if he had suddenly fallen into apoplexy <note>original: "apoplexiam"; in the 2nd century, this referred to a sudden stroke or internal collapse, often associated with the lifestyle of the gluttonous.</note>. They believed this would be easily credited to him, as it was well known he was frequently accustomed to gorging himself on immoderate feasts. But before all else, it seemed best to choose a man advanced in age and of modest character for the empire, through whom they themselves might be safe and everyone might breathe again after such a cruel and immoderate tyranny. Therefore, after long consultation, they found no one so suitable as Pertinax <margin>Pertinax</margin>. 

Pertinax was an Italian by birth, famous for his achievements at home and in war, and distinguished by many trophies he had erected against the Germans and the Eastern barbarians. He was the only one remaining of those most venerable friends whom the father <note>Marcus Aurelius</note> had left to Commodus; the father had bestowed the most honor upon him of all his companions and generals. He had remained safe until now, either because Commodus feared his very gravity or ignored him because of the man’s poverty. Indeed, it added to his praise that although he had administered more offices than anyone else, he was yet the poorest of all. 

They approached this Pertinax, therefore, in the dead of night while all were asleep: Laetus and Electus with a few of the same faction. When they found the door closed, they woke the gatekeeper; when he opened it and saw the soldiers and Laetus the Prefect present, he was terrified and, struck with fear, announced them to Pertinax. He ordered them to be admitted immediately, saying that the evils he had long foreboded would soon come to pass. Furthermore, such was his constancy of mind that he did not even move from his bed or change the expression of his face. But when Laetus and Electus entered, believing they had been sent to kill him, he said with a face full of boldness and not at all pale: "For a long time now, I have expected this end of life every single night, as I was the only one left of all my father's friends. Therefore, I wondered why Commodus deferred the matter for so long. Why do you stand there? Why not carry out your orders and free me at last from this sad and perpetual dread?" To this Laetus replied, "Cease..."

To this, Pertinax replied: "Stop mocking an old man, and proving my cowardice by trying to deceive me before you kill me." <margin>Pertinax to the soldiers</margin> <note>Though the margin says "to the soldiers," Pertinax is currently addressing the conspirators who have come to his house at night.</note> And Electus said: "Since you trust us so little, take this booklet (for surely you recognize the handwriting of Commodus) and read it yourself; you will undoubtedly realize how great a danger we have escaped. When Pertinax had done this—having decided he must trust men who were already his closest friends—and understood the whole affair, he placed himself entirely in their power.

It was decided first to go to the army and test the minds of the soldiers. Laetus promised he could easily bring them to his own opinion, since as their Prefect <term>Praetorian Prefect: the commander of the Emperor's elite bodyguard</term> he would have some authority among them. Therefore, all who were present hurried to the army camp, as much of the night had already passed and the day of the Kalends of January was approaching. <note>January 1st, the day the new Consuls took office.</note> Furthermore, they sent out faithful men to spread the rumor everywhere: that Commodus had passed away, and that Pertinax, who was now to rule, was hastening to the army. When this rumor spread, the entire populace suddenly began to rage like people possessed, running through the streets and joyfully announcing the news to their friends—especially those who possessed high rank or riches. For it was upon them that the greatest danger from Commodus had loomed. They went therefore to the temples and altars to give thanks to the Gods, some shouting one thing and some another. Some cried out that the tyrant was dead, others called him a gladiator, and some used even fouler names. Those things which fear had suppressed until now were now being thrown about with impunity, born of this sudden license and liberty. But the greater part of the people rushed with quickened pace toward the army camp, fearing that the soldiers might not receive Pertinax as emperor with enough goodwill. For they expected that a moderate prince would not be entirely to the liking of soldiers who were accustomed to serving a tyranny and exercising all manner of violence and plunder. Thus, as if to compel their obedience, the crowds flocked to the camp.

When they arrived, Laetus and Electus entered together with Pertinax. There, having summoned the soldiers, Laetus spoke in this manner: <margin>The speech of Laetus</margin> "Commodus your emperor has died of the disease of apoplexy. <note>Laetus is lying to the soldiers to hide the murder; 'apoplexy' was a common euphemism for a sudden stroke or heart failure.</note> No one else caused his death but himself. For while we were suggesting the best and most healthy things to him in vain, he—behaving as you all know—was choked by excessive food and drink. Thus he died, extinguished by his own fate. For the cause of death is not one and the same for all men, but varies from person to person, though all tend toward the same end of life. But in his place, we and the Roman people bring to you a man grave in age, moderate in life, and most skilled in military discipline. You veterans have frequently experienced his warlike virtue, and the rest of you have judged him, as Prefect of the City for so many years, most worthy not only of honor but also of admiration. Therefore, fortune gives you not only a prince, but also an excellent father. His principate <term>Principate: the reign of an emperor</term> will be most pleasant not only to you, who protect him here, but also to those who defend the banks of the rivers and the borders of the Roman Empire, as they surely remember his illustrious deeds. No longer shall we have to win over the barbarians with gold; rather, remembering what they suffered under this leader, they shall be subdued by fear."

As Laetus said this, the people could no longer restrain themselves. Even while the soldiers were still hesitating and doubting, the people declared him Augustus <margin>Pertinax is hailed as Augustus</margin> and called him Father, following up with all manner of favorable acclamations. The soldiers then did the same, though not with equal eagerness; however, the crowd of people surrounding them on all sides—unarmed but celebrating a festival day—easily forced them to join the acclamation and call Pertinax 'Augustus.' Soon, having sworn the customary oath in his name and performed the sacred rites, the people and the army, all wearing laurel wreaths, followed him. But after he was led to the imperial palace through the night by the soldiers and the people (as we said), he was tossed by great waves of anxiety. And though he appeared to be of a brave and constant mind, the present circumstances terrified him greatly—not that he was particularly worried about his own safety, for he had scorned graver dangers at other times, but he was turning over in his mind the sudden change from a tyranny and considering the nobility of certain Senators. He believed they would by no means allow the principate, after a most high-born emperor, to fall back to a man of private and obscure stock. For even if his own life was well-spoken of as temperate and frugal, and he had achieved the greatest glory in military affairs, yet he was unequal in the nobility of his birth.

Therefore, after dawn broke, he went to the Senate House. He allowed neither the sacred fire to be carried before him nor any of the insignia of the principate to be raised until he could learn the opinion of the Senate. <note>Ritual required the 'sacred fire' and the axes (fasces) to be carried before an emperor as signs of his power.</note> But as soon as they saw him, they all received him with joyful acclamations unanimously, saluting him as Augustus and Emperor. But he began to refuse the name of empire as an invidious thing, making excuses for his old age and begging for pardon, repeatedly saying there were many patrician men for whom the empire would be more suitable. At the same time, taking the hand of Glabrio, he tried to draw him forward and urged him to sit in the Imperial chair. <margin>The nobility and modesty of Glabrio</margin> For he was the most noble of all the patricians, tracing his family lineage back to Aeneas, the son of Venus and Anchises; he was also a consul for the second time. ### **Of Herodian**

...and his daughter, along with a crowd of parasites: urging him to leave the table, hurry out, and learn what was happening. They repeatedly exhorted him to seize the empire while it lay abandoned, promising that he would surpass all others in bribery since he possessed such vast wealth. Therefore, when he reached the walls, he began to shout: promising that he would give them whatever they wished, for he had great resources, <margin>Sulpitianus</margin> storehouses full of gold, and heaps of silver. At the same time, Sulpitianus—a man of consular rank, the Urban Prefect <term>Urban Prefect: The high-ranking official responsible for the administration and public order of the city of Rome</term>, and the father-in-law of the late Pertinax—was also bidding for the Empire. However, the soldiers held him in suspicion because of his close relationship with Pertinax; they suspected some trickery was afoot to avenge the former Emperor’s murder. Consequently, they lowered ladders and lifted Julianus up over the walls; they did not dare open the gates until they had agreed upon the amount of money to be paid. Once he had entered the camp, he first promised to restore the honors of Commodus <note>Commodus had been declared a public enemy after his death; Julianus hoped to win over the soldiers who had loved the former tyrant</note> and the statues that the Senate had removed. He also promised to grant them the same license and freedom they had once enjoyed under him. Furthermore, he promised to give each individual soldier much more silver than they had dared to ask for or expected to receive, and he assured them there would be no delay in payment, for he kept that money stored at his home. Swayed by these things and raised to such great hope, the soldiers declared Julianus the <margin>Julianus Augustus</margin> Sovereign <term>Sovereign: The Latin 'Princeps' literally means 'First Citizen', the title of the Emperor</term>; at the same time, they bestowed upon him the name of Commodus. Then, raising their standards and attaching his image to them, they prepared to escort the man out. Therefore, after the customary sacrifice was performed in the camp, he went out with a larger military escort than other Emperors had been accustomed to. Indeed, because he had purchased the empire by force, against the will of the people, and through such shame and disgrace, he rightly feared a violent outburst from the multitude. But the soldiers put on their armor and surrounded him on all sides in a *testudo* <note>original: "testudine" — a 'tortoise' formation where shields are locked together for protection</note> formation, so that they might fight if the situation required it. Having taken their Emperor into the center, with shields and spears raised above their heads to be safer if stones were thrown from the rooftops, they escorted him to the palace. The people did not dare resist, yet neither did they follow him with favorable acclamations as was the custom. Instead, they shouted curses from a distance, <margin>The corruption of the soldiers</margin> bitterly reproaching him for having purchased the Empire with money. Then, for the first time, it became clear that the morals of the soldiers were corrupted; a foul and insatiable greed for money and a contempt for the majesty of the Emperor began to take root. For since there was no one to act as an avenger for an Emperor so cruelly murdered, and no one had prohibited the Empire from being put up for sale and foully auctioned off, this was truly the beginning and the cause for the soldiers to become most shameful and rebellious in the future. Thus, their avarice and contempt for their rulers grew daily, even to the point of bloodshed. Indeed, Julianus, having obtained the empire, immediately gave himself over to delicacies and drunken revelry, being negligent toward the public business and leading a most soft life overflowing with luxury. But he had also deceived the hopes of the soldiers, as he was unable to fulfill his promises. This was because he did not possess as much wealth at home as he had boasted, and the public treasury had long ago been exhausted by the insane expenditures of Commodus. For this reason, he not only found the soldiers hostile toward him, but he was easily despised by the people who were aware of the whole affair. Consequently, they followed him with insults as he passed by, reproaching him for his shameful and questionable pleasures. This reached the point where they openly attacked Julianus even in the Circus <term>Circus: The Circus Maximus, a massive arena for chariot racing where the Roman public often gathered to voice political grievances</term>, where the greatest force of men congregates, calling upon Niger to be the avenger of the Roman Empire and the leader of the highest office, <margin>Niger called to the empire</margin> praying that he would arrive as soon as possible and deliver them from such insults. This Niger had served as consul and was then in charge of all Syria, which was by far the greatest command at that time. Indeed, the Phoenicians and the entire region up to the Euphrates were under Niger’s command. He was already of an age approaching seniority, and having been involved in many great affairs, he had obtained a reputation for mildness and skill, such that he was thought to emulate the life of Pertinax. It was by these qualities that he seemed to have won the favor of the people. Therefore, the constant and frequent cries of the people implored him; while they tore the present Julianus apart with insults, they all followed the absent Niger with imperial acclamations and favorable voices. When he understood this, Niger—thinking that everything would succeed according to his wishes, seeing that Julianus was neglected by the soldiers (whose trust he had failed to keep) and despised by the people as unworthy of the throne—conceived the hope of claiming the empire. At first, he would send the commanders, tribunes, and other soldiers who held the most authority back to their homes at various times, after they had been informed of everything being reported from Rome. He did this with the intention that rumors would be spread as widely as possible throughout the entire East. In this way, he thought he would join as many people as possible to his cause: if he appeared not as one seizing the empire through plots, but as one bringing help to those calling and imploring him. Consequently, everyone immediately flocked to him, each one for his part entreating and beseeching him to take up the governance of the republic as soon as possible. Now, the Syrian people are by nature fickle and prone to revolution. Furthermore, they loved Niger vehemently because he had governed them most humanely and had kept the multitude occupied with games and celebrations. The Syrians are, by their very nature, quite fond of such amusements; among them, the people of Antioch, inhabiting a very large and prosperous city, celebrate games and festivals almost the entire year, either in the city itself or in the suburbs. Therefore, by constantly putting on spectacles and allowing their minds to be cheered by leisure, he had so attached the common people to himself that he was greatly cherished by all. When he understood that this was the state of affairs, having ordered the soldiers to be present on a set day, along with the rest of the flowing multitude, he spoke from a platform <note>original: "pro suggestu" — a raised dais or rostrum used by generals to address troops</note> constructed for that purpose.

The people of Rome, however, did not hide their indignation. They openly showed their hatred for Julianus, regarding him as a man who had purchased the Roman state as if it were a common piece of merchandise. They gathered in the Circus and shouted against him, calling instead for Pescennius Niger—the governor of Syria—to come to their aid and save the Empire. 

<margin>The speech of Niger</margin>
Niger was at that time in the East, where he was well-loved by the soldiers and the provincial people for his moderate and just rule. When the messengers arrived from Rome telling of the people’s desire, he gathered his troops and the citizens of Antioch. He spoke to them, explaining that he was not moved by personal ambition, but by the cries of the Roman people who were suffering under a shameful usurper. 

<margin>Niger is greeted as Emperor</margin>
Upon hearing his words, the soldiers and the inhabitants of Syria immediately hailed him as Emperor. They clothed him in the imperial purple <note>The "purple" refers to the Tyrian purple robes reserved exclusively for the Emperor</note> and conducted him to the temples of Antioch with great ceremony.

However, while Niger was being celebrated in the East, another contender was rising in the West. <margin>Severus the African sets his path toward the Empire</margin> Septimius Severus was then the governor of the legions in Pannonia <term>Pannonia: A strategically vital Roman province located along the Danube river, covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</term>. Severus was an African by birth, a man of keen intellect, tireless energy, and a stern, even harsh, disposition. He realized that the Empire was up for grabs and that Julianus was weak, while Niger was far away and distracted by the luxuries of the East.

<margin>The dream of Severus</margin>
Severus was further encouraged by several omens and signs of divine providence. <note>original: "providentia" — the Roman belief that the gods or fate directed the course of human events</note> The most famous of these was a dream he had experienced: he saw a magnificent horse carrying the Emperor Pertinax; suddenly, the horse threw Pertinax from its back, but when Severus approached, it allowed him to mount calmly and carried him safely through the center of the Roman Forum. 

Believing that he was destined for greatness, Severus began to win over the spirits of his soldiers <note>original: "animos" — the morale or will of the troops</note>, joining them to his cause by promising to avenge the murder of the beloved Pertinax. He kept his true intentions for the supreme power hidden at first, focusing his rhetoric on justice and the restoration of Roman dignity.

# XI **Of Herodian**

<margin>Severus’s crafty nature.</margin> Therefore, Severus, seizing the opportunity, easily led them wherever he wished. He pretended that he was not seeking the empire for himself or striving for supreme power, but rather that he was going to avenge the blood of such a great prince <note>Referring to the Emperor Pertinax, who had been murdered by the Praetorian Guard</note>. For just as the men of that region possess very strong and tall bodies and are most ready for battle and slaughter, so they are of a thick-witted nature <note>original: "pingui sunt ingenio" — a common Roman stereotype that those from the northern frontier were physically strong but intellectually simple</note>; therefore, they do not easily perceive if you do or say something cleverly or craftily. Consequently, when Severus had convinced them that he wished to pursue the killers of Pertinax, he so won them all over that he was proclaimed Emperor, and he received supreme power from them. But as soon as he had tested the spirits of the Pannonians <note>inhabitants of a Roman province in modern-day Hungary and the Balkans</note>, he immediately enticed the governors of the neighboring nations—all those subject to the Roman empire—with great rewards. Severus was, above all other mortals, uniquely suited to feigning affection, so much so that he did not hesitate to break an oath if necessity demanded it; he carried one thing ready on his tongue while keeping something quite different hidden in his heart. Therefore, having introduced himself through letters to all of Illyricum and the governors of the provinces, and having gathered soldiers from everywhere, he took the surname of Pertinax, which he suspected would be most pleasing not only to the Illyrians but also to the Roman people. Having called everyone together into the field, he is said to have spoken from the platform <term>suggestu</term> <note>A "suggestus" was a raised tribunal or stage from which a commander addressed his army</note> in this manner:

<margin>Severus’s speech</margin>

**H**ow much either of faith or of religion toward the gods—by whom you have sworn your oaths—and how much honor you show to the Emperors, whom you so greatly venerate, you easily demonstrate, soldiers, when you are so greatly indignant that the urban cohorts <note>The Praetorian Guard stationed in Rome</note>, who are administrators of pomp rather than of valor, have committed so foul a deed. As for me, it is my prayer now, as I first embark upon such great hope (for surely you know how I have always been obedient to the commands of the princes), to bring to a conclusion and explain those things that are dear to your hearts, and not to allow the Roman Empire to fall into neglect. Indeed, among our ancestors, the Empire was always conducted with the highest authority and seemed venerable to everyone. But after it fell to Commodus, even if it often faltered because of his youth, yet every vice was overshadowed both by the nobility of the prince himself and by the memory of his most holy father <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>. His errors did not deserve hatred so much as mercy. Indeed, we did not attribute the things that were done to him so much as to his flatterers and the other practitioners and ministers of evil arts. This continued until the empire was bestowed upon that most holy old man <note>Pertinax</note>, the memory of whose virtue and integrity still resides in our minds. Yet those men were so far from being able to tolerate him that they removed such a man from our midst by a wicked murder. Since his time, someone—I know not who—has most shamefully auctioned off the empire of the land and sea; he is hateful to the people, as you have heard, and he finds little loyalty even from the soldiers upon whom he imposed himself. Yet even if they were to defend him, they are not to be compared to you, neither in their total number nor in the valor of individuals. Furthermore, military matters have exercised you. For you have been accustomed to meet barbarians foot-to-foot, to endure all labors, to despise cold and heat, to tread upon rivers frozen with ice, to drink from wells you have dug rather than drawn, and to remain watchful in the hunt. In short, you have acquired all the provisions for valor, so that it is not easy for anyone to resist your strength. For a soldier is proven by labor, not by softness; those men, satisfied and nourished by luxury, will not be able to endure even your voices, let alone your battle. And if the affairs of Syria <note>referring to his rival Pescennius Niger</note> seem formidable to anyone, let him consider even from this how weak they are and upon how thin a hope they lean, since they have not yet dared to move forward...

Naturally, a great fear gripped all the cities of Italy at the sight of such a massive army. For the people in Italy <margin>The trepidation of an Italy unaccustomed to arms.</margin> had for a long time been completely removed from the use of weapons and war, occupying themselves instead with their fields and the pursuits of peace. By subduing both Greeks and barbarians, they won for themselves the dominion of both land and sea; nor was there any part of the world, or any region under heaven, where Roman arms did not extend their power. ### Herodian

...his own soldiers, acting in the manner of an enemy: wounding or striking no one, but instead forming a circle to keep them trapped in the middle. They pointed only their daggers and spears so that, out of fear of being wounded while unarmed, the few would not dare to resist the many who were fully armed. Once he held them closed in as if by a net of weapons <note>original: "indagine armorum" — a hunting term for driving game into a net</note>, he addressed them with a loud voice and a turbulent spirit in this way:

<margin>Severus’s harsh speech.</margin>

**S**urely you see for yourselves that we surpass you in wisdom, strength, and even in number. You have been captured as easily as possible, and you are held with almost no effort. What shall become of you is entirely in my hands. You stand here now as victims subject to our command. If you were to suffer the punishment truly owed for your crimes, you would never find one sufficient. That most holy old man, the best of emperors <note>Referring to Pertinax, whom Severus claimed to be avenging</note>, whom you were bound to preserve and protect, you yourselves murdered. The Roman Empire, famous for its perpetual glory—which our ancestors took up in the name of either virtue or nobility—you have basely and foully sold, as if it were some piece of private equipment, like common auctioneers. And you, most cowardly of men, did not even dare to protect or defend the very man you had raised to power, but instead betrayed him. For these crimes and your wicked deeds, a thousand deaths are owed to you, should anyone seek a punishment equal to your guilt. Therefore, you surely see what is fair for you to suffer. I, however, will abstain from blood, nor will I imitate your hands. But since justice and divine law forbid that such men should be the bodyguards of a prince—having violated your oath, polluted your hands with the blood of a citizen and an emperor, and betrayed your trust—our humanity will grant you your lives and bodies. Furthermore, I command my soldiers thus: let them strip you and send you away naked, deprived of your military garments. To you, however, I command that you depart as far as possible. I likewise edict, swear, and announce that you shall pay with your heads if any of you are hereafter seen within the hundredth milestone from the city <note>About 92 miles from Rome; a traditional legal limit for banishment</note>.

Upon these commands, the Illyrian soldiers <note>Severus's elite troops from the Danube region, known for their toughness</note> immediately rushed forward and snatched away those short daggers which they wore decorated with gold and silver for ceremonial use. Then, having forcibly removed their belts, clothing, and all other military insignia, they sent them away, every one of them stripped and discharged from service. Indeed, seeing themselves betrayed and captured by a trick, they remained patient—for what could naked men do against the armed, or a few against many?

<margin>The discharge of the soldiers.</margin>

They departed, therefore, bewailing their lot and interpreting their spared lives as a gift; yet they were weary and grieving that, having come out unarmed, they had offered themselves to be captured so basely and ignominiously. Severus also employed another strategy. Fearing that the stripped and discharged men might, in their desperation, return to the camp and take up arms again, he ordered the most elite and trusted of his soldiers, sent ahead by other paths and trails, to secretly break into the empty camp and lock out those returning by occupying it with their own arms. Thus did the killers of Pertinax receive their punishment. After this, Severus, with the rest of his army drawn up in arms, sought Rome. The Romans were equally astonished and fearful at the first sight of him, reflecting on the man's audacity and his fortune. Indeed, the Senate and the entire populace, wearing laurel wreaths, received him—the first of all men and emperors to achieve such a great feat without blood, and even without dust <note>original: "citra puluerem" — an idiom meaning without effort or struggle</note>. Everything about him was marvelous, especially his sharpness of mind, his endurance of labor, and the audacity with which he maintained high hopes for the greatest undertakings. 

After the people received him with auspicious acclamations and the entire Senate greeted him at the gates of the city, he entered the Temple of Jupiter, performed the divine rites, and having similarly greeted the other sacred buildings according to custom, he finally retired to the imperial palace. The next day he entered the Senate house <note>original: "curiam"</note> and there delivered a mild speech full of the best hope. Embracing everyone kindly, both publicly and privately, he said he had come to the city to avenge the murdered Pertinax, and would see to it that the foundations of an aristocratic state <note>original: "optimatium"</note> were laid under his rule. No one would be put to death or stripped of their goods unless condemned by judgment; he would not tolerate informers; he would be a rival to Marcus Aurelius in his governing of the empire, and would possess not only the surname of Pertinax but his mind as well.

<margin>Severus in the Senate.</margin>

By speaking in this vein, he won favor and trust for himself. However, some of the older men, who knew his usual character, were already whispering to the others in secret: that this man was a "chameleon" <note>original: "versipellem" — literally "skin-changer" or one who can shift his appearance</note>, handling everything with trickery and art; a master of pretending and dissembling, holding nothing as sacred as long as it achieved what he believed would be of use or profit to himself. The judgment of these elders was proven true by events not long after. Therefore, Severus, having stayed a few days in the city, gave a most bountiful gift to the common people and rewarded the soldiers abundantly. Choosing the most robust from among them to guard the empire in place of those who had been discharged, he immediately prepared for a journey to the East. For Niger was still hesitating and indolent, occupying himself with the luxuries of Antioch; Severus thought he must hurry so that he might overwhelm his rival unexpectedly. Having issued an edict for the soldiers to gird themselves for the journey, he gathered forces from everywhere, held a levy of youths throughout all Italy, and ordered the remains of the Illyrian army which had stayed in Thrace to meet him. Likewise, having assembled a huge fleet and filled the triremes of all Italy with armed soldiers, he prepared for himself vast supplies of every kind with incredible speed, for he understood that no small strength was needed against the eastern nations...

**Book III. Folio XI.**

...living in the part of the world opposite Europe, who all followed the leadership of Niger in a single order. Thus Severus prepared for war. However, as a forward-looking and sober man, he held some suspicion regarding the British armies—which were indeed the largest and most warlike—commanded by Albinus, a man of Senatorial and patrician stock, raised in the greatest wealth and luxury. Severus thought it wise to join this man to himself by a clever trick, lest Albinus, spurred by his wealth, lineage, armies, and the great fame of his name to desire the empire, might claim supreme power for himself and occupy Rome (which is not far from Britain) while Severus was entangled in Eastern wars. He decided to bait him with a show of honor—Albinus being otherwise light-headed and simple-minded, and at that time even believing Severus’s sworn letters. Therefore, by calling him Caesar <note>At this time, 'Caesar' was the title for the designated heir, while 'Augustus' was the title of the ruling Emperor</note>, he anticipated the man's hope and greed by sharing the power. He also sent letters full of kindness, begging that Albinus himself should especially take up the care of the empire; he claimed that a noble man of such integrity was needed, and that he himself was now old and afflicted by gout <note>original: "morbo articulari" — a disease of the joints, typically gout or arthritis</note>, while his children were still infants. Albinus believed these things and gladly accepted the honor, happy to have achieved his wish without a fight or any danger. Moreover, to make everything more credible, Severus reported these matters to the Senate and ordered coins to be struck with Albinus’s image and statues to be erected; by conferring these and other honors, he proved his good faith and gratitude. After these things were wisely provided for, and with no fear now looming from Britain, he gathered the Illyrian armies around him and, having prepared everything else for use, set out to lead his forces against Niger. Thus, the places where he stayed on that journey, the speeches he made at each city, the signs that appeared by divine will, the regions he crossed, the battles and the number of those killed on both sides—while many historical authors and especially poets have treated these most abundantly in their words, choosing the life of Severus itself as the material for their entire work—it is my purpose to commit to the monuments of literature the events of seventy years, which I know very well, performed under various emperors and gathered into one body. Therefore, we shall next follow the most excellent and principal things done by Severus, neither inventing anything for favor (as we see those who wrote in that age have done), nor passing over anything in silence, provided it seems worthy of mention and memory.

**BOOK THREE.**

**I**n the previous book, we explained the death of Pertinax, and that of Julianus, along with the departure of Severus for the city and the expedition soon undertaken against Niger. Indeed, when Niger heard that Rome had been occupied by Severus and that Severus himself had been called Emperor by the Senate—expecting no such thing—and furthermore that the entire Illyrian army and both infantry and naval forces were being led against him, he was vehemently disturbed in spirit. He warned the governors of the provinces to guard every approach and harbor, and he sent requests for aid to the kings of the Parthians, Armenians, and Hatrenians <note>Residents of Hatra, a powerful fortress city in Mesopotamia</note>. To this, the Armenian king replied that he would take neither side, but would only defend his own affairs upon Severus's arrival. The Parthian king replied by letter that he would command his Satraps <note>original: "Satrapis" — regional governors in the Persian and Parthian empires</note> to gather forces; for he was accustomed to doing so when preparing for war, since the Parthians have no mercenary soldiers or standing armies. From the Hatrenians, however, auxiliary archers came, sent by King Barsemius, who then ruled in those regions. Niger forged the rest of his forces primarily from the soldiers who were present; many of the common people, especially those of Antioch, also joined—impelled more by the levity of their age and their devotion to Niger than by any prudence. But Niger also blocked the narrows of Mount Taurus <margin>Taurus.</margin> and the steep places with a strong wall and fortifications, thinking that mountain would be a great bulwark for the East. For the Taurus, raising its ridge between Cappadocia and Cilicia, separates the nations subject to the East and the North. He also occupied Byzantium <margin>Byzantium.</margin> with a garrison, the largest and most fortunate city of Thrace, which at that time flourished in strength and wealth. Since it is situated on the narrowest strait of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara</note>, it receives taxes and fishing from the sea, while also possessing very large and fertile fields; it makes profit from both elements, as it were. It seemed right to Niger to occupy such a city with garrisons so that fleets and ships would be prohibited from crossing through those narrows from Europe into Asia. For the city was fortified by a strong and huge wall, which, constructed of Milesian square stone, had such fine joints that the work appeared to no one as a composite, but as if it were made from only one continuous stone. Even now, when you see the ruins and remains, you would certainly marvel either at the skill of those who first built them or the strength of those who afterwards demolished them. In this manner, therefore, Niger organized his affairs, with what he himself thought to be a most provident and safe plan. But Severus hastened with his forces as much as he possibly could, leaving no place for idleness or rest. Learning, however, that Byzantium was held by garrisons—as he knew it was a most fortified city...

...the city: he turned his attention toward Cyzicus <note>A strategic ancient city located on the coast of the Propontis (Sea of Marmara) in modern-day Turkey</note>. Upon learning this, Aemilianus, the governor of Asia—to whom Niger had entrusted the supreme command of the entire war and the highest authority—also set out for Cyzicus. He brought with him all the forces that either Niger had sent or he himself had gathered. But when they came to blows, after several very fiercely contested battles, victory finally rested with Severus, for Niger's army was routed and put to flight. Consequently, the spirits of the Easterners were immediately broken, while great hope was inspired in the Illyrian <note>original: "Illyricianis" — referring to the battle-hardened legions from the Danube and Balkan regions that supported Severus</note> troops. Nor were there lacking those who believed that Niger’s cause had been betrayed from the very beginning by Aemilianus. They offer a twofold reason for this suspected treachery: some say he envied Niger, bearing it with ill will that a man who had recently been his successor in Syria <note>Aemilianus had likely been governor of Syria before Niger</note> should suddenly become his superior, and even his emperor and master. Others claim he was persuaded by letters from his children, who pleaded for their father to consider their life and safety. Severus had found these children in Rome and was holding them in custody, for in this matter he had employed a most provident plan. 

It had been the custom of Commodus <note>The Emperor whose death sparked this period of civil war</note> to keep with him the children of those who went out with imperial command to govern the provinces, serving as a kind of hostage for their goodwill and loyalty. Therefore, as soon as Severus was first hailed as Emperor, while Julianus <note>Didius Julianus, the short-lived emperor who "bought" the throne from the Praetorians</note> was still alive, he secretly sent men to spirit his own children out of the city, so they would not fall into another’s power. However, as soon as he entered Rome himself, he seized all the children of the generals and others who held public office in the East and throughout all Asia, keeping them in custody. By holding these "pledges," he hoped to persuade Niger's commanders to betray him out of a desire for their children's safety; or certainly, if they remained loyal, he would be free to take revenge by executing whichever sons he wished. 

Once defeated at Cyzicus, Niger's soldiers fled as best they could: some retreated past the mountains of Armenia, while others hurried through Asia and Galatia to cross the Taurus <note>The Taurus Mountains in southern Turkey</note>, seeking to take refuge within their own fortifications. Meanwhile, Severus’s army marched through the territory of Cyzicus toward the neighboring region of Bithynia. But as the news spread that Severus had conquered, a sudden sedition and discord immediately invaded the cities of those regions. This arose not so much out of hatred or zeal for the rival emperors themselves, but rather from a certain rivalry and contention—a most deadly envy <term>inuidia</term> among people of the same race. This is an ancient vice of the Greeks: while they stir up seditions and try to destroy whoever is most prominent among them, they have by now consumed all of Greece. Indeed, having grown old and worn down by internal strife, they were first made captives of the Macedonians, and then became the slaves <term>mancipia</term> of the Romans. Yet that blight of rivalry and envy has persisted, falling even upon the flourishing cities of our own age. Therefore, in Bithynia, immediately after these events...

**N**or should anyone accuse me of fickleness because of past actions, nor think me unfaithful or ungrateful toward him whom I held as a friend. **Book III. Folio XIII.**

In the first clash of these most powerful armies, the battle line leaned toward neither side. According to some authors of that age—who speak for the sake of truth rather than favor—the battle line of **Albinus** was far superior in the sector where **Severus** himself was commanding, to such an extent that **Severus** actually fled, fell from his horse, and hid after casting off his general’s cloak <note>original: "paludamento," the distinctive cloak worn by Roman commanders</note>. However, while the British troops were now pursuing and shouting in triumph as if they were clearly the victors, **Laetus**, one of **Severus's** generals, suddenly appeared with an army that was still fresh. Indeed, he earned a poor reputation for this, as it was said he had waited for the outcome of the <margin>Laetus's deceit.</margin> battle, intentionally delaying by holding back his soldiers so that he might claim the empire for himself. For he did not move a foot into the fight until it was reported that **Severus** had fallen—a suspicion that the eventual outcome later confirmed. Indeed, after all matters were soon settled to his liking and he was living in the greatest security, although **Severus** bestowed great rewards upon his other military leaders, he punished **Laetus** himself with death, remembering his treachery as was only fair. But those events happened later. At that moment, however, once **Laetus** was sighted (as we have said), hope was restored to the Severans; **Severus** was lifted onto a horse and draped again in his purple cloak. But the followers of **Albinus**, thinking themselves already the victors, had broken their ranks; when a strong and fresh hand of the enemy unexpectedly rushed upon them, they resisted only briefly at first before finally turning their backs. <margin>Albinus is defeated.</margin> Thus, having scattered and put them to flight, the Severans pursued them and reached the city itself, causing a great slaughter. The number of those killed or captured on both sides is reported differently depending on the views of the writers of that age. Soon **Lugdunum** <note>Modern-day Lyon, France</note> was plundered and burned, and the head of **Albinus** was cut off and sent to **Severus**. Thus two massive trophies were raised in the East <margin>Lugdunum.</margin> and the North, such that there is nothing one can compare to the struggles or victories of **Severus**—whether you consider the multitude of forces, the movements of nations, the number of battles, or the length and speed of his marches. For while the achievements of **Caesar** against **Pompey**, with Roman soldiers on both sides, were certainly great, as were those of **Augustus** against **Antony** or the sons of **Pompey**, and those carried out earlier by **Sulla** and **Marius** in civil and foreign wars: yet it would not be easy to find another single man <margin>Severus's outstanding victories.</margin> who overthrew three Emperors <note>Didius Julianus, Pescennius Niger, and Clodius Albinus</note> who were already in possession of power; who circumvented by cunning the city guards who held Rome and the palace; who managed to have one of the princes killed in the Palatine hall itself, reduced another to his power who was holding the reigns of government in the East and had been called Emperor by the Romans, and further reduced a third who was endowed with the honor and authority of a **Caesar**. This was the end of the life of **Albinus**, who enjoyed his fatal honor for a very short time.

Furthermore, **Severus** immediately poured out all the anger and cruelty of his soul upon Albinus’s associates in Rome. First, having sent the severed head of **Albinus** ahead to the city, he ordered it to be publicly fixed to a pole; at the end of the letter in which he informed the people of his victory, he also added this: that he had sent that head to be viewed publicly on a pole so that they might take it as an example of what they themselves would have to suffer. Therefore, having organized the affairs of Britain—after he had divided the administration of the whole island into two parts <note>Severus divided the province into Britannia Superior and Britannia Inferior to prevent any one governor from having too many legions</note>—and having settled all of Gaul to his liking (as it seemed) and taken punishment from the friends of **Albinus** (whether those joined to him by their own will or by necessity), he immediately set out for Rome. He brought his entire army with him so that he might appear more terrifying. Having completed the journey with great speed as was his custom, still hostile toward the surviving friends of **Albinus**, he entered Rome. He was met by the people wearing laurel wreaths and receiving him with great honor and auspicious acclamations, and by the entire Senate saluting him—though fear had dismayed most of them, as they believed he would by no means spare them, being cruel by nature and bloodthirsty, and needing no great cause to inflict injuries when he now had plausible reasons for hatred.

But after he entered the temple of **Jupiter** and performed all the sacrifices according to custom, he returned to the palace. He granted the Roman people a large gift of money <note>original: "congiario," a traditional imperial distribution of cash or goods</note> in the name of the victory and distributed coins to the soldiers, while simultaneously indulging them in many other things they had never received before. For he was the first to increase their grain allowance, and he permitted them to wear gold rings and to live at home with wives. All of these things seemed unlikely to produce men who were disciplined <margin>The corruption of military discipline.</margin> or ready for war; he himself was the first to subvert their hardness and the austerity of their lifestyle, their endurance of labor, all discipline, and their respect for commanders, as the soldiers became accustomed to gaping after money and cultivating luxuries.

Therefore, having established these things as best as he saw fit, he then entered the Senate house and, sitting in the Imperial chair, began to accuse the friends of **Albinus** in a savage speech. He produced secret letters from some of them which he claimed to have discovered hidden in Albinus’s possession, reproaching some because they had bestowed more splendid gifts upon him, and others because they were better known as friends to the Easterners or to **Albinus**. In this way, he punished every distinguished member of the Senate—whenever someone excelled in a province by birth or wealth—all without distinction, avenging (as he pretended) his enemies. But in truth, he was driven by greed, a vice from which he suffered more than all other Emperors. For while his mental endurance, his perseverance in labors, and his military glory were second to none—even the most praised—he was <margin>The greed of Severus.</margin> so addicted to profit beyond what can be said that he collected money through unjust killings and from every possible source, retaining the empire through fear rather than goodwill. Nevertheless, he particularly wished to be seen as a man of the people, putting on all kinds of most magnificent spectacles, often even killing hundreds of wild beasts which he searched for in all our regions and those of the barbarians. **Book III. Folio 14.**

<margin>Of Plautianus</margin>
...banis. This Plautianus, as they say, was of modest fortune from the beginning of his life; he was accused of sedition and other crimes and punished with exile. However, he was a fellow townsman of **Severus**, being African by birth, and (as some believe) even a relative by blood. Others affirm, however, that he gained favor in the bloom of his youth through shameful acts <note>original: "per stuprū," implying a sexual relationship used for political advancement</note>. From this small and humble beginning, **Severus** had elevated him to the greatest wealth by awarding him the property of the condemned. He enriched him far beyond all others, nearly making him a partner in the empire itself. 

<margin>Insolence.</margin>
Abusing this wealth and freedom, Plautianus omitted no act of cruelty or violence in his dealings. He was more atrocious than the leading men of any age. Consequently, **Severus** gave this man's daughter in marriage to his own son <note>Antoninus, better known to history as Caracalla</note>. However, **Antoninus** himself was far from happy with this marriage, having been driven to it by necessity rather than will. He hated the girl and her father so bitterly that he would not even share a bed or a home with her. He was so opposed to them that he daily threatened to kill both her and her father as soon as he obtained sole power. When the girl repeatedly reported this to her father and revealed how much she was loathed, it greatly provoked the man.

Therefore, Plautianus, seeing that **Severus** was now an old man and often suffering from illness, while **Antoninus** was a fierce and bold youth, became terrified by those threats. He decided to commit some desperate deed before he himself could be crushed. Furthermore, many things inflamed his desire for the empire: wealth such as no private citizen had ever possessed before, the obedience of the soldiers, and the highest honors among all people of the Roman dominion. 

To these were added the manner in which he appeared in public. Indeed, he constantly wore the **laticlave** <term>laticlave: a broad purple stripe on the tunic, signaling senatorial or high equestrian rank</term> and was numbered among the consular ranks. He also carried a sword and all the other insignia of supreme dignity. Whenever he walked abroad, he was so grim and terrifying that not only would no one approach him, but even those who met him by chance would turn their eyes away. Furthermore, several attendants preceded him whenever he traveled, announcing that no one should stand nearby or dare to look at him, but that all should turn their eyes away and look at the ground. 

When **Severus** learned of these things, he did not exactly take it well; he began to find it more troublesome and serious, to the point that he even began to strip away some of his authority and tried to persuade the man to diminish something of that great insolence. 

<margin>Plautianus</margin>
<margin>Plots against the emperor.</margin>
Plautianus, impatient with this, did not hesitate to seek the empire itself through treachery. Therefore, he engineered a certain plot. There was a certain tribune named **Saturninus** who observed Plautianus with great devotion. Although all the others did the same, this one man had crept further and further into his favor with a greater show of veneration. Thinking him to be the most faithful and the only one who would keep a secret and carry out orders, Plautianus ordered him to be called to him toward evening. 

With all witnesses removed, he said: "Now is the time when you must put the finishing touch upon your love and devotion, of which you have so far given me a specimen, and I can reward you according to your merits and return the debt of gratitude. You are given a choice: do you wish to become the very man you see me to be and succeed to this great power, or to die immediately as punishment for a stubborn mind? Do not fear the magnitude of the deed, nor tremble at the names of the Emperors. You are permitted to enter the bedchamber where they sleep alone when your turn for the night watch returns; secretly and with no one to stop you, you will easily accomplish what you wish. There is nothing else of mine for you to wait for but my command. Go now into the Palace of the Princes, as if you have some secret and weighty mandates from me, and as fits a brave man, slaughter one old man and one boy, each within his own chamber. For when you have shared in the danger, you shall also succeed to the greatest honor when the deed is finished." 

As these words terrified the mind of the tribune, they by no means shook his resolve. But as a man by no means lacking in sense—for he was Syrian by race, and those mortals toward the East are generally of the sharpest wit—having recognized the madness and folly of the plan, and being well aware of what was permitted to him, he did not dare to refuse, lest he be punished immediately. While pretending to listen with joy and readiness, he first bowed to him as if he were already Emperor, and then asked for a written warrant <note>original: "libellū," a small book or document</note> concerning the murder mandated to him. 

Indeed, it is the custom of tyrants, when they order someone killed without trial, to urge it specifically through letters, so that no lack of evidence remains of the commanded slaughter. Here, Plautianus, blinded by excessive greed, gave the warrant to the Tribune and, sending him to the murder, warned him diligently: that once both princes were killed, and before the crime was made public, he should order Plautianus to be summoned, so that he might be seen in the palace before anyone heard the empire had been seized. 

With this agreement, the Tribune departed and, according to custom, freely entered the entire house of the Prince. Recognizing how difficult it would be for one man to slaughter two princes living in different chambers, he went to **Severus** and dealt with the doorkeepers so they would admit him to the prince. He claimed he brought news pertaining to his safety. They reported this to **Severus**, who immediately ordered the tribune to be summoned. 

<margin>The plot discovered.</margin>
Having entered, he said: "I come to you, O Lord, as one sent for your slaughter and butchery—as he who sent me believes—but as I myself desire and wish, I come as the author of your benefit and safety. Plautianus, seeking the empire through treachery, has mandated the murder of you and your son to me, not only in words but also in writing. This warrant is the testimony. I indeed undertook to do what he commanded, lest another should take up the task if I refused. But I am here to reveal the matter to you, lest his audacity crush you while you are unaware." 

As the Tribune said these things, weeping profusely, **Severus** did not immediately believe him. Indeed, much of his love for Plautianus still resided in his breast; moreover, he suspected that this whole business was a manufactured and fabricated tale, thinking his son had...

**Book 4. Folio 16.**

And so, all the city's officials and anyone of honor or dignity were pulled in different directions. Each brother sent secret letters separately, attempting to win men over to his side with great promises. In time, the majority favored **Geta**, <margin>Geta</margin> as he displayed a certain reputation for integrity, showing himself to be moderate and mild in his dealings. Furthermore, he pursued the most honorable studies. Indeed, he was frequently surrounded by those celebrated for their learning, and he occupied himself in the <term>palestra</term><note>An ancient Greek wrestling school or gymnasium</note> and other noble exercises. Being calm and refined toward everyone, his excellent reputation and glory enticed many into his friendship and goodwill. By contrast, **Antoninus** <note>Better known to history as Caracalla</note> <margin>Antoninus</margin> conducted all his affairs with greater harshness and ferocity. Shunning the pursuits mentioned above, he strove to appear as a lover of the military and of war. Doing nothing without anger, he sought friendships through threats rather than persuasion, and through fear rather than goodwill. But when their mother had long studied in vain how to bring the discordant brothers back into favor with one another, it finally seemed best to both to divide the Empire between them, lest while living in Rome they should be vulnerable to one another's traps. Therefore, having summoned their father's friends, they debated the division of the Empire in the presence of their mother. It was proposed that all of Europe should go to Antoninus, while the land opposite—which is called Asia—should be adjudged to Geta. <margin>A division of the Empire is proposed.</margin> For thus, by a certain divine providence, the two continents were separated by the rushing waters of the <term>Propontis</term><note>The Sea of Marmara, which separates Europe from Asia</note>. It was agreed that Antoninus would maintain his camp at Byzantium, and Geta in Chalcedon, a city of Bithynia; being thus positioned opposite one another, they could protect their respective empires and prevent any crossings. Then, whoever of the Senatorial order was from Europe would remain in the city itself, while the rest would follow Geta. Geta intended the seat of his Empire to be Antioch or Alexandria, cities not far below Rome in size. Then, of the nations to the south, he would concede the Moors and Numidians to Antoninus, while Geta took the rest reaching toward the East. While they were discussing these matters, and all the rest looked toward the ground with sorrowful faces, their mother Julia spoke thus: <margin>Julia’s speech to her sons.</margin> "You have indeed found, oh my sons, a way to divide the land and the sea; and as you say, the Pontic waves separate the two continents. But in what way will you divide your mother? How shall I, unhappy as I am, be distributed between the two of you, or be cut asunder? Kill me first, then, and let each of you bury his half with him; so that I too may be divided between you along with the sea and the land itself." Having said this, with many tears and wailing, she threw her hands upon both of them, embracing them and trying to reconcile them. Out of this, a shared pity arose, and everyone departed, the plan having been rejected; and they themselves returned to their own quarters.

But their hatred and discord grew daily. If any leaders or magistrates were to be chosen, each would vote most strongly for his own friend. If they sat in judgment, they always held opposing opinions, to the great peril of those whose cases were being heard. For they valued their own partisan zeal more than justice or equity—even in the public games, they always supported opposing factions. Furthermore, they omitted no form of treachery. They repeatedly attempted to bribe cooks and cupbearers to commit poisoning. When these efforts proceeded too slowly—because both took their food with great diligence and care—Antoninus finally became impatient. Driven by a lust for total power, he deliberated whether to do or suffer some great thing; he began to plot with the sword and slaughter. Since hidden traps had failed, he thought it necessary, setting aside all danger and hope, to finish what he had started by any means. Therefore, having burst into his brother’s bedroom while Geta expected no such thing, the cruel brother struck him down <margin>The slaughter of Geta by his brother.</margin> as he clung to his mother’s breast, gushing with much blood. This done, he immediately leaped out and, running through the entire palace, cried out that he had escaped a great danger and had barely survived unharmed. At the same time, he commanded the soldiers guarding the palace to seize him at once and lead him to the camp, <margin>Antoninus is received into the camp.</margin> where he might be kept more safely, repeatedly saying he would perish if he delayed any longer in the house. They, taking his words for the truth and being ignorant of what had happened inside, ran along with him as he fled. A great tumult arose among the people as the Prince hurried through the middle of the city at dusk. As soon as he reached the camp and that small shrine within which the standards and images of the army are adored, he fell to the ground and gave thanks, as if making vows for his safety. When this news was announced to the soldiers—some of whom were bathing and others resting—they all rushed there at once in terror. He, stepping forward into their midst, did not immediately confess the deed exactly as it had been done, but cried out that he had escaped a danger...
