# Herodian

...escape: for the slaughter of one's own household immediately seems hateful as soon as it reaches the ears; the very word, when first heard, brings a heavy weight of scandal. Indeed, mercy follows the unfortunate, while envy follows the powerful; the defeated appears to have received an injury, while the victor appears to have inflicted one. But if anyone were to weigh the matter with true judgment rather than out of some devotion to the deceased, and were to seek out its cause and its purpose, he would easily find that it is right and necessary to avenge an injury rather than to suffer one. Furthermore, to the disaster of the slain is added the infamy of cowardice. The victor, beyond being safe, has also gained the glory of courage. As for the other plots which he frequently directed against me, both with poisons and every kind of treachery, it is easy for you to investigate through torture. Indeed, for that reason, I have ordered all his servants to be present so that you may discover the truth. Some of them have already been tortured, and you may hear their confessions. Finally, while I was with our mother, he came bringing certain men girt with swords. But I, having learned of the matter beforehand, took vengeance on my enemy. For he no longer bore the mind of a brother, nor was he acting as a brother. To take vengeance on one who is the first to plot is as just as it is now common practice. Indeed, even Romulus, the founder of this city, did not endure his own brother <note>Referring to the legend of Romulus and Remus</note> when he mocked his works. I will remain silent regarding the Germanicus of Nero <note>Likely referring to Britannicus, Nero’s adoptive brother and rival</note>, and Titus the brother of Domitian. Even Marcus himself <note>Marcus Aurelius</note>, that pretender of philosophy and gentleness, did not endure the insults of Lucius his son-in-law. But I, with poisons prepared against me and a sword hanging over me, have taken vengeance on an enemy. Indeed, his own actions imposed that name upon him. You, however, should give thanks to the gods that they have preserved one prince for you; do not divide your minds in different directions, but looking only toward one Emperor, lead your lives in security. For just as Jupiter himself alone rules among the gods, so too does he adjudge the empire to only one among mortals. Having spoken these things with a loud voice, full of rage and looking upon his brother's friends with a grim countenance, he returned to the palace while most of them were trembling and pale. Immediately, therefore, the slaughter began.

<margin>The cruelty of Antoninus <note>Antoninus is the formal name used here for the Emperor Caracalla</note>.</margin>

All of his brother's household and friends were killed, as were those who lived in the houses he had inhabited; likewise, all his ministers, such that not even the age of infants was spared. Furthermore, the corpses themselves were placed upon carts with every kind of insult and carried outside the city to be burned in heaps or thrown haphazardly onto pyres. Nor did anyone survive who had even a slight acquaintance with Geta. Even athletes and charioteers, and every sort of actor, and finally anything that had been pleasing to either his eyes or his ears, were killed everywhere. Moreover, anyone of the Senatorial order who excelled in nobility or wealth was killed for the smallest reason, or clearly none at all, on the slightest accusation of being among his friends. He even put to death the sister of Commodus, though she was an old woman and held in great honor by all Emperors as the daughter of Marcus <note>Lucilla, the daughter of Marcus Aurelius</note>, using the excuse that she had wept over the death of Geta with his mother. And he killed his former wife, the daughter of Plautianus, who had been relegated to Sicily, and his cousin named Severus, and the son of Pertinax, and the children of Lucilla, the sister of Commodus; finally, whatever remained of the Imperial kinship or of the patrician nobility in the Senate, he cut down as if from the root. He also put to death all the governors of provinces and procurators as friends of Geta; entire nights were spent in the widespread slaughter of mortals. He even buried Vestal Virgins alive <note>The Vestal Virgins were priestesses of Vesta, goddess of the hearth; Caracalla accused them of breaking their vows of chastity</note>, as if their virginity had been defiled. Finally, in an act never before committed: when the Roman People at the Circus, while he was watching, teased a charioteer whom he favored for some reason or other, he believed an insult had been offered to him. He suddenly ordered the entire army to attack the people, and to seize and kill whoever had spoken against the charioteer. But the soldiers, having once received the power of violating and plundering, since they could not distinguish from the rest who had spoken more perversely—and with no one in such a great multitude confessing the truth—killed people everywhere as they happened upon them, or, having stripped them of everything, barely let them go alive as if they had ransomed their safety. After these deeds, spurred by the consciousness of his evil crimes and loathing city life, he decided to leave Rome to organize the soldiers and visit the provinces. Therefore, departing from Italy, he reached the banks of the Danube and the northern parts of the Roman Empire. There he either exercised his body by chariot-driving and killing all kinds of beasts in close combat, or he administered justice—though that was rare—immediately rendering a sentence and response after hearing only a very few words. Furthermore, he joined all the Germans there to himself and won them over in friendship, so that from them he selected the strongest and most beautiful as companions in war and bodyguards.

<margin>Antoninus adopts the customs of the Germans.</margin>

Often, having set aside Roman dress, he wore German clothing and was seen in their silver-variegated <term>sagula</term> <note>A short military cloak worn by Gauls and Germans</note>; he even placed blonde hair upon his head in the manner of a German haircut. The barbarians, delighted by these things, loved him wonderfully; the Roman soldier also rejoiced, whom he followed with the most lavish gifts. He himself was ready to perform every military duty, and if anything needed to be dug, he was the first to dig; if a bridge was to be placed over a river, or an embankment built, or any manual work or labor undertaken, he was the first to take it all on. He was content with a meager table and wooden cups and vessels, and even ate bread made haphazardly. Indeed, he was accustomed to grinding with his own hand as much wheat as was sufficient for one man, and from that dough was made and cooked on the coals, which he ate. Finally, he scorned all elegant things and used the cheapest items, being most easygoing with the poorest and common soldiers. Thus he preferred to be called a "fellow soldier" rather than "prince," and for the most part made his journey just as...

Aware of the situation (for the affairs of princes can in no way remain hidden), everyone nevertheless, out of fear and flattery, decreed all honors for his victories. After this, Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, better known to history as Caracalla</note> stayed in Mesopotamia, intent on his passion for chariot racing and hunting wild beasts. Therefore, the Emperor frequently mocked Macrinus in public as someone insufficiently military and far from brave, not even refraining from insults. For having heard that he adopted a more refined lifestyle and despised the cheapest, most wretched foods in which Antoninus took a soldier’s delight, and that he wore a cloak <note>original: "chlamydem," a Greek-style mantle often viewed as less "soldierly" than the Roman military cloak</note> and other clothing in the city fashion, the Emperor slandered him as if he were degenerate and suffering from a womanly disease, even threatening to kill him. Macrinus, unable to endure these things, was vehemently provoked. 

However, an event of this kind occurred—truly, Antoninus’s life was destined to have an end at some point. Since he was by nature quite curious, he was eager to know not only the affairs of men, but also to search out the secrets of the gods and demons. In his constant fear of conspiracies, he relied on every possible oracle, summoning magicians, astrologers, and soothsayers from everywhere; <margin>He consults magicians.</margin> indeed, not a single person who professed such deceptions was overlooked. 

But suspecting these men as well—thinking they spoke too little of the truth and prophesied everything only to flatter him—he wrote to a certain Maternianus, to whom he had entrusted the care of all his affairs in the city <note>Rome</note> and whom he considered the most faithful of all his friends, having shared all his secrets with him. He ordered him to seek out the best magicians everywhere and, by summoning the spirits of the dead <note>original: "manibus," refers to the spirits of the deceased in Roman religion</note>, consult them regarding the end of his own life and whether anyone was plotting against his rule. 

Maternianus, having performed this service for the prince—whether the spirits of the dead had truly indicated it or because he otherwise hated Macrinus—wrote back to Antoninus <margin>Maternianus's reply.</margin> that Macrinus was the one plotting against the Empire and that he should be put to death. Therefore, he gave these letters, sealed as is the custom, to couriers who were unaware of what they carried. Using their usual speed of travel, they reached Antoninus just at the time he was preparing himself for chariot racing and was already boarding his chariot. They handed him the entire bundle of letters, among which was the letter concerning Macrinus. 

But Antoninus, with all his attention and mind now focused on the racing, ordered Macrinus to inspect the letters himself separately and to report if there was anything of greater importance; otherwise, he should carry out his usual duty as prefect. Indeed, he was accustomed to assigning such tasks repeatedly. He then proceeded to his pursuit. 

Macrinus, having unsealed all the letters in private, came upon the one that brought ruin upon him. Realizing how much danger hung over him, and knowing Antoninus’s anger and cruelty—especially with such a plausible pretext—he withdrew that letter. However, he reported the contents of the others to the prince as was his custom. But fearing that Maternianus would write again about such matters, and preferring to act himself rather than wait and suffer, he devised a certain plan.

Knowing all this, Macrinus called Martialis to him—for the man had been grieving deeply for the death of his brother and was incited by his own insults. Moreover, the informers <note>original: "delatores"; professional accusers who were paid to denounce citizens for treason, a practice that flourished under Caracalla</note> and all those slaves who had betrayed their masters were nailed to the cross <note>original: "patibulo suffixi"; a humiliating and painful form of execution</note>, and the whole city—and indeed the entire Roman Empire—was thoroughly purged of wicked men: some were afflicted with the ultimate punishment, while others were penalized with exile. If any, however, remained hidden, they kept quiet out of fear, and even they presented a certain image of freedom during that one year at least in which Macrinus held the empire. 

Indeed, he failed in only this regard: that he did not dismiss the army immediately, and having ordered each man to return home, he himself did not at once seek out Rome—which was longing for him—even as the people were calling for him daily and shouting the name of Macrinus. Instead, he lingered at Antioch <note>A major imperial city in the Roman East, now in modern-day Turkey</note>, growing out his beard and walking more slowly than was his custom, responding very sluggishly and barely at all to those who approached him.

**Book V. Folio 20.**

[Macri]nus <note>The text begins mid-word, completing the name "Macrinus."</note> contemning the whole affair as if it were child’s play, and maintaining his usual alacrity of mind, stayed at home and sent one of his generals, providing him with as many troops as seemed sufficient to crush the rebels. But when Julianus (for that was the prefect's name) arrived and was already approaching the walls, the soldiers shut inside the city immediately began to show the boy <note>Bassianus, later known as Elagabalus.</note> to the hostile army from the towers and battlements. They cried out that he was the son of Antoninus <note>Marcus Aurelius Antoninus, better known as Caracalla. The rebellion's legitimacy rested on the (likely false) claim that the boy was Caracalla's illegitimate son.</note> and held up bags full of coins as bait for their treason. The attacking soldiers, believing him to be the son of Antoninus and—since they wished it to be so—thinking his face and features were very similar, cut off Julianus’s head <margin>The slaughter of Julianus</margin> and sent it to Macrinus. The gates were opened, and they were all received into the camp. Thus the rebel forces were greatly increased, not only for enduring a siege but for engaging in open battle, as a great number of deserters joined them every day.

When Macrinus heard this, he hastened with his entire army to attack the camp. However, Antoninus’s soldiers did not wait to be besieged but dared to meet them, and he led out all his forces. The two armies clashed on the borders of Phoenicia and Syria. Antoninus’s soldiers fought more fiercely out of a guilty conscience and fear of punishment if they were defeated; conversely, Macrinus’s army engaged in the battle more sluggishly, and many soon began deserting to Antoninus. When Macrinus realized this, fearing he would be stripped of all his troops and taken prisoner—and knowing he would suffer every possible insult—he stripped off his cloak and other imperial ornaments while the battle line was still standing. <margin>Macrinus flees.</margin> Accompanied by a few of his most faithful centurions, he took flight. He shaved his beard so he would not be recognized, wore common clothing, and kept his head covered, traveling day and night. He even outpaced the news of his own downfall, for his companions urged the carriages on with great zeal as if they were messengers sent on urgent business while Macrinus was still in power.

He escaped by flight in this manner, as we have said. Meanwhile, the soldiers on both sides continued to fight. Macrinus’s bodyguards and attendants, whom they call Pretorians <note>term: Pretorians (original: "praetorianos"); the elite unit of the Roman Imperial Army that served as personal bodyguards to the emperors.</note>, stood bravely and alone sustained the weight of the entire opposing army; they were notably tall men, hand-picked from the whole service. The rest of the multitude fought for Antoninus. But when for a long time they saw neither Macrinus himself nor the imperial standards, those fighting for him grew ignorant of where he might be—whether he lay dead or had fled. Uncertain of what plan to follow, they decided not to risk themselves further for a man who was nowhere to be found, yet they feared surrendering themselves to the enemy’s power. When Antoninus heard from captives that Macrinus had fled the battle, he immediately sent messengers to tell them they were fighting in vain for a most cowardly man and a fugitive. He promised them a full pardon and an oath that all would be forgotten, and he invited them to join his own guard. Believing this, they all surrendered.

Antoninus then immediately sent men to pursue Macrinus, who had already covered much ground. He was found in Chalcedon, a city in Bithynia <note>In modern-day Turkey.</note>, where he was gravely ill and exhausted by the continuous journey, hiding in a suburb. There, his head was cut off. <margin>The slaughter of Macrinus.</margin> It was said he was hastening toward Rome, relying on the favor of the people, but while crossing into Europe by the narrow strait of the Propontis <note>The Sea of Marmara.</note> and approaching Byzantium, he was driven back by an adverse wind, as if the blast itself were pushing him back to his punishment. Thus Macrinus failed to escape his pursuers and met a most foul end to his life, having waited too long to return to Rome, which he should have done at the very beginning. He failed in judgment as much as in fortune. Thus was Macrinus killed, along with his son Diadumenianus, whom he had already named Caesar. 

Afterward, the entire army hailed Antoninus as Emperor, and he took up supreme command. <margin>Antoninus is Emperor.</margin> After arranging matters in the East as urgently required—guided by his grandmother <note>Julia Maesa.</note> and his friends, for he was quite young and inexperienced in statecraft—he announced his departure. Maesa was especially hurried to return to the Roman court, to which she had been so long accustomed. When the news reached the Senate and the Roman people, they received it heavily. But they had to yield to necessity, as the soldiers had already chosen the prince. They blamed Macrinus’s negligent nature and loose morals, saying that no one but himself was the cause of his own misfortune.

Antoninus set out from Syria and wintered in Nicomedia, as the season required. There, he immediately began to revel beyond measure <margin>The insolence of Antoninus.</margin> and to celebrate the cult of his ancestral deity <note>Elagabal, the sun god of Emesa.</note> with superfluous dances. He wore luxurious clothing woven with gold and purple, adorned himself with necklaces and bracelets, and even wore crowns styled like a Tiara <note>A high, often conical Persian-style headdress.</note> and decorated with gold and precious stones. His appearance was somewhere between a Phoenician robe and the garments of the Medes. He plainly despised Roman or Greek clothing made of wool, which he claimed was a most cheap and vile material; he did not deign to wear anything but Syrian fabrics...

It seemed he was performing the duties of a priest; at the same time, he sent a painting to Rome of the likeness of the deity whose priesthood he held. He also issued an edict that all Roman magistrates and those performing public sacrifices should invoke the god Elagabalus <margin>The god Elagabalus.</margin> <note>The sun-god of Emesa, represented by a black conical stone.</note> before the other gods they were accustomed to mention during sacrifices. Therefore, when he arrived in the city, the Romans saw nothing new, as they were already used to the painting. After distributing a gift of money to the people (as is the custom for those taking power), he put on most magnificent spectacles of every kind. He also built a very large and beautiful temple to his god, surrounding it with many altars where every morning he sacrificed "hecatombs" <note>original: "Hecatōbas" — a grand sacrifice, traditionally of a hundred oxen.</note> of bulls and a great multitude of sheep. <margin>Fruitless sacrifices.</margin> He heaped all kinds of perfumes upon the altars and poured out many jars of the oldest and finest wine, so that streams of wine and blood flowed everywhere together. The entire Senate and the equestrian order stood around in the shape of a theater. Furthermore, the entrails of the victims and the spices were carried in golden basins upon the heads, not of servants or low-born people, but of army prefects and those holding the highest dignities. They were dressed in long tunics reaching to their ankles with sleeves <note>Romans traditionally viewed long sleeves as a sign of foreign effeminacy.</note>, wearing purple in the center. He also wore linen shoes, as is the custom of the prophets in those regions. Indeed, he thought he was bestowing a great honor upon those he allowed to participate in such sacrifices. But while he seemed to be constantly establishing dances and performing rituals, he nevertheless killed many illustrious and wealthy men who were reported to him for being unhappy with that way of life or for mocking him.

Furthermore, he married a very noble Roman woman, whom he also called Augusta; however, he divorced her shortly after and ordered her to live a private life, stripped of her honors. After her, pretending to be captured by love—so that he might at least appear to do something manly—he snatched a Vestal priestess <margin>A Vestal Virgin snatched.</margin> <note>The Vestal Virgins were sacred priestesses of Rome required to remain celibate on pain of death.</note> from her temple to be his wife, whom the laws require to remain chaste and a virgin forever. He consoled the Senate, who were grieving at such an outrage and sacrilege, by letter, saying it was a human failing and that he was captured by love for her; moreover, it was fitting for a priest to marry a priestess, and for that reason, the marriage would be even more "august" <note>A pun on the title 'Augustus'.</note>. Nor did he only play with human marriages, but he also sought a wife for his god. This goddess is held in great veneration by the Carthaginians and all of Africa, and is believed to have been established by the Phoenician Dido <margin>Urania.</margin> at the time she built ancient Carthage by cutting a hide into strips. The Africans call her Urania; the Phoenicians call her Astroarche <margin>Astroarche.</margin> <note>The "Queen of the Stars," often identified with Astarte or the Moon.</note>, claiming she is the Moon. When it was brought and placed near Elagabalus, he ordered the whole city and all of Italy to celebrate with public and private festivals, as if for the wedding of the gods. He also built a massive and most magnificent temple in the suburbs, to which, at the turn of the year in the height of summer, he would bring his god. He believed the people were delighted by him with chariot races, theatrical plays, feasts, and all-night vigils. The statue of the god itself was placed on a chariot <margin>The god Elagabalus is carried in a chariot.</margin> adorned with gold and precious stones and was led from the city to the suburbs. It was drawn by six horses of spotless white and great size, remarkable for their abundance of gold and various trappings. No mortal ever mounted that chariot; instead, everyone stood around as if the god himself were the charioteer. Antoninus, however, ran backward, facing the statue itself, and preceded the chariot, holding the reins in his hands. He completed the entire journey running backward in this way, always looking at the god. And lest he should fall or slip, being unaware of where he was going, they spread golden sand on the ground, and soldiers held him up on both sides so he could retreat more safely. The people also ran along on both sides with torches, throwing crowns and flowers. Then the statues of all the gods, whatever was notable in the temples, the imperial regalia, and the most precious furniture, along with the Knights and the entire army, followed in a procession of this kind. But when he had led the god there and placed him in the temple, once the sacrifices and celebrations were finished, he would climb the highest and tallest towers built for this purpose. Many people died while scrambling for these items—partly trampled by one another, and partly pierced by the spears of the soldiers—so that the celebration brought calamity to many. **BOOK SIX.**

The end of the life of the elder Antoninus <note>The author uses "elder" to distinguish the deceased Elagabalus from the new, younger ruler</note> has been demonstrated in the preceding pages. Alexander, following him, now bore the name and the insignia of the empire. However, the administration of business and the steering of the principate <note>term: principate (the early period of the Roman Empire characterized by a single emperor ruling in partnership with the Senate)</note> fell to the women <note>His grandmother Maesa and mother Mamaea</note>, who endeavored to transform everything back to a state of modesty and gravity. Indeed, they immediately chose sixteen men of the senatorial rank who were preeminent for their age and the sanctity of their lives to be the prince's assessors and counselors; nothing was said or done without their consenting vote. This form of government was pleasing to the people, the soldiers, and the senate alike, for it had been restored from a most insulting tyranny to the governance of the best men <note>term: optimates (the traditionalist, aristocratic faction of the Roman leadership)</note>. Therefore, they first restored the statues of the gods—which the former emperor had removed from their proper places—to their own temples, shrines, and sanctuaries. Then, those whom he had rashly raised to honors and dignities because of their vices were removed and sent back to their former lives and trades. They entrusted all matters, both civil and legal, to men distinguished in learning and most skilled in the law, while military matters were entrusted to men famous for their bravery in war. While the empire was being ruled in this manner for a long time, Maesa <note>Julia Maesa, the grandmother of the emperor</note> died in extreme old age; she received imperial honors and (as is the Roman custom) was counted among the divine <note>A process known as apotheosis, where a deceased member of the imperial family was officially declared a god</note>. But Mamaea, seeing that she was now the only one left to her son, sought to guide him in the same manner. When she saw the young man was now coming into full authority, she feared that his youthful energy, combined with supreme power and license, might stumble into some inherent vices. She guarded the palace on all sides and did not allow anyone whose life or character was questionable to approach the youth, lest his good nature be corrupted by flatterers who might provoke his awakening desires toward extreme lusts. She persuaded him to devote the better part of the day to public duties, and to do this as often as possible, so that no time remained for bad habits while he was occupied with the more important and necessary affairs of ruling. **BOOK VI. FROM HERODIAN.**

The soldiers received him with eager cheering and showed themselves most ready for battle. Having distributed a generous <term>stipend (a payment or bonus given to soldiers to ensure loyalty)</term>, Alexander ordered them to prepare for the march. Soon after, having spoken to nearly the same effect in the Senate, he set a date for his departure. <margin>Alexander’s departure for war</margin> When that day arrived, and the customary sacrifices had been performed, he set out from Rome, escorted by the Senate and the entire populace. He looked back repeatedly, weeping. Nor was there anyone among the citizens who watched him depart with dry eyes, for he was beloved by the entire multitude, having been raised by them and having administered the empire with great modesty for so many years. Traveling with haste, he reviewed the Illyrian tribes and their armies, gathering great forces from there as well, and pressed on toward Antioch. In that city, he diligently prepared what the needs of war demanded, focusing on training the soldiers and handling other military duties. He decided, therefore, to send an embassy to the King of the Persians a second time to treat with him for peace and friendship. Since he was now personally present, he did not despair of either persuading the King to his will or, at the very least, terrifying him. However, the Barbarian <note>The Romans often used "Barbarian" to refer to any non-Roman or non-Greek power, here specifically the Sassanid Persians</note> sent the Roman speakers home without achieving their goal. He himself sent four hundred of his own men to Alexander—men distinguished by their great height, dressed in elegant clothing and gold, and conspicuous for their horses and bows—thinking the Romans would be terrified by that sight and the Persian style of dress. <margin>The Ambassadors of Artaxerxes.</margin> The message of this embassy was as follows: The Great King Artaxerxes <note>original: "Artaxarem"—Ardashir I</note> ordered the Romans and their prince to depart from all of Syria and all of Asia situated opposite Europe, and to permit the Persians to rule as far as Ionia and Caria, and over all those regions which the Aegean Sea and the Black Sea <note>original: "pontusq[ue]"—the Euxine Sea</note> separate. Alexander ordered these four hundred ambassadors to be seized; stripped of all their finery, he banished them to Phrygia, granting them villages and fields to cultivate. He was content with this punishment of forbidding their return to their homeland, for he considered it a wicked and unmanly deed to kill those who were not captured in battle but were merely executing the commands of their king. After these things were done in this manner, as Alexander was preparing to cross the rivers and lead the Roman army into the Barbarian lands, some soldiers summoned from Egypt revolted, and others in Syria also plotted revolution against the empire; however, all were immediately suppressed and punished. Alexander also moved certain parts of the army to other regions so that Barbarian incursions could be more easily warded off from there. <margin>The division of Alexander's army.</margin> Once these matters were settled and a great army had been collected, and as soon as he believed himself to be a match for the enemy's forces, he distributed the soldiers into three parts based on the advice of his friends. He ordered one part, facing the north, to march through Armenia—which was a region friendly to the Romans—and from there to invade the borders of the Medes. He ordered the second part to likewise head north through the Barbarian lands, where the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates is received by very thick marshes, and for that reason, their exit from that side is said to be difficult. Alexander promised that he would lead the third part of the army against the Barbarians by the middle route. For he thought that by these diverse routes, he would overwhelm them while they were unprepared and unsuspecting, and that the Persian forces, always rushing to meet the encroaching Romans, would be distracted and made weaker, and would undertake the battle in a less orderly fashion. For the Barbarians do not use mercenary soldiers as the Romans are accustomed to do; nor do they have standing camps for the army to be trained in the arts of war. Instead, the entire multitude of men—and sometimes even women—gather at the command of the king. Once the war is finished, the crowd is immediately dismissed to their own homes, carrying away only what remains of the plunder for each person. They use bows and horses not only in battle in the Roman fashion, but they are nurtured with them from childhood. They are constantly watchful in hunting, always equipped with quivers, and never dismounting from their horses, whether they are waging war or hunting wild beasts. But although this plan of Alexander's seemed by far the best at first glance, fortune immediately failed him. Indeed, the army ordered to march through Armenia, having only with great difficulty overcome the very rugged and precipitous mountains of that region—though the summer made the journey more tolerable—made an attack on Media, burned the villages, and drove off the spoil. <margin>The army around Media.</margin> But the King of the Persians, having understood the situation, immediately arrived with the greatest forces he could muster to help. However, he was unable to drive the Romans from there, for the rugged terrain provided a stable footing and easy passage for the infantry, but the Persian cavalry found their course more difficult and their path hindered by the roughness of the mountains. Then it was announced to the King that another Roman army had made an attack on the lands of the Parthians, which look toward the east. <margin>The army in Parthia.</margin> Fearing that if the Parthians were easily defeated, the Romans would soon advance into Persia, he left behind as many forces as seemed sufficient to protect Media and hastened with his whole army toward the eastern parts. However, the Roman army, with no one appearing or resisting, marched rather negligently, thinking that Alexander, with the third part of the forces—which were the strongest and most powerful—had already attacked the Barbarians in the center. Therefore, while those others were holding back and delaying their army, this group thought they did not need to hurry, believing themselves safe and expecting to meet at the prearranged place with all the driven-off plunder and captives. <margin>Alexander failed the army.</margin> But Alexander failed them; for he neither came himself nor led his army. It is uncertain whether he was held back by his own fear—lest he risk his life while defending the empire—or because his mother restrained him with a womanly dread and an excessive love for her son.

[Marginal note: The Rhine & the Danube.]
... are carried: the Rhine and the Danube, one of which flows past the Germans and the other past the Pannonians <note>Pannonia was a Roman province located in what is now parts of Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans</note>. In the summer, they are indeed navigable with a very deep and wide channel; then, in the winter, they are frozen solid with ice and are ridden across as if they were plains. Indeed, the ice of that channel is so solid that it supports not only the hooves of horses and the feet of men, but those who wish to draw water from there do not bring urns or other vessels with them, but rather axes and mattocks, so that they may carry away the water they have cut from the river like a stone without any vessel. This, therefore, is the nature of those rivers. 

Alexander, however, was preparing against the Germans many Moors <note>Mauri; North African light troops</note> and a huge force of archers whom he had brought with him from the East—partly from the territory of the Osrhoenians <note>People from Osrhoene, a kingdom in Upper Mesopotamia</note>, and partly deserters from Parthia <note>The Persian Empire</note> or those enticed by money. Sometimes, however, the business was conducted in a pitched battle, from which the Germans very often departed not unequal to the Romans. While Alexander was engaged in these matters, he nevertheless decided to send ambassadors to them to discuss peace. They were to promise that the Roman prince would provide all things they might need and would give money in great abundance. [Marginal note: The Germans are greedy for gold.] For the Germans are particularly greedy for money and are always ready to barter peace with the Romans for gold. Therefore, Alexander tended to buy peace and treaties from them rather than risk the dangers of war. 

Otherwise, the Roman soldier bore it with an ill will that he was wasting time in vain, with no opportunity to perform anything bravely or spiritedly, while Alexander (as they said) was intent on chariot racing and luxuries—even though he ought instead to take vengeance on the Germans and demand penalties from them for their boldness. [Marginal note: Maximinus the shepherd.] There was, moreover, in the army a man named Maximinus, from a certain village in the interior of Thrace: a semi-barbarian man who had been a shepherd from childhood, and then, in the prime of his life, because of his tall stature and great strength, had joined the cavalry. 

Finally, with fortune leading him as if by the hand and going before him, when he had ascended through all the ranks of military service, he had even reached the commands of armies and provinces. Therefore, Alexander had placed this Maximinus—because of that military skill I mentioned above—in charge of all the recruits, so that he might train them in military duties and make them fit for waging war. Since he left nothing undone in that business regarding all diligence, he naturally won the greatest favor from the whole army. He did not only constantly teach what needed to be done, but he was also the first to perform the tasks that necessity required, so that he had not only students but even rivals and imitators of his courage. He also attached them to himself with gifts and every kind of honor. # **Book VII. Folio XXV.**

In the city of Rome itself and among the subject nations, slaughter was unleashed! What benefit was there in the spoils of war or the driving away of captives <margin>Most severe demands for money.</margin> if the people living under Roman rule were daily stripped of their own fortunes? Indeed, not only was every kind of liberty suppressed, but informants were even encouraged to corner whomever they wished. They were permitted to revive—if it served their purpose—crimes that were unknown or undetected since the time of a person's ancestors. Nor was anyone merely summoned for some specific offense; rather, once accused, they were immediately convicted, losing both their status and all their property. Thus, you could daily see those who had been most wealthy the day before now reduced to begging for alms. Such was the greed of the tyranny that had taken hold, using the excuse of constant handouts to the soldiers.

Furthermore, the Emperor’s ears were open to every slander, so that he showed no consideration for age or rank. Consequently, he ordered many who had been in charge of armies or provinces—men of consular or even triumphal rank—to be suddenly seized upon the slightest and most trivial accusations. He commanded them to travel alone in vehicles, without any servants, journeying day and night from the east or the west, or from the south as far as Pannonia <note>A Roman province covering parts of modern-day Hungary, Austria, and the Balkans, where Maximinus was stationed with the army</note>, wherever his anger had fallen. Then, after being stripped of everything and covered in disgrace, he would punish them with exile or death.

As long as only one or two people suffered such things, and the calamity did not spread beyond their own families, it did not seem to greatly concern the common people or the various nations. For the misfortunes of the wealthy and blessed are not only ignored by the common folk, but some people of a wicked and spiteful nature even take delight in them, out of envy for those who are more powerful and successful. However, after Maximinus had reduced many families of illustrious men to poverty—and <margin>The sacrilegious greed of Maximinus.</margin> finding these smaller thefts insufficient to satisfy his greed—he turned his mind toward public wealth. Therefore, whatever civic funds remained, whether they were set aside for the public grain supply or for distribution to the common people, or intended for the theaters and festivals, he claimed them all for himself.

Beyond this, the offerings from all the temples, the statues of the gods, the honors dedicated to heroes, and whatever public works, civic ornaments, or materials were suitable for minting coins—all were equally melted down in the fires. This, above all else, wounded the spirits of the multitude and created a kind of public mourning. It was as if the city were under siege without a battle or weapons, so much so that some of the people dared to resist, attempting to protect the temples; they preferred to fall before the altars of the immortal gods rather than see the spoils of their fatherland. It was from this point, especially throughout the cities and nations, that the spirits of the common people began to swell with anger. Even the soldiers did not take these events well, as their relatives and household members reproached them with hatred, repeatedly saying that it was by their fault that Maximinus was committing such deeds.

Therefore, these causes, which were by no means trivial, provoked the people toward hatred and rebellion. However, they acted only through prayers, imploring the wounded deities, as no one dared to declare himself a champion of the cause. This continued until, after three years of his reign, a small and slight occasion—as the affairs of tyrants are always on slippery ground—led them to first take up arms. The Africans rebelled for the following reason: There was a certain procurator <margin>The Procurator of Africa.</margin> <note>A high-ranking imperial financial officer</note> in Carthage who lacked nothing in terms of extreme harshness and cruelty. He sought the Emperor’s favor by condemning men in court and extorting money. Indeed, Maximinus was accustomed to especially favoring those who acted as he did.

Therefore, whoever managed the affairs of the treasury, if they happened to be honest men (which occurred very rarely), either lost their posts or, terrified by the immediate danger and knowing the Emperor's greed, imitated the others against their will. For this reason, the procurator of Africa, while committing many other violent acts, had recently intended to immediately extort money from certain noble and wealthy youths who had been trapped by a legal conviction, thereby stripping them of their inheritance and ancestral goods. Enraged by these matters, the youths promised they would give the money, but asked for a period of three days. In the meantime, they conspired with all those who had either suffered some grievance or feared they would soon suffer. They ordered the young men from the countryside to come at night with clubs and axes. Following the commands of their masters, these men arrived in the city before dawn, hiding under their clothes whatever makeshift weapons they could find. A great force of people gathered, since Africa, being most fertile in men, had many tillers of the fields at that time.

When day broke, the noble youths ordered their band of slaves to follow behind them as if they were part of the general crowd. They were told not to show their weapons or use force until they saw someone from the soldiers or the people rush against them to avenge the deed they were about to commit. The youths themselves, with daggers hidden in their robes, approached the procurator <margin>The murder of the Procurator.</margin> as if to discuss the payment of the money; they immediately put him to death while he suspected no such thing. When his soldiers drew their swords and wished to avenge him, the country folk suddenly fell upon them with clubs and axes; fighting bravely for their masters, they easily put them all to flight.

With the business succeeding in this manner, and the youths having risked everything, they realized their only remaining safety lay in following this crime with an even greater one. They decided to bring the governor of the province into their shared danger and urge the people to revolt. They knew this had long been desired by everyone out of hatred for Maximinus, though held back by fear. Therefore, with the entire multitude, they went to the house of the proconsul in the dead of night. He was Gordian <margin>Gordian.</margin>

Many innocent people were likewise killed. Thus, under the guise of liberty and the pretext of peace, they committed the crimes of a civil war. Indeed, they even murdered the Prefect of the City, Sabinus, <margin>The killing of Sabinus</margin> as he attempted to stop such actions, striking him on the head with a club. They carried letters in which the Senate expressed the mind of the **Roman People** <note>original: "P.Q.R." for *Populusque Romanus*</note>, urging the governors to take up the cause of their common fatherland and protect the Roman Senate. They were to persuade the nations to remain in their loyalty to the Roman people, to whom the empire had belonged by right since ancient times.

But when they reached the plain, scouts reported that **Aquileia**, the greatest city of Italy, had closed its gates; the Pannonian troops <note>Maximinus's elite vanguard from the Danube frontier</note> who had gone ahead had fiercely attacked the wall, but despite many attempts, all their efforts had come to nothing. Thus, they were now retreating, exhausted, as stones, spears, and a great force of arrows rained down upon them from above. But **Maximinus**, angry with the Pannonians as if they had fought with too little energy, hurried forward with the rest of the army, hoping he would take that city with no trouble. 

But Aquileia was already overflowing with people (as was the great size of that city), and being situated near the sea as a kind of emporium <term>emporium: a major center of commerce and trade</term> of Italy, it served as a boundary for Illyria. It supplied a wealth of goods brought from the mainland by land and river to those at sea, and from the sea itself it provided necessary items for those who inhabited the interior—lands which, because of the harshness of winter, were less fertile. Above all, it supplied wine in abundance, of which there is a massive yield in that region, to neighboring nations who do not even possess vines. 

As a result, beyond the vast number of citizens, a great force of guests and merchants frequented that city. Indeed, at that time the multitude had increased even further, as people flocked there from the fields, leaving behind the small towns and villages nearby, trusting in the size of the city and its ancient walls. These walls had previously been destroyed in large part, for during such great Roman power, the cities of Italy had no need for walls or arms, leading a life of profound peace and having been admitted to a share in the Republic. But then, under the pressure of necessity, they renewed and restored the walls, and furthermore raised towers and battlements. With the entire city fortified in this manner and the gates closed, the entire population stood before the walls day and night, most bravely repelling the enemy. 

[Marginal note: The site of Aquileia.]

[Marginal note: Preparations of the Aquileians.]

The leaders were two men of consular rank chosen by the Senate with supreme power, **Crispinus** and **Menephilus**. These men had provided with the greatest diligence for everything necessary to be imported into the city, so that even a longer siege could be sustained. There was also a great abundance of water in the city, partly from very frequent wells and partly from the river flowing past the walls, which served both as a barrier for the trench and a source of water. 

When these things were thus prepared within the city, and **Maximinus** first heard that the walls were being diligently defended and the gates closed, he decided to send envoys under the guise of legates to speak to them and, if they could, persuade them to unbar the gates. He had in his army a certain tribune who was a citizen of Aquileia, whose children, wife, and entire household were shut up in the city. For this reason, he sent him and several centurions as spokesmen, hoping the townsfolk would easily follow his authority. When they approached the wall, they spoke to this effect: 

"The common Emperor commands you to lay down your arms and cultivate peace, to receive him as a friend instead of an enemy, and to devote yourselves to performing sacred rites rather than slaughter. He pities your fatherland, which will soon fall (if you persist in your obstinacy). You are permitted (if you wish) by a single action to consult your own safety and that of your country; for the best of Princes promises oblivion and pardon for all you have done, since none of it was your own fault, but all was brought about by the fault of others." 

The envoys shouted such things under the wall with a loud voice, so that they could easily be heard, if not by everyone, certainly by that multitude which stood atop the walls and towers. Indeed, everyone listened to the words of the envoys in silence. Therefore, fearing that the common people, with their usual inconstancy, might be driven by those promises to exchange war for peace and open the gates to the enemy, **Crispinus** ran along the walls, asking and imploring each man to remain bold, resist bravely, and not betray the faith owed to the Senate and the People of Rome. 

[Marginal note: Crispinus's exhortation to the citizens.]

He urged them not to despise the title of having saved and defended all of Italy, nor to believe the promises of a perjured and fraudulent Tyrant, nor to be enticed by a kind speech and rush into manifest destruction. Instead, they should consider the fortune of war, which is often so doubtful and uncertain that a great number are often conquered and overcome by a very few, and those believed to be more powerful by those held to be weaker. Nor should they be terrified by the size of that army. For those who fight for another, when they see the happiness of their victory will pass to someone else, certainly fight less fiercely, since they understand they are admitted to a share of the danger, but the final fruits of victory will reach another. 

"But those who fight for their country," he said, "besides the fact that they ought to be in better hope (for they do not strive to occupy what belongs to another, but to protect their own), are also greater in spirit, as they are driven not by another's command, but by their own necessity—since the fruits of victory are owed chiefly to themselves." 

Pouring out such things now to individuals and now to the whole group, **Crispinus**, a man venerable by his very nature and powerful in Roman eloquence—and moreover beloved by all for his mild and modest command—persuaded the multitude to remain in their duty and loyalty. He ordered the envoys to return to **Maximinus** with their business unfinished. **Crispinus** spoke so boldly to sustain the war because he was also encouraged by the response of the soothsayers, who reported favorable omens from the entrails. For the Italians are accustomed to have great faith in signs of this kind. Furthermore, certain oracles were also being spread promising victory from a certain native deity, **Belenus**...

[Marginal note: Belenus.]

### The News Spreads through Italy

The news of the emperor's downfall spread with great **speed and frequency** <note>original: "frequentia", suggesting both the density of the crowds and the rapid succession of reports</note> through the surrounding territories. High-speed couriers were dispatched to the cities of **Altinum**, **Ravenna**, and to the various camps where troops were stationed.

### The Proclamation of Victory

When the messengers arrived, **announcing the death of Maximinus** and the son who shared his name, and reporting the **consensus** <note>original: "consensumque", the formal agreement or harmony of the army with the Senate's decrees</note> of the entire military force at Aquileia, the atmosphere shifted instantly. After the news was **announced**, Maximus immediately performed a **solemn sacrifice** <note>original: "sacrificatum", a religious ritual offered to the gods in gratitude for the end of the civil war</note> to celebrate the **victory**.

This was **not** merely a fleeting moment of relief, but a **continuous** celebration that transformed the city.

### The Enchiridion of Epictetus the Stoic
#### Chapter I: Which things are in our power, which are not, and of what kind they are.

<note>The OCR reads "Lorum," but this is a transcription error for the Latin "Eorum" (Of those).</note>
Of those things that exist, some are in our power, and some are not. In our power are opinion, impulse, <term>conatus: the internal drive or effort toward something</term> desire, aversion, and, to say it in one word, whatever are our own works. Not in our power are the body, property, reputation, high office, and, in one word, whatever are not our own works. Therefore, the things that are in our power are by nature free, and cannot be hindered or blocked. But the things that are not in our power are weak, enslaved, subject to hindrance, and belong to others.

#### Chapter II: What results from the ignorance or knowledge of which things are ours and which belong to others.
If you think that things which are by nature enslaved are free, and that things belonging to others are your own, you will be hindered, you will grieve, you will be troubled, and you will find fault with both gods and men. But if you think that only what is yours is truly yours, and...

# Chapter XII.

Do not wish for things to happen as you wish; rather, wish for things to happen as they do happen, and you will fare well. Sickness is a hindrance to the body, but not at all to one’s **purpose** <note>original: *propositum*, referring to the Stoic concept of the 'will' or 'moral choice' which remains free even if the body is constrained</note>, unless the will itself chooses to be hindered. Lameness of the leg is a hindrance to the limb, but not at all to one’s purpose. And consider this in every event that occurs: you will find it to be a hindrance to something else, but not to yourself.

# Chapter XIII.
### That the things commanded are not impossible, since the mind possesses strengths against all things.

In every event that occurs, remember to ask yourself what power you possess for dealing with it. If you face a hardship, you will find a beneficial power: such as self-restraint against pleasures. If labor is offered, you will find strength. If an insult, patience. Once you are accustomed to this habit, you will not be disturbed by mere **appearances** <term>appearances: (original Latin *imaginationibus*, translating the Greek *phantasiai*) the initial mental impressions or "images" we receive of external events before we have time to judge them rationally</term>.

# Chapter XIIII.

**How duties are derived from nature: how each person should conduct themselves toward anyone else is considered; then concerning duties toward men. Chapter XXXV.** <note>In modern editions of the Enchiridion, this section is categorized as Chapter 30</note>

Duties are measured by our relationships <note>original: *habitibus*, referring to the social roles or the standing one has in relation to another</note>. A man is called "Father"; he must be cared for, and you must yield to him in all things. He must be endured whether he scolds you or even strikes you. "But he is a bad father," you say. .XXX. **Of Epictetus**

**On the duty and care toward a wife. Chapter LV.** <note>Standard Chapter 40</note>

**Women** are called "mistresses" <note>original: *dominae*, implying a position of authority or a title of respect</note> from their fourteenth year onward. For men flatter them for the sake of sexual intimacy. Therefore, by the fault of men, they subsequently take too much pride in themselves. They must be warned, then, that they will be held in honor among us for no other reason than if they are modest and show reverence to their husbands.

**A sign of a base nature; and concerning excessive care for the body. Chapter LVI.** <note>Standard Chapter 41</note>

**It** is a sign of a base nature <term>degeneris</term> <note>literally "degenerate" or "not living up to one's kind," referring to someone of low character</note> to dwell upon things that belong to the body, such as excessive exercise or excessive grooming of the body. Indeed, it is a sign of a certain superfluous agreement. For we agree with those things in which we find joy. It is necessary, therefore, to consider excessive care of the body as something secondary. Truly, one should have the greatest care for that which uses the body itself <note>referring to the soul or the mind</note>.

**A precept for patience and gentleness. Chapter LVII.** <note>Standard Chapter 42</note>

**When** anyone does you wrong or speaks ill of you, remember that he acts or speaks thinking that he is doing his own duty. It is not possible, therefore, for him to follow what seems right to you, but only what seems right to himself. And if it seems wrong to him, he is the one who is hurt, for he is the one who has been deceived. For if anyone thinks a true logical connection is false, the connection itself is not hurt, but rather the one who is deceived. If you are moved by these thoughts, you will show yourself mild toward the one who reviles you. Speak, therefore, in every such instance: "So it seemed to him."

**That all things partly agree with one another and partly disagree. Chapter LVIII.** <note>Standard Chapter 43</note>

**Every** matter has two handles: one by which it can be carried, and another by which it cannot. If a brother is unjust, do not take hold of the matter from the side of his injustice. For that is the handle by which it cannot be carried. But rather take hold of it from the side that he is your brother, and that he was brought up with you; and thus you take hold of it from the side where it can be carried.

**On the consistency of speech. Chapter LIX.** <note>Standard Chapter 44</note>

**These** statements do not follow logically: "I am richer than you, therefore I am better." "I am more eloquent <note>original: *sapientior*, literally "wiser," but here implying skill in speech/logic</note> than you, therefore I am better than you." These, however, follow better: "I am richer than you, therefore my possession is better than yours." "I am more eloquent than you, therefore my speech is better than yours." But you yourself are neither a possession nor a speech.

**On the exact judgment of things. Chapter LX.** <note>Standard Chapter 45</note>

**Someone** bathes quickly: do not say he bathes badly, but quickly. Someone drinks much wine: do not say he does so badly, but that he drinks much. For unless you know his motive, how do you know if it is bad? Otherwise, it will happen that we grasp the deceptive imaginations of some things, while we give our assent to others.

**Against glory and ostentation. And first regarding knowledge. Chapter LXI.** <note>Standard Chapter 46</note>

**In** no way call yourself a philosopher, nor talk much among the unlearned about philosophical theories <term>speculationibus</term> <note>original: *speculationibus*, referring to the theoretical principles or doctrines of a school of thought</note>; but rather do something according to those theories. For instance, at a feast, do not say how one ought to eat, but eat as one ought. Remember that Socrates also removed all ostentation from himself. And if talk of some theory should fall among the unlearned, keep silent for the most part. For there is great danger in vomiting up what you have not digested. And when someone says that you know nothing, and it does not sting you, then know that you have begun the work. For even sheep do not show the shepherds how much they have eaten by vomiting up the grass; but rather, by digesting the food within, they produce wool and milk on the outside. And so you, likewise, do not show your theories to the unlearned, but show the works that come from those theories once they are digested.

**Against the ostentation of sobriety and endurance. Chapter LXII.** <note>Standard Chapter 47</note>

**When** you have disciplined your body to a simple way of life, do not take pride in it. Nor, if you drink water, should you say on every occasion, <margin>Others have physicians.</margin> "I drink water." But consider how much more frugal and more enduring the beggars are than we. Also, consider that we do not have other goods which others have. If you wish to train yourself for labor and patience, do this by yourself, and do not wish to be seen by outsiders. Do not be like those who, suffering violence from those more powerful, climb onto statues to call the people together and cry out that they are suffering violence. For the ostentatious person turns entirely outward and destroys the goods of patience and abstinence when he makes their goal the opinion of the many.

**A description of the threefold character: of the unlearned, the philosopher, and the one making progress. Chapter LXIII.** <note>Standard Chapter 48</note>

**The** state and character of the unlearned person <term>ineruditi</term> <note>the *idiotes* or layperson who has not studied philosophy</note> is this: never to expect benefit or harm from himself, but from external things. The state and character of the philosopher is to expect all benefit and harm from himself. The sign of one making progress <term>proficientis</term> is this: He censures no one, praises no one, complains of no one, accuses no one, and says nothing of himself as if he were someone or knew something. When he is hindered or forbidden in anything, he accuses himself. And if anyone praises him, he laughs at the one praising him in his own mind. And if anyone censures him, he does not defend himself. He goes about like an invalid, taking care not to move any of his parts before they have reached firmness. He has removed all desire from himself. He has transferred his aversion only to those things which are contrary to nature among the things that are within our power. He uses his efforts toward everything with moderation. He does not care at all if he is called foolish or ignorant; and, to explain it in a single word, like...

# Handbook. Folio XXXIIII.

...he observes himself as an adversary and as one lying in wait. <note>This concludes the previous chapter's thought that a developing philosopher treats their own ego as a potential enemy to be guarded against.</note>

**¶ That words are for the sake of actions. Chapter LXIIII.** <note>Standard Chapter 49</note>

**When** anyone boasts because he can interpret the sayings of Chrysippus, <note>Chrysippus (c. 279–206 BC) was the third head of the Stoic school and its most prolific writer; his works were notoriously difficult and technical.</note> let him say to himself: "If Chrysippus had not written obscurely, <note>original: *operte*, likely a variant for *obscure*. The logic is that if the text were easy, the interpreter would have nothing to brag about.</note> I would have nothing to boast of." But Chrysippus did not write so that someone might merely interpret him, but so that one might act according to his teachings. If, therefore, I use his writings, I have attained the good that they contain. But if I only admire the interpreter, or if I myself am only able to interpret them, I have become a <term>grammarian</term> <note>In antiquity, a grammarian was a scholar of language and literature; here used to mean someone who studies the "shell" of the words rather than the "meat" of the philosophy.</note> instead of a philosopher. Indeed, what does it profit a man to have found certain medicines described in writing, and to understand them and pass them on to others, if he himself, being sick, does not use them at all?

**¶ That one must persevere in these principles. Chapter LXV.** <note>Standard Chapters 50–51</note>

**One** must persevere in one's purpose as if it were a law. Stand firm, therefore, as if you would be unholy <note>original: *impius*</note> were you to transgress these things. And if anyone should say anything about you, do not worry. For that is not your [concern...] <note>The text cuts off at *non e*, likely *non est* ("is not yours"). The philosopher reminds us that other people's opinions are "indifferent" things outside of our control.</note>

**13 A defense of Epictetus.**

...honor, or I favor Epictetus as much as I know for certain you favor him: But so that we may sustain the <term>persona</term> <note>original: *personam*; here meaning a role in a formal debate or a literary character.</note> imposed by you upon us, as much as is within our power. I will, however, first bring some matters into the open and cast them like seeds: from which—just as the fables say earth-born men were born at Thebes or Colchis from the sowing of teeth <note>A reference to the myths of Cadmus and Jason, who sowed dragon's teeth that instantly grew into fully armed warriors.</note>—so may all the most pugnacious and well-equipped forces of our Epictetus arise. But as Homer pitted Salaminian Ajax against Hector rushing into the Greek camps, so we shall pit Athenian Plato against you. That Plato, therefore, in that book titled *On the Nature of Man*, <note>This refers to the dialogue *Alcibiades I*, which was historically subtitled *On the Nature of Man*.</note> introduces Socrates disputing with the famous Alcibiades, whose surname was "The Beautiful." In this book, he proves that the thing we call "man" is nothing other than a soul participating in reason. "For just as a <term>cobbler</term> <note>original: *cerdo*; a common laborer or craftsman.</note> uses an awl," he says, "so a man uses his hand for acting." This being granted, he takes up a second point. "Now, that which uses a thing," he says, "is different from the thing it uses." Nature...

...would have commanded. <note>original: *precepisset*; the suffix of a word ending the previous page.</note> You might reason thus: whatever he commands in this entire book is within our power, for he would have commanded foolishly if it were not.

Is our Epictetus, then, obscure or complex? You would not even dare to wish for anything more plain, more clearly explained, or even more lucid than him. He is so clear that not only your "lynx-like" eyes <note>original: *lyncei oculi*; a common classical metaphor for incredibly sharp or penetrating vision.</note> but even the dullest sight could look into his meaning. 

"But," you say, "the things he commands are too arduous, and beyond the strength of man."

What exactly? This, for instance: if you love a son, or if you love a wife, tell yourself that you love a human being; for then, if they die, you will not be disturbed. <note>A paraphrase of Chapter 3 of Epictetus’s *Enchiridion*. The Stoic goal was not heartlessness, but a constant awareness of mortality to prevent being shattered by grief.</note>

Now, is it what he commands, or what he promises, that you criticize as being difficult to do? If it is what he commands, then you must consider things that are tossed about every day in common life, in the forum, and at the crossroads to be difficult to do. For who does not sometimes think about what might happen in the future?

<meta>This page concludes Angelo Poliziano’s introductory letter to Bartolomeo Scala regarding his translation of Epictetus and begins a new work: a translation of Alexander of Aphrodisias’s "Physical Doubts and Solutions." The transition demonstrates the Renaissance humanist’s interest in both Stoic ethics and Aristotelian natural science.</meta>

**Of Alexander**

For what is more famous than Plato himself! Yet, you might say, he could have gathered those arguments of his into a few brief points. He could have, but it would not have been so fitting, for he delivers precepts in this little book and proclaims them like laws; he does not fight with contentious arguments. Every profession has a fixed boundary; if you step beyond it, you should be summoned to court for "claiming property by force." <note>original: *ex iure manu consertum*; a Roman legal formula used in disputes over ownership, where parties laid hands on an object in the presence of a judge.</note> Do you see how mathematicians do not prove the starting principles of their demonstrations, but leave their defense to the one we call the "First Philosopher"? <note>A reference to Metaphysics, which deals with the fundamental nature of existence that underlies specific sciences like math.</note> For to him belong those things called "universals." Euclid says a point is "that which has no part." <note>The classic definition from Euclid's *Elements*.</note> If you deny that, the mathematician will fall silent. But the philosopher comes to the aid of the one in danger. And what does he say? He says that whatever limits a thing is one dimension <note>original: *intervallo*; literally "interval" or "dimension."</note> less than the thing it limits. Once he has wrested that point, he proceeds: a body has three dimensions. It is enclosed by a surface, which has only two: length and width. It has no depth at all, for it lacks one dimension compared to the body. A surface, having two dimensions, is bounded by a line, which has only one: length. Finally, a line is bounded by a point, which beyond all doubt lacks any dimension. This is because it is a most certain rule that every boundary lacks one dimension compared to the thing it limits.

Therefore, Epictetus also begins this little book by taking for granted what was proved by Plato; and from that, he weaves together the entire sequence of his precepts. Thus, just as Teucer in Homer protects himself with the shield of Ajax, so too our Stoic here fights boldly under Plato's reasoning as if under a shield. He decided not to overstep the limits within which he had circumscribed himself, lest (as the saying goes) he be forced "to dance outside the chorus." <note>An ancient Greek idiom for acting out of place or straying from one's proper role.</note> These thoughts in defense of Epictetus occurred to me for the moment, and I realize they have been more numerous than the nature of a letter required. Yet they are not more numerous, nor explained at greater length (I believe), than was necessary. If you accept them, my dear Scala, let our right hands join in a pact; if you reject them, then come, show yourself as great a champion for Epictetus as you have shown yourself an attacker. 

And yet, everyone reports that he was a great man, and having reread him a hundred times, he pleases me perpetually. I must fear, however, that my labor might flatter me like a charming little son, and that this might win favor for the author himself in my eyes. But I am grateful to you for provoking me to this "battle," as it were; for as Aristotle says, "contentious debate" contributes to the progress of the mind. <note>Aristotle often noted that dialectic and debate help sharpen the intellect.</note> Even the divine Homer calls battle itself "glory-bringing," <note>original: *κυδιάνειραν* (kudianeiran); a Homeric epithet for battle that brings renown to men.</note> and our own poet <note>Likely a reference to Virgil.</note> no less excellently spoke of "ignoble leisure." Therefore, I ask you again and again to stir me up often. For, my dear Scala, we must struggle against these turbulent times with the study of literature and philosophy, so that we may claim ourselves for ourselves as much as we are permitted. I will use your help, which you promised most generously as is your custom, no less confidently when the need arises than I have used it up to this day. Farewell. August 1st, 1449. Fiesole.

**The Book of Solutions by Alexander of Aphrodisias regarding several Physical Doubts,**
**translated into Latin by Angelo Poliziano.**

**P**ROBLEMS are of various kinds. Some are believable and well-known by their very nature, free of all ambiguity and questioning. For who, I ask, in their right mind would doubt why nature granted wings to creatures that fly? Any sensible person would say it was for the sake of warmth—as if they were first wrapped in clothing—and then for the sake of appearance, just as hair was given to walking animals, bark to snakes, scales to those in the water, or shells to those called "testaceous" <term>testacea: hard-shelled creatures like mollusks or tortoises</term>. Why, furthermore, did she grant horns to some, stings to others, and sharp claws, beaks, or something of that sort to others? She armed them with all these things as if with "natural spears" so they could protect themselves from injury. 

And since nature made all fruits and all seeds both to reproduce and to sustain their kind, she fortified them with husks, or soft bodies, or things mimicking wood or skin. She hid them as if inside a "little cabinet" <note>original: *scriniolum*; a small box or chest for valuables.</note> so they might avoid the damage of cold, heat, or even certain animals. In most cases, she did not even leave the wrapping itself useless, but made it suitable for food. She clothed the plants themselves with leaves, bark, and other similar things in place of feathers or hair, because she foresaw they could be struck or weakened by immoderate cold or heat. Indeed, she even armed some of them with thorns like small arrows to repel the injury of animals. She crowned them with a variety of flowers, partly for beauty and ornament, and partly so they might act like "heralds" announcing the coming birth of the fruit. Therefore, those who demand that these clear and obvious things be explained to them are, without doubt, "captured in mind" <note>original: *mente capti*; insane or lacking intelligence.</note>. Likewise, those who doubt whether heat is innate in fire lack the sense of touch; those who doubt whether nature and a providential plan look after these things...
