<meta>This page continues the "Physical Doubts and Solutions" (Problemata) attributed to Alexander of Aphrodisias, as translated by the Italian humanist Angelo Poliziano. This section transitions from a philosophical defense of the "First Philosopher" into the study of natural phenomena and "occult" or hidden properties of the physical world.</meta>

### Problems. Folio 36.

Those who do not believe in the things that rise and set, nor in their order, motion, position, path, colors, and other similar things, are worthy of punishment. Thus, these things are known by their own nature. Other things, however, are utterly inexplicable, known only to God—that is, to the author of their essence. For even a craftsman, who has ingeniously engineered some work, understands all the causes of its actions. But he who is unskilled in that work is also completely ignorant of those same causes. 

Inexplicable questions are of this sort: why do those whose wings <note>original: *alae*; likely referring to the armpits or the "wings" of the torso</note>, or feet, or sides are tickled, laugh? Why, for some people, when marble is rubbed or cut, or when iron screeches or is filed, do their teeth immediately go numb just from the hearing? Why is the numbness of the teeth, which comes from cold fruit, healed by purslane—which is itself cold? For these are not "remedies of opposites," but of likes. Or why does a magnet stone attract only iron and is "brought to life" by its filings? Why does amber only gather dry leaves and stalks and stick to them? And why does a lion fear only a rooster? Or why does a village hen, having laid an egg, purify her body on all sides with stalks? Quails feed on hellebore, which is toxic to humans. Starlings eat hemlock. Scammony <note>original: *Ascamonia*</note> draws out yellow bile. Bitter cucumber, agaric, white hellebore, spurge <note>original: *Epholbion*</note>, and Cnidian berries <note>seeds of the spurge flax</note> draw out phlegm. Black hellebore and dodder of thyme <note>original: *Epithymum*</note> draw out black bile. For some, the belly is settled by things that purge, while conversely, it is purged by things that settle. Then, one person is more delighted by one food than another, and digests it more easily. 

Who is ignorant of the sea-torpedo <note>the electric ray</note>? Does it not drive numbness into the body even through a fishing line? <margin>The Torpedo fish</margin> And if an apple is held in the hand, it is effective against the torpedo's sting! Finally, I could enumerate infinite things of this kind which are known only through experience. For this reason, they are called "secret properties" by doctors. For what is offered regarding the property of these things is almost entirely a secret when it comes to providing a cause. Indeed, some propose many depraved solutions for these things which are utterly useless and improbable. 

For they say that purgatives, being very hot, draw out humors; this is undoubtedly false. For it would be necessary that whatever is hot would also be a purgative. Yet now pepper, though it is hot, does not draw out humors, but rather aids digestion and firms them up. In the same way, so do mastic and aloe. We say, therefore, that the logic does not work both ways. For if whatever moves the bowels is held to be hot—having the power of emptying—it does not follow that everything that is hot also has the power of moving the bowels. They also say that the ostrich <note>original: *Struthochamelum*; literally "sparrow-camel"</note> digests iron, not by some special property, but by its heat; this is surely absurd. For a lion, which is hotter than this animal, does not digest iron. 

Nor are there certain properties only among doctors; they are likewise among philosophers and grammarians, as those things called "affections" <note>original: *pathe*; referring to Greek *πάθη*, meaning passions or conditions</note> are noted in common use. Therefore, we should inquire only into those things that occupy a middle ground: they are not too doubtful to be known, and they can fall under an explanation. For the things that are false are known to all; of the things that represent the truth, some are known and conspicuous, others are obscure and inexplicable. Others, however, are of a certain middle nature, the exposition of which we now undertake. 

Every problem must be solved either from its own habit, or from its composition, or from action, or from agreement toward something similar, or from color, or through deception of the senses, or by shared names, or by how the forces of that thing act more or less, or by how anything is harder or rarer, or greater or smaller, or from time, age, and habit, or by the reasoning of its essence, or from an accident, or the condition of similar things—the kind of things discussed in "problems." You will find, therefore, if you set these formulas before you, that whatever thing is doubted, you may call it into dispute. Since, however, we must not rest only on those things which are brought to the whole world, but the one who is being taught must be led by the hand, come now, let us approach the solutions themselves. 

**I.**
Why did Homer call men "gray-templed" <note>original: *πολιοκροτάφους* (*poliokrotaphous*)</note>? Because people begin to go gray most often from there, since the front parts of the head have more moisture and phlegm than the back parts. 

**II.**
Why does only the front of the head go bald? Because those parts are soft and loose. Since the hair lacks nourishment because of natural dryness, it easily falls away from those parts; for it does not stick easily, as it does on the back of the head, which is both drier and more compact. 

**III.**
Baldness, however, has its origin in dryness. Hence it happens that those with curly hair, because they have a drier head, go bald sooner and go gray later, as the dryness consumes the waste products of phlegm. They are also more wakeful than others. For sleep arises from moisture. The proof is in infants, who are equally moist, sleepy, and full of waste products. So too are those with moist temperaments, and drunkards, and those who bathe frequently. They also discharge less through the passages, such as the nose, mouth, and eyes. But for those with softer hair, such as those with a moist head, the opposite happens. For they rarely or never go bald. But baldness also happens by a defect of the lineage, just as gout and certain other conditions are inherited by family relation. They go gray sooner, are sleepy, and full of waste. Gray hairs are white, for they imitate the color of phlegm.

->IIII.<-
**Why are the elderly full of waste products and wakeful?** They are indeed full of waste products <note>original: *excrementosi*; in ancient medicine, "excrements" were any metabolic byproducts, including phlegm and bile, not just feces</note> because, being colder and weaker due to age, they digest less and accumulate many waste products through the passages of the body. Yet, since they are dry in their solid parts, they are also wakeful for that very reason. <note>Ancient physicians believed sleep was caused by moisture rising to the brain; thus, the "dryness" of old age caused insomnia.</note> For infants are moist both in the structure of their pores and in their solid bodies. 

->V.<-
**Why do boys, who are naturally moist and full of waste products, produce no gray hair?** Because they are moist and hot. <note>Gray hair was viewed as a kind of "mold" or putrefaction caused by cold phlegm.</note> Phlegm, however, is moist and cold. Boys also have a forehead that is skin-like and porous, through which superfluities are excreted. This area hardens with age, becomes bony, and thickens. For this reason, nature later provides it with sutures <note>The OCR reads *futuras*, but context indicates *suturas*, the seams where the bones of the skull join.</note> through which superfluous vapors might be exhaled. The solution is found in the condition and structure of the body. 

->VI.<-
**Why do women and eunuchs go gray more quickly?** Women, indeed, because they are cold by nature and exercise less; thus, they accumulate more waste products, especially once their monthly cycles have ceased. Eunuchs, however, because they no longer emit semen; instead, the waste humor from which semen should have been formed is spread throughout the whole body along with the blood. This humor has the nature of phlegm. 

->VII.<-
**But why do they lack body hair?** Women, because they are cold and have dense body passages. For cold condenses and tightens; hence it happens that there is no path through which hair may break out. Eunuchs, however, because both hu- <note>The text cuts off mid-word, likely continuing "humid" or "humors" on the next page.</note>

->**Alexander**<-

...it is burnt up, it will produce a short fever occurring every four days; but if it occurs in small passages, it creates a longer-lasting quartan fever <note>original: *quartanam*; a fever (often associated with malaria) that spikes every fourth day, believed to be caused by "black bile"</note>. For a cold and thick humor <note>original: *humor*; one of the four vital bodily fluids—blood, phlegm, yellow bile, and black bile—that were thought to govern health and temperament</note>, which is very difficult to change, meets with a narrow space that does not allow all the bile to be burnt up and consumed at once. XII.

**Why do the armpits of some people sweat when they are overcome by shame?** Because they have very porous passages <note>original: *raris meatibus*; ancient medicine held that some body parts were more "rare" or porous than others, allowing fluids to pass through more easily</note>. For Nature, withdrawing itself from that which is worthy of honor or reverence, retreats moderately along with the blood into the largest veins and arteries; and once these are filled, they drip. Yet this also happens to those who are joyful, because the body relaxes and becomes more porous, especially the armpits. XIII.

**Why do those who are afraid grow pale?** Because our nature—that vital force which has the care of the body—wishes to suffer nothing from external threats. And just as we take refuge inside our houses, so Nature herself, seeking security, retreats into the innermost parts of the body as much as possible. Moreover, she drags with her the blood, which she uses for nourishment and as a vehicle, provided it is of the best quality. This <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence; "Is" likely begins an explanation of how the withdrawal of blood from the surface causes the pale color.</note>

->**Eighty-Five: Alexander**<-

...and is dispersed. Hence also lions, who are mostly of this temperament, cannot walk through the sun; and seeing fire during the day, they flee. One can also see that their pupils are exceedingly bright, and they have the moist parts of their eyes very transparent. XXI.

**XXII. Why does sudden and intense joy sometimes kill?** Because the vital power and innate heat <note>original: *insitus calor*; the internal fire that ancient doctors believed was the source of life and digestion</note>, when they are carried, expelled, and dissolved excessively toward the outside, cause a person to sweat and turn red, since the blood is present there. For the innate heat, being fire itself, migrates both because of its warmth and from its proper place; it moves upward, but then downward again out of an appetite for fuel. If either of these movements fails, the heat itself is destroyed.

**XXIII. Why do those in pain, those in love, and those who are angry sigh so much and so frequently?** Because the soul of those in pain is turned toward the cause of the pain itself; the soul of those who desire is turned toward that which they crave; and the soul of the angry is turned toward that which incites their anger. Therefore, the soul, being intent on that by which it is moved, neglects and in a way forgets to provide power to the muscles of the chest. Thus the heart itself, neither receiving air through the expansion of the chest—and therefore being neither ventilated nor cooled—nor likewise expelling "sigh-making" waste <note>original: *singultifica excrementa*; literally "sob-making" or "hiccup-making" waste products</note> (which are produced from the burning of the blood) through contraction, fears suffocation. It compels and warns the soul to provide as much movement as possible to the muscles and to effect a greater inhalation and exhalation, so that it may receive a greater force of cold air and pour out a greater force of waste. Thus, one large breath accomplishes what many small, frequent breaths would have done. Hence the ancients gave the Greek name for "sighing" from the "anguish of the chest" <note>original: *suspirio ex angustia*; likely a reference to the Greek *stenagmós*, related to narrowing or distress</note>. They sigh for a longer time and frequently because the soul is always turned toward that which moves it. Nature, however, compels it to occasionally send more motive power through the heart to the muscles of the chest. What respiration is in the chest, perspiration is in the body, which occurs through the arteries. Dilation is similar to inhalation, while contraction is similar to exhalation; both dilation and contraction are understood under the name of the "pulse."

**XXIV. Why is minced meat difficult to digest?** <note>original: *isicium*; a dish of minced meat or sausage</note> Because, due to its lightness, it floats upon the moist food within the belly and remains in the middle, failing to apply itself to the body of the stomach, by which application digestion occurs. Then it overflows around the throat, whose function is appetite, not digestion. Indeed, if it is placed in water outside the body, it floats and does not sink, because while the meat is being ground, it takes in light air <note>original: *spiritum*; here referring to air or breath trapped in the meat</note>, which spits the body upward and forces it to float on the moisture. Hence it is also "joyful," since it partakes of air.

**XXV. Why do we urinate warm liquid before we enter a bath, but while we linger in the bath, we urinate cold?** This happens, of course, as if by comparison to something else. For the emitted urine is of a lukewarm quality and moderately warm. Outside the bath, because our body is cold, the emitted urine is warm relative to the body. In the heat, however, since the body is heated much more than the urine, the urine seems cold, even though it is warm in its own way. This is also apparent from another example: to one who enters a bath to get warm, if he enters a hot tub, the water seems very burning because it is hot; but if he enters when he is already heated, it does not seem equally burning to him.

**XXVI. Why do we find sweet water when digging in maritime places?** Surely because in the sea, the thinner water is sweet, while the thicker water is salty. The thin water, therefore, flowing through the passages of the earth, is hidden in the earth itself, which we then find by digging. It is sweet because it is lifted into the air during the winter <note>original: *brumam*; mid-winter or the winter solstice</note>. But thick water, when dried and purified, becomes salt. On the shores, however, which have wider passages, salty water is found, for even the thicker water of the sea is filtered through there.

**XXVII. Why is well water warm in winter and cold in summer?** Because everything always flees its opposite as an enemy. It is clearly apparent that cold is the opposite of heat and destroys it. Therefore, since heat occupies the air during the summer, the cold flees into the depths of the earth and, for that reason, makes the water cold. In the winter, however, since cold is more powerful in the air, the heat again flees into the depths and warms the water. For it is against the law of nature for opposites to remain in the same place and time together <note>This concept is known as *antiperistasis*, the supposed increase in the intensity of a quality as a result of being surrounded by its opposite</note>.

**XXVIII. Why are men of short stature usually wiser than tall men?** Because their soul is concentrated and compact throughout their whole body. In tall men, however, it is stretched out and dissolved in length. For this reason, Homer describes Odysseus as short and wise, but Ajax as tall and more dull-witted.

**XXIX. Why do the less wise, when they walk, seem to "suspend" themselves?** <note>meaning they walk with an unsteady or staggering gait</note> Because just as an invalid pilot does not steer a ship in a straight line, so a weaker soul steers the body.

**XXX. Why do many dull-witted people produce wise and robust children?** Because the more dull-witted, greatly succumbing to pleasure during intercourse, have their soul greatly immersed in the body. This results in their seed partaking of the greatest power—both rational and natural—making those who are born wiser. For the wiser, and especially those who are learned, it happens entirely otherwise. For the power of wisdom—always considering something else, even in the act of love, such as external necessities—and being therefore more "suspended," causes that which...

**XXXI. Why does the dung of wild beasts not smell so badly?** Because they consume a drier diet with very little waste, and they exercise a great deal. Indeed, the dung of gazelles <note>original: *dorcadum*; referring to gazelles or species of deer</note> and certain other animals even mimics the scent of aromatics to some degree. Human dung, therefore, smells the worst of all: because humans eat a varied and moist diet, and do so even beyond satiety, at improper times, and when they have the least need for it. Furthermore, they exercise less and possess less heat <note>ancient medicine viewed digestion as a "cooking" process performed by internal "innate heat"</note> than other creatures. Therefore, since the body neither fully digests the food nor is it purified due to its abundance, but rather it sort of rots, it has a bad odor. XXXI.

**XII.**
Why does **yellow bile**, which for the entire duration of life is contained within 그 membrane called the **gallbladder** <note>original: *bilis vessica*; literally "bladder of bile"</note>, not corrode the vessel itself—even though that vessel is the part of the body most exposed to its effects? This is because it has been so ordained by nature that the bile should dwell only in that specific organ, and therefore it harms it the least. For the very name of "Nature" is a great remedy against pain.

<meta>This page continues the series of "Problems" regarding human physiology and natural phenomena, likely attributed to Alexander of Aphrodisias. **Problems. Folio 39.**

**L.**

Why do those hiccuping from swallowing bread stop hiccuping when they hear something sad? It is because they turn their mind toward the thing that brings the sadness; as a result, the mind is less intent on moving the chest. Furthermore, when the breath <note>original: *spiritus*; referring to the "pneuma" or vital breath thought to regulate bodily movements</note> does not burst forth but is gathered more copiously, it stops the hiccup, as we have learned before.

**LI.**

Why do paintings show flat colors when viewed up close, but appear partly concave and partly protruding to those standing far away? It is because the power of sight stretches and weakens over a long distance; thus, it does not discern the depths of the colors exactly and clearly. Instead, it sees white colors as protruding and black colors as concave. For white, when it moves toward something bright, shines outwardly; but black, being dark, shines inwardly. Some arts transform their material, as when a statue-maker casts a bronze horse or an ox, or when someone hammering metal shapes a man; here, the material of the bronze is changed from one form into another. Other arts work by addition, like a molder of wax or clay. Others by subtraction, like those who create an animal by carving. Others by joining, inserting, and gluing, as in building a house or a ship, in weaving, or in carpentry. Others are made by an alteration of the internal state <note>original: *habitudinis alteratione*; a change in the fundamental quality or "habit" of the substance</note> and through the depths, so to speak—just as nature creates living creatures from seed. Others happen by a simultaneous alteration of state and the addition of mass, just as nature increases parts of the body by nourishing them. But others work by the mixing of colors and the modification of bodies, such as painting.

**LII.**

Why, if cold water is an enemy to the nerves, is hot water not a friend—or rather, why is it also an enemy? If one thing is harmful, surely its contrary should be useful? For contraries cannot act upon the same thing in the same way. In the first place, heat in and of itself is not simply hostile to the nerves because it is hot; rather, it is hostile because it is both hot and humid. Those who have injured nerves require a great deal of tension and tightening, because nerves possess a high degree of sensation. By their own nature, nerves are dry. Humidity, being a contrary, softens them, relaxes them, and causes them to rot. It is clear that heat itself is not naturally harmful, for a draught of hot oil is useful, as it also contains a power of tightening <note>original: *astrictionis*; an astringent or "drawing together" quality</note>.

**LIII.**

Why, if apples are harmful because they are cold and humid, does water not harm us, even though it shares the same qualities? Because water is subtler <note>meaning "thinner" or "finer" in consistency</note> than apples and is excreted more quickly, so it does not cause as much damage. Indeed, it even moderately firms up the parts of the body.

**LIIII.**

Why do things that are difficult to digest and have a thick humor <note>referring to the four humors of ancient medicine; "thick" humors were thought to be sluggish or heavy</note> digest much more easily—such as beef—than those that are easier to cook and have a thinner humor, like rockfish? Some attribute this to habit. Others think a certain natural, secret, and inexplicable disposition is the cause. Some say that because of excessive heat in the belly, those things which are more "digestible" than is proper (being more prone to change) are consumed and ruined by the great force of the internal fire. However, things that are less suited for digestion (being difficult to change) are only "cooked" <term>concoctio: the process of digestion, which ancient doctors viewed as a form of internal cooking or ripening by body heat</term> because they do not change too much. In this same way, straw is more prone to being affected and turns to ash in a large fire; but this does not happen to oak wood, which burns properly.

**LV.**

Why does the countenance of those in pain turn pale? Because nature (as we have said) retreats to the innermost part of the body along with the blood. It is the blood that usually warms the face and makes it "rare" <note>original: *rarefacere*; meaning to make the skin flush and the pores open</note>.

**LVI.**

Why is cold wine produced in Egypt, which is a very hot region? For the same reason. Cold flees to the roots of the vine and makes them cold. Indeed, vines are much more prone to being affected by their surroundings than other plants.

**LVII.**

Why, when hot water is poured into a well, does it make the water very cold? Because the cold that is in the well resists the heat. Since the abundance of cold overcomes it, the cold pursues the heat with all its might. Thus, much cold flows through the warming water, and in this way, it cools it down significantly.

**LVIII.**

Why, when a tiny insect flies into the eye, is it immediately pushed out if the other eye is closed? Because the "visual spirit" <term>spiritus videndi: the "pneuma" or airy substance thought to flow through the optic nerves to enable sight</term> can no longer exit through the closed eye, as we have already learned; instead, being gathered into itself and rushing in great quantity into the open eye, it fills it, makes it swell, and pushes outward from within. In this way, the insect is driven off and expelled.

**LIX.**

Why do those struck by blows see fire? Because the visual spirit, thinned out by the blow, becomes greatly ignited; as it exits into the air, it is seen as that which it has become. The same thing happens when you rub two stones together, or iron against iron. The air trapped between them is greatly thinned and becomes fire. The same thing also happens in the clouds <note>an explanation for lightning</note>.

**LX.**

Why is fire not struck out by the rubbing of all stones? Because many are too yielding, too light, and have loose passages. They do not thin the air equally when struck, because they neither strike vehemently due to their lightness, nor do they prevent the air from fleeing and receding into their pores. Therefore, the air is not struck all at once and does not ignite. The same happens with the rubbing of wood. But fire is created from the sun and water: because the rays of the sun, broken against glass—as also happens in mirrors—become more ignited and are reflected back upward.

That which is heavy is naturally carried downwards. ->**LXXXIIII.**<-

Why, if phlegm is cold, thick, and viscous—and <term>black bile</term> <note>original: *nigra bilis*; the humor associated with the earth element, believed to cause melancholy and certain types of persistent illness</note> is likewise cold and thick, yet much less abundant than phlegm—is a **quartan fever** <note>a fever that recurs every four days</note> nevertheless longer-lasting than a **quotidian fever** <note>a fever that recurs every day</note>?

Black bile, however, is cold and dry, which results in it being very difficult to alter or change. Thus, these substances deceive by their shared quality of coldness and the abundance of bile, while they hide their other contrary qualities. Beyond this, phlegm is more in harmony with nature than black bile. For this reason, when a healthy person is dying of hunger, nature converts that very phlegm into nourishment. Therefore, in a daily fever, whatever useful phlegm the body encounters, it consumes it all for nourishment...

**Problems. Folio 41.**

...show. For oak is by no means suitable for such things, nor are they of the kind that easily catch fire. Reeds are much more suitable and more exposed to catching fire, but <term>tow</term> <note>original: *stuppa*; the coarse, broken fibers of flax or hemp used for spinning or as kindling</note> is much more so than these. But if someone takes wet tow and green reeds, and chooses the driest among them, or sprinkles it with sulfur—which was least suitable for catching fire—he will make it most suitable if he brings it near the flame. By this same example, you can also solve another question: for what reason does it happen that weariness produces a daily fever rather than one arising from putrefaction, or that which is called a "habitual" fever? For we say this happens because of the state of the body’s disposition. For the body possessed natural spirits and humors that were not at all superfluous. But all solid parts are very dry, and the cause of the fever runs into them. And why does the sun's heat excite sleep in some, but not in others? But he who has a dry head, when it becomes more and more dried out, is afflicted with wakefulness.

->**LXXXIX.**<-

Why does the sun make a man black, but make linen white, soften wax, and harden mud? It is again because of the disposition of the material being acted upon. For all humors, except for phlegm, when they are heated beyond measure, appear black around the skin itself. But linen, stained with either <term>natron</term> <note>original: *nitro*; a naturally occurring salt used as a cleaning agent</note> or saltiness, becomes white when the sun consumes its impurities. Again, when the sun draws out the moisture that is deep within the wax, it happens that it softens. But in mud, the sun devours all the moisture—of which there is much, and which overflows on the surface—and thus dries it out and makes it hard. If, therefore, the agent is directed toward that which is being acted upon, it can be of great use to us. For if we arm the mind with piety and adorn the body with moderation in food—stabilizing ourselves in a life that does not seek possessions but is content with what is necessary for living—then we shall avoid all the troubles of life as much as possible. Nor shall we offer ourselves as suitable subjects for an evil agent to act upon, whether that agent is a <term>Daemon</term> <note>here referring to a supernatural spirit or influence rather than a modern "demon"</note>, a star, or any other external cause.

->**XC.**<-

Why do those with <term>jaundice</term> <note>original: *icterici*; a condition causing yellowing of the skin and eyes</note> have difficulty moving their bowels, and why is their stool white? Because yellow bile is diffused throughout their whole body—as both the eyes and skin indicate—and it no longer flows to the intestines as the primary law of nature requires. Thus, it does not color the stool, nor does it irritate the evacuative power of the intestines with its sharpness to expel the waste. Because of this, medicine—which like other arts imitates nature—comes to the aid of the patient’s strength when the body is in the danger of sickness. For because the stool is cast down when bile irritates and provokes the intestines and muscles to its expulsion, and the stool itself is soft and slippery because of those sticky humors in and around the intestines, an <term>enema</term> <note>original: *clyster*</note> rightly contains honey, which has the power to expel. Likewise, it contains natron, which has the power to expel and stirs the intestines and muscles toward evacuation. It also contains <term>hydreleum</term> <note>original: *hydreleum*; a mixture of water and oil</note>, which is oil diluted with water, to moisten and soften the stool that has been dried out by fever. One ought to know, however, that sometimes nature acts of its own accord without the physician's help, as in the "judgments" of illnesses or in the <term>concoctions</term> <note>the process by which the body "cooks" or matures humors to overcome a disease</note>. At such times, the physician is like a spectator, an arbiter, and a judge between two adversaries: the disease and nature. At other times, the physician acts alone, as in the setting of broken bones or the reduction of joints. And at other times, the physician and nature act together, as in foul and hollow ulcers. For the physician cleanses the ulcer of filth with those things that pertain to such purging, and then provides relaxation to those hidden passages; for he cuts away whatever acts as a lid over them, so to speak, and clears them so that they may receive pure blood. Nature, through the passages of the ulcer, supplies pure blood—which is created from nourishment—and transfers it to the generation of flesh. This is then thickened by drying medicines, and suitable flesh is formed.

->**XCI.**<-

Why have those who labored under a continuous fever had very black skin for some time after the time of judgment, which they call the <term>crisis</term> <note>the turning point of a disease</note>? Because continuous fever happens from yellow bile, which, in the very peak of the sickness, is burnt and changed into black bile. And so, in that crisis we mentioned, it is driven to the skin by nature itself and stains it, just as the skin is also white in cases of <term>vitiligo</term> <note>original: *vitiliginibus*; a condition causing loss of skin pigment</note>. Because of the thickness of that humor, such a color is difficult to dissolve.

->**XCII.**<-

Why does black bile cause corrosion when it goes to the breast or the leg, but does not do this in those called "melancholics," even though it flows into the brain itself? Because in the breast there are many large veins for the generation of milk, and for that reason, a great amount of bile flows there. Similarly, much bile is drawn down to the leg, since it is carried to the lower parts. But into the brain—both because it is high up and because it has tiny little veins—only a small amount of bile ascends, which has the power only to sting, but not to corrode. Furthermore, the brain is cold and moist, by which it happens that it opposes the quality of black bile in some way and softens it. Therefore, that which is truly black bile produces a corroding <term>cancer</term> in the breast; but in the leg, it produces a <term>Chironian ulcer</term> <note>a persistent, difficult-to-heal wound, named after the centaur Chiron</note> and what they call <term>nomades</term> <note>original: *nomades*; from the Greek word for "wandering" or "spreading," referring to ulcers that consume the surrounding flesh</note> from their devouring nature. In the brain, however, it produces "wild melancholy." But that which is not properly black bile, but melancholic...

**LXXXIII.**

Why, in those who suffer from intestinal difficulties, do they roll up papyrus and find it beneficial when inserted into the anus? It is because when the muscles of the seat are constricted, the moistened papyrus stimulates the muscles through its own relaxation. It acts in the same way in <term>fistulas</term> <note>original: *hypophoris*; deep, narrow, or "undermining" ulcers that drain fluid</note> as it does when it encounters ulcers. Therefore, once the muscles are relaxed, the stool is cast out as if it were no longer held back. 

**LXXXIIII.**

Why do those vessels that the Greeks call <term>baucalia</term> <note>original: *baucalia*; a narrow-necked vessel or cooling pot, likely named onomatopoeically for the "glug-glug" sound made when pouring</note> emit a certain sound peculiar to themselves when they are filled with water, from which the name of the vessel itself was derived—just as there are other names among the Greeks created from sounds, such as <term>lapping</term> <note>original: *phloesbos*; the rushing sound of the sea or water</note> for water, and <term>rumbling</term> <note>original: *borborygmos*; the sound of gas moving through the intestines</note> in the belly, and others? It is because when a vessel of this kind is empty of water, it is filled with air, which is a very thin substance. When, therefore, water is suddenly poured into it, by its own weight it presses upon and excludes the air, which is thin. For they cannot remain together in the *baucalia* until it is full.

Why is the treatment of ulcers in the kidneys and in the bladder of urine difficult? Because as we descend into it, the water that meets us also undergoes an effect; that is, while it heats our body, it is itself cooled by us in some way. For we have learned that whatever acts in <term>generation and corruption</term> <note>A fundamental Aristotelian concept referring to the birth and decay of all physical things; the author argues that every action has an equal and opposite reaction</note> undoubtedly also undergoes an effect itself. Therefore, since the water has been cooled in some way, it no longer heats us in the same way, and it is clear that we have become accustomed to it and no longer feel its heat as we did at the beginning, since its excessive heat is diminished by us. <meta>This page continues the "Problems" attributed to Alexander of Aphrodisias, moving from physical properties of glass and liquids to the physiological development of the human body and the effects of motion on the senses.</meta>

**Of Alexander**

Why do the voices of boys break around their fourteenth year? Because at that time, <term>nature</term> <note>original: *natura*; referring to the innate biological force governing growth</note>, which moves through human bodies, effects a great and sudden change of age. The physical reality itself provides proof of this. For one can see that the breasts of women increase because of the collection of milk, and those areas around the hips expand so that a fetus may remain within. In men, however, the chest and shoulders grow, so that they may sustain heavy weights placed upon them. Furthermore, the testicles develop, within which the <term>seed</term> <note>original: *semen*; the reproductive fluid</note> can be produced and stored, as well as the genital member, so that the seed may exit more easily. Moreover, the entire body dilates. This is indicated by the changes in diseases and the recoveries that occur around the fourteenth year, and by the roughness of the voice, which is called <term>branchus</term> <note>original: *branchus*; from the Greek *branchos*, meaning hoarseness</note>, that is, hoarseness. This name is clearly a metaphor taken from the voice of goats <note>original: *hircorum*; the Latin *hircus* means "he-goat," and the term *hirquitallio* was used for the voice-breaking of puberty</note> crying out in that manner. For since the <term>windpipe</term> <note>original: *aspera arteria*; literally "the rough artery," the classical term for the trachea</note> dilates from the beginning, it happens that it dilates more in some parts and less in others, and the internal surface of that body is, as it were, unequal all the way to the throat itself. Therefore, the breath exiting through those parts, and being hindered as it were because of the inequality of the path, renders the voice unequal, rough, and in a way hoarse. The same happens to those into whose windpipe <term>distillations</term> <note>original: *destillationes*; a reference to "catarrh" or mucus flowing down from the head</note> flow. For when the moisture flows down, the smooth internal membrane is filled with inequality, causing an unequal exit of the breath. Know that such is the windpipe and throat of goats, namely because of an abundance of moisture. The same is true of those who drink a great deal of oil. Yet, because of their frequent and intense shouting and the roughness of their windpipes, they are thought to have an unequal voice. To cranes, however, and to all those birds that have a rough voice, their windpipes are given by nature to be entirely rough. But after the year of puberty, boys cease to have this "goat-voice," because the entire windpipe dilates plainly and takes on its natural equality. **CXXXVI.**

Why does swallowed oil induce vomiting, and especially of yellow bile? Because since it is light and tends to be carried upward, it provokes the nutrients in the stomach and lifts and suspends them. And thus the burdened stomach rouses its expulsive power to vomit, and especially <term>yellow bile</term> <note>original: *flavam bilem*; one of the four humors, associated with fire and heat</note>, because it is both light and made of subtle parts, and thus is more easily carried upward. Indeed, it is evident that oil is carried upward by its very nature. For when it is mixed with any liquid, it runs out to the higher place. **CXXXVII.**

Why is oil alone least able to be mixed with other liquids? Because since it is viscous and compact within itself, it cannot be cut into individual parts and in that way be mixed with the remaining liquids; for which reason, even when it is poured onto the ground, it does not enter it quickly. **CXXXVIII.**

Why are oil and water constrained by cold, but wine, vinegar, and <term>fish sauce</term> <note>original: *garus*; refers to garum, a fermented Mediterranean fish sauce</note> not at all? Because since oil is devoid of "quality" <note>original: *qualitatis expers*; perhaps meaning it lacks a strong primary quality like inherent coldness or heat compared to other fluids</note> and is prone to confusion, it cools quickly, and so vehemently that it is chilled by even extreme cold. Water, being cold by its own nature, easily freezes when it becomes colder than itself. But fish sauce, as it is made of subtle and warm parts, does not cool quickly. The same is true of wine. But vinegar, being composed of very subtle parts, does not tolerate freezing. **CXXXIX.**

Why do opposites produce the same effect? For the moist is constrained by the cold just as much as by the hot. For snow and broth are congealed by coldness, but <term>poultices</term> <note>original: *cataplasmata*; soft, moist masses applied to the body</note> and bladder stones are hardened by heat. This happens, indeed, but by different actions; for heat feeds upon and consumes the abundance of moisture, while cold, obstructing by its excessive density, squeezes out the "sordid" moisture, just as a sponge pressed by a hand casts out the water it holds within its passages. **CXXX.**

Why does shivering often cease when something frightening happens, such as a crash heard by one who is suffering, or when water is suddenly dropped? Because frequently, when the humors have been digested and thinned over time, all the natural heat flees together suddenly from the skin to the innermost parts of the body, and in doing so, it consumes and dissolves the disease-causing humor. <term>Theriac</term> <note>original: *Theriaca*; a famous ancient "universal antidote" and cure-all made of many ingredients</note> does the same, as do many of those things that are hot and dry in nature when they are taken after digestion. **CXXXI.**

Why do those who spin around, but are not accustomed to doing so, usually fall down? Because they force the <term>animal spirit</term> <note>original: *animalem spiritum*; the subtle vapor in the nerves believed to control sensation and movement</note> which is in the brain to be disturbed, and to be whirled around together with the moistures. This spirit then, being made less fit for receiving the "animal power"—namely the power of sensation and motion—does not allow action to pass into the muscles and nerves. Wherefore it happens that the weight of the body, being neither carried nor sustained by the soul, is borne to the earth toward which it inclines; and because of this same thing they see darkness, since the "seeing spirit" is disturbed and does not function in the same way as the other senses. But to those who have become accustomed to spinning gradually, this rarely happens. For habit ensures that the soul and nature are not, as it were, strangers to one another, but in time they become reconciled. For that which happens gradually and continually remains hidden from the senses, and when it has proceeded furthest, it no longer strikes as something foreign those who have become accustomed to receiving it. **CXXXII.**

Why do glass mirrors shine so brightly? Because they are smeared on the inside with <term>white lead</term> <note>original: *albo plumbo*; likely referring to a tin or lead backing used to create a reflective surface</note>, the nature of which is to be bright; when this is mixed with glass, which is also itself bright, it shines much more. Transmitting its rays through the passages of the glass, it doubles what is on the surface and outside the body of the glass, and thus it becomes greatly bright. **CXXXIII.**

Why do we see ourselves in mirrors and in transparent waters? Because the quality of sight...

**Problems. Folio 44.**

...[splen]did bodies, migrating through reflection back through the rays of the eyes, returns to the sight of itself. That qualities <term>migrate</term> <note>original: *migrare*; the theory that physical properties like color literally travel through the air to the observer</note> from the face, and that this is not absurd, is shown by those who stay near trees, who are accustomed to have a green appearance. For the green quality of the green leaves migrates to the face itself. Similarly, migrating into flowing water, it also shows the water as green. **CXXXIIII.**

Why do clean caves and very high, clear places produce and send back an image of the voice? Because these places also, by sending back the strike through reflection, give forth an image of sound. For the voice strikes the air, and the air strikes the place, which, the more it is struck, the more it strikes back, and thus makes a more vehement sound of the voice. Damp places, however, being softer and yielding to the strike and dissolving it, do not give forth an image at all. The quality and quantity of that image, which is called <term>Echo</term> <note>original: *Echo*; here treated as a physical "image of sound" rather than just a sound</note>, is returned according to the quality and quantity of the strike and the voice. Some wrongly tell stories that this Echo is a certain goddess; others say <term>Pan</term> <note>the Greek god of the wild and shepherds</note> was captured by love for her: which is undoubtedly false. 

For there was a certain wise man who first both desired and investigated to understand the cause of this voice; and just as those who love, but do not possess the object of their love, suffer with a troubled mind, he was likewise distressed until he found the solution to the cause. Just as <margin>Endymion</margin> Endymion, who first discovered the course of the moon by staying awake at nights, observing its course and inquiring into its movement, slept during the day. They tell the story, therefore, that he was loved by the Moon, and that she came to him while he slept, because she, as it were, handed over the solution of her own cause to the philosopher. Indeed, they also report that he was a shepherd, who looked up at her movement in pure and high desert places. And they attribute to him a <term>joined pipe</term> <note>original: *compactam fistulam*; the pan-pipes</note>, either because high places mostly provide them, or because he was investigating the harmony of shapes. Similarly, because <margin>Prometheus</margin> Prometheus was a wise man and investigated the cause of the <term>starry air</term> <note>original: *sydereae aulae*; literally "starry hall" or "starry court," referring to the heavens</note>, its nature and position, and was as it were eaten away by the desire for learning, he finally gave birth <note>original: *genuit*; likely meaning "brought forth knowledge"</note> when <term>Hercules</term> <note>representing strength of intellect or a later teacher</note> solved every doubt with his wisdom. **CXXXV.**

Why does standing water, whether on the surface or deep in the earth, make many circles when a stone is thrown into it? Because the stone follows the water by the intensity of its throw from any part of its body, and thus a circle is made, specifically as far as the descent of the throw reaches. But if the intensity is immoderate, the circle becomes larger; and the stone descending all the way to the ground, subsequently drawing the water itself with its body, deservedly makes many circles. For first, by moving the surface of the water, it draws it apart. Then, perpetually descending through it to the deep, it divides the water again and makes another circle. And this happens in succession until the stone has settled and come to rest. Moreover, since the intensity of the stone gradually lessens as it descends, it is necessary that each subsequent circle be more contracted than the previous one, because the water is similarly divided by the strike of the stone itself. **CXXXVI.**

Why do many think that laughter arises from the <term>spleen</term> <note>original: *liene*; in ancient medicine, the spleen was thought to be the seat of laughter and the filter for melancholy</note>, asserting that those with a diseased spleen do not seem affected by laughter in the same way as those with a healthy one—indeed, that they are greatly sad? I personally think it happens by accident, and the cause of laughter does not properly consist in the spleen. For if it is healthy, it draws all the dreggy and <term>melancholic humor</term> <note>original: *melancholicum humorem*; black bile, associated with sadness</note> from the liver; so it happens that when pure and filtered blood travels through the whole body and into the brain, it delights the nature and the soul at once, and exhilarates them like wine, leading them into tranquility, and thus laughter is moved by it. **CXXXVII.**

Why do <term>mules</term> <note>the sterile offspring of a horse and a donkey</note> not give birth? Because they consist of different species of animals; then, by the quality of the differences and the nature of the seeds, the mixing—producing something else besides what was before—abolishes the nature of those who generated it. Just as the mixing of the extremes of white and black, by abolishing those colors, generates another color which is brown <note>original: *fuscus*; dark or tawny</note>, which is nothing like the extremes at all. Therefore, the generative quality is abolished, along with the suitability of the forms. **CXXXVIII.**

Why are those who are deaf by nature also mute? Because those who have not heard cannot speak or express themselves. But some physicians say there is one connection of nerves that pertains to both the tongue and the ear, so it happens that a consensus of affections occurs in them. Those who are mute by accident, however, are not entirely deaf; a local suffering of the nerves arises. **CXXXIX.**

Why do those who have fasted for a long time shiver soon after taking food? Because in the interval of taking food, they abound in bile and thus accumulate acidic humor. After food, therefore, those refreshed particles of the body drive the bile away from themselves into the skin, and thus shivering arises, as the bile nips at those very particles and excites them to follow it. **CXL.**

Why are pigs silent when they are carried looking upward? Because above other animals they always incline toward the ground. For they delight in stench and seek it out. Therefore, in that sudden change of sight, they are as if strangers and guests, and being astonished by so much light, they offer silence. Some say the windpipe, which is a narrow passage, closes up in that supine position. **CXLI.**

Why do pigs delight in dung? By the opinion of physicians, they delight in it naturally, for they have a very large liver, in which desire resides. Aristotle, however, thinks the cause is in the width of the snout; for it has a sense of smell that resolves itself and, as it were, struggles with the stench. **CXLII.**

Why does itching arise when ulcers are healing and the <term>phlegm</term> <note>original: *pituita*; one of the four humors</note> is ceasing? Because the healed and consolidated part pursues the remnants of the humor which is present against nature and which had caused the ulcer. And so, exiting through the skin and resolving itself, it causes itching. **CXLIII.**

<meta>This page continues the "Problems" attributed to Alexander of Aphrodisias, moving from the physics of sound and echoes to medical questions regarding the human body, specifically the eyes and the respiratory reflex of sneezing.</meta>

**Of Alexander**

Why are the afflictions that affect only one eye more severe and long-lasting? This occurs for two reasons: first, because the <term>flux</term> <note>original: *fluctio*; the movement of bodily humors (fluids) believed to cause inflammation or disease</note> is concentrated in only one eye. For whatever is divided among many parts becomes weaker than itself and acts with less force; the more it is spread out, the more ineffective it becomes. The second reason is that when the healthy eye moves during its normal actions, it forces the sick eye to move just as many times. We know, however, that the greatest medicine for any diseased part of the body consists in rest itself.

->CXLIII.<-

Why does a human being sneeze more frequently and more forcefully than brute animals? Because man consumes more abundant and varied food and drink, and does so beyond the point of satiety. Since he does not <term>concoct</term> <note>original: *concoquat*; the process of "cooking" or ripening food through internal heat, which we now call digestion</note> this food as is proper, he gathers much <term>spirit</term> <note>original: *spiritum*; here referring to internal gases or "vapors" produced by the body's moisture</note> on account of the excessive humidity. This spirit, being thin and subtle, ascends to the brain and frequently forces the body to be aroused to an excretion, and so he sneezes...

<meta>This page transitions from the specific scientific queries of the "Problems" to the introductory front matter of the printed edition. It features a dedicatory letter from the editor, Pietro Crinito, to the Prince of Mirandola, discussing the history of the translation and its scholarly value, followed by a letter from the translator Angelo Poliziano (Politian) to Pandolfo Collenuccio.</meta>

**Problems. Folio 45.**

Pietro Crinito to Giovanni Francesco Pico della Mirandola,
Prince, sends greetings.

[Decorative initial H] Until now, Prince of Mirandola, I was of the mind that Poliziano’s *Problems* of Alexander of Aphrodisias should be suppressed rather than released to the public. Not because I thought Poliziano had put little effort into them; indeed, I knew that whatever the spirit of these pieces, they were rendered into Latin so they could be read, and composed so they could be approved. Although some will read these just to argue, and many more to find fault—with whom the wicked usually agree, though the virtuous do not—I was hesitant. Since this work had already been translated by Theodore Gaza (found in the Pope's library and elsewhere) and much later by Giorgio Valla, I feared it might not seem a worthy enough endeavor to be brought into the light and public view under your <term>auspices</term> <note>original: *auspiciis*; historical patronage or protection provided by a high-ranking figure</note>. But it has come to the point where I have decided to "move every stone" <note>original: *omnem movere lapidem*; a Greek proverb meaning to try every possible means</note>—as they used to say in <term>conjectural cases</term> <note>a type of legal argument focusing on the facts of what happened</note>—encouraged by both ancient examples and the persuasion of Giovanni Mainardi. He, given his authority and devotion in the sacred matters of philosophy, made me believe that I would be serving young students well if this labor of Poliziano were fully restored to them. Furthermore, the minds of scholars will achieve something more certain and, as Jerome used to say, more refined, through the comparison of these multiple and varied interpretations. Indeed, it is easy to see that this was a common practice among the ancients. Marcus Cicero once presented Aratus's *Phaenomena* in Latin to his fellow citizens; he was soon followed (to name but a few) by Prince Germanicus and Sextus Rufus himself, who devoted much labor and sweat to this same task for the sake of the Latin language. Even several of Plato's books are said to have been translated into Latin by Lucius Apuleius, who played with the <term>Milesian tale</term> <note>original: *Milesiam fabulam*; a reference to "The Golden Ass" or "Metamorphoses" by Apuleius</note>, and later by Boethius Severinus, with similar effort but a different style and prose. There are many other examples, but I so disregard the pursuit of authority in these matters that I would sometimes rather appear to lack a cause. 

It will be much better, best of Princes, if we move on to the questions themselves. Theodore Gaza, a most learned man (as the scholars agree) and a Greek of the highest judgment, in no way believed these *Problems* should be attributed to that famous Alexander of Aphrodisias, who was a wonderful commentator on Aristotle’s opinions. Indeed, the style itself is not the same, and the meaning—especially regarding the soul—does not quite harmonize. While we know that this work has been accepted by most people until now as Alexander's, we wish to leave the opinion free for those who will judge it hereafter. As for Poliziano's translation, I would only remind you that if Poliziano himself had lived a little longer among the living, he would have added or changed much here; everything would be fuller and more refined. Nor should I omit, most kind Prince, that Latin readers once read "oracles" from Hippocrates along with the commentaries of Claudius Galen (for that is what he called the <note>original: τοὺς ἀφορίσμους</note> *Aphorisms*). A part of that work still exists; he once told me that he exhausted a great deal of labor and late-night study on it. But some of his dear friends have fulfilled this labor. In part, I am delaying because we have also added at the end Plutarch of Chaeronea's *Amorous Stories* dedicated to Pandolfo Collenuccio, who so admired Poliziano <margin>note</margin> and respected his erudition that he almost professes to recognize our own study (for why should I deny it?) as if he were its foster-child. Farewell. April 1, 1497. Florence.

Angelo Poliziano to Pandolfo Collenuccio of Pesaro,
Jurist, sends many greetings.

[Decorative initial M] Remember, when you were reading through Alexander of Aphrodisias's *Problems*, which I recently translated from Greek, you were delighted by the novelty of the story that imagined the fury Erinys was loved by Cupid, because some people had loved too perversely and (as he says) too impiously. Therefore, when some of Plutarch's *Amorous Stories* <margin>note</margin> fell into my hands which explained this very thing clearly, [I dedicated them] in your name...

<meta>This page transitions from the introductory letters of Pietro Crinito and Angelo Poliziano into the main body of the work: Poliziano's Latin translation of Plutarch’s "Amatoriae Narrationes" (Love Stories). The focus shifts from scholarly correspondence to ancient Greek tragic romances.</meta>

**Plutarch**

**PLUTARCH OF CHAERONEA’S TALES OF LOVE**
**TRANSLATED BY ANGELO POLIZIANO.**

[Large decorative initial I] In the city of Haliartus in Boeotia, there was a girl of surpassing beauty named Aristoclea, the daughter of a certain Theophanes. Two young men were in love with her: Strato of Orchomenus and Callisthenes of Haliartus. Strato was the wealthier of the two, and much more consumed by his passion for the girl. For he had happened to see her by chance in Lebadia while she was bathing in the spring of Hercyna <note>A river and spring in Boeotia associated with the cult of Trophonius</note>. She was there to carry the sacred chest for King Jupiter <note>original: *Ioui regi*; referring to the Greek Zeus Basileus</note>. Theophanes, unsure of what to do (for he feared Strato, who surpassed almost all the Boeotians in both wealth and noble lineage), considered consulting the oracle of Trophonius regarding the choice. But Strato, having been persuaded by the girl’s servants that she leaned more toward him than toward Callisthenes, worked tirelessly to ensure the choice of a husband was given to the girl herself. However, when Theophanes openly questioned his daughter and she preferred Callisthenes, it immediately became clear that Strato took the news with a very bitter spirit. Two days later, he approached Theophanes and Callisthenes, affirming that he wished to maintain the friendship established with them, even though some god had envied him the marriage. They praised him and invited him to the wedding feast. But he gathered a great band of companions and servants, ordering them to be scattered here and there within the crowd itself and to remain as if hidden, until the girl should go down, according to custom, to the spring called Cissoessa to perform the sacred rites of the nymphs which they call the <term>Protelea</term> <note>original: *Protelea*; ancient Greek sacrifices performed before a marriage</note>. Then, making an assault, those who had been placed in the ambush seized the girl. There, Strato tried to pull her toward himself; Callisthenes, on the other hand, tried to pull her back toward him (as was right). The companions of both sides did the same, each striving with all their might for their own leader, until the girl, torn apart between the hands of the combatants, perished <note>original: *dilacerata exanimataque est*; she was literally pulled apart in the struggle</note>. Callisthenes then immediately withdrew from the sight of everyone, and it was never discovered by anyone whether he killed himself or lived as a fugitive in exile from Boeotia. Strato, however, in the sight of all, cut his own throat over the body of the maiden.

When a certain Phidon was plotting to take the leadership of the Peloponnesians, and wished for the city of Argos—which was his own homeland—to rule over all the others, he first directed a trick against the Corinthians. He sent messengers to ask them for a thousand young men, preeminent in both the vigor of their age and their courage. They were sent, therefore, under the leadership of Dexander. Since Phidon intended to trap them so that he might make Corinth weaker and use it at his own will (for he understood that it was, as it were, the single <term>bulwark</term> <note>original: *propugnaculum*; a fortress or defensive point</note> of the entire Peloponnese), he communicated the whole matter to certain companions...

<summary>This page contains the tragic story of Aristoclea, who is killed in a violent tug-of-war between two rival suitors, and begins the political account of Phidon of Argos's plot to weaken Corinth.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the "Tales of Love" (Amatoriae Narrationes) by Plutarch, translated by the humanist scholar Angelo Poliziano. It follows the tragic story of the daughters of Scedasus and begins the story of the daughter of Phocus, focusing on themes of divine justice and the consequences of violated hospitality.</meta>

**Tales of Love. Folio 46.**

...out of love for the maidens, and because they were restrained from daring anything by the integrity of Scedasus. They proceeded to Pytho <note>Delphi, the site of the famous oracle of Apollo</note>, which was their intended destination. Having consulted the god (as the situation required), they were returning home, making their way through Boeotia. They took shelter again at the house of Scedasus. He happened by chance to be away on a journey, but his daughters received them according to custom. Having found the girls unguarded, the men committed violence upon them. When they saw the wretched girls grieving beyond measure at the outrage they had received, they killed them both and, having thrown the bodies into a well, they departed. 

When Scedasus returned, he saw his daughters nowhere; however, he found everything he had left behind safe. He remained uncertain of the situation for a long time, until a little dog began to whine, running now to the master and now more frequently back to the well. He guessed what had happened and thus drew out the bodies of his daughters. When his neighbors told him they had seen those who entered his house the day before—those Lacedaemonians <note>Spartans</note> who had stayed with him on previous days—he understood beyond doubt that the crime had been committed by them. For on those previous days they had often praised the girls and proclaimed that those who would marry them would be most blessed. 

Therefore, he decided to set out for Lacedaemon and report the whole matter to the Ephors <note>The five senior magistrates of Sparta who oversaw the kings and public conduct</note>. But when he reached the territory of the Argives, he was overtaken by night and stayed in an inn. There he encountered another old man, a citizen of Oreus, which is a town in the district of Hestiaeotis. When he saw him both groaning and cursing the Lacedaemonians with dire oaths, Scedasus asked by what evil he had been affected by them. The man told him that he was subject to the rule of the Spartans, but that Aristodemus, who had been sent to Oreus to serve as a magistrate, had practiced every form of cruelty and injustice. "For," he said, "when he fell in love with my son and could achieve nothing through pleading or promises, he turned to force and attempted to snatch him from the wrestling school <note>original: *palestra*</note>. When the master of the wrestling school forbade it and several youths brought help, Aristodemus immediately departed. But the next day, having equipped a trireme <note>A Greek warship with three banks of oars</note>, he seized the youth and, having carried him across to the farther shore, tried to violate him. When the boy resisted more bravely, he cut his throat with a sword. Then, returning to Oreus, he celebrated a banquet. Meanwhile, I heard of the shameful crime and committed my son's body to the earth. Then I hurried to Sparta and reported the whole matter to the Ephors, who took absolutely no account of it." 

Having heard these things, Scedasus was violently disturbed. For he thought that no account would be taken of his own case either; thus, in turn, he told his host of his own calamity. The host urged him not to go to the Ephors but to return to Boeotia and build a tomb for his children. Nevertheless, he did not persuade Scedasus. He proceeded to Sparta and met the Ephors. Ignored by them, he went to the kings. Soon, soliciting the common people one by one, he complained of his calamity. When all these efforts failed, Scedasus ran through the middle of the city, stretched his hands toward the sun, then struck the ground, invoked the Furies <note>Ancient deities of vengeance who punished crimes against the family</note>, and after all this, he killed himself. 

Not long after, the Lacedaemonians paid the penalty. For while they ruled all of Greece and had secured all the cities with garrisons, Epaminondas of Thebes slaughtered to a man whoever held the garrison of his city. When the Lacedaemonians rose up for war, the Thebans met them at Leuctra <note>The site of the famous Battle of Leuctra in 371 BCE, which ended Spartan hegemony</note>, seeking the omen of the place. For previously they had recovered their liberty in that very spot, at the time when Amphictyon, driven into exile by Sthenelus, fled to the city of the Thebans; he, having made the people of Chalcis tributary, rendered the Thebans immune from tribute, since he had killed Chalcodon, the king of the Euboeans. Thus all the Lacedaemonians were routed and slaughtered to a man at the very monument of the daughters of Scedasus. 

They say, however, that before they went out into battle, Scedasus appeared in a dream to Pelopidas <note>A famous Theban general and statesman</note>, one of the soldiers of the Theban army, who was terrified by certain signs that were thought to be adverse. Scedasus told Pelopidas to be of good cheer, for the Lacedaemonians were coming to Leuctra to pay the penalty to him and his daughters. At the same time, he ordered that they should not go out to battle until he sacrificed a white foal, which would be ready, at the tomb of the maidens. They say that Pelopidas, while the Lacedaemonians were still campaigning in Tegea, sent men to Leuctra to inquire about that tomb; and when the whole matter was confirmed by the locals, filled with the best hope, he led out the army and thus brought back the victory.

Phocus was a Boeotian by race, from the line of Clifas. He had an only daughter, surpassing in beauty and modesty. <margin>The daughter of Phocus / Clifas's daughter <note>original: *Phocí filía / ἐκ κλεία / σανρος*</note></margin> Thirty of the primary youths of the Boeotians each demanded her for himself as a wife. Phocus, however, wove one delay after another for the marriage, clearly fearing lest some violence be inflicted. Finally, when they asked, he said he would consult the Pythian oracle about the choice. They took this news very badly and, making an attack, killed Phocus himself. In the midst of the tumult, the girl fled and wandered through the fields, with the youths following her. But when she came upon farmers who were piling up wheat on a threshing floor, she found safety through them. For the farmers hid her in the wheat, and thus she was passed over by the pursuers. When she had escaped, having observed a festival common to all Boeotians, she proceeded to Coronea and sat as a suppliant at the altar of Itonian Minerva <note>Athena Itonia, a major deity of the Boeotian League</note>. There, telling of the injustice of the suitors, she made known the name and homeland of each. The Boeotians therefore pitied the girl and were enraged at the youths. When they heard this, they fled to Orchomenus; being rejected by them, they went to Hippotae, which is a village near Helicon between Thebes and Coronea...

It also introduces the story of Phocus's daughter, who flees to a temple for protection after her father is murdered by her thirty suitors.</summary>

<meta>This page concludes the "Tales of Love" attributed to Plutarch and begins Angelo Poliziano’s famous introductory lecture, the "Lamia," which he delivered at the University of Florence in 1492. The first section finishes the tragic account of the daughters of Alcippus and the divine retribution following their deaths, while the second section transitions into a philosophical allegory using the myth of the Lamia to critique meddlesome critics.</meta>

**Lamia.**

...had been placed. They were received by these people. After this, the Thebans sent envoys to demand that the killers of Phocus <note>Phocus was a Boeotian youth whose murder sparked a local war</note> be handed over to them. When they by no means obtained this request, the Thebans, along with the rest of the Boeotians, waged war against them. The commander of this war was Phaedus, who was then the leader of the Thebans. Thus, after a very well-fortified village was captured and those within it were reduced to extreme thirst, they burned the captured killers of Phocus; the inhabitants themselves they led away into slavery. Having destroyed the walls and houses, the Thebans and the Coroneans divided the land among themselves. It is said that on the very night preceding the captivity of the Hippotae, a voice was frequently heard from Helicon <note>The mountain home of the Muses</note> saying, "I am here" <note>original: "adsum"</note>. Thirty suitors recognized that voice as belonging to Phocus. On the day they went out to war, it is handed down that the monument of the old man, which was in Clisante, flowed with saffron. Moreover, to Phaedus, the leader and commander of the Thebans, upon returning from the battle, it was announced that a daughter had been born to him, whom he—having accepted the omen—called Nicostrata <note>The name Nicostrata translates to "Victorious Army"</note>.

<margin>The daughters of Alcippus.</margin>

Alcippus was a Lacedaemonian <note>Spartan</note> by birth, and having taken Damocrita as his wife, he had two female children by her. Since he was both consulting the best interests of the city and doing those things which he understood to be for the benefit of the Republic, he stirred up the envy of those who favored the opposing political faction. The Ephors <note>Senior Spartan magistrates</note>, persuaded by the false speeches of these men that Alcippus wished to dissolve the laws, punished the man with exile. He left Sparta; however, his wife Damocrita, who wished to offer herself as a companion to her husband along with her daughters, was forbidden. Furthermore, they confiscated his property so that no dowry would remain for the young maidens. But when several men asked for the girls as wives on account of their father's virtue, they were forbidden from taking those wives by a decree of the senate instigated by his enemies, who were heard to speak a vow concerning the girls' mother: that they hoped children would be born to the daughters as quickly as possible who would avenge their father. When Damocrita was being attacked from all sides, she observed a certain common festival of the whole people, at which it was the custom for women to assemble together with the maidens, all domestic servants, and infants. Those who were of the nobility stayed overnight by themselves, apart from the others, in a large Great Hall <note>original: "Androne"</note>. There, having girded a sword under her garment, she led out her daughters with her and set out by night to the temple. Having observed the time when everyone was participating in the mystery <note>A private religious rite</note>, and since the doors were closed, she piled a great mass of wood against them. Indeed, the wood was at hand and ready, having been gathered for the use of the sacred rites. Then she set it on fire. While the men were running to help, Damocrita killed her own daughters and then herself with the sword. Therefore, since they had no one upon whom to pour out their anger, they cast out the bodies of Damocrita and her daughters beyond the borders. On account of this, because the god was angry, it is handed down that a huge earthquake occurred at Lacedaemon <note>Sparta suffered a catastrophic earthquake in 464 BCE, often attributed to divine wrath</note>. THE END.

**Angelo Poliziano’s lecture on Aristotle’s Prior Analytics. Title: Lamia.**

I wish to tell a story for a little while, but one with a purpose (as Horace <note>original: "Flaccus"</note> says). For even little stories which are thought to be old wives' tales are sometimes not only a basic lesson but also an instrument of philosophy. Have you ever heard the name of the Lamia? To me, indeed, even as a small boy, my grandmother used to tell me that there were certain Lamias in the wilderness who would swallow crying children. At that time, the Lamia was my greatest fear, my greatest terror. Also, still neighboring my little country estate in Fiesole <note>A hill town overlooking Florence where Poliziano had a villa</note>, there is a clear little spring—for that is its name—hiding in a secret shade, where even now the common women who come frequently to draw water say the seat of the Lamias is located. Therefore, that famous Plutarch of Chaeronea—I know not whether more learned or more serious—says this Lamia has removable eyes <note>original: "exemptiles"</note>, that is, eyes which she may take out and remove when she pleases, and again, when she pleases, take them back and attach them, just as old men are accustomed to do with spectacles <note>original: "ocularia ſpecilla"</note>, with which they assist their sight which is dulling through age. For when they desire to look at something, they put them on as if by fitting a pair of shears to the nose. And when they have looked enough, they hide them away in a case. Some people even use teeth that are equally removable, which they put away at night no differently than a toga, just as your little wives also do with that hanging hair of theirs and their curls <note>A satirical jab at wigs and hairpieces common in Renaissance Florence</note>. But indeed, this Lamia, as often as she goes out of the house, attaches her eyes to herself. She wanders through the forums, through the streets, through the crossroads, through the alleys, through the shrines, through the baths, through the taverns, through all the meeting places, and she looks around at every single thing, scrutinizes, and tracks them; nothing is so well covered that it is hidden from her. You would believe her eyes were those of a kite <note>A bird of prey known for keen sight</note>, or even "prying eyes" <note>original: "emiſſitios"</note> like those of the old woman in Plautus; no tiny detail, however inseparable, escapes them, no hiding place, however remote, evades them. But as soon as she returns home, on the very threshold she removes those eyes from herself and throws them into her boxes. Thus she is always blind at home, but always sighted abroad. You might ask, perhaps, what she does at home. She sits busy making wool, and meanwhile she hums a little tune. I ask you, men of Florence, have you ever seen these Lamias who do not know themselves or their own business, but spy on others and other people's affairs? You say no! And yet they are frequent in cities, even in yours; but they walk about masked—you would think them men, but they are Lamias.

<margin>Lamia.</margin>
<margin>Removable eyes.</margin>
<margin>Teeth.</margin>

<meta>This page transitions from the previous discussion on the "Tales of Love" into the famous introductory lecture titled "The Lamia," which Angelo Poliziano delivered at the University of Florence in 1492. In this opening section, Poliziano uses a personal anecdote to address his critics, who mock him for transitioning from a literary scholar to a teacher of philosophy.</meta>

**The Lamia. Folio XLVII.**

Therefore, some of these creatures <note>The "Lamiae," or mythical blood-sucking witches, used here as a metaphor for meddlesome critics</note>, having by chance caught sight of me passing by, stopped and, as if they recognized me, inspected me quite curiously, just as buyers are accustomed to do. Soon, with crooked nods to one another, they whispered among themselves: "It is Poliziano, his very self; that trifler <note>original: "nugator"</note>, of course, who has so suddenly emerged as a philosopher." And with that word, they flew off, like wasps that have left their sting behind. 

But as for their saying that I have suddenly emerged as a philosopher: I truly do not know whether it is the whole idea of being a philosopher that displeases them (which I certainly am not), or whether they think I *wish* to be seen as a philosopher, despite being so far from being one. Let us see first, therefore, what kind of creature this is that men call a "philosopher"; then I hope you will easily understand that I am no philosopher. 

Nor do I say this because I think you believe it, but so that perhaps no one else ever will. It is not that I am ashamed of that title—if only I could truly live up to it in reality—but rather that I freely abstain from titles belonging to others. I do this lest, if by chance the flock of birds should one day come to reclaim their feathers, the little crow <note>original: "cornicula"</note> should provoke laughter <note>A reference to a fable by Aesop, popularized by the Roman poet Horace, about a bird that dresses in borrowed feathers to appear more beautiful than it is</note>. We shall deal with this first, and soon after with the question of whether...

<summary>Angelo Poliziano recounts a fictionalized encounter with malicious critics (the "Lamiae") who mock his transition into teaching philosophy. He modestly denies being a true philosopher to avoid the charge of intellectual vanity or "borrowed feathers."</summary>

<keywords>Angelo Poliziano, Lamia, philosophy, critics, Horace, Aesop’s fables, Florentine humanism, academic titles</keywords>
