<meta>This page continues Poliziano’s introductory lecture "The Lamia." Having just compared himself to a crow in borrowed feathers to deflect the title of "philosopher," he now describes the difficult search for truth and the character required of a true seeker, contrasting Socratic modesty with the arrogance of the Sophists.</meta>

...will either never, or only with difficulty, discover it. He who calls upon other hunters will easily reach the very lair. And so, in this "hunt for truth," as it were, there are many steep and rugged places, enclosed by trees and dread shadows, which you could not survey alone. 

But just as certain ancestral marks of noble families are recorded—such as <margin>The sign of the philosophers.</margin> the anchor of the Seleucids <note>The Seleucid kings of Syria were said to have been born with an anchor-shaped birthmark.</note>, the ivory shoulder of the Pelopids <note>In Greek myth, Pelops was restored to life with an ivory shoulder after his original one was accidentally eaten by the goddess Demeter.</note>, and the red beard of the Ahenobarbi <note>A Roman family name meaning "bronze-beard"; legend said their ancestors’ beards turned red upon witnessing a divine miracle.</note>—so all philosophers ought to have this above all else, as if it were their emblem: that they be haters of lies and lovers of truth. 

Although a certain kind of "lie" is also suitable for a philosopher—namely, when he belittles himself and his own accomplishments. This refers to the elegant irony Socrates is said to have used against puffed-up sophists <note>Professional teachers in Ancient Greece whom Socrates often challenged for their arrogance.</note>; by acting the part of an ignorant man while refuting them, he made them understand more easily that they themselves actually knew nothing at all. But indeed, if any people shamelessly claim for themselves those qualities from which they are furthest removed, they are troublesome everywhere, but especially in these intellectual pursuits. For truly, the love of money must also be absent. Nor further...

<summary>Poliziano describes the search for truth as a difficult hunt requiring cooperation and defines the true philosopher as a lover of truth who practices Socratic irony and avoids greed.</summary>
<keywords>hunt for truth, Socrates, irony, Seleucids, Pelopids, Ahenobarbi, sophists, greed, philosopher's character</keywords>

--- Page 435 ---
<meta>This page continues Poliziano’s lecture. Having previously discussed the "hunt for truth" and the modesty of Socrates, he now moves into the common human failure to see one's own faults, the historical persecution of philosophers, and finally, a defense of philosophy as the essential path to a virtuous and happy life, citing the Pythagorean Archytas.</meta>

**The Lamia.        Folio XLVIII.**

...in others' matters: they keep the front bag for others' faults, and the back bag for their own <note>Poliziano refers to Aesop's fable: every person carries two bags (manticæ), one in front containing their neighbors' vices, and one behind containing their own, which they never see.</note>. From this, it follows that men do not see their own vices, but see those of others. And would that these bags might one day be turned around, so that each could look upon his own vices and not those of others. Thus, that old Athenian <note>Socrates.</note>—who stood head and shoulders, and indeed even in heart, above the rest—sketched for us such an image of the true and legitimate philosopher. He used to say that as long as he lived, he was always "practicing for death" <note>original: "mortem commentari." A central Platonic idea that philosophy is the practice of separating the soul from the body’s distractions.</note>; and yet, that he alone was happy and blessed even in this life. 

However, such men are found so rarely that they are almost rarer than white crows. Now, if I were to call myself such a man, or even imagine myself to be the kind of philosopher I just described, I would be more foolish than Coroebus <note>A legendary figure in Greek proverbs synonymous with stupidity.</note>. For I have scarcely touched those disciplines that belong to a philosopher, and I am far removed from those habits and virtues I mentioned. 

But suppose I were such a man: should I be blamed for it? Is philosophy a vain or evil art? I know it certainly seemed so to some in the past, especially the powerful. The Empress Agrippina is said to have discouraged her son Nero from the study of philosophy for that reason, claiming it was useless to those who rule. <margin>Expellers of philosophers.</margin> Domitian drove the philosophers from the city and from Italy for no other crime than that they were philosophers. The Athenians took away Socrates, the very father of philosophy, with hemlock. The once-fortunate city of Antioch attacked the Roman Emperor Julian with insults and mockery for no other reason than that he was a philosopher and grew a beard (which was the custom of the ancient philosophers). 

What of the fact that a barbarian Tyrant once intended to burn all the books of the philosophers? And he would have done it, had not Al-Ghazali <note>original: "Algazeles," the famous Persian theologian and philosopher.</note> turned him from his purpose with a certain pious, though not very honest, story. Truly, I do not wonder at these men. For those who are wicked in their habits, criminal, and corrupted by luxury and pleasure, could not bear the stern brow of philosophy. 

I wonder more that it has been attacked so many times by the learned and otherwise good men—and indeed, to our indignation, with public support—that is, with great success and high praise for the attackers. For the Roman Hortensius, a most eloquent and noble man, when he had criticized philosophy, earned the honor of having Cicero name a book after him <note>Cicero’s lost dialogue *Hortensius*, which famously inspired St. Augustine’s conversion.</note>, thus handing him down to posterity as more illustrious. And that Dion of Prusa <note>Dio Chrysostom.</note>, who was the first to bear the nickname "Golden-Mouthed," is considered more eloquent in no speech—though he published many—than in the one directed against the philosophers. And [underlined in red: Aristophanes, the author of Old Comedy], is believed to have exerted as much charm or power in no play as in the one he titled *The Clouds*. In this, he most wittily described the philosopher Socrates measuring the leap of a flea. 

But even Aristides <note>Aelius Aristides, a 2nd-century rhetorician.</note>, because of that speech he wrote against Plato in defense of four Athenian leaders, seems to me to have become much more illustrious and celebrated than from all his other works, of which he composed many—even though that speech is devoid of art and does not quite fit any rhetorical form. Nevertheless, it flourishes with a certain secret beauty and grace, and it is wonderful how much it delights with its very names and words. What of [underlined in red: Timon of Phlius], who composed the bitter work *The Satires* <note>original: "Sillos."</note>? Did he not also gain a great name for himself from mocking philosophers? 

However, what has been criticized by some should not immediately be seen as evil. <margin>A most elegant collection.</margin> For even sweet flavor is considered the most excellent of all, yet it is unpleasant to some, even those who are healthy. These little chats and rumors of men are like shadows. Just as a shadow grows or shrinks while the body itself (which casts the shadow) neither grows nor shrinks, so no one becomes better while being praised by the crowd, nor worse while being criticized. 

If one must not philosophize, one must not live according to the virtue of the soul. But just as we live by the soul, so we live well by the virtue of the soul. Just as we see with our eyes, so we see well by the virtue of our eyes. Therefore, let him who does not wish to live well not philosophize. Let him who wishes to live basely not pursue philosophy. 

Behold, there come to mind [underlined in red: certain truly golden words of the Pythagorean Archytas], selected from his book titled *On Wisdom*, which—unless it is bothersome—I will repeat word-for-word in English <note>original: "latine," as Poliziano was translating from Greek into Latin.</note>. <margin>Selected words of Archytas.</margin> He says: "Wisdom excels in all human affairs just as sight does in the senses, the mind in the soul, and the sun among the stars. For sight reaches the furthest and encompasses the most forms of things. And the mind, like a queen, accomplishes whatever work is needed through reason and reflection; it is a kind of sight and power of the most excellent things. And the sun is the eye and the soul of all nature, through which all things are seen, born, nourished, increased, and cherished. Man is by far the wisest of all living things, for he possesses that power by which he can observe everything and draw forth knowledge and prudence from all things, as if that greatest God had impressed and sealed universal reason within him, where the species of all things could be distinguished and the meanings of names and words could exist, such that certain places were even assigned to the sounds of voices." Thus far Archytas. 

It seems to me also that he who does not wish to philosophize does not wish to be happy. <margin>Philosophy makes one happy.</margin> For if we are happy when many good things are present to us—but present in such a way that they are useful—and they are not useful unless we use them, and only knowledge ensures we use them well: and philosophy either seeks or possesses that knowledge: then surely, to be made happy, we must philosophize. Shall we then care for what is ours—that is, the body and wealth—but...

<summary>Poliziano defends philosophy against historical persecutors and critics, arguing that despite mockery from figures like Aristophanes or suppression by emperors, philosophy remains the only path to "living well" and achieving true happiness.</summary>
<keywords>Socrates, meditation on death, Aesop's bags, persecution of philosophers, Aristophanes, Archytas of Tarentum, definition of happiness, virtue of the soul</keywords>

--- Page 436 ---
<meta>This page continues the defense of philosophy from the previous folio. Poliziano is transitioning from the character of the philosopher to the internal structure of the human soul, arguing that neglecting philosophy is equivalent to starving one’s own humanity while feeding the "beasts" of passion and desire.</meta>

# **Lamia**

...ourselves, that is, shall we neglect the soul? Just as medicine treats the body, so philosophy heals the soul. But since there are three parts—or powers—of our soul: reason, anger, and desire <note>Poliziano is referencing Plato's tripartite theory of the soul from the *Republic*.</note>; the first being divine, while the latter two are as if bestial—tell me, shall we gently nourish and strengthen desire (that is, the "beast of many heads") and anger (like a "raging lion"), yet allow Reason—which is truly the "human" within us—to be consumed by hunger, left weak and half-dead? Shall we let it be snatched here and there by these twin monsters, just like Hippolytus in the myths <note>In Greek mythology, Hippolytus was dragged to death by his own horses when they were spooked by a sea monster.</note>, to be torn limb from limb and mangled? 

If we shun a solitary life and instead pursue a civic and urban one, do we not understand that there are arts in the city to provide the comforts of life? That there are others which utilize the work of those arts? Again, some that serve, and others that command? And that among these, insofar as they are nobler, the "Good" itself is chiefly found? But the only art which holds right judgment, which uses reason itself, and contemplates the universal good, is certainly the one that can, by its very nature, either use or command all others. And such an art, besides philosophy, is none at all. Why then should one be ashamed to practice philosophy?

**But you will say the knowledge of philosophy is too difficult. On the contrary, if it is tracked by its footprints, almost no noble art is easier to learn.** <note>The text in bold was underlined in red ink in the original manuscript.</note> For those things which are primary are always better known than those which follow. And things whose nature is better are also easier to understand than those whose nature is worse. Let this also be an argument for its ease: that philosophy reached its greatest growth in a short time, even when no reward was offered. And how many men of talent are there whose only prayer is for the leisure to practice philosophy? This surely would not happen if philosophizing were a labor and not, instead, a pleasure. What of the fact that we can always practice this study and meditate upon it, as it requires no external tools and no place is unsuitable for it? Wherever you are, the truth will be at hand. 

But while philosophy is not the most difficult thing to perceive, it is not simply lying in everyone’s path or exposed to the casual observer. It offers itself to the wakeful, not the sleeping. We, however, are so ridiculous that for the sake of the cheapest scrap of copper, we sail beyond the Pillars of Hercules <note>The Strait of Gibraltar, considered the end of the known world in antiquity.</note> even to the Indians; yet to obtain philosophy, we will not endure even a few short night-watches during winter. 

But as for what we said regarding the greatest pleasure being found in philosophy: so that you may understand this more easily, imagine someone flowing with every delight, who yet knows nothing at all, who is utterly devoid of wisdom—would anyone want to live such a life? I certainly do not think so, just as no one would choose to be always drunk, or always a child, or to sleep forever in the manner of Endymion <note>A beautiful youth in myth who was granted eternal sleep by Zeus to remain forever young.</note>. For although there are some joys even in dreams, those are false, shadowed, and imaginary; they are not true, solid, or distinct joys. 

Why do almost all of us dread death? Because, I think, what is unknown is terrifying to everyone, just as what is dark and gloomy is. Conversely, what is understood is lovable, as it is open and bright. From this, I believe, it follows that we most revere our parents, by whose kindness it was brought about that we might look upon this sun, the stars, and this public light. Indeed, we are most delighted by things we are accustomed to, and we love those most with whom we have spent the most time; in common speech, we even call friends "acquaintances." If, therefore, things that are known delight us, why should "knowing" itself and "being wise" not delight us? But that is the most defining characteristic of philosophy: therefore, either nothing should be done in this life, nothing sought after, or we must rest in philosophy alone as if in a harbor.

Let us, I pray, place the life of men before our eyes. What is it all, except a hollow shadow, or as Pindar more meaningfully says, "the dream of a shadow"? <margin>Man.</margin> **Man is a bubble**, as the ancient proverb says. For how much are we surpassed in strength by the elephant, and in speed by the little hare? <margin>Glory.</margin> This boastful glory, which so often drives us headlong—is it anything other than mere trifles? Is it anything other than a mist? If you look from afar, you might think it something great; when you approach, it vanishes. <margin>Beauty.</margin> Furthermore, the beauty and dignity of the body seem fair and honorable to us only because we are dim-sighted. For if we were like Lynceus <note>An Argonaut famous for his "X-ray" vision that could see through trees, rocks, and the ground.</note> and could penetrate bodies with our eyes and look inside, we would look upon even the most beautiful person with nausea: so many foul, filthy, and utterly deformed things would meet our gaze. Why should I mention obscene pleasures, which are always accompanied by regret? 

Come now, what is there in all our affairs that is either solid or lasting? Our own weakness and the shortness of our age make us think that something stands or endures. **Thus, the opinion of certain ancients—that our souls are cast into bodies as if into a prison to pay the penalty for great crimes—though not entirely true, may nevertheless not seem plainly absurd.** <note>Poliziano refers to the "Soma-Sema" (body-tomb) doctrine of the Orphics and Pythagoreans.</note> For since the soul is joined and glued to the body, and stretched and unfolded through every limb and every passage of the senses, it seems to me to be afflicted by no different a punishment than that which Mezentius, in Virgil’s poem, used to inflict upon his miserable citizens. For our Poet <note>Virgil, in the *Aeneid*.</note> sings of him thus: 
*He even joined dead bodies to the living...*

<summary>Poliziano argues that philosophy is the highest human calling, essential for governing the soul's base passions. He refutes the idea that it is too difficult, contrasting its eternal truths with the fleeting vanities of physical beauty, worldly glory, and the "prison" of the material body.</summary>

--- Page 438 ---
<meta>Continuing from the previous page, Poliziano is defending the philosophical life against his critics. He has just finished describing how the philosopher ignores the petty concerns of the forum and the marketplace, and now he transitions into a famous allegory to explain why the philosopher's perspective is so different from that of the common person.</meta>

**NOTE**
**The Witch <note>Original: *Lamia*. In this context, Poliziano uses the term to refer to his critics, whom he likens to mythical eye-removing witches.</note>.**

...to be able to see anything, except what is directly in front of them. Behind them, however, and far above them, a very great fire shines; and between that fire and those we have described as bound, there is a path, as if suspended high and loftily, and next to that path is a wall. Then, along that path, many people pass by, carrying in their hands vessels and other tools, and statues of living creatures, either of stone, or of wood, or of any other material. All these things being carried, while they are moved along, project above that wall we mentioned. As for the men carrying them: some are silent, as often happens, and others talk among themselves. In short, this entire **Scene** is just as when stage-magicians <note>original: *praestigiatores*; literally illusionists or puppeteers</note>, having placed a screen between themselves and us, show us certain tiny little figures above that screen, like puppets <note>original: *pupas*</note>, ridiculously talkative and gesturing, quarreling among themselves and running together in play.

What, you might ask, does this image so exquisite and so strange mean? I will tell you. Let us believe now that those men, whom I said were immobile and bound by chains, are not unlike ourselves. What, then, will they see here? Indeed, they certainly will not see themselves. Nor will those bound see each other; nor likewise will they see the things being carried. For they themselves are in darkness, and they are unable to look back. I think, however, they will see only those shadows which that fire, which we mentioned, casts onto the opposite face of the cave. But if it should also happen that they talk among themselves, I believe they would say those very shadows were clearly real things. Furthermore, if the playful image of a voice, which is called **Echo** <note>original: *Echo*; the Greek personification of reflected sound</note>, should resound and bounce back from that very face of the cave when those who pass by are speaking: do you think they would believe anything else was speaking than that very shadow which was passing? Truly I do not think so. Indeed, I suppose they would suspect nothing at all to be true except the shadows.

But come now, let us release them, and take them out of their chains, and (if we can) deliver them from such great foolishness. What will happen? I believe that when you order the handcuffs and tight bonds of each of them to be eased—when you compel them to rise up quickly, to look back, to walk, and to behold the light—at first he will be pained, and his eyes will be dazzled by the rays; nor will he be able to look at those things whose images he had beheld until now. But if someone should speak to this man thus: "Hey you, you saw trifles before this, but now you see real things"; and if, showing him the things themselves, he asks what each of them is: do you not think this man would hesitate for a long time, and being in doubt, would stubbornly believe those things he saw before were more true than the things now being shown? What if someone should compel the same man to eventually go out into the pure light—do we not believe his eyes would hurt? Would he not turn away from the rays? And who would doubt that he would take to his feet, as much as he could, so that he might return as quickly as possible to those images of his?

Come, if someone should drag him by force through steep and upward paths toward the light, will the man not be indignant and struggle? And soon, having been carried out plainly under the open air, he will surely twist his gaze, just like that **Cerberus** of Hercules <note>The three-headed hound of the underworld, whom Hercules dragged into the sunlight, causing the dog to vomit in pain from the brightness</note>, and he will be able neither to bear the day, nor to look upon those things which are called good, unless he should gradually become accustomed to them. Therefore, he will see shadows first. Then the image of the Sun in the water. Then the bodies themselves, free from the glare. After these things, however, he will also lift his eyes to heaven. And at night he will first look up at the moon and stars. Soon even by day he will dare to direct his gaze toward the sun itself. And he will think to himself that this is the one that distinguishes the seasons and completes the turning of the year. That this is also the author of those things which he himself, previously in that foul cave, had been accustomed to watch. 

Tell me, what will he turn over in his mind here, what will he do, as often as he remembers the blind prison, as often as the chains, as often as that truly shadowy wisdom? Truly I think he will give great, immense thanks to the gods that he has finally emerged from there. And he will grieve for the lot of his companions, whom he left in such great evils. But if also in the cave they had been accustomed to be praised, and rewarded, and honored—whoever saw those images more sharply, or who remembered more easily which of these were before, which were after, or which ran out together, or likewise who predicted as if by divination what would most closely follow these—do we think it would ever happen that this man of ours would covet those honors, those praises, those rewards, or finally envy those who had achieved them? I do not think so, but rather I believe: he would choose to flee beyond the **Sarmatians** <note>original: *Sauromatas*; a nomadic people of the far north, used here to mean the ends of the earth</note> and the frozen ocean, rather than to rule among those people. 

But let this same man now return, as if by a **right of return** <note>original: *postliminio*; a Roman legal term for the restoration of rights to a returning prisoner of war</note>, to that very seat, unpleasant and blind: will he not himself now be blind, having come from the sun into the darkness? If a contest should by chance be held there, as to who among all of them sees those same shadows most sharply: will not this man of ours be surpassed, and will he not be a laughingstock to everyone? So much so that those bound men would cry out with one voice: that their companion had returned into the cave blind, and that the journey outside was dangerous. And if anyone should try to release another of them again and lead him to the light: that person, whoever he might be, would surely resist with hands and feet, and would fly at the eyes of those dragging him with his nails, if he were able. 

I would certainly interpret the meaning of this image, if I were not speaking among you, O Florentines, men of great genius and great skill. Now I will only remind you of this: the men bound in darkness are none other than the common people and the uneducated. 

<margin>The philosopher alone is free.</margin> 

But that free man, in the clear light and exempt from chains, is this very philosopher of whom we have been speaking for a long time. And would that I were he! For I do not so much fear the envy and the accusation of this name that I would not wish to be a philosopher, if it were permitted. But I seem to hear those **Witches** <note>original: *Lamias*</note> again, responding to me briefly and sharply to these many and deeply-recounted things: "You labor in vain, Poliziano, to prove and declare to these listeners that you are not a philosopher. There is nothing for you to fear; no one is so foolish as to believe this of you, nor..."

<summary>Poliziano retells Plato's Allegory of the Cave to illustrate the divide between the "shadow-watching" uneducated public and the enlightened philosopher. He uses this to address his critics (the "Witches"), claiming that while he aspires to be the philosopher who sees the light, his critics remain trapped in the darkness of their own prejudices.</summary>

--- Page 439 ---
<meta>The previous page concluded Poliziano’s use of Plato’s Allegory of the Cave to illustrate how those trapped in ignorance perceive the world. On this page, he shifts from allegory to direct confrontation with his critics—whom he calls "Witches"—who have accused him of being a "pretend" philosopher. Poliziano begins his famous defense, arguing that his role as a scholar (a "Grammarian") gives him the right to interpret all subjects, including philosophy.</meta>

**The Witch. Folio 50.**

As for you, when we were saying that you had suddenly come forth as a philosopher (a word which, as we see, stings you far too much), we obviously meant this: that you are a philosopher; nor are we so ignorant or perverse as to hurl philosophy at you as a crime. But we were indignant at this: that you act, to use no harsher word, somewhat arrogantly—you, who for three years now have been professing to be a philosopher, though surely before that time you never devoted any effort to philosophy. For that reason, we also called you a trifler <note>original: *nugatorem*</note>, because you have already been teaching things for a long time that you do not know, and which you have not learned.

Indeed, I hear now, and I understand what you are saying and what you mean, my good Witches. But in turn, you also listen to me for a moment, if you have the time. <margin>On the Interpreter</margin> I profess myself an interpreter of Aristotle; whether a capable one, it is not for me to say, but I certainly profess to be an interpreter. I do not profess to be a philosopher. For even if I were the King's interpreter, I would not think myself a King because of it. Nor among us do Donatus, for instance, or Servius—nor among the Greeks, Aristarchus and Zenodotus <note>These are all famous ancient scholars and commentators on literature</note>—immediately profess themselves to be poets, simply because they interpret the poets. Is not that famous Philoponus <note>John Philoponus, a 6th-century Christian commentator on Aristotle</note>, the disciple of Ammonius and fellow student of Simplicius, a capable interpreter of Aristotle? And yet no one calls him a philosopher; everyone calls him a grammarian. What of Xenocritus of Cos, the two Rhodians Aristocles and Aristeas, the two Alexandrians Antigonus and Didymus, and that same most famous Aristarchus? Were they not all grammarians? Yet all of them (as Erotianus is the authority) interpreted the books of Hippocrates <note>The "Father of Medicine"</note>, just like others whom Galen enumerates; yet no one thinks they are doctors because of it. <margin>The duties of Grammarians</margin> For these are the duties of Grammarians: to examine and explain every kind of writer—poets, historians, orators, philosophers, doctors, and legal experts.

Our age, being little skilled in ancient matters, has enclosed the "grammarian" in too narrow a circle; but among the ancients, this rank once held such great authority that the grammarians alone were the censors and judges of all writers, for which reason they were also called "Critics" <note>original: *Criticos*</note>. So much so that they allowed themselves not only to mark verses with a kind of "Censorial mark" <note>original: *Censoria virgula*; a shorthand mark used by ancient critics to denote spurious or faulty passages</note> (as Quintilian says), but even to remove books from the family line, as if they were illegitimate, if they seemed falsely attributed. Indeed, they could either rank authors as they wished or remove them from the list entirely. For a grammarian is nothing else

<summary>In this passage, Angelo Poliziano defends himself against critics who mock him for teaching philosophy without being a "philosopher." He argues that as a "Grammarian" (a broad scholar of literature and language), he has the historical right and duty to interpret all fields of knowledge, including Aristotle and medicine.</summary>
